Plantetary Annihilation (PA) gets a very bad reputation, however my personal experence with the game has been a good one. The developers are indeed greedy, there is no doubt about that. But I am writing a review of the game and not of its creator. I know that if I had bought the first game I would have been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about Titans. As a stand alone game, distanced from its makers and previous games, it is very good. It is not, mind you, forty dollars good, but on sale, it is perfect. You have most likely already read about constant bugs, crashes and glitches. The game is buggy, I'll admit that much. But at worst they are mildly annoying and few in numbers. Many are easy to avoid after you encounter them once or twice. They are not game breaking or a reason not to purchase PA. I have seen quite a bit about the AI pathing for units; it is sometimes frustrating to work with for certain troops but is decent in general. I think that covers the things that I need to spend a few sentences on and I am going to hop right into some lists about this game not the other or the developers.
Cons:
- AI Pathing not great at times
- AI is a 'cheating AI' (can be fixed using the Queller AI mod with is better anyway)
- Serious multiplayer boils down to spaming a few basic units; whoever spams faster wins
- No true storyline (The Legion Expansion mod has more story in their trailer then the entire game has put together)
- Campaign is minimal and get easier as you move along due to AI allies that you get after every battle (I just start battles now and tell the AI to have fun; five minutes later I win and get another AI)
- Controlling base on more than one planet is hard but I don't use the UI tools that makes it easier
- Tutorial is tad bit unclear
- AI builds useless massive armies on deserted planets causing lag (Queller AI fixes this)
Pros:
- Non-toxic community (That is a first for me)
- Can build your own systems
- The sheer scale of the battles; thousands of units over many planents
- The number of different units and tactics
- NUKES, DEATH STAR, TITANS, PLANETARY DESTRUCTION ECT.
- Many mods available (Quellers AI, Legion Expansion, More Pew Pew, just to name a few must haves)
- Great graphics
- Huge customization
- Play with friends
- RTS at its best
The Neutral:
- Losing your commander knocks you out of the match (commander sniping is easy)
- Game relies on mods; some are pre-installed when you download the game
Now so that you will only need to read one review to get a clear grasp of the game I will summarize nearly all of the negative reviews out there:
- Dev suck
- Cash grab by greedy dev
- Paid for first game and this and they are same thing
+ Crashes and bugs
- Dumb
+ Stupid AI pathing
- Old game sucks then bought new game after reading that it is the same thing
- Dev just don't care
- Commander reskin for ten bucks (Is this really a reason to give a game a bad review)
I would advise you to look back up at the negitive review summary as the only problems that have to do with the new game are the ones with a +. Here's a hint: there are only two. As I previously stated both the AI pathing and the bugs are not a big enough problem to be game breaking, but are only mildly annoying.
In summary, buy on sale, not for the full price. I rate the game, not taking into account the price, the developers or the previous game an overall 85/100. RTS fans, buy this now.

It was supposed to be a spiritual successor to games like Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander, but it is pretty much a washed-out version of those games with a couple of interesting ideas executed to varrying degrees of success.
I only recommend this on a discount, there seems to be a decent active playerbase to have multiplayer games, and skirmishes are also pretty enjoyable once you get the better AI from community mods, the same mode now exists for single player "galactic war" mode which is another way you can play the game solo (it's quite fun honestly). So, definitely look into this game if you enjoy classic RTS, especially games like Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander.
Update: Multiplayer meta is really stale right now, early game there's some interesting things you can do, but lategame is almost always teleporting Manhattan with Helion into the enemy base which, if timed correctly, you can't predict where it will go and respond (basically you get a nuke teleported into your base or commander, zero counterplay. It's not even that hard to do). So, if you're thinking about multiplayer, just beware that it can get rather stale.
What I like about the game the most is the pacing and visual style. The game incorporates all the classic basebuilding found in classic strategy games, while cutting all the unnecessary downtime. As the result, units build fast, you can assemble defences and armies reasonably easily, which untimately leads to more fun due to often skirmishes between players. In my opinion it also makes the game have a bigger skill ceiling, because you don't have a lot of time to think about the macro, your economy can grow at a very rapid pace, and expanding your production must be done quick and effectively in order to stay efficient, basically the same process that can be found in other games but very accelerated which I really like. You get to more fun and powerful units much faster, which makes the game also last must shorter, giving you nice and relatively quick bursts of fun. The visual style is really nice to look at, very clean and intuitive. I'd say it's one of the best ones I have seen for strategies, it's stylish and adds to the clarity of the gameplay. I also like the whole planetary warfare dynamic, it makes you pay attention to a lot of things at once, and gives a lot of room for creativity. I often times ended up killing players that were much stroner than me because they got careless and I got a devilish idea. That's the best part of the game, huge multiplayer skirmishes on large systems, they are really epic and are a real test of your skill. It's incredibly satisfying to win a 10 player FFA with your clever scheming (UPDATE: If you've not read it at the start, there's currently one preveling and boring meta, which makes those large multiplayer games rather dull if everybody plays to win, because that one strategy that involves teleporting Manhattans has virtually zero counterplay).
The biggest problem with it is that there is very little diversity. You only have one race, and that race doesn't have that many units to choose from, relatively speaking of course. You could argue there is a unit covering almost every niche use, are you would be right, but that still makes you fight the tanks with the same tanks, there is no racial diversity to those units which made matchups in games like Total Annihilation that much more interesting. Titans helped to bring some varriety, but it still feels like you are fighting the same thing over and over again (mainly because only a few of them are viable). There is a fan made race that is available for multiplayer custom games, It's actually decently made, but the quality is not there compared to the original. I also take offence to the ridiculous in-game microtransactions. Sure, they are cosmetic and they are literally only different commander models, but locking away cool in-game content behind a 5$ A PIECE paywall is scummy AF. The single player "campaign" is also very lackluster, it's basically a set of AI skirmishes with added technological shenanigans which COULD be cool if the AI wasn't completely braindead even on the highest difficulty (UPDATE: there now exists a mod that changes and improves the GW AI, the same one that was implemented for skirmishes, and it makes it SO much more fun! Actually worth playing right now!) There are also little things like unit pathing sometimes getting a little wonky, or performance absolutely sucking♥♥♥♥♥when the game gets crowded with units (which is understandable to a certain degree, but i encounter performance issues even with a 1070 and overclocked i5 which is a little silly), but overally I think those are the most major complaints.
The game is a mixed bag. I would still recommend you to pick it up on at least -50% sale if you like to play strategy games, even just AI skirmishes. Otherwise you probably won't enjoy the game if you aren't into RTS, it's not the easiest one out there to start with.

I have about 20 hours played on the PS3 version of the game. I picked up the Steam version on sale hoping another honest shot with PC-quality graphics would be enough to re-awaken a game I hoped would be amazing.
It didn't.
Long story short, it's no "Burnout 3: Takedown" and it's for two major reasons:
1) The camera angle.
The camera is at just a low enough position and angle to be annoying. I spent my ENTIRE time wishing I could just..grab it and...move it...up..just a little bit....but no. The game doesn't let you. I don't mind if I can't control the camera precisely but this is a FAST-paced racing game. I need to be able to see CLEARLY what's ahead of me. My car takes up too much of the screen and there's no way to get the angles you want. It's an ongoing frustration that really became a dealbreaker for me over time. The camera is too low and at too shallow of an angle.
I know it sounds nit-picky but it's one of the absolute first things I noticed when I started playing the game. The camera is your worst enemy.
-------------
2) The fact that the entire career mode takes place within the open world.
On paper this seems pretty cool...except it means they should have titled this game "Burnout: Orienteering". This design decision means that the game is reduced to "memorize the city layout and use the same roads over and over again".  Don't feel like trying to navigate a brand new city at 100 MPH? Too bad, you have to do that before you can do ANYTHING else in this game. This game demands that the player spends too much time memorizing street names, locations of gas stations, etc. rather than enjoying the fast-paced action that the Burnout games are best at. Don't get me wrong, the action is still great...but it gets lost behind this annoying navigation layer that's present for 100% of the game!
Countless times I wished I could just tell the game to screw off with the city navigation stuff and just give me a track with flashing yellow signs that shouted "THIS WAY, DUMB-BUTT!" with occasional shortcuts hidden around, like Burnout 3.
This problem is further compounded by the fact that all races end at 1 of 6 locations. This means no inner-city circuits, etc. Growing up on Burnout 3, yes you played the same stages over and over again but it worked much better because the stages were discrete levels. You didn't get the feeling that you were spending all of your time in the same square chunk of land from 0% to 100% completion. Effectively, the game turns into "Themes and Variations on 6 tracks".
If this game had discrete tracks like Burnout 3 I think I would have enjoyed it much more. Burnout 3 still stands out as my favorite game in the series and one of my favorite racing games of all time. This game....ehh, I really wanted to like it because it did a LOT of things right - it kept the core of the "racing/crashing game" that burnout was best at but it obscured it with obnoxious camera angles and mandatory city memorization that just killed the experience for me. Discrete tracks let you memorize the game's levels in doses - one track at a time. Bastion impresses from the start with detailed, colorful environments and sharp isometric combat. You’ll visit many visually exquisite levels, expanding your hub base and unlocking a variety of weapons and upgrades. The game encourages experimentation by allowing you to choose attributes for weapons, mix and match passive bonuses, and even tweak the difficulty in original ways.  Each weapon feels distinct and needs surprisingly precise skill to use effectively. Bastion’s brutal challenge stages demand that you master the peculiarities of each weapon to succeed at unique tasks, and the wave-based arena modes provide an excellent playground for the extensive customization. Perhaps the game’s most memorable feature is the narrator, whose iconic voice and salty commentary propels you through the well-paced story. These different elements ensure that Bastion engages you moment to moment, as every step treats you to a new flavor of combat, visuals, music, or character dialog.  Bastion tightly packages quality gameplay with gorgeous presentation.

What on the first glance looks like a generic high-school-romance visual novel in fact turns into a dramatic SciFi / mecha / military-themed universe which took many influences from other franchises such as

franchise was actually so successful that meanwhile it expanded into numerous sequels, spin-offs, light novels, anime series and much more.
To begin with, this particular release of

and
.
can be considered as a lighthearted introduction to the main characters while
finally introduces you to the serious SciFi world in which the franchise mainly takes place.
Personally I interpret both games as an overly long prologue to the amazing 50 hours long
, the third game of the original trilogy which many players consider one of the best visual novels ever made (
included in this particular release, sold separately). That being said you need to bring up the patience and effort to read through both
and
, since in total it takes about 30 hours until you've seen all the endings. And to be honest, some routes and story branches in both games are not even that interesting. For instance I found
route in

BUT (and here it gets interesting) it still pays off if you read through everything and therefore immerse yourself into
's characters and world, since later in the third game a huge chunk of the story touches upon that. After sucking in all that what
and
offered, finishing the third game will be one of the most rewarding and complete visual novel experiences you might ever have.
Therefore especially
may leave you rather unimpressed at first, but the experience definitely takes epic proportions by the time you finished both games and finally start
.
In case you never played any visual novel before, here's the deal: You read yourself through textboxes and occassionally make decisions that to some extend change the outcome of the ending. Everything is accompanied by CGs, an appropiate soundtrack and sometimes even by voice actors. What may sound pretty boring to many is in fact pretty intense. Visual novels have the pace and format to tell such detailed and immersive stories that animes, movies or TV shows can't equally pull off due to their technical limitations. What a movie cramps down to 2 hours, a visual novel makes you experience in 40.
The story of
puts you in the shoes of Takeru, a regular, rather lazy Japanese high school student who's into mecha arcade games, good food and the comforts of life. He is best friends with Sumika, the girl next door who spent all her childhood with him. When he's not spending his spare time with her or his other buddy Mikoto in the local arcades, he's usually goofing around at school and interacting with his mostly female classmates. But everything changes as one day Takeru wakes up in his bed - next to a unknown, mysterious girl...
Telling anything more would already result in spoilers, but rest assured that you'll adore the
trilogy if you like SciFi-themed anime with military / mecha / conspiracy / traumatizing vibes to it. The later parts specifically reminded me of Verhoeven's
, which I already mentioned before.
Now the
games initially started as
visual novels with some kinky +18 scenes in it. This particular Steam release (also known as
version) has all of the H-scenes removed due to Steam's content policies. The developers / publishers solved this problem by offering a separately available
that unlocks the +18 CGs in the game. While that's technically a good solution, the bad news is that you need to fork out another $10 for that patch, which is quite a rip-off in my opinion. In the end it doesn't even affect that many CG's and scenes, which are
anyway due to Japanese pornography law. Furthermore personally I didn't like the kinky scenes that much since they kinda feel out of place considering the intense story and all - but that's up to you.
So, should you get it?
If all that already sounds too long and tedious for you, then just leave it be. You'll most likely get bored after a few hours of listening to Sumika's annoying chatter.
But if you're ready to dive into this universe that later shines with excellent world-building and geekiness, then come on board and enjoy this rollercoaster full of excitement, emotions, blood and tears. Consider this release as an overly long prelude to
, which will most likely blow you away completely.

Bastion is a fine action-adventure game set in a fantastic world after a near apocalyptic event. The scenery is superb, beautiful places that show some of this world's former glory. The gameplay is quite varied, as there is a wide variety of weapons, each with their respective upgrades and secret skills, that you can combine in every way you want. You can also customize the difficulty by invoking different gods that will make foes stronger in a variety of ways, while providing you with greater rewards.
The soundtrack is another strong point for this game. Each song seems fitting to the situation you're currently in, and there's plenty of them.
Finally, the story is very well crafted. The narration aspect is quite interesting, and as you progress, it begins to make more and more sense. Not to mention that a second playthrough, in New Game+, will add new details.
All in all, a highly recommendable game.

I played most of the early burnout games back in my console days and loved every last one, Burnout Paradise lives up to all of my expectations and then some. Its an adrenaline fuelled, carnage filled automotive masterpiece. Usually I prefer sims when it comes to driving games, but who dosent love to jump into an arcade racer and let loose every now and then.
From its open world, multiple event types, and freedom of progression it really is a "do it your way" experience. Dont like a specific type of event, then dont do them. You can upgrade your licence by picking the events you want to do. However to get to 100% completion will require you to complete every race, including ones you had done but got reset when your licence upgraded.  The world is beutifull, and with a day night cycle really comes to life.
The crash physics......why we all came here. They are still amazing to watch and have evolved like the rest of the game. Not only do we get those gorgeous cut scenes to better see the result of our screw up, we can now go one step further and enter "showtime" a beutifull ballet of carnage as you control the crash and attempt to cause as much damage as you can.
Multiplayer is brilliant with all kinds of challenges to take part in, a minor omission is no text chat for us PC users. Now something that always bugs me is why PC racing games don't include a splitscreen function. But fear not, when you have friends over there is "Party Mode" so everyone can join in the fun. Its a pass the pad "hot seat" style mode  with verious challenges to choose from.
Pros
Amazing visuals
Crash Physics
Huge open world
Day night cycle
Motorbikes
A non online multiplayer option
Cons
You will do the same events a few times
No text chat in online multiplayer
Only a few bikes to choose from
All in all i would rate this as the best arcade racer of recent years. A game where even a crash can become a beutifull specticle, enough to make you not mind that you just lost the race. Highly reccomend this to arcade racers and sim guys looking to go a lil nuts and bow off some steam :)

While I kind like the artstyle of this game (brings me back to the good old days of playing Theme Park World), it's sadly the only thing I liked about this game besides one other thing. I'm quite into sim games in general, but this game really did not cut it for me.
In this game you play a cartoonish airline manager (there are a few to choose from, each with their own special trait like getting better deals at on-flight meals) and you have to be the most succesful one: aka be the most profitable. You buy planes for your fleet and customize to your liking, balancing airplane quality, fly range, maintenance and transport size. You can also buy plance from the scrapyard, which is a nice touch but I doubt beneficial due to very high maintenance and the planes often being too outdated (yes, planes technology evolves in this game). You have to get your crew together (balancing skills versus salary), arrange stuff for you planes, etc.
But in the end there is one mayor issue: the game is TERRIBLY slow. You (and your competitors) advance at the speed of a snail... While this does resemble real life better, it sadly just isn't fun. This combined with a very steep learning curve as the tutorial just doesn't cut it, causing me to feed that I really have no idea what I'm doing nor what I ought to do. And that's bad for a sim game. You should have the feeling that your decision matters and you should get feedback on the consequences of you choices. But sadly, it takes too long to get that feedback and if easy to miss it as the gains are often very small.
This game disappointed me. If your time is valuable to you, try some other game instead of this one. Or be willing to ask google to help you play this game, because without it you'll surely fail :(

Ha, Delta Force. It's one of those games where you must have played it when it came out to fully understand how great it was. In terms of FPS, and most precisely in the realistic warfare genre, this game was one of the greatest upon release. Years later, the two leading warfare game brands, Battlefield and Call of Duty, would use many elements the Delta Force franchise came up with in its first installment.
Delta Force pioneered in multiple departments. First of all, one must remember that 3D shooters were pretty new. Delta Force not only had good graphics upon release, it offered extremely large areas to fight on when compared to its rivals. It also was one of the first FPS which allowed the players to customize their arsenal before starting their mission, and, correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe it was one of the first FPS, and perhaps THE first to allow players to select a playable female character.
One of the best elements of this game is that it didn't stray from its main goal which was to offer realistic combat. The diverse missions all seem like they could have happened for real. You can run out of ammo. Your AI-controlled squadmates can die just like everyone else. This might sound funny in 2017, but Delta Force was one of the first 3D FPS to include a somewhat effective "alert" system where enemies would not be aware of your presence until they would spot you or hear gunshots. This allows the player the chance to complete an entire mission using stealth with the aid of their knife and silenced firearm.
I briefly touched the topic of diversity. The missions in this game are very entertaining. Back in the day, FPS games were pretty generic in terms of design. Delta Force offers missions all around the world, so you get desert, snow and jungle maps, all with various types of buildings and land configurations. You almost immediately get access to those different places right away, so when you get tired of the jungle, you can always switch to some other place with a different scenery. As you complete your missions, you unlock others too. The objectives that you need to accomplish aren't always the same, which is very good.
As I said, graphics weren't bad at all back in the late 90's. The sky looks pretty good, the ground has some sort of grass thing going on ( which was pretty new back then ) and the characters are pretty detailed. The guns and other weapons could've had better animations, but overall it's more than tolerable. Sound effects aren't bad either, but you kinda wish there would be a little more, considering the fact that there will seldom be a second or two of complete silence even in the middle of a firefight.
Since the Delta Force is a unit, you have some AI soldiers to help you on your missions. Unfortunately, the AI in this game is quite limited, so they will more than often just go to their scripted waypoint and shoot at the enemies when the time comes. They also offer some radio support, giving you the position of specific enemies. When things get rough, don't expect them to do much. If you are lucky, they'll kill one or two bad guys. They are decoys at best.
I guess that the weakest thing about the game is its AI. It was already pretty bad when the game came out. The enemies follow a pre-designed path and once they have reached their ultimate destination, they'll just stand at this position. This will sometimes lead you to search all over the place, trying to find the last guy to kill. Luckily, you'll hear him yelling or shooting during your search. If you do the mission a second time, you'll understand that the enemies always do the exact same thing. This hurts replay value a lot. The other bad thing is that, obviously, this game has aged. Unless you are the kind of gamer who isn't repelled by old FPS games, I think Delta Force will mostly appeal to older people in search of cheap nostalgia.
Overall, I recommend this game for senior gamers, but also for younger gamers in search of a cheap FPS which paved the way for many others. I think that when you buy this game, you also buy a little part of video game history, in a way. It's the best game of the franchise, in my opinion, since it offered multiple groundbreaking elements. The other Delta Force games aren't half bad either, though, but they nevertheless picked up on what the first opus created, so I consider them a tiny bit inferior.

Speaking after hours of experience, Trove has much to offer, yet the Developers of the game doesn't care about the player-base on full potential. The game is experiencing high-tier server issues. (I suspect they are using an overcloaked potato as their server.)
About what the game offers;
There are two paths you can chose, first the "pay to win" one.
By chosing this path, you can pretty much get into end-game quite easily with the in-game currency "flux" you obtain from most of the chests and by using the marketplace buying all the required resources. This way also allows you to obtain a higher mastery level faster than the others beacuse of the market-exclusive items which most of the players won't be able to obtain by their effords. (They can obtain these but it takes quite large amount of flux to obtain all of them.)
Anyways, the "Patron system" allows you to get better items, better daily rewards, more daily chests ("chaos chests"), and most important of all, default experience point boost. The benefits of patron pass also lets you obtain even larger amount of "Daily bonuses" which change through the week.
Now knowing the semi-superiority of the way of pay to win, lets proceed to the default player path.
This is pretty much about the grind. You will need to grind resources and most importantly "flux". I would suggest the gardening method to obtain moderate amount of flux early-game which is through the "Gardening bench".
You can use this flux for mostly the same purposes of the other path.  (Getting resources, buying stellar - radiant gear etc.)
This path is mostly about the grind. At Mastery level 100 (Not so sure though) you will be gifted a "Chaos Coin" which will let you get chaos chests daily. (I think patron-pass gives you around 4 chests daily)
Anyways, that's pretty much it I guess ? Before starting the game, I would suggest not to if you can't handle high levels of server issues which you will be your daily route.
Without the server issues, I would definetly recommend this game, but with the servers' current conditions, I honestly don't.

Bastion impresses from the start with detailed, colorful environments and sharp isometric combat. You’ll visit many visually exquisite levels, expanding your hub base and unlocking a variety of weapons and upgrades. The game encourages experimentation by allowing you to choose attributes for weapons, mix and match passive bonuses, and even tweak the difficulty in original ways.  Each weapon feels distinct and needs surprisingly precise skill to use effectively. Bastion’s brutal challenge stages demand that you master the peculiarities of each weapon to succeed at unique tasks, and the wave-based arena modes provide an excellent playground for the extensive customization. Perhaps the game’s most memorable feature is the narrator, whose iconic voice and salty commentary propels you through the well-paced story. These different elements ensure that Bastion engages you moment to moment, as every step treats you to a new flavor of combat, visuals, music, or character dialog.  Bastion tightly packages quality gameplay with gorgeous presentation.

Very nice game so far, gives me the old Knights and Merchants / The Settlers vibe. I've been wanting to dabble in this genre again without resorting to the older titles, so I'm very glad to see there's still interest in it.
The good:
Game size (as in bytes), surprisingly small. Very quick and easy installation.
Graphics, I personally like the cartoony style- not too cutesy. Additionally the clan selection screen features gorgeous art (hope there will be more of this spread throughout the game) and the weather effects/season changes really set the right mood for this game.
Music, compliments the artstyle nicely but I'd like to hear more diversity.
Mini-tutorial, though lacking an 'official' tutorial, the game does a good job of explaining how it works. Easy to learn for players new to the genre.
Use of territories, you can build a set amount of buildings per territory (varying amounts depending on the territory), which makes it important to choose what to build next instead of just building "everything". Some buildings are more effective in certain areas than others and you will often have to choose which buildings to destroy and what to replace them with in order to gain the most benefit.
As for 'The bad', none so far! The games run really smoothly and does what it's supposed to do, even at this early stage of development. Shiro Games' direction is promising and I hope they can make an already good game even better with it's full release.

When SFV came out it wasn't worth the money for most people. Even if, like me, you mostly only cared about online gameplay, the poor netcode/netplay still made the game not fun a lot of the time. Fast forward to now and the game has been vastly improved and is definitely worth getting. Put together the fact that they've added a cinematic story mode as free dlc, made improvments to netcode netplay and lobbies, as well as added 4 dlc characters which can be obtained relatively easily for free, and you've got a damn good game. Not to mention they've added lots of cosmetics, which, if you're anything like me, you'll appreciate.
Does this mean the game is perfect? No. The game still lacks directinput support and grinding through survival mode to get colors is a pain. However, given how easy it is to fix these two problems I find it difficult to take people's complaints about these things seriously. I use joy2key, which to my knowledge does not add latency, to circumvent the directinput issue and let's just say there are ways to get around grinding through survival. I'm sure a little digging on google/reddit could help you there.
SFV at it's core has always had great gameplay. The figthing itself is balanced, fun, and very solid all around. However, on release it was held back from it's full potential by a myriad of problems, but I'm happy to say that most of these have been fixed. With the large amounts of improvements and additions they've made to the game, and with more on the way, SFV is definitely worth buying and playing.

Pros:
+Fun RTS/city builder
+Actually requires some strategy with limited buildings per territory and win conditions
+Survival elements with harsh winters causing your people to consume extra food and (fire)wood
+Combat is really fun even with limited unit variety
+Bug-free for me so far!
+4 different victory conditions
+Graphics look very nice, I really enjoy the style
+Nice music
+Pretty smart AI
Cons/Suggestions:
-Could use some more military units, at least a ranged unit (archer or throwing axes)
-Scouts get hurt while exploring (which is a good feature), but if you send them back to your territory to heal, they automatically leave to find new territory even if they aren't at full health
-Needs more customizations for skirmish matches like modifying the victory conditions, map type, etc
Overall I am really enjoying this game and definitely feel it is worth $20. It's kind of a blend of rts and city builder where you're limited on the number of buildings per territory so you want to expand and pick up more territories, but each one costs more food than the last. Winters are harsh and you consume more food and wood so you want to stockpile a bit beforehand. Villagers are your core unit and you assign them to different roles by sending to a certain building corresponding with the job you want them to do (woodcutter lodge to be a woodcutter, etc). There is no campaign or multi-player yet but they said those will be coming in the next couple months. So far I haven't experienced any bugs which is amazing for early access! Also, there are currently 4 victory conditions: conquest, research, trade, and fame. There are 3 clans which are essentially the races you choose at the beginning and there are at least 2 more getting released soon. Strongly recommended if you enjoy RTS/city builders.

It's an early access, and so far the game is quite fun.
3 different clans, with unique bonuses and slightly differing technology trees fight over a map defined by an area control mechanic.
Basically, the map is divided into small areas with unique bonuses and/or resources, differing from plain forest to Yggdrasyl, the World tree. You need to colonize an area by defeating foes and bying it through recources to be able to use the bonuses. IT sort of remids of CIV5 city construction, although here you are operating one settlement and have to engage into action instead of plain buing cells.
This mechanic is both source of fun and frustration. Besides exploring tombs and fighting draugrs, wolfs and other wyrms, you have to build economy around resources available at the start. And the map is randomized. The result is as follows. Only one out of three clans posesses perks to sustain economy despite unfavorable resource distribution. Other two actually need a good start to be able to compete. Like CIV, again. If your first city is badly placed, you're in deep doo-doo. Also, having too many different resources in the same area is not good, either.
All these issues will be balanced out, I think. But the feel of the game is actually quite good. Winters FEEL harsh. exploration IS fun and the music is great. UI is easy to read (Unlike something like Endless Legend). The only bug i found is that game does not load out from the map correctly. It outputs an error when you close it after playing and if you try to start new map after playing one.
Recommend it. Really want to see the game to advance.

This is the first time I've ever felt that my choices of building and expansion actually mattered in an RTS!
I've played about 5 games as of this review, the first one I starved to death during winter about 40 mins in.
After my 3rd game, I chose the Wolf Clan since I started to get the hang of it and managed to pull my first Victory by capturing and holding a location called Hellheim, a "hidden" victory condition. After that I ran with the Stag clan and won using  "Wisdom" Victory conditions (plus it just feels good to fill out that tech tree as far as you can go!) and my final Victory I earned last night was with the Goat clan, who now may be my favorite clan for the moment, I never ran out of food and instead held many many feasts that kept my production fired up nearly the whole game when it was available, I won through Fame.
Clans:
Wolf - Military based, offers "happiness" and makes your warriors eat less food.
Stag - Begins with extra resources, focuses on production from buildings.
Goat - Reduces the amount of food your clan eats, makes feats much more worthwhile with less risk of running out.
Tips:
-You can use houses to convert your workers back into Villagers to build things so be smart about where you place houses the farther out you go.
-There is a Repair All button on the right side of the screen (for when your town gets hit by an Earthquake or other event)
-It's a good idea to establish a food source, wood and coin early on so you don't run out during winter.
Store sheep in a sheephold, don't just slaughter them for quick food unless it's an emergency
-When Healers aren't healing anyone cause they are all at full health, turn them back into villagers to gather food until you get tech that allows healers to gather food
-Villagers will only build or gather in an area if they are ASSIGNED (click on them and send them to that area, they will gather food until they see a building that needs worked on or assigned a different job) to that area, so if you plop a building down in an expansion with no villagers, nobody will go build it.
-Hopefully those will help you as I wish I knew that when starting out!
-Pros:
-Vikings!
-Norse Mithology tie into the gameplay with Boons from the Gods based on your research amount.
-Meaningful choices, from the first building to the last is a tactical decision that you must be ready to defend at a moments notice
-Tactical expansions, get to know what the land offers you before you claim it, each tile offers different resources/opportunities.
-Seasons that make you plan ahead (and they come and go often so you'll have to adapt fairly frequently).
-Heroes you can buy that add that extra bit of strength to your Militia
-Random Events in the game that keep you on your toes (atm Earthquakes)
-Locations that can be held for bonuses and boss like enemies to fight for a big reward
-Fair Territorial warfare, though the AI is a bit easy to manipulate making them a bit less of a challenge
-You can play just by yourself as in, NO AI factions so it's just you against the wild beasts and monsters of the world offering a unique PVE experience for a more casual playthrough about survival.
-The Art Style is beautiful, I am a sucker for games like this.
-The sound is nice and clean, though the Warriors shouting the same thing with each order gets a bit repetitive.
Cons:
-No Female/Children to make up your village, so there's a lack of diversity, but the Devs are apparently looking into this at some point
-There are 2 factions not yet released, but the other 3 are great to use for now
-No Multiplayer implemented YET, but it's coming! :)
-No Campaign implemented YET, but it's coming :)
-There's a lack of customization in game generation, Just pick your name, clan, color, and enemy amount atm.
-The game doesn't tend to explain all of it's mechanics very well when starting out, but you'll get the hang of it after a couple 2-3 games.
-Tiles only allow you to build a certain number of buildings, now this is only a CON as I feel the number is a bit too small, I think 1 extra building for each current space would help, but for the moment it still works and it's just a matter of thinking critically about each expansion you make.
-Ship gameplay is pretty barren (practically non-existent in my games), given that these are Vikings I would really like to see that expanded upon in the future.
-There isn't a good way to really track your opponents progress in relation to your aside from Fame, which makes it a bit more tactical when you wanna be sneaky, but if you play competitively this may be a turnoff? I'm a filthy Casual though so take that with a grain of salt.
-It's less of a City Builder and more of a tactical expansion builder as you can't make booming utopias with city streets and the like, but the game has an incredible amount of charm to it's gameplay that is so different from anything I've ever played before, that i really like it (kind of a Pro and Con here I guess)
-Most of these things can or will be attended to given that this is Early Access yet, and for what's on the table now this is very solid and I love the groundwork they've laid for this game.
So if you like Age of Empires/ Settlers with maybe a bit Civilization mixed together, then my recommendation is a resounding YES!

Fallout 4 features a boring, monotonous story about a distressed parent looking for their child, set in an empty uneventful post-apocalyptical land. Other than random encounters with weak pushover enemies, nothing happens in this barren world. Most locations are empty except for the end-of-dungeon loot chest.
The story features some of the most uninteresting NPCs you'll see in a videogame. Most of the quest objectives are 1. Get in 2. Kill them. 3. Interact with the thing at the end. The factions are awful, the only one that's worth anything is the Railroad, and most of my appreciation for them stems from my transhumanist convictions. Also, they are the most good looking faction in the game, with the Institute just after.
The Minutemen quests are more or less the same for the whole game, going from settlements to settlements doing radiant quest (or would be radiant quest, as the quest are scripted to happened at the same location). Settlement building is one of the worst feature in the game, but with the Automatron and mods, you can replace your settlers with robots, being the only reason to buy the DLC.
The protagonist is the worst in the serie, being stale and boring, with little of the wit from New Vegas and even from FO3. I highly recommand the mods that make them silent and that lock the camera on the person you're talking to. I also highly recommend a mod that override the main quest and disable it, to get you out of the horrendous distressed parent act.
About the gameplay, combat is much more interesting than FO3 and NV. Guns feel better, enemies are more interactive  (though not much more intelligent) and visually speaking the game looks good. However, don't expect the same variety in enemies and weapons as NV. There is like, 7 guns in the game and just a few types of enemies. Though there is more options in weapon customization, most are thrash, and in the end there is always one that is better than the rest. The real issue lies in the character progression. As it's been said before, there are no more skills, instead everything you can do is determined by your perks. Meaning if you want to deal more damage, you need perks, if you want to lockpick doors or safes, you need perks, if you want to hack, you need perks, etc. This really slows down progression, the "upside" being that you level up faster, but leveling up is much less interesting. There are no more unique weapon, despite what the game wants you to believe. Unique weapons have the same stats has the normal one, but with a unique legendary affix. With mod, you can share those affix, there is even a few such affix that can be swap in the vanilla game.
Fallout 4 is not the worst game ever made. It is playable, and it qualifies as a game. However, it suffers from a dull, tedious storyline, little diversity, uninteresting exploration with little to discover, scarce sidequests, and few likable characters. While it is playable, it is a huge disappointement, and it is even downright incredible to think that this took nearly 10 years to develop, with as little content as it has, and so little quality, while Fallout New Vegas was made in less than a year.
So, I repeat, it is playable, but it is not fun. I had the most fun with this game by modding an overpowered character and run amok, killing everything. This would have been alright when I was 12, but now that I am 22, I'm looking for a little more in my game than mindless carnage with poor voice-acting. If that is what your looking for, go play Hatred.

Northgard is one of those games that you like immediately in the menu. When the game loads up, it feels crisp, clean, intuitive, and runs like a gem. Some people have mentioned stability issues, but I guess I was just lucky because it ran smooth throughout for me; just a second or so freeze when Winter starts and goes.
People seem to like reviews that are pros and cons/suggestions related, so here we go.
Pros:
- Butter smooth, awesome visuals.
- Combines Survival with RTS, you really need to keep an eye on your resources, a bad winter really messes with your tribe- love that!
- Not purely warfare based; you pick your clan, each with their own playstyle, and though you can have warriors and chieftains in every clan, you can win by playing it your way, bringing us to the next one:
- Multiple victory conditions, from establishing trade routes to warfare, or conquering Yggdrasil, there are multiple ways to stay in the game, I honestly can not WAIT for Multiplayer
Cons / Suggestions - baring in mind it's Early Access
- Fairly limited at this point; 2 hours into play, 1 hour to learn and 1 hour to play a full game from start to finish with medium AI (3 of them) and I won my first try as Trader, and I really, really didn't do it very well. Looking back I made all sorts of horrible decisions.
- Map size;
discovering other factions happens way too fast, and once you do, you're basically out of room for improvement. This may be by design, to force interaction between players earlier on, but in AI mode it feels a bit stuffy- this may be the way the devs have playtested it and it maybe feels right in multiplayer to force interaction with each other
- Early Access. Typical of early access titles, this one just over all feels like it needs "more" - but that's precisely the point for releasing it now, it gets rid of bugs and optimizes performance, as well as getting some much desired feedback for the devs.
Overall:
This game is the first Early Access title that I personally find extremely promising; the reason for that is simple: this is the first Early Access game that I will continue playing, since it is
a proper functioning, well fleshed out game, that simply needs a bit 'more', to keep us hooked. This is a solid gaming investment.
Keep up the good work devs!

So it's been 4-5 months this game has been out. It was released on February 16th in a pretty early state to let competitive players put their hands on the game before the Capcom Pro Tour events began. Now that the big content patch has been released and the game is in the state it would've been if it was launched in June (as it was previously planned), what can you expect from SFV?
I played this game since launch. As you can see I spent quite a few hours on it, almost more than all other games in my library together, so I'll share my experience about how the game is in its current state.
First of all, as you might have guessed by many reviews, this game originally had a heavy focus on multiplayer. As an online pvp game, my experience is overall amazing, with hundreds of almost flawless matches against both PS4 and PC players thanks to the rollback netcode that prevents you from missing inputs. That being said, there are some issues to be aware of before starting to play:
- forwarding the right ports on your router is very recommended for an overall better online experience.
- while the netcode allows perfect gaming on good ping, a lower ping or a bad kind of connections (like wi-fi) can easily turn the game into an unplayable teleport fest.
- the blind matchmaking is sometimes a little shaky and it is prone to 3 kinds of issues: long waiting times between matches, being matched with players way above/below your actual rank and putting you against people with worst connections than you asked for. While the first two issues seems to have been fixed with latest patch, it seems that you can still get laggy matches.
- there is still no proper punishment for ragequitters after 4 months, meaning that anyone can leave the match before the end and keeping his/her ranked points while preventing you from gaining them. This is totally annoying and you will need a lot of patience if you really wanna play ranked.
- battle lounges searching still isn't optimized and you need to enter a lobby to know the country and ping quality of your opponent.
Even with all these issues though I still managed to play countless matches against many different players from my own and from neighbouring regions and have tons of fun.
As for the single player content, the game doesn't offer a lot. Trials are OK, Survival mode is a pretty tedious and unbalanced and there is no "classic" Arcade mode (though a VS CPU mode is coming soon). Instead you have character stories and general story; the first ones are very easy and quick to finish, while the other one is 3 hours long including all the cutscenes and can be replayed in a harder difficulty to get extra money. The advantage is that general story lets you play ALL SFV characters - including those that you don't have who still haven't been released yet - so it's perfect to test them out before spending your FM on them.
Overall I still wouldn't recommand this game to those who thought of only playing it alone. But if you have friends or like to play online, this is definitely one of the best and most balanced fighters around there and will probably be the main fighting game on PC for the next 5 years. Rise up!

Street Fighter V has kept my attention for the past 2 or 3 months with ease.. and that was just the bare bones fighting system with some characters.  Now there is a story mode that is actually well put together and entertaining and the ladder matches me with similarly ranked opponents?
This was my first serious fighting game and the community really did a good job at pulling me in.  It really has this friendly atmosphere where players are taking jabs at each other one second and then cheering the next.  Wednesday Night Fights weekly makes me cheer for russian dudes in their underwear 69ing in the air before getting pounded hard right into the ground.
What I love about the game is it is challenging.  You have to think about what your opponent is doing and you have to counter it.  You may even play mindgames with your opponent to get them to open up.  You have to practice your combos, learn your characters normals, and work your way around problems that other games seem to solve for you.  Each fight is exciting.. and the fight after that fight is more exciting because they just figured out what you were doing and you have to change it up or lose the entire set.
Even the fact that my friend beats my♥♥♥♥♥70 times a night in a private battle lounge is a good thing because we're both getting better.  Sometimes I double down on losses and say if I win, it counts as more.. and then I have 140 losses.  This game tears us apart and then glues us together.. and the glue is made of pure hatred.   It doesn't matter that during the fight a fire is burning in my chest.  It wells up inside of me for hours.  I try to sleep and I dream about it.  It doesn't matter if I go to work and all I can see is blinding flashes of light as Chun-Li kicks me in the face with her big♥♥♥♥♥legs.  All that matters is that I kill my friend.  And I can't kill him while he's sleeping or while his back is turned.  It wouldn't be satisfying.  I have to crush him from the front, repeatedly.  I want to destroy him physically, emotionally, and spiritually.  And for that, I need to practice and learn and adapt.
Street Fighter V brings people together.

On the surface, Sanctum 2 is a basic tower defense shooter, with much better than indie graphics and voice overs (I want to marry Sweet), and a strange fixation on irrelevant details (why all this modeling of bars and security points that have nothing to do with the game?).  In contrast to Dungeon Grinders.. I mean Defenders, Sanctum eschews the farming and looting in favor of straight game play.  It does have experience and levels, but they're mostly a minor annoyance.  Like DD, the first person shooter element isn't strongly emphasized as the enemies are all very predictable and tower placement usually dominates your chances of success.
Where Sanctum really shines is the point after you've beaten the normal levels by randomly throwing down some towers and running wildly around blasting everything.  Flip on all the bad guy boosts and suddenly you have a very serious co-op puzzle game.  Which perks to take, what guns, and how to lay out your towers become hard questions, with different answers for every map.  Climbing the leaderboard becomes a competitive challenge.
If you enjoy cooperatively solving hard optimization problems, I strongly recommend Sanctum 2 with a friend.
Sanctum 2 does have some weak points.  The experience/level system just gets in the way and should've been scrapped.    There are too many perks and even when you know them all, it can be hard to find the one you want.  Number of players scaling is sometimes a factor.  Hoard avoided this by having specific maps for specific numbers of players.  Sanctum tries to pretend boosting the health of enemies is close enough.  It isn't and it makes leaderboard comparisons problematic.  The mind control tower introduced in the dlc substantially changes the game and ruins the leaderboard for people without the dlc.  The developers should've had separate ladders for dlc and without.

Having played and enjoyed Sanctum 1, I was excited and curious as to how Sanctum 2 would improve upon it.
Sadly Sanctum 2 just made me wonder, what the core gameplay of a tower defense game should be like.
Surely it would be building towers, right? And of course you are able to do so but in such a limited fashion that it just takes away what was so great about it in its predecessor for me.
Building a maze of blocks or tower bases to guide your enemies to their death before they can reach your core.
Limiting the amount of tower bases you can build from the beginning brings its own challenge with it. Having to switch up your maze design to account for where and what enemies attack you is good. Now if only you could fill up all your tower bases with towers...thats the problem.
As long as you had the space and credits you could build as many towers as you'd want in Sanctum 1, whereas you'll only be able to build 15 towers at max in this game.
Most of the time the levels will be big and you'll have to come up with the right placements for your towers or having to move them around. This is where I found that the limit of 15 towers just doesnt feel right.

Even with the window title bar blocking the top 2% of the screen's gameplay - the only real negative for this package -  this is enormous fun. One of my favorite games from quite a long time ago, a no-frills FPS with (very evolutionarily early) squad tactics.   The more difficult missions will still pack quite a challenge, and the graphics bring back memories.  Fairly revolutionary for its time, and runs silky smooth on Windows 10 / Alienware Alpha with no nasty compatibility difficulties.  Try it, you may fall in love with it!  Not beautiful, but she's got it where it counts... a perfect introduction to the Delta Force universe.

The game features three campaigns (Russia, U.S., Germany) that take place on a global map. Heavily scripted missions against superior enemy numbers typically involve capturing locations or destroying specific units, and are difficult in nature. You are given some flexibility in choosing units, as new recruits are earned following victories. Research can also be conducted between missions to improve stats. Skirmish games against the AI or online are also available, but only on five different maps. Blitzkrieg 3 has the typical units (infantry, tanks, anti-tank), plus off-map artillery and air support. Assaulting buildings with infantry is mildly interesting (units duke it out indoors), and powerful units can be countered with the appropriate opponent. Games progress at a fast pace (befitting of the game’s title) and units are generally fragile, especially infantry. The AI is decent at the game on higher difficulty settings and definitely benefits from superior numbers and its initial defensive placement on the map. In the end, Blitzkrieg 3 lacks that new, defining feature to set itself apart from all the other real-time strategy games.

I will get one thing out of the way first before starting my review. RTS games are my favourite genre of games, demolishing an enemy while steadily expanding my base is far more satisfying to me than landing a headshot in a FPS. While I have not played the previous two entries in the Blitzkrieg series, I have played more than my fair share of RTS to judge the third entry in the franchise as a new player.
The first thing you will notice is the lack of base building present in the game. Golden games like Age of Empires and Rise of Nations had such an immersive effect on the player due to the immense kingdoms you could create in them. Aside from a few missions and moments, that feeling is mostly absent here. If you are a base-builder who likes to see his empire or base grow, Blitzkrieg 3 is not the game for you.
But the thing about the old games were that they took long intervals of time before throwing you into the heat of the war and sometimes grew monotonous as you progressed through the same things before doing the actual fighting. The benefit Blitzkrieg 3 has from the lack of proper base building is that it throws you right into the battle without much ado. It fits perfectly into the modern generation’s quick battle scenarios and the amount of time a player can give to it, but it lacks the sense of achievement and satisfaction due to this.
Blitzkrieg 3 is designed mostly for multiplayer focused battles but that does not mean that it completely berefts the player of a proper single player campaign. It features three fully fledged campaigns with three factions namely US, Russia and Germans.
While the story is mostly throwaway and completely skippable, there are a few really well designed maps which makes these campaigns feel like something instead of empty maps stuck together and called a campaign.
These campaigns also feature side missions aside from the main story missions which give you special units and other rewards. To progress in the story though, you need to complete the main story missions which are strung together by a few pieces of dialogues which advance the story.
The unit system in Blitzkrieg 3 is much different than most RTS’s I’ve played. At the end of every battle you get a chance of getting units which differ in their rating. This is mostly a gamble as you can get either a basic unit every match or an epic unit only a few missions in. Rather than building your bases and upgrading your units in every game, Blitzkrieg 3 allows you to use the unlocked units right away if you choose to take them into the battle. While it is a different twist on the formula, it isn’t necessarily for the better.
Where does Blitzkrieg 3 falter though? For starters, it has a very basic and feeble cover system and the game would not have changed much even without it. The very lack of it means that most strategy is thrown in the pit and you start spamming units at your enemies while they do the same to create mayhem. The artillery system also feels limited and most of the artillery has very short range aside from also being limited to being immobile.
There are a few maps which are so unbalanced and the situations so unfair that you can only stick to one strategy and anything other than that will kill you instantly. The fast paced nature of the game also means that it has smaller maps in comparison to some other games of the genre and there is not much room for exploration.
Another major problem for the game is the fact that despite it being multiplayer centric, the condition of its servers is dire at the moment of writing. You cannot start a multiplayer match and expect it to finish normally. Lag is the most common thing even when you are playing singleplayer. The game sessions just disconnected for no specific reasons whatsoever and the crashes to desktop and screen freezes are more frequent than heat waves in India.
To top all of that, the load times are excruciatingly long and the game suffers a lot due to this. For a hefty price tag of 30 bucks you would at least expect a working game with a certain level of polish applied to it, but Blitzkrieg 3 does not deliver on that front.
The visuals present in Blitzkrieg 3 are simply fantastic. The flying debris, smoking charred buildings, a platoon of troops marching towards a destroyed city, everything has an astonishing amount of detail at Ultra which makes the game a visual spectacle. Even the world map looks pretty good with the shiny textures and clean UI.
Nothing remarkable but it does its job well. The soundtrack is fairly generic and is what you would expect from a game like this and the sound effects are just enough to keep your mind in the game. It is not something that you will remember after you quit or download it separately but it is not bad in any sense either.
Blitzkrieg 3 might be the RTS equivalent of Michael Bay movies. It is visual dumb fun at times but never reaches the heights it promises. It does more to keep you out of the game than in and while there are certain redeeming features, it is way too unpolished and buggy in its current state. It can be fun once it reaches its full flow but those times are far and few between. You should probably wait for a few patches or a sale before you shell out its high price of admission.

Delta Force is better than whatever dumb shooter you like from this time period.
In a world where Call of Duty was never tactical, Rainbow Six had tiny maps, and SOCOM had broken AI, Delta Force is the premiere tactical shooter of the late 90s. Imagine Rainbow Six, worldwide, on giant outdoor maps. The size of the maps, quality of teammate command, and loadout choices combine to provide encounters that are never the same twice. Each mission can be approached from any direction. You can run into bases and twitch shoot, or you can paint it with air strikes, or you can snipe everyone, or you can send your buddies to get seen so you can ambush troops in valleys. The choice is always yours with Delta Force.
Delta Force 1 and 2 use a unique raycasting engine that directly draws voxels to screen every frame based on what you look at. In laymen, this means the game has infinite draw distance and maintains a consistent framerate on machines with absolutely no graphics hardware. This game will run on anything, provided its windows.
The only bad thing I can say about this game is that resolution is hard-coded to the executable, and the highest choice is 1024x768. To my knowledge, there are no tools to fix this or enable widescreen. It's a shame, because the voxel art style can get in the way when 1 game pixel is 4 on your actual monitor, and you have to force your monitor into 4:3 to stop stretching.
Still a great game, highly influential, was doing things with giant maps that games like Tribes would later get praise for. Every shooter fan should get this if they see it on sale.

Sleeping dogs is a GTA style game but set in Hong Kong and with much more focus on melee combat. Which is great because the combat is very well done aside from a few hitches here and there it never really gets old throughout the playthrough as you unlock new moves and abilities. There are guns but the main focus is on melee, though when you are armed with a firearm its still nice as all guns are good, feel good, sound good, and are pleasant to use. Graphically the game looks great though at times the world can feel to static and scripted but at others you will chuckle as an NPC yells angrily at a guy stopped at a stoplight to get moving.
All around sleeping dogs is pretty arcadey stylized in its gameplay, the story is more down to earth and interesting revolving around an undercover officer as he struggles to make it in a criminal underworld. Its not hugely innovative or anything we havn't seen before but in all its a good story.
The only downsides are that it can be glitchy at times, I once had my care flinged miles into the sky without any reason, waypoints just dissappear and need reset, guns will dissappear (though less of a problem as the melee combat is more fun), and some other hitches here and there. The minigames can get very boring, unlocking boxes becomes a huge chore and is just awful, hacking cameras is sorta fun but almost impossible to really fail at once you have a system down, are the main problems. There just isn't enough minigames for as often as the game puts you into one so you end up doing the same ones many times over until you hate them. Controls can be wonky at times making you target the wrong enemy or just not responding at all when trying to open your cell phone or making you instead of hire a taxi instead initiating a car jacking. Girlfriends is handled very strangely. After having one date with two girls the first girl called and started flipping out how I was cheating on her when I hadn't even realized she was a GF. Apparently after one date one becomes a intimate love partner in Hong Kong even if that date was just singing Karaoke with a ♥♥♥♥♥ at her job..... In general character development could have been done a little better. Some of the characters are thrown at you fairly quickly while you may have trouble remembering them at all or knowing what they speak of.
The combat is very nice, its like playing in crazy Hong Kong beat 'em up movie. Driving is also pretty good, though at first you may dislike it. Its like an arcadey racing game and it grows on you.
In all though the sum of the parts is greater than any one part. There are many cool features that you may dislike at first but they grow on you and you eventually enjoy and have fun with. Any one part of the game focused on wont looks so great, but put them all together and you get a very fun and good game. The world is full enough to keep feelings of emptiness away while not being over filled and over bearing.

Do you like competitive fighting games? If yes, stop reading and buy Street Fighter V.
If you play fighting games sparringly (heh), consider waiting. This game is not worth it for anyone who isn't going to pour in a lot of hours of practice to play competitively. The single player content is boring and lacking. There's two story modes which are nothing more than lore with 1 round fights between two random characters you may or may not know how to use.
The new story mode is a joke. It's essentially a short film made using the in-game engine which looks passable. What is not however is the completely nonsensical story with equally bad writing with some seriously cringeworthy moments.
There's an awful survival mode which should be avoided.
There's no single player way to unlock all the content. If you're a completionist, this game will require hours of winning in online play in order to aquire all the content.
With all that being said, if you play a fighting game to battle against a human opponent, SFV is a masterpeice. The gameplay is tight and the characters are varied and balanced. Fights are filled with intense moments, layered between theories of combat from various mindsets of your opponent.
Capcom is done with releasing new iterations now, no more Super, Turbo, Championship editions. All new content is delivered to the base game. Paying for new content is now optional, but requires enough online play to do so for free.

The best fighting game around, people love to create hyperboles to strengthen their points so that's what they'll do when it comes down to the game's weakpoints, while gladly overlooking its strengths.
Since the last patch the online has been improved tremendously, matchmaking seems to work quite good at this moment. It doesn't have an arcade mode right now, boo hoo really. If you are looking for casual CPU play, it has Trials, the newly added Story Mode, the obvious Practice mode, several Character Stories to play and a rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Survival mode.
Seriously though, fighting CPU's in any FG's pretty much always sucks since the SNES era, so I don't see much point to it in any case. Do Casual online play if you are scared of an online ladder, atleast you'll pick up on how to play vs actual humans.
Character variety is there and greatly increasing with each new released character, most characters do not play alike and several characters are easy to pick up and play (& hard to master).
Capcom is improving this game as it goes, it was unfortunate it released in a rather shoddy state as the gameplay that's offered is fun and addicting, with the current improvements & content added it shows they are committed for the long haul with this game.
I would not have recommended it on release unless you would be a FG fanatic, but with the content released in July I feel the game starts to deserve that recommendation.
It boils down to: Do you like fighting games? Yes? Then you have to get this, the only game that comes close to as fun gameplay is Guilty Gear Xrd and that game is extremely niche even for a fighting game, thus has an even lower player count.
Do you want to dip into a fighting game as a newbie? To be fair this is one of the better choices, the community behind this game is by far the largest and most competitive, the game's core gameplay is straightforward to pick up compared to some of the other, more obstuse mechanics found in different FG's.
Do you not like fighting games? Don't get this. Crazy concept I know.

Having taken approximately 42 hours to complete one ending for Extra and one for Unlimited, I feel I am now worthy to review this VN. Let's start from the beginning. Extra starts rather slow. It has solid amounts of comedy. Your typical slice-of-life setting. However, it really takes off in Unlimited. It is worth the wait, that is all I will say. Given the nature of Muv-Luv's narrative setup, the promotional videos and descriptions unfortunately kind of spoil the eventual flow of the plot, which makes Unlimited a tad less impactful, but by no means does it spoil the lot of it.
It honestly reminds me of Steins;Gate, Sunrider, and eden*, all games which I have played/completed. Steins;Gate in the respect of it being slow to start, with a sudden significant realization that entirely shifts the narrative flow, and the pace gets exponentially faster. Sunrider with some of its sci-fi aspects. eden* with its narrative premise. Having solid knowledge on all four of the games, I have come to realize that they are related in more ways than one, and the satisfaction of that realization is/was amazing. Like an "Ah-hah" moment. In no way am I saying they were intentionally related, I am just mentioning what I realized and became so gitty about.
Furthermore, it stands the test of time. For being a VN from 2003, it's animations, character/background CGs, and audio are fairly impressive. And, for not being 4:3 aspect ratio, I salute this game. I'll admit that some of its soundtracks get kind of annoying and repetitive, but that was really no big downside. They were still enjoyable.
TL;DR: Can't wait for Alternative!

I write this review with deep regret; because the games themselves (when you can actually play them ! ) are first-class entertainment; really very good indeed. The problem I have is with the 'Steam' system itself, which may be very good at taking money from those who wish to play the games available; but (certainly in my case ! ) is virtually worthless at remembering who's purchased games from them or when. I've spent approaching £100 on three games linked to the Steam system (Civilisation 6 £40, Blitzkrieg 3 £40 and War of the Clans Free ) in the last couple of weeks. The only one amongst them I can still play is Blitzkrieg 3, but for how much longer that will remain possible I really don't know.
Repeat.
The problem is Steam's 'security' system, which is excellent at shutting the games down, and/or restricting access to them; but pretty worthless at allowing them to be reloaded for continued problem-free play later.
With the last three weeks experience of just how unreliable/difficult to access these games really are to base my opinion on; I'd not recommend anyone to send Steam a penny piece; because it doesn't buy the fun that's advertised; just endless stress/frustration and disappointment fighting with a useless 'security' system that insists on shutting down, misloading and/or blocking access too the accounts it's guarding as if they're the miser's hoard.
Quality of the games themselves ?
100%

I myself never was into fighting games but SFV has changed that. This game is much more approachable than almost any other fighting game. This is largely because the combos are easier to pull off than they were in SF4.
They have a Challenge mode in the game now where you can learn some basic combos for each character, but you still will have to go online to find some more advanced techniques. If you are new to fighting games or Street Fighter I would recommend looking at Gief's Gym on the SF subreddit. It will teach to a lot of basics and some advanced stuff that will definitely get you past the novice stage.
If you have a fightstick or are considering getting one to play this game (though you do not in any way need a fightstick to be good) you may have to use a third party program (Joy2Key or x360ce) to make it work properly. Its pretty easy to set up but it can be a minor annoyance.
One of the worst parts about the game is Survival Mode where you face off against AI in a bunch of matches in order to get Fight Money (to unlock characters, stages, colors, etc) as well as the first 10 colors for a character. The AI is extremely frustrating to play against and it takes a lot of time to get through it even if you don't lose on one of the later rounds. Luckily for us PC players, there are mods that will make this mode very easy and fast so should you decide to use that mod it will make getting the colors a piece of cake plus lots of Fight Money. Capcom has stated that they support PC players using mods and as such nobody has or will be banned for using this mod (or any other mod).
Overall, this game is worth a buy now. $60 is still a bit steep but this game will continue to be supported for years to come so over time it will only get better. If you are looking to give fighting games a try, this is definitely the one that will have you hooked. While there are still some issues with the game, Capcom recently has been fixing a lot of stuff so I would expect to see most of the current issues disappear as time goes on. As I write this review the game is on sale for $40. At this price point or any lower it is 100% a good purchase. The season's pass is worth it but I would recommend not buying it until it goes on sale or if you really are interested in the DLC characters/ the premium costumes that they include in the season's pass.
Even though I loved the game on its release and up until this point, I would not have recommended it to someone who is new to fighting games. With the new story and stuff you can buy in the Shop as well as the new and improved netcode, I believe this game is finally ready to have new players jump in.

This game is quite decent for a completely different iteration of the Blitzkrieg franchise. I've played through the first two a while back, and I honestly don't see any problem with this one. In fact, I feel like this game in particular offers more replayability compared to the previous two games because of its sandbox-like elements (There isn't an actual ending). That and the achievement of getting 1,000 units being a thing. Now, it isn't perfect, but it is by no means a bad game. In fact, with some additional fixes and patches implemented, it could be an even more impressive game to play.
As for those who have complained about the gameplay, I will have to just say that you just might be doing it wrong. The most common thing I hear is that "infantry is useless". I can assure you that you are not using them correctly, because infantry can be quite formidable when used properly. Anti-tank infantry are some of the most vindictive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s I've come across (particularly the Russian ATR teams) that can ruin your tank force if you aren't careful or let them get too close. Assault infantry can soak up a lot of damage and can dish out just as much in return, and MG teams can suppress enemy infantry, which is something very few tanks can do (current exception being the A9 Cruiser Mk.I). Light vehicles have different purposes, be it anti-aircraft duties or reconnaissance, and tanks and tank destroyers are quite usefull for certain situations. Also, a tip for those who are failing to use infantry to their fullest potential would be to use cover such as buildings, trenches, and emplacements to enhance effectiveness and their chances of survival.
My only complaint is with the Barbed wire and tank traps. I have over 15 hedgehogs in my inventory and the most you can put down is usually eight altogether. With that said, I'd like to see if the devs would implement a limit on how many mines and obstacles you can have. Otherwise I'll be staring at my screen contemplating why I have over 200 AT mines that I can't even place down. (Exaggeration is fun)
Overall, I enjoy this game a lot. It might not be for everyone, but it is still a game that many will enjoy playing if they give it some time. It's not going to be like Men of War or Company of heroes, but in the end the payoff is worth it in my book.
