═══════════════════════════════════
OVERVIEW
In Crossbow Warrior- The Legend of William Tell, you take on the role of folk hero William Tell to rescue his kidnapped son from an enemy general. Gameplay consists of mainly sidecrolling platforming although in certain levels the view changes. Defeat enemies with your crossbow or save your ammo and instead jump on top of them. Collectibles exist in every level for achievement hunters along with a hidden apple for you to shoot with your crossbow. A few minor glitches exist, although gameplay is very smooth. Something not mentioned in the tutorial was that jumping from a crouch launches you higher which is needed to clear some obstacles.
═══════════════════════════════════
PROS & CONS
Pros:
Cartoony graphics suit the humor in this game
Some levels are challenging, and there are no checkpoints in a level!
"Expert" time cutoffs for speedrunners and replayability
Cons:
In the city escape level, possible to get glitched under the level, forcing a restart
Jumping is awkward and hard to control sometimes
Enemies have inconsistent hitboxes when you try to jump on them
═══════════════════════════════════
SUMMARY & FINAL RATING
This is a fun, lighthearted, although challenging platformer where you get to play as the legendary folk hero William Tell. Great buy for all ages!

Dreamscapes 2 tries to venture into the hidden object game territory, but at its core it is still a casual point ‘n’ click. The story is a direct sequel, but with shorter dreams of somewhat wavering quality.
Shaman Games likes to create games that look and feel like hidden object games, but are actually lightweight point ‘n’ clicks. Dreamscapes 2: Nightmare’s Heir is a rare exception: it retains most of the developer’s usual clever puzzle design, but this time there is a larger focus on item gathering, and there are even a few traditional hidden objects scenes.
The story brings us back to Laura (the damsel in distress of the first game), who, despite her new-found superpowers, is only present as a supporting character; it is up to the new protagonist to save her husband. His dreams are probably more mundane than Laura’s were, but there are many of them, so even the duller ones quickly give way to the better segments.
Still, it becomes obvious fairly early that despite their number, the new dreams don’t last long. This naturally results in a very short game (about half of an afternoon long), even by casual game standards.

The voice acting, graphics, game play, and story are about par for the genre (in the main game, anyway).  Nothing really stands out either way.  The bonus chapter, though, is of far less quality than the main game (it's only about a half an hour of play, so it's not a big thing).  There, the story really turns dumb and the game play becomes trivial.  Also, the developers seem to have neglected their English translations more.  There's a lot of "something must be applied" flying around there.  Also, at one point, a character lies on the floor with an implication of being dead.  The text reads something about being deafened.  Yet, the character is revived by something trivial (with an odd name).  In the main game, the only real translation difficulties I noticed was the use of the term "balloon" for tank (twice, I believe).  My only real complaint with the whole game is the bugs ("Beholders") that we're supposed to find.  If you finish taking everything out of an object without first getting that bug, the object will close and you're SOL:  can't re-open the container, no saves, no checkpoint.  Ditto if you finish a dreamscape area.
I got a total of 3.8 hours of acceptable play out of the game.  By my dollar an hour metric, at it's current list price of about $7, it's a bit overpriced.  Look for it on sale for less than $4 and that would be better.

NOTE: I did not play 400+ hours of this game, it's a Steam bug that multiplied my playtime. I inquired about it but got not response from support.
INTRODUCTION:
Wei Shen a police officer trained in the USA, now working with the Hong Kong Police Department has been sent on a dangerous mission. To infiltrate and gather information on one of the largest and most dangerous Triad Organization in Hong Kong. Will he break under pressure or will he do his duty as one of Hong Kong's finest?
PROS:
+ Nice Graphics: -I like the visuals but you can clearly tell it was developed with consoles in mind. The only redeeming factor on this area is that a free high-texture DLC pack is available for download. The world is adequately populated by NPCs though at times some parts of the City does look empty. It has a day and night system as well as a weather system which adds to the game's atmosphere.
+ Expansive Map: -Though not geographically accurate to the real Hong Kong, the game still provides a massive Island to explore, populated by a number of NPC citizens as well as a number of drivable vehicles. Driving and exploration on this fictional representation of Hong Kong is very fun and oddly calming.
+ Interesting Combat: -The combat focuses primarily on punching people using street style Kung Fu martial arts, taking inspiration on the Batman Arkham games. Extremely violent and extremely satisfying in my opinion. This is further amplified by the fact that wearing different combination of clothing has benefits to your over all performance in hand-to-hand combat.
CONS:
- Very POOR Optimization: -As I said, this game was developed clearly with consoles in mind. Unexplained crashes, errors and FPS drops occur more than I would like. Not game breaking but It can be annoying and disruptive of the otherwise fluid gameplay.
- Story: -Though I found it interesting and fun, it's still rather predictable and rather cliche. Even going so far as to have one (or several), "The Godfather" moments. My primary complaint is that there is only one ending to this game and your choices never really affects the ending which makes both "Triad & Police points" a bit useless outside of the combat skill tree.
- Side Quest: -The game has a very good concept of side quest, offering both Police and Triad missions but they clearly weren't either finished or polished. I personally would have liked the "Drug Bust" missions to include proper detective work rather than have the game spoon feed who I should arrest.
CONCLUSION:
PRETTY GOOD. Notwithstanding the fact it's "like GTA", Sleeping Dogs is unique in it's own sense. The story has just the right feel to keep you interested and the gameplay offers enough action to keep you satisfied. Though it's current full price is good, I'd wait for a sale.
If you want a break from the fun and mindless violence of GTA, Sleeping Dogs can provide a fresh story based alternative.

Welcome to Paradise island, the island where you can run over almost everything, jump over everything else, and crash with little to no consequences. Burnout Paradise is an Open World racing game developed by Criterion Games and released in 2009.
You start the game with a quick introduction to Paradise Island, after your introduction you try to accumulate “marks on your licenses” to progress to the next licenses and unlock new vehicles.
You earn Marks on your license by completing the various challenges, there is always a challenge at every intersection.... leaving you plenty of races, bumper cars, stunt drives, and chases to keep people entertained.
The primary vehicles you'll play as are Cars, but they do have some motorcycles in the game and some “toy vehicles”. In general this has a lot of vehicles which are very much wasted on me, because I just crash into the other vehicles because I'm childish and want to play bumper cars.
There are three car “classes”, and different stats with each car. Stunt class cars will get you boosts by preforming tricks, Aggression class cars get you boosts by being a jerk (I really like playing Aggression cars and cackling evilly as I push an NPC into the wall), and lastly Speed class cars, which you fill by near misses, upon filling the boost you can preform “burnouts” which let you boost after your boost meter runs out, so in a way you could just keep boosting... as long as you don't crash in between boosts.
Like most car games, there are also specific stats on the various vehicles, some cars have high Speed, others have high boost, and still others have high Strength. Speed = you go faster. Boost = you have more boost you can charge up. Strength = your car can take a bigger beating from the competition.
There are no steam achievements for this game, at this time. However there are plenty of in-game unlockables that you can obtain. It's important to note someday there might be steam achievements, because on the Xbox there are 60 achievements on the core game, + 10 with the various DLC expansions.
Burnout Paradise is priced at $19.99, you can easily spend an hour for every dollar spent playing this game, there's a lot to do. That is the theme of Open world games. As I commonly do in my reviews, I suggest you wait for a sale to purchase this game, if you purchase it... I got my copy of the game on a Humblebundle.
There are a number of reviews out there on this game saying that this game has been falsely advertised. I cannot speak from experience because I never played this game anywhere else. You're only getting the core game with the Purchase of “Burnout Paradise: The Ultimate Box”, in other words if you look up DLC for this game, all of that is unavailable. You cannot even purchase the DLC on steam. For die-hard-Burnout Paradise fans, that's a tough knock. So it's worth noting that you're not getting “the Ultimate Box”, you're just getting the core game.
To quickly recap: Story – not really a selling point. Gameplay – fun, even if you're not very big on car and/or racing games. Very forgiving when you crash early in the game. Achievements – Nonexistent. Price – Fair, I suggest waiting for a sale. Remember – you're only getting the core game.
All in all, this is a fun car game which can be appreciated regardless of how obsessed (or couldn't care less) about cars. I recommend this game for people who enjoy racing games, or want to give a driving game a shot, keep in mind the open world aspect is a big appeal to certain gamers rather then others. (Open world is my favorite)
As always, thanks for reading my review.

Alright, lets get this over with.
First of all, I love this game, I think that it can bring lots of fun and a ton of hours of FPS gameplay. Its moddability is awsome and is what drives me to this game. I like and play this game like I would any other FPS and just unleash hell onto any poor raiders in my sights. Mindlessly tearing apart enemys like tissue paper.
But as a storybased RPG, it fails completely.
The "RPG" part of the game is a joke in my opinion. A shell of its former self when compared to previous fallout titles.
The first big mistake Bethesda made when creating the game is to give a voice to your "created character", ripping away of any chance to make your character unique, you are forced with an avenge your family story that is boring and downright not worth it. Another big problem with the game is the horrible dialouge options, almost (if not all) of the options you are given is 1. Sarcastic 2. Persuasion 3. positive remark 4. negative remark. In older games, you can choose exactly what you want to say and even have your perks and skills matter in some dialouge options and could completly change the side-story (and sometimes the main-quests) completly.
Then they ruin the perk and skill system, when in previous games where you can actually suck in one area (like using energy weapons) and be the master of something else (like using explosives). Now your "perk" system is filled with slight tweaks to make you slightly better in one very specific aspect that will only come in handy in one or two situations in the entire game. You cannot suck in one aspect or another, you can use any weapon without fail, you can mod any weapon no matter how much you use it or neglect it. Dumb.
Another failed part is the settlement system. Don't get me wrong the feeling of building what is the equivalent of a small town or fort to call your own is amazing in of itself, its when it has absolutly no effect on the wasteland or characters itself is the problem here. There is no reason to build settlements, absolutly none, their is no downsides to creating settlements just as their is no positive benefits. Unless you want to create your own town/house/fort to dump all of your stuff in there is no true benefit that is worthwhile.
And, the worst of all, the quests. While in previous fallout games where side quests and things you say actually matter, and can have unchangable events happen, here it is completly stripped away and remade into this "go here, kill enemies, get paid" system. There is no wrong answers or choices in this game, its all super happy funtime land where you have no choice but to obey the braindead sidequests for absolutly no reason but to shoot things.
The only reason I play this game as much as I do is the fact that modding can help the game soooo much. But the fact that I had to download sooooo many mods (and I mean a LOT) in order to get this game feeling close to a proper fallout game is a negative in itself. It goes to show how much Bethesda is willing to assume that the Modding community will fix the game shows how lax and lazy Bethesda is getting with their RPG games as of late.
I rate this game a 6/10 if you play it as a brainless shooter with light RPG elements. But as a fallout game, with all of the "perks" and the sorry excuse of side quests, I rate this game as a 3/10. It could have been the best fallout title to date if only Bethesda realized that the people who play the fallout games are not a bunch of 8 year olds that need their hands held through every moment.
If you want a good Fallout game, buy Fallout: New Vegas, or Fallout 1 and 2. If you want to be treated like a little kid and have copy and paste side quests and have your hand held through every situation with no possiblity of bad things happening, buy Fallout 4.
Do you know what we need? Obsidian to create a new fallout game with the RPG aspects, DLC, and stories of Fallout New Vegas with the gunplay and crafting system of Fallout 4. THAT would be lightyears ahead of this failed attempt of a game.

Why do I love this game?
Great graphics, everything is well detailed, you can zoom in to get close to the action.
Now this is just like when you were a kid with your toy soldiers, tanks and jeeps etc., but X100!
If you don't take the road when you move your troops to your desired point, they crash through fences, mow down trees, the damage is very detailed!
The battlefield's are about 1kmX1km, and you can pan around the landscape to plan your attack, but it will not show you where all the enemies are.
In the beginning (where I still am), the first level was fairly challenging, and I battled towards the goal as a crow flies. Yay, I won, but my battle report was poor and lower rewards etc.
Try the first round again to kill ALL enemies was a completely different story,  It just gets harder and harder the more you try to fully complete a round.
There are several seperate battles on the map.  Inbetween some of these battles, you receive exp. points that you can spend immediately on reserve troops and tanks etc. and bring them into the battle. How cool is that?
There is a 'watch replay' button, but I haven't used it yet. Sweet!
Very intricate, detailed, in-depth, the sound is great, damage is great and stays that way.
Would you like to hunker in a bunker? Your soldiers can build a trench anywhere you like, and you can also build up defences around tanks in areas you want to defend.
Game is FUN to play!
Update after 50 hrs: Before going into battle, there is so much military to choose from.
In battle you use your selected units for certain situations, don't send your machine gunners to a gun turret!
From the detailed characteristics of soldiers, to the dust on the road...
Incredible game, just incredible.
Super replayable, even if I'm victorious I may replay the same battle and try it completely different.
I hate to cut this so short, but I would like to play this game now. Cheers!

I wanted to be generous.  I know that the HOG industry relies on shovelware and hasty localizations.  I tried to be forgiving. But just too many things are wrong with Dreamscapes: Nightmare's Heir.
First, the game is very short.  I completed the whole thing, including the Bonus Chapter, in under two hours.
The voice acting is subpar, and some of the translations are rather shaky.  The typical supernatural antagonist is particularly sketchy -- his goals and motivations (other than general maliciousness) change every time he monologues.
The ending, and the second ending, after the Bonus Chapter, are both abrupt and unsatisfying.
The HO scenes and puzzles are all very easy, with one possible exception, if you've never encountered the Eight Queens problem before.  At least one HO scene in the Bonus Chapter, however, commits the cardinal sin of including multiple objects that satisfy the target description, and demanding that you find the right one.
The video sequences, in fairness, were up to the standard for the genre, and the music was mostly good, with the exception of one ear-grating synth chorus effect.
A few flaws are always forgiveable in this genre, but here, there are just too many.  I cannot recommend.

I discovered this VN series back in 2013, and it took my breath away when I was done, so much that I backed the Kickstarter for western localisation. Basically this is a rather long prolouge to Muv Luv Alternative, and it lays the groundwork for it. Overall this VN might feel a bit mediocre and chlichéd, but that is the way it is supposed to feel. Standalone Muv Luv might be a bit unfullfilling, but it was supposed to be released with Alternative which is basically the third part of the story, so think of it as Part 1 and 2 of a trilogy. It's also important to read EXTRA before UNLIMITED since EXTRA is basically the groundwork for the whole series.
The characters are quite stereotypical, exaggerated to make it as cliché as possible. The humor is usually silly and filled with references to pre-2000 anime and gaming. The main character Takeru can be a bit annoying at times, but he is mostly quite likeable when it counts, he learns as story progresses and you can tell by the end how much he has changed. Most of the EXTRA ARC is based around mindless sillyness and High School shenanigans. The UNLIMITED arc on the other hand is where things go all Sci-fi on you and make it a tad more serious. Once you're done with this VN and get into the third and final arc ALTERNATIVE later this year, they you'll understand the fruits of this VN.
All in all this is like whatching a "never ending" episode of anime and not like a video game so bear that in mind, it all story and player interaction is kept to a minimun
I highly recommend this VN series for those who like anime, scifi and robots.

Full Disclosure: I backed the Kickstarter for Muv-Luv to the tune of $300, thus I do hold a bit of bias if only for the sake of justifying my puchase
Muv-Luv is an interesting visual novel conceptually, a Sci-Fi trilogy that at the time of its original release was sold simply as a romantic comedy. This is a remake of sorts, it runs on a new engine, some voice work was redone, there's support for widescreen and the biggest change of all is the fact that the plot twist is now shown upfront most likely due to it being a fairly old title that has had plenty of time for said twist to be considered less integral.
This particular iteration consists of Extra and Unlimited, with the third part Alternatvie being a more linear experience but just as long if not longer than both previous parts combined. Extra is the first part, taking place in a traditional school setting. It's a romantic comedy wherein the protagonist, Shirogane Takeru must choose between five different girls, the main two love interests being Mitsurugi Meiya, the mysterious heir to a large financial conglomorate whom Takeru finds in his bed one fateful morning and Kagami Sumika, Takeru's long-time childhood friend who's beginning to desire their relationship to be something more. Your route in Extra is determined by various choices you make over the course of the game, one of the typical choices involving which girl's lunch you choose to eat. It's recommended that you go through the routes of both main heroines before entering Unlimited.
Unlimited shifts both in tone and setting, while still retaining the root of Extra, it's much more serious in comparison taking place in an alternate world where Kagami Sumika doesn't exist and an alien threat referred to as the BETA have ravaged the world, leaving only one billion humans left on Earth. This part acts mainly as a setup to the world of Unlimited, Takeru's growth as a person and to show the differences between the worlds besides the painfully obvious. The routes in this part are much easier to get, as it's left down to about three divisive choices around the end, and five of the six possible character endings have both a Normal and Good variant. Unlimited primarily acts as build up to the finale, Alternative however it still acts self-contained as does Extra so you don't have to progress down the line if you don't want to.
All in all I'd recommend picking this up if you're a fan of VNs and mecha, it's not everyone's thing but is fairly unique in its concept and execution and I certainly enjoyed it more than I expected to.

In the interest of full disclosure, I’d like to begin by saying that I backed
during its Kickstarter campaign. I’ve also read
and its sequel,
prior to reading the official Steam release, so my hours played (51 hours as of this writing) don’t accurately reflect the amount of time I’ve actually spent reading this series. Regardless of my status as a Kickstarter backer, however, I don’t intend to pull any punches in my review.
For those who are unfamiliar with this title, Muv-Luv is actually comprised of two visual novels:
and its sequel
. Together, they comprise part one and two of a trilogy, concluded in their sequel,
.
Taken on its own,
—the first installment in the trilogy—is an unremarkable school life comedy mired in well-worn harem anime/manga tropes and stock character types (the childhood friend and the mysterious transfer student, to name two). True to the conventions of the harem genre, a clueless and insensitive male protagonist finds himself surrounded by five young women who pine over him in spite of his complete obliviousness to their thinly veiled romantic advances. Aside from a few amusing moments that arise from the absurdity of the situations therein, the most polite way to describe
would be that it is forgettable. One of its most egregious issues lies in the overlong, circuitous writing style on display in particular sections, where the story grinds to a halt in service of back and forth exchanges that have no significant impact on the narrative. This could have been greatly improved by simply removing “problem” scenes or dialogue sections wholesale. All that being said, you’d be doing yourself a huge disservice by skipping directly to
without at least playing through Sumika and Meiya’s routes (more on this in a moment).
In spite of
’s failings, however,
it more than makes up for most of them in its direct sequel,
. Without giving too much away,
—and its sequel,
(not yet released as of this writing)—are extremely different in genre, tone, and overall themes to their predecessor,
.* This shift is crucial to understanding how
succeeds in many areas where
fell short. Its greatest triumph arguably lies in the way it recontextualizes everything the reader knows about
’s world, while anchoring it to the characterization of its female leads in ways that are by turns expected and surprising. Now, you may be wondering: if
is so much better than its predecessor, why bother with
at all? The answer is simple: you'll miss out on valuable plot and character information if you decide to skip it; I strongly recommend reading through at least Sumika and Meiya’s routes in
before diving into
.
Unfortunately, however, some serious issues from
persist, including its heavy-handed harem antics and thoroughly unlikable protagonist. While not quite as pronounced as they were in
, they nonetheless detract from
's much more interesting story (the same holds true for its sequel,
).
If you have the patience for a slow-burn story with a great payoff and are willing to forgive
overbearing genre idiosyncrasies, I would strongly recommend
. Don’t make the mistake of skipping
, though; it will pay dividends if you stick with it, greatly enriching your understanding of
’s characters.

Every sequel tries to do one of two things: either iterates the same formula and perfects it by being bigger and better, or the sequel evolves enough to become a completely new experience. This formula is the same with movies, as it is with games. Generally speaking, both publishers and developers want to create a better sequel than the previous one as much as it is financially viable. Fallout 4 however shows no such interest at all: it is one of the rarest sequels I’ve experienced so far that introduces so few and tiny improvements to its design. Fallout 4 suffers from the lack of ambition and focus from its developers – there is no courage to make a quantum leap forward in its design while at the same time relies too much on the Bethesda’s way of crafting open-world games that they’ve perfected, and is slowly becoming stale and obsolete. New open-world games are showing up that are wiling to experiment and give something unique to the player, while Bethesda keeps making the same games since Oblivion, only with very minor upgrades.
PROS:
+ Shooting mechanic is improved significantly
+ Fairly-well implemented opponent AI
+ Beefy customization and upgrade system for weapons and armors
+ For an ageing engine, Fallout 4 still manages to look gorgeous both visually and artistically
+ Music is above average, and sound effects are great
+ Very good level design
+ Settlement creation and resource management sim are both potent and promising (for those who are interested in it)
+ Easy to modify and apply mods
INDIFFERENT:
o Changes to the leveling system and perks don’t really differ that much from previous Fallout titles, only difference is you can choose from all available perks and you’re not blocked from some perks by fulfilling certain experience requirements: You don’t need at least Barter 50% and Speech 50% to get a Negotiator perk as was the case in previous Fallout titles, you just have to have high enough basic ability and enough experience points. This is a two-edged sword, since you have many perks to choose from the start, but all of them feel weakened and severely hampered.
o Voice acting is average: It’s held back by the low quality writing. Better than Fallout 3, worse than Fallout New Vegas.
CONS:
- Main quests, faction and side quests are significantly worse and shallower than in any previous Bethesda games
- Dialogue’s quality (or the lack of it) has not changed from Bethesda’s previous titles in the slightest
- New dialogue wheel severely limits player’s options and breaks immersion
- Exclusion of skills, coupled with bad dialogue wheel destroys role-playing part of the game
- Game is fraught with bugs, and glitches
- While the companions have been improved since Skyrim, they are still one-dimensional and represent a major setback from what Fallout New Vegas offered
- Every ending is basically the same, as was with Mass Effect 3
- Barebones mechanical systems make F4 less challenging
- Greatly overpriced and underwhelming paid mods on offer in Creations Club: Imagine if you could get sizeable expansions for F4 years after its release that are on par or better than Far Harbor with brand new texture work, or having new companions that are more fleshed out and complex than the vanilla game has to offer, and custom-voiced too. Creation Club had a chance to introduce paid mods in a proper way, but it was done with a minimum effort and to the detriment of the entire modding community. Right now there are a couple of texture reskins for the pip-boy and power armor, a few new armors based from other Bethesda franchises, one dull-looking furniture set, and a few new weapons (inspired by other Bethesda games again), and not only do they look entirely unimpressive and unappealing, they are overpriced compared to what they offer. A single power armor reskin costs around 5$, while entire story DLC in other games costs that much, with hours of new content. As a DLC, Creation Club costs as much money you put into it, while offering back very little, which makes it the second priciest DLC on Steam, right after the ridiculous costume DLCs Dead Or Alive 5 offers.
In conclusion, Fallout 4 is a letdown in being the same game as previous cookie-cutter Bethesda open world games. It offers so little of new, and what is here, has been degraded significantly. I know that Bethesda will never create old school Fallout games like the first two and New Vegas were, but I was hoping there would at least be more effort put into F4. It’s not the worst entry in the Fallout series (that crown of shame still belongs to Brotherhood of Steel for consoles) but it is too stale. Now that they have made more money from F4 than ever before, they have the capability to create the next fallout game that is truly going to excel, because for many gamers what’s on offer here simply doesn’t cut it anymore.
Fun Fact #1: Main antagonists in F4 have been neatly suggested for the first time in Fallout 3, in the side quest called “The Replicated Man”
Fun Fact #2: Emil Pagliarulo, main designer of Fallout 4, started his carries working on a sneaking classic: Thief II The Metal Age.

This game is the most fun racing game outside of Mario Kart (the series in general) that I've ever played.  I played this years ago for quite a bit of time on the PS3, and then now it's even better on the PC.
* Most of the "vehicle combat games" don't really do it for me because they wind up distracting from the racing and just get crazy in terms of all the weapons around your screen.  This game solves that by making "combat" (insofar as it exists) totally about running others off the road.  Very fun.
* Most games that have racing in an open city have some sort of checkpoints you have to hit, but this one just has a start and and end point, and you can use any shortcuts if you know them.
* Most games with a map of this complexity wind up being hard to navigate around, and I have to practice a given race a lot of times before I learn an optimal route.  Here it gives you a great minimap and lets you pause to look at another map to see what you're doing.  It also gives you great left and right turn signal blinkers that tell you the way to turn coming up for the shortest path the game can currently tell you to get to the finish line (minus any shortcuts, of course).  Really, really good.
* Most games with a bunch of cars wind up having most of them feeling pretty crappy.  There are a few that don't feel good to drive here, but mostly they feel great and then just get better and better.
* There's a lot to unlock, and a solid feeling of progress.
* There's a completely separate motorcycle progression that feels just as fun (and is a bit different), even though it's smaller than the main cars progression.
* This really is a sandbox, and the city is impressively detailed in an amount of space that feels large but never empty.  They really nailed the perfect size here.
Recommended at full price!

Well, this is long overdue, I know, but ti's still worth writing, so here goes: My Burnout Paradise Review!
This is, in essence, a very simple game. You're presented with a decently sized open world, a mid-tier car, and a goal: get your full licence. Beyond this, the game gets very subjective, so I'll stick to the pros and cons.
PROS:
-Tight, responsive controls (though best with a controller, I used an Xbox 360 controller for my testing)
-Wide variety of cars, all of them with their own unique style and handling
-Good open world, it's certainly not the biggest or or most detailed you've ever seen, but it could be a lot worse
-A variety of challenges and new races to try your hand at
CONS:
-Terrible soundtrack! I know what you're thinking: "Who cares, it's just a soundtrack!" Well, when you're going at 200 MpH along the highway, scenery whizzing by you, all your focus on not totally destroying your car, music is arguably the most important part of making that experience incredible. The soundtrack is boring, often times hilariously so, and does the game a huge disservice. Trust me, just use your phone for music.
-Lack of true car customization. Now, I know this isn't The Crew, but it'd be nice if I could fine tune my cars specs, not just the paint job.
So there you have it, sort of. My summary: It's a fantastic open world racing game with some truly awesome cars, scenes, and races. Terrible soundtrack, but, overall, still a phenomenal game.

Before I start, I would like to say that Starbound is one of the BEST games I have ever played.
Pros:
-The graphics are my favourite- pixelated but detailed. The avatars look sweet, the monsters cute but scary and the backgrounds... amazing.
-Storyline that looks set to be pretty darn sweet and overarching.
-Epic weapons for all types of fighters- melee, tank, speed, ranged, rocket launchers!
-The soundtrack is beautiful.
-Minibooks (lore) that you can find in NPC villages and dungeons that are interesting and intertwined.
-NPC AI is pretty good.
-Except for when they get stuck in the ground lol
-Active dev blog
-7 different races
-Upgradable spaceship
-Sandbox is seamless and well-intergrated into the gameplay
-Spaceship pets are adorable
-You can have tennents and get stuff from them
-Microdungeons
-You can be a savage plant-person that elongates their 'S's
Floran ssssstab!
-^best bit of the game right there
Cons:
-Now, I know this game IS in early access and features are bound to disappear and reappear without much notice but what was one of the defining features of the game, and the thing that made it stand out from others in its genre was that monsters didn't do damage on contact. They had specialized moves that hurt you if you touched them, for example you could stand in front of a monster and then it would swipe upwards, damaging you. But this is now gone, replaced with the whole 'damage on contact' as WELL as the melee and ranged attacks. The damage-on-attack thing never really made sense with me, and the specialized attacks were great and made the more fun to RP in.
-AI is pretty good... but, uh, they get stuck in holes sometimes and just keep walking. It's kinda funny (and I'm glad that the sideways NPC glitch is fixed)
-Fullscreen doesn't work very well. If I click the expand button on the game window, it expands up to my top hotbar. No further. If I want true fullscreen, I have to select it in Options, and that means I can't switch to other windows whilst in that mode. Since the stupid El Capitan update, I can't use Steam Community in-game so if I want to talk with someone whilst playing I have to have it in small-windowed mode since the expand button now just crashes the game.
-Loading time. 5 minutes at best.
Overall, Starbound is an amazingly fun game and I highly recommend it. I love it so much, it's the most played game and I have over 100 hours- and that's since July last year, on top of an immense homework load, limited screen time and frequent holidays.

As far as LEGO games go, this game is definitely... well, a LEGO game.
What I mean by this is that if you have ever played a LEGO game in your life then you already know everything there is to know mechanically about this game. In my experience, LEGO games are not so much about ground breaking, innovative gameplay; but rather, immensely enjoyable fun for the whole family that comes in all kinds of assorted flavors. Personally, I find the Star Wars flavor to be the best out of all of them, but for the same reason that a die-hard Harry Potter fan would tell you that the Harry Potter LEGO Games are the best.
On a more specific note for this title, if you've seen the LEGO Movie then don't expect anything new from the game; of all the LEGO titles I've played in my life, this one definitely feels the laziest. Muv-luv is a collection of visual novels, with the series overall regarded as a top-tier entry in the genre. The two games out right now are Extra and Unlimited. The order of the series is Extra -> Unlimited -> Alternative, and it is highly recommended you play them in order. I jumped into these games without knowing much of anything about then because I heard a lot critical acclaim for the series, and I don't regret my decision.
Extra is considered the least intriguing of the group, and I would have to agree. It’s a fairly time SOL game. The kind where the extremely average, nearly faceless lead character somehow amasses a handful of girls who are eager to aim right for his groin with the precious of a heat-seeking missiles. It features a lot of slapstick comedy (most of it based on tried-and-true genre clichés, some of it actually funny). It took me a while to warm up since it wasn’t all that interesting (no overarching plot), but in the end I enjoyed the characters and the various scenarios their personalities brought about.
Unlimited is where the series starts to reveal its true colors. Starting a short while before the conclusion of Extra, Takeru awakes in his bed one morning to find the world outside a devastated wreck. Although he initially believes it to be a dream, he is soon confronted with the fact that he has somehow ended up in a parallel world where humanity has been at war with aliens since the 60s. Seeing the ways in which the world and the characters that had become so familiar during Extra have diverged due to this new history is one of my favorite things about Unlimited.
The game comes with the option to play either entry whenever, although again if you're a newcomer you'll want to go in order. There are a ton of save spots, always nice when a game features a lot of choices, and I like that the game instantly resumes from where ever I felt off when I reopen it. That a pretty neat feature I've never come across before.
The spritework is interesting as well. Characters move into the foreground and background accordingly, providing some depth and additional animation to scenes. There aren’t a ton of CGs, and some see a fair amount of re-use. Some silly scenes see the inclusion of chibi drawings that look like they’re drawn with crayon. I have noticed sometimes the characters seem to lag or freeze when they’re in the middle of changing poses or facial expressions, and while it doesn’t happen often it is noticeable.
The music is alright. To be honest, while I realize music can add a lot of emotional impact I generally don’t ding games much on that area unless a significant portion of the soundtrack is actually bad. For the most part the music is certainly… there, some of it is even a little catchy, and the tracks chosen match up with the flavor of the scenes they play in, but at this point I haven’t heard anything that blew my socks off.
The series does have a large amount of time investment, and while I wasn’t entirely sold during the first few hours with Extra I can now see places where the hinted at the series’ true nature. I grew to really enjoy the characters, and so far Unlimited has me enthralled.
I'll update this review with more thoughts as I finish the games. Maybe.

(This review contains minor spoilers for Muv-Luv Extra/Muv-Luv Unlimited/Muv-Luv Alternative; however, it shouldn’t detract from the overall enjoyment of reading the Muv-Luv franchise)
This review covers Muv-Luv Extra/Muv-Luv Unlimited and Muv-Luv Alternative.
What is Muv-Luv Extra/Unlimited/Alternative?
__________
Muv-Luv is a Visual Novel franchise that is divided into 3 parts, namely (Part 1) Extra, (Part 2) Unlimited, and (Part 3) Alternative with each subsequent part following on the previous one.
Extra starts off as a generic romcom story without much depth. The main character Shirogane Takeru tries to gain affection from a variety heroines to unlock each heroine’s respective ending while comedy ensues. However, events take a much darker turn during Unlimited and Alternative where the peaceful lives of everyone turns into a bloodbath and fight for survival.
The Muv-Luv franchise gets the majority of its praise from Alternative which is considered a masterpiece from several people among the anime community (myself included). The unfortunate part is that, except for being a slightly above average romcom Extra doesn't have much depth and just can't compare to its sequel (Alternative); however, it still plays a vital part in building the foundation of the Muv-Luv franchise and thus shouldn’t be skipped.
I do however recommend to rather wait for Muv-Luv Alternative to release before playing Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited.

Story:
__________
If I were asked to describe the story of the Muv-Luv franchise in one sentence, it would be the following:
“The Muv-Luv franchise tells the story of Shirogane Takeru and his quest to find meaning to his existence and the role he can play in shaping everyone's lives around him.” This holds true to all 3 parts in the Muv-Luv franchise, albeit in vastly different ways.
During the first part Muv-Luv is a casual romcom and Takeru has to solve the problems from each heroine in Muv-Luv while also romancing them to unlock each heroine’s ending.
During Unlimited and Alternative Takeru finds himself in an alternative timeline from his own. Instead of facing trivial problems like training for a lacrosse match from his initial timeline he is caught up in a war with aliens called BETA to determine the fate of humanity. It tells the epic story of how Takeru faces hardships and how he tries to overcome each obstacle that is thrown his way, while still maintaining his sanity.
Characters:
__________
Q: What defines a perfect character?
A: An imperfect character.
Muv-Luv contains a large cast of characters who all get a fair amount of screen time, however the one similarity all of them share is the fact that none of them are perfect.
During Muv-Luv Extra the opinion you will initially have regarding the characters will be that most of them are without any glaringly obvious flaws and that they are perfect. As you continue with Unlimited and Alternative these specific characters that you might have idolized will crush your expectations of them when you realize that they are also merely “human” and that they can also only deal with so much before finally breaking.
The whole cast of Muv-Luv remind me of a form of art called Kintsugi. Kintsugi (金継ぎ) means “to repair with gold”. It is the process in which a broken pot or bowl would be pieced together with gold or silver to form something stronger and more beautiful than before it was broken. Each character in Muv-Luv has flaws, but it’s these flaws along with their progression and growth that make them unique and makes you feel attachment towards them.
Gameplay:
__________
Muv-Luv is a Visual Novel and as the word suggests it is a novel with visuals and sounds. It doesn’t contain any gameplay elements and the only real interaction between the reader and the game is making choices during dialogue and seeing the outcome of said choices.
If you are looking for a game with gameplay, then skip this it’s probably not for you. However, if you don’t mind treating it as a book with sound and visuals then you might find yourself pleasantly surprised.
Sound & Art:
__________
Seeing as Muv-Luv is a Visual Novel the sound and art play a great role in influencing how the reader perceives the characters as well as the world itself.
Muv-Luv’s graphics, sprites and CG no longer hold up to more modern Visual Novels; however, they fulfill the task that they set out to do which is delivering an immersive experience.
Muv-Luv has excellent music, sound and voice acting and despite it being almost 3 years since I originally read Muv-Luv (Fan translation) I still remember what each character sounds like as well as most songs from the soundtrack.
Overall thoughts:
___________
Muv-Luv is a visual novel and should be treated as such. It contains virtually no gameplay elements. The story of Muv-Luv Extra starts slow and quite generic; however, after you reach Unlimited it becomes a lot more interesting and the overall pace of the Visual Novel picks up and continues to do so until it finally reaches its climax delivering a truly epic experience.
Who is it for?
__________
Patient people who want to read an exceptional story, and are willing to sit through a few hours of mediocrity to achieve it.

From what I've played of the new version, both the actual text and the image translations (signs/banners/in-game images that originally were not readable in English) that were translated to English vastly improve the experience of reading the first part of the Visual Novel, Muv-Luv Extra. Dialgue flows much better and many of the characters' personality that were less compelling when originally reading the visual novel due to the difficulty in conveying their sense of humor/intention with the fan translation are all much better, to the point that first-time readers are much more likely to enjoy the experience of reading all of the routes in Extra as opposed to just Sumika and Meiya (the two main heroines) routes like how most read it originally. What most people considered a chore to work through originally to get to why most find the Muv-Luv series worth the title of "The Most Highly-acclaimed Visual Novel Series of All Time" is now a much more enjoyable slice-of-life read that is much easier to recommend.
Full of references to the entertainment present when it was originally released, with a new translation full of material that can be enjoyed by newer readers, the first installment of the Muv-Luv trilogy is much better thanks entirely to the team behind the translation and Kickstarter. Although older fans will be dissapointed by the lack of features that have been absent in visual novels by the original develops for some time now, the experience of reading the first installments of the Muv-Luv trilogy is far better off with the work put in by the English localization team, who have every step of the way tried to make the experience of bringing Muv-Luv to the west as accomadating as possible and have communicated to the best of their ability with the community in numerous ways both as a part of their job, and as fans of Muv-Luv.

Planetary Annihilation is a large-scale rts where a bunch of ancient giant robots awaken to duke it out planet to planet over the abandoned suns of the galaxy. It's an interesting concept of 3d battlefields incorporating land, air, sea and space units of all types. Unfortunately the game is let down by a lack of any real story or structured progression through the game, a great complexity of mechanics that belie a very shallow depth of strategy, poor ai and some ui and optimization issues.
This game is plagued by a number of poor design issues. The planets themselves make awkward maps; although your tiny units might see the battlefield as relatively flat, the scale of the players attention (and camera angles) compared to the size of the planet means you will frequently find yourself zoomed either to far in or too far out. Simply navigating a spherical map presents plenty of challenges. However, it's part of the draw of the game, and could have been presented in such a way as to gradually familiarize the player with the mechanics; instead you are thrown headfirst into it and left to figure it out on your own, as is the case for much of the game, which lacks a true story or campaign. There is only a token attempt at one which is little more than a number of 1v1's strung together, similar to the campaigns of earlier Battlefield style games. The ai is so smotheringly stupid that the most basic strategies will win handily.
Perhaps these issues could be excused; after all, plenty of great games present only a few mechanics, but have great depth in pvp due to the emergence of many different, well-balanced strategies and possiblities. This is where PA really kills it for me: While there are plenty of units and all sorts of mechanics, there are really only a handful of basic strategies that are effective. Because there are only two resources, metal and power, and the mechanics incentivize the player to produce units on a large scale, the game is essentially about expanding your base and exploiting resources as efficiently as possible. While you could argue that almost all rts's are about that, to me PA just feels so one note. In almost every game I have played or seen played, people simply build a number of identical factories and just pump out one or two basic units... whoever does this the most efficiently will usually steamroller the other. The only significant deviation from this pattern is when one player finds a way to sneakily kill the enemy commander, but even this rarely feels very satisfying. All in all, while the pvp is at least fairly balanced, it's the empty balance of tic-tac-toe; something to pass the time, but not exactly fun.

The single player is not very lenghty but it compensates for that  with variety, offering the possibility of playing with 3 unique and completely different species, meaning specific gameplay mechanics for each of the characters.
As a Marine you have a tipical FPS experience, but with a very high amount of tension and atmosphere that gets to the nerves of those of you with a faint heart, and is no slouch in action as well, as hordes of enemies are lurking around almost every corner.
As a Predator you feel like you are a total badass, with all the arsenal and gizmos we all know and love.
It is especially gratifying to stalk your prey from afar, distract it and then lure it to it's untimely demise.
As the Alien, you have to rely on speed and surprise to ambush your prey. As a totally melee based specie, you need to stick to the shadows and pick your battles carefully, but it is possibly the most gratifying of all the species you can choose from in this game, it relies mostly on skill and less on acessories (by acessories I mean weapons).
It is far from being perfect though, the game suffers from a huge amount of glitches that were never properly patched and fixed by the developer (Rebellion), and if you plan to play this game online versus other people... You are in for a huge dissapointment. The amount of hacking and glitching in this game is fairly high, and the AvP community despite being small, it is one of the worst uneducated, childish and ridiculous group of children you will likely to ever meet. I recommend this game for it's single player mostly, and if you can get a decent group of people to play with you on fair matches, the MP can be a lot of fun, with the modes Species Team Deathmatch ( 3 teams, one alien, one predator and one marine), Mixed Species Team Deathmatch (2 teams, all species allowed in each of them), Predator Hunt (one player is a Predator while all the others are Marines. The Marine who kills the Predator becomes the hunter and therefore has to try and kill the Marines; Highest scoring player as a Predator wins), Infestation (one player is an Alien, all other marines, the Alien player must kill the marines; When a marine dies he then respawns as an alien to try and kill the remaining humans) and Domination (two teams, one alien and one Marine fight over the control of checkpoints in the map).
Also worthy of mention is the co-op, there is a mode in the game called survivor, in which you fight waves of unending Aliens as a Marine with up to four people, and it can be a huge challenge, and it's fairly fun as well.
I recommend this game mostly for it's single player, the three different campaigns are unique, even if they are a little short. MP can be fun, but try to stay away from public servers. The rage, hacking and glitching is usually big on those places.
The Good
-Three different campaigns, and three different perspectives on the same story
-Good visuals and sound, particularly the sound effects
-Lance Henrikssen as Bishop
-Trophy kills
The Bad
-Glitches are abundant on MP
-Hackers are common on public servers
-Most of the AvP community are raging 10 year olds

As of the time of this review, I have logged 455+ hours on Fallout 4.  I've played through all DLC, modded the game a ton, and built and tore down countless settlements.  Simply put, the game is an advance visually for the franchise, and I genuinely looked forward to see what was around the corner next.  But the game is too easy, and the RPG elements have been removed to the point that they are unnoticable now.  You can't really be evil, and you can't really be neutral.  It forces you into being a "good-ish" character, who has to choose to side with a faction.  Frankly, the game could have been so much more, if the story was more original (better thought out), and they truly allowed you to embody a role (type of character) that you choose.  One last criticism....they should have just removed the "romance your NPC followers" option.  They are such a let down, and just seem misplaced.  If you never played this game, should you buy it?  Yes, so long as it's on sale.  But don't expect it to keep you interested to the very end, and don't expect any big moments that make you remember the story.

While I'm sure everyone has their opinion on the story, I want to address something not so popularly noticed, the engine and interface.
The Steam release of this game is 13 years after the original, and the age of this game can be seen well.  1024 x 600 resolution (strangely not the 4:3 of the original), a very busy menu screen, old art style, lack of choosing color of character text, no live2D idle movements, etc. The game, look-wise has far from stood the test of time.
Still, you can't help at least see that Degica tried their best to make the interface work. Text size is larger than the original Japanese text. The interface is skinned using extremely large text to fill up the giant buttons on the menu. There is even an advanced interface to decide how many cores the game should use (why a simple VN should need more than 1 core is beyond me)
If I were to mark down for something, it'll have to be the fact that the text in the game is now center aligned. Because as a reader, you can't tell where the start of the line will appear when you ask for the next line, your reading speed will drop. This is not a problem with the original JP version which is left aligned, so I'm very confused about the change.
All in all, Degica did try their best to make what they could of an outdated engine. It is perfectly fine and usable, but you'll know instantly you're not playing a VN made in 2016, but something from a less modern age.

Traveller's Tales has created another fantastic entry in the LEGO videogame universe.
I have completed the entire game including the collectibles, and I must say, I am impressed. In this game the story adheres to the movie's story rather well, and uses cutscenes from the movie too, which is a nice touch.
The game follows the same formula of platforming with action sequences and linear level designs that is common in other LEGO games, although the main quest was noticably shorter than the others I have played; it took me just under 30 hours to finish the story and go back through the levels to find the collectibles and unlock every achievement. I have also noticed there are less levels and they are dragged out to be longer than usual, which I personally didn't have an issue with.
In some areas, things have changed a bit. The game's presented in a similar manner than that of the movie. The characters are modeled in what seems to be a more realistic form, and their movements match that of the movie's. In addition, almost everything is gorgeously rendered in LEGO form and is a marvel to analyze. Batman also provides some hilarious commentary at times. Fans of the movie should feel right at home.

I would hesitate to even call this worth the $4 base price. It's fine, but it's easily beatable in around 30 minutes, without really all that much to show for it. The environmental message is topical enough now, but the game doesn't give itself time to really explore that with any depth other than "manmade pollution is bad and we should maybe start doing something about that".
The game does a good job of contrasting natural beauty from the past to the bleak, Silent Hill-esque landscape of the present, but there's not really much around to explore. Gameplay is mostly a combination walking simulator and stealth, with a few soldiers here and there that you have to sneak around, but most of these sections are easy enough to get past on the first try.
Sound design is pretty solid, and probably the thing that stands out the most to me about this game. The voice acting is pretty good, the soldiers' voices in the distance are garbled and appropriately menacing, and even the sound of labored breathing is done to surprisingly unsettling effect in places. Still, I wouldn't say it's quite enough to make up for a bland, cliched message, uninteresting characters, and fairly barebones graphics and gameplay. I was glad to give it a try, but it didn't leave much of an impression.

My favourite games from this series will always be the Original Trilogy episodes of the Star Wars games. There was something simple and charming about those games that will always appeal to me more than the quagmire that a few of the later games sunk into, in my opinion. I felt later games disappeared into a hole of fiddly complexity regarding character abilities and level design that sucked the fun out of playing.
In saying that, The Lego Movie: The Game rises above a lot of the others I've played, giving you multiple open-world hubs to play around in, as well as some entertaining levels that expand competently upon the movie's premise and retain the sense of fun and variety that Lego embodies as a product.
The voice acting is very good considering that the actors are mimicking the original stars, and it's rare that you feel like you're not ACTUALLY listening to the movie's actors.
My only sizable criticism comes from that point when you realise that there isn't actually much gameplay in these games, and it mostly relies on your compulsive desire to keep collecting studs to keep you entertained. At that point I found myself wondering whether I was either playing a cheap cash-in, or whether I was playing a decent Lego game and it was just that the series is designed in such a way that, by exploited our completionist desires, they can squeeze the most amount of fun out of the least amount of effort. If it's the former, it's hard to tell, and if it's the latter, I feel like I have to applaud the developers for their ingenuity.
Either way, I had fun while I was doing it, alhough I probably won't feel any reason to come back to this particular game after I've finished, as opposed to the Original Trilogy games, as my attachment to the Lego Movie was not great enough to make that a specific draw for me.
One last criticism is that I found the music to be annoying as ♥♥♥♥. I'm not a fan of the ethereal electronic soundtrack, and in the film the Everything is Awesome song is supposed to be a satirical take on bland, emotionless, corporate-built pop that is intended to be an ear-worm in the most annoying possible way. So when the developers decided to slap it all over the place in this game and have it haunt the dreams of everyone who plays it, they either missed the point of the film entirely in that regard, or they're ♥♥♥♥ing with us.

First of all, I kickstarted this game with the intent of having it reach a broader audience. I was already fond of the original trilogy's release in its full glory, so my inmediate opinion would have been biased. Instead I opted for having someone else play it as I watched, getting their feedback as a fresh starter and comparing it to my  own memories.
Not 100% of the translation agrees with me based on word choice, but it seemed to resonate with the test player; fortunately core concepts remain.
The characters managed to retain their "charm". By a twist of fate, their opinions of them aligned with my old. Specific ones were praised, others hated, a few cringed at. They went in no spoilers and enjoyed Extra with no problem, which I feel is needed to mention as there is a general hate for that part from some in the community. I personally find it charming in a (what now is) retro-anime way.
The story requires a definite suspension of disbelief for starters. In both parts there is a degree of setup before growing into their tone. Are they prefect? no. There is some wishy washy instances between well paced tense or endearing setups, some more prominent per route. Here is where lies the flaw of jumping into Unlimited. Character aspects and revelations are thrown in with varying level of assumption that you might be familiar or at least clued into them already.
If anything, this is where I would focus my dissapointment. Between characters and their stories there is an inconsistency in strenght of narrative. It is a normal ocurrence in multi-route VNs but when you have some character designed like Tama and you are supposed to take her seriously, it felt just impossible whenever she was involved; the fact was even made worse in the 2nd half.
While still holding onto the ideal of not spoiling the trek, this is an alright intro to the series. Many emotions were personaly felt, but just as many I could see reversed on others, or even just taken from an alternate perspective. That may in fact be its greatest strenght, that there is something for many a player here, not everyone but many.
Notes:
- I believe the original release required you to beat Meiya's and Sumika's routes in EXTRA before unlocking Unlimited. That is still recomended. Even if not your primary choices.
- This still remains an excellent prologue for what is/will be Alternative.
- After all these years, and even by the test player's words "Can we just get rid of that trio?"(players will know who)

The Lego Movie Game is, sadly, one of the worst Lego games to have come out for a while, on par with some of the first to be released. This game is first and foremost a movie tie-in, make no mistake. There is no original story, movie clips are used instead of in-game cutscenes, and don't expect any inivation beyond two bland mini-games.
I've loved all the Lego games so far, and I got this one with the express purpose to play as Unikitty, and on that it delivered. What it didn't deliver is that scope that we've come to expect from modern Lego games, such as sprawling open worlds, a large cast of characters, and a host of special skills that are drip-fed to you throughout. Let's look at these in more detail:
The character select screen may seem healthy, boasting 90-odd characters, but take a moment to consider who these characters are. Most are generic citizens who got mere seconds of screen time, or the mini-figured you find in the blind bags: Panda Man, Taco Tuesday Guy, and Larry the Barista are among the memorable characters you can play as, who only differ in apperance and the object they throw. The main character Emmet has not one, not three, but thirteen variations, all seperate (unlike most Lego games that stack variations of the same character on one spot) and all exactly the same, with two exceptions. Also, only the main characters have facial animations, and not even they get lip-synching when they talk.
The world is divided into four areas and a bonus zone; Bricksburg, The Old West, Cloud Coocooland and the Octan Tower. These areas consist of more or less two rooms, with missions scattered around, with no central 'hub' to begin them. Characters are bought from the character select screen, as with the newer games, but the mini-figures can also be found scattered around to buy in-person, which is completely redundant. Within 10-hours of gameplay, taking my time, I have already finished the game, bought all the characters, and bought all the red blocks, making this the shortest Lego game I've ever played (and I've played most).
The unique skills in this game are nothing mind-blowing: silver needs explosives, gold needs a laser, only construction-workers can repair, only women can be acrobatic (that's right, Batman cannot climb walls or jump around), only Master Builders can make objects, only Unikitty can use rainbow blocks, etc. etc. All very standard and mostly things we've seen before, too. Aside from Lord Buisness, who you get at the end of the game, most bonus obstacles can be cleared by the half-way point, let's say 6-hours in. It's a Lego game, so obviously you'll be going back and playing it all a second time in Free Play mode to unlock everything, but this certainly won't take anywhere near as long as the comparative colossus, Lego Batman 2.
~In summation: This is a game for people who loved the movie. You'll get to see it all again and play with characters you probably won't otherwise get to, such as Unikitty. The gameplay is exactly as you'd expect, nothing breaks the formula, and anything new is few and far between. And you'd best hope you like the soundtrack, because you'll be hearing three particular songs an awful lot. In short: It's silly, short fun, but don't expect much more for you money beyond a playable advertisment. I recommend it because it is exactly what it is: It's not great, but it's not bad either, but it most certainly IS a movie tie-in game, and should be treated as such.

I really can't recommend this game, which is a huge disappointment because I truly love Lego products and their games.
For starters, the voice acting is downright awful. Personally, I preferred when Lego didnt have people talking and just had squeaks and grunts for "voice acting", but besides personal predjudice, it sounds like the actors aren't even trying. They sound like really badly done robots, until the part where they're supposed to be robots, and then they sound like even worse robots. It feels like the actors put all their energy into making the movie and did the game while they were half-asleep. Not only that, not keeping all the same voice actors from the movie has really damaged it, especially since they actually PUT IN SCENES FROM THE MOVIE. They voiced over the scenes again? Really?
On top of that, the game was obviously designed for console first, with very little effort put into porting it to the computer. Evidence? On many occasions there are minigames. These minigames are insanely difficult with the mouse of keyboard, because you have to be very fast and make as few mistakes as possible, whereas if you had a controller you can use the 8 directional movement of a stick with ease. There's also a dancing minigame that doesnt even use keyboard keys; it says ABXY for directions, and if you don't own a controller for your computer and you don't know the key layout of a console controller by heart, it's incredibly difficult.
With most lego games, when they add areas and things, it's really fun, seeing possible parts of the storyline the movies don't go into; with this, it feels cheap and dull, mostly. It's not necessarily a bad game, but falls far, far short of my expectations and hopes, and far from the movie and other Lego games.

I spent a very long time playing this game and regret it immensely.
I wanted to like this game, the genre and just the entire idea of the game is awesome.
After spending 16 hours between 2 days of playing the game, I find myself very sad.
First, lets go over my first impressions I had. I started a campaign, where you basically try and take over the galaxy, one solar system at a time, a great idea for a game mode I believe warhammer did first, but maybe someone else did it before them too.
My first game was the most horrible, not fun experience I have had with a game in years. I put the game on the normal difficulty which is recommended as it's auto-picked and it was not well balanced. The enemy never does ANYTHING. if a cat walked on your keyboard for an hour it would probably win somehow and I am not kidding or exagerating. I spent 1 hour afk, came back and the enemy still only had one single base of about 5 buildings. I had over 30 buildings from the TEN MINUTES I spent playing. Leaving the AI alone for an hour had no effect, he basically never expanded, never attacked me, never did anything.
I then put the game onto hard mode and tried again, it was a lot more fun, but sadly still.. too easy. The enemy never does full attacks against you, they can but VERY rarely. They usually just send 5 units to poke you which is literally just wasting units of theirs. I defeated a campaign on hard mode easily, then did one more and found the worst balance decision in this game by far.
There's a perk that allows you to have an AI partner, the issue is this partner is actually a god. I challenged the main base of a faction ,set up some turrets around myself then afk'd. My one ally beat all 3 enemies on his own. He is ridiculously OP to a stupid extent.
I then tried the game in the next difficulty and found the game is actually flawed, period. Everytime the game ended up giving me a match where there is two planets, the game can't end.
It's so much easier to defend than attack. Basically you end up each owning a planet, you have a planet and the enemy has a planet. The planets are both covered in anti nukes so you can't attack each other at all. You can send units with the launcher, but the launcher can only send incredibly pathetic and weak units. I tried building 10 which is a huge amount, but they literally died instantly. I then tried building around 30 nukes, I could then bypass the AI's anti nukes, but still they'd just.. rebuild fast enough..
I spent about 5 hours in a game like this and now I think I am just done with the game and forever will be.
This all mixed with that this game has horrible pathfinding, sometimes making units run in circles for ages or running back and forth a few times before actually going where they were told. Horrible balance on Vehicles compared to Air units or Bots, as vehicles are just clearly superior as they have more HP, more damage, more utility and only at the cost of speed. Compared to air which is so squishy it's horrid and bots which are fast, but so weak it's pointless against vehicles anyway. Navy has some very powerful units but ocean is so rare and such a gimmick that it's pointless. Not to mention, why would we make navy units WHEN WE CAN FLY. Just put rockets under the damned ship.

After completing Bastion, I realized that the ending is actually really thoughtful, you have two ultimate choices; restore the world to a time before the calamity which is the apocalyptic catastrophe that caused an outbreak in plague, monsters, and fighting factions, or evacuate the Bastion, the mechanical floating island that the old man, Rucks, and you, the kid, live on. That's the central point of the game, to get the Bastion back in working order, gathering shards and minerals to fix the Bastion.
Along the journey, the old man, Rucks, narrates every move you make which might sound annoying but was actually intuitive because of all the context he is able to give. Later on in the game, you figure out that he's narrating to one of the Ura, a girl named Zia who comes to the Bastion after meeting the kid.
I can't say much about the gameplay, as it's rather repetitive, shooting down enemies, blocking, and hacking, no depth to it. But the options you get in weaponry and special abilities and the leveling up make up for it. The game's design is isometric but also 2D, kind of cel shaded. And the floating islands which are part of the world was an interesting way to represent how society has turned out.
Very good game though, with heavy depth in narrative.

Takes me back to the days of Half Life mods that were quirky, rough around the edges, but insanely fun with friends despite being buggy.  Don't count on getting much done with randoms since there's a fair amount of teamwork and coordination involved to operate effectively.  But the game doesn't penalize you for losing, you gain xp by carrying out various tasks so there's some incentive to stick around even the worst game with the worst crew ever.
The upsides, a well coordinated ship feels good to be a part of, switching between reloading, firing cannons, repairing the ship, and pumping water out of a cannonball riddled sinking ship are all pretty fun and rewarding to perform.  The captain role is very unique, and can definitely make the difference when you're in the middle of the action.  Despite some lag and bugginess I never felt cheated out of a potential kill or missed shot, a certain amount of innacuracy is expected, and feels appropriate regardless of weather you're hitting all your shots or missing them.  On the inverse, getting wiped out by a well placed shot by the enemy doesn't feel bad either.  Respawn times are reasonable, and you can get back into the action relatively quick. It's pretty mindless but with enough strategy to reward you if your ship is coordinated well enough and your captain has a good feel for the game.  Very accessible, and you'll definitely get better with time once you get a hang for some of the subtlty woven into the game.
Now for some downsides, granted this is in Early Access at the time of this review, and I'm sure some or any complains may be addressed at a later time (if they aren't, it won't be a deal breaker unless the player base gets super toxic), but my biggest gripe currnetly (and it's not a major one, it's just mildly annoying when it comes up) is with the team killing.  For a game that's predicated upon teamwork and coordination, nothing can really sour the experience more than some butt-hurt 12 year old who decides to start chopping up his crew until he gets kicked from the server.  Also would be nice to tone down the damage between friendly ships for all those rogue captains who have a tendency to ignore everything and ram into any ship friend or foe.  Might be advantageous to have more factions, or introduce a free-for-all mode for folks who need to satiate their urges to murder anything in site.  I suppose it's "more realistic" the way it is, but we're talking about a game where you swing hammers to magically repair large holes in your hull, use the same hammer to repair torn sails, and chug tea/rum to magically recover from non-fatal stray cannonball hits, it's not exactly a true to life experience.
Minor complains aside, if you wanna get together with some buddies online and take to the fake seas and do some 1700's style high seas combat, you won't find a much more accesible and fun way to do it than here.

Early Access Review;
I was looking for a fun pirate game that involved team cooperation and I'm happy to say I've found this! I've overall enjoyed playing this game and for the most part the team cooperation is good. You have the opportunity to make repairs, fire cannons, use an assortment of weapons in different classes, heal yourself and others, freely run around the ship, repair sails, and captain the ship. It's highly recommended that you have a mic as it makes the game more enjoyable and your team can work together much better. As the Dev's have mentioned, the one big downside to this game so far is that it becomes stale fairly quick. Besides deathmatches there really is not much else to do and after just over 4 hours I haven't played anymore. That being said, there are sneak peaks of 3.0 updates and I patiently and excitingly await their completion!
As of right now I would recommend this game and the full price of the game is worth it. Supporting the developers, who have shown they want to continue making the game better, will allow this game to grow further and become even better.
My two cents for the Devs that I'd love to see considered : Re-loading the cannons by going back and forth to the ammo boxes becomes tedious, and you have to pause a moment before using your action button to pick up an item to put in the cannon. It doesn't make the player feel very immersed compared to when you are ramming the items down the hole. Some of the icons used to show the commands given by the captain should be re-done to be more understanding and remain there until the next command is given (unless the captain selects to have no current order). There is little difference between loading a side to fire and preparing to fire and the team never seems to respond much to them. Other than that I look forward to there being more re-playability to the game and thanks for the dedication and keeping us players in the loop!

Once upon a time I would have listed Left 4 Dead to be in my top 10 favorite games of all time.
Now I'm sad to say that L4D has become a shrivelled husk of it's former glory, any attempts to replay it have ended in quitting out of boredom half way through a campaign, which is a major sour point in a game that was made to be replayable. Any replayability in the game can be attributed to different dialogue and zombies and items that spawn in different places, and that's it. The developers somehow believed that those three factors alone would make L4D stand the test of time and blow people away for generations to come.
The Versus component of the game is not much better than campaign mode, if not worse. I find the teams to be unbalanced and always in favor of the survivors and although this next point isn't exactly related to the game itself, the VS community is rather childish and on the same behavioral terms I'd expect from a daycare for spoiled little brats. While this isn't a development flaw it clearly shows that L4D's competetive scene attracts the wrong kind of crowd and soured an entire half of the game for me.
While it's easy to rag on the negative points, it's also easy to forget what has drawn us to the game to begin with: The atmosphere is perfect (which is more than can be said for it's rushed sequel), the coop serves as an excellent hangout for friends and once in a while you just feel the need to partake in a bloodbath that is clearly scaled to your favor.
It almost pains me to say that L4D has aged as well as milk that has been sitting out for a month. But it's true, L4D just didn't hold out in our hearts and minds.
