Back in the all too distant past at university a guy on my corridor had one of the burnout games which featured an amazingly fun looking mode where you had you cause as much damage as possible by crashing into an intersection and that is why I bought this game. Much to my disappointment the equivalent mode in this game just wasn't that great. You just start a crash on any stretch of road with limited degree of control and all the cars swerve towards you until you reach a required target. The older version was more like a puzzle to solve with a fixed arrangement of traffic.
That was only the start of the disappointment, the biggest problem is with the phrase “Ultimate Box”. When a game proclaims to be a superlative edition my expectation is that it is the base game combined with all the available DLC but no this is the base game with the free updates only. When you try and access the DLC it takes you to a store front that no longer works and they are not available on Steam either. There are apparently ways to buy the DLC but I didn't like the core game enough to want to investigate this option.
The actual game continued to disappoint me. The game has an open world environment however the actual races all end in a small number of locations making all the races seem unnecessarily similar. The races do not follow any fixed route but the navigation system is terrible, you have a compass that shows you the overall direction to the finish but the only clue about which road to take  is a little road sign that pops up too late to make the turn in the faster cars. There is also a mini map but looking at that is a sure fire way to crash into something so effectively you just have to learn the map. The game progression is too unfocused for me, you just complete an arbitrary number of races to unlock the next licence. Also there is no option to quit or restart and event you have to complete the event and then drive all the way back to the start point.
The other annoyance is all the collectables. I do love a nice set of collectable items in a game but this just has too many for it to work. There are 400 gates to smash through, there is no way you can collect all these while still having fun, you must just be driven by the desire for completion. You are bound to miss a few and then end up painstakingly going through a walktrhough revisiting all the locations till you find the ones you missed. And there is not just the gates there are jumps and best times on every road and biggest crashes on every road.
One of the items of DLC that did come with the ultimate box was the multiplayer party DLC which was again (I keep coming back to this word) disappointing. It had no split screen options, the events are repetitive and the load times are just that bit too long so it starts getting aggravating as you are passing the controller between players.
All of these problems are a real shame as the core game engine is excellent with great driving, spectacular crashing, a decent range of cars, a good map and variety of events. And in the sale this cost less than the price of a bus ticket. Given all the annoyances in the game I can't bring myself to recommend this game.

If you're not, this is the best place to start experiencing them.  It's one of the best VNs available and is something you'll want to read again.

I had to think long and hard before writing this review, since it's difficult to simply say "Yes" or "No" to whether or not I recommend it: it's much more of a shade of grey.
Planetary Annihilation: Titans (PA:T) feels like a spherical successor to Total Annihilation (TA), designed for fast-paced multiplayer games. It lacks a solid single-player campaign, but is charming in its simplicity if you are just after skirmishes and series of conquests.
The problem is that this game came out after Supreme Commander (SC) and its standalone successor (SC:FA) Forged Alliance. (Supreme Commander 2 [SC2] was such a step backwards that I'm ignoring it entirely.)
PA:T ignores the simplications, improvements and progress made within SC and SC:FA, instead returning to the simpler TA model, which is a significant step backwards. It ignores any grid system, which isn't important to most people and which some people wrongly claim isn't possible on a sphere but which affects how playing the game feels.
If you enjoyed SC:FA, then instead do a Google search for "Forged Alliance Forever" (FAF) before getting this game or try a demo of it first. If you didn't enjoy SC:FA and preferred TA, then you well well enjoy this much more.
Whilst I do not recommend this game, I was fortunate enough to get it at 85% off, so I got it for less than £5, so in terms of the value relative to my payment, it's not terrible. The problem is that it should have blown the socks off earlier games in this genre but didn't.
If you're after a newer game, you'd be better placed trying out something like Ashes Of The Singularity or simply sticking with FAF.

It is incredibly difficult to explain what makes Muv-Luv as good as it is without at least partially ruining one of the major events within this game. So difficult, in fact, that the marketing blurb on this very steam page 13 years after the Japanese release (yes, this game is 13 years old) does just that. I will try to give my thoughts without revealing anything the store page has not already, but with that said *POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD*
At first, you may think this game another typical dating sim-esque visual novel, in the vein of games such as NEKOPARA which have appeared on Steam in the last couple of years. You could be forgiven, as you wouldn't be
wrong. This title is split into 2 parts; a light-hearted and cliche slice of life comedy (Dubbed 'EXTRA'), and a significantly more serious, alternate universe affair that parallels the first half of the title (Unlimited). Curiously enough, the developers of this localisation have decided to allow both routes to be immediately playable upon launching the game, though I cannot stress enough the importance to play this game in the correct order. The contrast, foreshadowing and tonal shift are all essential elements which elevate this game, particularly the first section, to something greater than the sum of its parts.
The general consensus among fans of the franchise is that the first portion of this game, EXTRA, is something worth slogging through in order to reach Unlimited and the (as of yet unreleased on steam) sequel, Alternative. While I cannot deny that the latter 2 games are definitely the meat and potato of the series, with Alternative in particular considered by many to be the greatest visual novel of all time, I have to confess that personally I find EXTRA to be legitimately enjoyable. While it is nothing special on its own by any standards, it is a genuinely funny, short and sweet experience with very likable characters that manages to never take itself too seriously. I would happily give it an 8/10 on its own merits.
Unlimited, on the other hand, is undoubtedly the highlight of this game. Introducing the world and story that will carry over into the sequel, Alternative, the game begins to show its true colours, and is a tense, sobering sucker punch of a follow-up act to EXTRA. At this point, the series really does become one of the all-time greats of the mecha genre.This chapter of the game, paired with Alternative, is what I consider to be quite honestly one of the best works of science fiction ever made. If EXTRA is an 8/10, then Unlimited is quite easily a 9/10.
As a reader of the original release and a backer of the Kickstarter that accompanied this steam version, I can say that Degica have mostly done a fantastic job and porting this game on to Steam. They listened to the fans when it came to features we wanted to see implemented, and the game has released in a very polished state. Particularly, the ability to switch between English and Japanese text on the fly is a fantastic feature. The official translation reads very smoothly, and is less overly literal than the fan translation sometimes had a habit of being. The dialogue does at times feel almost
colloquial however, with mannerisms feeling a little too '2016 America' for their own good. This is clearly an intentional decision by the translation team, however, and is really just a matter of personal taste.
Some people also seem to be unhappy with the presence of censoring in this title when compared to the original release, particularly with regards to the 'adult content'. These scenes were few and far between in the original release anyway, and in my opinion took more away from the game than it added. There is supposed to be a patch eventually from the developer's website to rectify this regardless, if that's your cup of tea.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Overall, if you have an even a fleeting interest in the concept of this visual novel, I cannot recommend it enough, and the sequel alone makes this game an absolute must-buy.

This is the shortest Lego game that I have played, by a long way. I really enjoyed that. The movie humour is present and very enjoyable but does not become tedious. There has been a lot of improvement in gameplay mechanics: the camera was great, the level length was just right, the free play areas were enjoyable and there were no frustrating 'jump just right' challenges. The graphics are a whole level above the graphics of other games because of the way they incorporated Lego scenery, and it's fantastic. The building minigame was too fast for me but was infrequent (unlike Lego Hobbit) and there were fewer collectibles of all sorts. Each level had 5 gold instruction manuals and one pair of pants (Honey, where are my pants?!). Gold bricks are not collected but represent your overall completion (there were 70, while Lego Marvel had 250). The variety of collectible characters is spot-on, there are relatively few, but they are all fun to play and can be unlocked easily (once you complete the appropriate level). The music within levels and in free play areas was never odious. Doing each level was fun - Lego games are often criticised for having no challenge to them, i.e., break stuff until you complete the level - but this game has the most variety (and least repetition) yet.
In short, this is a really fun game to play. There is a lot of variety and humour; the game is colourful, the graphics are great and the levels are balanced. It's a lot shorter than other Lego games, and I have thus been able to completely finish it while still enjoying it.
I'd say it's 'as good' as Lego Marvel, but there is a lot less of it. This game was released around the same time as Lego Hobbit, and this game is far better. I hope they continue with this style rather than Hobbit.
Overall, I'd give this game a ... maybe 9 out of 10? [I'm having trouble figuring out why I shouldn't give it 10, though...]

With the success of open-world titles such as Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row and Just Cause, developer United Front Games had big hopes for True Crime: Hong Kong, set to be published by Activision. Wait – True Crime? Yes. You could say the development story around this game might be more interesting than the in-game story.
Hoping to reinvigorate the True Crime series, Activision had plans to merge United Front Games’ newest title into it – even going as far as announcing it and releasing a trailer (and eventually changing the naming to just “True Crime“). As time went on, and delays plagued the release, Activision gave up on the project. Some rumors state that the game was almost finished, and could even be completed by players in its current state.
To the angst of gamers everywhere, with thoughts of what could have been, this happens often in game development. What also happens on occasion is that another publisher will spot the diamond in the rough, inherit the project, and ultimately publish it. That’s what happened here; when Square Enix first laid its eyes on the game, it’s been said that it was a done deal right from the get-go. There have even been quotes from Square Enix calling Activision “crazy” for abandoning not only a game so far in its development cycle, but a game with such potential.
Those who enjoy open-world games such as the titles mentioned above will be pleased with Square Enix’s decision on this one, because Sleeping Dogs is a great game, offering just enough uniqueness to set itself apart from the games it’s going to inevitably be compared to time and time again.
What’s not so unique is its story, but it involves a not-so-unique mechanic that makes it unique (get that?). You’re Wei Shen, a Hong Kong-born undercover cop that lived in America for so long that his accent is almost non-existent. Back in Hong Kong, Shen’s job is to get in good with the Triad gang Sun On Yee (based on the real-life gang Sun Yee On) and ultimately take it down.
Throughout the game, Shen will have to perform duties for both his gang and the police department, and as missions are completed, XP will be earned for the respective skill tree (Triad or Police). Each of these are split into two sections, and as each level is earned, you’ll be able to unlock the next available skill in either section.
Where the unique comes in is that ultimately, you may sway more to one side than the other, depending on your playstyle. When on a police mission, if you run into people or damage the environment, XP is taken away from that tree. This doesn’t matter much, as Police XP comes easier than Triad XP. In addition to these there’s also a “Face” tree, which is leveled up based on various actions throughout the game; when a new level is earned here, it adds a new self-benefiting ability, such as having buffs last longer.
Buffs, you ask? Yes, Sleeping Dogs is more RPG-like than most other open-world games, with the game coming close to the mechanics Saints Row 3. By either eating or partaking in some activity, Shen can earn buffs that increase his damage, helps him regenerate health or boost other abilities. Each buff disappears after a certain amount of time; faster if it’s more beneficial. While it’d be nice given the difficulty of some fights, there are no healing items that Shen can keep on him.
One thing that sets this game apart is that it takes place in Hong Kong, while most open-world games, such as Grand Theft Auto, Mafia II and Saints Row, take place in more Americanized locations. If you’re indifferent to Asia, this might not matter, but if you do happen to love the cities of any Asian metropolis, you’re going to be pleased with the world here. I’d argue that this is the most detailed open-world game ever, as the cities feel genuine with their layouts and design, and rarely did I stumble on anything that I knew was a direct copy / paste (things like advertisements aside).
Adding to the realism, most of the NPCs in the game speak Cantonese with no subtitles, while all important characters speak in clear English with occasional Cantonese thrown in. This is appreciated, and to me, required. It’d feel a bit odd to traverse through Hong Kong and never hear the official language.

I initially hated this game, but the constant updates throughout the year has solved some of my frustrations. For example there's a weekly challenge now where you can accumulate fight points easily other than fighting the ranked matchs. Of course, being a ftg game playing the ranked/casual match is a must to hone your skills and there's no fault giving fight points in that so the weekly challenge is considered a booster for beginners. Those who have kept playing the game since day 1 should be able to use the points to unlock multiple character/stages (tho some content cannot be unlocked with points and must be purchased) if they took advantage of the weekly challenge. While SF5 gameplay is much easier than USF4 on basic level, the depth game is where it shines. Utilizing V-triggers to do reversals/counters/boost and combo extention greatly enhances gameplay on top of some very easy combo's already applied in each character (Ryu's MP > HP > HK for example). Crossplay PS4 vs PC is another welcome addition in SF5 that must also be followed with other ftg games, SF5 have survived the problem of decreasing player community from time to time just by having this feature so rest assured you're gonna be playing this game for a long time if you love it. SF5 is now sold multiple times cheaper than it's initial release during sale so the issue of having small number of fighters for the basic edition does not devalue the game too much as you can purchase the deluxe edition for a cheap price now or decide to unlock the season pass characters with fight points (keep in mind you might not like some of the fighters so just focus on unlocking the ones that suite your playstyle). That said, SF5 is a game that constantly tries to redeem itself while still making sales from both valuable & cosmetic contents. Sounds fair to me.

Whenever I want to play a GOOD game, and get tired of the generic games out there,  I re-install this game. I have cleared it 4 times already, and I would do it again if I wasn't this god-damn lazy. It's going to sound like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to most of you, but I do think, that this game is the one that got most close to perfection. And I ain't joking arround here. I usually talk about the BAD parts of a game first, in the reviews, but I just can't find anything bad about it.
It's not THAT long, but it's cheap, and has replayability, New Game+ and some extreme challenges. The enemies never feel cheap or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly programmed. The world is well-crafted. The soundtrack is as perfect as it's narrator, who is, at this point, the Morgan Freeman of video-f#cking-games. It also has a good amount of weapons, skills, combinations... What's bad about it!?
The only bad thing, is that the "plot-twist" can be a bit obvious. THAT'S IT. And that's the only thing that makes this game unworthy of getting a 10/10. But you know what? Who needs perfection, when you can get so near, it doesn't even matter.
Bastion starts with "Kid", a young buy who's drifting in a world of lego that's being undone day by day. Uppon leaving what used to be the walls of the city, he joins the narrator, Rucks, and some other people later on. The "Bastion" works as your hub, and you rebuild it, adding a place to hold and change your equipment, to hold your liquor (seriously, the Kid is like 12 years old, SHAME ON YOU, RUCKS), or even pray to the golds, to make the game unholy-f#cking-hard. There are also, like I said, a bunch of challenges, in either pictures that will unlock by doing special stuff like killing multiple enemies with an arrow, or in special arenas where you have to fight and fight to survive, from waves and waves of enemies, while the dream (or rather, the arena of the dream) falls apart, while you get to learn more lore about the game.
The soundtrack is just perfect. The songs with lyrics are just beautiful. The narrator makes a perfect job to narrate the game, not like in other games, where he just would spam selected audio files, but in here, he DOES narrate what you do.  You fall down a pit? He makes a comment about it? You forget about enemies, and start smashing down things on the map? He will also talk about it. He will even comment how nasty and over-powered your loadout is (try to carry the grenade-launcher with the Bazooka, the line cracks me up every god-damn time).
The gameplay is as solid, as the snake on my pants. I wasn't trying to reference Metal Gear, that crap just happens. You can equip two weapons, and a skill of either of them. You can also upgrade your weapons, and at times, you can choose what to upgrade. You want the rifle to load faster, or to pierce enemies? Your choice. But with the amout of weapons, you sure can go whoever you feel like, and enjoy the game.
Oh, and if you didn't know, after playing the game, and going New Game+, you can get the skill to summon Portal Turrets. Seriously. That just blows my mind how much they managed to make futuristic turrets that talk fit so well in the game. Those guys are a bunch of geniuses, and they deserve your money for making this piece of digital art. It also has multiple endings, and the key moments of the game can seriously reach deep into you. Well, not in me, I'm too much of a man, but it sure was close.
I give this game a Super Saiyan Morgan Freeman / 10, now buy it before he fuses with Samuel L. Jackson.

Sanctum 2 (S2) is a sequel, tho I never played original.  Bottom line, Sanctum 2 is a great strategy game with some shooter elements, although the difficulty may make you cry Uncle or throw your laptop across the room in fury.  So if you are seeking a real challenge, and not some scripted "interactive movie" shenanigans, this is for you.
S2 takes the tower defense game of Warcraft 3 fame and adds some twists.  First, now instead of controlling towers, you control a hero FPS style, running among your towers and shooting the monsters.  There are multiple characters, weapons, and perks (i.e. talents/talent tree), giving the game another layer of real strategic depth.  Monsters have armored, regular, and weak spots to shoot as well.  While there may be 20ish towers to use, you can only pick 4 to take with you into a level.  And these choices become agonizing.
Tower defense game basically is an advanced puzzle game: you start with a grid.  Monsters spawn and at Point A and walk towards your Base at Point Z.  You can layout a maze of walls and towers that shoot them as they pass.  In S2, each level has 10 waves (give or take) of various monster layouts, but on a certain level you only face about half the enemy types at once, meaning each map must be customized differently.  You must learn which towers take out fliers, baby monsters, and big monsters best.  There are also Bosses, which add another layer of strategy to the game.
Now I said S2 is maddenly frustrating.  This is because going into a level for the first time, you don't know what to expect at all.  So you have to play it say 10 times to learn what monsters spawn and where, all the while failing by narrow margins.  Then, lets say, you get to wave 9, where the hardest boss on the level spawns.  Well, guess what?  You have to design your entire tower layout to beat this one boss.  Time to restart the level...  So this is both frustrating and quit involving.  (I can't stop playing this game I am beginning to hate...)  All this would not be bad except a level takes say 20 minutes to complete, so you are looking at hours of experimentation to beat a level.  You might also simply make a mistake, like jumping and hitting the wall rather than jumping over it, at a critical time, which costs the game at wave 10.  ZOMG... I was SO mad.
This really comes down to difficulty.  As you are levelling up, you HAVE to make a customized strategy to beat the level.  That makes for great strategic depth, but it personally feels a little too difficult to progress.  But maybe that's the charm.  Who makes a hard video game these days?  No one.
MULTIPLAYER
Multiplayer takes the form of cooperative play.  Up to 4 players can team up to take on a level.  Monster health increases equal to number of players (2x for 2 players, 3x for 3...), as does the amount of money to spend.  The advantage is you can each take 4 different tower types into level with you.
The default mode of playing campaign is to have your map be public, so people can join.  PuG'ing is a really bad idea.  Other players can kill you with their weapons.  And since every noobtard has to play sniper or rocket launcher... yeah you're respawning a lot.  Furthermore, all players can rearrange and destroy everyone else's towers and walls.  I once lost a level because I knew I needed to send monsters direction F, but MR I AM LEVEL 40 SHUT UP AND LISTEN TO ME had to send them direction G.  As I mentioned previously, this strategic decision was based on my knowledge that because of the boss that spawns on wave X, so we lost wave X... sigh.
Because Pug'ing is a bad idea, you will see many high level players joining low level games to find friends.  However, because we (or rather I) am still learning the game, I'm not ready for my guild interview and they think I'm bad.  No, just inexperiened...  Also I don't have all the towers and gear and talents yet.  SIGH.
REPLAY VALUE
Once you beat the level on regular mode, you can beat it with any number of 5 hard modes (like skulls in HALO) turned on.  You have "beaten" the game when you complete all 5 challenges for all levels (in any combination, including individually).  And the challenges really do change dynamics quite a bit.  There is also survival mode, where you can play a level up to 200 waves (if you can kill the 2 billion hp monsters that come out at wave 200...)
And of course, you can do all this with friend in co-op and you won't get far if your don't.
PROS
* Novel twist on a popular game type
* Refreshing to see a strategy game
* Lots of replay and strategic depth
* 4 expansion packs of equally challenging content, with new twists.
NEUTRAL
* Hair pulling frustrating at times.  (Is this good or bad?  Depends on the player I guess.)
CON
* Pugging is a nightmare.
* Need good friends to enjoy the full depth of game.
* It's hard to see the map.  There's no zooming feature.  An interactive map that allows you talk and communicate and strategize with your fellow players would be really great.  To do it right, you gotta teamspeak.  But what elese is new?

Game Review:
** Sanctum 2 **
So Picked up Sanctum 2 last weekend for me and a friend. I was a little skeptical about a first person TD but I figure EH why not!? My friend and I have dropped seven hours into this game so far, and let me tell you. It's pretty solid! The lighting and graphical quality is good. The music is well done, it doesn't get repetitive or annoying, and honestly fades into the "background" if you will during the action. The controls feel tight and responsive. The enemies and level layout give you a challenge, even on repeated play throughs. The weapons and power-ups give a fun and interesting twist to each play through. The game makes use of the typical tower recycling to reposition on the in between a critical part of the early waves, and it was a pretty great call. They also adding the reduced returns you would have in a normal TD back in as a challenge. The tower / Hero dynamic is a good hand in hand balance. You go down and your towers are not going to stand up to the waves. You go in with no towers, You're not winning, as beating a wave let alone a stage is hard if not impossible to do without the towers even with multiple players. I still haven't gotten very far in the campaign as my friend and I thought it would be great fun to try and beat the levels with every challenge active as we go, and I'm pretty sure those are meant to be done as a second pass through the game. If you haven't played it and like TD's give it a try.

Premise: it's my second time reading Muv-Luv, which means that I'm familiar with both the fan-translated version and the Steam one.
Muv-Luv contains the first (Extra) and the second (Unlimited) part of the trilogy. The conclusion will come out later this year (Alternative). Let's start by introducing the story.
EXTRA
This is the part that you'll want to play first (this version allows you to go straight for Unlimited, which you should NOT do). It's a generic slice-of-life rom-com in a highschool setting, and it features Takeru, your run-of-the-mill carefree protagonist who's surrounded by cute girls but is totally unaware of their feelings for him. Takeru wakes up one day to find a mysterious girl sleeping in his bed. His childhood friend, Sumika, who comes wake him up every morning and has a crush on him, is not very happy about that. Shenanigans ensue. In order to ensure the best possible experience, you should at least read Sumika's and Meiya's routes, but I'd still recommend going for all of them.
UNLIMITED
PLOT TWIST! Takeru wakes up one day and finds out that the whole city around him is in ruins. Not only that, it seems that a huge mecha has crashed into Sumika's house! Understandably confused, he starts walking around town towards his highschool, which is now... a military base, for some reason. It soon becomes clear that our hero has stepped into an alternate dimension where humanity is on the brink of extinction after decades of war against a seemingly undefeatable race of aliens, the BETA. How did he end up there? Will he ever be able to go back to his own world? Or will he stay and help humanity's struggle for survival?
I really need to make this clear: Muv-Luv is nothing special by itself. It's not supposed to be played by itself. It's not self-sufficient at all. If you buy this, then you'd better be ready to buy Alternative in a few months, otherwise don't even bother. I promise it will be worth it. This trilogy has a pretty high barrier of entry, you'll need to invest at least 50-60 hours in it before it really gets good (most likely more than that), but the payoff will be immense. MLA will take you on one of the wildest rides you've ever experienced, but it wouldn't be even half as good without Extra/Unlimited. So yeah, don't expect this game to be good on its own, it's not, it was never meant to.
Now, to be fair there are some differences from the original version that I feel I have to point out. First of all, the default resolution is 1024x600 instead of 800x600, which means that most CGs had to be cropped. I wasn't particularly bothered by this, but others might be. Secondly, a couple tracks from the soundtrack had to be replaced because of licensing problems. I don't particularly mind about the one in Unlimited (I don't even know what it's called), but I really miss the other one (Warudakumi, a.k.a. the "Livin la Vida Loca ripoff"). That was one of the best things in this game, and I'm completely serious here. The new translation is pretty good, some might dislike it for not being 100% faithful but I don't really care, I personally think that a good translation should read well in the target language, and this one certainly does. I would have done without the Linkin Park reference though.
So, to sum things up: this VN is not for everyone. If you don't intend to read this trilogy "seriously" (if that makes sense), don't bother, you'll just waste time and energy. If, however, you have the dedication to go from start to finish, you won't regret it.

Whenever I want to play a GOOD game, and get tired of the generic games out there,  I re-install this game. I have cleared it 4 times already, and I would do it again if I wasn't this god-damn lazy. It's going to sound like complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to most of you, but I do think, that this game is the one that got most close to perfection. And I ain't joking arround here. I usually talk about the BAD parts of a game first, in the reviews, but I just can't find anything bad about it.
It's not THAT long, but it's cheap, and has replayability, New Game+ and some extreme challenges. The enemies never feel cheap or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly programmed. The world is well-crafted. The soundtrack is as perfect as it's narrator, who is, at this point, the Morgan Freeman of video-f#cking-games. It also has a good amount of weapons, skills, combinations... What's bad about it!?
The only bad thing, is that the "plot-twist" can be a bit obvious. THAT'S IT. And that's the only thing that makes this game unworthy of getting a 10/10. But you know what? Who needs perfection, when you can get so near, it doesn't even matter.
Bastion starts with "Kid", a young buy who's drifting in a world of lego that's being undone day by day. Uppon leaving what used to be the walls of the city, he joins the narrator, Rucks, and some other people later on. The "Bastion" works as your hub, and you rebuild it, adding a place to hold and change your equipment, to hold your liquor (seriously, the Kid is like 12 years old, SHAME ON YOU, RUCKS), or even pray to the golds, to make the game unholy-f#cking-hard. There are also, like I said, a bunch of challenges, in either pictures that will unlock by doing special stuff like killing multiple enemies with an arrow, or in special arenas where you have to fight and fight to survive, from waves and waves of enemies, while the dream (or rather, the arena of the dream) falls apart, while you get to learn more lore about the game.
The soundtrack is just perfect. The songs with lyrics are just beautiful. The narrator makes a perfect job to narrate the game, not like in other games, where he just would spam selected audio files, but in here, he DOES narrate what you do.  You fall down a pit? He makes a comment about it? You forget about enemies, and start smashing down things on the map? He will also talk about it. He will even comment how nasty and over-powered your loadout is (try to carry the grenade-launcher with the Bazooka, the line cracks me up every god-damn time).
The gameplay is as solid, as the snake on my pants. I wasn't trying to reference Metal Gear, that crap just happens. You can equip two weapons, and a skill of either of them. You can also upgrade your weapons, and at times, you can choose what to upgrade. You want the rifle to load faster, or to pierce enemies? Your choice. But with the amout of weapons, you sure can go whoever you feel like, and enjoy the game.
Oh, and if you didn't know, after playing the game, and going New Game+, you can get the skill to summon Portal Turrets. Seriously. That just blows my mind how much they managed to make futuristic turrets that talk fit so well in the game. Those guys are a bunch of geniuses, and they deserve your money for making this piece of digital art. It also has multiple endings, and the key moments of the game can seriously reach deep into you. Well, not in me, I'm too much of a man, but it sure was close.
I give this game a Super Saiyan Morgan Freeman / 10, now buy it before he fuses with Samuel L. Jackson.

Attain goals, gain power, use power to upgrade for even more power, and then attain ever greater goals.  This game basically takes that formula and stretches it out to make it the entire game.
The basic goal of the game is to see how powerful you can get, and how quickly and efficiently you can attain that goal.  Though quickly is a relative term since this game has hundreds or thousands of hours of playability.

This game is a 2D side Scrolling Rpg/Adventure. Yet it might look like Terraria, but it's far from it! Space travel and a Colony of your own await you in this massive adventure! Loads of Pro's and very minimal Con's(Pro's heavily outway the Con's), but all in all I give this game a 9.5/10! Trust me it's worth every penny!
Ok so to start off, I'm not super far into the story of the game just yet. I've only just made it to the Ark. Which I know is only the second story mission, but I may have gotten lost(maybe on purpose) on a random planet and LOVED IT! Seriously this game may look in a way like Terraria, but I can assure you it's not! I really loved Terraria, but the new game +++ gets old. I'm only about 6 hours into this game and I love it more than Terraria! The fact that you can just go get lost on any random planet and be killing random space men with an iron spear in a matter of a few hours and find GUNS! Yeah that's what I'm talking about! On top of that the armor is beautiful! I gotta say though. That first helmet you get really looks like something you might find in dragon ball (over 9000...), but hey. It's amazing! So now that's out of the way let me say some Pro's and Con's of what I've seen so far.
-Pro's:
-Game runs with almost no lag(I ran into a bit when I went into an underground Tomb and on the Ark when I first arrived)
-Npc's that give quests!
-Quests in general!
-Very beautiful backdrop in space and on planets.
-Monsters are very well put together and I have yet to see one (Glitch, lag or despawn)
Con's:
-As of right now there are not many Con's, but sadly there are a few.
-No fullscreen support for resolution (1360x768, It's not a huge Con, but I think it needs to be addressed. I would like to play Fullscreen too!)
-Quests are nice, but I got lost on where to go after I made it past the first mission...(I don't know if it was just me reading to fast and wanting to play, or if the game wasn't 100% clear on telling me where and how to get to this mysterious "gate".)
-Are there bosses?(This is not a Con, just I have been to 4 planets and I have yet to find any bosses. Although I have found "Challenge Portals, but I haven't been able to complete one yet. )
All in all I give this game a, -9.5/10

First thing's first. I loved Muv-Luv Extra. I loved the characters. The humor made me laugh. I enjoyed the world. I enjoyed the different routes I played. I enjoyed the harem aspect. I enjoyed working to find one route/girl to pick and seeing where it went. I enjoyed the cartoons/journal drawings. I think Meiya is best girl, but ayamine is most interesting. I backed the kickstarter a while back when it first launched, and do not regret it. I haven't read to much of this VN ever but really wanted to get into the series. From the many many reviews i've read over the years, Muv-Luv turns into a god level VN, but it just takes some time to get to the epic mech/sci-fi/romance because of the slow world building and character development in Muv-Luv: Extra.

Thoughts so far:
-The voice acting is actually really good.
-The art is dated (but not bad), but its to be expected with such an old title.
-It is pretty slow, but keeps you entertained with silly dialogue between MC and his childhood friend.
-It doesn't throw oppai in your face every five minutes to try and keep you in. However there is a bit of fan service here and there. (so far at least)
More thoughts on the series...
From what i understand, Muv-Luv: Extra is usually rated as a 6-7 out of 10. So far i'd agree with it. TL;DR:
Muv-Luv: Extra is the Star Wars episode 1 of the Muv-Luv series, it exists, you have to acknowledge it for the important character development and setting of the plot. And deep down, you, or one of your friends actually really likes it.

revolving around familiar characters. Again, the ending for Unlimited can serve as a standalone story without Alternative despite mixed opinion, but it definitely offers a greater story when read together with Alternative.

Simply put, the game is an advance visually for the franchise, and I genuinely looked forward to see what was around the corner next. Yes, so long as it's on sale.  But don't expect it to keep you interested to the very end, and don't expect any big moments that make you remember the story.

As a campaign backer and longtime fan, I’m pleased to see this awesome VN finally on Steam. When I first laid hands on the Muv-Luv series a few years ago, two thoughts instantly crossed to my mind:
1. This looks like a fun trip.
2. Best Girl’s easy to spot by her purple hair and elegant demeanor.
There was never any doubt about the second point. But boy, was I wrong about the first one. So yeah: you're in for one hell of a ride. Though there’s a bunch of words to describe the journey, you’ll need to look closely at the end of the line, to finally find “fun”. But we’re still talking about Extra and Unlimited here (and not Alternative, which will hit Steam on a later date) so let’s stick with “fun” for now.
All starts as a whacky and lighthearted romantic comedy, with your typical dense protagonist Takeru and his gang of potential love interests. It’s all nice and cute, but there’s nothing outstanding there, so a lot people ask, if there's any loss in skipping or rushing through Extra. - Well, there is. Because at some point into the series, you’ll notice, that it’s all part of the greater picture and every part’s crucial to grasp the saga and its impact as a whole. In fact, it’s pretty reasonable to see Extra as one long prolog to the core story, which starts with Unlimited and also a drastic change in tone and setting.
Through mysterious circumstances, Takeru awakes in an alternative timeline, where mankind is stuck in a desperate fight for survival against an alien race known as BETA. Gone are the dull days of Extra and you’re thrown right into a far more serious and darker universe, with very strong SciFi/Mecha themes. Saying much more about the story would be high treason, but let me assure you: it was worth every single one of the many hours, I spend in front of the screen. The story sometimes drags itself through extensive explanations, yes. But overall, it’s woven nice and tightly (there’s no perfection when it comes to time travel/alternate timelines) and plays with some interesting concepts.
In short: this is a definitive worth-your-money recommendation. And if you perchance still think of “fun” when the credits roll, keep in mind: by the time Alternative arrives, you’ll have to learn the hard way, how utterly and dreadfully wrong you were.
Pros:
- Intriguing Story, which –with Extra- lulls you into a false sense of mildly amusing harmlessness and sets the stage for the magnificent main event, known as Alternative.
- Still nice production values for a VN originally released in 2003.
- Length. You may want to reschedule your golf lessons, meetings and dinner with your waifu  to dig through this. You’ll be busy for a while. Roughly around 50 hours (and more), I’d say.
- Reasonable price
- Meiya
- Kasumi
In that order.
Cons:
- Extra alone is barely nice, tumbling on the brink of boredom here and there. Nonetheless a day will come, where you’ll yearn for this innocent times gone by
- Story drags here and there with its excessive explanations. Not as extreme as in Alternative, but still more than enough.
10/10 Everything is awesome!

So I will preface this by saying that I kickstarted these VNs without having played them before - this is my first experience with these VNs so take that how you will =s
Instead of writing a huge♥♥♥♥♥wall of text, I'll just give a quick little rundown and more or less an overarching review of both VNs.
8/10
+ The biggest positive these two VNs have going for them is definitely character development. Throughout both Extra and Unlimited, you're introduced to the main characters of the series and you'll get to know them very well. You'll see each person's personal development, which makes you all that more attached to them.
+ The writing is well done. Each character has a pronounced personality that shows through their dialogue. Not only that, the dialogues themselves are funny, emotional, and impactful.
|
-----> I'm going to say here that the plot is lacking, but not horrible. Extra is a typical romcom type harem VN, and Unlimited is more or less the same with a different setting. Both have their strong plot points, especially Unlimited, but it all feels like a huge build-up for Alternative and as such, don't really stand out on their own.

In my opinion, Realm is an incredible game. I've been playing for the past few years, and I am quite an experienced player now. With Kabam in control, the game has had its ups and downs (mostly downs), but Deca's takeover seems to be reviving realm. Since July 19th (when MOTMG started), the number of active accounts has risen from 115000 to 145000.
Anyway, onto the review. While there is much to praise about realm (exciting dungeons of all difficulties, wide variety of equipment sets, and unique skin-dye combos just to name a few), there is still much that needs to be fixed. Deca has already begun to remove bots, hackers, dupers, and others of the sort, so I won't be focusing on that issue. One big issue that most veterans have gotten over is death due to bad home wifi or server wifi. However, I feel like there still needs to be a fix. Just yesterday, I lost an 8/8 priest with 2200 fame with bulwark, prot, puri, shendyt, and crown in a Lair of Draconis due to a 3 second disconnection on my end (Deca pls revive :D). I'm not an expert programmer, so I'm not sure how this would be fixed, but I would assume there is a way to determine if connection is lost between an account and the host server.
The next thing I'd like to address is pets. There is lots of controversy going on regarding pets and how they may make certain players too overpowered. Personally, I don't think pets need to be nerfed. I understand that as a team, Deca (and any other company running a game) wants money. In my opinion, pets don't make the game "pay-to-win," they make the game "pay a crap ton to win," and if anyone is willing to pay 3000 something dollars for a max divine, then good for them. However, I think it would be cool if certain weaker pet abilities were buffed, such as rising fury, attack close, mid, and far, and savage in order to lead to a variety of pet types. In order to please the people who want pets nerfed, Deca should host events in which no pets are allowed, leading to an entirely skill-based competition.
One final issue I think should be addressed is the 16x16 skins. So far, Deca seems to support the idea of 16x16 skins with the release of their new ivory gladiator skin (at least it looks 16x16). Although this is quite a small issue, I am opposed to 16x16 skins. They look awkward and out-of-place surrounded by 8x8 skins. I have already seen a good 8x8 remake of the geb set skin on reddit. This is a small issue, so I am not too worried about it, but I would personally like to see it changed.
I, along with everyone else, also have a few ideas and suggestions to make realm a more enjoyable game. One idea I have thought of before is the addition of new vanity (or completely new) items every holiday as opposed to the same ones that Kabam uses. This can be used to add a variety of weapons, increase balance among classes, and show a player's experience. It would be neat if 6 months after the event ended, all vanities from the event went soulbound. This could start by deactivating the winter vanity weapons and releasing new ones this Halloween. One other thing I think would be interesting is allowing dyes to change more than two regions of a skin. Instead, I think each skin should be divided into some number of regions (8?) and dyes can be applied to each region as desired. In order to do this, dye cost would likely have to be cut from 50 to about 20 gold and cloth cost from 150 to about 50 gold. this would allow for even more uniqueness in dye combinations and could lead to some pretty cool (or silly) looking characters. These are just a couple ideas to add to the list of hundreds that Deca has, and while they may not be the best, I think something could be done with the general framework.
There are two methods Deca could approach this game with. Based on Deca's original announcement and Q&A in June, it seems that Deca wants to maintain a community of loyal veteran players and build the game upon them. This would require Deca to implement more endgame content, create balance between classes, and keep pets strong. By doing stuff to improve the experience of veteran players, Deca's profit would come entirely from multiple-year veterans who have been around since the heart of the Kabam years. This would be the easier, less risky, and preferred approach for current players.
However, if Deca wants to take a larger risk, they could approach Realm with a second method. Instead of focusing on current players, they could attempt to bring in new players and increase the size of the game. This would be very risky and would require lots of change to the early game. The other day, my 14 year old cousin tried out realm for the first time. He played for about three minutes, died, hopped on a new character, said "This is boring and it makes my eyes hurt" and shut the computer. The biggest issue with realm is stories like this. Sometimes when I play Realm in a cafe, some teenager will walk up to me and ask "Is that Realm of the Mad God?" I would answer with "Yes, do you play?" The response would always be something on the lines of "I played for thirty minutes and gave up." According to Realmeye, 70% of accounts ever created are Rank 1 (1 Star). The 1 Star they got when their first wizard died and they shut their computer in frustration, almost shattering it into a million pieces kinda like how Kabam almost shattered Realm. If Deca were to try this second method, it would be a high risk, but if pulled off well, there would be a massive reward.
All in all, Realm is a well-built game branching off six years of improvement. Kabam made it seem like the end, but with Deca, there is a new beginning. At this point in time, I would rate realm four stars out of five. I know that my review seems much more negative than that, but that's because I want Deca to focus on making the game six stars out of five. Realm has so much potential and if Deca can unleash that potential, the game could achieve greatness.
Thanks for buying the game Deca! I'm excited to see what comes!
-Andrew; IGN: Slaasher

Planetary Annihilation is a well-crafted RTS, with the foundation to become a great strategy game for the history books. However, it is plagued by numerous problems that the developers, who have had monetary issues (and were kickstarted to begin with), simply have not been able to address. Nevertheless, its only real issue that should keep you from buying it is the lack of a playerbase and high pricetag.
The premise is simple: destroy all your opponent's commanders to win. There are single planet matches and multi planet matches. At the beginning of the game, you are given areas in which you may spawn, either on one or more planets depending on the map. You send your commander in one of these areas - which are unique for each team/player - and begin. There are two resources: metal and energy. Energy can be produced by building energy plants or certain units, while metal requires specific areas on each planet to build metal extracters on. Metal and energy can also be produced by farming gas giants, but they are not always in maps.
One of the things PA does right - for the most part - is combat. There are 5 types of units in the game: Vehicles, aircraft, naval units, bots, and orbital units. With the exception of orbital, all of these types have different units with different abilities, strengths, and playstyles. Aircraft are weaker, but can cover more ground and are faster. Bots are cheap and can be churned out quickly, but have low damage and health. Vehicles can get expensive, but enough of them can wreck an opponents base. Naval units are only useful in water (obviously), but are excellent at base defense and turtling. Orbital are easy to destroy with towers, but build enough and you can deal massive damage to the ground below. All of these unit types have good variety: vehicles can have guns, flamethrowers, or be Anti-air. Bots can build land mines or have anti-orbital missiles. Aircraft can carpet bomb an enemy base or carry units around. Naval units can bombard far-away bases or use a rocket turret to turtle like a pro. Orbital, though, is pretty straightforward. Either they attack other orbital or attack the ground. Using these combinations of units makes unit variety a necessity, and means that knowing what your enemy is using is crucial.
If you buy the TITANS expansion - which you really should - you will get the Titan units. There are 5 titans in the game that each have a lot of health and deal a lot of damage. There are two land titans, a flying titan, and an orbital titan that also acts as an interplanetary teleporter. There is also a "Doomsday Titan" - see later. You could consider them the "endgame," but they can be killed easily if you have the right units.
Another unique part of PA is the ability to destroy planets. You can build catalysts on a metal planet to use a death sta- I mean annihilaser to destroy any planet instantly - if you can build all five catalysts without them getting nuked. Or, you can use Halleys to move planets or asteroids into one another, destroying them entirely. There is also the Ragnarok, a Titan that just blows up whatever planet it is on. For some reason, you can build this on a single planet match and just have everyone lose.
PA excels at combat and economy, the backbone of any RTS However, there are issues with the AI and numerous bugs that still have not been removed.
On single planet matches, the AI is great. They know how to win, how to use unit composition, not to destroy their economy by running out of metal and energy, and are extremely hard to beat on the highest difficulty. HOWEVER, on multi planet matches, the AI is clueless. AI units will land on a barren planet with 4 metal spots total and build massive land armies, even though the only way anyone would attack them is probably with orbital units. They also never use teleporters enough to transport those large land armies to attack where the other players are. Instead, they often send one orbital fabrication unit to build a teleporter, and then send land fabricators through to build factories. Normally, it is much smarter to build a portal and have an army already built up to send through, rather than try to build a factory on the planet you are invading. Also, the AI rarely seems to use the Helios orbital Titan's teleporter. they always try to build a regular teleporter which is much easier to destroy. Another AI flaw is their reliance on Nukes. Although nukes are devestating, one anti nuke gun can destroy three nukes at a time. The AI rarely launches multiple nukes at the same target, even on higher difficulties. This means that proactively building an anti-nuke gun will defend you from most AI attacks. Finally - and this is perhaps the biggest one - is the AI's inability to realize its own power. Though they often to a good job of attacking you, usually with constant harassment of units that slowly build in strength, the AI fails to recognize easy attempts to destroy your or other AI's commanders. the AI could send a land force into your base, destroy every anti air unit and gun, but lose all their units. Rather than send the 40 bomber units they inevitably will have back at their base doing nothing, face no resistance and easily bomb your commander and kill it, they will do nothing. They just hoarde units and do not use them, even in situations where it would give them the win. Because of this hoarding, the game will slow down and become a huge drag on your processor. This effect is exacerbated on multi planet matches, where, as I previously mentioned, the AI creates large useless land armies. This does, though, give you greater motivation to destroy entire planets, de-laggifying the game.
The only other problem is the bugginess of the game - even after all this time of it being released. Units, especially bots, will get stuck in terrian. Vehicles have a hard time pathfinding making them difficult to use on larger planets. Sometimes launching a multiplayer server sends you into a weird glitch, where you will be taken into a game as a spectator in an all AI match. It's happend to me 4 times. Loading into servers and creating them takes too long sometimes, where the game will freeze up and not respond. The game occasionally crashes when you switch your map in a lobby. Elevation on metal planets sometimes causes glitches where units can be teleported into non-accessible areas, and the only way to kill them is to teleport units there yourself, as nukes will hit the air above them and explode (where the actual, pathable land is for units). Most of the time, though, these glitches are just inconveniences and not game breaking.
Finally, the lack of a community is just devestating to this game. Half of the people who do play it don't have the TITANS expansion, meaning it is hard to find game servers open with TITANS. Half of the servers are not even in America, so they often are a bit laggier. Nobody plays ranked matches, either, so you'll be hard-pressed to find someone to play ranked. Usually, I just play with my friends.
I believe this game still costs about 40 bucks when not on sale. Don't buy it then. I got mine for like 16 dollars. If you can get it at that price, it's a steal. I don't think this game should be 40 dollars, though. Developers are a bit greedy in that respect.
Despite its shortcomings, PA is still an excellent RTS that has all the elements of a great game and is fun to play with your friends. If you can get it on sale, go for it. Otherwise, I would be cautious about paying full price.

Bastion combines a wonderful mix of story, art, music, and gameplay all in a way that feels unique to itself.  The game starts you off with little direction but the narrator's voice as you get used to the controls, combat system, level flow, and most importantly the signature level design.  Every environment is Bastion "builds" itself from the ground up around you creating a very unique take on the "fog of war" style exploration you commonly see in strategy games.  Story-wise all of this is the result of some far-flung calamity that literally destroyed a good chunk of the world.  This puts the story's focus half on keeping up the progress of the Bastion's buildings and exploration of what's left around you.
The graphics are wonderfully rendered and everything looks like a mix of semi-realistic 3D and hand-drawn sprites similar to a sort of top-down version of Braid.  Despite the bleak undertones, the colors are vibrant even in the darker levels and every place feels both desolate yet full of life as you see what's become of the world around you.  All of these are explored via your home base- the titular Bastion which acts both as a hub for missions, power ups, weapons, and side-quests, but also serves to both tell and fill in the holes of the story you missed through the narration that goes on throughout the levels.
There are only four named characters in the game counting the protagonist, but all of them are surprisingly well-developed for how little any of them actually speak.  All of them have special reactions to pretty much everything you bring back with you on each trip and each has a backstory to explore through special bonus levels.  While interaction with them is minimalistic at best, you really grow to know who they are and care about their well being just as much as in games where you spend most of the story talking to them, which is quite the accomplishment on part of the frankly stellar narration.
For how much of the game you're going to spend in combat, it sometimes feels like it takes a back seat to everything going on around you.  However, you'll never get distracted from it and each of the game's unique weapons has its own bonuses and downsides making no combination (you can take two with you, plus one special move of your choice) a bad call.  It really calls to create your own fighting style and do what suits you best.  Due to how you can upgrade any weapons in a variety of ways, there's really no wrong way to go into battle and it's always fun.  What makes things more interesting is that depending on what weapons you pick, how you choose to go about a level, and even how well you're doing or whether you decide to simply derp about, the narrator has a response to pretty much EVERYTHING you do, which adds a bit of flavor and life to the game that feels a lot more like you're actually being watched and having your story told.
The soundtrack of the game is just as varied as everything else in it and always manages to hit the perfect mood, particularly with the wonderfully done vocal songs.  Many levels or situations have their own music and no two songs really feel the same or reused whenever they appear.
Overall Bastion is a wonderful experience that takes roughly seven to ten hours to complete in one playthrough.  It's not a long game, but at the same time it's not any longer or shorter than it needs to be.  But you'll be thankful for that because it means you can easily play it again.  If you ever see it appear in sales or the Humble Bundle as it's often wont to, I highly suggest picking it up if it even sounds remotely interesting to you.

After a very long wait we finally have the un-official 3rd game in the True Crime series. If you've played the 1st game knowing Nick Khang then it's painfully obvious that's who was originally suppose to be Wei Shen in Sleeping Dogs. This does not detract from the game and in a way I think Wei much better suits the quite serious storytelling of the game. I loved Nick Khang and his one liners immensely. True Crime was self aware of how looney it went with the magic, that dragon, the over the top final showdowns, and the borrowed action movie lines. In this way Sleeping Dogs makes an almost complete 180. The story is very serious and without a whole lot of humor but by no means is it made bare or uninteresting. In fact, I honestly think it's one of the best "crime drama" stories I've seen and somewhat up there with L.A. Noire. I mean you actually start to know and feel some way about the characters, like Jackie Ma who is Wei's best friend. Without spoiling too much you are going behind his back and over his head a whole lot through the game and let's just say it never gets resolved. Then there are characters like jimmy Chan who you'll probably end up hating at first, but later come to respect and like him. A whole lot of attention was put into the story and I was extremely surprised probably because I went in with low expectations. Last thing I'll say about this aspect is that I was tickled pink to hear James Hong voicing Uncle Po. I think at one point he says that something is "really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off to no end!" but maybe that's only wishful memory at work.
The game itself is pretty solid. I'm actually conflicted on about half the mechanics because while none of them are really broken some of them could have been much better. For instance, I liked the action car jack sort of borrowed from Just Cause. It means you don't have to stop during a chase to get a new car which is potentially fatal, and you also don't have to completely destroy someone you are chasing either. I do think it could have been better, as when you are hanging on trying to make your way around a truck or something you are prompted to press the "Y" button in order to regain your grip else you will fall off. Not only is it always the "Y" button but it always happens at the exact same time, so it's not even something to keep you tense it just becomes a bit tedious. So again, it's a good idea that falls a little short of what I wanted and it's a nitpick I can live with.
Next thing, the optional missions. They are pretty much worthless as far as what they give, being money and other small helpful things that are rightfully optional. I did every one of them and while they are okay for a distraction they aren't nearly as well thought out as the main storyline and also felt somewhat tedious. I found the races to be way too easy and I never had to restart and I always won by a mile. The karaoke mini game was actually somewhat okay but I'd be surprised to find anyone who would want to play each song more than once unless they had to. I will admit that I do like some of the street missions included Calvin, who is a gang member that will usually blow up something unexpectedly or rob a bank or get into some trouble and then ask that you get him away from the cops. I just feel like most of these missions weren't extremely well thought out and merely a way to prolong the game play a little. That said, seeing as they are optional I can't say it's that big a deal.
Oh and this gets it's very own paragraph. I was phenomenally disappointed by the drug bust side missions. You go in and install a camera after taking out some gang members, and then you're supposed to monitor the camera from your home television. So then it tells you when there is triad activity, and you have to point out who is dealing to have them arrested. Well I was very excited by this and thought I'd have to look very closely as guys shuffled passed each other slipping drugs and money into pockets or between handshakes or maybe a drop of the suit case somewhere. But no guess what you get? You get mostly the same scripted characters doing the same scripted stuff and most of it is standing in place talking or whatever. Oh and that's not the best part, it labels the target for you after 20 or so seconds with a little arrow. It's one of the stupidest things I've seen and definitely the worst part of this game by far. It just feels so lazy and perhaps they got too ambitious but didn't have time to make it better. In any case it was such a letdown and I wonder how it finally got put in the game at all?
The driving is actually a pretty nice mix of arcade and somewhat realistic. You're never going to spin out unless you want to, but at the same time you are going to have to slow down to make tight bends. It's no GRID but for the genre I think it's satisfactory enough for everyone to enjoy it except for the most extreme fans of Realistic Driving. Some of the lower end cars feel a bit too weak for my liking but it makes the Bugatti's power feel like a gift from the heavens. So overall the driving is very good and I have no bad feelings about that.
The gun play to me is a mixed bag. You see, the game encourages some very John Woo style action as True crime did. While I can appreciate that I am myself a very conservative type of gunman. I try to play strategically and slowly without exposing myself too much or running out of ammo to the point it's probably only hurting me. So just try to get it into your head that you are not an average human being, you are Wei Shen, an apparently near invincible killing machine who can hop over tables and steal guns on the fly making ammo simply a fleeting number with no real consequence. Seriously though, live in the moment and go all out or else you wont be able to fully appreciate the gunfights very much.
The melee fighting is in my opinion quite good. It is very reminiscent of the Batman Arkham Asylum or City games, both of which I like. I do think the targeting system during said fights can be quite a problem when you can't target the person you want. I still don't appreciate the fact you get circled by 10 guys and they attack you basically 1 by 1, as a gang of guys who normally work together to beat people up are going to understand how to come at an opponent in at least pairs. All those little nitpicks aside I like it. The Dim Mak counter is easily my favorite and if only it had been accompanied by Bruce Lee vocals.
That leads me to the next nitpick. I was not a fan of the whole Face XP mechanic. You see, you can start off or find and unlock a lot of cool clothing and other accessories. For example, Chen Zhen's outfit from Fists of Fury. Oh but there is a catch. You have to have a high enough face level. Face is gained mostly through the side missions I mentioned earlier and unlike the useful Cop XP and Triad XP that gets you different skills as you unlock them, it only let's you equip clothing. Now some of the clothing has bonuses attached to them when worn, but you'll only ever need Triad XP Bonus due to the fact it's probably the most difficult to obtain. So again, face is something optional but I couldn't use most of the clothes I wanted to use until the game was nearly 75% completed. I felt cheated by this but it didn't stop me from liking the game.

To begin this review, I would like to start off by saying that I am a tad biased as I have been a huge fan of the Steet Fighter games before this new iteration and am an avid supporter of the Fighting Game Community (FGC). I love fighting games and I have played most modern fighters (Street Fighter, Tekken, Smash 4, etc) in an effort to become well-trained and to, as the community so eloquently puts it, "git gud."
All of this being said, I cannot, just
recommend this game to anyone who is a casual player.
Street Fighter V, upon its initial release, lacked little to no content for roping in a new casual playerbase. That's strange considering that that was one of their main goals with SFV. Capcom wanted to bring in new players, competitive or not, to produce mass sales for the game and also perhaps expose the general public to fighting game tournaments as well. Those who weren't really interested in the competitive scene could slowly be introduced to Capcom Pro Tour (CPT) and perhaps even be molded to be competitive players. Capcom failed to do this, however, by not even giving the simplest of features such as CPU versus or even the classic arcade mode.
Every other aspect that recognizes the competitiveness of the game is completely fine and actually very well-made. The netplay can be a little wonky here and there, but other than that returning cast members have been reimagined in unique and exciting ways while some stayed pretty much the same. New original characters are fun and not too overbearing. And with future DLC characters, the roster is ever-expanding for at least the next few years.
All of this being said, I can't bring my heart to recommend this game to anyone who isn't looking to be competitive no matter how much time I put into it. The release was a mess and Capcom, almost 5 months later, are just now getting around to adding some solo modes to the game, including the story mode. There's also the lack of communication on their end (and in their defense they have gotten better at it), but I don't really blame them for that. That's more of a part of Japanese culture when it comes to video games, it seems.
Overall, for competitive players, the game is probably a solid 8/10. For casual players, I can't even really give it a score. All I can say is to stay away and give it a proper year or so to develop, maybe even just look for it when there's a price drop or a sale. If you're looking for some type of casual fighting game on PC, I'd recommend
a very fun Super Smash Bros. style game.

Capcom really wanted to make a game that is easier for casuals to pick up, but still have things that appeal to competitive players.
The result?
A watered-down fighting game that gets repetitive and dull.  The game is very linear with how strong offense is and how weak zoning is.  Many mixups are strictly between throw or shimmy, and playing risky is usually a lot more rewarding than playing solid.  Combos are very limited with variety.  Most v-triggers are recycled versions of each other, which is really disappointing.  All v-skills are literally just a special move that is bound to mp+mk but they think they invented something incredible by calling it v-skill.  If they had v-skills as a regular directional input like any other special move, no one would have thought anything different.  The combos are also ridiculously easy to do, as they got rid of tight links that you'd see in any other fighting game.  Some might say this is a good thing, but I always respected good execution, or going for different combos in certain high-pressure situations.  Instead, you now have high-level Zangief players who mash for their links to connect (and it works), which is embarrassing for a competitive fighting game like Street Fighter.  Speaking of Zangief, Capcom really went out of their way to make him so bad in this game.  It's certainly possible to win with him, but you have to work so much harder than anyone else.  (I'm not a Zangief main, but it's just an observation)
I feel bad for anyone who buys this game that doesn't take it remotely seriously (basically if they button mash and just wanna have some fun for a little).  The single player mode is dreadfully bad, though it's never really been that great with the other SF games.  Story mode just came out, so that'll give it a little more spice.  Getting more colors for your character requires you to play through survival mode on different difficulties, which is a boring grind.  Unless you play online against other people, this game really offers nothing interesting for anyone to care about for the offline content.
This game is a rushed, incomplete fighter that should have been much better.  If they let USF4 ride out one more year while they carefully worked on SF5, I'd say the result could be a lot different.  It's a shame, because I was really hyped up for this game, but after trying to give it a chance multiple times, it's not fun.  Capcom said they may add changes to the character balance or game mechanics at the end of every year, so maybe things will turn around at that point.  However, the character balance is mostly fine.  It's the game mechanics that really make the game boring and not hype. No matter how excited you get for the next DLC character coming out, you always need to remember that they will still be restricted to the game mechanics.

So I will preface this by saying that I kickstarted these VNs without having played them before - this is my first experience with these VNs so take that how you will =s
Instead of writing a huge♥♥♥♥♥wall of text, I'll just give a quick little rundown and more or less an overarching review of both VNs.
8/10
+ The biggest positive these two VNs have going for them is definitely character development. Throughout both Extra and Unlimited, you're introduced to the main characters of the series and you'll get to know them very well. You'll see each person's personal development, which makes you all that more attached to them.
+ The writing is well done. Each character has a pronounced personality that shows through their dialogue. Not only that, the dialogues themselves are funny, emotional, and impactful.
|
-----> I'm going to say here that the plot is lacking, but not horrible. Extra is a typical romcom type harem VN, and Unlimited is more or less the same with a different setting. Both have their strong plot points, especially Unlimited, but it all feels like a huge build-up for Alternative and as such, don't really stand out on their own.
- I also docked some points for the music, as it didn't have as much of an emotional impact as I thought it would. By all means, the score is good, but not as inpactful as it should be, especially in a VN.
Overall, if you were to compare these two VNs without knowing about their relation to Alternative (the third installment and widely considered the best VN), you'd still get really solid reads worth your time, especially if you're a fan of VNs. The plot is enough to get you to keep reading, and again it's really well written but it's the characters, I feel, that really make you stay.

Muv-Luv Extra/Unlimited is now my personal standard to compare purchases for VNs.
The game is effectively a Part A and Part B set up, Extra striking along the usual slice of life romantic comedy that if you are even a novice anime fan will be more than familiar with the tropes.
Part B, Unlimited is a set up where your doofy Male Harem protagonist of Extra finds himself in a world on the brink of annihiliation, his saving grace is that it is aparently a very parallel world and many of his closest friends (*cough* harem *cough*) are still present and he forges new relationships with cadets on the verge of placing themselves on the frontlines of a losing war.
The VN while presented in a familiar "chose your own adventure" set up that the experience is almost expectedly done so that as the reader you experience each route at least once, for my personal experience I ran a Miki route for Extra and conluded with a Chizuruin Unlimited and found an engaging emotional read.
Afterwards, I backtracked to Extra and found many blatant call backs in Unlimited and found a significant lore connection between the parts with further route run throughs.

It takes a long time for this game to pay off, but it's well worth it.  It's actually a prequel to a better game, but stands well on it's own.
Muv-Luv Extra, the first half of this game, is fairly typical.  It would be an okay game on it's own, but nothing particularly outstanding.  It follows the standard template of a harem/comedy visual novel.  Anyone familiar with the genre won't be much surprised by anything.  If you happen to not be especially fond of them, for the sake of the other games' story you really only need to finish either Sumika or Meiya's route.
Muv-Luv Unlimited, the second half, is quite different, in a good way.  Building on the first game, the characters you've known get thrown into a much more serious situation, and it draws you in to that upside-down world quite well.  It's a war story, with some of the original game's comedy thrown in.
And while Umlimited is good, it can all be considered part of the build up to the final game which is not included here, Muv-Luv Alternative.  Alternative is one of the best visual novels out there, and you don't get the full experience unless you play this game first.

Bastion....where to begin. That's much the premise for the game itself, amusingly. Starting off, it may not seem like much.
But really. The music, as many have mentioned, is absolutely amazing. High quality, soulful, it conveys much of the world to you.
Even more amazing then the music is the story. Playing the first half of the game, you would laugh at this statement. The narrator's tone is intially sardonic, dry, and deprecating, mocking your failures lightheartedly.  It feels like a light-hearted 3rd person brawler with a floating twist and a strange setting. Really, it's just setting the stage for the parts to come. Trust me on this.
Halfway through the game, everything comes together, and you begin to see the true feeling of the game that the first half has been building up. The proper tone and framing of the game is set, and I just about broke down crying when it did. The game gives you true agency in deciding what happens, and the moral of the game is literally what you make it - akin to Deus Ex: Human Revolution, except less heavy handed.
The mechanics are amazing. The guard system is your friend, and after the intal warm up period once later weapons are unlocked the game may appear to get easy. The weapon upgrade system gives you plenty of options, and Bastion's building system has upgrades as well. Of particulary note, The Shrine acts as a hard mode, and it gives you rewards for such - use it if things start to get too easy. They won't be at the end of the game, no matter what it may seem like earlier then that, I can guarantee.
This is the only game I have ever gotten on sale that I wish I had not, that way I could have given more money to the development team, because I feel like this game is worth the full $15. The soundtrack is amazing - if you're going to buy it, buy it directly from the development studio, cut the middle man out.

This game is unique due to its more mature tone, sophisticated storylines, and relative realism when compared with its contemporaries.  Wei (the main character) is a fully realized character about whom you really care.  The supporting cast also ends up leaving you feeling surprising invested in their individual fates and motivations.

Overall, this game  has a LOT to offer and shouldn't be overlooked or seen as a lesser game in a genre dominated by giant hype machines.  It is my opinion that this game is a MUCH better game than anything the GTA series has pumped out in years, surpasses Saint's Row 4, and can easily trade blows with Saint's Row: The Third.
