I played all Fallouts to date, and my favorite is Fallout 2, by far. That being said, I think Fallout 4 is a great game and a good Fallout game. Those who say otherwise are usually purists that haven't explored everything this game has to offer. The world is fun to explore and full of surprises. It has some neat and original locations, cool quests and quite a few interesting characters. Sure, it also has its own share of flaws, but the backlash it's been getting is wildly unwarranted.
As for the "paid mods" scandal - I don't think paid mods is such a bad idea at all. It really depends on the execution. NWN1's paid mods (which were called Premium Modules back then in 2002) were a great success and produced some very high quality adventures. Plus, they didn't hurt the free mods community one bit. Bethesda should be given the chance on that matter.

Nothing else than a masterpiece, but what else to expect from VALVe? Left 4 Dead was the flagship of the zombie apocalypse genre. With a fairly interesting story-line, as interesting as it can get when zombies are trying to eat you. The game is split up into episodes, or movies, where the four protagonists make their way through all imaginable zombie infested areas.
I think Left 4 Dead didn't start the zombie culture, as there were books much earlier, but the game obviously did a great part of magnifying the genre, not only for games but for movies and TV-shows as well. The game has a lot of gore and darkness flowing through it, and I remember being terrified in my first play-through of the game. Looking back - this game didn't have a long lifetime, not as it's "competitor" Killing Floor, that is still kicking.
Valve kind of screwed Left 4 Dead over with Left 4 Dead 2 being released only a year after the original. The sequel wasn't even close to having the same atmosphere as it's predecessor, with all that darkness and grain film filter. Valve later ported over the whole Left 4 Dead into the sequel, which gives no reason to play the first game at all, which is very saddening, indeed.

I have beed following this game from update to update since the very begining of this game. With 77 hrs of playing, I have to say that this game was intriguing at first, with the new systems and mechanics that are unique. You have a ship to build, some randomly generated dungeons to conquer, millions of planets to set foot on, which are indeed some cool features of sandbox. However, behind this cool concept the game seems not to be so well executed. First this game currently does not have a well-plotted storyline to follow but a penguin-themed army. The quests are irrelevant as NPCs just ask you to burn your fuel and find stuff. Second, combat is boring, moves are rigid, you do not get much reaction from monsters. Third, upgrading your gears becomes boring as you feel that mining is repetitive after you reach tier 3 gear.
That is why I prefer Terraria. Once the player cannot see the main story, quests do not provide enough feeling of immersion. Plus that the targets players focus on are thrown into this vast ocean of planets, which inevitably prolong your gameplay. And that will result in your exhaustion after hours of playing, and you will find that you are repeating what you have done.
I have read some info in the archive and notice that the developers have actually done a lot in building the background. And the frescoes in that ancient ruin are magnificent too. And that's why I still recommend this game because in the future updates there might be more culture in this game. It is still in early access anyway.
**Edit**
When this game came out of Early Access as Starbound 1.0 I have to admit that this game is fairly complete now. Now we have a proper intro, a main story line, and a lot more cool stuff, which will surely grant another 100+ hours of gameplay if you choose to create a new character as I did. And when you beat the final boss there is still the awesome Frackin Universe mod you can download and try which will give you another 50+ hours of gameplay (if you don't cheat). With the support of steam workshop, this game is good enough.

As one of the Kickstarter Backers for Muv-Luv, when I saw it coming out in English, I knew I had to have it.  Only in the first couple of hours, so the review is going to be based not on the entire plot, which is a good long plot and therefore to be experienced over time, but the technicals of the game. (Particularly Extra - the review will be updated as I go through the rest of the game.)  So let's begin.
Voice Acting: Check.
Visuals: The Visuals are not the most recent, but Muv-Luv has done a lot more work visually than most Visual Novels bother with, which lends a very different feel to the game and enchances the overall system.  For example, the sprite's lips move when the voice acting is playing, which makes it feel like an anime cutscene.  Characters turn and aren't always facing the same direction, and so forth.  At the same time, they do have scenes that use very little in the way of art budget, but have done a decent job in making those scenes feel like they are supposed to be in that art style for comedic effect.
Music:  The Music is nice, worth hearing, but it hasn't yet moved to levels of To the Moon in that last finale.  I'll update if that changes.
Scenes and Story: To be done, once I have gotten another 10 hours into this game.
I would totally recommend this game to anyone who likes Visual Novels.

Something about Don't Open the Doors speaks to my inner child. I guess you could just call me a sucker for claymation. It all goes back to when I was much younger. That playdoh just seemed like a world of infinite possibilities. To be fair, I made infinite snakes, so many snakes. I wasn't very talented. That never changed the fact I was impressed with people who could create worlds with paper and clay, so I find these types of games alluring. Combining two mediums is always a fun idea and usually rife with imagination and expressions of art. From Kirby's Epic yarn to Armikrog, and Tearaway, these games are full of wonderful art and look completely different when compared to most games.
As you can imagine, when I saw Don't Open the Doors, I was very excited. Now unlike Armikrog, this title was an action/adventure title. It has more in common with games like Bastion, where the action is intense, and hordes of enemies and bosses await.
So much so that there is a tiny little cameo from The Kid in the game. There are some key differences between the two, but they share a strange universe, RPG elements, and a top down view of the action.
Upon loading up the game you immediately feel like you've lost your footing. While a reference to Alice tumbling down the rabbit hole feels cliche, it really does fit the universe of Don't Open the Doors. Sarcastic talking vegetation, and merchants who won't barter until you learn their name; the universe is quite strange and it takes some time to get familiar with things.
The basic gist is that Doors have appeared all over the place, giving people the creeps and making wildlife become dangerous and hostile. You are given the Megabomb to detonate the biggest door and hopefully stop this plague of spreading doors.
Of course, you lose the Megabomb and your wacky adventure begins.
That is about as straight forward a story as you're going to get from this game, because Doors' story is nonsensical. One second you're joining a bug hating tribe, the next you are using red apples to smash red porcupines so you can paint yourself.
It's a weird game, but weird in a good way. Just try and relax, enjoy the journey and don't worry about details.
The games main selling point is obviously the unique art style. Your quest takes place on this huge over world map that is filled to the brim with dungeons, shops, doors, and more cactus than you can shake a stick at. The claymation is so well done that you almost forget that it's there. Especially during combat. Then suddenly you'll focus on something and see all the shapes and moulds. There are dozens of different designs and all the environments are blended beautifully with the action on screen. There is a bit of palette swapping for certain plants/trees, but you will find more unique designs more then not.
The only gripe I have, is I would've liked a bit more cut scenes or more voice work in the game. Just to give the characters more personality. Not that its lacking whimsical charm but I felt it would've been enhanced even more.
Despite the game being called Don't Open the Doors, you actually spend the entire game doing the exact opposite and opening them. This is where you find a bulk of the progression, power ups, and equipment you will use throughout the game. Each door is an isolated area that has a unique level design and varying degree of difficulty. Some doors are a straight forward smash/grab type of deal, others can have you going through a labyrinth. The level design is very impressive and it's one of the things I loved most about this title. You never knew what was going to be behind a door and it kept things fresh and exciting.
Progression is pretty simple and the game isn't exactly cutting edge. The way it works is the farther the door is away from where you started the harder it is to beat. You start the game off with a basic hammer, no armour, and no skills. As you complete more doors you get all of the above and more.
If you play the game smart and complete areas as you advance into them, the progression isn't hard to keep up. There are no difficulty spikes, but the game does ramp up the chaos quite efficiently.
By the end I was at 4000HP and I destroyed everything that crossed my path. The reason I mention this, is that if you do skip around doors, you can become easily overwhelmed. The game doesn't do much in the way of hand holding.
Fans of destruction and chaos can rejoice, as nearly everything in this game is destructible. You can squish and blow up everything and the game encourages you to for exploration purposes. One neat thing is that mostly everything you wreck drops something that has a use. While the inventory system is on the simple side, if you collect a bug antenna, someone needs it, corn seeds? Use it in a popcorn gun. Found a diamond? Upgrade your armour. You get the idea. The inventory screen is mostly there for informative purposes. I used it for the map on occasion but the game automatically equips the best gear. It's nice that it is there, even if slightly unnecessary.
Combat is something I feel might be divisive in this game. One of the key differences between this and something like Bastion, is that Doors combat can come off rather cumbersome. It takes a good full second to swing your hammer and the primary way the game makes combat difficult is through being stunned. You have to time each one of your shots perfectly or get hit and watch the animation reset. It's annoying at first, I will admit, but eventually you learn to master it. Ranged weapons help quite a bit when you finally get one, but limited ammo makes them a non-reliable method.
While the combat grew on me, there were moments I spent far too much time running from a bug that hit way faster than me, thus I couldn't kill it. I had to back off a good pace, time my shot and squish. This is a tactic you will become quite familiar with by playing this game. A simple solution, I felt, would've been a dodge button or maybe a faster primary weapon that does less damage. One thing I did find curiously lacking, was different types of primary weapons. There are four different ranged weapons, three bombs, but only the hammer and its upgraded versions. Maybe in the sequel? Thankfully, the game does feature full controller support so this helps alleviate quite a bit of heartache.
Doors is always is giving you something to do and the game is incredibly addictive/fun. I found myself playing for hours at a time and with the secrets hidden everywhere, doors everywhere, there is always something to collect, upgrade, or a quest to complete.
The game lasted much longer then I expected and the over-world is bigger then is let on. This was a pleasant surprise, but nearing the end it does become a bit of a rinse-repeat scenario with doors, and upgrades. I got a solid ten hours out of the game but I might have missed a couple of things here and there. There is some potential for replay, but I think that is for people who are looking to 100% the game. There are some different dialogue choices, but I doubt it leads to any other outcomes.
Speaking of outcomes, the games door bosses and final boss are all really fun. While you mostly just end up bombing the hell out of them, they all look really distinct and feel epic in scope. The ending of the game is on point with the rest of the game, weird. I won't give it away but the game sets up for a sequel and just ends. To be fair, it's not like the game is about saving a princess or anything.
Other areas of the game are just unique as the games art style. The music starts off as a soothing and harmonious instrumental music and then breaks out into rock suddenly. The soundtrack is an area you could tell that they spent quite a bit of time developing and it shows. It's fresh and weird, and I personally enjoyed it. You can purchase the soundtrack as part of a bundle or on the side, which is always great.

This game reminds me of a great series as a kid called ‘The Trap Door’ that was also made with clay, and i swear this game was inspired by it.
So ignore any hate on this game its wonderful, the art direction the animation its amazing and you can tell straight away the amount of effort gone in to creating this.
So the story is straight forward to understand, its not complicated or confusing it just gets straight to the point and is pretty basic, the doors have taken over the land and your job is to get rid of them its a simple as that.
But it will make you laugh, the dialogue and characters are great and all fit in well with the game, nothing or nobody feels out of place and merge in well with the story.

Don’t open the doors:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

At some stage in our lives we all been introduced to modelling clay, predominantly in our youth! Hold on you old fellow, haven’t you heard? Doors are appearing all over the city and everything within their boundaries is starting to talk. . . Mushrooms, Pumpkins. ..  all want to kill you! Oh my God, the vegie killers are upon us! Help our yellow clay friend to save the city, but beware of opening the doors!
Don’t open the doors is a RPG/ adventure/action game where you take control of a loveable yellow clay character whose goal is to find the main door and destroy it with a Megabomb to save the city!
At the start, your character is naked; vibrant yellow but naked!  You will be given the task of delivering the Megabomb to the city guards. However, after taking reception of this powerful item, the guards have other plans for you. Your next challenge is to kill a monster in a terrifying dungeon.
As you reach your objective, you will be quite surprised with the outcome! You will acquire a massive hammer to squash enemies throughout this incredible journey. As you travel the world, you’ll meet other clay characters who will give you quests to complete. This interesting clay world is full of danger; cacti will throw their spikes at you, hedgehogs will take some of your health each time you touch them, and bugs will run at you from all directions to inflict as much damage as possible. But that is not all - bees, flies and spiders will also make challenging opponents.
Then you‘ll see the doors - you can’t miss them, as each one has a green globe on top of its frame. When you enter the doors, you are really going to have fun! There are challenging dungeons full of coins to collect and plenty of enemies to kill. There are a lot of chests to find and open: yellow ones with coins, green ones with pills (big and small, to regenerate your health, and you might even find some purple ones, which will have a combination of both. At the end of each dungeon, you might pick up a book or a special potion. The potion will give you an extra 50 health points but if you find a book then you will meet the white clay guy! He is a wise character and will teach you a special ability in exchange for the book. Oh, I nearly forgot - in some dungeons you might came across keys. These keys can unlock special doors in the clay world and they have great goodies behind them!
In terms of bosses, well, I haven’t been that lucky so far, as they are quite challenging - which is really good! The big red cactus is surprisingly tough! I keep running around, dropping exploding fruits (yes; haven’t you heard of them? Big yellow fruits that explode) with no success killing the cactus at all!  Maybe I should work on improving my strategy.
I really like the artwork in this game and the combination of RPG/Action (hack and slash) is really fun. The soundtrack is also really cool. The only downside in my opinion is the controls, which are a bit rough around the edges, but still playable. I would have expected them to be smoother.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great artwork
-	Great soundtrack
-	Good humour
-	Original world, fun to play with plenty of doors to open
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls could have been smoother
Don’t open the doors is an original game in a world build of clay. Really fun to play!

Overall: 9/10 - This game is really fun to play. If you're into games like Werewolf and Mafia, Town of Salem is a perfect hybrid between the two with even more roles and being able to play it online is genius. I've always enjoyed card and board games, but it's difficult to get enough people for the optimal experience. Town of Salem is the first online multiplayer version of one of these games that hasn't flopped due to poor programming.
Replayability: 10/10 - Town of Salem has so many different gamemodes and roles that it never gets boring. Even once you've played as every role, it's unlikely you'll get bored because getting the same role more than 2 times in a row is near enough impossible without scrolls (items which boost your chance of a certain role).
Multiplayer: 7/10 - One possible downfall of the game is that it's availible for free if you play it in a browser. The fact you have a paid-for Steam version as well is what makes me feel this is unfair. I've seen some people take advantage of the fact that the game can be free-to-play and completely broken the rules. The inclusion of 'Last Wills' and 'Death Notes' are usually a good thing. They allow Town (good) roles to keep a log of activity and can even be used to pass on suspicion, however they can be used by the Mafia to reveal fellow Mafia members which is unfair.
I can understand that all games that are traditionally card games need rules, but some of the features of the game can make rule-breaking a lot easier. There is a report system, though getting temporarily or permenantly banned is not too much of a punishment if players can make another free account. ToS needs to decide if the game is free-to-play with in-game purchases or a paid-for game.
Pros:
- One of the first games of its kind to work
- Fun to replay
- Endless methods of winning
- Enjoyable alone or with friends
- Most roles are fun to play as
Cons:
- A mixture of free and paid-for accounts means that Steam users have to deal with people who make free accounts to cheat until they get banned
- Rules are easily broken
- Customisable items can make players identifiable to friends
- The few boring roles likely to make players quit are all Town roles, making a carefully balanced game a lot more difficult.

I've bought this game without knowing a lot about it, I've just seen a gameplay.
So, the game basic idea is a tower defense, actually a first person tower defense where the main objective is protect a core. You can build your turrets and barrier and, when the horde comes you can use your two weapons (a main weapon and a secondary weapon) for killing the enemies.
About the scenary...is simply amazing! the background is well done (as you can see on the screenshots) and the musics are enjoyable.
About the enemies, I have to tell you that the hordes come randomly, I mean that when you play a level and then you play it again, waves are not always the same. The monsters you have to kill are a lot and differents, some small, fast and weak, others big...very...VERY big, slow but with a solid armor. Of course flying enemies are in this game too. Sometimes you have to defeat a BOSS that is a bigger and freakingly strongest version of one of the other enemies with a stronger attack or a different (but always strongest) one. Some monsters have weak points so if you can you can use them for a faster massacre.
There are a lot of different towers with different strength, speed and specialized again different tipe of monsters that you can unlock by levelling up. Same thing happens for the secondary weapons and the skills you can give to your pg, a lot of secondary weapons and skill that suit better to a particular pg more than to another one.
A thing that I have found quite fascinating is the possibility of the multiplayer, you can choose to play alone by playing a private campaign or you can allow other players to enter in your map and play with you.
So if you are looking for a game with a quite good plot, a lot of action and sometimes very difficult enemies, Sanctum 2 is the game for you.

I have to admit, I didn't have a lot of confidence in this game. Everyone I knew was talking about it; my friends were talking about it, gaming magazines and online articles were raving about it, even one of my teachers at school talked about how great the game was. But I did not yeild, the game did not look interesting to me and I had no way of trying it for myself without paying for the game so I didn't risk it. That was until I played around with the google chrome apps.
One of the apps was actually a demo for Bastion. One of my other friends had talked about the game but never played it himself so we both decided to try out the demo and see what we thought of it. Well for starters, the light humor of the game caught my attention. Starting up the game, a narrarator announces almost everything you do. "The kid wakes up from bed. He walks on a path forming in front of him." Then I accidentally fell of the edge of the stage only to hear, "Then the kid fell to his death... just kidding" as my character fell from the sky back onto the stage. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, but that doesnt mean the story isn't a grim one, but I won't spoil that for you.
The graphics are gorgeous, the kind of sprites I wouldn't have imagined of existing when I was a kid, in combination with the blooming effects, this game is gorgeous. I can't think of a single way to improve its looks. As for the gameplay itself, it's set up like a Diablo styled game; it's a top down, isometric view beat em up of sorts. The combat is really fun and fast paced; mixing together melee and ranged weapons is extremely fun. You are given a variety of weapons to destroy your opponents, with the option to level up each individually at the level hub. But the customization doesn't end there, you can also choose special alcoholic beverages that work as perks to power up your character.
Admittedly, I am not going to tell you anything else about the game. I didn't even know this much going into it so I won't spoil the rest for you. Just buy it and enjoy, this game is most definitely worth it.
Definitely a different game then the one's i've played in the past with GTA and Saints Row series. The overall mechanics of the game I very much enjoy!

This game is the kind of pirate game I have been waiting years for. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED! This is a hidden GEM of a game and more people should know about it. It is currently in early access alpha but don't let that discourage you, because I have never had so much fun in a game as compared to moments when I am commanding a crew of people who are dilligently following my every order. Believe me, if you like to lead, Blackwake lets you exercise your leadership skills out there on the ocean in high intensity naval warfare. The community doesn't lean towards toxicity, however there may be an occasional teamkiller but they usually get kicked fairly quick. There are always servers, battles range from 16 to 50+ man servers, the 16 player servers for players who like 1v1. Got servers for 2v2. Also a treasure hunt gamemode where you race to an island to grab a treasure chest and try to defend it once you got it aboard your ship. Boarding enemy ships is great fun too, delivers very satisfying moments.
Thoughts on captain -
Personally, I prefer to be the captain and steer the ship and shout orders, it's real fun to do when you have a mic and feels rewarding when you have a crew that works together and listens to you. In order for a crew to be successful, it cannot be captained by someone without a mic. It technically CAN be done, but it's harder to do and as I said, you can't properly command a ship without being able to give vocal commands.
Thoughts on crewmen -
You manually reload cannons and aim them at however many meters away the enemy ship is from you. Repair holes from enemy cannon fire, sails, etc. Pumps so that the ship won't sink once it has holes in it. Basically, hope for a captain that has a mic and can tell you and everybody what it is you're doing and when you're doing it. Pay attention to commands.
TL;DR
If you love pirates, if you love naval warfare, if you love teamwork and communication and strategic elements in games then this game is for you. Most importantly, if you love being out there on the seven seas with cannon balls flying through the air and seeing your crewmates being ripped to shreds by said cannon balls, then THIS is the game for you! Buy without hesitation!

I've been playing fighting games for the majority of my life and while I definitely enjoy playing this game I am not able to offer a recommendation to buy it.
First off, if you're playing this for a single player experience you're in for a huge disappointment.  The current story mode allows you to pick one of the cast and play a few mindless battles puntucated by boring cutscenes that offer little in the way of depth or even clarity.  Purportedly an updated Story mode is to be released soon but new cast members were supposed to be added every month and we saw how that hasn't quite worked out. Ergo don't hold your breath.
Next if you're primarily intersted in the multiplayer experience like myself you will probably be frustrated as well.  As of the most recent patch the match making system seems to have been reblanced quite nicely for Ranked Play from the previous iteration of having to fight against players of vastly disparate rankings from your own.  This seems to have been done however a the cost of stable connections.  If you've read much about SFV you are probably aware that the net code for the game is attrocious and this recent patch does not seem to have done much in the way of fixing this.   Add on top of this the meager penalty that is currently in place to prevent rage quitting from matches does little to nothing to deter players from abandoning games even after a loss to negate both point loss to them and point gain to you.  The combination of the two can and does create a highly frustrating state of play that only seems to escalate at higher ranked play.
Lastly, it's impossible to communicate with the player base on any social level other than prefabricated text lines in Battle Lounges.  Nothing substantive can be expressed as the lines are simply "GG" or "Potato!".
The bottom line is the game is enjoyable but it certainly seems like this is a case of a pay to play version of extensive beta testing for a product to be released at a later date.  The game may be worth purchasing in the future but that day is still pretty far off.

For the multi-player aspects of the game, I almost want to  recommend giving the game a shot. I can't do that and feel honest about it, saddly.
I loved the first Sanctum. The combination of tower defense and FPS was brilliantly done and made multi-player even more interesting as one could choose to focus on either towers or weapons when spending resources. This made the experience more versatile than other games out there. The mazes one could craft could be complex and powerful all on there own, needing only minimal FPS support to bring down the enemy.
In Sanctum 2, that has all gone away.
The addition of a seperate resource for tower bases means that some maps, while having the potential for gread mazes, allow no more than a very basic level of defense and no real ability to slow the advance of enemies that are much more dificult to bring down than in the original game.
The ability to upgrade weapons has also been removed, meaning that all attention from resources must be given to the too-few towers players are able to build. The weapons start off feeling a bit under-powered against the early waves and regress from there to seeming useless by the later waves.
Many of the maps seem poorly made as well. Some do not allow bulding on the path of the enemies at all, while other have such narrow, short paths to the core that bulding more than a half-dozen towers is simply out of the question. Some maps seem like they should be well suited to certain characters (good sniping points for one, narrow turns perfect for shotguns or rockets on others) but the inability to propperly maneuver enemies severly limits the effectiveness of those advantages.
Having set weapons for each of the four characters also takes away a lot of the customization options available in the first game. Each character also gets a passive ability to help make the most of their primary weapon. It seems to me that if the makers wanted to create four classes, it would have made things much more itneresting to give them each some kind of active ablities to use. While the passive abilities are nice, they tend to vanish into the background during gameplay.
The two things that make the game playable for more than one sitting are the leveling system and the multiplayer. The leveling system makes replying maps a viable option and gives players something to look forward to. Multiplayer increases playability by allowering the player to have a fighting chance on later maps. Saddly, the map designs also make certain characters useless in muliplayer. For instance, if a map has lots of cliffs to fall off, or water (oh-so-deadly water!) to fall into, you can forget using the shotgunner in multiplayer. He will spend most of his time re-spawning after having been blown off the map by a teammate's rocket.
I enjoy certain aspects of the game, and it might be worth getting on sale, but for the full price of this one, you can pick up much better games. Dungeon Defenders or Defense Grid come to mind, and I would recommend either.

The good, the bad, and the ugly....
Good:
Even though its early access (and therefore limited missions), great looking game. I like it, and can see huge potential.  A nice WW2 RTS, that builds on B1 and B2. Will cater to both vets of the original series and new players to the series.  Some innovative ideas, like having a base that can be live 24/7. I like having both single player campaigns and PVP. Very good tech support.
Bad:
A few  bugs (eg, can't save game), units doing funny things sometimes, server problems, lack of tutorials, initial single missions too hard (so will turn off new players). No encyclopedia or help functions. As B3 is still in development phase, changes to game interphase, AI, etc annoying - but to be expected with early access.
Ugly:
Too expensive for what you get at the moment (Oct 2016).  USD $15 - $20 would be about the right price for what you get because its sort of a third of what the full game will be, and still buggy.
Official website for B3 very poor in terms of game information and details.
In summary - the full release should be very good, but the early access version is a bit too expensive for now. A great WW2 RTS strategy game, big potential if Nival get it right.
I recommend it (the game) - simply because I can see the potential once its fully functional, and early access (despite the price) gives a great feel for what the full release will be like in 2017.

There is so much that I love about this game I don't know where to begin.  The first Sanctum was a very good game in my opinion, but it had its shortcomings, most of which were remedied here in the sequel.  The new class system is so fantastic!  A TF2 addict like myself is going to love the classes.  The ability to jump over  your walls is very handy!  In the first Sanctum, you needed those lousy elevator whatcha-ma-call-ems to get over them.  The new character perk system trumps the old weapon upgrading system.  Who wants to have to deal with that each round? Jeez, I just want a simple layout, I'm here to shoot stuff! This sequel let's you focus your time on the towers, rather than having to allocate funds toward weapons each round.  One thing I really enjoy about S2 is that they give you just a small amount of towers each round instead of a bunch at the beginning.  This  has made co-op much quicker, and makes it seem more like a cooperative effort.  Believe me, the bickering about towers in the old Sanctum were so annoying.  There was always that "artist" who wanted to create some amazing design, and it would take them FOREVER to finish it.
Buy this game.  Its suits the shell-shocker and the logical strategist alike.

This my first time experiencing MUV-LUV asa visual novel.  I backed the project on kickstarter merely on a whim (300 dollar tier).
I read the twitterfeed and played EXTRA first.   This review will be based on the first hour and a half of playing through Muv-Luv Extra.
You take the perspective of Takeru Shirogane a teenager who is actually a genius mech pilot...at least that's what the first two minutes of EXTRA are teasing only to find out that all a dream.  You're actually just a normal Japanese high school boy being awoken  by your childhood friend Sumika as part of a daily routine. Along the way you meet your other classmates Meiya, Tama, Sakaki, Ayamine and Marimo all of which take up stereotypical heroine roles in this visual novel such as the transfer student who you promised to marry when you were kids, the class rep, the underclassman, etc.
Now I've played plenty of visual novels, and I thought that extra was gonna be dry.  I was really tempted to start unlimited first to jump into the drama but digressed after reading the twitterfeed.  Boy am I glad I stuck to playing extra first.  The character reactions are so hilarious (even if they aren't animated) and every character (including the dog)  just meshes so well together.
Another feature I like is when you close the game and open it again you start off in the same spot as before so you don't have to accidentally worry about accidentally closing the game without saving.  Second is no text boxes, just text.
The music is pretty catchy and the visuals are more than just character cutout portraits.  Overall, the hour and a half I played just passed by in an instant.  I'd recommend this novel for anyone who enjoys visual novels or is just starting to get into visual novels.

Muv-Luv is a visual novel split across three parts: Extra, Unlimited, and Alternative. This Steam version contains both Extra and Unlimited, while Alternative will be released at a later date.
Extra plays like a very typical visual novel from Japan: a childhood friend of the opposite sex, a sudden change in the main character's life, multiple potential love interests in a high school setting. Extra is considered the weakest entry of the Muv-Luv trilogy, but it's there for a reason. It introduces the characters that will be present in the future parts of the triology, and allows you to get attached to them. This Steam version does allow you to access Unlimited without playing through Extra, but I strongly urge you to give Extra a shot first.
To avoid spoilers (I strongly recommend people to go in to Muv-Luv blind), I'll have to be vague in describing Unlimited. The high school romantic comedy setting of Extra is completely wiped away and replaced by... well, something, and this is when the story REALLY takes off. Muv-Luv follows the typical VN format: a slice of life comedy portion for you to get you attached to the characters, and then a major event that completely turns things around and you're caught up in a swirl of emotions.
Having read my fair share of visual novels, the Muv-Luv trilogy is among the best for good reason. If you enjoy visual novels, I strongly urge you to give Muv-Luv a shot.

Well... It was nice.
10 hours and I had beaten this game 100% (not all achivements though).
You know, nowadays it is rare to me, to actually finish the game.
Usually it is too long, with not so engaging story, and lots of fetch quests.
This game on the other hand, was fun, was fresh, and, dare i say, was "handcrafted" (see, what I did here? ^_^)
Closest analogy, that I can think of this game - is mix between Bastion and Neverhood.
Creator of this game do not shame themselfs from this comparisson, proudly wearing "badge of honor", on their sleeve.
Hell - they even made one of the optional "door" levels - full reference to Bastion.
Lets now talk about pros and cons. (+ and -), as I see them.
- Probably poor control scheme on keybord. I used controller, and had lots of fun, but some fights and "dodge puzzles" will be probably be hard without fluid movement.
- Story ends abruptly, and lacks "impact", in comparison to whole "crazy journey", that is leading to it. It's not because it is bad, but because game world is bright, colourful and funny. If I would give any advise to developers - I'd said to make like several minutes long animation film, and give it as an "end prize". (I know, that this requires work and time, but without it, I cant think of any possibility to make ending of this game feel "good", or like an actual end.)
- There is no "full completion" bonus, and some side quest reward just appear in game later down the line. I got at least several of armors/helmets/weapons, in quantity higher then 1. I suppose it's fine, but I just wanted even more content, I gues.
- Some in-level passes closes behind you. Not a generally bad thing, because it allows "different routs" for beating levels, but still annoyed me from time to time (cause I tried to look at all available to me nooks and crannies)
+ Fixed camera angle. This is actually wery good, because not only whole game looks super nice, but also there are a lots of "secrets", that use this camera angle thing.
+ Difficulty. It is well balanced (for controller at least). At no point in game was I frustrated, overwhelmed, or needed to "grind" anything. I died several times on bosses and some "puzzles", but was not mad at game of control sheme at any time. Nicely done.
+ Visuals - 10/10 (and some warm fluffy thing on top of the score)
+ Humor. Game doesn't take itself too seriously, or too unseriously, creating fun "living" world, that you can totally belive in.
+ Music. As I am gettig things - it was specialy made to this game, enlarging game experience even more.
+ No need to "open all doors", to beat game - so around of 70% of the game is optional. Also, there are several ways to complete like hath of the quests, which is super nice, and allows you to play "your way".
All in all - I do recoment this game, to buy and play. It is not "the new" Bastion, or Undertale, but a good game non the less.

I spent the next few minutes trying to "return the favors" as it were, before I decided to call it quits.
Now, you may be asking, why am I recounting this tale of comical deaths and seemingly futile respawns? Am I trying to get you to not try this mod? No, I'm telling you the tales of my recent demises because that's what playing on most JC2-MP servers is like; pure anarchy mixed with an equal measure of psychotic rampages. You have infinite lives... but they're short ones. There is absolute chaos, absolutly everywhere you turn. You honestly can't go into this mod and play on most free-for-all servers thinking "OK, I've got a plan and objectives!" because that kinda crap'll go right out the perverbial window after about you're 3rd respawn, which is when you'll finally realize the truth; not one other person on that server has any goals, they're just there to wreck things... any maybe take in the occasional limo race. You'll die, you'll kill people, blow stuff up, wreck cars, planes, boats, military vehicles, lay waste to every man, woman and child... and still, it's all just pure, unfiltered, unthinking chaos. No goals, just explosions.
Now some people may not like this whole "no goals, just explosions" mindset, but bear in mind that as of right now (12/20/2013) this mod is still just in beta version 0.1.0, so the whole experience is stripped down to the bare essentials... which, admittedly, in this game amounts to anything you can drive, fly, sail, shoot or explode. Yourself included. However, since this mod is avalibe for the low low price of Free, there is no real reason for JC2 owners not to check it out. Hell, host your own private server, invite lots of friends and see how quickly you can destroy everything on the islands! It's worth spending at least a little time in this mod, if only to get a taste of what it's like and to see the sheer potential presented here, not to mention the genius it took for the mods developes to not only look at game with such an odvious single-player bent and say, "Hey, what would this be like multiplayer?", but to actually pull it off as well. My hat goes off to them... but I'm keeping my pants.

Summary: Real time party based dungeon crawl
Multiplayer: No
Completion: 5 hrs
Cards: No
Cloud: Yes
Super Dungeon Run was a rather fascinating experience. It's rare for roguelikes to feature entire parties these days, and SDR takes that up to eleven by allowing you to gather 20 allies at once (or more if you find and free them) and wander around with your lynch mob to stomp over the opposition. It's a chaotic game, and easy to jump in and start whacking away at things.
Super Dungeon Run is a realtime isometric dungeon crawler. I'm not exactly sure if the game uses procedural generation. At the very least quest floors are all the same, but I haven't really noticed any other floors repeating. Combat is nice and simple. Merely move your men in the vicinity of an enemy and they will gang up to beat the poor sobs. Two units cannot occupy the same space, so it is recommended to bring some ranged classes along to maximize damage.
The party structure in the game takes some getting used to. Classes you hire are not automatically a part of your party. To actually make use of classes, you must find them in chests, which upgrades one of your peasants. I like that you can occasionally free a prisoner and add him to your party, which helps offset a bad room that nearly wiped the party.
The loot system is a bit odd. There's no equipment in chests. Instead you may find potions, crafting materials, class upgrades, or cash. Completing a floor quickly while grabbing all the coins and killing all the enemies will net you better rewards at the end of the floor. The crafting materials are used to upgrade your class equipment, which affects all units of that particular class. The drop rate isn't too bad and doesn't require an excessive amount of grinding.
At this time the game balance is a bit out of whack. Early on it is difficult as you have a small party with low levels. But a few upgrades turns that all around and makes floors significantly easier. By the end of the game enemies were nothing more than a nuisance. While there's a fair amount of enemy variety, they are all definitely susceptible to simply being mobbed. If there were some enemies immune to ranged or melee, that could help spice things up a bit. Huge bosses with aoe attacks could also be fun. Maybe some enemies who uses status effects such as poison or charm that can only be countered by a cleric would be nice to have around.
Traps are highly lethal in this game. As your party grows in size, it becomes very clumsy as your death blob moves around haphazardly trying to follow your mouse cursor. Otherwise easily avoided traps become meat grinders because your poor men do not know how to move intelligently or one at a time. It's not always easy to spot traps in time either, such as flaming traps firing from a south wall. If there's one class I would like to see in the game it's a rogue to disable traps because boy those traps kill.
This is the first game I've seen where a mere table can kill you by doing nothing. It manages this by blocking a path, so your troops may end up getting stuck and left behind. I've had a few rooms where I had to walk at snails pace trying to get everyone to avoid walking into a table. I would have liked the ability to change formations, such as single file, because rooms such as these, or traps you must walk around are among the most lethal in the game.
The graphics are pretty good. They are very clear, and show no slowdown, and the animations are fun to look at. For being early access there's a surprising amount of polish here. The music is is also good, though I would have liked a few more songs, as they get repeated often. I haven't noticed any bugs, so good job on that front.
The game doesn't exactly end as best I can tell. Once you've hit max level and finished the last quest, nothing new opens up. I can't help but want that last bit of closure. Thus I judged the end of the game to be max level and completing all quests, which all in all takes about 5 hours. Even though Super Dungeon Run is still considered in early access, in it's current state it's entirely enjoyable. Even the base price is quite reasonable for what you get. I give Super Dungeon Run a 8/10. It's unfinished, but you can definitely see the potential they've got going.

Buggy and serious design flaws aside, is Sleeping Dogs fun?  The short answer is yes.  The story is predictable but satisfying -- several characters that I expected to die, did -- with the exception of one.  The fact that the bugs result in ridiculous behaviour only makes the fact that the game plays itself straight all the more hilarious and adding to the entertainmnet value.
Cover-combat is nicely broken up with movie-style stunts, favouring bold, aggressive play that is movie-like, entertaining and rewarding both visually and tactically but is otherwise pretty standard.  The Free-Running is perhaps too down-to-earth considering the rest of the game isn't and while a nice attempt is probably one of the weaker game elements.  The fighting has some serious design flaws that really keep it from being as good as it could be; enemy classes weaken what could have been entertaining free-flow combat by giving them uninterruptable attacks or grapple immunity which bogs down the combat flow in a forced way.  The driving seems fine, but the catch-up logic is irritating as it only applies to the computer-controlled cars making racing rely more on luck than it should.  Said driving is not keyboard friendly.
Finally, the bugs.  Oh the bugs.  Bugs were the first things I encountered because during the initial chase, the person I was supposed to follow quit running halfway through and in order to continue I had to dash ahead while the game nagged me that I was leaving him behind before he promptly teleported ahead.  Sometimes key events won't fire if you are genre-savvy and plan ahead.  NPC's will get stuck frequently and occasionally have amusing pathfinding difficulties.  One time the security camera wouldn't let me exit.  And the fact that many critical actions are crippled after completing a mission will mean occasionally thugs will steal your car trying to escape you because you couldn't do anything useful until the summary finished summarizing and you dismissed it.
Overall  the mechanics work with the general feel, and while fans of GTA or Saints Row will probably prefer those games to this one, it's still fun and its own unique quirks made me feel it was a enjoyable romp.

Paid Mods, The Game.
That was the short version. The long version is that Fallout 4 is on release a bare bones game. It's actually the skeleton of a game, waiting to be filled by the community.
And yes, the community has filled that skeleton, building upon it transforming it into a great game. There are thousands of mods, I personally play with 130, others play with over 200. Using this great library of FREE Mods you can turn Fallout 4 from the empty shell it is, into one of the best games on the market.
So what do the creators of this game do? Well, dear ol' Bethesda decides to implement PAID Mods, 5$ per mod even, so you can enjoy their game. Not that they are good mods, weapon and armor skins mostly, not mods that actually fix or improve upon the game in any other way.
But that in itself is actually fine. Let them have PAID Mods separately, so folks can nicely ignore and let their Creation Club just wither away. Which has been happening. So what does dear ol' Bethesda do?
Well... here's the kicker... they keep releasing "Updates" that don't do anything to the game itself, just modifications to the PAID Mods Creation Club Market, and these "Updates" break F4SKE.
The real thorn is that 99% of the mods out there use F4SKE, which is fan made, as an essential tool in their mods. So without F4SKE, you have no FREE Mods, forcing unnecessary updates from modders who either are not active anymore or have little time to spare.
To make it short, Bethesda is intentionally releasing Hack Updates to break Free Mods so you are forced to buy Paid Mods. So instead of paying your 60$ for the Game and it's DLCs, you also need to pay 8$ for the Creation Club and then pay 5$ per mod to make the game PLAYABLE!!
So yeah, Bethesda wants me to pay 130 mods (after finding their PAID equivalent) * 5$ (assuming they would all be this cheap) a minimum of what? 650$ to just play their freaking game in a actually Working and Fun manner?
Fallout 4 has been turned by greedy executives into Paid Mods, The Game.
As a conclusion, if you don't mind being constantly reminded by the game to buy Paid Mods, and you enjoy paying for what used to be free content, then yeah, go buy the game. If you do not want to be treated like a cow to be milked for your hard earned money, then do not purchase Fallout 4. There are plenty of other games out there that respect you as a consumer than go play Elex or Witcher 3, games that respect you for buying them.
Which reminds me of something else, something a lot of people have been asking for lately: Bethesda, please... I beg you, please let Obsidian make Fallout games from now on. They actually make good games.

Don't Open the Doors! is a lovingly hand-crafted game which appealed to me the instant I saw the promo screenshots!  It's
claymation -- no computerized 3D graphics here -- but created entirely by the hands of the developers.
Pros:
+ Number one on my list: the story is HILARIOUS!  Super funny dialogue!  Throughout my play the whole thing has been extremely entertaining.  Many are "inside" jokes to gaming :-)
+ The environments are colorful and vibrant, and the different items, landscapes, foliage, bricks, props, etc. are well-fashioned.
+ Combat is challenging: there are a variety of mobs, each having a different style of attack, which necessitates a bit of strategy when fighting.
+ There are a few fun little puzzles in the game.  Because of different effects (air blowers, etc.), some platforming skill is required to get bonus items.
+ The Quest Log reminds you what you need to pick up and where you need to go.
+ The world is mostly open -- you can complete quests in any order.  (Though some places open/unlock only upon completion of other quests.)
+ You can destroy TONS of stuff in the world with your amazing hammer!  (Can't reach the spitting cactus?  Destroy the bamboo that's blocking your way!)
+ The game has a very light and entertaining tone.  A nice casual game to feel carefree with!
+ Besides being very funny, the premise of the story has gotten me curious, and I am very interested to see what happens!
+ The music is quite excellent!  (At first I thought the intro music was a bit odd, but during gameplay it is quite enjoyable and covers several different genres).
Neutral:
~ Some of the combat is a bit wonky: e.g. you swing your hammer on a diagonal, but it doesn't hit the enemies.
~ There are save points, (versus "save where I am right this moment").  Love the tiny claymation disk! haha
Cons:
- There are some items which don't look immediately dangerous -- and then you get harmed by them.  (The thorns, for example).  But once you get used to their appearance, you should be fine.
Overall:
I am thoroughly enjoying playing the game, and I think I will play the entire thing on my YT channel!  (At the time of the review, I am only a couple of hours in!)  It's so much fun to explore the different environments, and I am excited with anticipation at wondering what new kooky characters I will meet next!
For me, the most important aspects: 1. the humor is great! 2. the game IS a game, which requires a bit of skill!  Don't Open the Doors! hits both of the pleasure points.
I definitely recommend this game.  If you are unsure or just want to see a little more, please check out my Let's Play series here:

People often say Muv Luv is slow at the start and gets better as you go. I'll just say how it went for me.
There are three parts in the Muv Luv Trilogy. Extra, Unlimited, and Alternative.
When I first started reading Extra, it seemed inane and cliche. It took me several months to get through it, because I wasn't really particularly invested.
When I hit Unlimited, suddenly it became pretty interesting! Still a little slow, but I was hooked. I played it when I had spare time over the course of a week or so.
When I hit Alternative, I literally could not put it down for anything. I literally did not sleep for nearly 72 hours until I finished it. By the end I was a complete emotional wreck.
Coming back to Extra, it's very emotional experience on your second playthrough. Everything I didn't care about before seems much more important, and there's lots of subtle little foreshadowing.
I'll admit that this game is the weaker half of the trilogy. But I still think it's absolutely worth it, and if purchased with its sequel (expected release winter 2016), then I'd absolutely recommend it. It goes places you won't expect, and has one of the roughest emotional rollercoasters I've ever experienced.

Blitzkrieg feels like it is now a franchise which has lost its soul, the essence of what made it fun and unique. The first Blitzkrieg was and still is unique in how it handles strategy, it gave you huge amounts of detail and background information to every unit and plenty of information prior to each battle so that players could make informed and calculated choices when executing their strategies. the gameplay itself was almost Total War-esque in its execution, you start each real time battle with a limited pool of units and make use of their individual talents to overcome the enemy to secure victory, Infantry for Urban battles, neutralizing garrisons, scouting, and cannon fodder. Tanks were used to overwhelm infantry in open spaces, combat enemy armor, and execute rapid, aggressive advances. Artillery was the hard counter to everything in the game (except air units) but is practically useless without effective positioning, thorough recon, and a little luck and patience. Tanks and artillery both carried veterancy through missions so if you could keep your units alive for long enough you would start the game with a sizable advantage over your enemies units but if they died you had to start from scratch with a new unit. Air units were often the deciding factor in each battle but were almost useless if you hadn't neutralized the enemies anti-air and air force prior to their deployment.
As you have read, each unit felt like it had a purpose and had to be used intelligently to attain the most beneficial outcome and make progress. Blitzkrieg 3 feels like it is trying to be something it is not, and by doing that is losing what made it so special in the first place. Blitzkrieg 3's revolves around the same stale selection of maps, a hard counter combat triangle making it so units lose their versatility, practicality, and individuality and also game mechanics and campaign missions that fall flat due to their shallowness, lack of meaningful engagement, and cookie-cutter nature, you feel more like you are grinding through a chore than actively participating in grand strategy.
How would I improve Blitzkrieg 3? I would advise Nivals games designers to go back and play the original game so they can recapture it's essence and improve on its mechanics with more modern game design ideas, then play the mods for the game such as Achtung Panzer! so they could see how to improve mission structure and presentation to the player, then finally openly and actively engage their community since in this new games development environment having closed communication channels for your audience to engage you will only prevent you from seeing how passionate fans want to help make this game great and live up to the legacy of the existing franchise.
I cannot recommend the game in its current state as it is not a Blitzkrieg game, it is currently a bland, generic, cookie cutter, attack / defence style strategy game which genuinely feels like it was built for a microtransaction style economy and still feels and plays that way.
TL;DR This game mechanically needs to be Blitzkrieg 3 and not Clash of Clans. I love you Blitzkrieg but you need to go home, you are drunk.

Muv-Luv contains the first two parts (Extra and Unlimited) of an amazing visual novel series that tops the favorites list of countless fans. Degica has made some fantastic improvements in art and technical quality to go along with a retranslation of the original fan work that made Muv Luv famous.
The series as a whole shifts from slice of life romantic comedy to hardcore science fiction, taking characters you already know from a normal setting and putting them in a world where humanity is on the brink of extinction and human-piloted mechs are their only hope for survival. There’s plenty of action and emotion in the latter two parts, while the first focuses on romance and comedy, and you should definitely play them all in order to get to know the characters.

Muv-Luv Extra is a mixture of normal comedy, hilarious exaggerations and absurd truths that will probably keep you laughing for most of its length. Some might describe it as a run-of-the-mill rom-com but it sets the scene for other instalments in the series and I personally find it to be great fun.
If you thought the Muv-Luv series itself was entirely romance and comedy, though, you would be horribly wrong. Unlimited launches the characters introduced by Extra into a sci-fi mecha setting where humanity is on the brink of extinction at the hands of the terrifying BETA. Seeing those characters you've built connections with face the adversity of unadulterated war is hugely entertaining, and Unlimited is still only setting up for the amazing final chapter of Muv Luv Alternative.
Of all of the visual novels, video games, TV series, movies and books i've read before, Muv Luv Alternative sits at the top of the list in terms of sheer entertainment value and Muv Luv is the game that paves the way for it. Any fan of science fiction in general  -needs- this story in their collection.

.

Left 4 Dead is the game that started this recent wave of coop games and it's by far one of the best ones available despite it's many problems.
The basic game mode, campaign, pits you and three of your friends against the undead hordes in an attempt to flee to safety. You play through a series of maps fighting common infected as well as various special infected that provide a greater challenge. As you go through the maps, from saferoom to saferoom you pick up consumable items and get better and better weapons. Although the lower difficulties are so easy a child could complete them the higher ones provide a great level of challenge and are nearly unachievable without a team of good players.
In the second game mode, versus, you play a four vs. four matchup where teams take turns at playing survivors as well as infected. As the infected team you spawn as one of the various special infected and try to inflict as much damage as possible before the survivors reach the saferoom.
While campaign is mostly a smooth play, provided you have friends to play with, versus has a number of problems that make it hard to enjoy in the long one. Chiefly is that the game was never balanced in any meaningful way so the survivors can quite easily complete every map taking a minimum of damage. Without imposing some sort of house rules on what the survivors are allowed to do any organized versus game quickly becomes a rather boring affair.
Another rather large problem is the number of bugs still in the game, despite Valve doing almost weekly patches for several years the tank, the infected's only real game changer, will still occasionally spawn outside the map and instantly die or spawn on top of a burning barrel which works much the same.
Although underneath the horrific balance and game ending bugs is a rather solid game it is also a game that requires organized team play. You can't simply jump on a random server without expecting to get disappointed. I was lucky enough to have a number of great friends to play with yet whenever I booted the game up by myself I always found it to be a frustrating and bland affair trying to get any sense of game going with randoms. It's a game that can only really be enjoyed in gathers.
Graphically the game is quite good despite being on the now aging Source engine. Various poor design decisions mark the experience though, most notably the unusually low skyboxes on certain maps.
The sound is fairly functional, each breed of infected carrying with it a number of distinct sounds that'll always keep you on your toes.
Left 4 Dead is a good game but it does have some problems, the most important of which is that it isn't a game you can just buy for yourself, you have to have friends to play with and while I enjoy playing coop with people I know not having to option to occasionally jump on and play a quick session without planning it beforehand really hurts the game in the long run.
Also, any review of Left 4 Dead would be incomplete without a mention of Left 4 Dead 2 because that's what killed this game. These days you'll only find a few games going at any given time and for a Valve game to have such a short lifespan is just atrocious.

Maps, maps, maps.  And then more maps.  The game is very similar to Risk, but moves faster and has a broad set of options to alter rules and cardplay.  The matches may not be the most involving of strategic thinking - most games can be played in 10 minutes or less - but the sheer diversity of maps wrings every bit of potential generalship out of the player; many maps play with the basic map features in interesting ways that highlight creative approaches to your campaign.  User-created maps are scored on a scale of 1-5 so you can winnow the wheat from the chaff (and suprisingly, most are very solid indeed!).  I'm not certain this is a game that I will grind at to the exclusion of other games (there just isn't enough consistency, naturally, between the vast collection of maps) but it is a game that I can drop in and play a few matches easily.  Any game this good that is that approachable is a keeper.  Highly recommended!

Buggy and serious design flaws aside, is Sleeping Dogs fun?  The short answer is yes.  The story is predictable but satisfying -- several characters that I expected to die, did -- with the exception of one.  The fact that the bugs result in ridiculous behaviour only makes the fact that the game plays itself straight all the more hilarious and adding to the entertainmnet value.
Cover-combat is nicely broken up with movie-style stunts, favouring bold, aggressive play that is movie-like, entertaining and rewarding both visually and tactically but is otherwise pretty standard.  The Free-Running is perhaps too down-to-earth considering the rest of the game isn't and while a nice attempt is probably one of the weaker game elements.  The fighting has some serious design flaws that really keep it from being as good as it could be; enemy classes weaken what could have been entertaining free-flow combat by giving them uninterruptable attacks or grapple immunity which bogs down the combat flow in a forced way.  The driving seems fine, but the catch-up logic is irritating as it only applies to the computer-controlled cars making racing rely more on luck than it should.  Said driving is not keyboard friendly.
Finally, the bugs.  Oh the bugs.  Bugs were the first things I encountered because during the initial chase, the person I was supposed to follow quit running halfway through and in order to continue I had to dash ahead while the game nagged me that I was leaving him behind before he promptly teleported ahead.  Sometimes key events won't fire if you are genre-savvy and plan ahead.  NPC's will get stuck frequently and occasionally have amusing pathfinding difficulties.  One time the security camera wouldn't let me exit.  And the fact that many critical actions are crippled after completing a mission will mean occasionally thugs will steal your car trying to escape you because you couldn't do anything useful until the summary finished summarizing and you dismissed it.
Overall  the mechanics work with the general feel, and while fans of GTA or Saints Row will probably prefer those games to this one, it's still fun and its own unique quirks made me feel it was a enjoyable romp.

The face of the video game scene has been undergoing major surgery in the last few years. With works such as the literary Bioshock, thought-provoking Shadow of the Colossus and mindbending Limbo hitting the mainstream- and succeeding- the world of the humble “game” has been slowly but unstoppably moving from a wasteland of bald space marines and western male fantasies into the realm of art.  One reason for this shift lies in the accessibility of the indie gaming scene in the last few years- with the internet, and particularly with Steam, more and more creative works are gaining attention, and slowly reshaping the medium itself.
Bastion is one such game changer.
This humble little indie project, the first effort by Supergiant Games, starts out sharp but unassuming. You, as the enigmatic “Kid” wake up on a “rock in the sky” to find out that you have landed smack dab in a post-apocalyptic waste that was one a floating country in the sky. You find yourself part of a constantly unfolding story as a gruff, Tom Waits-esque voice narrates your actions in real time, as the world shapes itself around you with every step.
The gameplay is simple, go through various decimated floating islands, fighting hoards of baddies, to retrieve items which will revive the Bastion- a mysterious paradise for the remaining survivors capable of restoring the world. It is not the play that makes Bastion so effective, though it is, despite somewhat repetitive format, extremely fun without being overly difficult.
The eye to the aesthetic, even over the gameplay, are what makes Bastion special. Anyone can kill in a video game. Bastion is one of the few that makes you think about what you’re killing and why.
The game is in many ways, extremely provocative. Combining a schizo mix of Firefly-esque Western music with a distinct Indian flair creates a compelling mood and sense of culture- driving home all the more tragically the loss of everything before the start of the game.
Combined with this bold score is the use of narration to tell the story. Rather than weigh it down with dialogue, the plot and characters are given in narrated snippets by a gruff, oft-disembodied voice. The sense of being placed in a story gives a certain dreadful inevitability to the tale, even a sense of darkness that belies the simplistic play and cheerful colors.
The art style itself, a simplistic yet painterly style provides a sense of detail and loss, rendering a sense of culture to compliment the mythos of the story. Despite being a relatively short game, the world which it creates is compelling and has a sense of life and vastness as the narrator unfolds tales of lost gods and desperate wars, old friends, and lost loves.
While a game appropriate for any ages, the game unflinchingly deals with dark topics, ultimately addressing issues of grief, revenge, racism, and forgiveness, which culminate in allowing the player to choose the ultimate ending of the game- whether the cycle is to be perpetuated or broken- whether it is better to leave the past and let the story unfold as it will, or to cling to what seems safe, like a rock in the sky.
This deceptively simple game keeps its eye, evermore, on the more intellectual aspects of itself. This almost backwards approach to video game creation has produced a game familiar yet somehow completely unlike any other game ever produced. A game which, perhaps, more than any other, causes the player to stop and question his own choices as much as the character’s. This game renders itself, for all of its simplicity, utterly unforgettable. And as it sits in a stew of top sellers on Steam, bearing the distribution of Warner Bros. Entertainment, and a myriad of well-deserved awards, one hopes it will never be forgotten, not just as a video game, but as true art.

Now one of my favourite games of all time. To sum up this game, it's like GTA but with better driving, fighting, shooting, and immensely better plot; I couldn't stop playing. Actually, I don't want to compare this game to GTA. This game isn't misogynistic (any in-game misogyny is portrayed as bad), and the point I feel makes this game shine is its depth, both absent in GTA. It shows that nothing is truly black and white. The Triad are originally shown as 'bad' and the police as 'good,' and this concept it destroyed by the end of the game by showing that things are not that simple to label. The Triad are shown to be more than just 'bad guys,' and the police are shown to be more than the 'good guys.' This fact, along with excellent gameplay, made this game for me. I actually felt sad during certain plot points and felt a sense of what Wei Shen was feeling through playing the game. This is what makes this game for me. I loved this game and I can't wait for the sequel.

Old RoTMG Review: The game was never very bad. Before DECA bought it, it was in a decaying state for a few months (multi boxers being a regularity and spam bots in every nexus) but this was negligable (sorry that I can't spell). The game didn't feel entirely broken, and these were just some of the major anoyances.
New RoTMG Review: DECA hasn't really changed much. They elimnated multi-boxing as far as I know. I haven't seen any yet at least. I didn't notice spam bots at first, but I recently logged in an instantly got a PM from one. Emphasis on ONE where as with Kabam I'd get a combined text wall from 3-5. So that's an improvement there. DECA is definetly trying their best to revive the community though, with new events almost everyday for month of the mad god (and an extended week of it). Last year's MotMG had an "event" every week. Another improvement.
Overall, DECA is doing great work. They haven't made any major updates, but they've only had the game for about 9 days now. They what's important and they're doing what needs to be done first (eliminate unwanted "players", revive the community, fix bugs) before actually adding content. So far, they've earned my trust with the work they've done, and I think good things are coming for RoTMG. I also like how they aren't blatantly trying to win over the community by overloading us with free stuff. It's coming in moderation.
TL;DR: Anyone who stopped playing RoTMG because of the lack of care shown by Kabam, NOW IS THE TIME TO COME BACK. If you've just heard of RoTMG and you want to give it a try, the one thing you need to know is this game is perma death and it will test your patience. A lot. At the same, it's a great time to try this game if you've ever been tenative about giving it a go, if you like bullet hells and ARPG's try this game.

"Time is the cruelest kindness" - Kouzuki Yuuko
The Muv Luv trilogy is a coming of age story of the protagonist Shirogane Takeru, who is thrown from his idyllic high school life into a war-torn universe where humanity is on the cusp of extinction after a protracted war with the BETA (Beings of ExtraTerrestrial origin which is Adversary to the human race). This new universe he finds himself in is a twisted parody of his home. His hometown is a ruin, his childhood friend, Kagami Sumika's, house is crushed by what seems to be a giant robot, and the high school he attended is now a U.N. military base. Upon arriving at said military base, he is immediately thrown into prison after a thorough cavity search and interrogation. Herein lies his salvation, Kouzuki Yuuko, his (in his universe) high school physics teacher. After some cursory questions, he is released into her custody and summarily informed of his new circumstances.
In this unfamiliar and nightmarish environment, Takeru does what any teenager would do in his situation; he panics. He's completely unwilling to accept reality and rationalizes his experiences as a crazy dream. Shortly afterwards, Kouzuki Yuuko, who is revealed to be the base XO assigns him to squad 207b, so she can keep an eye on him. When he heads out to meet them, he's stunned to find himself surrounded by familiar faces--people who he's supposed to know, but finds out are completely different, at least on the surface.
After being introduced to the squad, he begins his basic combat training, where he discovers one of his many shortcomings, namely his pathetic physical state. This is a recurring theme, where his utterly civilian background does not lend itself well to any of the drills squad 207 is assigned. Even in the CCSE (Comprehensive Combat Skill Evaluation), the final test before cadets are allowed to undergo eishi (pilot) training, he almost causes the squad to fail because he caught a cold in the middle of it. Somehow, they pass, and in a twist of irony, the boy who near-failed at everything related to the military scores the highest in the aptitude test. With this reversal in fortune, Shirogane Takeru coasts on his newfound talent to become the strongest cadet, using skills gained from countless hours of video games.
In true Muv Luv fashion however, happy times never last, and on the eve of Christmas, right after a Tanabata-Christmas party, the base CO (General Paul Radhabinod) reveals that Alternative V, a mass exodus from the blue planet, has gone into effect. 100,000 people, chosen by the government, will head for a planet with conditions similar to Earth, effectively abandoning the rest in the fight to take back the Earth. Their departure will herald the start of Operation Babylon, the mass deployment of G-bombs to clear the Earth of hives while the armies follow up with their TSF units.
Muv Luv Unlimited ends with one of the romanceable companions (Mitsurugi Meiya, Sakaki Chizuru, Tamase Miki, Yoroi Mikoto) and their [Shirogane's and her] daughter pointing out a distant Sun in the night sky, while engaging in a heartbreaking dialogue.
Throughout all of Unlimited and Alternative, Shirogane Takeru learns many hard lessons. He learns how truly fragile and transient happiness is, and the lengths he will go to in order to preserve it. He learns the definition of nationalism, both its positive and negative aspects and what it means to truly be Japanese. He learns about responsiblity, both taken on willingly and not, and the consequences of abdicating it. He learns of the burdens of power, of both having it and lacking it, and that to truly affect change, he must not be afraid to bloody his hands. Blitzkrieg franchise... one of the finest real time wargames I ever played. So many sleepless nights and short days with the common feeling  - just one more mission...
Years have passed, many new wargames were released and I did my best to try them all. Some were good, some not that good ... and the rest just plain awful.
And here is where I would place Blitzkrieg 3. Shameful use of the old franchise name to make a game, that has hardly anything in common with its legendary predecesors. If you loved the first (still the best) and the second part (had potential). Then please DON'T spoil yourself your memories on those great games and avoid Blitzkrieg 3 as a plague.
I did try to like this game, I really did. But to no avail. The core basic of the new game is flawed and no matter what they update this is still a dumbed down wanna-be wargame aimed at... God knows whom.
So in short:
- forget about nice missions from the originals. You will get some annoyingly scripted missions without a darn auto save.
- forget the use of single soldiers (except snipers), here you get a whole squad as in Company of Heroes series
- forget the usage of combined arms as in the original. Here you only need a ton of tanks/tanks destroyers and a sniper/scout vehicle. Infantry you say? Not really needed here where you are on offence and a really limited value on the defence only.
- graphic are nothing special for today's standard. Animations are ok. Maybe too spectacular... but hey... kids like BIG BANGS.
- Multiplayer is boring. Base building in Blitzkrieg franchise? No thanks...
Rest in peace Blitzkrieg franchise and thank you for nice memories.
