- In short it is a science fantasy kind of title. Expect space unicorns (there are no space unicorns).
- Unlike the Heroes Rise series, this is more episodic (Indeed the devs point this out at the end of the game). By this it is meant that it is like an episode of a TV series, thus incomplete.
- A lot of new lingo to understand. It's fed to you with narrative dumps, so be careful when going in. Also some xirhir going on, take that as you will.
- The story will jump around a lot (one minute you are in Camelot and the other you are chasing the Holy Grail, next you are Robin Hood).
- Like the Heroes series you are very much nudged in the direction of becoming a specific archetype, thus there is perhaps less roleplaying and more "what choice is x or y archetype".
- Plenty of romance options, you can bang guys, gals, goddesses, chicks with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(hearts, huge hearts). At the same time if you want to. Not robots though, but you can romance one.
- Full character customization as usual (except last name). It does not have a major impact (since the story tailors characters to you), but it's there.
Let me start by saying I think this is a good title, and I did want more after I finished it. I personally don't mind the episodic feel to it, but once you finish it then it is certainly evident. It does not close up the plot as neatly as the Heroes Rise series did, but it is not meant to. Personally I am fine with that, I'm a sucker for episodic content, but you should probably keep in mind if you are as well, or at least know what you are getting into here.
The writing is generally good and while the author does use a lot of new terms and smashes you with them, then it does serve to paint their world as fundamentally other. It's not Earth, it's a universe of humanoids. Generally these terms makes sense by themselves and with the context that they are used. For me it's not too difficult to understand, though some might object.
I am not hugely experienced with "Choice of" games, but I have binged a lot on them this Christmas (I think I've emptied Steam of them by now), but I am uncertain as to how much choice you really have in this game. Perhaps the best way to explain the choice you do have in this game is to say the devil is in the details. By that I mean that you will not stop this train no matter what you do, but you may have conversations with people on this train, choose how to conduct yourself and indeed who to save from its impending doom. So huge choices? No. Small choices? Plenty. And if you like details then almost no choice is meaningless.
As mentioned above the author does push you towards archetypes, which you might be familiar with from the Heroes Rise series. It really does streamline your choices, responses and so on. I'm uncertain whether I think this is good or bad. In the grand scheme of things it really does limit your choices, but on the other hand it does make for replaybility as the game is focused around these four archetypes. Your game as an honest status quo guy will unfold differently than one as a manipulative rebel. Ultimately I think these archetypes are necessary to give a good narrative as the game will know how to respond to you based on them, which is good I think.
The romances... they're alright, but I'll be honest... There is too little talk going on between all of them to really be considered romances (I think anyhoo). They're more like a date and a hookup. I hope we'll see them grow though. I do like that, apparently, you are able to pursue several romances at the same time. What can I say, my completionist nature makes me greedy.
Also you cannot romance Prodigal, Chicken. That's the one true black mark on this game.

This is a very polished fast little roguelike.  The game is fun, and it is great to beat quests or watch your little minions die.
There are a few things that could be better.  In the game traps are way more deadly than monsters.  The designers clearly know this because some of the later levels are really trap heavy.  The monster variety is at best OK, and there are no powerful bosses to defeat, sometimes just rooms with more enemies.
As you get more peasants to your party and level them up, combat against the weak enemies becomes easier, but the giant blob gets harder and harder to avoid traps.  So, while traps start out hard, they become very very hard, and while monsters start out maybe average in difficulty, they become very very easy.
There is a crafting mechanic, but I found that I always had so many resources that I would craft all items as soon as they were unlocked.  Armor upgrades and level upgrades make your guys a little tougher, which offers a little help against traps.  Also, going into the dungeon without selecting a quest and I found the difficulty of the floors could ramp up quite high.
There are only two different looks to the dungeons.  Still the game is very fun and pulls you along.  Once you have maxed out your levels and unlocked everything there is not much else to do, but getting to that point will only take you a few hours.
There is more good than bad about this game, and it is still early access so more improvements to come.  I recommend buying this game.

When I played the original I was not a hardcore funder. I did not spend hundreds to see the game come to it's ambitious heights. I've seen and heard complaints that the team never went all the way. I was more interested in playing a game that looked and felt like the old school total annihilation rts of the 90's and enjoying the bonus of interplanetary battle and super destruction.
HIGHLIGHTS -- This game is very easy to learn, is not limited to resource depletion but rather resource vs builder managment. You can get to super destructive levels quickly, which is the point. The game rewards you for rushing to a climactic destrution of a planet or simply wiping out the commander. The balance between the bot/naval/tank/air units is surprisingly well done, and the conquer mode (single player) is not half bad and enjoyable. The best version of this game however is LAN or online multiplayer skirmishes which are absolutley insane at times, and remind me of the best old school RTS games such as red alert, Generals, and of course Total Annihilation.
I would say the cons are that the game can be too easy at times, especially when you are conquering the galaxy and most of the maps tend to have on planet, a small one at that, which doesn't allow for the huge levels of destruction that you would be looking for but there are ways around that. Also the AI while not terribly hard jumps a lot between difficulty settings.

I have been playing Fallout from the beginning, and am something of a fanatic when it comes to lore and the world of Fallout in general. Unlike many, I find Fallout 4 to be an excellent addition to the series, and am quite pleased with it. The combat system is substantially improved (I really couldn't see 'going back' to playing earlier editions because of this...the improvements are that significant), the settlement system (and associated crafting) add a new dimension to play that significantly enhances the 'feel' of the world, and updated graphics (a new color palette!) make the game a better aesthetic experience.
I do agree with many commenters that Bethesda could do a better job with the main quest (a huge weakness in Fallout 3 as well), but their side quests are quite good, and the DLC adds a great deal to the main game. The RPG elements of the game need some polishing (the choice of a voiced protagonist has proved to be somewhat problematic, though I have hopes for improvement in future versions), and of course there is the usual problem of "Bethesda Bugs"...the QA on the game really does need work.
With all of that, this is a superior experience, and one of my 'go-to' games when I have some time free.

What an hilariously fun little game.
It's extremely simple, and thanks to that easy to get into and enjoy. The Artwork is cute and fun, and the music adventurous and whimsical.
You simply click and hold the left mouse button to guide your mob of peasants on their adventures. Note, they really really aren't adventurers. They're peasants, they want to smash things and get loot, but are really really dumb. They'll often run into spikes and other nasty traps because they saw a vase they want to smash or some coins they want to pick up.
As such they can get all over the place as you increase your party in size. Thankfully you can upgrade them via outfits to transform them into pseudo-adventurers that are better armed than our yellow poncho clothed club swinging ones.
Not only that, but the peasant garb, and unlocked outfits can be upgraded and improved upon.
So head to your tavern, pick up a quest and click Dungeon to get started. The game is is time trial based, so the quicker you do things and better rewards you get. Although in many cases some quest rewards are so lucrative you really don't need to scrounge around wasting time smashing crates or looking for coins. Just rush through. Now while this does mean you miss out on bonus rewards and goodies, you can upgrade the Quest Rewards with level points. Further making them an even better option.
Sadly the dungeons aren't very random, and you can often get the same routes over and over. I do hope they add some procedurally generated versions, along with more quests.
So far it's fun, and considering the price it's well worth it in my opinion.

Would you dare vicious traps, monsters, and inevitable death all for some shiny loot and gold? Well the peasants in Super Dungeon Run would! SDR is a strange mash up of roguelike, endless runner and RPG. There are quests, upgrades, and plenty of randomly generated death rooms, and of course delicious amounts of treasure! As your peasants run and collect gold you will begin collecting upgrades in the form of potions and costumes. These allow your peasants to become much more extraordinary and wield incredible abilities, such as the Sorceroress or the mighty Knight. I was pleasantly surprised by the amount of replay value and depth SDR has for it's adorable simple graphics and gameplay. I wasn't expecting things like crafting, class upgrades and skill trees. Where things need more polish is in the dungeon running itself. Let me be clear, everything works very well while running, you unlock potions, classes and move your poor adventurers about in a hilarious drunken wave. The problem is there is a bit of lack of interaction when the action kicks in. You kinda just sit there and watch what happens. Using a potion occasionally to help your adventurers out of a jam. However, things like class abilities and spells are already planned for final release and will more then likely take care of this aspect. In all Super Dungeon Run for it's price is an absolute steal and highly recommended to those looking for a funny and relaxing roguelike.

The face of the video game scene has been undergoing major surgery in the last few years. With works such as the literary Bioshock, thought-provoking Shadow of the Colossus and mindbending Limbo hitting the mainstream- and succeeding- the world of the humble “game” has been slowly but unstoppably moving from a wasteland of bald space marines and western male fantasies into the realm of art.  One reason for this shift lies in the accessibility of the indie gaming scene in the last few years- with the internet, and particularly with Steam, more and more creative works are gaining attention, and slowly reshaping the medium itself.
Bastion is one such game changer.
This humble little indie project, the first effort by Supergiant Games, starts out sharp but unassuming. You, as the enigmatic “Kid” wake up on a “rock in the sky” to find out that you have landed smack dab in a post-apocalyptic waste that was one a floating country in the sky. You find yourself part of a constantly unfolding story as a gruff, Tom Waits-esque voice narrates your actions in real time, as the world shapes itself around you with every step.
The gameplay is simple, go through various decimated floating islands, fighting hoards of baddies, to retrieve items which will revive the Bastion- a mysterious paradise for the remaining survivors capable of restoring the world. It is not the play that makes Bastion so effective, though it is, despite somewhat repetitive format, extremely fun without being overly difficult.
The eye to the aesthetic, even over the gameplay, are what makes Bastion special. Anyone can kill in a video game. Bastion is one of the few that makes you think about what you’re killing and why.
The game is in many ways, extremely provocative. Combining a schizo mix of Firefly-esque Western music with a distinct Indian flair creates a compelling mood and sense of culture- driving home all the more tragically the loss of everything before the start of the game.
Combined with this bold score is the use of narration to tell the story. Rather than weigh it down with dialogue, the plot and characters are given in narrated snippets by a gruff, oft-disembodied voice. The sense of being placed in a story gives a certain dreadful inevitability to the tale, even a sense of darkness that belies the simplistic play and cheerful colors.
The art style itself, a simplistic yet painterly style provides a sense of detail and loss, rendering a sense of culture to compliment the mythos of the story. Despite being a relatively short game, the world which it creates is compelling and has a sense of life and vastness as the narrator unfolds tales of lost gods and desperate wars, old friends, and lost loves.
While a game appropriate for any ages, the game unflinchingly deals with dark topics, ultimately addressing issues of grief, revenge, racism, and forgiveness, which culminate in allowing the player to choose the ultimate ending of the game- whether the cycle is to be perpetuated or broken- whether it is better to leave the past and let the story unfold as it will, or to cling to what seems safe, like a rock in the sky.
This deceptively simple game keeps its eye, evermore, on the more intellectual aspects of itself. This almost backwards approach to video game creation has produced a game familiar yet somehow completely unlike any other game ever produced. A game which, perhaps, more than any other, causes the player to stop and question his own choices as much as the character’s. This game renders itself, for all of its simplicity, utterly unforgettable. And as it sits in a stew of top sellers on Steam, bearing the distribution of Warner Bros. Entertainment, and a myriad of well-deserved awards, one hopes it will never be forgotten, not just as a video game, but as true art.

Unless you play on playing offline a lot, don't even bother.
I'm just going to focus on the online because otherwise listing all the♥♥♥♥♥♥wrong with this game would take too long.
This game's online is a complete disaster. The matchmaking takes 5-10 minutes to find an opponent, and when you're starting out you can expect them to be several leagues higher than you. The skill of your opponent typically doesn't matter, because even if you filter matchmaking to only accept 5 bar connections, they will usually end up lagging anyway.
The netcode is absolutely atrocious. They saw the success of GGPO and tried to imitate with their own rollback netcode, but the execution failed horribly. You can try to hit confirm then get counter hit because the game rolled back the first hit. My favorite was when I got hit with an uppercut in the middle of a throw animation.
Even if you get a stable match, the inherent problems with the gameplay are still present. The game has 8 frames of input lag so "offline will feel the same as online", but this is 8 frames of always-present input lag in addition to whatever input lag you get from being online. You literally cannot block some things on reaction. This leaves the game feeling sluggish, and reacting to moves or punishing is almost impossible. You will constantly input moves that will either come out late, resulting in a counter hit, or won't come out at all. Also get used to learning new meaty timings every single game, because they will be completely different depending on your opponent.
If you like fighting games then just wait, Capcom will fix this game eventually, Third Strike and Ultra are two of the greatest fighting games ever, but right now V is a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥show.
Also, this game was made in 2016 and doesn't have a borderless option. If you attempt to launch it with borderless through steam it will most likely crash frequently.

Ultimately, a game like Street Fighter is defined by its online experience. Which is unfortunate, because the netcode is absolutely woeful and the community is filled with either ragequitters, or people so good at the game that they can beat you ceaselessly without you ever landing a hit on them. Unless you have a circle of friends playing in a lobby with you, of similar skill, the matchmaking system will demoralize you very quickly. You only need to see the average peak players of this title on Steam, and you'll see what I mean.
I was going to say that this could have been offset by its single-player experience. Delay after delay, we've yet to see the content delivered. Even with the addition of two new characters, the title still feels half-baked out of the Crapcom oven. If you're looking for a pretty-looking game with a fighting system based on a mish-mash of previous SF combat systems, you're going to do okay with the title. Where SFV shines is certainly in the graphics department, and the very rare occurrence of having a totally lag-free battle.
Capcom didn't release a full game after all their promises, and the table scraps on offer leaves a lot to be desired. SFV is only worth looking at if it goes on sale for 50% off, but don't pay full price for the experience.

I really had to think about this one.
I bought this game about 3 years ago. Not quite sure how I found out about it. I tried to play it, but there was something about it tht I didn't like. I only made it through the first level.
I would try to pick this game up again every 6 months or so, but I just couldn't. So now, here I am with the game finished. Finally.
It starts off with a narrator speaking to you. He will talk to you for the entire game, so get used to it. Anway, he talks about some Calamity. This is the first problem with the game. The Calamity is never explained. Sure, it explains why it happened. How it happened. But not what it is. But for the entire game. the ground builds itself beneath your feet. I can't tell if that is because of the calamity or because of a gameplay element. Bad choice, either way.
So, you find a hammer and bow, fight off some weird grim reeper things, that apparently used to be workers. They aren't talked about in a more thorough way, however. Nothing in this game is. Except for where you go next. The Bastion.
I like the Bastion. I like building it as I progress through the story. But to build the bastion, you must get shards. To get shards, you have to go to different levels.
The levels are so repatative it is unexcuseable. It teases you with backstory, but of course, doesn't go any farther. After an hour fo this, I was done.
The next day, I sat down. I was going to finish this game no matter what. And I did. And now I have even more to complain about.
The backstory isn't revealed until 2/3s through the game. It feelsl tacked on. I slaved 3 hours for a tacked on story. I clicked and pressed space aimlessly for an extremely poor story about xenophobia. I wish I hadn't.
The game is repatitive, the narrator is intrusive, the story is mediocre, the gameplay is repative and boring. Sure, you get a few choices about how you want to fight. But the choices lack impact. They don't make the game feel any different.
But of course, this game is praised for it's art style and music. And that is about it. Even those don't make up for the many areas in which this game lacks.

The Treasure of Montezuma 5 is the 5th game from the The Treasure of Montezuma series developed by Alawar. The game is a gem matching one with a variety of game modes: destroy tokens, collect gems(which is the most used one), collect flasks, find artifacts, collect fireflies, collect golden lizards, collect gold nugets and collect ancient amulets, and a total of 70 levels and 3 bonus level: destroy colored stones, destroy marbles and collect gems(can also be called classic mode) which have a basic time limit of 1 minute which can be extended via totems or bonuses.
In the last sentence I mentioned totems and bonuses. For each 5 completed levels you unlock a totem or a bonus(they come in the totem-bonus sequence). There are 7 totems, one for each gem color, and 6 bonuses, which can be upgraded four times in the store. The currency for the store is gems, which can be obtained by completing levels, completing the in-game achievements, from chests and from the slot machine. The rewards for completing achievements are gems and tokens for the slot machine. The chests each reward you with 150 gems and 3 tokens for the slot machine and require five golden keys which can be obtained by beating a given score for each level. The slot machine have 5 symbols: 10,20,30 gems , a token for the slot machine or a montezuma masks, making 3 masks giving you a jackpot, and 3 reels.

Exemplar of how NOT to be an author And game designer
I swear this author has gone out of their way to tick every box on the list for story telling faux pas. It starts with a cold opening filled with nonsense terms and jargon, then proceeds into a flashback having told you nothing about the story, world or characters.
The game is littered with invented words and terminology that are closer to a child’s attempts to pronounce words they misheard, than they are to phrases a living culture would develop. Cluttered with pseudo-English as if changing a vowel would adequately express how alien and new these things and concepts are meant to be. This problem is then exacerbated by the authors insistence on using the relatively unknown gender neutral pronouns Ze / Hir, incorrectly I might add seeing as their used in reference to a characters physical sex as well their completely unknown (as in our characters merely assume this) gender.
It then proceeds to brush off the magnitude of an alien landscape with our characters (who early on express their desire to see the world beyond their narrow horizons, having never before travelled the stars) strolling into alien buildings, habitats and situations as if they were down at the market buying vegetables. Should we not be amazed at this, and there by proxy, we the reader/player feel some sense of imaginative thrill?
But the crowning achievement on this monolith of unpleasantness is the unfolding character interactions. For you see, I had the Gall, the Nerve to try to play as a morally honest character who was also rebellious! The scandal, every time I picked an option that was deemed "honest" (by the author flagging that as the "honest" choice) I was immediately informed by the game that I was doing it wrong. For you see I the player am a mere spectator, how dare I try to impose my narrative on the writers scenario.
The reason for this was that as a morally honest character, I was opposed to the blatantly evil feudal lords set up as the early adversary. I selected a character goal of disbanding this corrupt organisation, picturing my character as a being who held all lives as equal and worthy. But this goal (the game later informed me) required me to support certain characters, and believe in subterfuge and dishonesty.
Which was why my character was chastised by the game (not a character, a meta-narrative construct) for daring to challenge another character who was attempting to trick someone who trusted them, into dying for them. A character literally described as a God, was trying to trick their loyal subjects into fighting a pointless battle they couldn't win, by lying to them. What was a morally upstanding character like mine to do?
To then rub salt in the wound, as the game continued to tell me how I was playing it wrong (Hah!), all my characters subsequent dialogue with those involved in my goal of bringing down the ridiculously villainous bad-guys, was phrased with my undying obeisance as I decried my foolishness for deciding that I wished to be a Morally upstanding "Rebel".

I want to make it clear first: yes, Steam shows I havn't played this game for long. It is because I played this on my tablet. I only bought the game on Steam because I was shocked that the game is receiving this many of bad votes, and I'd like to give my evaluation. Of course, everyone has their rights to dislike a game, I am just here to say that, in my opinion, this is a great choose-your-own-adventure game.
===========================
TL;DR version:
If you want to grab a quick read for your toilet & public transport time, no this one is not for you, because the plot and the writing don't allow a semi-attentive reader to fully apprehend and appreciate this novel. But if you are tired of all the shallow bull-sh*t Choice of Games sometimes pull out, and want to enjoy a REAL novel. This one definitively is worth considering!
And BTW, the ingame "optinal payment content" is not necessary at all. Basically it gives you some reminder like "Previously, you have chosen the Strategy A, so now, if you want to be coherent, you should consider the choice that stay in the same line."
============================================================
First thing first. Some people giving negative review were complaining about the confusing plot or/and the universe created by the author. It is an "understandable" opinion, IF you just want a quick short-novel to read while in the toilets. Because this novel is NOT a "toilet read". It tries to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ create a Sci-Fi universe!!! And of course, all novels like this (ranging from Tolkien's to Asimov's novels) take chapters and chapters to establish themselves. The author of Versus tries to condense all the necessary informations & background in an efficient way, and for me, he succeeded. You just need to set yourself confortable and enjoy the read slow and nice. Because yes, as the informations are very dense, if you try to read this as a transport pass-time, it will be hard to grasp all the subtleties.
As for the plot, it is one of the best plot I've ever seen in all my readings with Choice Of Games' interactive novels. I honestly dislike the previous trilogy of the same author (Hero Rise etc...), but I hugely appreciate this one: the choices I make truly give my the feeling of shaping the destiny of my character. And contrary to a lot of similar interactive novels which often tend to have really shallow plots, this one actually succeeded to build up the intrigue. This novel had me several times to stop and think "waite a minuit, does this mean that XXX is trying to... But what if...." whereas for most interactive novels, you just see the actions & motives of each character cristal clear. For me, this makes the novel a huge enjoyment. For some... I guess this may be qualified as "hard to follow" if they don't pay attention to details...
For me, it is best COYA novel Choice of Games had published so far. Before this, I'd rate Choice of Robots at top, but this novel just has so much more depth and perspectives. I am marveled by the universe built by the author. It is interesting and inspring like the TRUE Sci-Fi novels where you can glimpse thoughts about sociology, ethics and belief in every imaginary alien society that the author creates. The only regret I have is that, at several occasions, I'd like to have more choices: the given choices didn't correspond too well to what I'd like to behave. But I guess it's impossible for an interactive novel to cover and foresee all the options...

I've played through most games put out their by Choice of Games, including every one they've put out on Steam, and this is my least favourite that I've played, by a very large margin.
I have massive hours logged in this game, but that's not because I repeatedly played the game. At the risk of sounding hyperbolic, that was largely how long it took me to will myself to bother finishing it once. I don't like using those words to describe it, because these Choice of Games text adventures are generally quick, easy, and a lot of fun to complete.
I didn't want to miss out on let out before completing a COG adventure that could redeem itself.
At every turn I feel there was more disappointment, however. The game was left on in the background, as I continually opened it up with the intention of finishing it, but I instead god distracted while surfing the net, watching TV, doing work around the house, or anything at all, really. It could not hold my intention for more than a few minutes, or a few pages at a time.
It's tough when you're setting up and establishing a fictional world that no one has ever been to before, but I was continually losing track of things due to the incistence on using made up words, technologies, and powers to briefly describe what are complicated structures and devices within the story. By the time I began to figure out how one world worked, you get dumped into another world with it's own complex and hard to understand rules, morality, and way of life.
I felt little attachment to the characters, as their motivations got muddled up in that sea of things I couldn't grasp. It doesn't help that this game was ended on a cliffhanger, as an unsolved part of a larger story. It just felt as if the game almost abruptly ended.
The paid DLC prompt in the middle of the game was offputting as well. I know it was in the Heroes Rise games as well, but I think a pay to win plug in a single player text based game is just highly unecessary.
The game's heavy presence of ideas such as gender fluidity become overbearing, to the point where it begins to distract from the story, which as I've said was hard enough for me to get into. There's an incessant use of genderless pronouns like "Ze" and "hir", and many, many, points in the story, with various characters where the concepts feel shoehorned in for the sake of doing so. To the point that it feels less progressive and more outright preachy. Begins to feel more like there was an attempt to morally guilt me over unrelated real world issues, than keep me immersed in a survival space adventure.
Instead of this game, I would recommend a different Choice of Games entry in it's place. Tin Star, Champion of the Gods, A Wise Use of Time, Zombie Exodus, and Choice of Robots are all fantastic. Even this author's previous work, the Heroes Rise Trilogy is highly recommended.  But no, I would not recommend this game.

Super Dungeon Run is a fast paced, addicting game. In the game you control your greedy gold loving heroes fighting through dungeons, and dying to traps and enemies for a bit of loot. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
The controls are very simple as you use your mouse to guide you greedy heroes through the dungeon and use the 1, 2, and 3 keys to activate potions to help your heroes out.
The gameplay is very enjoyable. You start off with a set number of greedy peasants (you will know why I say "greedy" after) and fight through a dungeon to collect loot. In the game you can accept quest with the first one being to steal back a watermelon. The dungeons consist of floors which are anywhere from 10 seconds to 3 minutes long. As you continue to play this game you will unlock more heroes, more potions, and more quests in which you will get your butt kicked a bit. A key thing to note is that the heroes are very, VERY, greedy. More than a couple times a few coins would be lying around, and my heroes would run to the coins getting themselves, and most of my other heroes killed because of their greed. If you go too far away from one hero they will no longer be part of your party and you will need to go back to get them.  In the game there are 7 different types of heroes (including peasants) and 4 different types of potion.
The graphics are cartoony and seem a bit paper-like as of now. The area and village are rendered as a more 3D structure. The units are each unique in their design and very enjoyable to play. The music is done amazingly in this game. The music actually reminded me of an old game I used to play. Either way the music is very enjoyable.
+ Good music
+ Quick-paced
+ Simple
+ Quests are fun
+ Rewards you as you play and level up
+ Potions are fairly balanced
+ 7 different heroes and 4 different potions
+ Great art style
- Easy to lose a hero
- Slight grind
- Death is tasteless (they just flop over no matter what)
These are my personal suggestions for the game. My suggestions do not need to be taken seriously as they are my personal opinion for hopefully adding to the game to make it better.
- Controller Support
- Customization of heroes (different weapons and articles of clothing to choose from)
I have greatly enjoyed my time playing Super Dungeon Run. I have seen what the developer hopes to add and I am looking forward to it (especially funny deaths). The quests are nice and it was fun to play through this game. The only bad things that nudged at me was how easy it was to lose a hero, and how the heroes’ greed got me killed more than a few times. Overall I'm happy to have had the chance to play this early access game.
Super Dungeon Runner is fast-paced with floors in a dungeon ranging from 10 seconds to 3 minutes. The controls are simple as you only use your mouse and the 1, 2, and 3 keys. There are quests, potions, and of course your little dungeon running heroes in this game (7 heroes and 4 potions). The heroes are a bit greedy sometimes getting themselves killed for some coins. You fight through dungeon, gain money, get heroes and potions, upgrade said potions with crafting, and upgrade heroes as you level up. Truly fun and quick, Super Dungeon Runner is already a great game. Just in case you can check the features list to see if anything has been added since the time of this review.

So, after pouring a little over 180 hours into this game, I'm beginning to lose a lot of interest. It doesn't feel... like Fallout. It feels like some typical triple-A corporate game. With the controversy of paid mods, my opinion further decays. I mean, it's well made for a non-Fallout game. As Fallout, it's almost like it's not even the same anymore. The dialogue feels one-sided. You're absolutely forced to join the Minutemen. You have minimal freedom of character choice.
What I mean by that is this. You get the choice between a husband or wife. Get to choose their appearance, etc. They even put you in a scenario before the bombs drop. While this is nice, you don't get to really have a "history" like in the older games. You're either a military veteran, or a law school graduate. Don't get to choose much else aside from your S.P.E.C.I.A.L skills and appearance and name. Then you're shoved out into the game. You watch your wife (or husband, depending on who you choose) get killed, your son kidnapped. Then after thawing out of cryosleep, you go meet your robot butler and embark on an epic quest to find your son. While this has some emotional depth to it, the rest of the game feels mediocre and boring. Settlement building feels bland and boring, combat is sporadic, and the music is awfully repetitive.
So here's the mod issue. While free, user-made mods are fine and all, Bethesda thinks otherwise. Under the looming, ominous shadow of the Creation Club, paid mods are beginning to pop up. I mean, it's been mentioned before. But how many people is it going to take to tell Bethesda this isn't what we want. Paid mods vs. community made mods. I will list the effects of both.
Paid Mods
-Requires money to get (obviously)
-Are usually mediocre and rip-offs of other community mods
-Add little to no enjoyment to the game
-Ruins opportunities provided by user-made content.
Community Mods
-Requires NO money, not one cent.
-Are made with care, and by people, not just a few paid modders hired to make a mod in a small amount of time
-Can add endless hours of content and gameplay, moreso than DLCs at times.
-Create job opportunites or escapes for many people
-Opens avenues for improving the base game itself
With all this in place, is it really worth buying this game. A bunch of the DLCs seem uninteresting and generic to me. I've had a little bit of fun, but not as much as I would in older games. Heck, I play Skyrim to this day and still find enjoyment and fun. Because it's flexible. I wouldn't reccommend Fallout in its current state. Until Bethesda finds a way to fix this issue, I will more than likely uninstall it from my library so it doesn't take up space on my disk drive. If you enjoy this game and don't have anything against it, that's your thing. Just be wary of the current issues at hand.

So let me get this straight, you want to use my internet to download Creation Club bloated junk onto my harddrive space without my permission so that you can attempt to sell me things that I don't want? You're right Bethesda, that sounds like a great idea, said no one ever.
Let me start by saying that the game is fun. The combat is smooth, the shooting and the vats system streamline well into the game, and the settlement building (although with its own set of flaws) is a great addition to the series and fits well with the lore. Without mods, the game will keep you occupied for a long while. With mods, it will be a great experience. And I'm talking about MODS, not this Creative Club nonsense. REAL MODS made by generous people from places like the Nexus.
My major complaint with this game is the lack of RPG elements. I'm sure a lot of other reviews discuss this, so I'll jump into the big one, the one that sets me off: The voiced, set character and the stupid, linear story.
Now I know what you're going to say, "But all RPGs have a linear story!" And you'd be right, but it's the way that Fallout 4 approaches the story that forces you into a linear path regardless of how YOU, the player, wish to play the game. In most RPGs you make a character of your own imagining. You are free to be who you want, for the most part (given the limitations of said game). You know, the whole RP-Role Playing that comes with RPG. You have many adventures and quests to approach, some of them give you choices that (based on your style) can have different outcomes, not only for your character, but for your world.
So, Fallout, a nuclear apocalyptic wasteland. Are you a Wasteland Wanderer, a Raider with a heart of gold, or a bottlecap merchant looking for more loot? NO! You're a concerned parent looking for their son. Oh, and you have a wife/and/or husband depending on your gender. That's it. That's the game. And the story makes sure to remind you of it at every major turn, so even if you try to ignore it, even if you want to play differently, you can't. Not with such bread winners like, "I'm looking for my son, have you seen Shaun?" and "I'll find the men that took my son. I'll make them pay!" Oooo Hell hath no fury like a parent scorned.
Seriously though, what is this garbage? This is Fallout, a game of choices. I'm suppose to be able to be MY character and approach the story MY way. Nope. Not this time! Sure, you can "pretend" that, outside of the main story, your character is whoever you want them to be. Imagination is a large element of Role Playing, after all. But I shouldn't have to imagine! This is suppose to be My game, why are these decisions made for me? It only breaks the immersion further when I agree to help raiders loot a diner, yet at the back of my mind I recall - wait, didn't my character just wake from a vault? They went rogue immediatly? Sure, why not! I'm a real badass! But a badass that needs to find his son, desperately.
Even in games like Mass Effect and the Witcher where you DO play a singular character and you DO follow a semi-linear story, you are still presented with greater options than anything Fallout 4 throws at you. In the Witcher and Mass Effect, respectively, you are given choices, actions, and consequences, and based on how you respond, what you choose, and how you play, these choices will effect the game around you, and ultimately, effect your story. Pretty cool, right?
So does this happen in Fallout? No, you fool, of course not. Throughout the entire game's story you are given the ILLUSION of choice, but in the end, you follow through with the events the way the GAME wants you to progress, not the way YOU want to progress. It all boils down to these four dialouge options that you will encounter again, and again, and again.
1. You can accept the quest.
2. You can decline the quest. (Other than accepting it later again, if you can, why would you do this?)
3. You can ask for more information about the quest.
4. You can accept the quest - with sarcasm. (oooh, you badass, you!)
To add insult to injury, your open world RPG character has a voice. That means that they don't sound the way you imagine, they sound the way the game wants them to. In this case, like a nerdy yes man or a charmless mary sue. (And forget playing as any Race other than White, for all you other raced people out there - Your character will still sound like the above mentioned. What are you, some kind of supermutant?) Furthur more, the dialouge options presented to you are so vauge, half the time you're unsure of what your character will actually say. I would rather have text based responses for my character that add a large variety of depth and choice, as opposed to quick one liners that say nothing of who I am or what I want. Because remember, a voiced character means they had to pay a voice actor. It means that voice actor had to record every single line, it means that your options are going to be severly limited, because more options would require more money, would require more work. That's a no go.
ALL THAT being said, I would still recommend this game, because it is fun and does have its moments, were it not for the shady, money grab that is the Creation Club. You tried this a number of years ago with Skyrim and paid mods, remember Bethesda? It didn't work then, what makes you think it will work now?
Gone are the days of Role Playing in Bethesda, like the Morrowind of yore, or the great, gilded Fallout: New Vegas. (That was only good because Obsidian made it.) Instead we are left with the fun, yet souless shooter that is Fallout 4. I lament when I think of what new Bethesda game awaits us, and can only hope they've learned from their mistakes and will bring the power of playing back into the hands of the player.
But then I look at the Creation Club.

I have been playing Fallout from the beginning, and am something of a fanatic when it comes to lore and the world of Fallout in general. Unlike many, I find Fallout 4 to be an excellent addition to the series, and am quite pleased with it. The combat system is substantially improved (I really couldn't see 'going back' to playing earlier editions because of this...the improvements are that significant), the settlement system (and associated crafting) add a new dimension to play that significantly enhances the 'feel' of the world, and updated graphics (a new color palette!) make the game a better aesthetic experience.
I do agree with many commenters that Bethesda could do a better job with the main quest (a huge weakness in Fallout 3 as well), but their side quests are quite good, and the DLC adds a great deal to the main game. The RPG elements of the game need some polishing (the choice of a voiced protagonist has proved to be somewhat problematic, though I have hopes for improvement in future versions), and of course there is the usual problem of "Bethesda Bugs"...the QA on the game really does need work.
With all of that, this is a superior experience, and one of my 'go-to' games when I have some time free.

The graphics are incredible, and do a fantastic job of pulling you into the beautiful (albeit troubled) world the developers created; nothing instills a sense of urgency like seeing a massive alien creature in the distant city skyline, tossing buildings aside like LEGOs, and the whole thing is moved along by a soundtrack that's within a class of it's own!
The gameplay is, to say the very least, addictive; even post-game, with the plethora of weapons, towers, and gameplay style-defining perks all unlocked and the engaging story seen through to it's applause-worthy finale, the player will still have NO problem feeling the urge to return to their favorite maps time and again to assure the dreaded Lumes have had their fill of lead sammich!
All in all, Sanctum 2 stands as a shining example of an indie studio producing a triple-A product, while keeping the indie price tag!

I've been playing fighting games for competitively since 2000 and was a dedicated Street Fighter fan until this. It's no secret that Capcom's overall quality has steadily been on the decline and, for me, this was the last nail in the coffin. SFV is my final purchase of a Capcom game and I whole heartidly regret it.
So what's wrong? Let me list it for you:
- It was knowingly released as an unfinished product.
- Cinematic Story Mode is lackluster at best.
- PC vs. PS4 has a notable input difference. PS4 ver. has 8 frame input lag. Drastically impacting reactionary gameplay.
- Delays in character releases/glitches upon updates.
- In game character models are low end and varied in looks due to outsourcing to 3rd party model designers.
- Capcom's indifference to customer complaints and player concerns.
I say this as someone who has been a dedicated fan of the franchise and as a player who created a Steam account just to purchase and play this game on their PC.
If you're looking to SERIOUSLY play this game on a competitive level in the hopes of obtaining CPT points then you'll be willing to swallow this bitter pill and play it regardless of it's blatant flaws. This review does not apply to you and I wish you all the best on your endeavors.
If you're a casual player that's looking for a fighting game to play with friends online I strongly suggest you look elsewhere - Be it ArcSys' GGXRD or holding out for SNK's upcoming KOFXIV. This game is not worth your time or money, I'm sorry.

IMPORTANT: The playtime shown does not reflect my actual playtime for this VN. I previously read the fan translations of both Muv Luv and Muv Luv Alternative, and will base this short initial review on those experiences.
I should start by saying that the Muv Luv trilogy is the best piece of fiction I've ever read in visual novel format. From start to finish the story was very well thought out and designed, each instalment building upon and surpassing the last. Despite its flaws (read: Extra) you absolutely have to read the whole thing if you're a fan of visual novels.
Previously I'd found it difficult to review or recommend this VN to others for two reasons:
-because my words can not do it justice. I recommend reading the top reviews on this page if you haven't already;

-because it's inherently spoiler heavy. Originally Unlimited was not revealed to the reader beforehand, it would be unlocked after finishing Extra as a surprise. Fortunately the English release is not as secretive as the original.
I say fortunately because Extra on its own would be a very generic harem romcom in a tired high school setting. I don't think it would be unfair to say that it's actually a hurdle on the way to enjoying this trilogy, despite being a decent VN that contributes a lot to the series. It requires some commitment to get through Extra if the reader's tired of its kind of story, but you'll have to take my word for it that it's all worth it in the end. I recommend reading Sumika's and Meiya's routes at least, because this was the requirement to unlock Unlimited in the original release and they follow roughly the same story path with alternate scenes. I'd give this one a 7/10.
After enduring comedic shenanigans in his original universe Takeru the harem protagonist wakes into the darker world of Unlimited. Out of his comfort zone in a fundamentally familiar setting with familiar faces that don't recognise him, Takeru has to adapt to an unfair reality, unsure if he'll be able to return to the world he knew. Unlimited is a much more refreshing experience after Extra, and yet only dips into the depths Alternative goes to. I like to call it a boot camp coming-of-age story, and it's a solid 8/10.
At the time this review is being written Alternative is not yet released on Steam. It could be that playing through Muv Luv may leave you unsatisfied with Unlimited's ending since a lot of questions remain unanswered and closure is left to Alternative. I'd recommend to wait until Alternative's release if you prefer to finish a story in one go.

Short version: Muv-Luv is an incredibly good VN that requires a little patience. If you haven't read it before and like Visual Novels, then I highly recommend you buy this, but you may wish to wait until the final chapter, Muv-Luv Alternative, is released on steam, for the full dramatic experience. PLAY EXTRA THROUGH ONE TIME BEFORE YOU START UNLIMITED.
Long version: For those who are familiar with the fan translation, I'd also highly reccomend this release. It's a lot better looking than the original PC release, and uses some of the visual improvements introduced by Alternative such as lip flaps on sprites. The translation is much improved so far and I laughed far harder at a lot of the jokes, and in addition, there's an option for images to be translated too. I'm unaware if a H patch is in the works, but the all-ages versions are surprisingly enjoyable, giving us new CGs that don't deny the progression of the relationship, but merely remove the graphic element, so for this game I don't mind. The only downsides are that Unlimited is available from the get go; whilst this is convenient, it means the dream of gifting this to your unaware friend, so they jump in blind, isn't really possible. In addition, some of the music tracks have been replaced. Not a big problem, just don't expect to be Livin' la vida loca.
Highly recommended to fans and newcomers alike. I'm having the time of my life playing through all over again and I can't wait for Alternative to complete the set.

An interesting and thoughtful experience, well worth the miniscule price tag.
Obviously, in an all-text game, the most important aspect is the writing, and it's generally written well enough to elicit the proper emotional response: Fights feel tense, fantastic landscapes feel wonderous, and intrigues feel anxious.
The story is a puzzle, and it keeps asking you to input your guesses as you go, giving you some sense of involvement, rather than just being dragged along, having the plot explained to you.
That said, I'm not such a fan of the naming sense.  Everything tends to have an "exotic" name that's just one letter removed from a common adjective or object name it is like.  It's the sort of thing where you meet a rabbit-like alien creature, and it turns out it's called a "Vunny Vabbit", or something.  The abomination that dominates as a villain's name is "Bominate", for example.
There are far more decisions here than most games, but they tend to be in two categories: Action decisions and "what you think" decisions.
Action decisions are fairly cut-and-dry, and are based around your stats, both relying upon and empowering stats.  You have "forceful" versus "cunning" (preference for direct versus indirect confrontation), "weapons" versus "abilities" (technology versus superpowers), and different absorption energy levels, but which one you pick doesn't seem to mater so much as whether you pick them
.  Whether you take weapons or abilities, technical skill absorption or agility absorption, you're going to be flying, it's just a matter of whether the text says it's with a jetpack or a flight superpower.  It's like being drowned in multiple layers of the standard good/evil karma meter: You just pick one and keep picking it's options until the end of the game, taking away from the impact of choices by making them all equally viable, just for different playthrough paths.
The "what you think" decisions are much more nebulous, and seem to do little but push up a "growth" meter of unexplained purpose.  The game asks you constantly for what you think about some concept or person or what you want to set as a goal, but then someone busts in, teleports you out, or throws some other deus ex machina at you before these choices can impact anything.  The system seems to be there to punish "inconsistent" answers, but at the same time, encourage "growth in your viewpoint" as the game reveals more information to you.
The plot is one of those somewhat annoying types of mysteries where all the mysteries would largely be solved if you just asked the right questions, but the prompts never let you, and all your conversations are 3 minutes long before shoving you into some new, arbitrary crisis half-cocked, asking you to just make a blind assumption, and hoping you're right.
This is exacerbated by the fact that there are multiple concurrent plots in this game that have little to no overlap - that elite courte intrigue that's part of the game's main selling points has only the most tenuous connections with the blot plotline the game starts with, or the android-human war you launch into after that.  The plots have totally different actors, backstories, and even planets the characters come from, and you can't ask characters from one plot for help understanding the other plots.
To a degree, this seems to be a result of how the game handles the vast interation of possible choice combinations - they keep the plot from branching into geometric plotlines by just putting the results of your choices in one plot on hold while you get shoved into the next, unrelated plot.  I can understand the reasoning, but I can't help but see it as a weakness of the whole scripted dialogue branching choices genre, as it weakens the story as a whole.
Essentially, instead of having one long plot, you have three short plots, where the only actual divergence in the relatively linear story comes at the very end when plots all finally crash together... right before a "To Be Continued." Yeah, there's a yet-unreleased sequel, and nothing but the achievements being layed out chronologically hints that you're about to run out of game.
This hurts the replayability, as well: You have some choices to make that are flavorful and welcome, but then the only real way to play differently (or get the other achievements) is to purposefully make the characters you romanced last time hate you this time. Achievement-hunting basically counteracts the value of playing to express yourself, because you are required to befriend everyone, romance everyone you can, and make everyone hate you, while also going against your previous choices for weapons versus abilities. It's just busywork for cheevos, and that's probably why so few people get them, in spite of it being rather quick and easy to get them. Contrast this with Choice of Robots, which offers completely different vignettes for different character romances, and wholly different chapters for different specializations.
Also to be noted is this game's ludicrous level of customizable sexuality. You can play as a transgendered or intersex character who is attracted to male, female, or androgenous characters, and have an androgenous lover, or an android one.  Of course, you still get the option to just say you're a straight man or woman and the game respects that, too.

-Everybody placing his troops

-Player#1 wins
If you're the player #1 who is able to attack first, you win. If not you lose. Always.

I was expecting an OK game as I like RISK, but this was awesome!  It IS a RISK-type board game, but with such a fantastic wide variety of maps it really changes the strategy per map, especially when you get maps that are both sea and land based.  And there are just tons of options for AI behavior and skill level, and tons of community maps not to mention the multiplayer online games you can do.  I really like the idea of a few large cities across the map that also worth a bonus army or two; changes up the strategy.  Very cool.
The ONLY downside on the main game itself is that I really wish it had a "campaign" as the two DLCs do.  The DLCs give you the feeling of accomplishing a story or going through history, even if it is just a board game.  So I HIGHLY recommend the two DLCs:
and
.   Both, though dated, I liked even better than the core game maps, again due to the campaign nature of the DLCs.
The 11 maps included in the Core Game are all certainly good, but they are unrelated to each other.  Included there's a Castle Siege, a couple European maps, a USA map, a WW II map, a Pacific Theater map, and the Classic RISK map, but then you get some novelty maps too:  a Solar System map and a Silicon Valley map.
But along with the Core Game, there are many, many good maps that you can download (right from the main menu) or even make maps yourself.  I just far prefer 'campaigns' and not one-off maps, but that's me.
The core 11 maps took me ~ 4.75 hours; American History Lux was ~ 2.75 hours, and Ancient History Lux ~ 4.75 hours.  I consider the DLC's "must-haves" particularly Ancient History.

This is a consistent, but only mildly fun game. It probably won't be remembered as one of the best games of 2010, but it might be worth the cost if you enjoy the Aliens vs. Predator lore. This is one of those games where I neither felt disappointed or overwhelmed. It was just a solid title which will, unfortunately, inevitably be forgotten. Lux Delux is a Java-based implementation of the Risk board game. It comes with 11 maps by default (though you're free to download more) and there's a bit of variety to them (some maps have regions without bonuses, regions with one-way access, regions separated by single chokepoints, etc.). There are a good amount of options to customize the game rules.
You should be familiar with and know the rules of Risk because while there are in-game instructions, it doesn't go into full depth and there are mechanics that aren't explained at all (like combat).
While the attacker is supposed to have the advantage (because they roll an extra unseen die), I tended to make sure I had a good amount more units than the defender because it always feels terrible to lose your whole stack and not even take anything. Keyboard shortcuts make it easier to attack with large stacks.
I would've liked to have an optional window that showed the actual rolls (like in Blood Bowl) because I'd rather see under-the-hood how I lost a stack instead of having no idea what's going on.
Once in a while there are graphical glitches that require you to restart the game.
It's very easily missed but it also offers two expansion games, American History Lux and Ancient Empires Lux (and a third link that sends you to the 'buy product' page for a third title). These are a group of 10-12 scenarios with multiple difficulty levels that you can go through. They have no overarching story and are pretty much unrelated except for theme, so I wouldn't really consider it a campaign.
If you enjoy Risk, you might want to try out Lux Delux.

Organ Biker is horrible at communicating with the player. It first launches as a teeny tiny 256x240 window, which is the only place where the game outlines the controls, which make no sense to you if you've never played the game.
Once in the game, what you do is dodge cars (and later missiles from stealth bombers), collect pick-ups and when an "ambulance plane" comes on screen, you enter the green "launch zone" and shoot hearts at it for points. If you crash, your bike respawns on the right side of the road, and you're invincible for a while.
To move left or right, you need to have speed, or "MOJO" as the game intuitively calls it. Logically you lose your mojo when you crash, but your input is disabled for a while after you crash, leaving you watching a flickering stationary bike for a while.
The game doesn't in any way indicate the input is disabled, so the first time you'll likely not understand what's going on, and crash again, because, natureally, the cars *CAN* drive in the part of the road where you respawn. The next time  you'll be manically hammering UP to get your "mojo" on and be able to get out of the way of danger. Why this happens, I have no idea. It definitely doesn't add anything to the game. According to a recent developer announcement, there should be a six seconds invincibility period, but in effect this is usually wasted on waiting for input to become active again.
Your HP is called HOPE, which you refill by picking up heart pick-ups. You lose HOPE over time, whenever you crash and if you get hit by the stealth bombers missiles.
Picking up four heart pick-ups grants you one use of a screen clearing bomb that, unfortunately works on a delay, so more than once, not wanting to waste it, I tried using it at the last second, but because the actual clearing of the screen happens after the heart animation has played, I still crashed. Trying go gauge the right time to use the bomb is pretty difficult, and later in the game it's almost useless anyway, because of the time it takes to collect four hearts is very long in relation to the amount of hazards you face.
Organ Biker doesn't have
animations at all just static sprites (well, the bike sprite gets flipped when you "turn", but even then the sprite is almost symmetrical). Some of the "old school" effects just look weird (especially the moiré-effect looks like it's just a static texture).
The music is very hit and miss, luckily you can choose it manually so you can just opt to never to listen to the worse tracks.
Unless you disable the arcade-effects, some of the text is pretty hard to read, because your combo and score are not displayed in the same pixel font as the rest of the UI, but instead in a standard serif font, that the arcade effect makes pretty unreadable.
The game doesn't have a pause function, and no apparent way to quit mid game, appart from just closing the program with Alt+F4.
Bottom line is Organ Biker just isn't fun, the controls are iffy and some of the design choices are just arbitary and weird. Apparently the game is still beign worked on, which gives hope, but at this point, I definitely do not recommend buying it. If there are any updates to the game, I'll make sure to update my review.

Mechanically, this is honestly the most impressive of all of Choice of Games' products. The stats are very in-depth, the relationship mechanics are very complex, and it even has images embedded into the game, something which I believe very few other CoG games have.
Unfortunately, VERSUS' plot and characters is where it all goes to hell. I can understand that some or even many people would delight at the concept - Individuals taken from a gamut of different worlds around the galaxy to fight in some kind of strange, mysterious tournament. For me, however, the whole thing feels like it was written by an amateur high school "author" who thinks that combining twelve different genres into one is super cool. The problem with this game, then, is an issue of too many cooks spoiling the broth. Combining two or even three genres at once is viable for some creators, even if it is an exceedingly difficult task to do properly. Combining as many genres together as VERSUS does, though, just results in a chaotic mix where the game really doesn't seem to have any idea what it wants to be at any given moment. Sci-fi? Fantasy? Mystery? Action? Cyberpunk? Steampunk? In the end, the setting, plot, and characters are all just a complete mess, which means that the otherwise amazing system CoG has developed here has gone completely to waste.

Back in the heyday of Strategy games, casting our minds from before the influx of Freemium/online/casual strategy, we had nailbitingly tense and complex strategy games that truly challenged the individual. Whist the current trend of Casual gaming isn't a bad one, it is hardly satisfying. Planetary Anihilation Titans IS the personfication of satisfying RTS. No cheese. No light action. No consticted and simplistic gameplay. It is raw, unrefined Strategy, a reference to the classics such as C&C Red Alert, Warcraft 1-3, Dune and Supreme Commander, of which the latter has most definetly influenced PA:Titans. Never have I had the feeling of control juxtaposed so heavily with the feeling of exposure as I have had with this game. The scope alone is mind-boggling, and the first time zooming out from a lowly Dox, then into the Solar System over which vast armies are clashing in is perhaps one of the most amazing I have had in a Strategy game.
Of course, not all games are perfect, and PA:Titans stands accused. Yes we did lose features as engine limitations revealed glaring holes. Yes, this game does suffer from slow update cycles. Yet, I'll concede that this is the limitations of smaller developers whom can't afford continued time expendature (and money) on games that are defintely playable and worth a go for any Strategy gamer worth his/her salt.
TL:DR - Game's good and provides a deep and challenging experience that invokes a sense of size quite difficult to comprehend. Give it a go if one is a hardcore RTS fan who is tired of the casualised experience.

Probably one of the most underrated games of 2012, Sleeping Dogs brings to the table an unique experience. From the interesting story, to the refreshing Kung Fu combat, every single bit of it is really enjoyable, but as every other games, it has it shortcomings.
Story & Setting
Sleeping Dogs is a third-person, open world, action game set in modern Hong Kong. The story revolves around Wei Shen, an undercover cop from San Francisco that left Hong Kong with his family when he was young, and his journey to infiltrate in Sun On Yee , a criminal organization who is both feared and respected. The main plot line is focused on Wei`s struggle between the two worlds, between what is right and what is wrong, between law or emotions. The second plot line is focused solely on his    work in Sun On Yee, where family and respect are the most important thigs, leading to some really intense moments.
Gameplay
The Gameplay is the best part of the game, and what you are gonna by doing most of the time. Inspired from Batman Arkham Asylum ,but with a twist of Kung Fu, the combat is one of the most enjoyable when it comes to Open World Action Games.
The mechanics are simple : You have an attack button, a counter button, a run button and a grapple button.
The basic combo consist in pressing the attack button a certain amount of times, and sometimes you have to hold it to increase the power of the attack. Also, you can combine the attack with either run or grapple in order to performa even more combos. But beware, most of those will have to be bought with statues that you find in missions from the dojo.
You main defence will be the counter button. Just as in Batman, when an enemy is about to attack he will flash red. If you hit the button at the right time, you will stop the attack and initiate a counterattack. Of course this does not work on all enemies, some will have to be disarmed in order to be able to counterattack
Of course, as in every action game, there are gonna be guns but they are very rare, and only certain missions will have it. The gunplay is cover-based, from which you can also blind fire or jump over in slow-motion. Some of the cover is destructible, but most of it is not. Be careful though, because the enemy will come after you if you don't kill them. When in a car chase, the gunplay consists either in shooting the bad guys or in shooting their tires, resulting in an awesome slowmo scene.
The biggest flaw that the combat has is that it can become a little repetitive after a while.
Graphics & Sound
Sleeping Dogs has THE best rainy scenes and the most detailed city I have ever seen in a game. The models are very nicely detailed and textured, the city is full of things hanging or flying. The detail put in this game is absolutely amazing. Even if you can't run it maxed out, you will be able to experience the beauty that this game has.
As for the sound I have to say that it is very immersive. From Traditional Chinese music, to modern club music, to some metal the game provides something for everybody. The voice acting for every single character is top notch and very authentic.
Conclusion
Sleeping Dogs is not a perfect game, not by any stretch of the imagination, but it IS a really good game which offers a great story and characters, but also a really good combat system that is very enjoyable to watch. It is an underrated game that deserve much more than it got.

First things first, some people may be confused with the playing order. This listing comes with both Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited, but unfortunately, unlike in the original game, both Extra and Unlimited are accessible from the beginning, adding to the confusion. The order that I recommend you play, and the order that was originally intended is:
Extra > Unlimited > Alternative
I'd recommend you at least finish Sumika or Meiya's route (personally, I found Meiya's route to be more entertaining) before playing Unlimited as it continues directly from the common route of the two. Then once you hit Unlimited, pursue any route you want. Of course, this is the bare minimum so you can pursue other routes in addition to those mentioned, but keep in mind that the purpose of Extra is to familiarise yourself with the characters before diving into Unlimited. In Unlimited, knowledge of characters and their personalities is assumed and as such, you shouldn't start Unlimited before doing the above.
I'm not really one to beat around the bush, so here's a summary of pros and cons of both games.
In conclusion, Extra may be bearable for some and completely unbearable for others, but even so, it's very worth playing through Extra as it has a huge pay off once you hit Alternative and as it introduces the characters. It's not great by any stretch, but some of the issues it tackles can be very emotional, such as choosing a girl to pursue. While playing it, you may not realise that it does indeed tie into Alternative, so it is integral to the overall experience. Personally, I despised Extra at the time I played it, however, after playing Alternative, it blew my mind with how much it was actually related.
Unlimited, overall, is a much better experience and if you're a mech fan like I am and there's a lot of fun to be had with Takeru's shenanigans as well as the world design. There are also many references to other mech series in here that would delight fans. That's not to say it's perfect either, as the story is fairly generic and it still retains the light hearted nature of Extra which can be both good or bad depending on how you look at it. It assumes that you have played Extra, and as such, spares no time introducing characters but instead builds on the characters from Extra. Furthermore, some events can be overly patriotic, which may be annoying to some people.
As a standalone experience, both Extra and Unlimited are average, however, they lay the foundations for Alternative which continues straight from the end of Unlimited. If you like narratives that focus on characterisation, the Muv-Luv series is definitely something to experience regardless of if you're a mech fan or not. If you prefer a strong story, Muv-Luv might not be what you're looking for, but I would recommend it regardless as it may give you a few surprises. Doing the bare minimum in Extra and Unlimited will take about 20 hours altogether.
If you do end up playing the Muv-Luv Trilogy, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

Street Fighter V is an interesting beast. On one hand, the game is really fun to play. It eschews the tight links and high execution of the previous titles in the series, and instead focuses on the meta game. As a new player, you're probably going to like that. As a veteran to fighting games, it can be overly simple for you. From my point of view, I'll still play it, but I also think the game needs something else to make the game crazier to play and watch. It's a very vanilla fighter, with not a lot of the flash and flair of games like Marvel VS Capcom, or Guilty Gear Xrd.
Another thing is the lack of single player content. Quite noticably, the game is lacking a simple arcade mode, or a way to fight CPU opponents outside of Survival Mode. Much of the content is focused on multiplayer, which is fine for me; I play fighting games to play people, not computers. If you're looking for a fighting game to play solo, this may not be for you. Capcom is adding in a Story Mode to the game in this June 2016, so it'll get a boost to it's single player content.
As for the actual fighting mechanics, it's a little bare bones for my tastes, but still gets the job done. I do enjoy the focus shifting away from the execution (a high barrier to entry for beginners) and more towards playing the opponent, reading his/her habits, and adapting accordingly. Likely, this is a good starting off point for new players and newcomers to fighting games, but the game does not include a good tutorial to teach you the basics. Instead, you'll have to rely on the community for guides and tutorials on how to play. Luckily, there's no shortage of that content, but it's amazing that Capcom hasn't added in anything to teach.
Now, in the case that you're choosing a fighting game on which to focus on playing, should you make Street Fighter V that game? The competition is stiff; BlazBlue, Killer Instinct, Guilty Gear Xrd Revelator (a PS3/4 title, but rumored PC release), Mortal Kombat X are also games that could be on your list. Street Fighter V can definitely be played for a long time, and probably will last into the far future, as much as Street Fighter IV has. If this is your first fighting game, I would say decide between the aesthetics of Guilty Gear Xrd Revelator or Street Fighter V - whatever looks or character you'd rather play I'd choose. For veteran fighters, have a look at the fighting mechanics. If the meta game interests you (the shimmy, the crush counters) go for it.
It is by no means a bad game, but it lacks in certain places. I enjoy my time playing it, but at times it feels like it's lacking in the flash and pizzazz that other games have. I still recommend it to anyone who enjoys fighting games and newcomers alike.
