BitzComms Reviews: The Lego Movie Video Game
(This review covers the PC - Your experience may differ from platform to platform)
I have to be honest with you - The Lego Movie came to me by complete surprise. For all the time I spend on YouTube, no word was spoken of the movie (at least that I saw) until I first saw the trailer for it on TV...
But then I was surprised even more when a video game was announced for it - It wasn't even a full year after Lego Marvel Super Heroes came out, and Traveller's Tales came out with a new game already?
It was more surprising that the game was coming to all major platforms, INCLUDING next gen platforms like the PS4, Xbox One, Wii U, in addition to the PC, Xbox 360 and PS3... Yikes.
The short development period between this and Marvel seemed like a sign that this game was going to blow HARD... But then I played it, and it is probably my favorite Traveller's Tales Lego game of all time.
STORY:
The game follows the story of the movie down pat... Which might turn off those who haven't seen it yet. I suggest you see the movie before you play the game, but even if you don't, the game doesn't feature EVERY scene from the movie... Some of the scenes that are in the game have parts that were cut from the movie, most likely to keep from spoiling the movie for those who haven't seen it. I won't explain the story itself, because we have a movie for that, and I wouldn't want to spoil anything.
PRESENTATION:
The Lego games that have been developed by Traveller's Tales over the years have had a reputation of exceptional presentation, and this one is no different. The game is fully voiced, and either they got the celebrity voices from the movie to do the game, or they just got really, really good sound-alikes. If it's the latter, I wouldn't be able to tell the difference because the acting in this game is so damn good. As I said before, the story is presented through scenes from the movie, and while that may sound kind of cheap, you have to keep in mind the short period between the release of this and Marvel. Plus, the scenes look so good already that you won't mind at all. It kind of harkens back to the days of movie tie-ins on the Playstation, which generally used scenes from the movie for the cutscenes of the game. Anyone remember Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue? (also developed by Traveller's Tales) The game also makes use of a new animation style - The characters actually move like actual lego... No more bendy, stretchy lego limbs. This is probably done to stay true to the stop-motion style of the movie.
GRAPHICS:
The game looks amazing, as everything is made of Lego this time around. The game also runs really well on low-end machines like mine, and that's always a plus.
SOUND:
Everything is Awesome!
GAMEPLAY:
Here's where things get pretty iffy - The game itself is a mixed bag. While this is my favorite TT Lego title so far, I can't deny this game has some serious problems. Let's first talk about the character selection - There are over NINETY characters... NINETY CHARACTERS. Don't get too excited though, as most of the characters are either clones of existing characters, or very minor characters that no one cares about. Most of the characters are different suits for Emmet. Wild Style or Unikitty. There are some good ones in this game, such as Lord Business, Metalbeard, Batman, Super Man, The Green Lantern, Wonder Woman and even the Green Ninja from Lego Ninjago.
Emmet himself is a pretty boring character as well. For the majority of the game, all he can really do is use instruction builds. He can't use master builds, and he doesn't have any interesting attacks or gimmicks. Most of the time, you'll be playing as Wild Style, Batman and Unikitty, switching to Emmet only when you need to use an instruction build. Eventually Emmet gets the ability to use Master Builds, but that's very late in the game.
Next, let's talk about the gameplay. The game follows the same basic formula as any other TT Lego title before it - Go through the levels, collecting studs and accomplishing objectives with preset characters, then go back and play those levels as any character to find hidden unlockables - Only this time it's mixed with free-roaming hub worlds, and my GOD these are underwhelming. Compared to Lego City: Undercover and especially Lego Marvel Super Heroes, these free-roaming segments seem to be just an after-thought. They are very small and contained. Not very much fun.
Next, let's talk about the levels for a minute. The levels are probably the best part of the game, with only a few stinkers here and there. The only problem is that many of them are very long, and when there's a bad level, there's a REALLY bad level. Each level is quite interesting, with its own gimmick and setpieces. There's an entire level that takes place on an under-constuction submarine that's careening down an ablaze Cloud Cuckoo Land. Many of the level designs are very inspired and smart, but they are quite long, and if you don't have a lot of time for one session, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. There are checkpoints placed around the levels that allow you to save your progress, but some of them are placed in areas where you really wouldn't notice them... oops.
THE VERDICT:
As a whole, however, The Lego Movie Video Game is quite solid, considering the short development period. There's a lot of content in here, and most of the levels are fun, if not a bit too long. I'm giving this game a 7.0 out of 10.

Ok First off, I've played all three. What this means is that I like Extra much more than the first time I played it. Alternative has a tendancy to boost appreciation of the earlier games a ton. Mainly because... reasons.
But this isn't about ALternative or the trilogy.
This is about Extra/alternative. And Extra is ok. It feels like a 90's anime romantic comedy, with all the good and bad of it. It's not bad, in fact I'd rate it's story a solid 7/10 as an above average visual novel. But its not great, and can drag in some areas. If you've played a bunch of visual novels it might even seem like it's a bit stale because of the tropes being so familiar. But it is a solid visual novel, and there are some good story arcs, and I rather like the endings for Meiya/Sumika (the endings one had to reach in the original game to unlock unlimitted).
Now onto Unlimitted. Unlimitted is where things get interesting. IN this new world Takeru is a fish out of water and everyone's personality is slightly changed from extra (cause yeah... humanity is dying out and everyone kind of is aware of it but trying to beleive it can be stopped). This is definaitly a good visual novel and I wouldn't hesitate to give it's story a 8.5/10. Very enjoyable and fun. Love the atmosphere and world building.
But again these are only the prelude to the amazing, tear jerking, roler coaster that is Alternative. I'd say too anyone on the fence this is a game you should play before alternative realeases (if you don't care for extra, I'd say just play one route and then jump to unlimitted).
The Interface and game quality is definitly updated and has some of the higest levels for VN available. But I personally don't really care for that too much, I prefer story, but compared to the fan translated 200X version, yeah I can see the difference.
As a standalone i'd say it's worth the buy, but not everyone will like all aspects of it. They are good games.

After buying Bastion during the 2011 winter sale and playing the few minutes necessary to get the achievement for the coal-crafting metagame, I filed it away in my mental “play later” category, but never got back to it until just recently. (After all, I wouldn’t have felt quite right adding Transistor to my backlog until Bastion was done.)
Honestly, it took me a fair amount of time to warm up to Bastion. The voiced aspect of the narrative didn’t hook me right away as it did for many other players - in fact, I found it somewhat distracting and stylistically difficult to follow while beating away on the baddies. The combat, while serviceable, didn’t immediately motivate me to experiment with different weapons or special abilities. As a result, I pushed through the first half of the game primarily because I like to finish the games I start, and not because I was particularly impressed with it beyond the superficial stuff.
It wasn’t until all the cores were gathered up that I felt Bastion was finally starting to click with me. By that time I’d had a decent opportunity to upgrade a few different weapons, and the creature variety made me think a bit more about approaching each situation (although I certainly wouldn’t characterize any of the enemy encounters as difficult). In addition, I had put together enough of the backstory that the plot started to get interesting. Narration redeemed. After that point, I was much more motivated to play the game to completion.
The soundtrack and art were superb throughout, but I don’t think there’s a lot of disagreement on that, so no need to go into any great detail there. I can’t think of any area of the game that lacked in the visuals department, although I did find that forested area with the armored frogs to be incredibly annoying.
Regarding optional stuff, I didn’t spend a lot of time with it. First, I’d like to go back and try some of the idol challenges. I enabled one of the idols once, but lost interest in them when I noticed that it deactivated itself when I was done with the level. I didn’t really want to revisit the shrine between each area to keep them turned on. Second, I’m thinking about going through New Game+ after a short break (a month or two).
So, short and sweet, I’d give Bastion a decent recommendation. It wasn’t among the most compelling experiences I’ve found in gaming, nor did it really live up to the level it was hyped at to me. Regardless, it’s a good game and short enough for anyone to give it a fair shake. And it was most certainly good enough to make me look forward to buying and playing Transistor at some point.

Paid Mods, The Game.
That was the short version. The long version is that Fallout 4 is on release a bare bones game. It's actually the skeleton of a game, waiting to be filled by the community.
And yes, the community has filled that skeleton, building upon it transforming it into a great game. There are thousands of mods, I personally play with 130, others play with over 200. Using this great library of FREE Mods you can turn Fallout 4 from the empty shell it is, into one of the best games on the market.
So what do the creators of this game do? Well, dear ol' Bethesda decides to implement PAID Mods, 5$ per mod even, so you can enjoy their game. Not that they are good mods, weapon and armor skins mostly, not mods that actually fix or improve upon the game in any other way.
But that in itself is actually fine. Let them have PAID Mods separately, so folks can nicely ignore and let their Creation Club just wither away. Which has been happening. So what does dear ol' Bethesda do?
Well... here's the kicker... they keep releasing "Updates" that don't do anything to the game itself, just modifications to the PAID Mods Creation Club Market, and these "Updates" break F4SKE.
The real thorn is that 99% of the mods out there use F4SKE, which is fan made, as an essential tool in their mods. So without F4SKE, you have no FREE Mods, forcing unnecessary updates from modders who either are not active anymore or have little time to spare.
To make it short, Bethesda is intentionally releasing Hack Updates to break Free Mods so you are forced to buy Paid Mods. So instead of paying your 60$ for the Game and it's DLCs, you also need to pay 8$ for the Creation Club and then pay 5$ per mod to make the game PLAYABLE!!
So yeah, Bethesda wants me to pay 130 mods (after finding their PAID equivalent) * 5$ (assuming they would all be this cheap) a minimum of what? 650$ to just play their freaking game in a actually Working and Fun manner?
Fallout 4 has been turned by greedy executives into Paid Mods, The Game.
As a conclusion, if you don't mind being constantly reminded by the game to buy Paid Mods, and you enjoy paying for what used to be free content, then yeah, go buy the game. If you do not want to be treated like a cow to be milked for your hard earned money, then do not purchase Fallout 4. There are plenty of other games out there that respect you as a consumer than go play Elex or Witcher 3, games that respect you for buying them.
Which reminds me of something else, something a lot of people have been asking for lately: Bethesda, please... I beg you, please let Obsidian make Fallout games from now on. They actually make good games.

If you love 'choose your own adventure' type stories, this is a must-read.
I dove straight into the story with high hopes.  I have read and purchased many of Choice of Games interactive novels, the most recent being the Heroes Rise Trilogy.  Heroes Rise immersed me into a wonderful story line full of twists, turns, and an entire rollercoaster of possibilities.
VERSUS brings forth a sense of customization, while keeping the reader immersed in the world.  Giving you choice of name, gender (or lack their of), and sexual/romantic preference, this interactive novel truly gives the reader a further connection to the story: it allows the reader to place their personal identity into their hero.
This interactive novel also gives the reader philisophical choices paired with their personal agendas.  Was your hero raised under strict religion and views, but feels that fate has destined them to explore beyond their community limitations?  Or is your hero a hot-headed renegade, prepared to take on the world despite their homeworld's strict raisings?  Is your hero one that finds themselves suddenly captivated by an alien goddess?  Or does the idea of knowledge overpower the idea of possbile romance?
I hadn't a clue where VERSUS would take me, but I found myself torn between two opposing teams with equal rhyme and reason, debating my views on secular purpose, and coming to terms with what was morally right, given extreme circumstances.
If you have a few hours to spare, immerse yourself in the world of VERSUS.  And be prepared to test your limits, heroes.

Loads of fun to play solo or with friends. Roles as a crewman are very easy to learn, and one can be a competent addition to any ship within the span of an hour. Captaining is a tad bit more complex, but can be simplified as keeping close to friendlies, giving your crew the best shot possible, and getting out of danger when warranted.
The best advice I can give is to embrace the chaos. Things will go wrong fairly often. Shots will miss, fires will start, ships will sink, friendlies will die (either at the hands of the enemy, or otherwise), but always remember that it's a game above all else. Ship happens, try not to take it too seriously. Good stats are nice, but they will come more easily when you're having fun.
The only real issue, aside from the usual slight jankiness that is to be expected in an alpha/beta, is the stacking of ships with elite crews that go up against newbie opposition, but this is a short term problem while the playercount expands and the servers slowly fill up with new faces.
Repair the sails, load the cannons, and sing your favorite sea shanty as you turn your lightweight Hoy into a flaming torpedo of doom!

Also, this review was originally a post I made on the discussion boards when someone asked why they should read this.  If it looks familiar, that's why.
Muv-Luv is a single tale split into three parts. The first part, Extra, is one of character building. The generic high school setting and romcom story are meant to familiarize you with Takeru's mindset as well as the characters he is involved with. If you've ever read or watched Steins;Gate, it's kind of like the first half of that. It has a certain amount of charm and no small amount of humor in it, but also some clever foreshadowing that you probably won't get on the first read, but will look back to while reading the later parts and go "ohhh, that's what that was."
The new translation is vastly more readable than the old fan translation, but if you aren't interested in the romcom genre, Extra may be a tough read. Fortunately, just going through a single route won't take that long. And that's all you really need for Extra to serve its purpose.
The second part, Unlimited, is one of world building. It introduces you to the sci-fi setting that the majority of the story takes place in and shows how that world has affected the lives of the people you grew to know in Extra. Unlimited is more of a military academy setting, and the genre is more of a dramedy than a romcom, though there are still romantic aspects to it. Again, there are a lot of points in Unlimited that will be referenced in the third part, but even without that, Unlimited is a worthy read on its own. Keep in mind that original readers were waiting for 3 years after Extra/Unlimited to get the next part.
The third part, Alternative, I won't go into much detail on, except to say that if you have any interest in the Mecha genre at all, this is one of the best ones out there. Even if Extra and Unlimited were borderline unreadable(which they are not), I'd still recommend ploughing through them to get the most out of Alternative. It's the highest rated VN on VNDB for a very good reason.
If you've watched Total Eclipse, the Muv-Luv Trilogy isn't that. If you've watched Schwarzesmarken, that's only a pale imitation(and yet still quite good on its own). If you're asking why you should read Muv-Luv, then my answer is because the entire trilogy, taken as a whole, is just that damn good.

TLDR: Muv Luv series is one of the best visual novel series out there! Steam version is a definitive improvement from the old fan-translation. Price is good and fair. Recommended for fans and newcomers! If you didn´t like it before, you probably won´t like it this time either if you enter with the wrong mindset.
___________________________________
"Muv Luv Extra sucks so much!"
"I really love Muv Luv Alternative, but Extra was the worst visual novel I´ve ever read!!"
"WTF I thought this was some deep mecha-badass-action visual novel, not some generic school s***!"
First of all, let me say that Muv Luv should be looked and reviewed as a whole package. For many people (myself included) Muv Luv series is really the pinnacle of visual novels. It´s meant to be a trilogy and people really should treat it that way. Of course its possible to watch Return of the King or Return of the Jedi and skip everything before them, but you wouldn´t care as much about anything thats happening, right?
For all the haters and newcomers to the series I´d like to offer a few tips that should make the Muv Luv experience better:
1) The order to read is Extra -> Unlimited -> Alternative. One should play all the routes from Extra!
2) Don´t listen to people saying it gets better later on, because that just makes you really negative and critical towards Extra. You´re not in a hurry, so why not enjoy the story at your own pace? Extra is lighthearted fun for the most part, don´t make it a chore to read for yourself!
3) Extra has lots of comic relief, lots of moe, and quite a lot of drama too. If you´re too serious to handle the cutesy, sometimes cringy humor and moe, try to relax, walk a little, take deep breaths, and soul search yourself to the point that you can turn your Serious-mode off, even if its just for this one time.
All in all, maybe this was really more of a pitiful, overly defensive rant, but I really really really like Extra, Unlimited and Alternative all equally. Everything is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥contest these days anyway (Dark Souls X is harder than Y, this X anime is better than Y, why would anyone X when you can Y?), so remember to stay positive, try to be happy for once, have fun, enjoy, and share the Luv with everyone!

First look and clash of clans deja vu started flooding back and whereupon I read through the chat box, others were complaning about this that and the other. Update: Now "SLIGHTLY" Recommended
So, I wrote that *cough* review, a fair old while ago now, and given the discount which has fluttered along, I thought that, because I'm naive, that'd give Blitzkrieg another bash. And my oh my how it has come along over the past 9 months. For starters, the gameplay has been smoothed out substantially. It's not perfect, by any means, but units no longer get stuck, campaigns have been added and tweaked and such until they're now in reasonably enjoyable state and just general adjustments here and there to make it playable.
Now you might think I'm being a bit harsh, well to tell you the truth, I've been waiting for a WWII RTS game which has enough elements of realism (Tell me on what earth a 37mm can pen a Valentine from the front. I'd REALLY like to know), but retains a good arcade style to it that it can appeal to the mass audience, for YEARS. No don't say Company of Heroes 2, that game is all about humping the fuel point long enough and hard enough until you win through sheer numbers and unbalanced units. Sudden Strike 4 looks decent enough, but the lack of technical gameplay doesnt avail enough for me.
Anyway, back to Blitzkrieg 3; The game STILL retains some rather intolerable, if your reasonably learned on WWII, aspects. Such as nations only being the US of A, The USSR and Germany (Tell me what is wrong with that list, I'll wait) and what appears to be the bread and butter of this game; Clash of Clans, Blitzkrieg edition. Ok, perhaps I'm reading this entire game wrong from the start, but it's just my view. And the ATROCIOUS voice "acting". But other than that, this game has done ok to pull itself out from the rubble of a Lancaster bombing I gave it last year, but as a nice little distraction until that perfect WWII RTS arrives *cough* Steel Division *cough*, this will tide you over nicely until then.

This. Game. Is. AWESOME!
First off, I'd like to say that the developers really knew what they were doing when they built the game.  From world-generation to quests to mechanics to combat, everything is wonderful.  The world-generation can get a little bit boring after playing for 100+ hours, and the quests run out quickly after 100+ hours, but the devs have said multiple times recently that they're working on new quests and quest-generation, so that should bring that part of the game back to life for me quickly.  The crafting does get a little plain, but it feels like they're trying to make it a way to advance rather than a focus of the game.  Now, as for the combat, the recent combat update doesn't cease to amaze me.  There were a few things that I liked that they removed, but that's okay, since it may just be a bug they need to work out.
Now as for my criticism... I do wish that they would change how you get from planet to planet, the fuel is a bit too abundant for how little you really need to go to other solar systems, and space exploration needs to be improved.  I mean, it does a good job with planets, but space really isn't much of a thing.  The only thing you can actually do that's even worthwhile in space is on your ship, but then you don't even stay there for long because you want to go down to a planet and build an epic building.  Aseroid fields would be nice, which they already have, but in a previous update, they removed everything in them.  Not some things, EVERYTHING, excluding the asteroids.  Now they're plain and boring.  The only other thing I have against this game is that it runs slowly on my computer when I put it in fullscreen.  It runs just fine when I can barely see anything in a small little window in the middle of my screen, but I want to be able to see a whole lot of stuff, not just the next thirty blocks to my left and right.
Anyway, if you like adventures, mining, quests, or exploring, this game is for you.

The developers say this is the start of a new series for which they have many "episodes" planned.  Given how much content is in this episode alone, that's rather shocking!  Shocking enough that I'm worried the series might evaporate.  There's going to be a lot of writing to make "many" of these.  Fortunately, this game has enough content to be worth buying standalone, so I'm not going to let worries about what may be released in the future discourage me from picking them up along the way.  I expect to eventually own the entire series.
This part may be unfair or arrogant of me:  I have a strong suspicion about what the last episode will contain.  The writing seems transparent in some ways.  It will annoy me if it turns out I predicted the last episode's content while playing the first episode's content.  Fortunately, that's a long ways out.  There's a great deal of detail between here and there, and the journey along the way looks like it will be enjoyable and unpredictable.
The only jarring thing I'm going to spotlight is that the game tries to sell its DLC partway through.  That was terribly immersion breaking.  That said, read other reviews, too.  There are complaints in the other reviews that are potentially insightful about whether you will or won't enjoy the story.
I will say one last thing.  I have a high tolerance for text dumps.  I have sometimes preferred exotic and detailed worlds over smoothly flowing narrative.  I suspect one of the biggest predictors about whether or not someone will enjoy VERSUS: The Lost Ones is going to be how much they enjoy expository worldbuilding.  The game is packed full of descriptions of alien worlds.  Some of them are evocative and fragmentary.  Others are long and tell-y.  Whether a reader finds the overall effect to be dull or intriguing is very much going to be a matter of personal taste.

Reviewing Lux Delux is like reviewing Candy Land, these are games that are far older then I am and will be around long after I am gone and buried. Essentially when you break down Lux Delux, it's Risk with multiple levels and online player support. I could end the review here and call it a day however, there are some things that this game does right and does wrong. So as we move forward with this review, keep in mind that if you love Risk, you're going to love Lux Delux. I can't really say anything negative about a board game that has been around since 1959. Lux does capture the spirit and fun of its inspiration.
On the other hand it does have some issues, ranging from graphical to interface. When you first load up the game, the first thing that greets you is a very complicated looking menu.
This isn't the most friendly of sights at first glance. This looks like something out of the Windows 95 era. One could say there is a plethora of options, in that regard, that is very true. There are menus upon sub menus that let you tweak, twerk, twist and twiddle all of the rules and many other options that I could list here for quite a while. Needless to say if you're the type person who enjoys an extreme amount of customization, it's all there for you. The only problem is that this menu kinda sucks for lack of a better term. It's not very user friendly. Not only that, it completely fails in its Steam integration. If you load the Steam overlay, it completely over laps and messes up the entire appearance of the menu.
At the heart of the problem with Lux is that it doesn't work very well with Steam. Graphical issues abound inside the menu and in game as well. I had my game corrupted in the middle of play many times as the graphics just wigged out for no reason. This required me to save, reload the program, and continue playing. The current fix for it is to simply turn off the Steam overlay, which does work,  That doesn't excuse things like menu buttons not working properly and other weird issues that this program seems to have.
Now at the end of the day, do these issues really technically matter? No. Your playing this game cause you love Risk/Lux and want to play the 900 levels that are possibly at your fingertips. For all you strategy lovers out there, there are more maps then you can shake a stick at and more readily available for download, if you get tired of the basic ones. The levels range in designs, some of them are nice, others are clunky. There is still plenty for you to chew on and eventually find the one that you like. You can even create your own levels, if you have the patience for it.
So lets talk about the meat of the gameplay. The options of varying AI are quite abundant and seemed very well versed on how to kick your strategic bee-hind. I found myself several times struggling to maintain a border as the enemy smashed against my troops over and over again. I noticed though that sometimes the AI tends to work together against me.  This could be paranoia talking, it just seemed like one enemy would weaken me up and then the next would just smash through me. This particular AI strategy happened many, many times. I did not falter though and I did win the basic map after a while. Matches against the AI can last anywhere from 10 to 40 minutes. I still feel like there is plenty of matches left for the AI and I am scared to find out how the game behaves on hard.
Which brings me to Online multiplayer. This is a bit of sore area for me. You would think attaching itself to Steam it would take advantage of the platform in bringing players together. This isn't the case sadly, I only ever saw 8 or more players online at any given time. Port forwarding was another issue that I had heard about but thankfully was spared. I feel like if Lux did a little bit better with integrating itself with Steam, more players might be playing the game. Of course, that's speculation. As it stands Lux feels like a 3rd party program that you can buy on Steam. Instead of a game ON Steam.
The audio element of Lux is fine for what it is, simple and explosion filled. Music is fairly well done and varied amongst the maps. I only occasionally ran into songs that played on other maps. The tunes are jaunty and have a nice pace to them. The game offers bucket loads of replayability either through the AI or perhaps convincing a group of friends to meet up at a certain time. I should also mention the game does feature two extra expansions, American History and Ancient Empires. What these expansions boil down to is just extra maps, nothing that changes the rules or adds any other features.
As I said at the beginning, anyone who loves Risk is going to enjoy Lux. You are guaranteed to find some interesting maps, and if you're lucky, interesting players. Just don't come into Lux expecting anything ground breaking. This is what it is, and it works, however I do feel maybe some extra rule bending would've added some fun game modes. As to the games issues, the graphical issues will eventually be patched out hopefully; the menus are rather ugly but you grow accustomed to it. If you're not convinced you will enjoy Lux, keep in mind that the actual board game of Risk is going to run you $25 usually. This seems easier, cheaper, and gives plenty of bang for its buck.

Paid Mods, The Game.
That was the short version. The long version is that Fallout 4 is on release a bare bones game. It's actually the skeleton of a game, waiting to be filled by the community.
And yes, the community has filled that skeleton, building upon it transforming it into a great game. There are thousands of mods, I personally play with 130, others play with over 200. Using this great library of FREE Mods you can turn Fallout 4 from the empty shell it is, into one of the best games on the market.
So what do the creators of this game do? Well, dear ol' Bethesda decides to implement PAID Mods, 5$ per mod even, so you can enjoy their game. Not that they are good mods, weapon and armor skins mostly, not mods that actually fix or improve upon the game in any other way.
But that in itself is actually fine. Let them have PAID Mods separately, so folks can nicely ignore and let their Creation Club just wither away. Which has been happening. So what does dear ol' Bethesda do?
Well... here's the kicker... they keep releasing "Updates" that don't do anything to the game itself, just modifications to the PAID Mods Creation Club Market, and these "Updates" break F4SKE.
The real thorn is that 99% of the mods out there use F4SKE, which is fan made, as an essential tool in their mods. So without F4SKE, you have no FREE Mods, forcing unnecessary updates from modders who either are not active anymore or have little time to spare.
To make it short, Bethesda is intentionally releasing Hack Updates to break Free Mods so you are forced to buy Paid Mods. So instead of paying your 60$ for the Game and it's DLCs, you also need to pay 8$ for the Creation Club and then pay 5$ per mod to make the game PLAYABLE!!
So yeah, Bethesda wants me to pay 130 mods (after finding their PAID equivalent) * 5$ (assuming they would all be this cheap) a minimum of what? 650$ to just play their freaking game in a actually Working and Fun manner?
Fallout 4 has been turned by greedy executives into Paid Mods, The Game.
As a conclusion, if you don't mind being constantly reminded by the game to buy Paid Mods, and you enjoy paying for what used to be free content, then yeah, go buy the game. If you do not want to be treated like a cow to be milked for your hard earned money, then do not purchase Fallout 4. There are plenty of other games out there that respect you as a consumer than go play Elex or Witcher 3, games that respect you for buying them.
Which reminds me of something else, something a lot of people have been asking for lately: Bethesda, please... I beg you, please let Obsidian make Fallout games from now on. They actually make good games.

Should you read Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited?
I would say yes.
Muv-Luv is one of the greatest tales I have ever had the pleasure to read. Extra and Unlimited are the first two parts of the Muv-Luv trilogy which are in included in this release, with Alternative (the final chapter) coming out later this year. Muv-Luv follows the story of Takeru thru a plain old regular life at first, until he is thrown into another world fighting to keep itself from destruction, with each passing moment becoming more intense than the last.
Our story begins in Extra. Extra is your run of the mill High School Rom-Com visual novel, where Takeru enjoys his life at school and spending time with the five heroines (each with their own endings). Extra is a bit of an odd duck in that it is not at all representative of what the majority of the Muv-Luv trilogy is like. Does this make it bad? Not at all. Extra is the ground work for the trilogy, introducing characters and developing connections to them, showing what Takeru’s life was like before it is turned completely upside-down, and laying in place plot points that prove crucial later. You don’t need to complete all the routes in Extra (although it would improve the all-over experience), but it is highly recommended to finish Sumika and Meiya’s routes before continuing on to Unlimited. Muv-Luv Extra should take around 10+ hours to finish the two main routes and around 20+ hours to read everything if you wanted to.
In Unlimited everything changes. Gone is the life Takeru knew and in it’s place is a world teetering on the edge of destruction, with humanity making their final stand with giant Mechs. Unlimited role in the trilogy is to set up and show us the world in which remainder of the story takes place. We are also introduced to the main conflicts of Alternative. Unlimited has multiple endings but you only need to see one (unless you want to see them all). Completing one route of unlimited should take you around 8+ hours and reading everything would be around 10+ hours.
You may see some people saying that Extra and Unlimited are not worth your time and just read Alternative, but both Extra and Unlimited are incredibly important for increasing the impact that Alternative delivers. Think of it this way, you could just watch the last movie in Star Wars (original trilogy) or The Lord of the Rings (The Return of the King) and understand what the plot is and who the characters are but the experience is lessened. By watching the movies that came before you spend more time with the characters and the world they live in, becoming more attached to them and understanding their struggles. The same can be applied to the first two parts of Muv-Luv.
Should you read Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited?
As the key foundation supporting and enhancing one of the greatest visual novels of all time, Muv-Luv Alternative, the answer is a resounding “Yes!”.
10/10

To get it out of the way, some people recommend to skip the first part, Extra. Those people are big whiney babies. However 'generic rom-com' Extra seems at a glance, its humor is audacious, at times brilliant, and the novel keeps itself at a fast pace. Moreover, besides laying the groundwork for the characters' personalities, it's filled with foreshadowing for later parts of the series and necessary to fully appreciate the relationship between the protagonist and the heroine of the third part, Alternative.
But feel free to skip Chizuru's route, it adds nothing. I like the character, but her personal story is anemic.
================================
First and second parts of the most excellent Visual Novel series 'Muv-Luv'.
Extra is the story of a high school senior whose carefree life gets thrown in disarray with the sudden appearance of a comically wealthy, eccentric girl who sets about attempting to win his affections, and in doing so prompting our protagonist's inseparable childhood friend, a literal girl-next-door, to rethink their circumstances; the taken-for-granted notion that they'd always be together, whether simply being 'friends' is something is satisfied with, and insecurities regarding her own merits compared to the more colorful lives and personalities of the girls in our protagonist's life. A generally sweet, at times melancholic, romantic drama tempered by light-hearted comedy.
Unlimited is a military science-fiction drama, featuring much of the same cast of Extra. It introduces us to a world that has been ravaged by an alien invasion, with our protagonist forced into the role of a trainee pilot for the giant mecha used as the mainstay weapons of humanity in the war. While keeping the light-hearted comedy and romance aspects of Extra, its pace is slower, the general tone darker and more melancholic, with a narrative that deals primarily in looking at the lifestyle and values of a world thrown into a long attritional war and the protagonist's attempts to find his own place in it. Starship Troopers (the novel, not the film) meets anime, in a way.
Both stories are parts of the whole, meant to be read in order and play off each other.
Extra offers something of a branching storyline, with the main heroines Sumika and Meiya possessing a largely shared route, plus one short diverging path for each of the secondary heroines, and a pair of gag endings. All are worth pursuing, except for Chizuru's, and I personally emphasize completing Sumika, Meiya, and Ayamine's stories. Unlimited, on the other hand, possesses a singular story divided into distinct chapters, with choices providing small variations in scenes and determining the possible romantic pairings at the end. There are no routes, and while the particulars will vary, the story will always reach same ultimate conclusion. No advice to offer here but to grab some tissues and force the girl to board the shuttle.

A relatively historically accurate RTS in the vein of Company of Heroes or Men of War, at least to the degree that any top down RTS could be historically accurate. As in Company of Heroes tanks do not destroy each other with one penetrating hit, infantry are not immediately gunned down in swathes by machine gun nests and so on, but that is unavoidable in order to keep the game playable from an isometric perspective.
As in Company of Heroes there is a singleplayer campaign with historical missions as well as a traditional skirmish PVP mode.
The main difference from the competition, and to me the most interesting part of the game, is the Clash of Clans style base defence/offence mechanic. You establish a base on a front line and set up defences where the terrain favours them: minefields and tank traps on bridges, bunkers and tank destroyers hidden in forests, etc. Then other players attempt to attack your fortifications with assault forces that they put together. If you are online you command your defensive forces yourself, and can call in reserves and various other support such as artillery barrages, dive bomber strikes, strategic carpet bombing, etc. If you are offline the enemy player faces your defenses controlled by AI. Surprisingly the AI actually defeats enemy players attacking you from time to time.
As in any Early access game there seem to be a few balance issues, but on the whole the game seems quite polished at this point. I'm rather impressed with it so far and definitely prefer it to Company of Heroes 2. It's refreshing to be able to spend 100% of your time commanding units and microing, whether defending your own base or attacking an enemy base, as opposed to spending it on base building and build orders as in more traditional RTS.

Avoid this for now. This game is so bad right now after nearly a decade of writing perhaps 1 Steam review, I've found this so bad that it warrants a negative review.
Major issues:
♥♥♥♥♥♥ pathfinding
Battles that take way too long and and are way too short (I will elaborate later)
♥♥♥♥♥♥ difficulty curve
So the pathfinding. You have to manually, individually command units. If you do a big move order units get stuck, they get jammed and the best part is, if two units get stuck on each other they do damage! Brilliant game design choice there. It makes the most basic of features tiresome - moving your armies about.
Units get vaporised in seconds if you're not careful. The "artillery" (Including planes, hence the quotation marks) is incredibly overuses by the AI and will wipe your entire army if you do not react in time. Currently I have no AA vehicles and I have no idea if they are even in the game. You have defensive AA but that's only for base defense. So it's a tiring slog through a basic mission, meaning the whole thing becomes an over-extended bore. You have to carefully, slowly poke forward and with the pathfinding being so bad even that can fail miserably to stop you getting hideously punished.
So battles can and do end VERY quickly, often unfairly so.
Now why do they take too long? If you manage to somehow best the above, you have to take down the HQ and their radar (it calls for ENDLESS reinforcements from the AI - seemingly) meaning the longer you take the MORE enemy units there are. What a catastrophically♥♥♥♥♥♥design flaw - punish people for moving too fast, punish people for moving too slow. So battles are both too slow and too fast. There's no happy medium and the game becomes a chore.
Seriously, you can even check the ingame bars - it shows your unit score in blue. I start with nearly 600. They slowly die off, so does the enemies. Then BAM the enemy counter goes from 60 back to 600. Yet I have nothing now to counter?♥♥♥♥♥♥game design 101.
So you think to rush the radar? Bad idea. The enemy reinforcements spawn in the HQ, it's cluttered so bad pathing becomes even more painful and the way LoS works means they will be able to snipe you from the Fog of War with impunity. Another exercise in frustration.
So yeah.♥♥♥♥♥♥pathfinding,♥♥♥♥♥♥game design choices and a terribly balanced AI opponent have turned me so off this game it upsets me greatly. Avoid.

I originally read Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited using the English fan translation some time ago.  I'm happy that it has finally officially come to those of us unfortunate enough not to be able to read Japanese.  Degica has done a wonderful job of translating this visual novel even better than the old fan translation.  We even now have a game engine that isn't prone to crashing at particular locations!
As many others have stated, you really must read this story starting with Muv-Luv Extra (Sumika and Meyia routes), then Unlimited, before finally moving on to Alternative.  This story wouldn't be nearly so epic and complete without reading it in the proper order.  It is all an exceedingly well thought out and complete story.
It is true that Extra doesn't pack the same awesome punch that you will get later in Alternative, but that shouldn't be something to disuade you.
Having originally read these games slowly, over the span of months, I want to recommend that you don't prolong your reading of Extra and Unlimited.  Hopefully the Alternative translation doesn't take too long, as everything is best when the full story and all the little details are still fresh in your mind.

If you got a friend go for it.  Should only take up a few hours if you're bored.

The progression kind of hits a massive bump in the road at about level 10-12.  Found myself searching endlessly and never receiving much needed upgrades to progress to the next zone, leveling up had to do it and once upon reaching the new zone, worse loot than previous was dropping, completely halting my progression.  The progression is what kept me into it for the few hours but it's just dead now.  Why is lv12 zone dropping level 8 loot, where lv7 worlds dropped lv10 loot?
At the start, enemies die pretty quickly as usual and you're pretty much invincible.  A little ways in you might have
risk of death but otherwise enemies just takea bit longer to kill.  Then you'll be at the point where every enemy is just a pure damage-sponge that kills you in 1-3 hits and it's just rediculous.
Quite a bit of the game is locked behind premium currency, of which is quite expensive.  And some of it behind a massive grind that would make warframe jealous.  Spending money gets you massive boosts that people yell P2W over.
The game does a poor job of explaining things.  You get these tutorial quests that are pretty easy to do then it wants you to craft things using materials it never tought you to harvest so I had to check the wiki on how to progress.  Most of it was go here do this, complete dungeons on the map then move to next map.  And that's actually all the game is, doing random worthless dungeons for the slimmest chance that something decent might pop out.
The server lag is among some of the worst I've seen.  Say you jump and glide but then you teleport to the ground because the server didn't register your inputs.  There's countless rubberbanding here and there which massively interferes with combat, causing hits to not register.  Even stuff you can collect sometimes doesn't work.   You'll miss maybe 1% overall because while it looks like you collected it, you didn't.  It's invisible, and once you leave and reload the area, you can now see all the plants and stuff you missed that apparently didn't register.  You and the server often see two completely different things before they try to sync up in the most horrible way possible.
There's also a challenge you can take part of at the top of every hour but it's so poorly programmed that if you get in there just before the timer runs out you're just wasting your time you can't get the reward even if you ace the challenge.  Despite being eligible to enter at the time, you are no longer eligible for the rewards because you cannot re-enter the challenge.  It'd be like giving a 25 minute race on a 20 minute timer, they may complete the race but you won't give them the rewards.
Essentially the more I play, the more I see horribly wrong with it with nothing good to say.

Well, it's been awhile since this has been posted, and now I should go back and not how much damage has been done to the game. I'm not one of those idiots who say "THEY LIED TO US!!!" In partly saying that this is a 2D game, what could you possibly expect? Though, I expected much after my first hour of experience, and it led to OHHH's and AAWWWEE's as I flew over the early access version that was after they removed their touch damage based combat in change to something more decisive, more watch the opponent for the right time. In my last review, I stated that they have done wrong removing that system, making it what everyone could call popularly a "Terraria" clone. Sure, the Terraria team had some doing in helping get this game to a 1.0 release. But, before that they reverted back to the touch damage, and that threw me off for the course of enjoying this game. Because something is fluffy and cuddly looking doesn't always mean it should be considered a threat, even if it doesn't hit you. On top of that if you're surrounded, it's like you take a backstab in darksouls for crying out loud, and you die without anyone backing the fact those little cutie eyed bats were just flying in your face with their mouths closed. I absolutely hate touch damage in this game, it's the only thing that bugs me beyond playing or getting back into playing this nice game.
On another note, there was various monster sounds that would play in idle, or when getting attacked. For I loved the duck alien noises or many of monster sounds of the previous build. But I do not, repeat, do NOT love hearing a high pitch beep as if it was some kind of detected sound. For christ sake, the workshop can have lots of funny little edits and what not, but the default game becomes duller with little varying sounds between enemies. I know it takes time to make monster sounds, but when you made plenty of them, why in the world would you just get rid of them? This needs to be fixed.
A few more bits here for this review. This is a survival exploration game. To me, that means you subsequently get thrown into the fray, and are EXPECTED to explore lands and worlds by your own volition with little or some guidance and hits from townsfolk about land lore, or what happens when you combine A with B, or what terror rises from the mountain tops of said peak. This was one concept fits this game so well, I would love to just see that kind of idea in a space exploration game. Now we got QUEST!!!! No, this isn't too bad of a thing, but it dumbs down the whole explore to your heart's content and gives you an annoying check list that requires you to explore, so it all then feels like a chore. Now it isn't bad because it stops the player exploring, because that isn't at all what I am saying, it is just forced down on the player (Kinda like skyrim, just less veague) that they have or must do these things. And the survival aspect was minimized vastly. At first, you had your basic hunger meter which was simple and not final in anyway, but it worked. Then you had your temperature management, too hot on this planet, too cold on that planet or even night time travel. NOW, just hunger. It's not the good kind of hunger either, it feels just as place holder as the previous build. There IS planetary temperature problems, but it is dependent on specific planets, and not time of day. Not so survival, more like a feeding simulator if you ask me.
Finally, we get to another complaint of mine. One I take personally, but I understand to those who love the calm exploration music that is in the game currently: The battle soundtracks. WHY would you remove combat music from your game? I could see that people complained that it would interrupt their little travels to the calm music they love so much, but it makes battles SO much more anticlimactic. And after awhile, the calm music drives me insane. Might be because my preference to metal and rock alike, but let us face the fact that there are different moods to feel in any situation and that feel delivery is VERY important when it comes to combat. Sure, it isn't Kingdom hearts where every combat situation needs battle music, but it had added flavor. Since this section is about music, let's talk about the UNUSED music in your game. That's right, there are tracks that were never used that were going to be implemented. There was biome/planet based exploration that never made it fully to the game. There IS a couple, but at most, the whole soundtrack plays only a few on there. To me, music is important in your game, and if you don't use songs that were planed and sound nice, that is where I'll have plenty of questions and many others would too.
In conclusion, I cannot play this game anymore. I'm not mad that I paid for something that ended up being crapy, more just upset what the developer(s) have decided on the behave of the game. I could believe that the assistance of Terraria team might have done something to Chuckle Fish to go with a more "Terraria" ruled game, but this is just a mess. Too many ideas thrown together, and too many edits that just made this game what it is now: a workshop dependent. Not to say all is bad on the workshop, it's just sad to see so much more fixes and adjustments to the game that make it better from the community rather the developing team. In the end, early access can just lead to a game which doesn't want to identify itself as its own game and uses concepts from other games to make one.
AND yes I understand, this isn't a game I own, I just post my opinion on the internet because this is how I feel about this game. There is stuff to do here, but don't expect a perfect game

Not sure how anyone can recommend this game when the online lag issues are so profound.  The cost of the game is also high considering how many elements of the game have yet to be released, but I could overlook that if online play was more enjoyable.  Even setting your online preference to playing people with a higher connection speed doesn't work well.  What's worse is it seems that players are able to directly create lag to give themselves an advantage online.  Kinda annoying when my computer has an i7-4790K CPU and Nvidia GTX 970 Video Card, and
clocks my internet connection with 45ms of ping, a download speed of 17.17 MBps, and an upload speed of 1.05 MBps.
For example, I recently lost to a Platinum ranked player whose connection was supposedly 4-5 bars.  No big deal, losing is part of the game.  After losing the rematch screen showed he had a full bar connection.  Get the rematch, and the lag during our 2nd match is ridiculous, could barely input strikes let alone special moves.  What's worse is halfway through both rounds of this match the rounds speed picked up big time - 40 to 50 seconds of match play went by in less than 10 seconds.  Why play ranked matches online if you're going to cheat?  Casual matches and the battle lounge are great options if you're so concerned about losing ranking points.
The online matchmaking system is also a bust.  You'll work for hours to raise your ranking, only to drop back down because you'll keep getting matched against much lower ranked opponents.  While you should beat most opponents that are a few rankings lower than you, it can be frustrating to reach higher rankings and not be matched with opponents that are at least at your rank or 1-2 ranks lower because the point system is curved (more points won for wins against higher ranked opponents, more points lost for losses against lower ranked opponents, and vice versa).  It is not uncommon to reach a new ranking level and get consistently get matched against players 3-4 rankings below you, which means you need to win 9-10 out of 10 of those matches just to break even in rankings points.
The last game fighting game I played on steam was King of Fighters 13, which almost never lagged and had a better designed online matchmaking system.  Really hope King of Fighters 14 ends up coming to steam if Capcom doesn't fix Street Fighter 5's online lag issues.  I won't even bother going on about the rage quitting problem.

Starbound takes everything I loved about Terraria and massively improves it.  The worlds are varied and wonderous, and there is an ever-present, beautiful ambience that comes from all of the little details.  The soundtrack is absolutely perfect for this type of game, inspiring a sense of wonder and the thrill that comes with exploration.
The core concepts of mining, crafting, and building are all here, but without the frustrations of inventory management that plagues other similar games.  Unlike Terraria's "house" building for NPCs, Starbound features full-size colony building and a more robust quest system.  There is also your ship, which you can decorate and expand.
Starbound also has legitimate dungeons - you cannot simply place or break blocks to avoid the obstacles.  Bosses are also geniunely challenging because you can't simply build a "boss arena" the way you could in Terraria or Minecraft.  The combat update just further improves everything.

Update:
I've recently doubled my amount of playtime following a number of updates for the game and the resolution of the Rootkit debacle that put the games in the spotlight for very much the wrong reason.
While Capcom managed to add a large amount of Paid DLC and a security threat - it's unfortunate to say that the game is still plagued by many of  the same issues apparent during its launch.
There is still no support for customizing your bindings using a keyboard.
The game breaking stability problem during Online matches is still there. Many matches are unenjoyable due to the models glitching around constantly. The connection filter seem utterly sporadic. Even when set to "5 only" - I still found myself being paired with people on other continents. This raises a few eyebrows since I tested queueing for a ranked match alongside a local friend and the game failed to pair us despite a relatively close LP rating.
They do get some bonus points for actually providing free content like Story Mode, and maybe even Arcade Mode one day.
The verdict still stands:
It's a Street Fighter with simpler mechanics and a smaller roster than its predecessor, though it will grow over time. They made it easier for beginners to perform combos due to the removal of 1-frame links.
You have to rely on Third-party software to customize bindings if you use a keyboard which isn't that much of a hassle - but it shouldn't be necessary for a AAA-title.
The biggest flaw is the online play. Currently PC players are facing a major issue reportedly caused by either player minimzing out of the game which inflicts a desync that results in models teleporting all over the place.
There are also a lot of server downtime, and disconnects are not uncommon.
There's still a lot of content missing, which is scheduled to be released at a later time, but it keeps on being delayed.
It's absolutely not worth its current price unless you're a huge Street Fighter fan.

" ; this is blatantly misleading. Allright. this first bit is my honest review for Planetary Annihilation TITANS itself.
I love it.
Everything from sheer choice of units to the ways you can end a match is amazing.
It takes out what I don't really like about RTS which is micromanaging units to "upgrade them"
and limited resources in a map. the camera work is amazing and the Music is just.. bliss. its great.
Some downsides that I don't like are the META people use in pvp which is.. find commander, orbital laser platform x20, and rush.
Orbital in this game is too quick to get and easy to mass produce to the point any Ground orbital defense is useless if you can just choose where the orbital units arrive from (right over the commander's head) Unless there's only one planet or that you keep your commander on the move. you have no chance of retaliating. Even with your commander surrounded in catapults and umbrellas.
Basically, I don't like how Tanking/defensive strategies are void to such powerful divebomb units.
But. if you play with friends who doesn't want to cheese a game, its a blast. You have so many ways to play and to win that you can easely invest hours upon hours in it.
Here is my second bit. MODS.
The default AI difficulties in the game become easely exploitable when you first start to get good grip of the game. So with that said. I switched to Queller AI, which claims to have more human like behavior. which is great since.. default AI keeps attacking your metal extractors and being a general annoyance over Duels of massive armies.
Queller AI worked for the first few rounds. climbing from gold to platinum AI. until.. Uber.
So the game time counter says 40 minutes into a match, but.. the AI is building useless air units on a moon and continuously build millions of frigates in a tiny lake make the game run in slowmotion in the first 20 minutes. To the point where a minute in the game counter took over 3 minutes in real time. being a real pain to even try to shave the sheer number of units to fix the game. but the time it takes is too long so you end it by giving up.
The game Should be optimized for massive armies and its not my memory capacity that is the problem.
the game itself Is fine but that mod makes AI build larger ammounts of units until it slows the game and even crashes sometimes.
(Queller AI) so dont bother doing anything else but 1v1s with bots or 2v2 with human players. because.. only humans know how to build units in the right places without making a million of them. and more than two bots makes the game lag after 20 minutes.
(the previous review was me ranting only on the game's bad performance at handling a mod and I was tired so my head wasn't right. my apologies. Its now a reccomended game for me and not the other way around)

First let it be known that like many of the people who have already written a review here for the first two games of the Muv-Luv series the hours shown here do not reflect the actual time I have put into this Visual Novel. Like them I read the series long before the localization project was in the works and have come to love the series. When I finally heard a project to localize the series and officially translate it with the cooperation of the original production company Age I jumped at the opportunity to back its production (as well as securing my own copy of the games). Being that it was the first Visual Novel that I ever read I cannot shake my bias towards this absolutely fantastic series which sparked a number of spin-off animations and Visual Novels.
Now on to my recommendation. As a whole the Muv-Luv series is a highly in-depth, emotionally compelling, well thought out and loveable series. All of the heroines of this series are adorable in their own way with each of their routes getting emotionally deep and compelling as they do not avoid some tough issues. My personal favorite is Sumika as I'm always a sucker for the childhood friend. Although the series gets much darker as it goes on becoming more than the seemingly slice-of-life genre, especially in the case of its sequel Muv-Luv Alternative. Personally I loved the whole series and each individual game where as it is up for debate as to if Muv-Luv Extra and Unlimited (the two here) are really likable. Since this is the introduction to the series I highly recommend reading Muv-Luv and waiting for the release of its sequel Alternative regardless if you have ever watched one the spin-off animations or not. It is a great read and it should move you.
Hope you enjoy it!

Lux Delux is a fast-paced turn-based-strategy game involving risk and world domination which recently released on Steam. In Lux Delux you take control of a faction (what faction that is depends on the map) and your goal is to take complete control of the map you're playing on. The risk elements of Lux mean that a game can turn on its head in a single turn and this, combined with excellent AI, means you'll always get a unique experience even if you play the same map with the same AI.
+Basic graphics that suit the game well
+All of the maps are well designed
+Simple controls but tricky strategies give the game very addictive gameplay
+Over 900 maps, yes you read that correctly, 900!
+Depending on what map you play the game can be over in a matter of minutes so it's perfect if you just need something to play quickly
+Three different levels of bot difficulty, each with sub-levels of difficulty which change the way the AI behave, for example a defensive AI will only defend their territory
+A lot of maps have a unique mechanic and these can sometimes be a little confusing to begin with but also make each map unique
+Great soundtrack
+Excellent AI and Map creator/very easy to mod
+Very friendly dev who is active on the forum
-The Steam Overlay causes lots of graphical glitches with the game which make it unplayable so you have to play with Steam Overlay turned off
-It isn't very beginner friendly and the official guides aren't overly helpful, I had to have a friend explain to me how to play
Verdict:
9
A fantastic, fast-paced, risk style TBS game with fitting graphics, a massive amount of maps, fantastic AI and some interesting mechanics. If you're a fan of risk games or just want a more compact version of Civ 5 then this is an absolute must buy.

I played SF4 for literally thousands of hours and SFV is compared to the predecessor's vanilla a huge disappointment. The character cast is much smaller. The game has little to no content (at least they keep patching it) but I think they should've released this deliberately as an "early access version" of the game.
Of course, like many others, I bought this primarily for the online competitive component. This, however, is lacking in many regards. People keep rage-quitting every other game and don't get any punishment at all. You cannot put people on block lists whose connections suck so you don't have to face them again and the rank mode is not giving you the option to choose from a list of lobbies but you get automatically queued with the same rage-quitters and 56k modem players. It's frustrating beyond any comprehension. You can't message other players or add them to a buddy list on steam or ingame which is pathetic. And searching for "endless" lobbies (as they have been called in SFIV) can be a huge pain in the butt since you can't see the connection quality for most of the lobbies open. It is such a drag...
The ranking system features certain a similar naming as in League of Legends (Bronze to Platinum) but it is literally pointless since you get queued with everybody and you don't have any influence on the search algorithm. Basically, most of the games I play are against total scrubs with <2000 league points and rage-quitters with >6000 league points with the occasional good game against gold players around my level.
The graphics are ok; definitely a good step forward from SFIV. They could be better in plenty areas though; my GTX 980 barely has a 40% load playing with maxed out settings @1080p. But this only shows how consoles again drag pc gamers down with their garbage performance. At least the female characters look hot with one expection (*cough* Mika *cough* wtf is this garbage?).
The music is awesome! But I think this is not all too surprising. Each track of the game has something to it.
Gameplay? I think overall it has a lot of potential. But I deliberately speak of potential since there are numerous flaws in design and engine, problems with balance and an almost incomprehensible hurt box system. There are plenty differences in approaching the game strategically in this game. In SF4 you had tons of safe options with most of the cast to approach a fight. You could go for quick, safe block strings and follow up with a special move if you could open your opponent up for a hit confirm. In SFV footsies play a much bigger role due to the Crush Counter mechanic. You can land a Counter hit in a number of situations since opponents will also try to fish for counters with fierce and roundhouse. Getting a counter with these normals will grant you additional frames to follow up with a huge combo. It takes some time to retrain yourself.
What I hate most about the game mechanics standing jab hurt boxes. You can cleanly anti-air anything with almost any jab in the game. No trade, no risk, no execution or reaction required. Also these jabs allow for a strong kind of "reset" setup situation. Sadly some character rely heavily on jump mix-ups. Cammy can be beat out of her cannon strike with a mere jab. Jp.fierce and roundhouse get beat by jabs. It is ridiculous.
To unlock colors of a character you have to waste tons of time into survival. I managed to pass hard difficulty survival mode with Ken just by stupidly jumping in at the bots and trying to go for constantly maximum damage. But bots are programmed in a way you cannot play footsies against them. You cannot play the guessing game. Of course, vertices won't work neither. So won't ambiguous jump-ins. For for hard you have to win against 50 bots in a row. normal 30. easy 10. You have to do these 3 difficulties (90 games) successfully with each character and each costume to unlock all colors. It's no fun. It is a huge waste of time. I don't know what Capcom has been thinking...
What I also hate is the inavailability of certain costumes for players who didn't get a certain pre-ordered version.
But oh well. Since this is a beta at best I won't expect this to be completed until another year at least.

The story is very complex with many things to do. If the title was True Crime: Hong Kong, I would know EXACTLY why because, well... spoilers. I honestly wanted to rip my computer. This game does a very good job of getting to your emotions.
Gameplay: 10/10
The parkour in this game is quite impressive. The shooting is well done, as is the combat. However I WOULD like to see some more weapons in the story. But, with all the DLC I have downloaded, I don't care whatsoever.
This isn't entirely relevant, but anything bad during the game that happens to me is usually caused by a damn taxi.
Graphics: 20/10
It's developed by United Front Games. It's published by Square Enix.... GREAT combo if you ask me graphics-wise. I play Hitman: Absolution, and if a game is published by Square Enix, it's most likely a good graphics game. They sure did make the taxies look fabulous... I hate you, game devs.
Sound: 9/10
The chat from the civilians are always regarding you. Ha-ha. Yeah well, guess what? Rumor DOES fly around the city like a plane leaving the airport... bad example. But you get my point. Also, when I flash a weapon, and the civis start crying bloody murder, I want to kill them to shut them UP! Is that too much to ask?! Otherwise, pretty well done.
Controls: 9/10
When I sprint to get away from the cops, and I have a gun out, Wei drifts to the right and hits a wall, or does unnessisary parkour. Ends up getting my health down. I really hate it. But other controls like the action hijack and the Slo-Mo vault and other things like that (yes, even parkour,) are great.
Replay Value: 10/10
After you complete the game, you can replay the missions and re-immerse yourself into the Sleeping Dogs world. You may also go on a killing spree on cops and/or civillians. There's even this cool feature where you get to be ran over by taxies in the free-roam mode. It's quite exhilerating.
Overall Value: 9.75/10
This is an overall great game, and if you don't have it, GET IT! That's an order! Seriously, the overall game has itty-bitty flaws almost unnoticeable. I sincerely hope that you enjoy this game. I'd say the best part of playing this game was to witness the utter glitch-fest of taxies getting stuck in the ground, jiggling a bit, and producing a sound and sight that was both loud and bright. (I don't know what the word is, but for now I'll call it an explosion.)

Let me start off with this, during the Steam Summer Sale of 2013, my friend introduced me to this wonderful game by gifting me it (along with its soundtrack) while it was on an 80% sale. After only playing the game for one hour I wanted to pay him and the developers twice the full price of the game each. My friend for introducing me to the game, and the developers for making the game. Now, on to why I love this game.So, the Visuals. Need I say anything? This is one of the few games that can make a "cartoony" look work. And for me, this is the only game that made the "cartoony" look, well, look amazing!
Story, well, I don't want to spoil too much, so I'll explain the beginning. You're introduced simply as a Kid, and remain without a name through the entire story. You wake up and walk outside. Almost everything is gone, bit as you walk, the world assembles itself ahead of you. The Narrator tells you that this is the result of "The Calamity." I love the idea of making everything vague, and many will ask why. I say because it makes you explore to learn more. Throughout the game you can find Trinkets from before the Calamity and the game will explain to you what they are. And occasionally you will find special Trinkets that will make you fall asleep (for example a huge Smoke Pipe or Books... Or a Beanbag. I love the humor of this) and will send you into a place where you battle waves of enemies. Every time you defeat a wave of enemies, a piece of a character's past (or what a letter of the alphabet stands for in the universe in Bastion, for example "B is for Bastion, the *blah blah blah*") Each place corresponds to a certain main character, minus you. And the Narrator (who you meet after the first level, who is replaced instead by the alphabet). I love how the game doesn't just give the story to you and instead makes you work for it. It makes you feel more inclined to care about what it is telling you while still making you have fun and having a challenge.
Okay then, the Gameplay. Many criticize this game for being a "generic action hack-and-slash game" when it in no way at all is. There is so much variety in each weapon, your default weapon being a Hammer that can deal massive damage, and the last weapon in the game being a mobile cannon that shoots large, slow moving projectiles that can deal a HUGE amount of damage. You also can upgrade items with items that correspond with each weapon, and it grants you a tree of upgrades for each weapon. For example, the cannon (The Doom Cannon) can be upgraded to have Exploding Shots, Shoot Faster, Homing Shots, and more! Along with this, each weapon can be "charged" and released at just the right moment to deal a lot more damage, shoot multiple projectiles, and more! And along with THAT is a system of special abilities. Some, such as... Uh... I forget its name, but it lets you throw a Canister that spawns in a Turret from Portal, and doesn't require a specific weapon. And others, such as... Uh... I forget the ability names, sorry! But it lets you shoot a Barrage of Shots from the Doom Cannon in rapid succession, and since it shoots from the Doom Cannon, requires one of the two (yea, you can choose what weapons you can have and have two at a time) weapons you have with you to be the Doom Cannon. Also, each weapon (and the shield) has a trial course with it and let you get new things for the weapon. (For example, top prize being a new ability, and another prize being an item to upgrade it with.) Also, there are Brews you can bring with you to grant you special abilities, for example... The... Man I'm horrible with remembering these names... The... (Made up name, not ability) Heart Brandy that grants you the ability to carry 2 more than the original 3 health potions, allowing for a total of 5, and also the potions are instantly used if you would die from an attack. Finally, there is the idol system. What it does is, when you activate and idol, the game is harder, but you get more experience. For example... One idol could double the damage enemies deal but grant you 50% more experience (well, not that much). There is a grand total of 10 idols. Anyone who thinks the game is too easy, try doing the challenge levels I talked about in the last section with all 10 idols on.
Finally, the music. Absolutely stunning, must I say more? Well, I will anyway. The music is so fitting for any point in the game. You're in an intense boss fight? This game has the music for it. You are at the credits and are tearing up? This game has the perfect music for that. My favorite three tracks would be #3: Build that Wall (Zia's Theme) #2: Mother, I'm Here (Zulf's Theme), and #1: Setting Sail, Coming Home (Credits Music). Heck, I would pay the full price of the game for just those three songs from the soundtrack. The Narrator is not annoying in any way and is the cherry on top to this game.
This game gets a 10/10, no doubt.

It is a fun game, I've put in about 100+ hours into this game(disregard my time played, a lot was in offline). Could it have been done better? Yes. Would I have this many hours in the game if I didn't speedrun it? No.
The mechanics of using terraforming and telekenesis to solve puzzles and navigate levels is pretty unique and fun. When I first played the game I spent tons of time with friends in coop just trying to glitch to areas and cheese puzzles with the mechanics. Standing under boxes and launching myself hundreds of feet in the air and using coop to create elevator systems to get around the maps was awesome.
The game doesn't look the best and could be optimized better, these are true, but for a small company's first game as the result of a kickstarter it could be worse. The game seems to be made to show off the mechanics of (then)current VR and eye tracking hardware, I'm sure the game is cool with that equipment but the majority of the userbase will not have them and it's best to focus on that. I never have crashes or anything and the game runs near perfect on my PC(the sand can be stressful on some computers at times). I do hang on load menus into between levels and am sometimes forced to click, have the program go unresponsive and wait for prompt to click "wait for the program" then the game will load. It doesn't happen super often at all. Just something I've noticed.
The campaign will give you a small 6-10 hours of gameplay and the multiplayer is 100% dead, which is slightly disappointing for $20, but I'd say it's well worth it just to mess around with the physics engine. If the game is on sale it'd be a shame not to grab it.
Overall would I recommend this game?
Yes.
