This was one of those games I had heard about here and there, and when I saw it for sale, I thought, "Hey. Why not."
And then proceeded to ignore it for half a year.
Never have I regretted that choice more. Here's the breakdown:
Graphics:
Everything looks to be meticulously detailed and painted with loving care. The colors are appropriately bright in some areas, whereas others induce feelings of despair and melancholy. The characters', when viewed from the general view, aren't extremely detailed (being rather small), but do get various painted panels, which are really nice to see, Overall, the medium used to present this game is wonderfully atmospheric, and makes Bastion one of the prettiest games I've seen in a while.
Soundtrack:
It's fantastic. I really, really recommend buying the game with he soundtrack. Lots of emotional tracks, all of which seem to fit the game very nicely. I have no problem having these stuck in my head for the rest of the night.
Gameplay:
It's fairly straightforward, though I would highly recommend playing with an xbox controller if at possible. Lots of the timed challenges will be much easier with those controls. I enjoyed how you could select any weapon combination you wanted, as well as how many ways you could customize each. A fun touch was the narrator commenting on whatever combination you selected. That's actually a really nice tough overall, how involved the narrator seems to be with your decisions. Another aspect of combat that was interesting was how most of the fights were very fast and exciting. I say most, because there were a few where you could win simply by shielding and lettings the enemy ricochet off you until it died. But for the most part, fast-paced and fun.
Story:
This is what makes you marathon this game. Everything above complements the story and the way it's presented. The characters are sympathetic, though mysterious, and the story of the Calamity even more so. I very much felt like I had personal stakes in the outcome.
If the above is too much to read, just know it's worth buying and playing right away.

After the huge success of the TV series "The Walking Dead", which in turn appeared thanks to the comics, the game was for fans of the series the perfect gift.
The structure of the game similar to the TV series. The game begins with our protagonist being taken in a police car as the prisoner. The negligence of the driver, the car gets into an accident. Getting out of the car Lee (the name of the main character) discovers that the area is literally crawling with walking dead. Hence begins our adventure. Despite the short duration of episodes (each one takes approximately three hours), the game contains a high density of interesting events.
The game is in the genre of adventure. During the passage we will have to solve various puzzles, for example to find an object and somewhere to use it, but they are not complex and intuitive. There is a place and action points, but they only can count a few pieces. And yet in the foreground of the game - the survival of the people in a zombie apocalypse. The story is based on the relationship between the characters. During the game, quite often we will have to make a difficult choice, for example, saving one of two people from the clutches of the walking dead. All important decisions need to be made very quickly (for a decision given only a few seconds). Thanks that's not such cunning techniques give us the opportunity to create their own unique story, because even wrongly selected line in the dialogue can have far reaching consequences in the future.
Though I am not familiar with the comics of this series, but familiar with the series, which I love. With confidence I can say that this game sometimes looks even darker and more dramatic of the series

I saw this from a friend's list of games and I thought I would give it a try...it's along the same lines as Zombie Shooter / Alien Shooter but with more of a "Tower Defence" feel to it (although there's no central point to defend, it's just YOU and / or any buddies).  So, there is a difference to it.  You can either build your defences in the middle or take your chances and fight running battles...in the former, it's like the Battle of Rorke's Drift or The Alamo....with the latter, anyone who ever played the Flash game "Classic Daleks" will know the feeling of being 'boxed in' by the bad guys as you run around the map...well, this is the same feeling, but it's all in real time !
I like it a lot.  It's simple, it's VERY challenging and gets progressively harder without being too easy or too difficult; the balance is about right.  It is the kind of game that I could sit and play on a Friday night, look at the clock and then wonder where three hours just went (or on weekdays, half an hour, just to put in a quick round or two).
For $4, it's worth it (in terms of a comparison of 'how many beers would this cost me and would I get as much if not more enjoyment from it), the answer is YES.

Takes the Warcraft II ball and runs with it like a champ. In terms of gameplay, Wyrmsum fixes what needed fixing and adds and improves on what already works in every way.
What lets this game down I think is the art - not enough thought was put into it. Sure it looks fine for the most part, and never goes as low as terrible, but the tilesets are bland and merely utilitarian, and the units all look way too similar. Until you've played it for hours you can barely tell the differece between your peasants, warriors, archers etc even from their profile pics. Good luck telling them apart at a glance on the map. I feel it really needed a clear artistic and stylistic direction.
In warcraft II each tile felt like it was lovingly painted, not only to fit in with the overall style, but also to be unique and with its own fine details that gave maps character and made them interesting. Each unit, too, had its own instantly recognizable silhouette so that in the heat of battle you didn't find yourself at a complete loss as to who is who. It seems incredibly strange that the dev felt the need to make each individual guy have differently coloured hair and their own personal name, but put no effort to make the units actually stand out from one another.
Other than that, I kinda like the sound effects - the sword noises sound like cutlerly being gently tapped against each other and its kinda cute. The encycopaedia is nice (if badly implemented. Talk about having a wall of text thrown at you), the world building is solid and the moddability is a plus. If you liked warcraft II you should like this game, especially if you can wait for some graphics mods or are artistic and want to attempt your own (*hint hint* Please someone make some new tilesets and unit graphics)

Planetary Annihilation was riddled with bugs, hollow promises and an absolutely terrible launch. But after several years and this stand alone expansion, Uber finally got things right. What remains is a fast pace, remarkably balanced and incredlibly fun RTS which plays along the solumn principle of amassing  huge numbers of units to quickly expand across an entire planet and annihilate everything. Never have I played a game so satisfying.
The only cons of this game were what I experienced when I first started playing, which is that there is a big learning curve and that some of the UI mods are so useful they should be mandatory. With the last community update, Mods are now accessible right from the main menu and incredibly easy to manage.
As for the learning curve, the most helpful piece of advice I can give is that any strategy can work, as long as you never stop building 1) energy plants  and 2) metal extractors. Thats literally the only thing separating bronze level play from platinum.
Also bigger systems require more RAM to play, so keep that in mind when starting out.

You know, I enjoyed Bastion a lot, and played it a lot, but it's one of those games where I sort of gave up right at the very very end. And it wasn't because there were other things going on, or I was bored. It was because the controls and engine are ever so slightly finnicky. Both KBAM and controller were pretty tight but still leave you wanting. The game starts off something like an isometric beat-em-up, but quickly devolves into a bullet hell kind of situation, and while the right items and upgrades can help in some situations, you'll never have enough equipment set to handle all situations, requiring you to, essentially, use upgrades as a way of protecting yourself from one particular form of challenge.
As an example, the swords can be used for quick melee attacks, but can also be charged up and thrown. This means that if you're proficient with swords you could have two melee weapons instead of a melee weapon and a sword. On the other hand, two ranged weapons might also be useful. Each weapon is great for dealing with a specific enemy type, but you're limited to two, which means you'll want to upgrade the two you have and are good with to handle as many situations as possible.
This means that you'll want to collect more McGuffins to power up your town. But that eventually requires you to do challenges with weapons you aren't good at through puzzles you can't effectively solve (and these are muscle puzzles, so no amount of video watching or reading can help you. Pure focus).
Near the end I really wanted to get all the McGuffins, more than any other game, but hitting that solid wall of ability really took the wind out of my enthusiasm. The game is cloyingly easy when it comes to challenges you can overcome, but mercilessly difficult for things outside of your wheelhouse, and it doesn't have the difficulty curve to allow you to perfect your skills.
I always expect to come back to Bastion one day and just beat that final level, but then I realize there's a lot of skills I'll have to dust off, and relearn, and practice to do, and at that point I might as well play from the beginning, which feels like a waste. Also, while the art and narration are impeccable (what the game is known for) the story is only so-so, which is also nitpicky, but it only serves to weigh in on me more thinking about how easily the game could have a truly excellent story.
At the end of the day, everyone should play Bastion, at least once. Hopefully if you have the energy and skill you can find a game to really sink your teeth into. Otherwise you may find yourself spinning your wheels. You'll still have enjoyed you time here, however.

Bastion follows the life of a survivor of an apocalyptic event. It does this through a process of narrating the player as they make their way through the levels. I initially found the narration a bit jarring, but once I got into the game it became clear that this was a really good way of telling a story.
The gameplay focuses on top-down two-dimensional movement, using a variety of weapons & abilities. Everything is well varied and leads you about in a linear manner, but with enough space for you to get a feel of it being open-world.
Playing using a mouse & keyboard set up gave me no difficulties. The controls are easy to learn and use.
The graphics in this game are very "traditional" in feel, everything having a sort of painted-over imaginary look rather than being really precise. Yet it is still very high quality.
Given that there is a high emphasis on narration in this game I would reccomend you play about with the music/sound settings to get a good balance so you can clearly hear the narration. The music involved had a sort of "desolate" feel to it, and not quite to my tastes, but it is still very well composed.
Once the game is completed, you can unlock a game+ mode, which fully unlocks levels & extra challenges. There is also a pre-unlocked "no sweat mode" for people who want an easier play-through.
I found no bugs in this game at all, it is really well-polished.
This game is really worth a play if you like story-driven games, and if you like a (apocalyptic) fantasy type of setting.
A good return for the game. New items and mechanics really bring some new action into the gameplay.

When i first found starbound, it was in a lets play by paul soars jr. i thaught it was just him making this game seem amazing since i was never into terraria or games a like... until now.
If i called this game 'cute' then i feel like the community would cut me up and feed me to an alien, But wow did i get lost in this game! the music is brilliant, the game play is great and the content is forever expanding! And the reason why i love this game is as follows:
~ The Game play is easy to learn, and hard to master like everything should be. Its straight forward and even when the going gets a lil' complicated The game throws in helpful tips and guides to point the way. Its a really user friendly game what suits all ages and personalities.
~ The Game its self is wonderful to be a part of. In Terraria i could never be bothered grinding away to find bosses and make the content last longer. To me it was just one world were it all got old pretty quickly. But this is not the case in Starbound. The first thing i love is The Planet system! You begin in orbit above an amazing looking planet. a small planet none the less, and what i love is that if you keep walking in a certain direction, you will find your self back were you started having done a complete revolution around the world! I found a wonderful little planet with all the stores i needed to build a base and supply my trips, and immediately before i did anything i attached sentimentally to the planet. i remember the name of the planet and the solar system and i loved calling it mine! but there is no shortage of planets. In your ships navigation systems, a Giant star map allows access to a HUGE array of what i think is a proceduraly generated universe of endless stars with solar systems around them. venturing into the unknown out into the universe is a really amazing thing. there are Different types of stars that create different types of planets and solar systems around them! a frozen star creates cold planets were at first, you can't traverse further then a few feet from your camp fire wile walking on. there are radioactive stars and planets, even shadow planets were the sun can't create heat enough to supply light. i can get lost in my imagination before even coming into orbit of the planet!
~ The Time line of the game is helpful as well. at first, you are given a back story depending on what race you choose (with decent character customization included), and you are given a weapon and your matter manipulator. Its not like you have to follow, but the game will give you a line of quests to fulfill to get you into the game and its workings. after that, its up to you to expand, venture on and find new places like the outpost were Races from afar trade and chill among themselves in an amazingly detailed lunar base.
~Something that really gets me is how immersive this game is. The music has obviously had a lot of time spent on it. it gets me into a mode just as the game loads up were the real feel of this game comes about best. Things like being able to have a fridge with endless food choices to store in it like (since I'm an apex) Battered banana, banana bread, or just a nice juicy nana is what my character loves best! but there's everything from cakes to burgers! there's even a servo just outside the outpost that sells Erchius fuel as well as soda and chocolate! (the money system is great as well). and once all the niceties are out of the way, this game can even take very dark and scary turns. i still haven't found out what those ancient ruins do but don't tell me and leave my imagination to work its self up :D.
~ The Combat system in this is great as well - Swords, Knifes, Hammers and axes are still the favorite of most civilized races, yet Guns like Pistols, machine pistols, assault rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns and even rocket launchers are all available in the armory of starbound and all the good♥♥♥♥♥♥is hard to get when or wear ever you are in the time line of the game. there are shields as well, and grenade launchers as well! throwables like moly's and bombs are helpful as well!
~ The mining in this game is amazing as well! its pretty much Terraria but with different ores and different content all together! the caves and caverns rage through, the walls sparkling with precious gems and goodies for the taking. But its not easy. Who knows what is waiting in the dark for you.
~ There are man made structures as well. well when i say man made, i mean humanoid made because most of these villages, colonies and sometimes just tomes were built by the natives or visitors to the planet just like your self. and the detail is beyond measure, just how this entire game has been set out.
All in all, i would recommend this game. Its a great game that you can sink anywhere between 10 and 1000 hours into before you even touch multiplayer, and the game is still in Beta! i hope that the devs continue doing what they are doing, which is making a great game for people like me to really and truly enjoy (and even their Update names are Strange but give a sense of what the devs and their game is like; at the time of this review, I'm currently running the "Glad Giraffe update" which followed the "pleased Giraffe update" which was a long time after the "enraged Koala update". Never mind Minecraft and their "1.8.1's and their other mathematical excuses for names XD").

Once again, Capcom comes out with great core gameplay, a game you really want to play because of how well it plays only to botch literally everything else about it.
Do we even need to talk about singleplayer content? Probably not, for 60 dollars it has literally nothing in terms of singleplayer content. I highly doubt much will change with the cinematic free dlc coming in June. Absolutely unacceptable for a 60 dollar game, especially for people who don't play fighting games for the competative aspects.
Now the crux and the biggest complaint with this game.
This game has some of the worst programming I've ever witnessed. In a game that really requires stable connections and good netcode to even function (like most twitch games), they really dropped the ball. In a world were they easily could have licensed a version of GGPO3 (which works really good with Rising Thunder another 2½D fighting game) but instead opted for their very own netcode. Huge mistake.
We left the old delay based netcode and finally entered the rollback based netcode, but in return we get some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥product that have some of the dumbest decision making ever. They went out of their way to literally let the lag in a game be burdened by the person with the best computer/connection creating what most people by now know as one sided rollback. I dont know what they were thinking but they thought wrong.
The netcode suffers from other kinks, like extreme rollback from people that are just the street over which makes literally no sense. This type of rollback has also made it fairly impossible to play with people/friends across continents as you can not set a specific delay and it will just rollback really hard.
Its not good.
The matchmaking is pretty much not working. Capcom (geniuses that they are) decided to mimic League of Legends more rank based matchmaking, because everyone knows you should always just copy whatever is most popular/makes most money currently. It just doesnt work. The rank is useless as the game will still put you up with whoever is most available.
There doesnt seem to be much hidden MMR (or ELO) and LP (the in-game point system) doesnt matter at all, just like the ranks dont.
There is three different ways to play online. Ranked, Casual and Battlelounge. Ranked and Casual are just matchmaked (ie just sitting in que waiting for the game to pair you with someone to play with), but battlelounge is a game the player creates and people can join. This works the same as endless lobbies in SF4. At times it makes sense to play lounges because you might want to learn a new character but not play people who are "really trying", well lounges isnt the answer. For some reason Capcom have gone out of their way to make sure you cant play them.
When searching for lounges it will pop up a list of available games, the problem? The ping bars (which indicates how good of a connection you have to said person) load forever and 95% of them will never show up.
No worries one might think because you can also see what country the lounge starter is from and in that sense be able to pick and play a lobby via that to ensure less lag. No, because flags simply wont show up and will just show the usual "SFV" flag. The only thing that shows up properly is the rank of the player who made the lounge, but what good is this when I have no idea if he is from China, the US, Brazil or whatever else I know for certain I cant play with? It's basically a crap shoot of joining a lobby, then leaving because they're from a continent you cant play with and then trying again, but as salt in your eyes Capcom have done such a poor work at the programming that you will get stuck on black screens of loading and other error messages leaving out of lounges which makes this whole procedure extremely annoying and not worth the time.
Now for the social aspects. What is there to say? For a game that thrives on community interaction they've made sure you can't communicate with anyone. This time around there is no friends list, only a "rival list". It's sort of like a friendslist but you cant talk to them, only send them invites. This means if you want to interact with other players you have use external sources to make that happen. I guess they were scared people would use a messaging system to talk♥♥♥♥♥♥to people, but thats honestly a dumb decision considering if you make a decent friends list with decent features (only friends cant messages me) it wouldnt be a problem. There is literally no steam integration into that game as Capcom decided to use their own platform so you can not invite friends over steam like pretty much any other game.
Capcom has once again went out of their way to make a barebone experience that while the core game is fantastic, the surrounding parts are complete garbage. This game needs some serious Quality of Life changes to be sure to survive in the future. The only sad part is that games that really do well in the core gameplay AND in the features department cant hold no candle because it simply isnt Street Fighter. I think it's time the Street Fighter name and Capcom take a hit to their credibility if only to show this isnt acceptable for a 60 dollar game.
All of this culminates in what I can only explain as frustrations with the developer. They havent acknowledged almost any of the things pointed out above. Instead, just silence, with the monthly update on how hype we should be about the newest character coming. I'd rather have no more characters and a functioning game instead. Capcom is a developer with a bunch of great IPs but are a bunch of greedy suits trying to put out the least amount of effort in return for the max amount of money.
I dont recommend this game, but I'll continue playing it because it is Street Fighter, which is quite sad.
EDIT July 2nd:
While the new content patch should satisfy a lot of the more casual players of this game (this game actually has singleplayer content now), the game is still plagued with underlying basic problems. The battlelounge searching is still not working (wont show flags/ping/bars/anything) and the one sided rollback netcode fubble is still in effect and still hasnt even been acknowledged by Capcom.
I appriciate the new characters, they're fun and all but at the same time it's more important for me that the game works. Currently theres no real way of playing long sets with random people (think FT5 or FT10) in battlelounges because it takes too much time and effort to find a game where you have a decent connection with someone and (s)he isn't either way better than you or way worse.
If Capcom busts their♥♥♥♥♥and fixes the battlelounges at this point I can look past the netcode (as most of the time its fine) and will change the review to positive, but for now it will stay not recommended.

Looking at this game, the aesthetic and how it plays, it's obvious to see that this is heavily inspired by Warcraft II. Now, this isn't inherently bad, because that was a great game and a modern-day take on it would be refreshing and fun. This game also brings a Grand Strategy mode to the table, which could be an interesting addition to an engine and style that could implement it well.
As far as the traditional RTS side of things, this is not a modern-day take. This is basically a weird re-skin. Every detail of the interface is essentially the same, and that brings with it every bit of clunkiness that the original WCII interface had. There's no effort made here to streamline or improve, and because the developers failed to give this game the polish that its inspiration had, this ends up being a vastly inferior, near bootleg-tier clone.
This leads me to the Grand Strategy portion. I am honestly not sure of what I think of it, really. If you're good at Grand Strategy already, you might be able to get some mileage out of it, but as a beginner to the genre I found the barrier for entry cripplingly high, and the surprisingly exhaustive Encyclopedia function to be of little help despite how comprehensive it seems to be. All the Encyclopedia feature did for me was introduce me to concepts I didn't even think were in the game, and I left even more confused than I was before.
I don't really like the fact that I can't recommend this game, but it comes off feeling like an unfinished product, like the team behind this game needed more time and better people to help it really come to life. As it is, it's bland, it's confusing, it's clunky, it's not great.

Wyrmsun has many similarities to WarCraft II both in its visual style and gameplay mechanics.
The game supports both single- and multiplayer games and the shines, like any other RTS, when played with or against other people. The single player mode is very similar to the scenario mode from WarCraft II where you face one or more AI opponents on a selection of different maps but there's a big difference between these two games. While you have access to every unit and building in the latter you have to complete Quests in order to gain technology points. Once you decided which technology you want to unlock you can use it during you're next quest to see if you made a good choice or if you have to reset your technology tree to approach the quest in a different way. Besides that Wyrmsun features a built-in editor so players can create own maps to their liking.
And now we are coming to my personal favorite.
The Grand Strategy Game. It may sound like a different game but it's just the name of the second single player mode.
You may wonder why it is called like that. Well let me explain. This mode is divided into two parts. Unlike campaign mode you manage your production and research on a turn-based global map. If this sounds already good you will like the second part as well since the combat takes place on a terrain you are used to from other RTS games: maps in real time. Besides that there are also Quests for you to complete. Sounds good doesn't it?
It's just a different approach which I really happened to like.
Also there's another thing that separates Wyrmsun from your usual fantasy setting. The mythological creatures like the Dwarves don't exist in the same world as the Humans. The human campaign takes place on your favorite planet: Earth. While the Dwarves have their place on Nidavellir.
Since they both dwell in different realms in the campaign mode and won't face each, they will either fight against or alongside the fantasy factions in custom games.
For the people that are also into the lore of Wyrmsun the game features an in-game encyclopedia.
This allows players to learn more about the units, building and other elements of the game and additional to that about the sources of inspiration whether historical or mythological.
And the best part? Mods.
Wyrmsun is a game with high mod potential and features built in Steam Workshop integration.
So what does that mean for the game and the players? In the future there'll be, hopefully, custom made settings, units, buildings and more depending on the player base.
I don't think you could understand why this is a recommended game without playing it.

At its core Planetary Annihilation is a macro-heavy RTS where you build large formations of units to hammer at enemies. Production is important, composition is important, micro seems mostly unimportant, aside from things like basic maneuver war (flanking, envelopment, etc). It has a really cool map layout, because its all set on spherical planet maps orbiting a sun, with appropriate orbit, rotation and lighting. It has a lot of units, but no faction diversity? I think?
It’s a bit buggy, I’ve had huge slowdown happen infrequently when enemy units retreat into the fog of war while my armies pursue them, as well as when using the halley planet launcher or nuclear bombs. I’ve also had the game freeze on menus and it’s one of THOSE GAMES that has to load forever at the start of a new campaign because it’s generating the universe. But it’s very playable. That said, my machine is beefy. I have 16 gb of RAM, a 3.2 (3.5 with turbo) ghz quad core and a geforce 970, and I still had some problems and slowdown so, yeah.
Overall though if you have a strong PC this is a really fun supcom clone if you enjoy those.

I backed the Kickstarter for this, so I thought I'd mention that right off the bat as it will inevitably colour my opinion of the game.
I quite enjoyed PA when it was first getting made. When it was released, I thought it felt very incomplete compared to what I had expected. This was because of how Supreme Commander and Total Annihilation, and the fact this is very clearly based off of those games, were some of my favourite RTS games. This did not live up to either of those games.
So, I thought I'd just leave it. I'm happy enough with the small, physical items I got, and I did get some enjoyment out of the game, maybe it'll be better later on. That's when I saw that Titans was released.
I got Titans as a 'gift' for being a backer, but I definitely felt like this was an incredibly cheap shot for those who purchased PA after release, as they're basically getting charged for the complete package of what everyone always expected of the game (i.e. huge super-robots). I didn't really fancy taking another pass at the game then, so I left it until I could get a bit of time to play.
Cut to this weekend. I finally loaded up PA for the first time in a very long time, and then it directs me to launch Titans. Oh, it's a separate installation, not just extra content? So people can bypass PA and just get Titans? Wow, that's even worse than I thought.
Finally, I can't even play the bloody thing. Upon starting a Galactic War, I can't see any 'green area' to place my Commander and land, and then when I wait out the two-minute timer, I can't see metal deposits or unit icons. Wow. Give it a few minutes of drudging through in a less-than-fun experience, and I find that graphical glitches begin to occur. These include, but were absolutely not limited to:
- A black bar at the top of the screen, below the information pane
- Flashing purple lights everywhere
- Audio and video errors, including animations (I couldn't see gunfire, nor where turrets were facing)
- Random spiking of the planet's model, after I'd zoomed out a few times to look at the system
Overall, I was pretty unhappy with what I saw. I've got the latest drivers for my card, and most of the regular troubleshooting says the issues are Xfire or SLI related. Neither of those apply to me.
Even if I would have fixed the problems, I don't think it's reasonable, in this day-and-age, to be expected to have to find fixes when you load up a modern game. Something I've got going through an emulator? Sure, that's very much to be expected. Something that's a little dated? Absolutely, it's no surprise there. A 'brand-new' and 'complete' release on Steam? No. No I don't expect this at all.
All-in-all, I'm left with a sour taste in my mouth. Regardless of how I was a backer, this buggy mess is just a waste of time and money for anyone interested. I'm surprised about the large number of positive reviews when I find so many forum posts relating to these bugs, which are frankly game-breaking.
TL;DR: Buggy game for a number of people; double-dipped waste of money for those that can load it.

If you don't mind characters spouting the same boring phrases every few minutes, the companions done quite nicely. They have personal arcs, but I personally found them useful only for their perks, and it doesn't help that one of the best perks only works if you either use no companion or dogmeat.
-The side stories
There are some really interesting side stories happening in this game. From the Cabot quests, to discovering a pre-war cult's remains hidden in a mine.
The mixed:
-Voice acting
The decision to voice act the MC was quite divisive, with some people liking it and some hating it. Personally, I find it to take away a bit from the roleplaying, since the character now decides how something is said, rather than me choosing to interpret something. A great example of this is when the character is
-Large world, empty characters
There might have been about 4 characters in the entire game I could care about, with dogmeat hitting the top spot, and other dogs filling in spots 2-4. The world is quite big, and it's not empty of buildings and cool places to explore. The people in it, are about as useful as a 3 pound note. Most characters would die if you didn't remind them daily that breathing was a vital human need. I ended up adventuring alone most of the time, and just didn't bother with companions.
The bad:
- dialogue options
While the voice acting can be nice, it seems like they had to severely limit the main character's dialog options because of it. The dialog system is terrible. 4 options, and none of them ever tell you in detail what your character is going to say. Get a mod that changes this to actually showing every line the character will say, it'll save you getting into a fight because you disagree with how the devs interpreted "annoyed"
- The quests:
HOOOO boy, the quests. If it's not a "go here interact with object quest", it's a "go there kill that" quest. The quest variety in this game is exceedingly small, and while there's a large number of them, they all start to feel the same after a while. The stories behind them can be nice, but they all boil down to doing the same thing.
- alternate options
If like me, you really enjoyed finding alternate solutions to problems that aren't telling a person to go away, or a more "permanent" telling them to go away by accelerating pieces of plasma in the general direction of the local annoyance, you are going to find them in short supply in this game. In the whole of the game, there are about 3 skill checks that aren
't charisma. Most charisma checks boil down to "gimme money". There is one way to achieve a quest, and that's the path the devs laid out. Bloody disgraceful.
-the main story
As I mentioned before, I did not care in the slightest about finding my kidnapped baby. Why? Because the entire time I spent with the thing boiled down to it crying, pressing A on it once, and then nothing. I have literally no emotional attachment to any character in the main story. I literally only cared about elder Maxson, because I wanted his coat. Which is an awesome piece of gear, BTW. There was nothing in the main story that interested me, and in a game with this many chances to draw me in, that's a blooming disgrace.
All in all, the game is a mixed bag. If they had not thrown a fallout label on this, I could have accepted this as a good game, but this shares about as much with fallout as Dungeons and Dragons does with programming. While there might be people who enjoy both, don't expect this to be good if you liked the old ones a lot, but it's a decent game on its own.

Wayward Manor is a puzzle game, where you play as a ghost of sorts and try to chase the inhabitants out of their gothic manor.
It is also very much a mobile style game: you need to get six "scares" per level, and you get more options to interact with the room as you scare the person or persons more times.
Each level also has three optional objectives to get.
There is therefore replay value if you want a perfect run. The characters each have a distinct personality which makes them unique, and what ties the individual levels together is a short story written for this game by none other than Neil Gaiman.
As for the graphical style: it is based on drawings from the Victorian age, such as used in the original publications of Alice in Wonderland. This means superdeformed yet "cute".
The game is easy to get through, but can be really challenging if you want to perfect it.
It's not a perfect game, I encountered a few minor glitches, but none of those really detract from playing. But my overall experience is a very positive one.

I've been reading some bad reviews of this game, I think written by people who expected something different from what they got. It's a relatively short but cute, enjoyable point-and-click puzzle game. You play a ghost, who can make items in his house move in order to scare the residents. By clicking the items in the right combinations and at the right times, you are able to construct elaborate scares that will eventually cause your unwelcome houseguests to leave. The puzzles are rarely that difficult, but they can be tricky if you don't use a little imagination. I especially enjoyed harassing the old man with a crossbow, making him shoot arrows into people's butts and set things on fire.  It has an intro from Neil Gaiman and the art direction looks like something he would design, but don't buy this game solely on the Neil Gaiman name. Buy it if you like a clever family-friendly, puzzle game with some replay value and a unique art style.

Most people praise it as being technically sound, and for the most part it is. You can get good FPS even on old machines, but it should be expected, as it is a 6 year old game. The graphics still hold up (tho it doesn't really matter), and the overall experience is smooth. BUT....and this was a big, stinky but...I couldn't alt+tab out of the game. 4 out of 5 times, this would make the game unresponsive and I had to force close and restart it, which was unbelievably frustrating.
The map design is good, and Paradise city is a huge place, with lots of events to complete and things to do. I really enjoyed having to hunt down and smash new cars in order to get them. However, I found some of the events useless, like the "smash all the 400??? fences" or the "smash 120 bilboards" ones. Also, the fact that the map is so big, made it frustrating and tedious to go anywhere, because half the game (if not more) consisted of me bactracking to the starting poing of a race.

This is a neutral review, even if I placed it negatively.
Overview of Sanctum 2 - The Bumbling Monster Tower Defence game.
I played this game when it went on the weekend sale of Jan 25 - 26, of 2014, as of now, its locked and requires purchase to continue.
Graphics:
This game... it looks 'Ok', the AA is meh, the graphics don't really detect your optimal settings so you might have to adjust this on the first boot of the game. Textures are meh as well, I don't think you would notice it much either while playing.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is mostly about tower defence as it was branded, the FPS mechanism  is there as well, a rather odd one, you can basically do the first level of any stage just with your guns, however, you rely on this progressively as you play. The guns are mostly bad in their starting shape, the extra secondary guns were better, the rocket gun was nice, then you got the Prototype Lighting gun, which was awesome, however, you do NOT get much XP from it. Either this was a method to balance the gun (you just sat there and fried enemies), or something else with a similar aspect. The perks mechanism is odd, mostly you do not notice this at all, mostly they simply gave stuff like more damage every 3 shots. You get a limited amount of slots for your towers, which you unlock as you level up. This is ok IMO.
AI/ Logic:
This is where the game mostly sinks. At first when I started into the game, I am greeted with dancing men. (screenshot was not provided because I forgot to upload it when I 'had' the game) I was... well OK, great, dancing men, then I saw a man running around in a circle like an idiot. It just left me a peferct taste in my mouth. Then I entered the game itself, more problems.
I saw that my comrades were bulky spacemen with yellow eyes,  and did not know how to handle beyond a pistol. Great. Then I saw they died almost immedietly after a wave of monsters spawned. I supposed that added more to their value: nothing. Spacemen are usually like those in ME3 or Halo, defeatable but brave and standing, I got nothing but bumbling idiots.
Towers:
The towers are somewhat limited. In your starting position you are given a gattling gun and a rocket launcher. Later on you get more towers to your collection. They are mostly limited to a general 5 meter range. Even the largest and most perked gun didn't surpass this. The thing that did was a earthquake machine that did some damage to the enemies. It appears (quoting CyanideBillzard here), that Sanctum 1 had a better assortment of towers as well in terms of range and varierty.
Monster AI:
The monsters are fine, but mostly just a running animal that wants to destory the core, there is nothing wrong with that except that perhaps that an element of randomness could have been added, the badass warriors could have lept over the walls, flying monsters could have had more attacking AI, rihnos could have smashed walls. Perhaps I was too early in the game to see more advanced AI, but this is my opinion of the initial monsters. I was also pleased when I saw that the boss did bother to destroy all the towers, makes him look like an idiot, because naturally all the bosses go directly to the goal(AKA, the core). This boss didn't.
Hardware abuse:
Although I am running on a GTX 660M with 8GB of RAM, I suppose some lower end units might feel the pain, some people were complaining about lag. I didn't really notice much.
Bugs:
To be surprised I did encounter some. For example, some enemies did stupid things like taking a longer walk around the corner, I was flown into a fence and got myself stuck there( had to suicide to get out), and my shotgun got stuck in the tower creation mode.
The multiplayer.
The multiplayer is there, but it feels artificial.  I found the multiplayer communication in this game several times worst than any other game I have played in my life. There is no way of communicating with the other players(or if there is, I never noticed it or I'd knew where to input my help). The team works independently and you have very little idea what to do, just believe the team has a general idea in 1 minute. Also, be fast, or people will start to hit enter and the game starts regardless if you still haven't upgraded your turrets.
Overall:
5/10 game, - Game Feels like: It was a game you play, but you don't feel like you played it or will... in a long time. *
*This of course is my opinion and you are subject to see fit as how you please to read this review. This review was meant to extract the game's faults and pluses.

There are ways around this issue that they purposefully break with each and every patch.
Furthermore they are now, promoting paid mods through their own store, while actively hampering the "free" mod community that has existed for over a decade around their games.
Oh, and almost as a sidenote, the game is a terrible RPG (if it's even worth calling an RPG anymore) but pretty decent as an open world shooter.

Flyhunter Origins is a mobile platformer game that got released on pc.
I havent played the mobile version so I cant judge if this was a good port.
You can change resolution, full screen/windowed mode and controls at the start of the game. This game supports a controller.
This game is aimed at the family with a younger audience as a focus.
The creators all work (or used to work) at Pixar.
In Flyhunter Origins you play Zak, a clumsy one-eyed alien, who seems to be the only survivor of an alien spacechip. Because of an incident all precious cargo has been ejected from the ship and landed on planet earth. It's your task to return it. This precious cargo is a bunch of exotic flies, hence "Flyhunter".
Armed with a Fly Swatter (later you get access to a gun) and a jetpack you have to find these flies. On your quest you'll find numerous obstacles and enemies (earth's insects). Zak is a very small alien, so earths creatures are about his size or a lot bigger. You can collect eggs you can use to upgrade your weapon stats (add +1 to damage, very basic).
At the end of a level when you're about to catch the fly the game changes to a 3d racing game, in which you have to smack the fly a few times. Odd imo, but it works.
Its a typical platformer. Controls are easy (jump/doublejump/shoot/melee). There are plenty of spawn points. Anyone can play this.
The good
- Lovable and funny maincharacter
- Very easy controls
- Controller support
- Nicely priced
- Pixar style artwork and characters
- 3D Racing
- Upgradable weaponry
The bad
- Hit detection seemed to be off sometimes. I had a lot of trouble defeating the big spider. Could be me though.
- Might be a bit too easy for the more mature players.
- Graphics arent really impressive
Overall a nice game for the younger audience. There are more impressive platformers around though.

Town of Salem is a cartoony witch trial simulator. Quick matchmaking and large community fills up the wait queues very fast. Roles are handed in secret, play your role and help your team wins. The learning curve is very manageable as most of the roles are intuitive enough.
Value is not very clear here as the concept is a rip off from SCII custom map and the dev decided to add a cash shop on top of the game not being free to play. You can earn the rewards through enough grind and the rewards are mostly cosmetic except for an item which lets you pick a role.
All in all I have a lot of fun in this game, and everything that ruins other communities like immaturity and trolling end up reinforcing this game's concept, making the trials hilarious and all in all people really do want to play their roles and win so the competitive edge can be very present, and when things go wrong then it is comedy gold even when the reasons are a little dubious. If you find this in a bundle I would say you owe it to yourself to try this. However if you own starcraft II already you might find this version of the game is slightly underpar in comparison to the free custom map. Its up to the dev to raise the bar for its steam release.

Video Review -
Hello I'm Cosmic and welcome to indie puzzle title Wayward Manor developed by the odd gentlemen who are well known for their début title The Misadventures of P.B. Winterbottom. The story of Wayward Manor comes from best selling author Neil Gaiman and is published by moon shark..
Set in a 1920's Victorian Gothic estate, Wayward Manor places you in the role of a recently awoken ghost. The house itself is a sentient being voiced by Gaiman himself who tells to you about how horrific it's new occupants are and how you are now tasked with scaring them away as quickly and spookily as possible.
In terms of gameplay, Wayward Manor comprises of levels. There's five levels per chapter and five chapters in all. The sad thing is as puzzle game's go Wayward Manor just doesn't hit the mark in any respect. Levels are too easier and can barely even be described as puzzles. All you end up doing is clicking the various objects in the room at the right time to scare which ever family member is in the room. The more scares you accumulate, the more clickable objects become available to you.
The major issue with Wayward Manor is inherent in it's game design. Any good puzzler across the board whether indie or not has one major game design element in common, the progression of mechanics. The whole point of puzzlers is to take a mechanic and as the game progresses, add too it. Introduce new elements to that mechanic, introduce new difficulty. Sadly Wayward simply doesn't and the entire game is little more than a pointless point and click seemingly unsure of what it wants to be.
One thing that irks me in particular is that in a game about haunting the inhabitants of a maision. The utter lack of interactivity and dare I say creativity in terms of the gameplay shocks me most. As I ghost I want to be able to do more that shake a suit of armor just by clicking it. The entire game feels like a poor iOS title rather than a indie PC game.
On top of its lacking and ultimately repetitive gameplay, Wayward sadly suffers in the graphical department too. I was expecting more from both The Odd Gentlemen and Neil Gaiman in this regard. Both the visuals and soundtrack lack any real depth, there's no soul in the games characters, no atmosphere in the soundtrack. Graphically the game also suffers from an array of bugs and glaring oversights which just simply cannot be forgiven. One such oversight is at the completion of the level when you click the final skull and all the furniture begins to spin around the room, everything just clips right through the wall. It really does destroy what little immersion the game actually produces.
Sadly the biggest disappointment for me was Wayward Manor's story. I thought with Neil Gaiman on-board at the very least there would have been a good story, after all this is the author that brought us things like Coraline. However like the rest of the game, the story is just lacking in every respect. There's no depth, no character, no life to it thus ultimately it's just bland and disappointing. The whole story feels like it is tacked on to give purpose to the endless clicking of objects.
Overall Wayward Manor as an idea had tons of potential but in practice as a indie game, simply did not amount to any of it. The whole game oozes rushed, underdeveloped ideas and mechanics. Its easy difficulty and lack of content combined with a weak, soulless story leaves me with an utter feeling of disappointment.

1) a great story - because of Gaiman's involvement

The majority of the story are in the exposition between chapters. During the actual gameplay, there's maybe a bit of character background.The story stops during the gameplay and picks up when the chapter ends, which makes the flow very choppy.
2) repetitive music - I heard maybe four short tunes total so far. That's if they played correctly. Occassionally the music will glitch out and I'm left with the clock's ticktock background. The maid also has an irritating volume increase to her music when  she cleans the cobwebs or block the mouse holes.
3) decent mechanics - The puzzles are a bit repetitive, but each character has their own stage set and what will scare them. Some puzzles need good timing, and most of the achievements require a bit of thinking.
So far I'm not impressed with this game at all. Perhaps later on the story will pick up and the tunes will vary, but my hopes are not high. When I finish the game, I'll update this review.

A lot of people seem to not like this game. I'm not exactly sure why. I like it.
Neil Gaiman does an excellent job with the short narrations. And the entire concept of an old house calling on a ghost to haunt the current annoying residents out is in no way a new concept but it is done well here.
The artwork is interesting. You won't see much like it. Now some are really hating it because they just can't seem to get why everything is so...well ugly. However, I see that it is all based on Victorian style cartooning, (please go look up Alice in Wonderland and look at the original artwork by John Tenniel, you'll see exactly what I'm referring to.) So its not supposed to look pretty by todays standards, its supposed to look the way it does and I find that its quite charming.
The puzzles; if your an adult or near adult then I imagine this game will be rather easy and will just become tedious to you. If however, you have children or if you are a child then the puzzles will be challenging but not too much so.
Now the Music, at first the music isn't the worst thing in the world but yes it does become very very irritating. The sound effects are very repetitve and will make you want to shut off the sound. At least they did with me.
Lastly, the bugs, yes there are some serious bugs. One is that the objects sometimes don't interact with the enviroment like they are supposed to. Sometimes the items at the end of the level when they are all flying around the room will indeed go through each other or through the walls. And yes sometimes the game will in a sense freeze up because the people wont run out of the room but rather just run around the room trying to get out and you will have to restart the level.
As it stands currently I'd give it 3 out of 5 stars. If they fixed some of the bugs, then maybe would consider raising it to a 4 out of 5.

While for a while the game was great it's started to go downhill. Now maybe i'm just bad but before it felt like skill mattered and you could dodge enemies' shots. However now it seems like every new thing that has been added not only has the potential to one shot it can do so well before you can react to the shots. Along with that they've made every dungeon just a spam of status affects, damage, or piercing. Not every enemy needs sick, pet stasis, and weak. And not every enemy needs to resist any and all status affects. So many classes are made worthless because nearly every enemy is immune to their abilities. There's a complete lack of protection for the player while every enemy is immune to everything but raw damage and even then has multiple invulnerability phases. In DECA's attempts to make the game more of a challenge instead of adding mechanics or floods of enemies to fight they chose to add more instakills, status affects, and all around less enjoyable gameplay. When you do a tomb there are clear shots that you need to dodge and rolls that everyone needs to play, along with that the bosses have actual mechanics from shields for each other to heals to paralysis. New dungeons have so much shot spam that melee characters are nearly useless, and when they can get in the enemies are immune to stuns. And now with the newest dungeon, the Lost Halls there's basically no right way to do it, either you have too few people and you can't clear the rooms faster than they respawn, or you have too many people so that the game lags and causes instakills. I have no problem with dying in this game when it's my own fault, however far to often that's not the case, enemies will charge you apply so many status affects that if you aren't dead you will be soon after or will have shots that kill you instantly. Great core gameplay, but not without its faults. If you are interested in single player game modes then I would suggest holding off on purchasing this game until that content arrives, but if you are mostly interested in online then you would find a lot of enjoyment with this game. With that said, there are still some things to consider.
The biggest issue in my opinion is that this game (A PC and PS4 exclusive) lacks Direct input support on PC. This means that all of your PS4 arcade sticks won't work on this version of the game, you will need a stick that has X input (360 stick) or use third party software to get your direct input stick to work. Doesn't sound like a huge issue, but I have experienced noticeable input lag with using anything but Joytokey. Maybe your system will work better with the some software over others, I don't know, there are several of these sofwares but Direct input support has been promised on launch day by a Capcom representative and they haven't mentioned it since. For all the players who like to play 2D Fighters on keyboard, there is no key mapping, so you're stuck with the default mapping.
The next issue I'd like to mention is Ragequitting. Capcom's solution to ragequitting is laughable at best. These types of games will always have ragequitters and many games have implemented very capable systems to handle the issue, but Capcom's solution has taken too long to be implemented and has the posibility of locking out people who genuinely disconnect from the servers for up to two hours.
Again, the gameplay is solid,  but if Capcom would just do a better job communicating with the community about the issues in the game and when we can expect certain things to be fixed instead of constantly giving us the silent treatment I think the game would be doing a lot better.

Street Fighter V is a massive disappointment compared to Ultra Street Fighter 4. Not only is the game, after 3 months post-release, still littered with bugs and quality of life issues, the gameplay itself is mediocre, bland, and simple. The game essentially took everything that was complex and hype about USF4 and removed it, leaving a dry husk of a game.
Net play is absolute garbage. The implementation of rollback netcode was seemingly done by morons. Huge amounts of rollback is rampant even if you're playing someone locally.
Combo system is lackluster and trivial. The game itself prevents players from truly growing. Low skill floor, which is great for beginners, but an extremely low skill ceiling making this game feel very limiting.
Input lag is atrocious and causes extremely poor situations for reactions.
Do not recommend at all. If you are new to Street Fighter, I highly recommend purchasing Ultra Street Fighter 4 as it is an overall superior game. It is more complex and harder to get into as a beginner, but a monumentally more satisfying feeling when you begin to implement those complexities in matches.
Overall, stay away from SF5. Capcom doesn't deserve your money.

Excellent game. If you're looking for a fresh new experience in gaming, definitely pick this game up. The open-world is extremely polished and detailed, giving a truly immersive experience. The volumetric lighting, food vendors, soda machines, rusty air conditioners, high density vehicles and NPCs, real-time weather change, and local radio are all present as if you were actually in Hong Kong. The story is strongly focused and engaging as you control an undercover cop to reveal the dark world of the Triads. The gameplay is solid. The shooting mechanics are fluid and action-packed. The guns are big and satisfying to use. As for the driving component, you'll feel like a true asian ricer blazing through the night life. When you have to fight, the combos are easy to memorize and satisfying to execute. Unlike the original True Crime, there's actually strategy involved than just mindless button mashing.
However, the game is intended to be played linearly (which I prefer actually) and not like a sandbox. So, the replay value is limited if you're concerned.

TL;DR: A very hearty recommendation. Easily worth much more than the sale price I paid ($2.24). Visuals, music, and narration are just about perfect, and the gameplay is very satisfying and offers a lot of variety.
Bastion is an absolute gem. The game hits it out of the park on so many levels that it just feels very complete. Gorgeous visuals, excellent soundtrack, amazing narration (how many games can claim this?), and wonderful gameplay. I just finished the 1st play through which took me around 15 hours to 100%, and am now just starting my 2nd play through on new game plus.
At this point the game still feels fresh, even though some of the game is becoming old hat. What helps keep it fresh is that at any time you can equip 2 different weapons and a special skill. Every weapon is upgradeable up to 5 times, and every weapon has very obvious strengths and weaknesses, both overall and against certain enemies. By trying out new combinations you are forced into different styles of combat. On top of this, there is also a "shrine" you can visit where you can call on up to 10 Gods to make the game more difficult in a variety of ways. Lots of variety here.
If I had to come up with a negative, I'd say the story could have been a little better, and I can't say there was much in the way of character development. Steam has this game tagged as "story rich", but personally I found myself not paying much attention to it. Even with the lack of a brilliant story though, the combination of excellent visuals, music, and incredible narration give this game more than enough character. I have a feeling this will be one of the more memorable games in my collection.

Well, this is disappointing.
As an idea, it sounds pretty cool. You get to be a ghost in a manor, manipulating objects to scare people. And it's written by Neil Gaiman! It has to be at least
, right? Unfortunately, no. I've played the game for, admittedly, not a very long time. But the short time I did have with it, before closing it from boredom, was not really enjoyable at all.
Let's start with the basics. Wayward Manor's intro features Neil Gaiman giving me a somewhat lackluster reading of the talking Manor's thoughts and feelings about life. Gaiman doesn't sound like he's trying to play the part of the Manor here; if anything it's what I imagine a tired father reading aloud to his children, who aren't really paying attention, sounds like. The words themselves are perfectly fine. The delivery isn't.
Onto the gameplay. One word that comes to mind is bland. Another is repetetive. As a ghost you can manipulate objects in each stage to get a scare out of the characters in said stage. You start off being able to manipulate only precariously placed bottles of poison (I'm talking balanced on rafters and swinging from ropes). I understand that scaring people with these makes you more powerful in the room, able to play with more items. What I don't really get is why only some bottles are available to you at the start; it seems arbitrary and just "because we said so." to me. As the stages progress you get access to more of the objects, which sounds great. I think the problem is that you can still only interact with one thing at once, leaving combo potential almost out of the window. There are a few things set up in the stage that combo together but apart from those select few things, you're just left clicking on objects and hoping that the characters in the room will react in the way you want them to. It would be brilliant if you could move items around, using your own creativity to set up a big scare. But, no. All you can do is click things until you find two objects that interact with each other.
An example of above is a stage early on in the game. One character is walking around a room, cleaning it. Pretty much the only thing that you can do is make a rat run around. So it just becomes this tedium of making the character move to a different spot in the level, making the rat run out in front of them, rinse and repeat.
Now, I'm not really one to harp on about graphics in a game. But I will say this; Wayward Manor is not beautiful by any means. The character models are weird and sometimes glitch out or just walk through each other like they are the real ghosts here. A boy was meant to be hiding from a maid, but several times the boy ran out, stood
the maid, and ran away. In the settings menu the only graphical option there is is to change the resolution. Not a huge problem but some antialiasing couldn't have gone amiss.
I like Neil Gaiman. I like puzzle games. What I do not like is slow, boring, repetetive and simple puzzles with, honestly, some very un-Gaiman-quality writing. I was looking forward to this game, and I am very disappointed.

After reading some reviews, I was wary.  I could understand some of the points others were making and I went into the game worried about gameplay, graphics, and story; but I pleasently surprised.
There were a few bugs here and there, but it looks like the developer is taking care of them as they find them.  This would explain not encountering some of the bugs others had previously mentioned.  As time goes on, I am sure there will be little to none to speak of.
The graphics, although not up to the quality of some of the larger titles, has character and style.  It was actually an enjoyable break from the drab color-palatte of larger games.  And since this game is tagged as both indie and casual, I am to take into assumption that it isn't meant to rival a heavy-budgetted game and just live up to what it wants to be; fun.  Intent aside, the rooms are fun and visually enjoyable, the characaters are amusing to watch, and the resolution seemed fine for whatever screen I played on.
The gameplay was simple, a point and click combination puzzle game that didn't have me frustrated by level 2 by some overly-complicated design.  Even further in, the difficulty was raised, but feasable.  The complexity came into the 'secret scares' which would be the achievements for this game.
The story felt a bit loose, but the quick cutscenes between the worlds as well as blurbs from stuffed animals/gargoyles/tutorial-like house narration helped keep you tethered to the story and who was involved.  I didn't feel like it was a visual narration of one of Neil's books, which I can only assume others felt dissapointed by.  All in all, the focus was more on the fun gameplay than bogging the player down with too much story.
As a over-all whole, I enjoyed the game.  I even spent time trying to get all the secret scares, some of which took me a while to get, and some yet elude me.
TL;DR : It's a fun casual puzzle game with some character with a bonus of Neil Gaiman's narration.

Like other Neil Gaiman fans, I was excited to hear he was taking his story-telling talents to a new medium with this game. I was personally not disappointed. All I expected was that I'd like it. I'd learned that you can't expect much other than good story-telling from Neil; he mixes it all up too much. Between Neverwhere, Sandman, American Gods, Anansi Boys, Coraline, his picture books, Fortunately the Milk, the Graveyard Book and The Ocean at the End of the Lane (all of which I have read or seen), no two are alike. While I think it would be great to have more to the game, especially a longer story, I was pleased with Neil's work. I would love to see this as an illustrated novella of sorts.
That being said, I do have certain expectations about games, though keep in mind, this is from a very casual game-player. I expect them to run. I expect them to work. I expect a finished and released game to be complete and fully-functional. I expect them to entertain. I expect them to be worth the money. I expect them to be worth my time. It worked for me and all (I don't think I had any bugs, but I could be wrong), but I also expect narration to be coupled with text, particularly if audio is unavailable or undesirable (even if it is the wonderful Mr. Gaiman narrating). And I expect some sort of tutorial, even if it can be disabled, and there was none. I think an option to return to the menu between levels or chapters could be added; I had no idea I was almost done until the plot twist came.
Do keep in mind: a patch/update was released within a day of initial release, so any issues may have been fixed. The designers made some slight adjustments, too (i.e., there wasn't the magnifying glass when you couldn't click things before).
In all, I liked the game. I did not have ideas about what it would look like or what it would be about (save for the pre-release description), so on this I had no disappointments. Nor was I disappointed by the story, though as I said I wish there was more. The puzzles could mostly be solved multiple ways, which means you can play them differently several different times, and people who are great at these types of puzzles and those with less experience can all enjoy. Some were more challenging than others, but mostly, this is a casual puzzle-solving story. The background art was nice, though the moving pieces were rather square and jagged, as some others have complained (I don't put as much emphasis on graphics as most people seem to). The music had a nice haunting (but not quite scary) tone, which was pretty cool, too.
Bottom line: It was a cute, casual puzzle game, and I wish there was more.
Also, make up your own mind about it. Was it worth my time? Yes. Was it worth my money? I'm not sure, based on the length, depth, etc., but I don't mind supporting a favorite author and an indie company.

I did not play this game. I endured it. This product fails in almost every regard.
The graphics and animations are terrible, they look barely better than the original Playstation.
The sounds are generic and often are implemented wrong. In the level where you
the baseball bat makes a clanging sound even when you miss. On multiple occasions, I've heard enemies death sound effects when I plant explosives or pick up extra health.
The controls are terrible and you will die repeatedly (or at least more than usual) if you do not rebind them. The down button crouches, but the up button makes you crouch and move forward. Jump and melee are 1 and 2 for some inexplicable reason.
The combat is mindless and unfair. You just aim at an enemy and open fire with your infinite pistol or machine gun until they die. You will take hits from the enemies no matter how good you get. The game hides instant death traps behind foreground objects, and I have had humvees drive through walls and kill me.
In addition to ALL OF THIS, the game is glitchy. As I said before, humvees will occasionally drive through walls and kill you, falling off a building can crash the game, and I've even been hit by a humvee through a wall and ended up outside the play area. I was promptly run over by a humvee that drove through a building.
In short, this game is terrible in every way. Every way except its enjoyability. For some strange reason, I found an odd charm to it. Its story was as cliche as possible and the gameplay really shouldn't have been fun, but it kind of was. If you like games that are so bad that they're kind of fun, then this game could be worth picking up. For everyone else though, I would highly recommend you stay away.

This game is disapointing.  I did spent quite some time playing this game hoping it will get better as I progress. I finally gave up after spending over 30 hours on it.  First of all, all three factrions have the same unit types.  Tanks and infantry units do look different among US, Russia and Germany, but those units are the same type of heavy tank, tank destroyer, assault infantry and regullar infantry, etc.  They just look different but are with the same functions.  The buildings, defense units and structures look the same among all three factions.
Multiplayer is a waste of time.  The upgrading system and game progress take forever.  It takes around 600k - 800k supply to progress from a level 5 headquarter to a level 6 headquarter, and each battle won will give you only about 7k of supply.  You fight in the maps with defenses created by other players.  However, there are only a few player created defense maps (around 4-5 per level).  So you fight the same battle over and over.  Imagine fighting the exact same battle 20 times hoping to get enough supply to upgrade to the next level.
Another disappointment is that you will lose your supply to other player when your defense (controlled by AI) is breached while you are offline.   Lastly, this game is buggy.  For example, units don't respond to command, infantry won't be able to destroy road blocks as that's suppose to be one of their skill.  So it ended up my whole army got stucked and I won't be able to finish the battle.
However, I must say the graphics are nice and the sound effects are good.  But unfortunatly, the gameplay is boring with repeatable maps and opponents.  I would not recommend this game to anyone at this stage of the game development.  Save your money for something else.

Loving this game. It's not often if ever i find a sandbox game that can measure up against the great Rockstar. Having pulled this off with a team and budget that is only a fraction of Rockstar deserves nothing but applause. Enough about Rockstar though.
Set in eastern Hong Kong the city surely has a style of its own. I've never visited the real thing, but looking from pictures the virtual surroundings captivates the original in a great way. Differentiated in four distinct areas the world comes alive and you never get this 'empty' feeling that so many open worldgames leave you with.
I usually don't care that much about stories in video-games and i didn't care much at Sleeping Dogs' either. I did appreciate the level of violence and typical characters that i've known and grown to love from Asian Cinema. The cinematics are executed well.
The missions are great, although nothing out of the ordinary from what you've come to expect from sandbox games. 'Go here/follow this person/kill a bunch of guys over there'. One could view that as a critique, but for me it suffices. Also, even though the gun-action is pretty standard (but fun!), there is a large portion of hand-to-hand combat. Think Batman-games and you'll get the idea. As you progress you evolve as a fighter, and where i started out as a pretty pathetic brawler with a limited amount of moves, at the end you're fighting Bruce Lee-style. This is really satisfying. The fighting and the upgrading works great.
Last but not least, the island is filled with side-missions that reward you in different upgradable aspects of your character, wich keeps you motivated to keep exploring.
Once finished i don't see myself hanging around in the city much more. But to be fair, i hardly ever replay a game so i can't fault Sleeping Dogs for not being any different for me. I almost always just move on to the next.
All in all, a really great game, especially if you have an aptitude for sandbox games in general like me. For the sale-prices i see this game going for on Steam, it's an absolute steal.

This game engine has to be the BEST Indie that I have ever used. It is beyond fantastic although in the development phase. And believe me, I am not a new comer to game engines. My job, using Esperient Creator, is producing VR training simulations of electronic communications equipment and test equipment. I get paid big money to do it also... I'm not very fond of point-and-click adventures, but I can say, without a doubt, that the first season of Telltale's The Walking Dead is an important milestone in interactive storytelling.
Your actions in this gloomy apocalyptic world force you to get involved in its situations and with its seemingly complex characters. The important choices you make are rendered as very real, very serious decisions that will affect your playthrough greatly, even when they aren't actually that decisive in the end (it's a game created with limited resources after all). Gameplay and script combined make you think of the consequences of your actions, so you can really empathise and think as Lee, the main character.
Gameplay is reduced to filling a checklist of actions before the next cutscene plays out. Of course, there are some quick time events present during dramatic sequences, but they're not hard at all. Where's the real challenge then?
The real test is keeping hopes up in a cruel world infested with the flesh-eating dead and desperate people trying to survive. Whatever you do as Lee, someone is going to get hurt in the end. You will have to take responsibility for your actions and never stop believing in a better future. The Walking Dead is a very, very dark story about the best and the worst things in life and death, about the things we do, the relationships we make and the lives of those who are left after we're gone. It's a bloody parable both optimistic and pessimistic, because good and bad things happen all the time and we, many times, have no control over them.
In short, Telltale's The Walking Dead is not a great game. It is, though, an awesome story that reflects some of the true, most horrible, most beautiful facets of humankind. The best kind of tearjerker.

I went into this game with pure anticipation due to Neil Gaiman bringing out a horror comedy game. I was really looking forward to it having loved his previous work.
First Impression Video before it went sour
The  game was released, I dived in with high expectations. I loaded it up, and found that it only supported a maximum resolution of 1920x1080, not an issue it's still HD.
The narration starts and I fill with joy as I listen to Neil Gaiman narrate the plot while characters are shown on screen. The game certainly has a rather funky art style. It instantly reminded me of newspaper comics strips that made fun of politicians with their eccentric facial features.
I started off with a really good impression of the game, sure the graphics looked dated. The art style and music suited it somehow and it seemed fine. The puzzles start off slow and get more complex, but sadly there is no free roaming as a ghost. You're limited to a single room at a time for your ghostly deeds of frightening the denizens out of their abode.
Then, things went south rather quickly. I experienced a bug that locked the level, unable to knock over a vital bottle. No problem I say, I'll just reload the level, and sure enough it works and I continue my spectral adventure.
More bugs, and more, items clipping, clicks not registering and then...then dreaded chapter 3, part 2 where the game refuses to continue after spooking everyone. Five retries later and I was still stuck, not to worry I'll quickly email the developers.
Sure enough they respond in kind and have patched the level. I can still not continue. Sadly once again the same happens, this time the puzzle items are broken and you're unable to catch a drunk patriarch dancing to scare him. Several tries and the same issue.
Sadly due to limited gameplay with many puzzles just reusing the same items over and over again; broken puzzles, and game breaking glitches galore I cannot recommend the game. My first impression video is in direct contrast to what I have come to realise the game is like upon playing it to near completion. ( I cannot finish it due to the puzzle bugs)
The writing, although good, is also not to the level one has come to expect of the Author, leaving you wanting more.
The games needs more polish, better gameplay, and much more depth sadly. It's shame, as Wayward Manor had so much potential, although it seems Neil despite being a brilliant author does not know how to make a game. I hope that in the future he will make a second attempt and that everyone gets what they want: a successful and good game.
