I adore this game for so many reasons. I have been there through character and world wipes, awkward beginnings and cubersome quests - and now I am enjoying the smooth open-world quest-rich universe-building game. I will list my favourite things, and then cons that might apply to players. I will also suggest who I think this game would be great for, and who it is not great for.. and a tldr review.
TL:DR Review: Fun if you like games like Terraria, Minecraft, Creativerse etc. Crafting, open world, quests, you get your own spaceship! Guns, swords, farming, killable bosses, puzzles. Colony building. Teleporters! You can tp from one planet to another, from any depth to your ship! Buy it.
My fave parts: All of it. There is nothing I do not like about this game. Seriously. From having my own spaceship which can fly to infinite worlds to building up a huge planetary colony; from getting a quest from a mechanic who happens to also be a penguin to pocket dimensions with treasure; from tiny mysterious underground villages to deep underwater voyages where you don't have to worry about breathing cause you got a breathing implant from a quest; from an array of replayable instanced missions to scary boss fights you can actually win without tearing your hair out (bloodborne, I'm talking about you!) to buying and selling in an Avian market... this game has so much depth and replayability.
Parts people might not like: I can see how impatient people might not like figuing out some of the puzzles. It takes some thinking and some exploring and some revisiting. Secondly, I can imagine that for some, the repetitive nature of games of this genre can get tiresome - some people don't like games like Terraria and Starbound, Minecraft and Creativerse etc. But repetition can be said of almost every game, even the most popular games out there. If you don't like the genre, you might not like this one.
I do not recommend this game for people with super short attention spans that need constant hacking and slashing to keep them interested; for people that don't care for crafting; for people that only like first person 3D; for people that need staunch realism.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to people who like exploring, crafting, farming, quests that can take some thinking, town building, house building, decorating, hidden treasure, open world, and RPGs. Your characters progress, I won't spoil how. There are amazing races to choose from! each with their unique style, speech, and world views.
Teleporters!! I ADORE how they made the teleport beam you up from anywhere on the planet, even deep in said planet, to your ship. You can easily get teleporters to several worlds, I don't know yet if there is a max number but I have quite a collection, and access those worlds from any other part of the universe! Travel made simple and fun. Just be sure to remember which to goes where.
There is more I am sure I am forgetting as this game is huge. And it keeps getting bigger and better. Worth every penny, I suggest buying full price to support the devs as this is obviously a labour of love.

'Tis a thing of beauty.
Bastion is an RPG that harkens back to the days of games like Secret of Mana, choosing an action combat system rather than a turn-based one.  The mechanics of it are quite simple, but satisfying to utilize.  You have two weapon slots and an ability slot, and you can upgrade your weapons as time goes on and you find the materials for it.
The story is an interesting one.  Bastion, unlike most modern RPG games, decides to go for minimalism in its storytelling.  Rather than have you sit through a forty minute cutscene that explains things, it tells it to you on the fly through a narrator (who is superbly voiced by the way).  It's an interesting touch that allows you to stay engaged, and the narrator will even make little comments based on your actions.
The game starts after a world ending event known as The Calamity.  You play as The KId, a lone adventurer who seeks to restore the world through The Bastion, a place of immense power.  I won't say any more for the sake of spoilers, but I will say that there are a few twists and turns later on.  There are only two major choices you'll have to make in the story, but rest assured you will feel the weight of them.
The game also has a fantastic art style, with bright vibrant colors that are pleasing to the eyes.  So if you want a fun, RPG romp with a unique story and fantastic aesthetics, I highly recommend Bastion.  It's a very atmospheric and memorable game.

Starbound is a good game, but in my opinion a lot of its charm has been stripped away as updates have come out.
It has kind of gone from "Space Terraria" to some weird amalgamation of a few different genres. In my opinion, it should have stayed closer to how it worked early on before release. Terraria is pretty much the ultimate sandbox. The only goal is to wander around and build and craft everything in your menu. You slowly over the course of the game discover new things. You learn to summon bosses and learn to unlock harder diffuculties, you find strange weird biomes that you weren't strong enough to explore before.
Starbound used to be the same way, but in space, with infinite worlds to explore and uncover. Every single one was different, and it really stood apart from Terraria; mostly in good ways. Now, there are still multiple worlds to explore, and things to build, and most of the furniture and items that used to be in the game are still in the game, but now there is just a lot of weird stuff thrown on top of it. Stuff that doesn't fit or feel right or natural. I might be the minority in this, but I really think quests and an overarching story with cutscenes and characters and that sort of thing just doesn't belong in a Terraria esque sandbox.
When you created a game in the past, you would be greeted with a text box explaining the backstory of your character. Every race's backstory was unique. If you were a human "earth has been destroyed and you are one of the survivors, now go build and explore and stuff." Or if you were floran, you were exiled for not being savage and murder-ey enough. Every race had unique weapons and armors, but they removed the weapons and now only Novakids can craft weapons unique to their race. And now, every race starts with the -exact same- beginner mission and have the exact same backstory. And then you pretty much get thrust right into the story, which shouldn't exist at all. It just doesn't fit.
You can avoid the story in its near entirety if you want to, but there is a long mission and a really really long cutscene that you have to watch in order to get the ability to fly to different star systems. Even if you avoid the story though, it has damaged the game in order to make it more fitting for the story, there's the aforementioned things, but there are several quests in the story where you have to scan a bunch of items belonging to each race. So, for example, you have to "search a forest planet" for floran settlements and scan everything there. In the past, it was -rare- to find settlements, and it was more of an "oh neat" than an integral part of the game, but if it were that way now than the story would take -ages- to complete, so now you'd be hard pressed to find a forest planet without a floran settlement, or an ocean planet without a hylotl settlement, or a snowy planet without an apex one.
On top of that, you need certain reagents from certain types of animals to get further in the story. Previous to this requirement, pretty much every single monster in the game was randomly generated. And they had randomly generated attacks, randomly generated colors, and randomly generated parts. Pretty much no two creatures were the same. And as you explored a planet and ran into members of the same species of creatures multiple times you would learn more about the planet and its fauna. You would learn which creatures were hostile, and which weren't. You would learn which ones did more damage and which ones were easiest to kill for food. The randomly generated monsters exist, but now the vast majority of the monsters you see are pre-made ones hand designed by the developers. And you see the same monsters on different planets all the time. The game has completely lost that part of its charm, and it really makes me sad.
The entire game is wrought with scars left in the wake of the introduction of the story mode. Little things that were stripped or cut out that were such a big part of what made Starbound special. All for the singular purpose of making Starbound more friendly to the quests that have been roughly shoehorned into the game. It really is a shame. It wouldn't be as big of an issue if you could easily just download an older version, but you can't.
I still love this game, I have played it since near the beginning of its early access life, and still think, despite all of the strange and in my opinion nonsensical changes that were forced into the game suddenly right at the end of beta, it is still great fun, but it just isn't the same anymore.
It feels like every single thing that made the game special has been slowly peeled and stripped away for absolutely no reason, and that sucks.

Bethesda is so mixed in how they make games. They give you interesting stories and settings, but extremely buggy contents. They make a "creation club" where you pay to essentially get tiny cosmetics mods, but give you a very large open game to play through. They make it so you can't get achievements when you use mods, but give you power armor that you can give a jetpack fairly early on. Overall I can't deny that the game is fun when you're up for a Bethesda game. New Vegas is probably my favorite, and between this and three, I like this one more due to a myriad of problems I've had with 3. Synths are an interesting new threat, with anyone potentially an artificial human. Deathclaws look much more menacing than in previous installments, with animations mauling you. The weapon customization/creation is extensive, with improvised pipe weapons being all over the Commonwealth. And a lot of the followers are interesting or unique, with Nick Valentine being a Synth detective, or Curie being a forgotten about modified Mrs. Nanny made for medical purposes, or even John Hancock being a suave Ghoul mayor of Goodneighbor with a bit of a devil-may-care attitude. The base story is pretty uninteresting, but I can't think of a Bethesda game I've played where I've just loved the main storyline. The visuals are pretty good too, despite what complaints I'd heard before playing it. The power armor UI is the only bad thing I've found in that regard, which can easily be fixed in modding. The audio fits well enough, but the laser weapons sound more like a firearm than I'd like, and after a while the radio gets pretty dull, especially if you've played other Fallout games since a lot of tracks are re-used. In the end though it is very fun, but it could have been better, and Bethesda doesn't seem to care about what's already there and instead are trying to milk the modding market that has sprouted around their games.

Ok. I bought the game in April 2016 after some updates and only after reading many reviews and problems it had in advance. So before you buy it, here is what you need to verify:
1) Does your controller/stick has a default plug and play driver for windows 10? If no, do not buy it. It is a risk your fighting stick won't work and a 3rd part software will be needed. My fighting stick is a Hori RAP V Kai (XBOXone, Xbox360, PC) and it is plug and play on windows 10 to all games. I enabled the d-pad button and it works just fine. WARNING: this worked fine for this specific arcade stick. So you need to do a little research in the reviews pages and on the Internet to see if it works with yours.
2) Are you a competitive player? Do you like training a lot to improve? If no, do not buy this game. In its current state, there is no arcade mode, i.e., no offline things to do besides training. If you want to buy this game, make sure your objective is to train, get better offline, then test it on casual matches. After you have a solid performance on casuals, you go to ranked and start climbing the ladder.
3)  Given you have a controller/stick that works fine and you want to go multiplayer, here is the game review:
This game is AMAZING! The new system mechanics makes it easy to train and learn combos. The timing for the combos is slower than on SFIV, but the game is incredibly fast-paced. So all you need to do is set up your combos and develop your REACTIONS A LOT! This game is easy to learn but incredibly difficult to master real-time execution. I mean, you can train perfectly your combos, but if you do not have a fast-reaction time, they will be useless. I'll all about the mind game lol. Throws are incredibly difficult to tech and the punish is hard on any error. So be pacient. You'll get better.
You can play with friends offline or online on a lobby, the game has both.
Best thing of the online multiplayer: CROSS-PLATAFORM! I've fought many PS4 and PC players! Really nice. The matchmaking is good enough. Sometimes you'll get lag when fighting someone outside your country, but that's it. If you do not know if there are many people playing in your country, you should do a little research on the Internet to see how's it going, because you could end up lagged in every match vs other people outside your country.
You can farm fighting money and buy new characters when they are released.
That's it for the moment.

Trove is a game that requires a lot of time to really get to the endgame. I have played trove on and off for over a year now, and have always found it enjoyable and not dull. In fact, I can not recommend this game any higher! For a free to play game, it is incredibly fun and engaging.
Upsides:
Fast pace dungeon clearing.
dungeons are close together, making accessing them easy.
multiple classes, each very fun.
leveling system that is very unique but satisfying.
Downsides:
Leveling past level 25 is super slow.
grindy as all heck.
if you don't spend any money on gem related stuff, it takes much longer to progress.
if you do not know how to progress already, it is difficult to be effecient.
after a year, I only have 2 characters at endgame level.
Don't get me wrong though, after more than 230 hours playing this game, I have invested a fair bit into the game. I love the game and want to see it grow even more. The best way to level is to focus on not farming gear, and going into the highest level worlds you can still survive, and mooch xp off of better players. Feel free to add me as a friend and I will give a better explanation and guide you a bit, if you want.
Again, for a free to play game, this is pretty good! you CAN get to endgame levels without spending a cent, it just is easier if you do.

+ Amazing Gameplay (Solid as F*CK! FPS out the wazoo!)

A few things I should clarify up front is that I purchased this on steam winter sale for $5.99, and 3 DLCS for a few bucks as well. So for the amount of money I spent I wasn't expecting a whole lot, which is always nice because you're easily suprised.
The game revolves around you, a cop working on the inside of the Hong Kong mafia (more or less). Throughout the gameplay you're constantly trying to walk the line between cop vs gangster but the line is more often than not blurred and I found that a lot better than some games who will stick to the rules.
A lot compare this to GTA or call it a GTA clone but I don't think so, not in the slighetest. The only resemblence is it's open world and you can enter/exit vehicles. I found the game to be a bit more interesting with the combat system, which if anything reminded me of Assassins Creed more than GTA. At times you'll wish guns were easier to obtain (and retain, I should say) but the hand to hand and combos you learn make the fighting fun and a bit more interesting to watch than bang bang, Though I am guilty of spending a good while mindlessly trying to jack guns from cops. Another very cool feature was the hijack feature. You can jump from vehicle to vehicle in stuntman-like fashion, if you're close enough. This makes for interesting gameplay if you're like me and sometimes get sidetracked and have a lot of cops to get rid of. Car about to burn up? No problem, steal another ... while driving. Epic.
I think the story was pretty well. I felt for some of the characters such as Winston, and Momma. My biggest regret is that I didn't buy the super DLC bundle ecspecially since it was on sale too. I picked up Year of the Snake but have not played it yet. I can't imagine it being so terrible my impression of the game changed.
While I mentioned you won't often run with a gun you do enough so don't worry if you're looking for guns. Personally I had some issues with the firing of weapons. Most notabely while shooting from vehicles, almost everytime it wouldn't fire and I'd constantly have to re-duck in to the car and re-lean out, sometimes my gun would stay firing when I quit until I un-leaned from the car window. While taking cover behind some objects firing would not work either. This was both irritating but spiced up the game play a bit, and judging from the forums I don't think many had the issue I did. I am unsure the reason [still], but it didn't break the gameplay a whole lot for me.
So call this a GTA clone, a 'bad' console port, or whatever you want. For me, for the price I paid, I thought I made out quite well and picked up a pretty damn fun gangster game that lasted me a good while. I haven't even finished the race/cop missions (just storyline) and have much more to do outside of the DLCS.

I heard a lot of hype for this game before I tried it.  Usually I'm wary of such games, as it's difficult to live up to so many high expectations.  I'm glad to report that this is one of those rare circumstances where a game not only lives up to its hype, but exceeds it.  Bastion is an action RPG with the gimmick of a real-time narrator.  The story is quite good, but the variations in combat are really what shine with Bastion.  Multiple weapons and weapon pairings allow you to play this game as you choose, and also allow for different playthroughs each time you approach this game.  Add in one of the best video game soundtracks I've heard in a long time, and you have a complete package.  Bastion is one of the few games that upon completion I fired it up again to play it from the start.  I would give this game an outstanding 9.5/10.

Bastion's got good visuals and good music, and is a fairly polished game altogether. It's standout feature is its gameplay. The controls are tight and the mechanics are varied and fun to play. The weapons you collect throughout the game are interesting enough compared to one another to give you a lot of useful options for different scenarios. And the game will present you with a number of different scenarios where one weapons "build" may be better than another. You can't switch weapons on the fly, but with easy and frequent access to the game's hub world, it's not a big deal.
There are some RPG elements thrown in that add depth to the game, such as upgrading your weapons or purchasing special skills that you can use in combat. The weapon upgrades are useful and add to the game's fun, but the special skills are not. They're usually used in combat if you're in a pinch, but they're only useful for the first small portion of the game. By the end of the game, you'd be hard-pressed to find a skill that you'll actually use in combat. There's also an XP system used to level up, which unlocks the ability to equip more tonics. Each tonic augments your health or fighting abilities, adding modifiers to certain stats. Some of them give you a bonus to one area but a restriction to another, and it adds quite a bit to the game. There are also godly idols that you can invoke on your character, making the enemies more difficult in various ways. This allows you to gain more of the game's currency and more XP faster, which you'll sometimes want to do in order to achieve a more powerful character to tackle harder parts of the game.
All of these elements combine with the combat, which features a large variety of enemy designs, to make for a mostly fun experience. Mostly all of the enemies and levels are well-designed and are varied enough to require you to change up your strategy on the fly to get through different battles. The difficulty is fairly well-paced, though the game's harder scenarios can be frustrating. However, if you're having a lot of trouble beating a certain part, it usually just means you need to spend some time beefing up your character before you tackle it again. The game's not terribly long, but there's enough optional content added to it that will keep you busy if you're interested.
The big downside to the game is the story. It's narrated by a guy with a cool voice, which at first is good, but it later falls flat due to a lackluster story backing it up. The developers put some effort into the story, but it comes across as supremely generic fantasy with completely uninteresting characters. The character you play as has no name, no voice, no personality, and really no reason to be in the setting he's in. Some backstory is periodically told about your character, but with him literally not conveying anything at all to any other character in the game, it feels equivalent to the developers coming up with backstory for a sponge. Slightly more story is added to the game's other few characters, but it's all just simple, boring fantasy. The actual character behind the cool narrator just doesn't stack up, which causes the narration to suddenly seem silly and forced.
And if the narrator says "calamity" one more gotdang time...

According to my account details I bought this game in 2013.  I had been really enjoying Terraria and I felt enthusiastic about this as something I would be able to enjoy in the same way.  I hadn't been ripped off by Early Access games back then and I was entirely optimistic.  Shortly after beginning the single player version of the game I had to answer a phone call and my character died and I lost a bunch of progress because I couldn't find a 'pause' button.  After some research I discovered that 'pause' was a widely requested feature that simply didn't exist,
It is now 2016.  Since the 1970s a 'pause' feature for single player games has been widely accepted to be one of the most significant advancements in video gaming.  But not in Starbound.  The developers seem to consider that their precious game should take priority over anybody elses lives in any and all respects and that is basically the story of this project that I now very much wish that I had not supported.
The game remains in Early Access.  Large amounts of time has passed where nothing has happened.  Large amounts of time has passed where mechanics have been implemented only to be abandoned or scrapped and entirely reworked.  The game always had plenty of potential, I'm simply really pessimistic at this late stage that it will ever achieve it.
The game has become far laggier in its years of development, and it is starting to look dated before it is even completed.  It doesn't have the depth of Terraria in supporting different playstyles and it doesn't have the creativity in arranging various mechanisms to help acquire materials and beat bosses and so on.  There is basically just one way to play the game and progress, while most of the additions to the game have ended up entirely cosmetic or amounted to gimmicks.  Many of the 'improvements' add tedium rather than fun - who wants to worry about watering crops instead of going exploring?  It often feels like the game is going backwards in development rather than forwards...
The game isn't terrible and this does make me feel bad that the review system is as simplistic as 'yes' and 'no'.  There is a significant amount of content to explore and it is far more complete and entertaining than similar projects such as Edge of Space and Darkout.  But for a game this far into Early Access it is basically a textbook example of project mismanagement and in its current state I honestly couldn't recommend it.

I was hesitant at first to review Blitzkrieg 3, due to its “mixed” reviews on Steam. But given that it’s still in development, I figured I’d give it a shot, and I’m glad I did.
Blitzkrieg 3 is a fantastic strategy game, with features I haven’t seen elsewhere. The key thing to remember is that it’s not Company of Heroes. It isn’t about moving your troops cover-to-cover. It’s about blitzkrieg—lightning war. It’s Patton’s no “holding ground” strategy, and the strategy that allowed the then-evil Germans to steamroll half of Europe.
It also doesn’t feel like a WWII game. You can play as Americans and still fight against Americans, and the same goes for the Soviets and Germans. It feels more like a post-apocalyptic war-game with WWII weapons, where you build your defenses and raid the camps of neighboring tribes.
Now that we have that out of the way, let’s get to the point: these factors are what makes Blitzkrieg 3 fun. While one side needs to try and plow through the enemy, the other side needs to build a base to defend against the attack, and this means finding all kinds of creative ways to ambush them.
The game starts with you at your base. You get a set number of fuel and supplies to spend on upgrading building and units, or on your defenses. The base building is a game in itself, because your base is technically a full map that other players can attack at any moment.
Think of it like Home Alone, only with tanks and guns.

I apparently never reviewed this during its release period.  I didn't have to; sales and critical reception spoke so loudly that there was no confusion.  Fallout 4 is an exceptionally good game.
Apparently the masses have taken up arms against the Creation Club.  Sure, it's a dumb idea, and sure, I won't be buying into it.  If you want to compensate modders for the mods they make, pledge money to their Patreon pages.  Beth already got paid for the game and the DLC, they don't need a piece of the mod scene as well.
That being said, Fallout 4 is still an exceptionally good game.  Creation Club didn't impact the PC mod scene as delivered through NexusMods.  Players can still download and use mods as they always have.  The new addition doesn't change the game for the worse, as it did when Payday 2 released their loot crates.  It's an additional way to mod your game, and while I'd argue that you absolutely shouldn't use it, it's a shame people are saying Fallout 4 is a bad game out of frustration with a single optional feature.
Fallout 4 is the same great game it always was.  The only thing we lost with the release of the Creation Club was our respect for Bethesda.  All the characters, weapons, and stories are still present and accounted for and it's a shame the vocal minority within the player community has decided to tar and feather a great game over a paid mod scheme that is, admittedly, greedy, but that is also completely optional.

This is coming from a mostly casual fighting game player
I'd like to gradually get better at this game
So this is here to look at the game at a casual point of view
----------------------
Street Fighter V, I've been pretty hyped for this game for a good while (4-6 months)
When I recieved this game I was very excited to get into the fighting of the game
And I can safely say the actualy FIGHTING for a FIGHTING game is good!
It is remarkably fun to work with
----------------------
The fighting in this game is obviously fun but...
You are a bit limited to what you can do in the rest of the game
Don't get me wrong, this game is still pretty great!
But the game lacks things other fighters usually have
This game is still not complete and characters are still coming out
I really hope that in the future they will add more
The current modes you can fight in is:
Story, Versus, Survival, Challenges, Training, Ranked Match, Casual Match, Battle Lounge
----------------------
STORY
The story currently is very plain and simple
It has drawn pictures without animation and dialogue with voice acting
This is also where you recieve your story mode costumes (I'll explain this later, just bear with me)
BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE
Capcom wil be releasing a full and complete story mode this June!
Or atleast it's said to be released in June
----------------------
VERSUS
There really isn't much to say here, every fighter usually has a versus with two players fighting each other on the same computer
----------------------
SURVIVAL
This is not the most liked gamemode
Survival is where you will choose one of 4 difficulty settings and a character to fight with
Your 4 options are :  Easy   Normal   Hard   Extreme
You may choose any character in the game to fight with
You will have to fight enemies for a varied amount of time and recieve credits to get you temporary upgrades for the next enemy.
When you complete one of these you recieve Colors for the costume you are wearing
This leads to extreme grinding
Easy= 1 new color for the costume you're wearing
Medium= 3 more colors
Hard= 3 more colors
These battles are treated as any other: beat the enemy and win
Depending on what difficulty you chose will change how many battles you will have to fight.
Easy= 10  Medium= 30  Hard= 50  Extreme/Hell= 100
The upgrades you get are completely random which makes this unfair
You could be at level 29 and desperately need a full health recovery but instead recieve a low health recovery and lose everything!
These can be very time consuming and if you lose at that level 29 or level 49 or even possibly 99, you get nothing back.
I honestly get bored of this mode rather quickly
But some competitive players might enjoy this
----------------------
CHALLENGES
This is in some fighting games
This is where the game teaches you combos for each character and currently they have 10 combos for each character you could learn through challenge mode.
----------------------
TRAINING
This is where you play as any character and...well...train!
You fight against a non moving CPU where you can establish your own combos, or train already known combos.
You are able to set up a good amount of CPU options.
----------------------
RANKED & CASUAL MATCHES
Ranked matches raises your LP when you win.
Your Rank depends on how high your LP is.
Platinum = 7,500 LP
Ultra Gold = 6,500-7,499 LP
Super Gold = 5,500-6,499 LP
Gold = 4,000-5,499 LP
Ultra Silver = 3,500-3,999 LP
Super Silver = 3,000-3,499 LP
Silver = 2,000-2,999 LP
Ultra Bronze = 1,500-1,999 LP
Super Bronze = 1,000-1,499 LP
Bronze = 500-999 LP
Rookie= 0-499 LP
The Higher rank you are, the more LP you lose when you...lose
Well, it's a bit more than just that
Lets say you are a Silver rank and you got paired up with a Rookie
If you beat the Rookie, you get a little bit of points and the Rookie loses a little bit of LP
If you lose, the Rookie gains lots of more LP compared to what you would get if you won and you would lose much more LP then he would if he lost.
CASUAL
Casual is a less competitive mode for people who don't really wanna rank up that much
This mode is a bit more focused to get you fight money (I'll explain this later)
----------------------
BATTLE LOUNGES
Find battle lobbies according to your search settings
For example
I wanted to find someone with a high internet connection stability and on a PC
you can find a lobby with these settings
you can somewhat compare this to how the Lobbies work in Skullgirls and Guilty Gear
----------------------
There are still 2 things I haven't covered
The Shop, Fight money and Fight Request
----------------------
FIGHT MONEY
Fight money is acquired from:
Story Fights
Winning Survival modes
Casual Matches
Ranked Matches
----------------------
SHOP
This is where you spend your fight money
You can buy:
Titles
Costumes for characters
Colors for those Costumes
Stages
Characters
----------------------
FIGHT REQUESTS
While you are playing some of the game modes, you are able to press the start button and select battle settings and wait for someone else with those settings to fight you at any time
----------------------
CONCLUSION

The way to unlock colors can be annoying

As mentioned the sound is mesmerising with the sound of poker chips clinking, background noise, and the music filling the air.
Card backings are of good quality too and the developers are constantly updating their games.
The AI however feels a little basic and there's room for improvement, with the gameplay being as expected: its poker.
It's certainly worth a look-see but maybe wait until a sale: as is I'd prefer other PC and console Poker games I've played and also some mobile games to.

Many people loved the first Sanctum, and I agree, it was the best of the series so far, this one is so far the utter downfall...let me show you the pros and cons
Pros:
Characters: Now instead of being Skye or one of her buddies, you can actually pick who you want to be, theres Skye, her sister Sweet, a Robot, a Soldier, and a Goth.
Smaller maps: Kind of harder to fight in a smaller map, in Sanctum 1 you had a huge map and could make a huge layout of a area.
Enemies fight back: Yes, the aliens actually fight you instead of run past you, and you do indeed have health, which means you need to start dodging them, on the upside they do go after you instead of the core, so if you want to try and lead some of them away you can.
Friendly helpers: There are some random NPC's that sit around the field and will actually shoot the enemy with you, but only if they are close, some help I suppose, or if you are feeling lonely.
Cons:
Characters: Each character has a Preset weapon, and you can't change it, for instance the Goth girl has a Crossbow and you can pick the side arm, what if you want to be the goth girl and change her primary? Well tough cause you can't
Maps: I honestly don't like having the map be so bloody small, it feels like your in a tight space and you can't really go anywhere.
Enemies: This kind of sucks honestly, yes they fight back, but you have health for gods sake, and you lose it quick.
Teleport system: Guess what? They took away the teleportation, seriously what the heck? That was one of the great things about the first game, if you were in the front and the enemies were in the back you could teleport over to them if you had a teleporter and start shooting them with your towers.
Death: Yes, you can die now, and guess what? If you die, you have to WAIT for a respawn, yeah, you fall off the map somehow? No teleport out, you have to wait till the respawn is done
Friendly NPC's: Well I know they can be of SOME use at times, but when they are dead they are gone, and you can actually kill them yourself, with a gun or by spawning a tower on them.
Tower limit: Now this got me very angry, and annoyed, in the 1st game you could put up AS MANY towers as you wanted (Provided you had enough space and money to do so) now you have a limit, AND GUESS WHAT?! It counts for co-op too, yes, if you are in a game with 1 or more friends, the tower limit is combined, IE, if a friend puts up a cannon or a gattling gun, it counts as a tower used for you too.
Boss battle: At the end of the chapter I think, there is a boss, and he can destroy EVERY, SINGLE, ONE of your towers and blockades, making all of your hard earned money basically be useless.
Can't upgrade weapons: Nope, this is removed AS WELL, you can't upgrade weapons, you pick a gun, that gun stays the same, no getting it stronger or faster, or quicker reload, it's just the same all the time.
Out of all the stuff they have put in and removed, I can only give this game a 4 or 5/10 It needs a lot of improvement, and it should have been kept at it's roots, not trying to branch off and be a stupid First Person Shooter clone, it should have been it's tower based shooting like it was before.

I had a lot of fun playing through this game so I figured I would do a quick review:
Story:
The story for Bastion was incredibly unique. For a game that is the price of a meal at a fast food reasturant (at least at the time I purchased it), Bastion delivers a well thought out tale that strings the levels together, without burdening you to pay attention to every detail in the game in order to understand it. The intrigue of the storyline is largely due to the brilliance of the added narrarator. The narrator truly kept the game intersting and enjoyable. Somehow, even dying early on in the game wasnt a drag due to the narrarator spewing out one of his quick blurbs right after you die such as "Just kidding, that's not what happened". The story isn't going to wow you like the Bioshock series, but it still has a fair share of twists and turns to keep you on the edge of your seat.
Graphics:
There seems to be a trend in indie games having unique graphics as part of the appeal. Either as retro 8 bit or more stylized. Bastion is no exeption. It has a very distinctive look with its fluorescent colours and lush hand painted environments. Bastion breaks away from the tedium of other platform games of its type. The reason I say that it breaks away is because of Bastion's unique style of varying environments. Unlike even some AAA games, Bastion is constantly changing the levels colour spectrum, enemies, and overall feel. From floating urban settings, to swamps and jungles, and finally to snow filled caverns. All the while, your presented to well made landscapes that are visually impressive due to their distinctiveness. As a side note, this game is not graphically intensive and runs on my basic Dell labtop perfectly.
Gameplay:
Bastion boasts a customizable expereince that categorizes it as an RPG. There is a wealth of close and far weapons that are really dependent on the player. Personally, I never really had a bread and butter loadout, but even if you look online, every setup is viable. Very few people have the same setup, as by the end of the game you are given so many options that your loadout is tailored to your personal play style and strategy. The charecter you play as, simply known as "The Kid", is very responsive and quick on his feet. The controls and movement are solid and tight. never will you worry about the gamer's dreaded "Button Lag". Bastion offers a solid layer of strategy due to your loadout  which includes your two weapons, a secret skill, and your selection of spirits. The weapons are all customizable allowing you to vary up even further how you want to play. A simple machete can be used as a fast, posion inducing blade, maybe a critical hit machine for taking down bigger foes, or even used as a sort of javelin. The options really alter the gameplay. Along with your weapons is your secret skill. The skills are extremely varied. Some are based on which weapon you have equiped, while others such as a hand grenade, or a skill that makes enemies fight for you, are independent from your weapons. Finally, is your spirits which you gain more slots for by leveling up. In other words, higher level=more passive bonuses. These drinks truely alter gameplay. Some boost basic things like health or your critical hit chance, while others can help you survive a blow that would have killed you.
Sound:
Unforunately, I am not a huge sound guy. I don't play games with headphones and therefore might miss the immersion that a shooter might bring with it's explosvie array of sounds. As for Bastion though, I was actually quite suprised with its sounds. Combat sounds were rich the feeling of a gun actually packing a punch. Blades had a slicing sound that made them seem as though they actually cut something instead of just air wooshing by. And the best part of Bastion's sounds, is its soundtrack. Very few times do i play games and find myself humming a tune from it hours later. Not the case with Bastion. The soundtrack is spectacular and suprised me with how catchy and infectious it was.
Replayability/ length:
In the case of Bastion, there is reason to go back and replay the story. After completing the game for the first time,  I was only around level 5 or so. There are 10 levels total that I know of, and with levels comes more spirits and more gameplay options. Plus, there is so much customization that can be had, that one playthrough means you neglected at least a weapon or two. Unfortunately for Bastion though, the replayability and it's length are the one true flaw for me. No spoilers, but towards the end of the game you make a few choices that seem like they would have a big impact. To great dismay, you never see the impact, there is hardly an epilogue showcasing what occured due to your final choice and so, that segment of the game seems almost unneccasary. This means that going back through the game to make a different choice is almost pointless. While I am already bashing Bastion, I have to bring up how it is very short. You can easily complete the game in a solid day or two. Combine that with a lack of story differential between playthroughs and this game could be a play, beat, and  collect dust depending on the person. In my humble opinion, I have yet to get bored, but I must mention, for the person wishing to spend hundreds of hours on a game, this probably isn't for you.
In conclusion, Bastion offers a great amount of enjoyment for a small fee. Although a tad short, it will keep you entertained the ride through with its amazing soundtrack, broad amount of  customization options, and a distinct art style that warrant this little gem an 9/10 from me.

I usually play games I'm unsure about for at least two hours so that I can get a good idea of how they work before the refund deadline, but it only took me half an hour to see most of what this game has to offer - and what it offers is a dull, repetitive and positively ugly attempt at a top-down shooter.
Built on a roguelike-style framework that features procedural generation, character progression and permadeath,
is a game that clearly prides itself on throwing the player in at the deep end - a fact that shows very well on the first level, where you're required to escape a self-destructing spaceship without a tutorial or even so much as a map. Randomly-spawning, godawfully-ugly explosions take significant chunks from your health as you stumble through the corridors, and though you catch glimpses of what could be enemies or friendly NPCs, they tend to get gibbed by the RNG pretty fast. It's only when you bump into an escape pod and launch yourself free of the doomed ship that the game 'opens up'. for want of a less promising term.
In reality, although you're now free to visit space stations, abandoned planets, wormholes to newly-generated map sectors and discarded chunks of former space liners, the promise of freedom rapidly withers when you find out that there's absolutely nothing to actually
out there. All of the destinations you can visit, though different in appearance, play out identically - you land your ship, shoot the mindless zombie-like enemies rushing towards you in single file, pick up poorly-sprited items and weapons that the game never really tells you the purpose of, then take off and try to find a use for all the indistinct junk you accrued. I'd like to be able to write a paragraph for each different type of destination you can land at, but unfortunately, they're so similar in how they play out that there's just nothing unique to be said.
Though the game does boast an impressive array of different collectible weapons to find in your travels, the anaemic levels of enemy variety make the point moot - an automatic pistol carves through a brainless line of whatever those sprites are meant to be just as well as a plasma rifle, so what's the point? The only time I actually managed to die to these foes was when a huge mob of them sprung onto me out of what must've been a spawn point as I approached. My other deaths - getting shot in the back repeatedly by a companion who I never asked to join me, getting hit by an asteroid that I had no way of predicting, and failing to luck my way to the exit during the starting level - were similarly unenthusing. There's also different spaceships to grab off space stations and derelicts to replace your initial ship, but there's even less point to it than getting a new weapon - besides their admittedly-decent sprites, all the ships are totally identical.
In all, between a music playlist that varies between 'generic' and 'actively unpleasant', a near-total lack of any artwork that could be called 'good', and mechanics so bare-bones that they almost don't need that tutorial that the game fails to provide anyway,
feels far more like a tech demo than a bona-fide game. The 'open world' the game puts you in is laughably bare, the exploration aspect falls flat once you realise you're not doing anything new after the first couple of landings, and frankly, I don't even think the area maps that you land on are procedural. Just spend the $10 on a cheap movie or a takeout or something, since both would keep you entertained for longer.

It's some great old-school racing fun, with a ton of content for a very small price.
You have an upgrade path with lots of cars in three main groups: speed, stunt and destruction. You collect these as you win races and challenges, both as rewards and as target which you have to take down in order to collect them.
You can play offline with challenges from simple races, not-so-simple races, stunt challenges and races where you are the target for other cars who are trying to destroy your vehicle.
You can also play online with friends and strangers, setting up races, simple ones or with multiple check points, car limits, boost limits or a free-for all. You will need a free EA/Origin account to play online and to add friends to your friends list requires installing Origin.
There are some annoying quirks (the UI navigation involves ESC, F1, F2 and Backspace!) and the theme song that plays every time you launch the game (To stop it: Go to Steam\steamapps\common\Burnout(TM) Paradise The Ultimate Box\SOUND\STREAMS and replace the file GUNS_AND_ROSES.SNS with a blank text file of the same name (including extension)) and there's this blank page that pops up requiring you to hit "Return to Game" every so often in the menu (The fix to that is to add  127.0.0.1
to your hosts file). I guess that's some hangover they forgot to fix when they stopped supporting whatever was on that page, but once you've done that, it's plain sailing.
It's a good little game!

A notable addition to the TA/SC series.  While it still has low unit variety, it is fun to play.  One note of caution, if your system does not meet the minimum specs, don't even bother, the game will crash.  Galactic war mode (PvE) matches usually take 15-20 minutes per system, with a selectable number of star systems from about a dozen to 40ish.  Smaller galaxies are usually harder as you will have to face the final bosses with far fewer number and variety of upgrades.  That said if you are trying to unlock the loadouts without cheating smaller galaxies give you more shots at the RNG.
Multiplayer is where it really shines though.  MP games usually last about an hour depending on how evenly skilled the players are.  The unlimited unt cap effectively makes turtling less of a game ender in the late game.  The multiple planets make rushing in the early game not effective, or in most cases even possible.
There is a free expansion to the game called legions, which some people like and others do not.  So there are always legion and classic games available.
If you are a fan of RTS games, and the TA/SC games in particular this is a must have.

25 Minute First Impressions:
An interesting if not extremely early and low-budget game. I like what I have seen so far but it took effort to keep going at the start. You begin the game on a starship that has been adrift in space for an extremely long time and wake-up to the sounds of explosions. You then have to quickly grab some starting weapons that are lying on the floor and attempt to escape the ship.
The 'the ship is disintegrating' effects are poorly executed and the whole first mission is seriously annoying. There are little balls of fire burning everywhere and you have to escape while avoiding them...but you have no idea what the exit looks like. Not only that, but the mission is time sensitive and the instructions are written in tiny distorted pixel letters on the left side of the screen. Anyway, once you realise that the exit is a circular lens-like protuberance (because, of course it is), you flee the stricken ship in a tiny fighter and begin roaming the galaxy.
This is what happened to me:
I cruised around in space for a bit in my new fighter. The game’s space-stage is a ‘top-down Newtonian drift shooter’ ala ‘asteroids’, so it was fairly easy to master. I quickly stumbled onto a planet. I landed, exited my ship, and began exploring. Crab aliens attacked me in droves but I gunned them all down easily enough with my shotgun, which seemed to miss randomly. I explored an old abandoned school and a factory, realising only after five minutes that the point of landing was to pick up these small circular fuel and O2...pods; themselves hidden amongst useless boxes and explodable barrels. Many of the crab-aliens were clipped into the wall and were stuck there, making the clearing task that much easier - also, the aliens never attacked unless they had direct line of sight, which made evasion quite easy.
After I had cleared and stripped the area, I reboarded my ship and took to the stars again. I boosted relative north, firing my cannons at space-junk. Just before my O2 ran out (at least, I think the little white bar was my O2) I came across a derelict ship floating in space. I boarded the ship and found that this was a little different than being planet-side - I was floating in an airless environment. So I floated down the corridors, encountered a whole heap of crab aliens again, shot them in zero gravity. I saw a hole in the bulkhead which was full of eyes, decided to avoid it and took refuge in a room. This is when I tackled the inventory system. I still do not know how to use it because, much to my surprise, being in your inventory does not pause the game. I was eaten by crab aliens.
This game has charm and, as they all do, potential. I like the concept and I like what they have done so far. The inventory system needs to be explained, the introductory mission needs to be overhauled, the AI needs epic work and the starting splash-screen needs to be more conventionally laid out. On that last point, it took me a while to even realised there was an options menu and that is not good when you are an indie game trying to make a good first impression. The last thing you want is for everyone to believe that it's such a shell of a game that it has no graphics or audio options.
It's a good early-access game and its first 20 minutes can grab you if you give it a chance beyond the unconventional splash-screen and the horrible introduction. In 20 minutes, I had fun and felt that there was more to come. Hope this review helps!

The main problem with the game is that they don't explain anything that would be important. You get the info that one key is for starting. Then realize it's also for accelerating.
Maybe at some point you get the info which key is for (emergency) braking, or reversing/braking.
But overall? "Just figure it out" seems to be the attitude. Especially when it comes to online racing - there is no real help in-game, and it seems that when you join a race, you stay where you are and have to find the others first. And figure out what exactly the race is about (time, stunts, specific courses, etc...).
Just to be clear - "find the others" means you may have to drive across the quite large map for a minute or more (depending on your driving skills) just to catch up with the other players. Who may already be engaged in some sort of activity.
To be fair, the game does give you a lot of information - but it doesn't explain it to you. While I was within a group of players, I saw constantly changing scores - "Air time", "crashes", "take outs", etc... - I had (and have) no idea what exactly they were counting. Is there an overall score? No idea.
When you try it, give it some time. It takes time getting used to the way the car behaves, the way the camera shows you only a little bit of what is in front of you, and especially the way the braking/boosting works.
Bottom line?
It's fun, but every time I play it I get frustrated with the way it works - or rather doesn't work.
Join an online game - and realize you're five minutes away from the next player. Try to get there - only to have them cancel the game. Yay.
Ride a bike and think about going online? Sure, but only with a car - not that the game will tell you so. You'll know when you're in your car instead of your bike.
All in all, if what you crave is reckless driving - go for it. You might want to take a peek at Nail'd as well, that doesn't have online mode anymore, unfortunately. But it does have progress (tournaments) of sorts.

Bastion is not a game that you play for the gameplay and if that's all you're looking for you might as well find the door right now. It is a perfectly servicable action-RPG. Nothing great, but fun enough to play, and only a positive for the die hard action-RPG fanatic.
However, Bastion is well worth your time for every other reason. The narrative is absolutely perfect. Wandering through a broken land, with only the voice of a single friend as your guide. He comments on everything: how the world used to be, the actions you take, and some hope for the future. Actually, one of the strongest themes of this game is that of hope. No matter how much we screw up, no matter how much we destroy, we can always rebuild. No matter your checkered past, there's always the future.
Frankly, the simple fact that a game has such a strong theme shining through is a rarity in itself (unfortunately), and for that alone I recommend it.

Starbound is a good game, but in my opinion a lot of its charm has been stripped away as updates have come out.
It has kind of gone from "Space Terraria" to some weird amalgamation of a few different genres. In my opinion, it should have stayed closer to how it worked early on before release. Terraria is pretty much the ultimate sandbox. The only goal is to wander around and build and craft everything in your menu. You slowly over the course of the game discover new things. You learn to summon bosses and learn to unlock harder diffuculties, you find strange weird biomes that you weren't strong enough to explore before.
Starbound used to be the same way, but in space, with infinite worlds to explore and uncover. Every single one was different, and it really stood apart from Terraria; mostly in good ways. Now, there are still multiple worlds to explore, and things to build, and most of the furniture and items that used to be in the game are still in the game, but now there is just a lot of weird stuff thrown on top of it. Stuff that doesn't fit or feel right or natural. I might be the minority in this, but I really think quests and an overarching story with cutscenes and characters and that sort of thing just doesn't belong in a Terraria esque sandbox.
When you created a game in the past, you would be greeted with a text box explaining the backstory of your character. Every race's backstory was unique. If you were a human "earth has been destroyed and you are one of the survivors, now go build and explore and stuff." Or if you were floran, you were exiled for not being savage and murder-ey enough. Every race had unique weapons and armors, but they removed the weapons and now only Novakids can craft weapons unique to their race. And now, every race starts with the -exact same- beginner mission and have the exact same backstory. And then you pretty much get thrust right into the story, which shouldn't exist at all. It just doesn't fit.
You can avoid the story in its near entirety if you want to, but there is a long mission and a really really long cutscene that you have to watch in order to get the ability to fly to different star systems. Even if you avoid the story though, it has damaged the game in order to make it more fitting for the story, there's the aforementioned things, but there are several quests in the story where you have to scan a bunch of items belonging to each race. So, for example, you have to "search a forest planet" for floran settlements and scan everything there. In the past, it was -rare- to find settlements, and it was more of an "oh neat" than an integral part of the game, but if it were that way now than the story would take -ages- to complete, so now you'd be hard pressed to find a forest planet without a floran settlement, or an ocean planet without a hylotl settlement, or a snowy planet without an apex one.
On top of that, you need certain reagents from certain types of animals to get further in the story. Previous to this requirement, pretty much every single monster in the game was randomly generated. And they had randomly generated attacks, randomly generated colors, and randomly generated parts. Pretty much no two creatures were the same. And as you explored a planet and ran into members of the same species of creatures multiple times you would learn more about the planet and its fauna. You would learn which creatures were hostile, and which weren't. You would learn which ones did more damage and which ones were easiest to kill for food. The randomly generated monsters exist, but now the vast majority of the monsters you see are pre-made ones hand designed by the developers. And you see the same monsters on different planets all the time. The game has completely lost that part of its charm, and it really makes me sad.
The entire game is wrought with scars left in the wake of the introduction of the story mode. Little things that were stripped or cut out that were such a big part of what made Starbound special. All for the singular purpose of making Starbound more friendly to the quests that have been roughly shoehorned into the game. It really is a shame. It wouldn't be as big of an issue if you could easily just download an older version, but you can't.
I still love this game, I have played it since near the beginning of its early access life, and still think, despite all of the strange and in my opinion nonsensical changes that were forced into the game suddenly right at the end of beta, it is still great fun, but it just isn't the same anymore.
It feels like every single thing that made the game special has been slowly peeled and stripped away for absolutely no reason, and that sucks.

Foul Play is an action-packed, side-scroller game which I think everyone should try, just ignore the metacritic rating 69 that is stated down below, and just read on to know why it's much better than it is given credit for.To introduce you guys into this game, I would like to start by stating that this game has nothing foul about it at all despite the title of the game. At first glance it may seem like a poorly made game with terrible graphics from the developers “Mediatonic, The Irregular Corporation”. However, this is where the magic of the graphics come in, through the rough and casual graphics, the game let's you immersed in its theatrical and comical atmosphere with its very own audience and humour added in.
You are in a staged performance to keep your audience engaged and happy by acting out your adventure-filled stories of Baron Dashforth. The aim is to max out the pleasure bar of your audience by performing crazy combos. Through achieving high scores on the level, you can gain access to even more combos and skills your character can make use of, to help with future scenes and acts.
Let's start with the good points, shall we?
1. This game is entertaining throughout the whole campaign, filled with creative ways to make players feel amused and interested. For example, the stage might be used as an advantage to bring out a cleaner who doesn't have any idea what is going on when stage crew suddenly drags him out of view.
2. Bashing up baddies is always fun,isn't it? Well, you could say the same for this game as you get to destroy your opponents for the joy and pleasure of the audience as you try to keep the audience engaged through the system of completing combos on your enemies in order to prevent the curtains from closing down on the stage.

As an early access game, Blitzkrieg 3 has a lot going for it.  However, early access also implies that you'll be receiving an incomplete or flawed experience from that of a retail (launch) game.  All of that said, I will try my best to provide an unbiased and objective review, detailing the qualities and deficits that Blitzkrieg 3 currently has.
Pros:
[+] Excellent graphics.  Beautiful, highly detailed maps--there are animals, roaming vehicles (trains, cars, etc.), and people who are doing daily tasks.  Trees fall down as tanks run into them, fortifications explode and crumble, and shots richochet off of vehicles creating an impressive realism.
[+] Base building.  Organizing your upgrades is always fun.  There are tradeoffs to consider as you are leveling up, because you can't possibly level everything up at once.  Do you want improved infantry?  How so?  Do you work on individual upgrades to existing units, do you upgrade research options or upgrade the barracks itself?   The tradeoffs aslo exist in how you upgrade your defenses.  Do you want a widespread defensive network, or do you want a few key structures that are hihgly upgraded?  The options are impressive.
[+] Strategy.  Despite what others are saying, there are lots of strategic options that open up conisderably the more you unlock and play.
-Command points can be spent on a variety of support options.
-Artillery to weaken defenses
-Smoke screen to hide advances
-Spies to scout the bases
-Reinforcements
[+] Army composition.  The options are pretty limitless here.  There are four classifications of vehicles and five classifications of infantry, and determining how many of each can be a very important decision going into battle.
Cons:
[!] Pathfinding.  This is something that will presumably get better over time, but right now tank pathfinding is horrendous, at times.  This becomes even more apparent the larger the vehicle is.  And taking into account that as you upgrade your vehicles, you replace them with a larger chasis (stug to jadgpanther for instance), this makes it even more problematic.
[!] No expanded multiplayer options.  Currently, there's only 1 v 1 asychronous battles.  I love the asynchronous battles, by the way, but I'd love to see 2 v 2 and greater options implemented.
[!] Building off the above, there are no integrated community options.  No friends list, no chat system, no way to invite others to look at your base and basically zero player-to-player communication.  [This is a huge negative]
[!] A lack of unit explanations.  I would love to see a detailed tactical tutorial or in-game guide.  Right now I have no idea how to use an MG squad versus an assault squad versus a normal rifleman squad.  All three seem relatively "samey," and I don't have a clue what their operational differences are (if any) besides different stat adjustments.
It's a good game. Not as replayable as other Bethesda games though.

According to my account details I bought this game in 2013.  I had been really enjoying Terraria and I felt enthusiastic about this as something I would be able to enjoy in the same way.  I hadn't been ripped off by Early Access games back then and I was entirely optimistic.  Shortly after beginning the single player version of the game I had to answer a phone call and my character died and I lost a bunch of progress because I couldn't find a 'pause' button.  After some research I discovered that 'pause' was a widely requested feature that simply didn't exist,
It is now 2016.  Since the 1970s a 'pause' feature for single player games has been widely accepted to be one of the most significant advancements in video gaming.  But not in Starbound.  The developers seem to consider that their precious game should take priority over anybody elses lives in any and all respects and that is basically the story of this project that I now very much wish that I had not supported.
The game remains in Early Access.  Large amounts of time has passed where nothing has happened.  Large amounts of time has passed where mechanics have been implemented only to be abandoned or scrapped and entirely reworked.  The game always had plenty of potential, I'm simply really pessimistic at this late stage that it will ever achieve it.
The game has become far laggier in its years of development, and it is starting to look dated before it is even completed.  It doesn't have the depth of Terraria in supporting different playstyles and it doesn't have the creativity in arranging various mechanisms to help acquire materials and beat bosses and so on.  There is basically just one way to play the game and progress, while most of the additions to the game have ended up entirely cosmetic or amounted to gimmicks.  Many of the 'improvements' add tedium rather than fun - who wants to worry about watering crops instead of going exploring?  It often feels like the game is going backwards in development rather than forwards...
The game isn't terrible and this does make me feel bad that the review system is as simplistic as 'yes' and 'no'.  There is a significant amount of content to explore and it is far more complete and entertaining than similar projects such as Edge of Space and Darkout.  But for a game this far into Early Access it is basically a textbook example of project mismanagement and in its current state I honestly couldn't recommend it.

Foul Play is a side-scrolling brawler. Nothing very original there, but the charm of the game lies in its presentation. The game is presented as a recounting of the past exploits of its main character, Baron Sebastian Dashforth (aided by his plucky sidekick, Scampwick Steerpike), performed by the pair on a Victorian stage. The setting & overall presentation is one of the game’s two major strengths. Its other strength is the unique way Foul Play handles its gameplay; you don’t have a health bar. Instead, your goal is to please your audience, which you do by stringing together combos against your enemies, which range from frill-wearing vampires to robed cultists and many more besides. Take a hit or fail to land a blow against someone for a period of time and your audience’s mood will drop, as indicated by a meter at the top of the screen. If it hits rock bottom, you’ll have to start the act again. There’s also a level up system, which unlocks new fighting moves each time you reach a new level.
Unfortunately, for all its neat presentation, Foul Play is still a beat em up, and is therefore subject to the same limitations as most of the other examples of the genre, namely repetitive action & a fairly short length. There are 4 ‘acts’ each containing four regular levels and a multi-phase boss fight, plus a final act featuring the last two stages, for a grand total of 22 levels, but even with all that content you should be able to finish the game in 5-6 hours, and that’s assuming you don’t have to replay any of the acts. The developers also included a number of challenges in each of the regular acts. These challenges can be anything from ‘Get a 50 hit combo during this battle’ to ‘stop the enemies from killing these innocent extras’ to ‘Use this move successfully x times during this act’. Completing all the challenges in a particular act rewards you with a Charm, which provides you with a boost of some kind. You can equip up to 2 Charms before tackling each act, and they prove to be quite handy, especially in the later parts of the game. The game also boasts a 2 player mode, with one person playing as Dashforth & the other taking control of Scampwick. Co-Op can be played both local & multi, but I cannot comment on whether co-op mode is any good or if the netplay was stable or not as this was purely a single player experience for me, so please bear that in mind.
Overall, Foul Play is a good attempt to take a well-established genre and put its own stamp on it. I’d recommend this game to fans of the side-scrolling beat em up but given it’s short length it might be worth waiting for it to go on sale before you pull back the curtain.

I love the way PA:T embraces the absurdity of its premise and its gameplay and creates an RTS that doesn't take itself too seriously but still delivers exactly the kind of gameplay that I want to have. I'm not interested in micromanaging every little unit to get it to do specific tactical things; I like managing armies of mixed units and sending actual rivers of soldiers into enemy bases and watching the fireworks. PA:T does this spectacularly well.
Managing literally thousands of individual units is made easy thanks to a very intuitive UI with many excellent keyboard shortcuts, both for unit and camera control. Being able to zoom in directly where the mouse is makes navigation a breeze. You can even go as far as to zoom away from the planet and zoom in on a different planet. What's better is that managing your armies across these planets is also easy. I'm generally bad at strategy games, but even I can build a teleporter on my planet, fly a fabricator (or twenty) to another planet, and build another teleporter there. Then I can tell the teleporter to send the units that go through it to a specific location, such as the enemy base.
It is absolutely essential that the controls be as fluid and easy as they are because your human brain has to manage these armies across land, sea, air, orbit, and other planets. The preposterousness of these armies is part of what lets PA:T be almost giddy amounts of fun. Thankfully, the art style both reflects and enables that, too. It's a very colorful, low poly visual affair, with lovely lighting and shadows as your planet orbits the sun. If PA:T tried to be super self-serious and pack as much detail as possible, this game would chug along at miserable framerates, and they would expect me to take the premise seriously. Instead, they imbued the graphics, the gameplay, and the minimal story and characters with a lot of personality by letting the game be light hearted and even humorous about the absurdity of strapping rockets to an enemy planet and crashing it into another enemy planet.
This is a ♥♥♥♥ing blast. Buy it now

Bastion is not a game that you play for the gameplay and if that's all you're looking for you might as well find the door right now. It is a perfectly servicable action-RPG. Nothing great, but fun enough to play, and only a positive for the die hard action-RPG fanatic.
However, Bastion is well worth your time for every other reason. The narrative is absolutely perfect. Wandering through a broken land, with only the voice of a single friend as your guide. He comments on everything: how the world used to be, the actions you take, and some hope for the future. Actually, one of the strongest themes of this game is that of hope. No matter how much we screw up, no matter how much we destroy, we can always rebuild. No matter your checkered past, there's always the future.
Frankly, the simple fact that a game has such a strong theme shining through is a rarity in itself (unfortunately), and for that alone I recommend it.

I have been playing sanctum 2 for only this past free steam weekand, but have invested the most amount of hours I possibly could during the time, and boy was it fun.
The game is a sequel to "Sanctum" in-case you didn't know, which is a tower defense hybrid/ fps-game, with some light rpg elements to it.
You have 4 classes to choose from I will list them in such a manner that will be easier for people to understand the quick and fast "assault class" with an assault rifle and a secondary weapon of your choice starting out with just 1 but collecting more as you level up.
Next comes the "grenadier class" think a mixture of soldier and demoman from tf2 she can lay down a good amount of fire power, which causes spalsh damage and is good for keeping control of large crowds.
Then comes an artificial a.i. which is "sniper class" just as it says in the name you can hit critical points of the monster from a far greater distance than everybody else and I recommend that he should stay behind everyone else as he is most useful from a distance.
Finally the "heavy class" you carry a shotgun with 4 shells and can do the most amounts of possible damage, your goal is to try to get as close to the monster as possible and shoot him at point-blank range, you can also charge up your shot to do 1 mega "buckshot" of supercharged ions.
Now comes into play the surprising and impressive tower defense mechanics they are pretty deeply implemented in the game and setting down the right guns and tactics for each monster are essential to survive, especially in the later levels.
While not particularly difficult from the get-go, players will have a trial and error session with mulltiple losses and learning which "turrets" are more effective than others depending on the upcoming enemys. Once you get in the final mission of the "first area" you will have a challenge on your hand which will require good communication and teamwork, oh and I cannot stress this enough "Sanctum 2" is meant to be played in co-op mode with 4 players if possible, the game is just built from the ground up with co-op in mind, so if you can try to find good teammates who work together and listen to each-others advice.
The sound of each weapon is appropriate for the guns belonging to them and feels good when pulling the trigger to each of them particularly charging up the "rocket" and letting it go for a barrage of missles, although some weapons do feel weaker in comparison and should be boosted up in terms of sound quality and volume of noise it creates, the voice-acting is limited but what the characters do say in there "one liners" is entertaining, cute, and cheeky.
Most of the story is told through non-dialogue graphic novels, comic book style with the main characters going around their world to try and stop these hordes of aliens from attacking the core's of oxygen which powers the area they are in. The core of oxygen is the main point of the game to defend "AT ALL COST" because if you don't, game-over and civilians and soldiers die so feel sorry for them.... heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Finally the graphics come into play the world around them and the level design are gorgeous and very stylized this is one of the better looking games i've come across that isn't a big developer, the character models ehh not so much. While they look cool in their mech suits and giant robotic arms, they lack proper detail which I would have liked to have seen for higher-res rigs like "sub-surface" scattering of some type and more detailed face, they seem to lack any emotion even when talking.
Also the anti-aliasing in the game im no sure if it has some issues that need to be taken care of but, the AA does no visual quiality improvement what-so-ever. I cranked it up to max 8x msaa is what im assuming and nothing really at all. Eh but don't listen to me im just ranting now, all in all it's a good looking game with some minor draw-backs, or maybe after seeing crysis 3 and battlefield 4 running at max settings, everything looks ugly to me now ;P.
Overall my final verdict on this game is an
8.5 OUT OF 10,
enjoy and cheers.

According to my account details I bought this game in 2013.  I had been really enjoying Terraria and I felt enthusiastic about this as something I would be able to enjoy in the same way.  I hadn't been ripped off by Early Access games back then and I was entirely optimistic.  Shortly after beginning the single player version of the game I had to answer a phone call and my character died and I lost a bunch of progress because I couldn't find a 'pause' button.  After some research I discovered that 'pause' was a widely requested feature that simply didn't exist,
It is now 2016.  Since the 1970s a 'pause' feature for single player games has been widely accepted to be one of the most significant advancements in video gaming.  But not in Starbound.  The developers seem to consider that their precious game should take priority over anybody elses lives in any and all respects and that is basically the story of this project that I now very much wish that I had not supported.
The game remains in Early Access.  Large amounts of time has passed where nothing has happened.  Large amounts of time has passed where mechanics have been implemented only to be abandoned or scrapped and entirely reworked.  The game always had plenty of potential, I'm simply really pessimistic at this late stage that it will ever achieve it.
The game has become far laggier in its years of development, and it is starting to look dated before it is even completed.  It doesn't have the depth of Terraria in supporting different playstyles and it doesn't have the creativity in arranging various mechanisms to help acquire materials and beat bosses and so on.  There is basically just one way to play the game and progress, while most of the additions to the game have ended up entirely cosmetic or amounted to gimmicks.  Many of the 'improvements' add tedium rather than fun - who wants to worry about watering crops instead of going exploring?  It often feels like the game is going backwards in development rather than forwards...
The game isn't terrible and this does make me feel bad that the review system is as simplistic as 'yes' and 'no'.  There is a significant amount of content to explore and it is far more complete and entertaining than similar projects such as Edge of Space and Darkout.  But for a game this far into Early Access it is basically a textbook example of project mismanagement and in its current state I honestly couldn't recommend it.
