I bought this on impulse during the Steam sale because I thought the graphical style looked pretty cool. It advertises itself as an endless runner with an Ikaruga color-switching mechanic. I thought, what could go wrong?
The controls. The physics. The visuals. It was a nightmare.
For starters, this game has absolutely no edge physics. None. For the unfamiliar, "edge physics" are a feature of just about every highly-rated sidescrolling platformer in the history of games, which gives you a few frames' window of opportunity to jump after walking off the edge of a cliff -- kind of like a tiny midair jump that feels like you're propelling yourself off the edge of the cliff. Mario does it, Sonic does it, every platformer character I can think of off the top of my head does it... but not this game. Here, upon stepping on the edge of a cliff, your character will immediately just slide off. This actually makes the game impossible at higher speeds, because if you get a bad combination of landscapes, it's possible to just trip down a bunch of stairs and into a pit with no way to save yourself.
There are only about 7 terrain shapes in the game which are just repeated in different orders ad nauseam. Certain combinations of terrain will make it impossible to grab pickups. Other combinations will make it impossible to grab a pickup without also jumping into a pit. As you speed up, certain combinations of terrain become outright impossible to survive. If you're going for a high score, you'd better just pray you don't get any unsolvable terrain.
The game makes you hold down the jump key to prolong your jump, yet it doesn't check to see if you've released the key and pressed again before making you jump again. This means you'll frequently bunny-hop to your doom if you're not careful.
The fire and ice switching is only useful for avoiding two kinds of death obstacles and picking up two kinds of powerups. That’s it. There are no other game mechanics.
The visual style, which is probably the best part of the game, is also a detriment. The ice pickups, as well as the ice character, have no contrast or outline, and are practically invisible on the game's bright-colored backgrounds. The scrolling terrain constantly stutters in a headache-inducing way.
And the music is one 60-second loop that plays during menus and gameplay. Over. And over. And over.
You will almost never hear me say this, but stay away from this game,
. I know you can fully complete it in about three hours, but with the infuriating edge physics and the luck factor, it’s just not worth the emotional abuse. Please. Just trust me on this one. This game is torture, and I suffered through it so that you don’t have to.
And I want my three hours back.

Game claims to have "full controller support" and has ZERO controller support.  Big turn-off.  Acually, you can manually go and re-bind your controller buttons onto the inputs on the keyboard through the launcher, takes a few minutes but it is possible.  However, this is not "full controller support", I would barely even call it "partial" support.
Then when you actually go to rebind your keys you realize there are only 3 buttons: jump, switch fire/ice, and slide.  You hardly even need a controller since you can't even move your character freely.  That's not a huge issue, though, the game was designed in a certain way that does not require movement.  You just walk along with the world.  Does the world ever speed up?  It seems so slow it's boring.  More like the "walk" of your life.  Sure you need time to think about what to do, and slower = easier, and it probably gets faster and/or more difficult later on, but initially it comes across as pretty lame.  Imagine Super Mario Bros except you have someone else holding down the button to walk and it is your job to jump.  I would much rather have the ability to RUN, like actually FAST, but the screen moved at a minimum pace, and was rewarded for running faster than the game wanted to go.  Having very little control over what is going on is a turn-off, definitely.  It becomes a game of rock-paper-scissors very quickly.
Sometimes, though you can get a really really bad game and it is still enjoyable if the leaderboard is up to par.  This way you can show off your achievements of torture.  Does this game have a good leaderboard?  NO!  It barely has one.  What I would have liked to see is this:
- see your rank globally
- see your rank among your friends
- browse through all the users' scores freely
Instead, we are given a list of the top 10 scores in the world.  If you are not in the top 10, you don't appear ANYWHERE.  Oh, and those scores are super high already, on the first day, so basically forget they even exist (and since this is a simple game, expect them to be hacked pretty quick).
So the leaderboards are basically non-existant, the gameplay sucks, the controller support is a lie, did I miss anything?  I'm not even going to go over the empty steam repository issue yesterday, mistakes happen.  Is the game worth $2?  Hm.  Sort of.  If it were a bit more polished maybe.  Give it a few months for the developer to fix all of these problems.  You won't miss much!

I'm a big Street Fighter fan and I really wanted to be able to recommend this game but.. I can't. I don't do reviews so this is probably poorly done but as it's a game I know about I felt I could put down some informed opinions. If you want a brief summary, scroll down to the conclusion.
Capcoms attempt to open the game to everyone has neglected the people who want depth in a game. If you're a die hard fan of the classic street fighter where basic is basic then sure this might be the game for you but if you want a game that's evolved and developed depth, you're better off waiting to see where they take this game or look somewhere else.
First off, the game is multiplayer. That's it, if you enjoy playing randoms or have other friends playing this then you won't mind. If you enjoy a nice little single player mode to waste some time like me, then you'll be disappointed. The single player is rushed and poorly done. Clearly a last minute thought.
Then saying that... It really feels like the netcode was a last minute idea (I'm not a pro in anyway about this subject). I would enjoy a more smooth online game play but whoever thought the netcode they've used was a good idea needs to rethink what gamers want in online quality.
If I had to choose between the small input delay of the USF4 online and the teleporting in SFV online play. I would choose a more polished USF4 online. Maybe I wouldn't care so much if it happened to both players and if it was temporary but its not. It mostly happens to the player who's defending... I don't need to explain why that's bad. Then once it starts, it doesn't stop it's there the entire match switching between whoever is defending.
Onto the characters, these have good and bad points. I do love some of the character designs and I love the new characters that have been introduced. I thought it was a great idea to have characters that have clearly aged or changed in appearance and they've tested the water with a few but left the default Ryu and a few others the same as they were back when SF started, hopefully this can be changed with new outfits or better yet, mods.
The characters playstyles are also a good idea (there is also a bad point to this in a moment), each character has their own unique way to fight, despite aggressive playstyles being rewarded more than others you do feel a difference and I like this.
The problem I have with the characters is their move/combo sets.. There is no depth, when I go to play Bison who's been my main, I already know it's going to be HK spam until I've broken the defence because that is literally his safest and only worthwhile move. Yes, against higher level players I can't just spam it I have to adapt but at the core it is just HK and that's the feeling I get with all the characters, they have one good option and one good combo.. That's it, nothing else is worth doing because it doesn't reward you for playing any different.
I do play other characters like Laura or Karin, I get bored just playing one character I like to learn all their basics then learn their more damaging/tight combos but their combos are either lacking or don't do as much damage as more simple combos I do with Bison. Which is actually a good idea and something I thought they would do. If you want to accommodate newcomers without losing the technical players. then just reward the basic combos and keep the more difficult combos. It doesn't need massively long combos but give it more than 3 parts to every combo (without the use of Vtrigger, even then that just becomes 4 parts of the combo).
The stages are also nicely made, the only downside to the stages which isn't a huge problem I'm probably just nitpicking but they're not all interactive. You have the one stage where you'll be knocked into another area of the stage or possibly knocked into a bus or get noodles on your head but that's it. It gives the impression that they spent 75% of their time on that one stage and then rushed the others.
Another issue with this is the restaurant that you can be knocked into (The other half of the stage) Is so nicely made, it gives a different atmosphere than when you're in the streets but you rarely get to see it unless you're always being pressured in the corner which anybody will know that's not where you want to be. It would be a great idea to have it switch between starting the game in the restaurant or in the streets.
To cover some points I'm seeing a lot of people make;
1: SFV has had an insane amount of people register at Evo - This should be obvious and expected, if you've stripped your game down so much to accommodate people who aren't the most skilled at fighters then why wouldn't they all want to compete for that big prize? Having depth to a game up to this point never stopped new people competing and breaking into the spotlight, Capcom shouldn't have felt the need to take such a different direction at the least they could have incorporated a way to accommodate newcomers into the evolved Street Fighter we've become so used to.
2: SFV still has depth with the Vtrigger/Vskill - You would think so but for an example, look at Biffotasty/Desks videos. Watch his SF4 videos and his newer ones for SFV. The SFV videos are plain in comparison, so much so that he's got creative by editing older SF games into the videos (Which he does so well). This isn't a dig at Desk in anyway, I love his channel and his videos you can always see the amount of effort he's put into every video. His quote in a video description of his sums it up:
"It's disappointing that it doesn't but since Capcom have tried with all their might to remove absolutely anything that's even slightly situational or anything that might be considered difficult to perform, it's not at all surprising."
And I'm not saying we need 100 hit combos we never did and with scaling, the longer combos in SF4 became a bit pointless. Only there to satisfy those who enjoyed the timing/technical aspect. I could give plenty of examples as to why these new simplified mechanics are a bad choice, including being able to mash combos.. Literally mash combos, I saw people in an arcade full on smacking the arcade machine and doing big combos. Then while I was practicing combos, I found that as Ryu I could do a combo, mash DP before the combo animation even comes close to ending and he would throw out the DP, seconds later. This causes problems with the whole negative edge (Will need to google it, hard to explain) aspect to inputs.
3: The games still new - Ok, I can't really argue this considering SFV to date has been a glorified early access. They do still have time to fix where they went wrong but the big problem a lot of people/critics have pointed out is that this was the games "full" release.. The majority of reviewers and gamers might not bother coming back to the game in a years time to do another review. It would of been a smarter decision to do an open beta/early access so people (the pros) could play the game in prep for the big tournaments without the expectations of having a fully fleshed out game.
Overall I really wanted to like SFV but I don't, I still have hope that they will change it's direction and because I am a big Street Fighter fan I don't regret buying the game. The characters, while really well designed (Seriously, Chun has never looked more beautiful), lack any depth to make each fight different from the last. The stages, while nicely done at first quickly fall apart (background FPS lower than the foreground FPS, only one stage being interactive). The new mechanics lack any depth for players to get creative. Then finally, the biggest problem right now. Netcode, teleporting is not an acceptable trade off for slightly reduced input delay.

Blackwake is a team versus game set in the age of sails and cannon in which you crew ships and try to sink the other side's ships. In some respects it may be a bit too true to the realities of antique naval warfare in that most of your deaths are going to be rather banal and senseless affairs where you get ripped to pieces by wooden shrapnel generated when a cannon ball fired by some guy six hundred yards away just happens to hit the hull adjacent to where you're furiously trying to load your own cannon as quickly as possible. You'll rarely see your death coming and even if you could there's not really a damned thing you could have done to prevent it.
Success in this game requires exceptionally high levels of teamwork and coordination and an incompetant captain or clumsy helmsman will turn your game into a futile series of hopeless wipes against any opposing vessel that has it's crap even partially together. For this reason and because of the way teams are created at the start of a match you usually end up either on a ship run by an elite clique of obsessive players who always run together or on a tub full of rookies commanded by some stuttering idiot with a thick foreign accent.
This game can be incredibly rewarding when you're doing well but to do well consistantly you're not only going to have to practice for many hours but you're going to need to socially network and get in with a group of guys who are truly comitted to playing it well. With a little less than four hours in at this time I'm still uncertain as to whether I want to invest myself suffciently or whether I'd rather just walk away. Blackwake is simply a game without middle grounds or viable casual play.

The Last Dream is a point and click game with FrOGs.  I had to look that one up - it means Fragmented Object Game.  You play as Ben, a young man whose wife Elizabeth has recently passed away.  Ben has started having dreams about Elizabeth as if she is trying to contact him from the other side.  The game consists of a series of stages that take you ever closer to Elizabeth.  Her ghost appears frequently to urge you onward to the next challenge.
The game uses live motion video for the cut scenes.  I think this worked better than having mediocre CGI as most similar games do.  At first I found it a bit cheesy as they try to force the emotional connection to get you invested in the story.  They had me hooked with the cat - whom you must use to aid you on your quest. I guess if the love story doesn't work - add an animal.  The voice acting is much better than normal for this type of game.
I think the locations were nicely drawn in a cartoonish style - I quite liked them.  The fragmented object puzzles were very well done - that was the best part for me. It is clear someone put a lot of effort into the FrOGs.  There are normal point and click style puzzle games too - these are also nicely executed. My compliments to the developers for a solid effort with strong attention to detail.
This game has thriteen Steam achievements and takes about four to five hours to complete. I bought it on sale in the Steam Summer Sale - I think I got good value for my $3.  I recommend this game to fans of point and click / hidden object games.

Of all the racing games I've ever owned, I have to say this one has been the most fun!
It feels like the game
really wanted to be but just didn't quite hit the mark.  It's typical Burnout: silly, crazy fun with lots of different race modes in a gorgeous open-world.  Unlock better cars at junkyards, learn bigger and better stunts, beat the fastest record for a myriad set of roads or survive brutal races where you must smash a given number of cars out of the race.  For those who find bikes more fun, this is two games in one!  You can start the game in car or motorbike mode instead, with just as many stunts and unlocks to achieve.
This game is also fun for people who don't generally enjoy racing sims.  It's very much arcade-style yet car handling is great with a variety of camera modes to choose from.  The AI is really well made (no rubber-banding or artificial 'cheating' that AI opponents in other games can display).  The difficulty level increases gradually and at the right pace.  It's all enormous fun, light-hearted yet challenging in all the right places.
The only problem I've experienced with the game is getting my G27 Logitech Wheel working nicely with it.  People can and do have success, but my wheel has a continuous, strong pull to the left in this game which I cannot resolve.  Your success might vary, and

is essential reading to get your wheel recognised and configured correctly.  Alas, my wheel pull was too much so I stick to a very old and loved Microsoft Sidewinder stick or my XB360 gamepad - still great fun!

Preface: the game is perfectly enjoyable on its own merits. You should know, however, that it takes place in a post-apocalyptic world in which the human race has been utterly eradicated by a race of sentient vehicles who now freely roam the streets and occasionally rally terrifying black-clad death squads to murder each other for no apparent reason. They also have inexplicably created an awkward computer program (robot?) responsible for maintaining a lurid facade of human culture through insipid daily radio broadcasts to nobody in particular--perhaps to subconsciously placate the few remaining humans they have trapped in stasis for unanticipated future exploitation? The developers have sold themselves short by failing to highlight these key plot points in the game's summary.
I challenge anybody to observe the complete lack of pedestrians, the fact that none of the cars have drivers, and the radio announcer's bizarre sense of humor and delivery style, and come to any other conclusion about this game's backstory. Driving through this environment is subtly unnerving after a while, evoking a sensation similar to observing desiccated corpses on Miranda and trying to figure out what the hell happened here. 11/10, would play again.

A triumph in controls, world design and story telling; Sleeping Dogs is everything you could want out of an open world game.
There has been something I’ve noticed with open world third person games that has annoyed me for some time. Usually compromises are made in order to create the over world and as a result I believe game play suffers usually from incredibly clunky controls and passable at best combat. Sleeping Dogs breaks this tradition by boasting a fairly large over world (Hong Kong with little surrounds) but manages to pack it full of enough things to do that you never feel like you are travelling through a barren wasteland just waiting to get from point A to B with nothing but traffic in between. You have plenty of extra content to do besides the main storyline, some of it does not appeal to me but I digress. The hand to hand martial art combat is a huge highlight in this game. Upgrading your skills and performing brutal moves never gets old (provided you mix up your moves a bit) and mashing buttons will usually get you killed. The shooting mechanics, while second fiddle to kung fu, are more than adequate, they are neither clunky nor particularly mind blowing. You have the ability to slow time when jumping over obstacles, or shooting from a car, which is appreciated and can be used in creative and satisfying ways that don’t feel like cheating. Want to take out a car? Send it flying by shooting out its tyres while it is moving at high speed.
The story starts a little cliché, and continues the trend for a while but you rather quickly get sucked into the storyline of climbing the triad ranks while also trying not to forget you are an officer of the law. More often than not the lines get blurred and you are usually rated at the end of a mission about how much of a cop or thug you were and earn points to spend on upgrading your abilities. I won’t spoil the story but I will say it is excellently crafted and thoughtful as well as satisfying at the end.

I REALLY wanted to like this game. It has great graphics and it's built well, it has good voice acting, and it isn't buggy. It is also published by Daedalic which I like. But sadly, it is just plain boring.
The story is simply terrible, repeating itself, barely any twists, boring ending. The dialogs are WAY too long and boring, most of them have no effect on the storyline and are just wasting your time, yet you can't progress unless you listen to all of them. Every time you click a character you are stuck in a long conversation that takes a few minute, but only has like one line that is actually important for the story.
Most of the characters are impossible to like, a very few of them are somewhat interesting but get no focus at all.
The jokes are awful and trying too hard, not a single joke even made me giggle. It's full of references for things, but none of them is being put there in a smart or funny way, it's like they are only there because they put a goal on this game to have a lot of references.
The puzzles also have no logic at all in them, most of them literally require random guessing, yet the achivements require you to get them all right at first try. That pretty much forces you to cheat and look for the solutions online, because it's impossible to randomly guess the solution at your first try when it has no logic behind it (ridiculous things like "if that Star Wars character would deserve to die, who would need to be the one to kill them?", that's literally a part of one of the puzzles).
The game is also VERY long, it has like 7 episodes, which are really hard to take when the story is so boring and is just full of long dialogs that are not even relevant, and as if the long dialogs are not enough, there are also a lot of pauses in them. A LOT of pauses.
Bottom line, I lost interest in the story at episode 2, and from then on I just waited for the story to end. The best part about this game story-wise is literally the ending credits.

I really can't recommend enough that you play this game. I just finished it and it is one of the best I've ever played. It is an action RPG, though with emphasis on the action with and incredibly engaging story and amazing music.
The real strength of this game is story and story telling. There is a Narrator who is telling this story and he has a lot to say. Most reviews I've seen say he narrates "everything you do". This is not correct, and thankfully so, because that would get dull. No, the strength of the Narrator is that he MIGHT comment on ANYTHING you do. You never know when you'll get a comment. It might be because you just beat up a big group of enemies without getting hit, or because you fell off the ledge a lot.
He is also constantly giving you insight into the city before "The Calamity", a catastrophic even that happened right before the game starts. I found myself not really caring what the Calamity was, but wanting to know everything about the city before. He tells you how many of the monsters you fight aren't monsters, but creatures that actually had important roles in society before the Calamity changed them and the world. There is even one scene that tries to make you feel bad for them, though once I recognized that, I felt it somewhat contrived.
The plot is also good, with information being given to you slowly, so you keep pushing forward so the Narrator will tell you more about what happened or what is going on. There are actually two choices at the end, which surprised me. The last choice had me thinking like no game ever has. I couldn't decide for awhile! I'm going to play New Game + to see the other side of both. There is also a scene where you base is attacked, and the game made me angry with just a few small words "Our little [pet]... didn't make it". It's something special to draw out emotion like that.
The action is fun. The combat comes in spurts, with some running around and listening (more on that later) so you have a breather and don't really feel overwhelmed. On the one hand, this makes the game easy, but it also keeps it from being boring.  Don't look for really stong RPG elements, as leveling is slow and only allows you to carry one more "tonic" which give benefits. You gain the tonics themselves independently. Some are found and some are bought. But there are a lot of weapons and each has 5 upgrage tiers, with 2 options for each tier and you can switch them whenever you want. There is a 2 weapon system, so you will probably find a favorite combo.
Finally, the music is also awesome. In most games, you might be too busy with the action to focus much on music, but the way this game plays, especially with the pauses between fights, you can really pay attention to the music. It is a fantastic soundtrack and fits the setting, which I'd describe a mix between fantasy and western, as odd as that might sound. A few tracks include excellent vocals.
This is a fantastic game, well worth your $15, and I'm the guy that waits for everything to go on sale. Buy it, buy it now!

Sky Knights is what happens if you take top-down arcade flight and turn it into a MOBA. Two teams have three foward operating bases each. Each team will also have a plethora of tanks and AAAs (basically "adds") to help them out. Teams can be comprised of 2-4 players or AI each. Your team's objective is to destroy all three of the enemy team's bases. Combining the arcade flight genre with MOBA is a very interesting take, something that I believe has not been attempted before. Kudos to Hampus Bankler for trying something unique!
Flying the planes is as simplistic as possible -- it's arcade, not simulator, so you'll only have to press one button to begin your takeoff. The camera is top-down; don't let the promotional screenshots on the store page fool you, there's no third-person chase camera available. There's also only one altitude that you can fly at, except when you're landing and taking off. As I said, simplistic. But it doesn't take a lot away from the gameplay, it just allows you to focus on the important stuff: flying to your objective, destroying everything in your path, and evading enemy missiles.
The major gripe I have with this game is that little is explained. The tutorial mission, while very well-done, only introduced you to the flight mechanics as well as how to use heatseekers and standard bombs. There's a couple of weapon types that were omitted, flares were skipped over, and the entire premise of upgrading your aircraft mid-battle was not explained at all. There's also a loot crate system (???), and some sort of passive abilities that you earn by leveling up. There's a whole lot that needs to be explained, whether in a second tutorial or in an easier-to-access game menu (there is a second text-only tutorial section hidden in the main menu's tutorial option).
I'm also fearful that this game may not live for very long. I enjoyed it, as I'm sure many others would (hence my recommendation), but indie multiplayer-based games tend to drop off very rapidly these days. I hadn't even heard of Sky Knights until Ace Combat Fan published a video on it and provided me with his second key to help promote the game's multiplayer (thank you to both him and Hampus for providing the key!). The game needs a lot more promotion to bring many more players in to help populate the servers and get things rolling.
Beyond the game's need to explain a few things and maintaining its population, I'm impressed by Sky Knights. It definitely deserves a buy. Particularly at its $10 price point, you can't go wrong. Hoping to see lots of updates in the future, and see you all in the skies :D

Despite huge gaps in realism, the game provides clear directions so players don't have to wrestle with fuzzy logic. There's a reasonably natural flow to everything, except in the few circumstances where you work towards solving a problem not yet exposed.
As is generally the case with this genre, objects are scattered in the most ridiculous places. Reveal, collect, use, activate and merge items in the environment or through a manageable inventory. A simple click handles most actions, except in situations that require your inexplicably devoted cat companion for extra help. The actual presence of this cat makes no sense but adds variety.
There is exactly one fragmented object scene per major area, with detailed parts to seek clearly visible at the bottom. Completed series turn into a usable object that activates another part of the scene until all has been found. These were very enjoyable and easily my favorite game segments.
While full motion video may be a welcome addition to some, what is seen here is almost intrusively amateurish. Developers opted to film themselves as the two characters in grainy video, a notoriously bad decision since the early days of FMV. Dub actors provide serviceable audio.
There's eventually a palpable level of repetition with objects and surrounding actions, including lots of power tools, handles, ropes or chains, water, buckets and containers, passwords and more all appearing on multiple occasions.
Mini games are mostly derivative versions of classics you've likely solved before, such as the 8 queen chess problem. Few of them were actually enjoyable, and certainly not memorable. Some even come with poor instructions and arbitrary undefined rules, causing unnecessary difficulty spikes in an otherwise fairly easy game.

I'l give this game a "recommend" because its positives outweigh its negatives, but don't expect a whole lot from this one. Yes, it's hidden object, but it feels like it's more of a puzzle game than a hidden object. Even the hidden object segments require you to find the parts to something that is then used to find  other parts that are then used to find other parts.
Voice acting is limited only to FMV cutscenes, which is a good thing because the voice acting is not good. The puzzle segments are very tight in that you only have a few areas at a time per section, so you don't have to go all over the place. In fact, there is no map because there is no need for one. The drawback to that is that if you want all of the achievements, you can't miss anything before you move on because there is no returning back. You'll have to start the game over again if you miss anything (unless you make copies of your game save areas).
As to the puzzles and storyline itself, it all takes place in a dream world. You're injured in a car wreck and you're fighing to regain consciousness to return to the woman that you love. It's contrived, cliché, and sappy; but this *is* a HO game, after all. That pretty much par for the course. Unfortunately, being in a dream world means that a lot of the puzzle solutions and actions that occur are bizarre and don't necessarily make sense. Whether that's because of using a "dream state" as an excuse for poor story design or to add a bit more difficulty is tough to determine.
Still, it's not an *awful* game. But I can't recommend getting it at full price. Grab it on sale.

Preface: the game is perfectly enjoyable on its own merits. You should know, however, that it takes place in a post-apocalyptic world in which the human race has been utterly eradicated by a race of sentient vehicles who now freely roam the streets and occasionally rally terrifying black-clad death squads to murder each other for no apparent reason. They also have inexplicably created an awkward computer program (robot?) responsible for maintaining a lurid facade of human culture through insipid daily radio broadcasts to nobody in particular--perhaps to subconsciously placate the few remaining humans they have trapped in stasis for unanticipated future exploitation? The developers have sold themselves short by failing to highlight these key plot points in the game's summary.
I challenge anybody to observe the complete lack of pedestrians, the fact that none of the cars have drivers, and the radio announcer's bizarre sense of humor and delivery style, and come to any other conclusion about this game's backstory. Driving through this environment is subtly unnerving after a while, evoking a sensation similar to observing desiccated corpses on Miranda and trying to figure out what the hell happened here. 11/10, would play again.

reviewing a poker game is actually kinda hard. If you’re reading this review, most likely, you’re already a huge Texas Hold’Em fan, and you know that these games aren’t really different in the big details, but rather in the small ones. I can imagine your primary concern being lag dropping you out of pocket aces. I can happily say, from what I played, I didn’t see many problems with the core online gameplay. The game runs smoothly, and I never experienced any dropouts.
The biggest fault Pure Hold’Em has, as any poker game does, is it doesn’t feel any different. It’s sadly the same game you’ve been playing for years. That’s at no fault to VooFoo Studios, that’s simply because you have a very simple game, that has set rules, and can’t be changed up or ‘innovated’. So, my review really has to come down to the smallest of details.
Something I really disliked was the fact that your opponents are electronic tablets sitting on a table. There’s no human models, no shadowy figures throwing chips- it’s a mini Facebook profile, with generic stock images as your opponents. Even worst, there’s no way to change your image, so any online opponents you meet display a generic cutout image. I should be able to make a profile, and use an image to represent my icy play style. Sadly, this is absent, leaving no shred of character in your seat.
There’s also no in-room chat. I know some don’t want that, and would rather play the numbers game, but I do enjoy talking with random people while playing poker. The game is void of interactivity with your fellow players. I’m dying for the day when I can stare someone down through webcam, and you can pick up on someone’s tells. Aren’t we all sitting at the same table; shouldn’t we be able to at least talk to one another?
The music is quiet enough that it does feel like a secluded casino, and the warm glow of unused slot machines surround the table. It does provide a nice ambiance, and Pure Hold’Em has set up a great mood with dim overhead lights, calming music and light sound effects. When the game wants to build tension, the camera pans into a slow motion reveal of the river, as the card slowly flips over. The overall experience is greatly increased through the game’s execution of tone.
The graphics are nice, and the camera floats around the table smoothly, keeping the flow going continuously as the hands are played out. The chips are stacked quickly, and there’s nothing that really slows down the action. For a such a beautiful game, it plays like one of those fast paced online options, but with a stunning presentation.
Finally, the in-game purchases, or as I’d like to call it, “pay to sit at the big boys table.” Want to actually play with people who won’t try bluffing every hand, than pull out your wallet again and pay for the privilege. I can understand playing with money on the line can add some excitement, but we’re not playing online poker- this is a video game. The reward should be getting to the Masters table, and picking up little perks along the way (maybe some customization of the absent avatars). Alas, it’s not a big deal- maybe people just like buying people at their table a pair of sunglasses or a fish with real money. Seriously, are we still doing the whole, “gift” system in these games? Can’t we have something more useful- like voice chat!?
Being a poker fan, I feel confident in recommending this newest entry. It’s fast-paced, visually dynamic, and offers a great atmosphere in a reserved casino. The game however does feature some bizarre choices, such as playing against small electronic screens instead of people. The options are also lacking, at least until they allow you to buy different sets of cards. The game also has a pay-to-play element, that makes this feel less simulation, and more like a real casino. The game also has no voice-chat, or even chat, making the table feel void of personality. If you’re in need of some hands though, this will fit the bill- even if you feel lonely playing it.

Still Not Dead is a very solid experience, especially factoring in the price.
Plenty of indie developers try to make retro style games. They can be less time consuming and more straight forward to create in general. The problem with many of them is that retro games often carry over the shortcomings of their era of video games.
The early first person shooter era of games like DOOM, Wolfenstein and Duke Nukem are well crafted games in terms of aesthetic and design, but most feel janky to move and control by the standards of today.
The developer of Still Not Dead wisely realizes this and created their game to make use of the aesthetic of retro titles, with the enhancements of today's industry.
Movement in Still Not Dead is smooth and responsive, there are no slow downs and the game feels frantic. You move quickly but enemies do as well. The jumping mechanic adds a bit of extra layer of strategy to come encounters if you are able to hop over a fence/low wall.
The combat is very well crafted. You start with a decent pistol but can also purchase more weapons during the levels. Each weapon packs a ton of punch and is used differently enough that you need to change up your strategies a bit when you get something new. There is also a melee system that has a lot of weight behind it. While limited to one button attacks, each slice and hit with your weapon is very satisfying.
There is a variety of enemies in the game both melee and ranged focused. Each looks completely different and has it's own attack pattern. Ranged enemies will have different types of attacks and patterns to deal with, while melee enemies, despite all doing close up damage, will also attack in specific ways instead of all of them simply running towards you.
The levels feature an upgrade/debuff system. Each time you clear a section, you are granted either a bonus or curse, alternating between levels. Most of these are more than just stat buffs with some fundamentally changing how you will have to play the game during that run. Things like less line-of-sight, exploding bullets, randomized weapons and plenty more are welcome additions to the experience.
The game is a rogue-lite, meant to be played multiple times. The maps are procedurally generated but usually get laid out pretty well. There are certain times where it looked like I could fit through an opening but it ended up being too small. Other than that, no major problems with the levels.
This is a pretty solid experience, especially for an Early Access game. Already worth the $5.00 price-tag and I'm looking forward to what the release version will be.

For starters, despite a
of reviews about Trove being PTW it is still a fun game to play
it is possible to play without
to put money into it. Play being the key word; it's a game, relax, enjoy it for what it is.
(I do not use the PVP side of the game nor do I do much Club (guild) events or Towers (dungeons), so my review will not have anything to do with those. As a main MMO I could see how Trove would both be lacking and frustrating (no real questing goal, just grind gear and hack away at mobs and build crazy cubed structures). As a
game there's really not much to complain about in my opinion.
You can spend time building your own 'home' (up to 5 of them I believe), you can go out mining, or you can run around hacking (or shooting, or throwing exploding flowers at) mobs and through dungeons (these are mini-locations spread out over the maps at random that hold 1-3 bosses that will offer up a loot chest when killed. Dungeons as other games refer to them are closer to what the Shadow Tower is in Trove). There's also fishing, crafting, gardening (I haven't really tied it yet), and now minigames -- and countless hours of grinding mats for just about anything you could possibly think of. It's an MMO. Grinding comes with the territory.
Unfortunately there
a lot of items on their gem store that can give people the upperhand, but there are also many of those items that you can also by with a second currency you actually can earn in game. That being said... Do I believe the store is filled with greedy prices and anticlimatic rewards? Yes. Have I seen worse microtransactions in other games? Definitely yes. But there is many ways to get many of those items outside purchasing them.. It just takes time.
Also, the ability to mod items is amazing. You can get your own creations added to the game if approved -- or you can make your own and run around wearing it yourself (only you will be able to see just how awesome you look, everyone else will see you wearing the craziest mis-matched outfit possible otherwise). Either way. It took some reading and lots of trial and error, but even I managed to redesign an entire costume for one of the classes (I keep it to myself though, the guidlines for approved mods was too long a list for my brain to handle at the time I looked into it).
, I do recommend it. For casual gaming. I come and go from Trove when the mood strikes (and for a lot longer than it's been on Steam). It's not a game to take too seriously, and if microtransactions are going to ruin a game for you then you should probably try picking up a book -- because sadly now that they are here, they are probably here to stay.

The real strength of this game is story and story telling. There is a Narrator who is telling this story and he has a lot to say. Most reviews I've seen say he narrates "everything you do". This is not correct, and thankfully so, because that would get dull. No, the strength of the Narrator is that he MIGHT comment on ANYTHING you do. You never know when you'll get a comment. It might be because you just beat up a big group of enemies without getting hit, or because you fell off the ledge a lot.
He is also constantly giving you insight into the city before "The Calamity", a catastrophic even that happened right before the game starts. I found myself not really caring what the Calamity was, but wanting to know everything about the city before. He tells you how many of the monsters you fight aren't monsters, but creatures that actually had important roles in society before the Calamity changed them and the world. There is even one scene that tries to make you feel bad for them, though once I recognized that, I felt it somewhat contrived.
The plot is also good, with information being given to you slowly, so you keep pushing forward so the Narrator will tell you more about what happened or what is going on. There are actually two choices at the end, which surprised me. The last choice had me thinking like no game ever has. I couldn't decide for awhile! I'm going to play New Game + to see the other side of both. There is also a scene where you base is attacked, and the game made me angry with just a few small words "Our little [pet]... didn't make it". It's something special to draw out emotion like that.
The action is fun. The combat comes in spurts, with some running around and listening (more on that later) so you have a breather and don't really feel overwhelmed. On the one hand, this makes the game easy, but it also keeps it from being boring.  Don't look for really stong RPG elements, as leveling is slow and only allows you to carry one more "tonic" which give benefits. You gain the tonics themselves independently. Some are found and some are bought. But there are a lot of weapons and each has 5 upgrage tiers, with 2 options for each tier and you can switch them whenever you want. There is a 2 weapon system, so you will probably find a favorite combo.
Finally, the music is also awesome. In most games, you might be too busy with the action to focus much on music, but the way this game plays, especially with the pauses between fights, you can really pay attention to the music. It is a fantastic soundtrack and fits the setting, which I'd describe a mix between fantasy and western, as odd as that might sound. A few tracks include excellent vocals.
This is a fantastic game, well worth your $15, and I'm the guy that waits for everything to go on sale. Buy it, buy it now!

If one looks at this game for the first time, it seems like it's a classical adventure game:
It has illogical puzzles, it has its own quirky style but for me that wasn't enough to make me like this game.
I have to admit that I don't like Star Wars all that much and as this game draws a lot of inspiration from science fiction, Star Wars was a really big portion of it.
The game's name already suggests that after a day has passed, Randal is sent back in time to a monday.
But as this game had no real direction where they wanted to make it head to, they went from one pop-cultural reference to next one which forced them to give up on this premise quite a lot at times just to be able to put those references in.
While the illogicacal puzzles led to funny situations at times, I simply wasn't willing to spend so much extra time just trying combining objects after a few hours, so I used the ingame cheat sheet that they probably put in because they noticed after creating the game that the puzzles made no sense most of the time even if they should be a bit out of the ordinary.
The insults that they throw at you for using it are a nice touch I guess, but tying to many achievments to it shows that they really predicted people using it.
While Monkey Island has an interesting cast of characters and Guybrush is a clumsy guy that achieves his goals by cleverly solving problems, Randal is just an unlikeable person to the core.
Deponia has Rufus as his protagonist who is also unlikeable at first judging by his personality, but the other characters understand to interact with him in ways that make clear that he is more like a small child living in his dreamworld and thus creating funny situations.
Rufus also comments on things in a way that supports this.
Randal is just always behaving the same with him harming other characters and never showing other aspects of the person you are forced to play for 10 hours in my case.
Other characters are also often bland and while some appeared multiple times, they stayed pretty uninteresting most of the time.
The story is like I mentioned made up by a lot of references to nerd culture that makes it sometimes appear like less of their own ideas were put into this game than things other people created.
At the end the revelations are pretty stupid why things went the way they did and didn't make me feel that it was worth to play this game.

Seeing as I have had many reservations about early access, the reason why I bought this was actually for the blitzkrieg one and two anthologies that I got with it and decided to give this a try anyways.

So nival decided to added an asynchronous multiplayer aspect of it. Blitzkrieg 1 and 2 has always been single player--Blitz3 is no different. You, your attack force, vs. loads of defenses and it's all up to you on how you would crack that defenses and stamp your boot-heel on your conquest.
Except those defenses are now set by others. What could go wrong?

Street Fighter is a series that has grown exponentially since it’s original launch in 1987. Coming a long way from the pixelated graphics we were initially introduced to, Street Fighter V brings a little bit more to the table than it’s predecessor Street Fighter IV injected into the series. Read more in our Street Fighter V review below!
Up until Street Fighter III, Capcom stuck with it’s original style of graphics. 3D graphics were dabbled with in the past but all iterations that tried to bring a new look to a much loved series seemed to flop. That was until we were first introduced to the new artistically designed Street Fighter IV in 2008. Personally, the new graphic style made my jaw drop and I knew I had to get it solely for the dazzling paint brush stroke methods used to spice things up a bit.
It’s now 2016 and Capcom have brought a new sequel for us to enjoy and bring destruction upon our keyboards/gamepads.
The gameplay in Street Fighter V is ultimately the same as everyone is used to albeit for a few changes here and there to how certain characters are played and some slightly different features.
For example, you can no longer chip an opponent’s health away to victory. Gone are the days of firing Hadoken after Hadoken at a blocking opponent to finish them off. Now you need to actually land a hit in order to fell your adversary if they have a pixel of health left. None of this small damage whilst blocking business.
Mandatory originals make a return such as Ryu, Ken, Dhalsim and more. Unfortunately though, some quintessential characters aren’t available from the get go, such as Guile, Balrog and Alex. So far Blanka hasn’t even been mentioned. Some characters will eventually become available to purchase with in-game currency.
Street Fighter V is a great new iteration on a familiar and well-loved series that doesn’t fail to live up to it’s expectations. I’m very proud to see that this sequel is yet again another great success. Well done Capcom!

Another Jim Sterling fanatic here. After seeing him to play this game I finally decided to give it a go and I must say that it was well worth it.
The player is thrown into Doom-like environment where they must search for food, gold, weapons, items and ammo while fighting against hordes of monsters. Not only that but you only have about two minutes before
Death starts chasing you. The exits won't open until you've killed a set amount of enemies so you'll better plan your actions accordingly... or rely on a huge amount of dumb luck to not end up dead.
The unique mechanic of the game is a blessing/curse system. At the beginning of each stage you'll get to choose one blessing (or curse) to either aid your battle or hinder it. You can also risk it by rerolling the blessings/curses (at the cost of losing health) or letting the game choose one for you instead. This not only makes the game more challenging but also gives the game plenty of replay value. The blessings/curses can dramatically change the way you play the game so you won't be having identical playthroughs anytime soon.
Finding different ways to play the game is fun but the game still has some issues. Some weapons are clearly better than the others (I'm looking at you, Hell's Hand) which means depending on the weapons you find you either blaze through the levels with ease or struggle to finish the first stages of your run.
Some blessings/curses can really screw you over without you even noticing. For example, there's a curse that halves the speed of your bullets but it also halves the range of your crossbow. There's a blessing that makes the explosions three times bigger but it also makes kamikaze zombies more likely to hurt you. Learning the pros/cons of each trait will help you plan your runs better, but I still feel like luck plays a huge role in whether you'll succeed or not. (This also applies to finding the right weapons in the stages.)
There are also some minor bugs left in the game. There was a time when I ran through an exit that was floating above the ground and I had to time my 3x higher jump to get through it. Once I was smacked by a spike ball before I even got placed on a level and had any time to react. Sometimes it's also hard to tell whether there are enemies chasing you but that mainly happens with the zombies who possess little threat and are easy to dispose. The enemies/levels also lack some variety but the developer has promised that more will be coming soon.
Overall, while I have some nitpicks with the game it's still a blast to play. The soundtrack is great and gets you pumped, the game runs without issues (apart from Steam notifications glitching out at times) and seeing the world turn dark when Death appears really fills you with dread. Yes, the game is still in early access but unlike the most "early access games" this one actually feels almoust complete. And unlike the most "early access game "developers"" this one seems to genuinely care about the game and interacting with people without trying to sue the crap out of them. That if anything makes this game stand out from the rest.
I paid 5€ for this game and I felt like I got my money's worth during my first run. I'm truly looking forward to seeing what the complete product will be like. Until then, I'm grabbing whatever gun I can find and go running at demon hordes pretending to be on the quest to avenge my pet rabbit.

For a $5 game, I was pleasantly surprised. This game is an interesting idea which, while a bit lackluster at the moment, is great because it explores a mechanic that it seems most other games in the indie genre have simply placed onto their games as more of a gentle push to the objective rather than a threat. That mechanic is the "time limit mechanic". To put it simply, after a certain increment of time (short enough that you'd be able to put a suit on provided that you don't have to redo anything, but that's about as long as it gets [actually probably around 3 minutes from a guess]), "death" appears, who is a large black skull that will chase you at a speed that the player can barely outrun, and because death does a lot of damage, you know that it's time to haul♥♥♥♥♥when you see the sky go red. However, you can't just sprint to the nearest exit: you need to kill a set number of enemies before that can happen! So off you go, pumping lead into zombies and floaty skulls and whatnot. That about does it for the core focus of the game. To aid you in your quest to do the aforementioned, you can buy guns using currency which can drop from enemies or is on the ground in large heaps. Usually ammo for guns is limited, so you're going to need to buy ammo as well, meaning you need to keep juggling your priorities. Regardless, if both of these options are unavailable and you've run out of shot, you have a melee attack (and using a certain blessing, can regenerate ammo for your gun). Now, blessings and curses. After each area, you are either given the option of choosing a blessing or a curse in a 1 0 1 0 1 pattern. Blessings, as the name would suggest, aid your quest. Curses disrupt it. I think that's good on a summary. Let's talk pros and cons:
Pros:
+Shooting is fun.
+The death mechanic really lays down the heat and forces the player to act fast.
+Blessings and curses usually (more on it) distinctly help your game or negatively impact them. They're not just pointless descriptions that seem to have a sort of "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥what else can I put here" vibe to them either, they all have a genuine and noticeable impact on the game. Examples: There is a blessing which increases your jump height by 3 times, allowing the player to vault most obstacles. There is a curse which fogs your vision and decreases your view distance, making it difficult to judge the number of enemies surrounding you.
+Visuals are nice.
+Music does a splendid job of conveying this sort of stressed out vibe as well as being action packed (I would definitely buy this OST).
+Environment plays a good role in the game and makes shooting more enjoyable.
Cons:
-Enemy variety is nil. There are only 6 at the moment (but the developer is planning to add more, so be patient).
-The reference to "usually" when talking about the blessing/curse system. It would seem that certain blessings or curses, while they still have a distinct impact on the game, find themselves on the edge of the coin, not on either side. Examples: There is a blessing which makes explosions larger, including ones made by these kamikaze enemies which will hurt you.
There is also a curse which remixes your loadout each level, and while my good weapons might have suddenly been replaced with something that has limited ammo and the effectiveness of an electric toothbrush, I have occasionally spawned in with the better weapons in the game while full on ammo.
-Enemies can be a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Zombies can be outrun while walking at a snail's pace and they won't hit you, as well as not being able to hit you if you hop onto a fence (I suggest the dev make the zombies move a tad bit faster or have longer reach, as well as being able to slowly vault over or onto a fence that you're standing on).
-The need to juggle ammo and the need for new weapons is challenging, but ammo is usually more demanding, making the player put all their currency into ammo and never really seeing much of the other guns. This can be remedied by a blessing which makes melee kills give ammo, but it's still a starter-revolver-fest. This could be remedied if on each level there was one free gun.
-This is a niche complaint, but the font is a bit tacky.
All in all, it's a good experience, especially for $5 bucks. The gunplay is satisfying and the experience requires that the player be on their toes. I wasn't really expecting something this good from a single dev.
While there are improvements to be made, the final verdict:
78/100
Especially for $5, the gunplay is satisfying and the experience requires that the player be on their toes.

For starters, despite a
of reviews about Trove being PTW it is still a fun game to play
it is possible to play without
to put money into it. Play being the key word; it's a game, relax, enjoy it for what it is.
(I do not use the PVP side of the game nor do I do much Club (guild) events or Towers (dungeons), so my review will not have anything to do with those. As a main MMO I could see how Trove would both be lacking and frustrating (no real questing goal, just grind gear and hack away at mobs and build crazy cubed structures). As a
game there's really not much to complain about in my opinion.
You can spend time building your own 'home' (up to 5 of them I believe), you can go out mining, or you can run around hacking (or shooting, or throwing exploding flowers at) mobs and through dungeons (these are mini-locations spread out over the maps at random that hold 1-3 bosses that will offer up a loot chest when killed. Dungeons as other games refer to them are closer to what the Shadow Tower is in Trove). There's also fishing, crafting, gardening (I haven't really tied it yet), and now minigames -- and countless hours of grinding mats for just about anything you could possibly think of. It's an MMO. Grinding comes with the territory.
Unfortunately there
a lot of items on their gem store that can give people the upperhand, but there are also many of those items that you can also by with a second currency you actually can earn in game. That being said... Do I believe the store is filled with greedy prices and anticlimatic rewards? Yes. Have I seen worse microtransactions in other games? Definitely yes. But there is many ways to get many of those items outside purchasing them.. It just takes time.
Also, the ability to mod items is amazing. You can get your own creations added to the game if approved -- or you can make your own and run around wearing it yourself (only you will be able to see just how awesome you look, everyone else will see you wearing the craziest mis-matched outfit possible otherwise). Either way. It took some reading and lots of trial and error, but even I managed to redesign an entire costume for one of the classes (I keep it to myself though, the guidlines for approved mods was too long a list for my brain to handle at the time I looked into it).
, I do recommend it. For casual gaming. I come and go from Trove when the mood strikes (and for a lot longer than it's been on Steam). It's not a game to take too seriously, and if microtransactions are going to ruin a game for you then you should probably try picking up a book -- because sadly now that they are here, they are probably here to stay.

While the game is short, relative to other games in the same genre, The Last Dream makes up for it with the real-world video cutscenes. The story follows a man trying to reunite with his wife, and there is some decent confusion as to what is real and what is a dream that help pique a player's interest.
Ultimately the gameplay is overly simple though. Hidden object scenes are few and far between, and are an odd mix of find-and-assemble, and find-where-to-use-it, all on the same screen. I admit to getting stuck in a few places as well, trying to figure out what to do next. Puzzles are an odd mix of easy and hard, making it difficult to pin down what age group the devs were targeting when making this.
There is a good variety of scenes and some interesting barriers to overcome, even though I felt it could have benefited from more puzzles and gameplay.

I am a huge fan of point-and-click adventure games, as well as a sci-fi nerd. Randal's Monday is full of references to things that I like. A lot. Still, I couldn't spend more than an hour on playing it and certainly cannot recommend it to anyone.
Worst aspects:
- The game feels painfully slow. Awkward silences & pauses between scenes or sentences, slow walking speed, even slow voice acting. Does nothing to engage you from the beginning.
- Speeches and cutscenes are too long and it's unbearable especially in the beginning of the game. Characters talk and talk and talk before you can do any clickin'.
- The character is defined as a kleptomaniac from the very beginning but in the first hour of gameplay, he will say he doesn't want to steal anything, that it would be wrong bla bla. He kinda seems like a decent guy. But displays no sign of real emotion when something drastic happens. Same dull tone of voice all the time.
- That look Randal gives whenever he stops speaking. Why does he look towards 'us' after every sentence? That's really, really annoying.
- The jokes are off. Mainly because the story and the characters are totally off. And you hear tons of obscene references to things that may have happened god knows when, and it's supposed to be funny but it's not, because it has no history for you, you don't understand anything from context.
- Puzzles feel off too. Usually they don't make much sense. At least they didn't make sense to me.
Pros:
- The only good thing about the game is the references to sci-fi culture. But even that is overused and most of the time feels annoying rather than amusing.
So, this was unfortunately one of the very few p&c games that I recently played yet cannot recommend. I couldn't bear to play it enough to actually get the real story. Because every minute in this game feel like ages for me.

This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly simple-minded and boring; that is my rating! It is not worth the $30.00 USD that it is being marketed for. Now what may I mean by that you ask; well allow me to explain.
Blitzkrieg 3 is nothing like it's predecessors; the infamous Blitzkrieg and Blitzkrieg 2. Both of these games were traditional RTS with different twists in game mechanics and plot lines. Blitzkrieg 3 has no plot line, and is more in line with a crappy Warlords or Clash of Clans (yes....dare I speak that name) in the sense that your only goal is to either bash endless amounts of "player-owned bases" or engage in poorly designed "Historical" missions. It is not an RTS but is more like a Mobile App game that has been given the skin of Blitzkrieg. There is no Map for you to conquer, only 3 Factions to choose from (typical German, U.S, U.S.S.R), and you are only able to use the same 12 units (6 Inft. and 6 Armor) throughout the game; as well as a few "Support" abilities (like Mortars/Smoke). I say all of this because it's system seems more like App graphics than a professionally designed PC "AA" or "AAA" game. Indeed I'd dare say this systme runs very much like War Commander; the MMO-Base Builder game on Facebook. Thus, in this writers opinion, it is not worth the $30.00; let alone does it belong on PC (should be a IOS game IMHO).
But you may ask what about the Gameplay, or the Graphics; for surely those must mean something with all those positive reviews. Allow me to explain from my first-hand experience. The Blitzkrieg series has always been more about large size battles and epic "on-map" destruction that leave the player feeling part of some epic war drama film. This, at least for this writer, is what made the past games so alluring. Burning wrecks, destroyed buildings, massive arty bombardments, and craters everywhere; all of these made Blitzkrieg a great game (and predecessor to todays total war-style games). Blitzkrieg 3 shows none of this, and in fact is a step back from it's traditional roots. Both the Graphics system and the Game Mechanics run more akin to Clash of Clans (yes....dare I speak that name again). Wrecks do not remain on the battlefield, gunfire is simple even on Ultra setting, maps are barely decent at best, the defense/offense systems are poorly balanced to the point of forcing a player to use mainly Armored units to succeed. While I could continue commenting on the poor Gameplay/Graphics I leave it to you to imagine your disappoint if you waste that $30.00.
In this writers opinion there are only 2 good things to take away from this project. The first is the base defense system; which is decent at best. I did enjoy the fact that my map extended beyond my given base design, and that I could move my defense where ever I pleased on the map. That being this very same system is broken because the defensive weapons tend to out perform even the Lvl 6 Armor/Inft; thus making it hard to swipe anyone's base on your own lvl and up (I can see the Trolls enjoying this). The other good thing was the nice Tutorial, which was very helpful (minus the glitch on the Panzergrenedier Mission). That being said it seem too.....bland......for this writers tastes.
Could this game become better, you may ask; worth it's $30.00 price tag. Sadly I'm afraid not, as many of my fellow gamers are slowly discovering. As I stated earlier this game is more akin to Clash of Clans, and not worth $30.00 (more like $10.00 at most). Early Access Constructive Criticism :D No Donkey sh1it!
1.	To my pleasant surprise, the narrative in the tutorial mission alternated between Russian, German and American forces. I love the way the developers choose to give different perspectives during the same session. It’s an interesting way of displaying what kind of impact, your actions have on your foe, as the perspective changes.
As you get the chance to play thru the eyes of your rival, you immediately see the aftereffect of your consequences. It’s a new take on storytelling, it’s very entertaining and refreshing.
2.	Cool moments: During a tutorial mission, you are given a few German infantry to clear out a poor Russian village. And here I was, in the middle of nowhere… hoping to spread democracy. Oh, well! We musn't disappoint our fuhrer, maybe we will find some MANA vodka.
I split my infantry into two squads. I started off by sending squad one to occupy an empty house on the outskirts of the village. This immediately started a firelight, my first squad was taking incoming fire from a house further up the street.
I tactically maneuvered my second squad thru a forest into an assaulting position on the flank. Using the new ability “assault building”, my second squad dashed forward out of the bushes into the house, screaming, pulling ears and vomiting on a chicken, ending up with five Russian KIA inside, oh and we found really fluffy teddy bear in the basement, to celebrate our victory, my heroic soldiers baptized it PUTIN.
3.	Sniper Unit - Sounds inaccurate in game. Last time I checked, yelling wasn’t part of the sniper weapons inventory. I swear to God, every time you give the sniper an order the dude goes ape sh1it, and starts screaming patriotic slogans.

The entire idea of having a dedicated unit going stealth, is silence. At least put some effort into making him act covert and whisper in response. Small changes to sound, can make a big difference to the atmosphere and characteristics of a unit.
4.	There seems to be no function at the moment to see your troops behind objects. And with such a rich and beautifully detailed environment, sometimes it’s hard to pinpoint your units in the field, you constantly need to reselect the units to find them.
Sorry, but I don’t want to spend my time searching for my troops on the battlefield. Especially when there is a mission timer involved.  Some sort of highlight is needed to distinguish your troops from the background, Men of war dose this brilliantly. Take note.
5.	Ability “About face” - Being a Company of Heroes player for many years. I found myself selecting a vehicle and trying to drag the front armoured part towards the enemy. I’m abruptly, startled and confused when I realise that no such function is available in Blitzkrige 3.
It’s 2015, happy new year! Ability’s like “About face” should be at my fingertips, and not hidden away in the far-flung-bottom right hand corner of the UI menu.
Yes, yes, I know! There is a Hot Key, you can press “R”. But that’s so… 2005, I’m not stating that simplification is bad. But coming from a CoH frame of mind, my RTS behaviour is tuned to having fast and responsive controls. In the current state, I don’t feel that responsiveness is coming thru in Blitzkrige 3.
I know there is a red compass-marker you can utilise to set your vehicles direction, but that option is way too sluggish and clumsy to use. Having an instant clock, with an arch of fire, popup underneath your vehicle is faster and better way to do it.
Why not include a more fine-tuned approach of controlling your vehicles for those that want that possibility. Instead of this barebones, point and click. There is definitely room for improvements to be made regarding this issue.
6.	At the current state Blitzkrige 3 does not offer any cover system for infantry. This is something that we should expect by today’s standards. There is a missed opportunity here in NOT letting the player use destructive environments as part of cover.
A lot of effort has gone into creating a detailed destructive environment for Blitzkrige 3. And the developers have succeeded. I just wish the developers made the collateral damage more than just eye candy.
Let me illustrate an example.  - Battle for Monte Casino, On 15 February 1944 the abbey was almost completely destroyed in a series of heavy American-led air raids. The bombing was conducted because many reports from troops on the ground suggested that Germans were occupying the monastery, and it was considered a key observational post by all those who were fighting in the field.
Only after the bombing were the ruins of the monastery occupied by German Fallschirmjäger (paratroopers), aiding them in their defence, because the ruins provided excellent defensive cover.
The point I’m making, is that the destructive environment in Blitzkrige 3 could have been utilized to benefit both sides. This could have created some unique variation of strategies in battles. What you get instead is repetitive gameplay, with limited paths of approach.
7.	Which brings me to my next point, I find it odd that the developers of Blitzkrige 3 strongly incentivise the concept of artificial intelligence for defensive purposes, in base mode. Calling it “core component of the multiplayer experience.”
Yet, the game is lacking any meaningful Ai behaviour, the way Ai responds to human players is with basic triggers, which activate on conditions. Example: A is true, there for activate B and repeat, basically.
Someone once said, “The best defence is an offense!” So far, I haven’t found any way to change Ai behaviour perimeters when defending your base to aggressive stance or turtle defensive, hit and run or balanced tactics.
It’s not fair to say that the Ai is inadequate. It dose its job, but it doesn’t like to deviate from a set path. Doing anything complicated like taking the initiative or making a surprise manoeuvre is out of the question. It’s all scripted and predictable behaviour, don’t expect to encounter General Rommel in the field, anytime soon.
8.	One more thing, the tip popup in the tutorial disappears to fast, it’s stressful and should be fix. This problem is especially hard on new players, who are trying to learn the game.  Your popups don’t have “next tip” or a “back to previous tip” buttons. WHY! WWwwwwhhhyy!!! WHHHHHYYY!!!!... . .. .why!
9.	OMG! I have no idea what the designers or concept artist were smoking when they created this Modern-bluish-sci-fi-metallic-transformers looking UI menu, I’m pretty sure it wasn’t water vapour. For the LOVE of GOD, the current UI doesn’t fit the WW2 themed framework at all, change it.
Other than that, it’s a good early access start.
Dont forget to thumbs up if you like my preview and would like to see more. Dont be a stranger leave a comment. Cheers 4 reading.

Longer Review:
Pros:
Starbound is incredibly fun, incredibly addictive, and even better with mods and friends. The 1200+ hours I've put into it speak volumes about the quality of the gaming experience you can get from this game.
Cons:
It's been early access for about two years now (it first was released on steam in December 2013). That said, the development has kind of been all over the place, at times there were massive gaps between stable updates (we're talking 6 month gaps) and the nightly builds aren't the best option for everyone due to the unstable nature of them.
Additionally, stable updates often make many changes regarding worldgen and universe generation (since the game is procedural) and often times updating the game from one stable build to the next will corrupt your worlds and/or your characters. If you don't like having to start from scratch, you'd best wait for this to leave Early Access.
Not to mention, with mods, an inevitable experience all modders/players who use mods will have is having all their mods no longer work when the game updates and either having to wait months for modders to update them or having to update them all yourself (if you mod the game).

A Guns of Icarus feel, it's pretty fun but sometimes you get stuck with captains that are too afraid to do anything but take potshots from miles away. Ramming, boarding, grapple hooks are where the game shines. What this game really needs though is more environmental effects. A Kraken that creates giant whirlpools, a wind system that effects how ships maneuver based on wind speed and direction. Inclement weather/Whales that can create large waves that can force a captains hand and open up opportunities. Smoke/Oil barrels that can be thrown off the back of the ship to create a trail of fire, or a cloud of smoke to make cover so you can perform repairs or blind your enemies. The game needs things like that that can force an opponent to alter their tactics instead of just broadsiding from a distance. This game has a lot of potential but just adding more ship types and guns aren't enough to mix up the formula. It's still fun as is, though  I hope the developers don't get too comfortable with the basic formula they have now, and continue to expiriment.

Foul Play, is very intresting game. Not because on the graphic or anything like that, but because of the gamplay comcept as well.
The game does not really have a life bar, rather have a thing called "Mood-o-meter". It's basically beating people up, mood-o-meter fills, do nothing during combat and/or get hit bu an enemy, loses some mood-o-meter, more mood-o-meter, more points, meaning more stars (maximum 5), lose Mood-o-meter to 0%, Game Over and must try the act again.
I love every second of this gameplay, espically with one of my budding who we Skype call and play together (He is playing the game first time, and I am playing it for 100% completion).
The story mode, while simple, really does make it intresting. Sure, it might be just there for the sake of being there, but I still do like it.
The graphic, while cartoony, fits the gameplay and the concept, FOUL PLAY, rather easily.
However, I really do enjoy this game, not because of having fun only, but having fun with friends and finding things rather enjoyable, even if it wasn't intended, Example: Lag in cutscenes. Plus getting all achievement can be very rewarding (haven't 100% it, but got some and proud of it too!).
So here's My Final verdict:
Recommen: beat-em-up, fun with a friend and/or 100% the game with hard but (mostly) fair challange!
Gameplay: Enjoyable, espically with friends during Skype calls!
Graphic: Cartoony, but fits the game perfectly.
Music: Really forgetful, but in a good way as you enjoy once listened to it!
