This is a FROG (Fragmented Object Game) with a simple story: you play a man who has lost his wife in a car accident and must find your way to her, in a series of dreams or whatever. The game is high on the adventure component: you search for objects, sometimes combine them, then use them on other objects in the scene to overcome obstacles. The rest of the game comprises puzzle minigames and looking for fragment object pieces in scenes, which are combined to form an object which you then can then use.
- More scenes & locations compared to other games of similar genre.
- Varied environments: from an old, dilapidated amusement park to a country cottage to a factory and much more.
- FROGs are more creatively done than other similar games, so do not feel as tedious.
- Lots of animated cutscenes (involving 2 real human actors too, though personally I'd have preferred CGI).
- You have a "cat helper" that can assist with solving adventure puzzles.
- Good mix of puzzles, adventure gaming, and FROGs.
- Hint system works well.
- Bonus (extra) gameplay available after you finish the game.
- Graphics are nice.
- I encountered 2 major bugs: 1 while solving a FROG, and the other while solving a puzzle minigame.
→ In the garage FROG, clicking on a fragmented object piece suddenly made the game say that I'd found the main object I was looking for, and the FROG scene then closed, despite my only having found about 5 out of 20 pieces.
→ In the puzzle minigame involving the pearls, clicking on one of the pearls suddenly "solved" the entire puzzle, even though I had not yet reached the solution.
- In the "Extras" mode, which you can access after completing the game, pressing "download" to see a wallpaper or concept art close-up, does absolutely nothing.
- Narration is too loose and fragmented (partly due to poor translation), so the "story" is poorly put together and never really holds any weight.
- Adventure game puzzles are mostly lame and/or involve stupid solutions
★★ out of 5 stars

Still Not Dead is a kind of arena-ish Doom throwback that plops you in the middle of procedurally generated maps full of assorted baddies that want to kill you. Your task: kill them, take their loot, eat their vegetables, buy bullets and better weapons, and make for the exit before Death arrives to offer you a sample of this new cookie recipe he's been working on. Between levels you receive either a blessing (a small buff or helpful effect) or curse (a small nerf or harmful effect) alternately. It's a cool system, though I mostly find myself letting the game select at random in exchange for extra cash. Once I can manage to survive longer than 2 or 3 levels this will probably amount to something, right now they represent fairly minor tweaks.
Movement is smooth and desperately fast, allowing use of environment to evade the hordes. Learn to love your jumpable walls, and the precise timing to mash 'E' so you can buy ammo without breaking stride. There's a primitive "radar" map in the lower corner to help orient yourself and lead you to objectives, which you'll need because otherwise there's not a whole lot of detail to steer by.
Graphics consist of these funky, retro sprites (or at least they're styled as such). Enemy and item designs aren't hugely detailed, but they are very distinct and read well from a distance. My personal favorite's the giant spiders with inverted crosses. In-game sound is bare-bones but excellent—enemies have their own audio cues to let you know when something's gnawing on your junk, and the soundtrack captures both the era this game's referencing and the frantic nature of play.
Not sure if this can realistically be called roguelite—so far I've seen no inkling of progression from one run to the next, which is something I'd expect from the genre. Rest of the elements are there though—permadeath, map randomization, etc. Maybe progression's coming, this is early access after all.
So yeah. 5 bucks for a nice little panic-inducing manic FPS. Count me in. Looking forward to see what this guy does with it.

Having played Sanctum, I had some expectations going into the sequel. Sanctum 2 spent no time in blowing my expectations away, for both the better and the worse.
First thing I noticed was the new FPS experience. The graphics are redrawn and enhanced, recoil feels more real, and enemies actually try to kill you on-sight. This makes the FPS aspect much more engaging, and the new direction is definitely for the better.
However, I was also quick to realise that the tower defense part is not the same anymore. The most significant change is that the number of blocks that can be built is severely limited. Now, I understand that resource management is a form of strategy as well, but tower defense is just not the same when a player can no longer design intricate mazes and death traps. I now have to be very careful about where to place my towers, which is also fun in its own way, but can also feel suffocating at times. Whether this is for the better or worse is something that you have to decide.
The game also introduced a leveling system. As the player beat stages, exp. is rewarded, and slots are unlocked as levels are gained. This gives the player the ability choose which towers and "perks" (i.e. special abilities) to bring into the mission. This is an interesting addition from the original game, but also suffers the same issue with resource management above.
Now, I want to spent a bit of time describing the "boss". The bosses in Sanctum 2 are still fat, but now they can destroy walls too. From a FPS point of view, this is thrilling because you got this badass enemy that stops at nothing and you are emptying your clips like mad in order to stop it. From a tower defense point of view, this is incredibly silly because the boss destroys your towers and ignores the maze that you spent so much time planning out. Again, the argument can go either way, and I certainly have mixed feelings about it.
There are other tweaks here and there, but this review has gotten long enough. Sanctum 2 grew as a FPS, but back-tracked as a tower defense game. Although the fun is still there, it is certainly lacking in many ways as well. Heaven knows what direction the Sanctum series is moving towards, but if there is ever a Sanctum 3, I certainly hope that Coffee Stain will hit that golden balance between FPS and tower defense next time.

Have you ever been to a stand-up show where you expect to get a good laugh? The guy looks funny and you know the production company behind him has some really funny comedians on their roster. Then the guy opens his mouth and with the most annoying voice you can imagine and no personality at all he spends 30 minutes telling a joke that is not remotely funny and tries to save it by explaining the joke and fakely laughs of his own joke. The awkward feeling you sit with when the whole room sits silently watching in disbelief of what this guy is doing is what this game feels like, and he doesn't stop for 15+ HOURS!
I was grasping at some hope that something funny eventually would happen, but I quickly understood that I would only be disappointed. I cringed basically every time I went into a conversation with anybody. Not only would you get misplaced and hopeless attempts at humor, but it'd last forever. The dialogues just goes on and on. The lengthy dialog would not in itself be a bad thing if the context was good, but it just isn't.....EVER. So, basically, you just sit there tapping your fingers and rolling your eyes waiting for it to finally be over so you can go and do the same somewhere else. The biggest reward in this game is just getting done with it.
That is a lot of negativity at the start of a review, but fortunately it is not all bad. I have to say I really like the artwork. There's some real talent in that department. Both the characters and the scenery are done well in a style i like. Some characters have ok to good voice-overs, though the main character is as uninteresting, emotionless and monotone as thew come. Don't know if I can blame the voice actor for this though as the script could scare the talent out of almost anyone. There are plenty of references to movies, series and other games (which is something i like). The main idea of the game and its premise seems like it could make for an enjoyable ride if it only had been done properly.
I have to question some of the game design choices too though. You know those pesky illogical tasks that you hear complains about in many games of this genre? Well, this game is setting a world record in it. There are so many mind bendingly stupid illogical tasks that makes no sense. And if you get a hint to what to do next it is so vague that you probably have no idea what to do. This means you'll end up pixelhunting and going back and forth through the scenes trying everything on everything. Everything is just poorly guided. The best part is when you have to do all of that just for it to end up being pointless. Oh well.
The game is also riddled with a few bugs that will hinder your advancement. I got black screens, set-pieces that didn't occur and characters that disappeared. Luckily there were easy workarounds or got fixed by reloading your last save. One tip: save OFTEN!
I'm sad to say that I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone, not even if you got it for free. It is just a waste of time. I'm trying hard to think of who would enjoy this for any reason, and I can't come up with anyone. Maybe, if your life has too much fun going on and you'd like to take some time off of that and practice your rolling of eyes and shaking your head, it could be worth it if you got it damn cheap or free.

I fell in love years ago with the genre of graphic point and click adventures playing Manic Mansion, Monkey Island and Sam and Max. For years I yearned for games with such well written dialogues, puzzles that are hard to solve, but also make you laugh out loud for their apparent simplicity, and memorable and lovable characters.
A couple years back, I found out Daedalic had the answer to my search. This wonderful point and click game I fell in love with is not Randal's Monday. I'm talking about the
(+ sequel, now!).
Randal's Monday lacks everything that make Deponia so fun to play. From the very beginning, Deponia puts you in a tutorial filled with meta humor "HAH, LIKE I NEED A TUTORIAL!... what am I supposed to do exactly?" that let's you get the gist of of the controls work. RM asks you how you want your commands set, then sets you free to watch a video with mumbled audio and no subtitles, then an awfully animated 10 minutes long sequence of people drinking at a bar spewing barely interesting lines that remind me of the level of writing and acting of the Big Bang Theory. All interrupted by unskippable animations of the characters gulping beer with loud as ♥♥♥♥ GULP sound effects (the same for every character). Meanwhile, every voiceline is delivered with a caricature of emotivity and passion that strides terribly with the fixed expression of everyone in the scene. The comicity in this part of the game revolves around puking from drinking too much beer, the friend being a geek, and Randal being... just mediocre.
By this time, in Deponia, you had already solved your first puzzle, and watched yourself fail to get to your objective in a spectacular failure that makes you love both Rudolf -the protagonist-, the setting, the animations, the secondary characters. RM sets you free to roam in a bar you can't do anything in except for a brief cringey dialogue, and kiks you out to watch yet another boring dialogue with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ animations, before the game finally "begins", giving you ANOTHER 10 MINUTES DIALOGUE about big surprise: another chiché:
Randal's monday reminds me of Johnny Rocketfingers, a flash game I played years ago, which had a similar structure, but was extremely better written. It feels cheap and rushed in every single aspect, from the drawings to the animations, from the dialogues, to the pop references. The game sounds are terrible, from loud steps and gulps and BINGS when your mouse cursor hovers elements in the menu. The soundtrack seems mostly ok, even though it seems taken from a compilation of royalty free generic music.
In sum, if you want to play a funny, well made, deep, smart point and click adventure that you will carry in your heart for years to come, go and play
. They even put all 3 chapters in a single very reasonably priced package. And the sequel is pretty good, too, even though it's still pretty expensive.

I cannot recommend this game, Randal's Monday. The game has a very nice Groundhog vibe to it with time span (that's not often done in video games), but it has very bad humour and references, and the gameplay is quite poor.
The game has the plot of Randal (the character you control) stealing a ring from his friend and repeating the same day over and over again, each day his friend dies in a different way. I always liked this concept in movies, as it can be quite interesting, and in video games it is a whole nother story. This concept has not been explored in a hell've a lot of video games (surprisingly enough, as it would be useful for using a minimal amount of sprites and characters), thus this is a new and refreshing thing in games. This feature is actually what originally drew me to the game in the first place.
The humour in this game is very, very bad, and so are the references. There are a ton of references, and at first the first two or three references you see are nice and funny, but after the hundreth one you sort of get sick of it, the game eventually gives off the feeling that it's trying WAYYY too hard. The humour at best is weak and at worse is offensive. There are homophobic jokes, and transphobic jokes. As well as a lot of suicide jokes, violent jokes in general, body shaming, sexist jokes, etc. It's essentially Deponia's humour on steriods. A few little violent or offensive jokes aren't great, but they are forgivable, but when they resort to implying that not only trans people are mentally ill, but gay people also, you sort of see a problem. The point of a game like this is humour, and if said humour is not funny, they aren't doing their job properly, this game would not exactly be played for it's plot anyway.
Randal's Monday is also plagued by really poor gameplay. Not only is it really annoying to activate the inventory, but travelling anywhere becomes a hassle. Puzzles in point and click games are supposed to not really make all that much sense, and help you think outside of the box, but this game takes that to a new level, there have been many times in the game when I have had really good stuff in my inventory, but none of it is anything I need, even if it seems I can use it.... Some of the diaogue puzzles seem to need you to be able to tell the future to solve them, or just read a walkthrough.... RTS for grown-ups is how I would summarize it.
I bought this game when it came out, a few years ago, and it was interesting as an asymmetric multiplayer base attack and defense game.
Still has that, but wow they added quite a lot of other stuff.
Campaign for each of 3 factions, through early, mid, and late war. You build your army by collecting units after winning battles, and they keep their experience and level up over time, getting a little bit better.
A skirmish mode against AI that is fairly challenging, but only a capture the flag control point type setup currently - no to the last man kind of battles, but it works well and keeps the games from getting too long and drawn out in this style. Boris is pretty good, can pop up with some surprises and a bear on harder difficulty.
Multiplayer custom games, which I don't play, so don't have anything to say about the experience.
So much to do in this, you can get lost with which to work on. Setting up base defenses, each unique for the 3 war periods, so 9 total if you hit tier 3 for each faction. Replaying the campaign missions to hit all the accomplishments, or just grinding for better war gear and legendary units you are missing.
Etc...
This game could easily keep you entertained for 500+ hours, assuming you are looking  for this kind of rts. Hopefully more people are and will wander in here and find this gem of a game, and play it long enough to see what it has to offer.
Great job devs, I'd love to see some  modding support to add custom missions and stuff like that, but man I'm already over 100 hours and still messing with things that I haven't touched yet. RTS done well, they took many creative design ideas and stuck 'em out there. I for one appreciate that alone and am really enjoying the game!

So Blitzkrieg 3 is in my opinion a WW2 light RTS game. The multiplayer is a carbon copy of Quest for epic loot with a WW2 theme. You dont actually fight online opponents. You build upp a base with defences and raid other players bases to get more resources and upgrade your base.
During these raids the opponents base is controlled by an AI same goes for your base when invaded. If you are into that its ok. But dont expect VS multiplayer couse there is none yet.
My biggest gripe at the moment is lack off control of your units, by that i mean you cant tell your tanks which way to face and you cant give your infantry units orders like throw granades, run, or take cover.. Your units do this bythemselves hence why i call it a light RTS game.
The graphics are Ok. The sound's are mediocer at best, machine guns sound more like pee shooters instead of machineguns. It has destructible environments but nothing compared to CoH2. Unit movement and behaviour is not very realistic. Tanks move and turn way to quick instead of feeling like lumbering metal beasts.
If you want a more standard WW" RTS i would reccomend CoH2 instead. Better audio, visual, and better control of youre units as well as a better singelplayer.
If you are more intrested in deep historic WW2 RTS game with maximum realism i would instead reccommend the Men of War series.
They have time to improve it since its early access but for now its a shallow RTS light game and i would pass..

Very reminiscent of Castle Crashers. Foul Play is a side scroller beat ’em up from Mediatonic and Devolver Digital. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
The artwork is great. The characters, the enemies, even the environments. Everything, right down to the smallest detail, was wonderfully well done.
The game has a campaign with a decent length. It’s not too long and it’s not too short.
There is a pretty sizable amount of enemy variety. This is always a good thing as punching the same thing in the face repeatedly can grow monotonous. Having a variety of things to punch in the face repeatedly is much better. After all, variety is the spice of life (or, in this case, variety is the spice of face punching).
If you’re like me, you hate desert themed levels in games with every fiber of your being. Foul Play gets their desert level out of the way first thing. The rest of the game has much less aggravating environments.
The characters’ dialogue is quite entertaining. It’s always nice to have some comic relief amongst the thronging hordes of enemies.
The block feature is, easily, the best feature. Not only can you block enemy melee attacks, you can also block projectiles, and send them straight back at the fool who sent it your way. Simply amazing.
The Bad
I don’t really have anything for this category. Foul Play is genuinely enjoyable.
The Meh
I felt like enemies were really hard to put down, where as the player character is relatively squishy. Maybe that’s just me, but I don’t know.
As far as equipment customization goes, Foul Play doesn’t bring a whole lot to the table.
Verdict: Yea
As I stated above, Foul Play is genuinely enjoyable. If you liked Castle Crashers or if you like games of that nature, you’ll definitely like this one. If you’ve been looking for something new, go check out FP in the Steam Store. As always, thanks for reading.

This is a simple game, that I enjoy a lot.
The first few dungeons are easy enough, you'll find some loot and learn the basic game mechanics.
At first you just have to tell raid members what to do. Healers heal, tanks tank, dps do damage.
Then you get a bit of micromanagement to do.
Sometimes raidmembers switch roles and you need to yell at them.
Somtimes raidmembers stand in fire and you need at them.
Sometimes the melee walk into the backline and you need to yell at them.
Sometimes the tank gets low and you need to yell at the healers to keep them up (which works, unlike in World of Warcraft).
Maybe a fight is too rough, so you go back to an older dungeon to gear up.
Later the fights get complexer. You'll need to pay attention to mechanics and macro manage your raid as well as micro manage your raid at the same time.
I find it enjoyable and considering it's price tag I'd recomend waiting for a sale.

The game is wordless right down to the menus, which doesn't make it all that intuitive at times. In fact when I first launched the game I accidentally exited whilst I was trying to navigate the menu, which didn't auger all that well. Then when I actually managed to start the game the first 'puzzle' was one where there are multiple buttons to choose from as to what to press, but then it turned out that none of these selections had any actual impact on the outcome of the scene so trying to work out the correct answer was just a waste of time. It also took me a while to work out that all the navigation in the game is done via thought/speech bubbles and any clicking on the rest of the screen just results in cosmetic effects.
The game is pretty linear and none of the choices you make will affect your ability to make it to the end. There are no real puzzles to solve and there are a limited amount of interactions available to you at any one time (sometimes there's even only one action to choose from). That said there is
exploration to be had along the way, but it's very easy to keep heading straight towards the end and miss things. Out of the eight total achievements possible six of them are missable and I managed to miss each and every one of those six.

I wouldn't say I regret playing it but at the same time I'm not sure how strongly I feel about recommending it to anyone. One thing to take into account is that it appears the game used to be Free-to-play but that doesn't seem to be the case any more, so any older reviews won't take into account the fact that it's no longer free.
I think there is something to enjoy here in terms of aesthetics and story, and I would rate it ambivalently, but seeing as I can only choose between making a positive review and a negative one... I think I'll go with a thumbs down on this.

(Adventure-lite/FROG)
Options are basic, with separate sliders for music and sound, cursor choice, and full-screen/windowed, and with four difficulty levels.  Tutorial is optional, though disabled if you are playing on the hardest difficulty.
Cutscenes are skippable, and are all live-action.  The music is pretty, and the acting is OK, though the English voice overs are nearly cringe-worthy.  The game does a very nice job of integrating the live actors into the game itself by using a graphic effect to make them more suited to the environment.  Definite kudos for that!  The graphics in general are very nice!
There is a rechargeable hint button and a task button to help you keep track of what you should be doing, but no journal.  On the puzzle scenes, there is also a button you can click on to get instructions.  Speaking of the mini-games, most of the sites I went to have a screen of the pearl puzzle.  Be aware that this particular puzzle is fiddly!  The pearls can take several tries to place, even if you're placing them correctly.  As long as you're following the instructions, keep trying!
Gameplay itself is primarily adventure-lite with some interactive FRagmented Object scenes, which are NOT repeated (unlike most hidden object games, who seem to recycle the scenes at least once.)  We have a scary-cute cat as a helper, and inventory items can be combined.
A pet peeve of mine is when we're expected to do things that make absolutely no sense, are dangerous, and/or defy the laws of physics.  Well,
does have us doing some nonsensical things, but because of the story line, they are not only forgiven, but expected... We ARE talking about dreams, after all!
I was pleasantly surprised to find that the story did not go in the direction that I expected... After all, predictable is boring!
- Bonus chapter (took me about 45 minutes)
- Wallpapers
- Concept art
- Puzzles (all 18 from the game can be replayed here)
- Achievements (only a couple that you'll have to work for -- the rest come from game progression)
Overall
took me about four hours to complete, and was a nice change up from action games I've been playing lately.  Definitely a good one for the casual game-lovers!

Reason being it seems like the best way to play it is get the runner gunner and the infinite ammo when your under 20hp blessings and just mow everything down with ether an uzi or an ak47 and pretty much become a glass cannon.

Look at my time played. I have enjoyed every hour I've spent on this game.
The developer is great about listening to the community, fixing bugs as they're found in a timely manner.
I STRONGLY RECOMMEND not reading a guide before playing, since a major part of the gameplay is figuring out each boss' mechanics on your own.
Essentially, IAW is a puzzle with multiple solutions. Which raiders you recruit, your group's class spread, balancing loot distribution, everything plays a part in your success, and there isn't a single 'right' answer. Do you take two rogues for higher damage, but knowing morale might suffer from loot disputes? Do you take two wizards, knowing they'll deal high damage, but have trouble swapping targets? Do you take a bard for the buffs or replace them with a different class?
I've played through the game with a lot of different spreads. Once with three warriors, once with only one, sometimes I take a bard, sometimes I don't. Once I took two druids, even. It's all about figuring out how the group will interact and doing what you can to keep things balanced.
Plus the humor is great. It's amusing even if you don't get the references, but is pretty great if you do.
So microwave a burrito, turn on voice chat and grab the rum: It's time to go raiding.

At first glimpse, nothing seems to actually stand out with this game. In its essence,
is a fragmented object game - or a FRAG as called by the veterans of the hidden object genre. Pretty interface, expected gameplay, a selection of puzzles... But its beauty in execution and thematic nuances centering the notion of dream; and a hopeless pursuit of love, hiding a heartbreaking truth that separates itself from the rest of its genre formidably in means of display, makes
a memorable experience.
As an interesting choice, we take the role of a male protagonist - which is quite uncommon in HOG genre to begin with. Ben has lost his dear wife, Elizabeth in a car accident some time ago. Since that dreadful day, he is getting haunted by the apparition of his wife in dreams. Elizabeth is calling for him, leading him to an obscure discovery through uncanny geography of their history. Desperate to reach his dear wife, to hold her hand once more, Ben takes on this strange journey, persistent to reach her with any means possible. A nameless, smiling cat accompanies him in this journey, leading him through bizarre environments and dangerous obstacles in each new dream. Can Ben reach his dear wife at the end?
With these kind of games, we are accustomed to encountering digitally rendered art work and animations for characters. Here though, the dream world and the real world are sharply separated from each other in means of display. Enacted characters and their interactions are presented in FMV cinematics in the real world, while dreamlike environments and gameplay sequences are arranged into digital art works. This way, the story presents a medium for you to emphasize with the character, making all nuances a bit more touching. I personally think the acting is quite decent, yet voice acting isn't that marvelous or emotional at all. There is a certain stiffness and a lack of theatrical enthusiasm in voices that wrecks the emotional quality. Dream environments are most certainly beautiful and fittingly uncanny with sorrowful, elegant and symbolic displays of memory streams.
For the gameplay, there is not much to talk about. You collect items, combine some, use them in the appropriate places and carry on with the story - with one difference of a dream companion. Selecting a cat as a dream travelling guide is a beautiful nuance borrowed from Egyptian mythology and well appropriate for the undertone of the whole story. You are given 10 FRAG scenes in which you'll eventually collect different items and 20 or so puzzles, which are not that hard to deal with anyhow. In 9 chapters - with each of them having a central theme with 3-4 places - you'll come to the end of your journey and the bonus adventure in 3 hours or so.
I suggest considering this beauty on a sale. If you like the HOG genre, it's one of the better ones out there which doesn't come from big name developers. Enjoy!

is a surreal hidden item game about a man trying to find his wife. The story is rich,engaging and heartfelt with voice acting and full  motion video cutscenes. Everything in this game blends together to create an experience that can be easily played in one sitting as you may find it hard to pull yourself away. This title is a beautiful piece of work and a prime example of how video games can be more than just games, and can also be great vehicles for storytelling.
On its surface the story is simple:  You are Ben, a man who believes his wife to be dead. Suddenly in a dream you see her again and begin your pursuit to be reunited. Through this journey we learn more about Ben, his wife and the love that they share. The game shifts from the enigmatic dream world to what seems to be the real world causing one to wonder what is actually real and what Ben is only imagining. The story is touching and sweet but also mysterious with its fair share of twists and turns. I won’t go into too much detail about the game's story but I will say that you should prepare to be very entertained.
The game plays as your standard point and click adventure. You click on items to interact with them and collect items when need be, some of these items can be combined to make a new item for you to use which is a feature I enjoy. You move between areas trying to advance and overcome obstacles. The game is filled with puzzles to be solved, a bit too many for my personal taste. There are also hidden item scenes, which I prefer, that entail finding pieces of items to create new items, which are then used to progress in the scene- so it’s still a little puzzle. You are aided by a cat that helps you reach places you normally cannot so bonus points from me right there. The game can be played on four different difficulties which do not affect any achievements.
Along with a great story and solid gameplay,
also offers beautiful artwork and FMV cutscenes. The artwork in the game is well done and invokes the dream-like mystique of the story. Nice colors and items that aren’t hard to find if you have bad eyes make for a pleasant experience. The FMVs in the game help move the story along, and the two actors portraying Ben and his wife tug silently at your heartstrings. There is also voice acting but not by the same actors in the cut scenes. The voice acting is pretty good with only a few awkward moments in the reading.The game also has a lovely musical score.
+ Offers a good amount of gameplay for the price.
+ Overall presentation is satisfying..
+ Story is wonderful as is the acting and audio.
+ There is a cat.
+ It has trading cards and achievements.
- Personally I would have enjoyed more hidden object scenes instead of puzzles.
- I felt there could have been a bit more direction on what to do next in the game.
I found the game to be nearly perfect!  I may just be nitpicking, so what annoys me may not annoy you. If you’re a fan of the hidden object genre then this is a must-have in your library, no hesitation. If you’re new to these types of games or not usually a fan of them, this game may change your mind- or at the very least offer a great experience you may not have expected. Video games can be a fantastic medium for storytelling,
tells a beautiful and relatable tale that is worth the money.
9/10

If it was the only game on the planet, it might be alright. Compared with an actually well-made game like Orcs Must Die 2, though, it's almost embarassing.
Want to pick your own loadout? Well too bad, the first slot is static.
Want to try a weapon out before the monsters start coming? Too bad, you can't. Would've been nice to be able to plant bombs or rocket jump somewhere BEFORE the wave starts, but oh well.
Like a weapon with punch to it? Too bad, even the grenade launcher takes multiple hits to stop weak enemies. The towers are worse since you can only afford one or two per wave and most if not all of them are worthless.
Want to upgrade your weapons and towers to be less useless? Can't do it. Towers can only be boosted in the current level during build phases (never in battle, which is something OMD2 lets you do), and weapons can't be boosted at all.
Want to know what your health is? Too bad, no health bar.
Do you hate waiting? Too bad. The initial game menu, level select, equipment select, and even the actual start of the level, all come with loading screens.
Do you sometimes have to stop playing to do human things, like eat or answer a phone? Too bad, there's no pause button, even on singe-player. The escape key only brings up a menu.
Worst of all, the action in the game feels stilted, awkward, and under-developed compared to the smooth, responsive combat of OMD2.
As for bugs, OMD2 had plenty, but at least none of them caused a crash to desktop. This happened my first time playing. Really nice first impression.
Overall, they just got so much wrong that it's hard to like this game. Again, if it was the only game I'd ever played, I might like it. But since I know other devs have done the same but much, much better, this is nothing but sheer disappointment.

This game is strange in a few aspects.
First, it doesn't tell you anything (or, if it does, hides it quite well). A few examples: Apparently I've completed 63% of the first zone, after finishing it. The completionist I am, I would now like to get 100% completion there. But I don't know how, because the game doesn't tell me how completion is achieved, though I assume by finishing the levels without damage to the core. However, there is no indicator in which level I have how much progression.
Another example is the interface in levels. In this kind of game you will have quite a full interface, and I found the map being very well done. However, there seems to be no information to the player's health. The next wave is announced by presenting the icons of the enemies approaching, paired with how many will appear. As someone who just started this game, this doesn't tell me anything ("Oh, these are fliers..." or "Oh, those things have a ranged attack..."). It is propably enough if you know the game well, but the enemy design is not distinguished enough to make this easy.
The second thing really bothering me is the shooting, which is just not fun for me. When you empty the magazine of one weapon and switch to your secondary, the game automatically reloads (after some time) the first weapon. This leads to situations where you would usually only use one weapon (e.g. if you want splash damage, which only one of your weapons has), but it's more effective to empty the magazine of one weapon, switch weapons, empty magazine, switch, and so on. This is quite dull and unsatisfying.
These are the main reasons why I just can not recommend Sanctum 2. The first things mentioned are just things I expect from a tower defense game to be any good, the second point is something which totally spoils the action part for me.
The game has some really nice aspects, for example the choice of four different characters, which play quite differently, a nice selection of towers, secondary weapons, and perks giving you advantages/disadvantages. I think you get these things too fast, which hinders motivation a bit and takes away the possibility to use all the new things you have obtained, as in the beginning you are rewarded with too many to try them all out. The progression is a bit off here. The game also is not too easy (which is positive, I have to add), you need to build a decent maze to survive. However you are quite limited, as you can only build on certain parts of the map. A positive point I found: You have two patches of ressources, bases and money. You use bases to build the maze, and money for the actual towers, sitting on top of the bases. Therefore you don't have to compromise between having a nice maze and having decent firepower, which is a great concept.
My direct comparison for this game are the Orcs must die-games, and those do most of the stuff in this game better. You don't build mazes in Orcs must die and have no shooter-aspect, but everything else is done equally good or better in my opinion; even the combat is more enjoyable there. If you don't mind the things I mentioned above and prefer the FPS-Shooter elements to Third-person action, give Sanctum 2 a try; otherwise avoid this and maybe think about getting Orcs must die, if you haven't already.

The Last Dream is a fragmented object game where gameplay takes a secondary role to make room for the beautifully rendered scenery and a strange, eerie atmosphere, tied to a story of a husband who chases the ghost of his wife through his dreams.
Technically, The Last Dream can be classified as a fragmented object title. In practise though, it has only ten fragmented scenes and roughly twice as many puzzles with a difficulty rating of almost zero (except if the player chooses expert mode for the first play through).
The main content is the story about a man who cannot shake the feeling that his dreams about the ghost of his wife mean something, so we follow him through nine scenes, each about 3-5 screen and 10-20 minute long. This kind of setup quickly eliminates any backtracking or chances to get lost, but it also severs any ties the players might have towards the game. Simply put, most scenes feel empty, lifeless.
This stands in stark contrast with the live-action story segments, which set an excellent mood and help us immerse ourselves in this story and make sure that anyone who buys this game won’t regret their decision.

I honestly really like this game, which makes me a bit sad to see most of the helpful reviews are the negative ones. I mean yes, the negative reviews are almost always correct with issues like optimization, constant crashes, and a hard difficulty curve and grind one has to do to overcome it. But I would still definitely give this game a recomendation, as this is possibly one of the most fun games I've played in a while.
To put it simply, Trove is like if Minecraft and CubeWorld had a child. It has the amazing combat system that CubeWorld had (Albeit, far less unbalanced, as CubeWorld's balancing was borderline unforgiving,) and the creativity perks of Minecraft, with a portable home (Or Cornerstone, as it's called) that can be pretty much anything you set your mind to. And it works amazingly as a game, I've spent countless hours both creating bases and exploring the worlds, fighting monsters.
The main gameplay mechanics are dungeon crawling and building your base. Dungeon crawling gives you loot, which can help you get both stronger and more stuff to customize with. There are numerous biomes, all very unique and fun to explore (My personal favorites being Candoria and the Fae Wilds,) and there's even a mining mechanic with different ores and even recipes you can find.
There are also numerous classes to play as, with different playstyles and strategies to play around with. They're all very easy to get used to, and very creative in some regards as well. You're limited to picking a limited number as a starter, but as you go along, you'll be able to unlock the others, either by gathering the material, earning class tokens, or if you really want to, buying them with real money.
The game also features a chat system you switch between. In fact, it has a chat where literally everyone can see, no matter what world they're on, which is extremely useful for both finding/selling gear, and asking for help or likewise giving help. However, it does have its share of spambots and elitists, but with every positive, there is a negative.
And storywise, you won't experience anything in game as of writing that contains a story. The opening cinematic is as much story as I've been able to find, and it makes me sad, since it does have a premise of being interesting. The idea is that the worlds you explored are shattered remains of a once glorious realm, having been broken apart to save the people from the wrath of the Moon Goddess, seeking to destroy the world in envy for her sister, the Sun Goddess, and her creation.
However, as much as I love the game, there are some pretty nasty issues to address. One is the extremely unstable nature of the servers. They crash EXTREMELY often, especially on the Dinosaur biomes. If they aren't crashing though, prepare for rubber-banding or delays with lag. The fact the servers are this unstable despite being a game with what I presume to be a steady playbase and income is very upsetting.
Two, it is quite pay encouraging in the later game. While it is possible to go with the game without paying, it's VERY slow and grind-filled unless you dish out some cash. It does seem to have gone down a more player-friendly slope recently, especially with the ability to craft classes now, but it's a very long grind.
And third, after a while, you may find it simply hard to continue. While the combat is fun and the dungeons are very creative, you'll eventually see it all and find no real encouragement to play. They have added some variant versions of the hourly challenges, and minigames seem to be on their way, so hopefully this may be resolved soon to encourge more people to play longer.
Overall, yes, the game has a plethora of problems. But even with it, the game's creativity and addictive nature has left me with hours of enjoyment, and one I would recommend to at least try out.

The Last Dream: Developer's Edition is a relaxing point and click adventure that follows closely all the characteristics of a HOG game; however it excels through several original elements that make it distinguish itself from the other games of this genre.
The first original element of the game is the protagonist - which in this case is not a woman, but a young man, Ben. After a tragic accident, the spirit of Ben's wife starts materializing in his dreams, appearing to call him and asking him to follow her. Therefore, Ben sets himself on the adventure to find the source of this mysterious call. The story develops itself around the Dream world that alternates with scenes from the Real world. And this is where the originality of the game kicks in - instead of having digitally designed cut scenes, the Real world is depicted through live action cut-scenes, with people playing the characters of Ben and his wife Elizabeth. The contrast between this beautifully painted Dream world and the acting snippets from the Real world adds even more immersion of the story, which is already emotionally packed. The main motif seems to be the classical "save the loved one" theme, although in this particular case, the story has much more depth, culminating with a plot twist and an intense ending. To me, finding out midway through the game that the actors that gave life to these characters are actually two of the game's developers (which got married afterwards) made me feel even closer to this game and enhanced the experience of playing it even more.
The classic HOG scenes have been replaced by FROG scenes (fragmented hidden object scenes in which you gather multiple object fragments in order to construct an item that will be used further to unlock other puzzles). The puzzles are also original and in general of moderate difficulty. And there's also a little cat helper that adds to the enjoyment of playing the game. Collectibles are also present, and they come in two categories - cat toys that provide funny cat animations and real pictures of the Ben - Elizabeth couple, all of these being not extremely difficult to find for a player that invests a bit of his attention into the details.
Overall, I enjoyed The Last Dream: Developer's Edition a lot and I would recommend it to all the HOG lovers out there - it provides a unique experience through the live-action cut scenes and the profound story centered around the deep-rooted idea of "love conquers all barriers".

Releases such as The Last Dream, should not get lost in the amazing mire of games that are produced in each year.....and I for one, am hoping that word of mouth gets out about this unique game.  It might fit the category of 'Casual Gaming; but the term Story Driven might be a better category for it.....because it is the story that MAKES one want to complete the game and help this man get to his wife.
There is an emotional content that is in the game, that really doesn't exist in most Casual Games where a "lost" significant other meme is a regular theme of the games.  You genuinely FEEL for the man and his quest….and the whole tenor of the game, juxtaposing cinematics that drive the story and sequences of game play that also alternate between very plausibly real to “What the Heck is going on Here?”
I for one, really thought that juxtaposition was part of the theme that kept me guessing what was going on….until the end.
It is supported by good art work and by mini-games that are quite challenging.  (thank heavens for the video walkthroughs!).  The "FROGS" that are a part of the gameplay, really don't feel as if I am playing a FROG or Hidden Object puzzle, and I didn't find myself sighing at the thought of searching the landscape for the objects that were needed, I just simply 'got to work' to help this man in his quest….and many of the mini-games were thankfully, quite solvable with a little work.
The art work gave us hidden clues that he was not searching in the real physical world....and gave us some unique problems, like how to stop a killer lawnmower or a garden hose, that suddenly take on life of their own.  There is a Helper Cat and I hope that people who object to such Helpers won't skip this game because of the existence of the cat.  She is obviously a construct of another world, from the first moment she speaks to the man....but, is far from cute....and not used very often....but, if anyone playing the game, is owned by a cat, the looks and behavior of it, will be quite recognizable…and, the main point, is that anyone who simply objected to playing a game BECAUSE of the inclusion of a “helper” would be missing out on what is a unique gaming experience.
The game kept up a juxtaposition between places and tasks, you would find in the real world and places that were obviously in a Surreal Zone that kept me asking "What is going on here?" and the cat, was simply another element of that not quite real....that sometimes became “Whoa…what has this guy been smoking?” sorts of scenes.
A clue to how interesting this game is?  I decided to replay it to get some awards I missed, and I have not been bored for one moment, even though I know now, what the end will be.

One Eyed Kutkh is a brief and abstract fairy tale. The vivid colours, soothing background music and cute voice acting add up to a beautiful game suitable for children. The art comes close to the mod psychedelic style of the 60s and 70s and feels unspent. Progression is slow-paced and the length of the animations require the player to be patient, which could be challenging for toddlers to endure. At best it's a lesson in patience.
The gameplay is broken down to the very basics of the point and click format. Clicking on signs, dragging pieces together and the rest is interpretation. With regards to that, One Eyed Kutkh is also completely devoid of script and identifiable spoken language, relying only on semiotics. The integration of language through signs can be confusing at first since menu and communication options are often ambiguous. It's funny how dumbfounded a player can be when confronted with easier and arguably more intuitive controls than what is standard.
Generally it seems as if One Eyed Kutkh was the result of an exercise in eidetic reduction, which works out well in this case. It's definitely a great game for children, adults may lose interest quickly though.

I haven't played this game in a long time. But, for the time that I did, I really enjoyed it. The experience was especially fresh for me the second time I played around in the story; since the first time I had just the base game, and the second time I had the Season Pass, gifted generously to me by a friend. Nuka-World and Far Harbor were, in my opinion, pretty great. They were two new areas that I personally really enjoyed; such as the diverse, yet stereotypical raider factions in Nuka-World, and the landscape of Far Harbor. Two completely unique areas -- done right.
Now, I'm not down-rating this because I think Fallout 4 is bad. Not by any means, which is strange for me, because I preferred an approach that was taken by Obsidian a while ago with Fallout: New Vegas. Story-oriented, good character building, diverse NPCs, and a live wasteland with creatures to stumble across all the time, like navigating the world map in Fallout 1 or 2, if you did a 'no fast-travel' run or something of the like. Fallout 4's gun mechanics, in my opinion, are great. Although it had little to no story, it was enough for me to fill in the blanks for when I didn't focus on the main story. It's not a 'traditional' roleplaying game, per se, even though it's very shooter-based. It's more of a pseudo-RPG, with many holes being left to fill for the player -- but that's about it.
Regardless: onto why I'm downvoting this. Todd Howard's curse of 'BuySkyrimBuySkyrimBuySkyrimBuySkyrim' has hit Fallout 4 hard... in the form of microtransactions. Yes, the thing everyone hates, because it interferes with the game so much. I hate them myself, especially when they're pushed in my face like: "hey buy this thing to do this thing!!!" I personally despised Bethesda's marketing of Creation Club. Yes, the club no one wants to seriously be a part of -- at least, if they're sane in the you-know-where. I hate Creation Club with a passion, even though I haven't played any of the games lately that have it (I think you can guess why) but many people have reported problems, and just outright hate. What I hate the most about this is Bethesda has tried this before, got shot down by the community, and is /still/ doing it. In fact, many of these mods are on the Nexus (not like you can download mods anymore because of Creation Club) and are, in many cases, better than their CC counterparts.
tl;dr: don't support paid mods, Bethesda is scummy, game is ok otherwise

Current Playtime: 68 hours.
The most recent entry to the Fallout franchise as of 2017, and at the same time one of the worst according to a lot of people. To me - a first time player of the series - the game made a very mediocre impression at best. While I really wanted to enjoy the game to get my fun out of the money, I really can't say it was that fun overall.
The setting is usual for the Fallout Franchise; Taking place in post-apocalyptic America, this time in Boston/Massachusetts. While the setting is great and still fresh, the game makes it really hard to enjoy the world and it's narrative, the latter not being very complex to begin with. It feels dumbed down, and as a lot of veterans to the series will tell you, the roleplaying elements of Fallout 4 are almost gone or vague to the point of taking away the player's control to predict what your character will say when you choose a dialogue option.
Another stone in the pathway is the poor optimization on PC. When first running the game, I had problems keeping the game at 20 FPS. Used some optimization fixes, and even then it never got me above 60 FPS. And that's sad considering that my PC can run Overwatch on Medium settings, but not Fallout 4 on lowest settings!
Speaking of the game's technical problems, the performance isn't the only thing that might bother people. Animations look extremely stiff as well, and that wouldn't even be that much of a problem if the questlines and dialogues were as varied and complex as in New Vegas, but they aren't. As mentioned above, the new dialogue system alongside vague dialogue options pretty much kill off the roleplaying aspect.
Another thing that kind of kills the roleplaying aspect is the fact that your choices do not matter, if you get choices at all, and that you cannot decide what kind of character you want to be. Even if you don't want to, your character will have goals and motivations that the story will progress towards, although you may not care about it at all, therefore taking away your ability to roleplay the way you want like you could in previous games.
And last but not least; The combat gameplay. The guns are extremely generic. Out of my head, I can only remember seeing less than 15 gun types in the entirety of the game so far, excluding special reward guns that can only be found once. So even the gunplay can't make up for it, especially because most guns feel like you are stinging your enemy at best.

Jawbone's 6-Point Review:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1.--Front Page BS: Don't watch the first trailer, it spoils almost every single "Unexpected plot twist." They never said they would be good, so no BS there.
2.--Characters: The voice acting is great. The characters themselves are unlikable and have spots of being poorly written. However, it is amusing to watch a jackass being a jackass to another jackass.
3.--Lots of humor and references?: The claims are legits. They ignored quality and had to bend space to shoehorn in as many references and joke attempts as they did, but they're there.
4.--Difficulty: Hard, for all the wrong reasons. Please don't be a tough guy like me and try to beat this without a walkthrough/hints. You're only hurting yourself.
5.--The ride: Wonderful at first. The puzzles slowly began to bog down everything as they got increasingly illogical, the repeatable environments got stale and fast travel didn't help much because of how secular some places were, and the overall mirth and good humor just plummited. I also figured out too late that "Unexpected twists" meant "**** it, I don't have any better ideas."
6.--Impression: I'll remember the game for 3 things. Pace killing puzzles, feeling let down at the end, and how Jason Mewes (Yes, he voiced Jay in this game) is exceedingly cringeworthy without Kevin Smith's creative input.

STREET FIGHTER V IS AN EXCELLENT BETA EXPERIENCE:
I don't want to be too hard on Capcom and the game because they are trying.  But, there are glaring mistakes and oversights that hamstring the game, and by extension its community. Just about every review that is critical of the game has mentioned that the fighting in the game is fun.  I agree with this wholeheartely.  Going from this game back to Street Fighter IV the controls feel slow and unresponsive by comparison.   The flaws need to be called out though, especially since this game is still "very much in development".  Problems wont be fixed unless they are voiced.
MATCHES TAKE TOO LONG TO FIRE:
This one is obvious and not really up for debate.  You can find a match in Street fighter IV much quicker, even with its player base on life support.
Searching for ranked matches from the main menu leaves you with nothing to really do until the match fires, which can include several failed attemps which is mildy irritating.  As an alternative you can search while in training mode.  This allows you to get some practice in while you wait, but the loading screen each time you enter training mode is too long.  You end up spending a healthy chunk of your playing time not playing the game.
Player lobby listings sometimes show invalid lobbies that you can not join when you search.
If a player disconnects for whatever reason mid-match, you get kicked out of the battle mode that you were in and have to reset (more on rage quits later).
RANKED PLAY DOESN'T DO ITS JOB
I will give Capcom credit for adding "best of three" functionality to the game.  They need to go one step further and make all ranked matches "best of three".  Why?  A multitude of reasons.  First of all, it will allow you to spend more playing the game and less time waiting for loading screens.  Secondly, best of three is pretty much standard in tournament play.  If you do what Capcom wants you to do, and participate in tournaments and try to make the Pro Tour, you need to be able to beat your opponent in a best of three match.  Lastly, I'll point out that simply giving players an option at the end of the first game, just creates an awkward meta-game where player can choose based on "what will give me the best chance to earn points" rather than, "we are going to have a real match".
Speaking of earning points, the number you lose when facing an opponent of a lower rank and losing is very taxing.  Don't get me wrong, it makes sense that you should lose more, however when you win, you shouldn't be earning a pittance.  The risk/reward for fighting lower ranked players incentivizes skilled players to dodge and/or rage quit, which isn't healthy for this game if it is to succeed.  We are seeing the best players create secondary accounts to avoid this dilemma.  There's nothing inhernently wrong with having more than one account though, it's just unfortunate when players feel forced to do so to preserve their rank when they wish to play a different character. The PP/BP system from Street Fighter IV wasn't the best, but it was easier to understand, and avoided *some* of the present issues.
Rage Quitters are going to rage quit.  I have quit before.  I will quit in the first round if the connection is horrible.  I've had to do that about a dozen times since the game launched.  The game has also crashed about a dozen times mid-match.  Capcom told players that they were working on the issue, but that in the meantime, players should submit recordings to RQ matches to them.  That was a horrible solution in my opinion, if you can call it a solution at all.  RQing essentially steals points from players who would have otherwise won, and creates this meta-game if the player you are beating is ranked higher than you.  Without a real solution/penalty for quitting, ranked really doesn't mean anything.  Asking the player base to police themselves by sumbitting video is obnoxious.  I've got tons of video footage of my matches that I look at to try to get better, and people RQ in many of them.  I'm not going to put people on blast on youtube just to *attempt* to back at them.  You don't get the points back for that W anyway.   I honeslty don't know why Capcom allowed this to be such a big deal in this game when Street Fighter IV handled it adequately.  Show a player's disconnect percentage.  Even if accidental disconnects were included the real rage quitters would be obvious to everyone.  Then just allow us to opt out of matches with people who have a certain disconnect threshold.  Problem solved.
CAPCOM SPENT RESOURCES ON FEATURES THAT DON'T MATTER
Survival Mode would have been a nice feature to have in the game provided the game was already feature complete.  As it stands it leaves a lot of people scratching their heads as it's not particularly enjoyable.  Most players only play the mode when trying to unlock colors, which really could have been unlocked through achieving more worthwile milestones.
Immediately after arriving at the main menu, you are reminded of how poor the user interface is. The heatmap is fine as a backdrop, but it doesn't hold any information that players care about.  What we might care about instead is information about the game, such as the next character release date, patch notes, etc.  Or if Capcom wants to really be ambitious, information about the next Capcom sponsored tournament/results from the previous tournament.  I don't think these are necessary, but I'm listing them as examples that would be far more useful than what is there.  I'm sure others could figure out better usage of that space as well.
Player profiles serve almost zero fucntion at present, other than a way to look at other players past matches.  Attack data isn't tracked at the moment, and though it looks like it will be in the future, I'm not sure how much that will improve the game experience if at all.
The Shop, by Capcom's own admission is a work in progress.  The timetable for in-game purchases with "Zeny" had to be pushed back.  While purchasing items with "fight money" is a cool idea, the implementation falls short.  I don't know how much time/resources Capcom is sinking into getting the "Zeny" store to work, but it's not worth it as it's not an insignificant amout.  The in-game store isn't something that is going to add value to the game, and as it stands it's holding other improvements up.
THE GAME LACKS FEATURES THAT SHOULD BE STANDARD
Traning Mode is significantly improved when compared to Street Fighter IV.  It's easier to test out situations; wakeup, mixups, etc.  However, features such as frame data, and hitboxes should be in the game.  There's really no excuse for this.  And while you can find all of this information online, it sort of flys in the face of the whole "self contained platform" that Capcom had been promising.  They could still eventually make good on these features, don't get me wrong, but it's hard to be confident that they will given how far behind they are on so many other things.
There are a number of features that were present is Street Fighter IV that are just missing here.  Though Tournament mode wasn't something I used too often in SFIV it would have been nice to see it return and be improved in this game.  Ways to communicate with other players would have been a real boon for the game; even if the messages were pre-defined. "Hey good matches", or "Wake up DP much".  Voice Chat, where art thou?
I CAN'T RECOMMEND THE GAME NOW, EVEN THOUGH I ENJOY THE FIGHTING.  I'LL RECOMMEND IT DOWN THE ROAD
Once the character and game content gets closer to what Street Fighter IV offered, I will be able to recommend it to others.  As it stands the players who are invested in the Street Fighter franchise own the game already.  If this was someone's first fighting game, there are other franchises that I could suggest before SFV.

Below is my original review, unchanged from when I published it.  I wanted to write an update.  As of 6/27/2015, the devs are adding real PvP against real players.  While I admit in my review that it isn't my cup of tea, it was also why I felt some may not like this game.  The fact that they listened to those who wanted real PvP is awesome-sauce.  And I wanted to send a big kudos to the devs for continually making this game better.
============================================
The single player campaigns are similar to Blitzkrieg 2, albeit the RPG element of it is lacking in comparison to Blitzkrieg 2.
The multiplayer campaign can be explained very simply.  It is Clash of Clans...world war 2 style.
Before you say "Cool" or "No way!" (depending on how you feel about Clash of Clans).  There are some differences.
The main difference is no waiting.  You don't spend "gems" or some equivalent resource which can only be obtained with real money.  You build your army, you go to battle and then you battle again and again and again.
Your whole army gets wiped out?  No problem, they are immediately available for the next battle.  No waiting for buildings to finish, no waiting for troops to build.  If you can afford to build it, you get it immediately and it is always there.
So, in my opinion, it has the allure Clash of Clans has minus the moneygrabbing nonsense clash of clans has.
If I want to play Blitzkrieg 3, I can play for as long as I wish.  I don't have to worry about troops or waiting, it is quite refreshing.
The RPG element is similar to clash of clans.  You want that Panzer IV?  Well, you need to upgrade your tank depot...but before that, your HQ needs to upgrade.  In order to do that, you need 3000 fuel or 5000 supplies, etc.  The only way you get it is to raid other players.
On the other side, your base is something you need to defend.  There seems to be a variety of maps players can start off with.  (You don't get to choose) and each map has 3 or 4 ways to infiltrate your base.  Your defenses are limited and you need to place them strategically.
When you raid others, it is awesome when you hit someone who has the same map as you...then you can say, "Hey, why didn't I think of that?" and improve your own defenses.
My hours aren't that deep at the time of this review.  I can't comment too much on single player.  I've been having so much fun with  multiplayer.  It really is odd, because my library of games is single player only.
This game stole a bunch of ideas from Clash of Clans.  It is NOT Blitzkrieg 2 reskinned.  I'm concerned about long term playability and freshness of new maps, but it is not an issue at the moment and the devs are updating the game frequently.
How does this compare to Company of Heroes?  In my mind, it doesn't compare.  COH1 or COH2 are true RTS style games where you gather resources and build armies, and attack and replenish losses until one player out attritions the other.   In this game, you have a squad of tanks and infantry.  You attack another player and you both have a static number of troops.  The other player has static defenses which are managed by the AI.  (You never actually duel a live human, only the defenses set up by that person before they logged off)
For many, this lack of true multiplayer may be a turnoff.  I'm a self professed lover of single player games...it doesn't bother me at all.  This game is more of a puzzle than COH.  You have a limited number of troops and you are trying to outwit the defenses.
I can see some folks truly disliking this game.  I hope I explained it well enough so you can determine it for yourself.  I did compare to two very popular games and apologize if you have never played Clash of Clans or Company of Heroes and were unable to garnish anything from this review.
Happy hunting.

While my steam profile doesn't show much time played, I've sunk in around 60 hours pre-steam.
So you always wished that your raiding guild in WoW/EQ/EQ2/SWtoR/GW/GW2/Whatever really had less people you had to deal with, and left you more in control of loot/tactics/etc?  Well theres good news!
It's A Wipe is a tongue in cheek (and sometimes outlandishly silly) guild management/turn based strat game where you 'hire' the guildies of your dreams and tackle raid after raid.  Each stage divies up some epic gear (and your guildmates whine when they don't get the phat lewtz).
While the guild management side can get quite irritating, especially if guild moral drops too much due to a lack of progression or decent loot drops, the overall game feels pretty much like a real MMO's raiding, only without the whole subscription fee's, annoying raid time brackets, trash mobs, and other issues in said games previously mentioned.
Pros:
-You get to tailor your guild to your own play style
-Classes each have easy to understand mechanics
-Random chance AI causes interesting side effects in combat (can also be a con from time to time)
-Funny encounters, Pimping orcs?  Why the hell not?
-Stupidly low specs required to run said game
-Some replay value if you really really like achievements.  Like really like them.  Alot.
Cons:
-Classes can feel kinda blended
-AI could be better on wizards and clerics on which spell to cast at which time
-Healing order can sometimes glitch causing tanks to not get healed very well, thus a wipe
-Random events can sometimes cause important spells/abilities to not fire in a round.  While this is intended, and basicaly emulates idiots screwwing around in the source material, it's just as annoying here as it is in those games.
-Graphics could use a mild tuneup, but considering the overall cost, not to mention obviously small team... not an issue personally.
Would I recommend this game?  Hell yes, even with it's faults it's good for a laugh, and most of the game isn't too hard, just a nice slow grind up in gear/dungeon difficulty.
Pink Horde Rules.  That is all.

The Last Dream is a beautiful casual adventure / 'hidden object' game. 'Hidden object' here is quoted since the game does share a lot of elements with HOG games, but doesn't actually feature any Hidden Object puzzles! Instead, all puzzles are either of the inventory kind, or where you're presented with a limited list of items to find on a static screen and have to combine them to create and find another object.
The story is told through full motion video and voice-over. When the video ends it transforms fluidly into the game screens, which are all richly detailed and partially animated. The Last Dream features beautiful environments which are at times similar to The Longest Journey in its fantasy, and at other times display real life locations. A credit to the studio here in that they manage to keep everything looking as if it is part of one world, not once did I see something that looked really out of place.
Static images do not do this game justice.
The sound in the game is good. The music is well done and fits the game perfectly, even if it didn't really stand out to me on its own. Everything fits together perfectly with the environments. Sound effects were fitting in all cases as well. The voice acting is good as well, for an indie game. I'm glad the studio decided to hire English speakers, there is no trace of a foreign accent. The one bad note I have is that at times spoken dialogue did not fit the subtitles.
Puzzles range from incredibly easy to a few reallly challenging ones, fortunately on the standard and lower difficulty levels there is a hint system that also functions as a skip button for if you get stuck. Each puzzle additionally has an information button which explains what to do, which I really appreciated a few times.
The game's story does get a bit dark at times, that combined with the at times hard puzzles means I wouldn't recommend this for young players.
What I loved:
-Beautiful graphics
-Animated environments
-Fitting soundtrack
-Challenging puzzles
-Cat companion!
This game is a real gem, and I definitely recommend it to everyone.

I ran guilds in both Everquest and World of Warcraft for a total of about 4 years all combined. My "thing" was to take a bunch of ragtag newbs, start them at the bottom, and see how far they could get if organized properly. I was quite successful and built several "uber" guilds this way.
This game doesn't quite capture that experience. The main things it is shorn of are cameraderie and discipline, which also happen to be the key human elements to making a successful guild.
In this game, every person who doesn't get a drop that they could potentially use gets upset about it every time. In my guilds, anyone who behaved that way got shown the door, swiftly and unceremoniously.
In this game, no matter what you do, some of your raiders wander off and do stupid things with surprising frequency. In my guilds, anyone who proved to be a loose cannon - you guessed it - got shown the door.
The rules were that on raid time I expected soldiers, and people could be as loose as they pleased outside of raids, but while the group was together everyone had to have the utmost respect for everyone else's time.
In this game I couldn't show anybody the door, because the roster of available players was so limited, and all those players came with the same flaws, so replacing someone doesn't help.
Nor could you give specific advice to any players to make them better.
Nor can you make a long term plan for individual players' development (a key reason why I was successful as a GM) so they didn't freak out when a usable drop went to someone else.
In this game, nobody is ever happy to see a drop go to someone else; at best, they are neutral. In the real thing, good players are very happy to watch the guild as a whole improve even if their own character doesn't see new pixels every raid.
In this game, your numbers go up but your raiders don't actually get better at raiding. In the real deal, the more people practice the faster and sharper they get.
There are a lot of other facets of GMing that this game doesn't bother to capture at all, but are important factors in the real thing. Players taking extended breaks then coming back. Dealing with groups of friends whose primary loyalty is to each other so they become a package deal. Husband/wife pairs and the impact of marital dynamics on the group. The child prodigies who despite being much younger than other players are so talented that you can't pass them up as raiders. There are a wide variety of player archetypes but only a tiny few are represented in this game, and even then they do not differ that much from each other. The game makes feeble attempts at modeling some of this but it's really half-hearted and not at all realistic.
As a MMO guild/raid leader, player availability was often the biggest challenge - who out of our key players can't make this raid? How do I substitute/adapt to those players missing? Do I need to find another player of the same class to replace a needed character ability, even if I'm taking a chance on someone new, or can I substitute with other classes from among more trusted players? If our best isn't available, do I aim for a lesser raid to bring others up to speed?
The absence of that factor is important, because it impacts other decisions. Do I stack my main tank first or distribute more evenly? Do I give the best loot to the best players, or the ones who show up most often, or the ones I expect to be around for the longest period of time, or just to the people who play the best on that particular raid? Each priority creates a different incentive to players, and players in turn react in a wide variety of ways to each type of incentive.
So... let me wrap this up. What this game is, is a good *prototype* of a guild management game. It's a prototype that needs to be developed by people with experience managing guilds, needs to have a much much deeper and more varied pool of players to work with, needs models of player development (including self-development), needs models of "real life" impact on player availability and guild dynamics, and other elements that, without which, you aren't really getting a good simulation of the real thing.
This game should give you a few hours of enjoyment as you figure it out and before you realize how sharp the limitations are. If that's enough for your few bucks, go for it.
In the end I cannot recommend the game as I think it fails its main mission of simulating what it is like to run a raiding guild. Wish rather than an explicit thumbs down I could give it a thumb kind of wagging to the side hoping to go up but lacking the willpower.

So you're wondering whether or not to buy Dominique Pamplemousse. As you're probably aware, it's a short point-and-click adventure presented as some kind of amateur musical. The trailer didn't give you much in the way of gameplay, but you did hear some off-key singing accompanied by some off-beat horn accompaniment. "What is the deal?", you ask. "Is it worth my time and/or money?"
Well that's a very tough question. Dominique Pamplemousse is a game that dares you to hate it. I hope my review proves useful, but ultimately you're going to have to decide for yourself. I experienced it, and came out the other side impressed and entertained, but at all times, I was a hair's breadth away from shaking my head and walking away.
At it's heart, Dominique Pamplemousse is a simplified point-and-click adventure. There are objects you need to pick up or examine and people you need to interrogate or manipulate. There's no inventory system to speak of; all items are applied automatically when you examine something relevant to them. The puzzles are usually fairly easy, and examinable items are typically made reasonably clear.
Outside of this adventure game core, there's a whole bunch of weirdness. As I've already mentioned, this game is also sort of a musical. In most locations, there's some kind of weird horn-based accompaniment on loop. Sometimes, for basically no reason, these characters will sing along to this accompaniment, which leads to a bunch of awkward pauses while they wait for their cue. While (thankfully) not all responses are in song form, it's a weird gimmick that comes off as more charming than annoying... most of the time.
DP is largely the work of a single person: Diedra Kiai. As if making the game musical wasn't enough, Kiai voices all of the characters, including when they sing. Kiai doesn't seem to have any formal vocal training (or acting training), and the characters are frequently off-key. Every character is Kiai putting on a different voice, and some of the voices are somewhat cringeworthy.
The visual design is another contentious point. The characters and many of the background objects are clay figures that are stop motion animated, and the whole game is rendered in greyscale. Everything that isn't clay is cardboard or paper, often with visible tearing or some other tell-tale mark that makes immersion impossible. The clay figures themselves tend to be rough, with visible thumbprints, wavy lines that are supposed to be straight, or just a general lack of detail. The clay people range from abstractly recognisable as a person, to something bordering on reptillian!
---TLDR--- There's a lot to criticise here, but depending on your disposition, it'll either come across as frustratingly half-baked, or charmingly hand-made and uniquely weird (in the good sense). I can't say it was the best story either. I would be  unsurprised if many of you walked away thinking that it was the worst game you've ever played. For me, it was an extremely unique experience, one that was initially off-putting, but I came away charmed and entertained nonetheless.
For most people, it's probably not worth the asking price, but it goes on sale often enough. Best pick it up then.
