Rated negative because of Creation Club. Bethesda, if you want to reward modders for their hard work, you're better off hiring them as freelancers and sell their creations as an outright DLC. Microtransaction-style implementation has earned the hate of so many people, it would be foolish to launch another attempt without expecting outrage from the community. You have been warned.
That said, here's my honest take on Fallout 4.
My god. Where to begin...
Main story, compared to the likes of New Vegas, is nothing to write home about, with the exception of Far Harbor. Limited dialogue choices make for a stricter characterization of the protagonist.
But the rest. Weapon and armor customization, settlement creation. A big, highly-detailed world to roam in. Fast, fluid, intuitive gunplay. Surprises in almost every new location to be found. Enemies that continue to challenge the player no matter how high their level is, keeping them alert almost all the time.
And then there are the mods.
They used to call these kind of games a sandbox. Fallout 4 is no sandbox - it's a huge desert.
Real recommendation: get it on a sale. It's a good game otherwise, just marred by questionable marketing tactics.

I don't know if Chucklefish had some sort of staff change, if the lead developer of the game "Tiy" got amnesia'd somehow mid-development and had to pull a whole new concept out of his♥♥♥♥♥after forgetting how to make what they had keep going, or the five people on the Chucklefish page that kept commenting "when is the game coming out???" pressured the developers into releasing the game haphazardly, but the condition the game released felt like an enormous downgrade. Rather than finish up what they already had in order to get the game to a "finished" state, Chucklefish's idea was to instead, and suddenly, cut the project down in size by removing anything unfinished and haphazardly implement an out-of-the-blue "story" structure just to bridge the gap of missing parts.
Numerous things such as cosmetics, armor, weapons, biomes, planets, mobs, bosses, furniture, blocks, and even more were outright removed from the game for no reason other than the haphazard release date that Chucklefish forced themselves didn't leave time to complete them. Hell, some things that WERE actually complete were outright removed too for seemingly no reason. For example, originally, every race was able to craft a melee weapon of each type for each tier - an axe, spear, hammer, broadsword, shortsword, knife, and possibly others I'm forgetting. Not only this, but each race had a completely unique name and appearance for each weapon of each tier from the other, even if they were statistically identical. At release date, these were all removed for absolutely no mentioned reason; not only could only two weapons of a type be crafted per tier, but every race now shared the same generic melee weapon, bar Novakids. Also, a suprisingly unique mechanic amongst other survival-based sandboxes, a 'heat' mechanic, would be removed along with all survival mechanics during an alpha update but nowhere to be seen with the reimplementation of the survival difficulty at release.
Numerous promises were left unfufilled. Each playable race having their own unique opening, story and ending were gone in favor of the universally hated Terrene Protectorate. Each race having their own unique ability - Novakids casting a natural glow in the dark, Florans regenerating themselves in the sunlight - would be nowhere to be seen aside from the already added mechanic that Novakids could only craft guns and all other races could only craft melee weapons. Novakids, the seventh and fan-made race that was officially accepted and said to be as flush with the game as the other races when the game was finalized, would have no representation in the underwhelming "campaign," no villages or tenants to meet or recruit, and would even still be using placeholder inspect quotes. While the second and third issues would later be added post-release, the first has yet to be remedied. Additionally, it was once stated that beating the game without ever fighting would be possible; you'd be able to humbly live farming animal and plant products and selling them. In the final game, you can farm animal and plant products...using tedious processes that were made even MORE complicated from the alpha, and to either be sold for minimal pocket change compared to exploring and looting, or to be used to make weapons to fight with. Additionally, the customization system would go on to be jarringly dull; some cosmetic items would recieve a visual downgrade, the dyeing system would be added and extremely limited, and as stated above, cosmetic items would be removed for no concievable reason, limiting character personalization. But don't worry! They'd be replaced by new cosmetic items...that are either hideous backer-created cosmetics that look terrible, don't match with anything and are never worn by anone ever, or just the old sprites for removed armors with their stats stripped and rebranded as cosmetics.
Numerous perfectly functional mechanics would be reworked for no reason. In addition to the removal of what was made of the unique racial weapons and the heat mechanic, the tech system would be the biggest and easiest-to-note victim of this odd choice. What was once a diverse system that let the player customize themselves how they see fit and give them an advanced sense of control and fast movement that rivaled Minecraft's simplicity, or even surpassed Terraria's and its similar usage of movement-enhancing accesories like running boots or wings, would later become a clunky and watered-down niche that feels and looks like an afterthought in terms of functionality. What was once a lovely variety of seven-ish techs per slot, each with their own uses, would be boiled down into four, with one being a starter version of the tech, and the other three being complete upgrades and thus rendering the first completely irrelevant once the others are obtained. The four slots you once had to mix and match with near-complete freedom would later be decreased to essentially three, with one slot being locked into only having the progressional 'nano-protection' techs that protect the player from increasingly dangerous planetary atmospheres, and later exactly three when the envirnomental protection techs were turned into mandantory equippable items. The racial system of mechs initially planned, with each race having a Mech that could be built or deconstructed around them that matched their race, would be removed at launched and revived later as an unusual new system with mechs that resembled less of serious combat mechs and more of what looked like child-sized gundams that have a limited and non-rechargeable usage on planets, can't navigate doors, can't scale sharp terrain, can't interact with usable objects, and can't even be brought on the game's missions without modding.
Also, let's talk about that campaign. What was, as preached previously, originally going to be seven unique campaigns with unique cinematics, levels and fights that all intertwined at certain points and with Starbound's core exploration and sandbox elements would instead be a single, lazily-written story with cheesy, unimpresive characters, a laughable opening and ending that both end up meaning almost nothing that literally forces you to go out and aimlessly ♥♥♥♥ around until you miraculously manage to find all the♥♥♥♥♥♥the random hag in front of the giant laggy vortex in the Outpost wants you to find before sending you to one of the most thematically one-note levels ever made to fight through unbalanced enemies and environmental hazards that no matter your armor, can kill you in like three hits, only to go fight a boss that probably has less health and damage resistance than whatever the weakest normal enemy in the stage does, and only to have a miniscule chance to get an important rare weapon or trophy. There are only seven mandantory levels not counting the tutorial. Seven. Short. Levels. Worst of all, there's not even a way to truly reset the game without uninstalling it and reinstalling it; if you make a new character and go back to the outpost after beating the game, while the questline itself gets reset and the playeris free to do them over again, all the NPCs remain at the central area, able to buy things from and interact with, and the gate that teleports you to the final level and boss remains unsealed, allowing the annoyed player to simply go "♥♥♥♥ it" and sequence break right to the end of the game if they want.
This game could've been so much better.

Sanctum 2. One of the first few games which I can honestly say have an amazing idea, a FPS with a Tower defense.
Sanctum 2 provides players the chance to actually get a gun, get into yoru own field or maze, and start blasting the enemies along with your towers. It takes the fun of a tower defense, and the fun of a regular FPS, and puts them both into one single game.
The multiplayer in the game is great, it is simple to make a room, invite friends, done. No need for port forwarding and all that extra nonsense. Just 2 clicks, done, they are invited and in. It is so simple that it is truly amazing.
The variety of towers and tactics leaves you thinking " What should I do? " or " Is that really the best choice? " Which makes the experience of the entire game even more greater.
Finding the game too easy? Turn on some feats of strenghts, it has just taken a turn for the worse, and it has become extraordinarily hard, which makes this game very replayable. You can keep playing throuhg all the games modes with the feats of strengths, or just go into a survival and keep going onto wave... 2,000! Just keep on going!
However, I do dislike how there is a small variety of characters and that each of them has a set primary gun which you cannot change. You MUST use that character if you want that primary weapon, which I honestly found a bit bothersome, but this can be overlooked easily, it isn't that big a deal.
There were times in the game that I wish they would ahve more maps without the need of having to buy a DLC, since it seemed a bit short after finishing all the maps, forcing me into buying a DLC for more things to do in the game.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game, it is fun with friends, easy to play, and will provide you with hours of fun.
This is definitely something you should not miss out on.

Liking the game ist currently not allowed because everything has to be free and 60€ for 300 hours is too much to ask. Don't ask me to explain
The Story and RPG parts:
While you could always wish for more variety and more choices, F4 offers a lot of options. The primary story hook -  a parent looking for their kid - might not be something everyone can identify with but pretty soon you get plenty other options. The world is largely plausible and brought to life by a lot of text or audio sippets from the world before the bombs. Most quests boil down to 'go to X and kill everyone and/or retrieve Y and/or push button Z' Might sound repetetive but which game doesn't use the same formula?
Combat and Weaponmodding:
There are a lot of weapons in the game and while most work like they all do: point at enemy and pull trigger they all have some unique characteristics. Direct aiming and VATS aiming are both valid ways and you will probably have to use both. At least I had to when playing with gamepad.
Difficulty:
I played on survival. The lower difficulties make no sense to me. The early levels were nerve wrecking with death around every corner. In time your level rises and you get more and more powerful, landmines and traps are less lethal you start to one-shot enemies that you ran away from for the first few hours. Highly satisfying even if you occasionallyu lose an hour or 3 of progress. I highly suggest you at lest give it a try in survival. Nothing beats the feeling of barely making it to a doctor on your last stimpack with enough sicknesses and radiation coursing through you to kill a small horse.
The game crashed a total of 4 times during 300 hours of play, losing me about 10 hours of playing time. I was highly unhappy at the time but in the end I got over it.
Inventory:
Creating a worse inventory is almost impossible. Like every Bethesda game you are a walking warehouse with attached trailer. The sheer volume of stuff you lug around is staggering and breaks a lot of the immersion for me. Which orifice did I store the minigun in? The obvious choices are already occupied by a missle launcher, 2 shotguns and a few pistols. Never mind where everything else the game happily labels as 'junk' goes.
With the sheer volume of stuff you have you might expect some smart inventory management  but instead you have to scroll through endless lists with little filtering or relevant sorting. Try to find the audiolog you just picked up in a list of about 100 Misc items.
Settlement building:
In theory a nice idea. Actually create something and rebuild the wasteland. However it is not the game I want to play - I want to have an adventure in the wastelands, not minecraft. Sadly the feature can't be ignored entirely especially on suvival difficulty since you need the supplies. It feels largly pointless to build a settlement and you have to do it too often.  The interface for building is anything but brilliant and a lot of magic conditions are only implied. You can also kiss your imersion goodbye when you magic up a bunker with all the furnishings within 10 minutes. Ignore the timetable: why am I the only one that does anything here?
Companions:
You get a choice of utterly moronic packmules that tag along on your adventures. They enjoy walking in the radiation, dropping to their death and carrying your stuff, like you needed another 3 assault rifles. Except for the occasional suicide and complete path finding fail they are still acceptable additions. The true idiocy starts once you start joining secret societies and get access to restricted areas. 'We need you to do the following thing to prove your worth and trustworthyness - and that of any random stray that tags along with you, even if they would normally be our mortal enemy'
And since everyone is up in arms about it:
Creation Club. You have the option to buy official mods. You also have the option not to do so. The game works fine without it. The game works fine with them. If you have a problem with CC, please have your power to make purchases on the internet invalidated by an attorney or go into therapy. Alternativly decide that you are entitled to get everything for free and go on a rating crusade. I know it is a horrible thought, but some people actually require payment for their work.

I liked most of Daedalic's games, but I cannot recommend this one for a couple of reasons (minor spoilers ahead):
1.  The characters are all a bunch of unlikable idiots.  For some reason, the main character is an amoral jerk, but for some reason he feels a need to save his drunken idiot of a friend from repeatedly killing himself.  Some people might find them funny, but I just found them a bunch of abrasive morons.
2. The game is repetative, with you going over the same locations repeatedly each timeloop, looking for whatever minor changes have happened in the world.  Sometimes there are noew items hidden away, sometimes the characters hive different dialog, but it is annoying to have to go over every screen looking for the one new plot hook you need to progress.
3.  The puzzles are often wildly illogical.  A good chunk of the game is devoted to finding a single quarter to use in a vending machine.  Of course, you cannot just look under the couch cushions or borrow one from someone.  Instead you have a multi-stage puzzle involving repairing a radio and making a working lightsaber just to get a single coin.
4.  The game is inconsistent with allowing you to do stuff ahead of time.  Sometimes the game allows you to pick up or use items ahead of when you need to use them, and sometimes the game does not let you.  This is annoying considering how you repeated visit the same areas each loop, so you are forced to try using everything with everything each loop to see if you are allowed to do something new.
5.  The game does not seem to be very consistent with the rules of time-travel.  Some things change each loop and some things stay the some, so the plot seems to progress at random with each time-loop.

Sleeping Dogs is like an Asian GTA. The graphical fidelity of the game is unparalleled by competitors such as Saints Row or Grand Theft Auto. The story line is different from the others in some senses yet remarkably similar in others. You play as an undercover cop in Hong Kong and you get to do tons of stuff from cockfights to local fight clubs to karaoke at local clubs.
PROS [+]:
-Amazing graphics
-Great storyline
-Usually quite inexpensive when on sale
-Tons of DLC if you want more
-Large map
-Tons of vehicles from boats to bikes
-Has a plot that keeps you on the edge of your seat
-Lots of little ways (or big ones) to help you make money in game
CONS [-]:
-Game is very needy (resource-wise) when playing on high graphics settings
-Not a lot of big choices in the story compared to games like Skyrim
-Weird camera angles in cars can be annoying some times
-3rd person camera only while on foot
-Only runs in windowed mode for me
-Little to no customizability of vehicles or guns
-No multiplayer
OVERALL:
If you are looking for a new open world game that isn't just shoot-em-up-crime-gangbang-city-in-America, look no further. Sleeing Dogs has an intense story and a plot chock full of back stabbing, lies, and death. This game is so good and is relatively inexpensive. If you have the money and are looking for a new single-player game, GET IT.
RATING: 8.5/10

AN: It says I have no hours on record, but that is not true? I spent quite a lot of the days leading up to Christmas playing SD. Man, that sucks.
Alright, here's the thing. I love crime-fighting games. I'm fine with mission-completing and do try to handle them as well and quickly as possible. Unfortunately, this game's glitched combat system makes it extremely diffcult to actually perform well against enemies, and the aerial third-person camera angles make it dizzying to navigate when fighting. Actually clicking the mouse to attack and/or counter is only registered by the game about 15% of the time; the other 85%? No idea. I really looked forward to playing this game, as Hong Kong as a setting in a game has always struck my fancy, and I appreciate the environment work done in this game's case. What this title makes up for in writing and scenery, it falls short on in character animation, particularly the facials. The models are extremely well-rendered, but their faces remain static, often uncannily expressionless, even when dialogue gets particularly emotional. To me, it feels like this game tries extremely hard to present a realistic story and characters, but at times things can seem so flat and, well... stale. 5.4/10. Hopefully, patches or software updates on the PC port of this will make me want to play Sleeping Dogs again. Until then, I'll just have to wait.

I bought this on a whim because it looked good and reminded me of Castle Crashers. Yeah, yeah everyone talks about that game but it's a damn good one that's why. Anyway...
I started playing the game with a mate, we grabbed the same foolish mindless goon and beat him into the sky. It was one of the most rewarding things I've done in co-op in a long time. It actually felt like co-op had a good purpose. It changed combat and that's not even all of it.

Another downside is that it's 2 player only. While that does perfectly allow for both players to be seen at all times and easily control the situation... I do wonder what it would be like to have 3 players or even 4.
Still, it was an entertaining game I hope to finish 100% one day. If there is ever a Foul Play two... I'd buy a co-op pack instantly. I'd mess about in another one of these no problem.

I hate to be that guy, but the game is simply lacking in the guild simulation category too much for me to give it a positive reveiw.
Don't get me wrong, it's still worth five dollars, and no more, but it fails to capture the true sense of guild interaction. I remember during my MMORPG days (long behind me) watching the chat while frustrated people waited for the cleric or tank to return from picking up fast food, or the absolute rage that would occur when someone with a terrible connection went link dead in the middle of a boss fight. This game tries to simulate that, but it does so poorly. For example, when Healzaur's cat walks across the keyboard, they miss a turn. When Sir Killzalot runs out to get a burrito, he misses a turn. When MagicMan goes link dead, he misses a turn. That's it, that's all that happens, when it would be easy to have each event do something differently. Cat walks across keyboard? Hit/Heal/Attack wrong monster/player. Leaving for a burrito? Takes longer than a few minutes, that should be a few turns right there. Goes link dead? Leaves the raid indefinitely, but dosn't take any damage. That's the raiding I remember, but sadly this game dosn't even take it that far.
The social aspects are also lacking. When Burninator and Sing-a-long discuss politics, it should have an effect on their morale, but it does nothing. It's just pointless flavor text that reminds me it could do something, but doesn't, especially given the odd morale system in this game. The fact that your guildies are selfish arses when it comes to handing out loot is a plus, but will sometimes leave you scratching when your head when taking something for guild funds does nothing for player morale, but giving an item to a player its best suited for causes a drop in morale across the board. Then there are the times when people are feeling neglected, even when you just spent the whole night talking to them, and everyone else is getting upset you won't talk to them, like you're the only conversationalist on the planet or something.
Again, I'm not someone who cares about graphics, and the game is worth about what is being asked for it, but if your looking to recapture that sense of leading a guild to disaster because raiders and responsibility rarely mix, you sadly won't find it here.

I spent a lot of time with Capitalism 2 many years ago and it's nice to see it on Steam. It is a pure economics Simulator- no getting sidetracked building a transport network or theme park etc. It's an old game, having been released in 2001.
As such it has a lot of depth. So much so, that (according to the website) it gets used as a teaching aid in business courses by several universities. It has, for instance got an in depth simulation of the stock market. It has complex production chains that will see you mine Silica (and other raw materials), process them in your factories and eventually sell computers through your own shops. But there are many, many steps required to achieve this, even with simpler goods.
With all the complexity, there is, as you'd expect, a somewhat steep learning curve. Capitalism 2 does have a campaign which starts with a tutorial. The goals then become progressively harder while introducing you to new game concepts. It is a good campaign but shows the games age: the explanations are given exclusively in text and are often pretty long.
The graphics also show the games age: even for a game this old, they're not great. And being able to select "lower resolution" or "higher resolution" from the main menu, without actually displaying what said resolution is (or if the resolution is even at its max), isn't ideal either.
Capitalism 2 is a niche game: it does one thing, it does it in depth and altogether very well. Because it is a niche game, about a subject that can be quite dry and quite old, it won't appeal to everyone. But to those who this sort of game does appeal to, it is a good game (and not to mention virtually without competition).

This game is not terraria. comparing it terraria is pretty much meaningless, the only thing they really have in common is that they are  both 2D. Starbound focuses on space technology, quests, and role playing while terraria focuses on exploration and adventure.
Starbound has very good building mechanics and atmosphere. The sound track is absolutely lovely and good enough to listen on its own. However Starbound lacks content compared to the vast size of the universe. This used to be a much bigger problem, but they have slowly been scaling back the randomness of the universe and increasing content. Its not really like Starbound lacks content, but that as a player you have to visit more worlds to find it. The vast majority of time playing this game could be spent just searching for a specific species. going from planet to planet, hoping there is a village or outpost there. One benifite though is that everyone is in the same universe, and some users have begun indexing the planets they visit which can assist other players hoping to find specific things.
A final tip though, start making a base as soon as you start. You might be able to fit all your stuff in your ship, but it will not be as fun and will be very cramped.
This game is most definitely a work in progress. However i am now confident that it will continue evolving and is worth a playthrough. Just don't be looking for a replacement for terraria.

AN: It says I have no hours on record, but that is not true? I spent quite a lot of the days leading up to Christmas playing SD. Man, that sucks.
Alright, here's the thing. I love crime-fighting games. I'm fine with mission-completing and do try to handle them as well and quickly as possible. Unfortunately, this game's glitched combat system makes it extremely diffcult to actually perform well against enemies, and the aerial third-person camera angles make it dizzying to navigate when fighting. Actually clicking the mouse to attack and/or counter is only registered by the game about 15% of the time; the other 85%? No idea. I really looked forward to playing this game, as Hong Kong as a setting in a game has always struck my fancy, and I appreciate the environment work done in this game's case. What this title makes up for in writing and scenery, it falls short on in character animation, particularly the facials. The models are extremely well-rendered, but their faces remain static, often uncannily expressionless, even when dialogue gets particularly emotional. To me, it feels like this game tries extremely hard to present a realistic story and characters, but at times things can seem so flat and, well... stale. 5.4/10. Hopefully, patches or software updates on the PC port of this will make me want to play Sleeping Dogs again. Until then, I'll just have to wait.

After the first one ends is where the game really takes off, and I wish the first day was a little more direct so the real story could start sooner.

An entertaining concept that will (briefly) tickle you with nostalgia, but falls short as an actual game. Before you dismiss this simply because it's a negative review - take note of the hours played on positive reviews. 2 hours here. 4 hours there. I personally want more out of the games I play, hence the downvote.
The primary draw of this game - the campy feeling that you're raiding with MMO players - is disappointingly shallow as far as content/depth/replayability. Seeing one of your healers AFK because of a "Bathroom emergency caused by too many Hot Pockets" is amusing the first time you see it, but not the third time it happens in the same raid. I progressed quickly from "Haha! That is SO World of Warcraft!" to "Ah, that one again." The game does well capturing the annoying and tedious aspects of raid/guild management (attention-starved guildies, loot jealousy) - so well that dealing with these issues feels like  the actual chores that they are and not much else. With the charming "MMO personality" aspect exhausted almost immediately, I was left with only a game of a game that quickly became boring.
Fights are slow, the loot system is underwhelming, and the mechanics can at once feel sparse and clunky - there is apparently no taunt ability for tanks, so the best way for your main tank to drop threat seems to be spending your entire turn switching him to a DPS spec, then back to tank, then when you want your pimrary tank to regain threat, you put your off-tank to DPS, then your off-tank to tank. If it sounds tedious or clumsy, that's because it is.
It's not so much that it isn't worth $5, it's that there are many other games that deserve your money more than this one.

Bastion is, without a doubt, one of the best narrative, atmospheric, story rich indie games I have ever played. However, let’s cut right to the chase; should you pay £11 (or equiv) for this game?
The straight answer is no. Why? Well, because although this game has many great aspects, for a game this short with such little depth, you pay something along the lines of £2 per hour of enjoyment. The game can be completed in less than 5 hours, and once you understand the mechanics, a second play through is completely unnecessary and adds nothing to the experience at all. Unfortunately, because this game received so much attention, its price is naturally higher to make up for the marketing budget. This is unfortunate, because if its price point was the price of an average indie game, somewhere along the lines of £6 to £8, I would have absolutely recommended it without a second thought.
But, if you are wondering about whether to purchase this regardless of its price point, read on, and find out why I'd recommend this game.
Firstly, Bastion's narration is some of the best I've ever heard, full stop. Not just from indie games, from AAA games too. The game is narrated in second person view; meaning as you explore and roam around the world, the narration will describe your movements and actions and directly refer to you as the character. The narrator’s voice is deep and brooding and when I first started playing it was somewhat disconcerting, largely due to the fact that the voice is slightly unnerving, and creates an atmosphere of uneasiness. However, it fits in perfectly with the themes of the game. I also love the way in which the story is presented through pretty much only the use of the narrative. At one point, you spot a man who is still alive amongst a mass of dead people, frozen into stone. The narrator however knows more than the boy you play as, and says “Just think, if we didn’t have people like him, we wouldn’t be in this mess, would we.” The character you play knows nothing about who this man is or why he’s any different from anyone else, but the narrator does. If I hadn’t replayed this part of the game, I wouldn’t have remembered that such an event occurs. It adds a refreshing layer into a game which otherwise may have held very little replayabiliy.
Another point is that this game does a magnificent job of engrossing you into the world. The soundtrack is fantastic, and, without a doubt, the greatest redeeming aspect of Bastion is its absolutely beautiful art style. It oozes with passion and you get the general sense that someone loved every second they drew the stunning watercolour masterpieces you see throughout the whole game. You control a character only known as 'The Kid', of which very little is known, or is ever known, apart from that he served in the military. Along the way, you gather increasing attachment to this silent hero who receives no thanks despite never stopping and never giving up. The world is reliant on him, and he pushes forward, absolutely emotionlessly, and this dark, brooding nature raises real questions about such a mysterious character. Honestly, I think the fact that we only learn tiny snippets about the character is one of the best things the developers did to this game. More often than not, character progression can go too far or not far enough, but in this case, it’s pretty much perfect for the type of game it is. I felt the slightest twinge of empathy when I learnt of The Kid’s situation, but not enough for me to feel like I was forced into feelings of depression or sadness, and was rather presented with facts and allowed to feel as I naturally would.
There are a few downsides, none of which I’d really say demean Bastion’s brilliance to an extent that I’d consider it not worth playing, but I will mention them briefly regardless.
A massive lack of replayability plagues this game. There is really no reason to want to replay this game. There aren’t any difficult choices which lead you upon a different path, there aren’t any new weapons or characters to find. It’s largely based on an immersive first playthrough. This leads to the question of value for money, as to which it isn’t great.
I found slight trouble with keyboard controls, and I’d greatly recommend a controller, as it makes exploring much smoother and enjoyable. Once I started to use a controller, I felt like I understood some of the mechanics much better.
It also suffers from a general lack of any sort of character progress in terms of stats. It’s not an RPG; in reality it’s more of a story-telling experience in which you play the protagonist. You have weapon upgrades, but even they fall somewhat through, since they’re largely passive and can be overlooked almost entirely.
When it comes down to it, I would recommend this game. Why? Perhaps not for its merit as a video game, since the mechanics are somewhat forgettable and simple, but instead because of its merit as a work of art. After you play this game, if ever someone proclaims the infamous ‘video games cannot be art’ statement, you will be infuriated, thrust Bastion in their face and declare them a ♥♥♥♥ing idiotic moron.

- The classes that characters are presented in It's A Wipe feel somewhat restricted and specialized. While this makes the game easier to play and manage it can make playing the game seem too simple (If you're a Rogue you can only single target damage. If you're a Mage you can only AoE damage, ect.)
-  While the overview for each guild mates' personality and needs is a nice feature, the social interaction amoung guild mates is lacking.There is no interpersonal aspect between the guild master and his guild mates other then some reoccuring flavor text that happens during the raid itself. The social part of managing a guild is just as important, if not more important, then the raiding itself. Having a relationship and knowing each guildie is something that simply can not be done through the automated skip sequences shown in game.
Overall the game for me personally has been a great return on my purchase. Its a wonderful time passer as it doesn't require you to stare at the screen. You can do other things while it plays in the background without fear of messing up too bad (for the most part). I would love to see a more fleshed out game (with a more fleshed out price tag to compensate) that had more complexity. The game has very strong potential as a starting point for a much more involved adventure/manager/socialsim game.
Tl;dr
The game is priced appropriately for the content it contains. Although features may seem lacking and it can be repetitive at times, it is a must have purchase for anyone who has Raided in MMOs and wants a light hearted, nostalgic strategy game to play on the side.

I can't give this game a totally 100% positive review so take the thumbs up with a grain of salt.
While it's fun to play there is too much emphasis on the honor system and too many players know it.
I can't say that there aren't any honest players out there but in all seriousness the number of people who actually play fairly are few and far between especially people with larger friends lists.
One of the biggest rules the game employs is NO OUTSIDE CHAT. This includes, Facebook chat, skype, etc and is to keep the game fair. Now, if you're in a game and six of the fifteen players are Skyping that's six people who can gang up and take the remaining eight down without having to worry about being killed by the Veteran or being shot by the Vigilante. Random chance or not this is a HUGE advantage over the other players and ruins the whole experience.
With that being said the game, when layed properly, is fun and can become addicting to a scary level. It allows for critical thinking and can sometimes give you an adrenaline rush when your character's life is on the line and sweating out the fear of being accused regardless of being accused correctly or not.
For what they're asking it's worth it but in the end you risk being consumed by the hivemind of cheaters who will ruin the game for you at some point or another.

Honestly, after the initial completion of this game, from koala to giraffe (alpha and beta codes names respectively.), I could only see that they didn't go to the creative side when making this game, as half the assets and features from Koala were taken out, rather than repurposed, until after release, with no known bug testing. Exploring planets on the first playthrough is a reasonable adventure, seeing all the different kinds of planets you can visit for resources to upgrade your ship, gear, and craft your race appropriate weapon.
And then after the second playthrough, you might realize things get a bit stale, and you don't really see the end game goal, with every new character, is a long journey just to get all those upgrades all over again. Sure, there's a chat command that lets you spawn what you need to forcefully upgrade, but it doesn't feel all too endearing.
The story is very stale, and the paths you take really feel like dead ends, having you treck to-and-fro just to see if you're going the right way, while you get expositional diologue about who and what and why you should care.
The only thing that really was the saving grace of this game was the Multiplayer, and the Mods you can add on their. The base game is nothing special without mods, but even with them, it will continue to feel empty.

Many changes have obviously taken place since I last got into it, so your experience may be totally different.
I've spent a lot of time in this game, in addition to making lists and checking off stuff I've collected. I have long since stopped keeping up with every update, but I used to visit the forums every day and was obsessed with it. Getting back into it is admittedly tough so before I drop it completely I'll say this.
In solitude, I enjoyed going through the randomly-generated worlds, fishing, mining, fighting enemies, and getting loot with the music quietly playing in the background, going through the same motions and seeing the sights. It was relaxing. It was also fun to draw out what kind of equipment I would give to each class and seeing how I could mix and match gear between them. As a single player, there was a pretty clear meta you'd follow to be able to go through dungeons very quickly, and I enjoyed it for a good while, but this game is more fun with other people. There's also that feeling of pride you get when you carry the team through a boss fight. If you're reluctant to go into chat though, I can see how it'd be very difficult to do some of the things the game has to offer.
On the other hand, there were ways to get random players to naturally congregate to each other without saying. Now I'm not even sure these are a thing anymore, but every hour there would be a challenge that involved going into a specific level and beating a bunch of dungeons. It was crazy, having dozens of players all move in this huge mass working as one to complete each reward tier. Reviving each other, working in chat to keep it all together and preventing splits, inviting people to help them out. If there's anything I loved about this game it would be how fun playing cooperatively was.
This game is one of the few free-to-plays that I was willing to put money in, so I hope people can still enjoy it regardless. I'd hate to see this game go down after all the enjoyment I got from it. From what I've seen in recent reviews and updates, there are some new paywalls and the issues I faced before with the servers are still there. If your goal in this game is to reach some sort of ending, 100% completion, or hit the absolute maximum in stats, then I can't honestly recommend it because that feels impossible. I played this game for so long because I liked the feeling of progress, setting my own goals in the form of items to collect or craft. I may have stopped playing, but I am grateful for the time I spent doing it.

I am a huge fan of anything stop-motion animated, I enjoy musicals, and bizarre indie games are a guilty pleasure for me.  It should have been impossible for me to dislike this game, but instead, it ended up being one of the worst I've ever played.  I really and truly wanted to give this game the benefit of the doubt, but try as I might, I could not find a single redeeming quality.
The first thing that hits you is the singing.  To call the singing 'music' would be quite generous indeed- the choice of notes breaks every musical convention, but that is overshadowed by the fact that the voice actor can't hit a note to save her life.  The rhythm is all but indiscernible, and the rhyming is strained at the best of times.  The fact that they're selling the soundtrack is a smack in the face.
The stop-motion is rough as well...  it seems like the developer only chose stop-motion because drawing the characters would have actually been more time-consuming.  There is a fine line between “artistically simplistic” and “shoddy,” and this game qualifies as the latter.
The game says it's about gender and the economy, but the only mention of gender is a running gag that nobody knows the gender of the main character. My suspicion is that the developer has some personal opinions on gender ambiguity, and I can sympathize with the sentiment, but it seems tacked onto the game, and serves no real purpose towards the plot.  Games with political undertones have their place, especially in the indie community, but it has to be done well.  In that respect, this game fails miserably.
My final advice is this: don't play the game.  But if you do, just to see what it's about, don't allow yourself to think “it's starting out bad, but it'll probably get better!”  It doesn't.  Feel free to quit at any time...  you're not missing anything.

Sanctum 2 is definitely worth the purchase.  The game is difficult but not too difficult or frustrating like most Tower Defense games.  The difference here is that you actually have control of the game in a FPS way.  Not only do you place walls, towers, and other goodies, but you are also in the arena fighting the waves first hand.
There are a few issues with the game.   For one playing by yourself is just not fun.  Difficulty scales with number of players but teamwork is far superior than lone wolfing.  Another issue is the controls being awkward.  Playing with a controller makes things easier, since the game is made for the Xbox 360.  But what makes the games' controls awkward is that you have to understand that it's an FPS so you also have to place/upgrade/sell the walls/turrets/dispensers in first person view.  The placement system is also bright and kinda distracting.  The weird thing is that you also see what other players are "planning" to build.  It makes for easy communication when building the path way but sometimes you get your build tool mixed up with your allies build tools.  At least the upside on that is if you misplace your wall/tower you can always sell it for all of your resources back.
Besides the issues which I would consider pretty minor, I would rate this game extremely playable and worth the purchase.  Tower defense games are naturally addicting but then you add in FPS too it?  Well I'm sold!

Dominique Pamplemousse has some negative reveiws. When I first saw this game in the Steam Store it had mixed reveiws. But this game is not all that bad. Yes, there are bad things about it, that's why there are negative reveiws, but I must say the game was worth the money I spent on it.
The bad traits of this game are clearly and without doubt, bad things. There's no arguement that makes the bad traits go away, but the good traits do outweigh it. Firstly, the game is quite short, surprisingly short. This SHOULDN'T be a surprise though, when you think about how hard claymation is to do, how long it takes, and it's clear that the game makers put a lot of effort into this game, just not enough to make it a full length game, and obviously the time  also depends on how good you are at completeing the game.
Secondly, the voices, Dominique Pamplemousse is about singing, about the music industry and opera. The bad singing voices at the start of the game are really cringeworthy, they make you feel uncomfortable, because we are not used to listening to people sing normally, and this game perfectly demonstrates that, (which is one of the reasons I love it!) it shows that some people sing normally. The singing is not so much bad, as normal. After a few minutes of the characters all singing you get used to it, and playing a game with an opera sort of stlye can get quite enjoyable, when you realise the voices aren't really THAT bad. And it's such a special experience seeing someone in a musical type setting who doesn't have a strangely perfect voice.
The game makes a lot of claims. It claims that it is a game about gender, and economy, which it really isn't about that much. Yes, the protagonist is non-binary, and appears to express their thoughts about this, and having all the rest of the characters confused about the protagonist's gender. It is clear that this game planned for this to be a big theme, but it didn't really turn out that way, because the game is clearly too short for them to have any discussions about gender or even the economy.
Dominique Pamplemousse does seem to have some bad things about it, but it is really worth buying, as it is a beautiful claymation game, and I really am in love with any type of claymation, or any game made with real life materials. This game really has some nice subtle discussions on auto-tune and the music industry, which is not a common plot for video games to have. This game is also in black and white, which is another rare thing for video games, as video games are too advanced to have really gone through a black and white period (if you don't count the time when games could only be in two colours) as televisions did.
One last little touch on this nice game, which barely has anything to do with the game, is that it has DLC that you can buy that will give you the sheet music, and sheet music is such a lovely thing to buy as DLC, which is really the whole reason I bought it, but I enjoyed it past the sheet music. This game isn't really that expensive and not really that long, but if you have around $5 you should think about buying it.

One of the greatest games ever made, and hands-down my personal favorite block building game.
You start off on a busted spaceship orbiting a world. You talk to your ship's AI and head down to the surface to build your new life. You chop down some trees, mine a little cobblestone, start building a house, make a workbench. Then, next thing you know, you're travelling the universe to hundreds of planets, building colonies for NPCs, setting up elaborate home lighting and security systems, always mining, always building, always flying to new planets and discovering new things.
You can craft a bajillion items, and you can also grab items from NPC colonies, underground strongholds, ancient ruins, etc, and 3D scan them. Then you can 3D print those items later. I cannot express how impressed I am with the sheer volume of amazing structures, furniture, and decorations. It's incredible.
Build an amazing house for yourself in a variety of styles and then build some neighboring houses and summon NPCs into them. The race and personalities of those NPCs will be based on how you decorate their homes. Sometimes they're shopkeeps, other times they're badass ninjas. Sometimes they just say cryptic things while looking off the edge of a cliff.
After building colonies on many planets, building heaps of stately manors, cozy homes nestled inside cliff faces, giant technological towers, spiraling tree houses, and moon bases, kick back and relax with your friends on your ship, each of you playing a different instrument, singing your favorite songs.
This game is for people who like to create. For people who want to build a weird little colony, call it home, and show it off to some friends now and then. There is plenty of combat, with boss fights, challenge portals with gauntlets to run, quests to help penguins test out their mechs... But at the end of the day, what brings me back every time, is the creation. I have yet to find a game that allows me to better express myself through building.

Trackless is a strange blend of first person exploration and text-based puzzles on a wonderfully mysterious sci-fi world. It's structured around the pilgrimage to see a sacred "object", and most of the game is about getting through various obstructions and trials on the way. Exploration is richly rewarded with snippets of information, some optional challenges and a score system that can be used to buy different skins for your phone (which sometimes give it new, unexplained abilities).
As you wander around, you can explore at your leisure and interact with objects in the environment. Most of them will give you some flavor text, but a few are marked as interactive; if you right click on them, a text box appears. So, for example you might find a machete next to some vines, and type "hack" into the textbox that appears when you interact with the machete. All puzzles are self-contained like that, though there are several that chain actions as you complete them. The game also rewards you with more score if you don't reuse words, and if you use a word that's not just functional but one that works better in context; for example, on that machete puzzle you could get away with just typing "cut", but it would give you fewer points. It's a pretty unique mechanic that's pretty satisfying when it works. As with any text-based game, it has some "guess the verb" issues, but since figuring out the intention of the interaction is part of the fun it doesn't grate too much. Its limited vocabulary is a bit more of a problem, since quite a few entries I tried didn't work (at one point throwing me off-track for a puzzle).
In any case, once you get into the spirit of things there's nothing too hard in there, which keeps things pacey. It also helps that the phone you carry around in front of you all the time points you in the direction of any objects in the vicinity, both interactive and not.
The world is beautifully realized with a wonderful soundtrack and a great, euro-comic style aesthetic, making exploration a joy. The writing does a great job of explaining just enough to keep you interested, with lots of little details building up to a very well realized sense of place.
There's nothing else out there quite like Trackless, and I enjoyed my time with it thoroughly.

At its best, Blackwake is one of the funniest games I've ever played.  I personally prefer those moments where you have a crew with a good sense of humor than to just win the round. With such a crew, it doesn't even matter if your ship is sinking and everything is going down the drain, You'll laugh loudly in the process and have the time of your life. These moments have been fairly common to me while playing, but it all comes down to using the mic yourself and at least let out a "yaaar" once in a while.
You don't have to be social in Blackwake, and it's possible to play the game without the use of a microphone. but the game is made with communication in mind so it's a must if you want to get the full experience. Other players are mostly happy as long as you're able to tell your crew that you need supplies downstairs, follow captains orders and basic stuff like that.
To be somewhat effective in this game, you really need a captain that knows what they're doing and a crew that are willing to do the orders they bark out. Playing as a crew member you'll be spending your time scouting for eneny ships, firing and reloading cannons and repairing the ship, sails and killing erupting fire with buckets of water..The tasks are simple but when those cannonballs start flying through your ship and you run around working those holes, you'll be thankful for the simplicity, because it can get pretty intense, at least with a headset. There's also the possibility of locking down enemy ships with grappling hooks to finish it off and the other way around. Ths is where your weapons get useful
Playing as the captain of a ship is different and in some sense more challenging than crew member. You'll need some ability to manage multiple people and tell them what to do and when to do it. And you MUST have a microphone and the will to use it if/when playing as captain on populated servers. Nobody likes a silent captain. Good captains keep the crew informed about their actions in time for the crew to be prepared and ready..
You'll spend most of your time in one position steering the ship in position to fire the broadside cannons on the enemy as well as evading incoming threats by staying out of their range and the angle of their devastating broadside cannons. This is the easy part. The real challenge isn't that or the enemy ships, it's your crew and how you manage it. The difference between firing off a full broadside at the right moment and individual cannons firing off cannonballs at their own convenience is the difference between winning a round or losing it.  Take control and demand respect. Your crew should only fire the cannons when you say so.
It's a type of game I jump in and out of for an hour or two rather than a game I play for full evenings and nights, but I fully recommend this game for its simple yet amazing gameplay and hilarious approach.

Liking the game ist currently not allowed because everything has to be free and 60€ for 300 hours is too much to ask. Don't ask me to explain
The Story and RPG parts:
While you could always wish for more variety and more choices, F4 offers a lot of options. The primary story hook -  a parent looking for their kid - might not be something everyone can identify with but pretty soon you get plenty other options. The world is largely plausible and brought to life by a lot of text or audio sippets from the world before the bombs. Most quests boil down to 'go to X and kill everyone and/or retrieve Y and/or push button Z' Might sound repetetive but which game doesn't use the same formula?
Combat and Weaponmodding:
There are a lot of weapons in the game and while most work like they all do: point at enemy and pull trigger they all have some unique characteristics. Direct aiming and VATS aiming are both valid ways and you will probably have to use both. At least I had to when playing with gamepad.
Difficulty:
I played on survival. The lower difficulties make no sense to me. The early levels were nerve wrecking with death around every corner. In time your level rises and you get more and more powerful, landmines and traps are less lethal you start to one-shot enemies that you ran away from for the first few hours. Highly satisfying even if you occasionallyu lose an hour or 3 of progress. I highly suggest you at lest give it a try in survival. Nothing beats the feeling of barely making it to a doctor on your last stimpack with enough sicknesses and radiation coursing through you to kill a small horse.
The game crashed a total of 4 times during 300 hours of play, losing me about 10 hours of playing time. I was highly unhappy at the time but in the end I got over it.
Inventory:
Creating a worse inventory is almost impossible. Like every Bethesda game you are a walking warehouse with attached trailer. The sheer volume of stuff you lug around is staggering and breaks a lot of the immersion for me. Which orifice did I store the minigun in? The obvious choices are already occupied by a missle launcher, 2 shotguns and a few pistols. Never mind where everything else the game happily labels as 'junk' goes.
With the sheer volume of stuff you have you might expect some smart inventory management  but instead you have to scroll through endless lists with little filtering or relevant sorting. Try to find the audiolog you just picked up in a list of about 100 Misc items.
Settlement building:
In theory a nice idea. Actually create something and rebuild the wasteland. However it is not the game I want to play - I want to have an adventure in the wastelands, not minecraft. Sadly the feature can't be ignored entirely especially on suvival difficulty since you need the supplies. It feels largly pointless to build a settlement and you have to do it too often.  The interface for building is anything but brilliant and a lot of magic conditions are only implied. You can also kiss your imersion goodbye when you magic up a bunker with all the furnishings within 10 minutes. Ignore the timetable: why am I the only one that does anything here?
Companions:
You get a choice of utterly moronic packmules that tag along on your adventures. They enjoy walking in the radiation, dropping to their death and carrying your stuff, like you needed another 3 assault rifles. Except for the occasional suicide and complete path finding fail they are still acceptable additions. The true idiocy starts once you start joining secret societies and get access to restricted areas. 'We need you to do the following thing to prove your worth and trustworthyness - and that of any random stray that tags along with you, even if they would normally be our mortal enemy'
And since everyone is up in arms about it:
Creation Club. You have the option to buy official mods. You also have the option not to do so. The game works fine without it. The game works fine with them. If you have a problem with CC, please have your power to make purchases on the internet invalidated by an attorney or go into therapy. Alternativly decide that you are entitled to get everything for free and go on a rating crusade. I know it is a horrible thought, but some people actually require payment for their work.

I feel as if I should add a disclaimer here: This isn’t the typical type of game you’ll see me play or review but I still wanted to give it a fair shot.
Starting out the game literally drops you into a train car with no direction or introduction at all and as someone new to the game without any background information as to what it was or how I should play it I spent several minutes just figuring out how to interact with the game and the world I was in. The controls themselves thankfully aren’t overly complicated, you use WASD to move around and right-click to interact with objects
The other interesting, and at times frustrating mechanic, is when you’re given the opportunity to type in a verb, e.g. to raise the water level, I was stuck at first because I kept trying things like “push”, “switch”, or “turn” thinking I needed a verb to tell the character how to interact with the control box rather than one to tell them the end task I was trying to accomplish with that control box.
I did see somewhere in the game that at times more than one verb would allow you to complete a task but that certain verbs would grant you more points than others, I would have liked to have seen the vocabulary increased to include additional words for some of those tasks that I felt made sense even if they didn’t net you many points.

The visuals are fairly simple and are 2-dimensional even though you’re wandering around in a 3-dimensional world and the character cut-outs that you interact with twist or turn at all times so that wherever you are in relation to them they are always facing you (aka, “Billboarding”).  The character designs reminded me of something you might see in the Cyberpunk 2020 tabletop RPG manuals. Though I didn’t see any information about this title going to VR, visually it seemed as if it could work with those platforms pretty well. The story itself creates a mysterious and intriguing journey and the music lends very well to the atmosphere and the story.
The other two things I felt worth mentioning are the cellphone, which is your constant companion that keeps track of the tasks available in each area and is from time to time used to send messages back and forth to some of the other NPCs, and the Save Game feature which you activate by standing on certain platforms in the game.  Fail to find and save your game means you could end up all the way back at the beginning, but these are fairly easy to find and spread out through the game. Activating it to save your game is as simple as walking up to it and standing on it briefly which you’ll then get a notification of the save.

Conclusion/Rating
Note: Bammsters score different parts of the game on a 1-10 scale, with 4-6 being the average.

Design:  6
The design for this title is 2-dimensional and pretty basic and yet still helps to create an interesting and at times mysterious atmosphere.  The music was really well done and was a nice compliment to the art and story.
Challenge:  3
Though there were moments of frustration at times trying to find the right verb to get something to work so I could complete a task to move on, I didn’t feel as if the game itself was all that challenging.
Fun:  4
As mentioned above, this isn’t the type of game I typically play, but it did provide an interesting distraction from the stuff I usually delve into.
Replay:  3
I don’t see much reason to play the game again once you’ve finished.
Price:  6
While $9.99 isn’t much to pay for a game, this is a title I would pick up on a Steam sale.  For myself I think at $5.00 it would be priced where I would be ok with purchasing it.
Overall Score: 4.4 out of 10 – Median

My my, glad I got this - a very funny platformer.
If you have previously played Castle Crasher, this game is similar but more action-oriented.
So what, we control a character that's supposed to perform a... foul play. While we're performing our play on the stages, we move forward, beating enemies and pleasing our audiences with good performance.
The campaign is divided into five acts, each acts have five levels, each levels is approx ten-fifteen minutes long, a bit longer if you're into boss battles. The objective is simple, you just need to beat each enemy waves with style - be it by performing chain combos to fill and maintain the meter gauge (audiences' mood). Don't let it get too low or the curtain will close and game over. A bit lacking aspect, though, is that the campaign is incredibly linear - you have no option to do anything else and can only follow the direction the game wishes you to. You can, however, replay earlier stages from main menu to achieve higher scores.
The combat mechanic is very simple, chaining normal and powerful attacks while deflecting the enemies or throw them against each others. And this what differentiates from Castle Crasher, it offers more lively battles and flexible ala Devil May Cry DMC but in 2D. By chaining you'll be increasing your scores and earns stars that'll be calculated at the end of each level. As you progress, you'll unlock more abilities/perks to use in game. Use these to... chain more enemies. Heh.
And of course, playing coop is much more fun than alone. It's hilarious, really, to have a messed up battle on the stages.
Graphic wise I'm incredibly amused. It really is that great - suitable for this game - colorful and innately bunch sense of humor drawn into the art and character designs. Special effects don't distract you from the battles and carefully blend with the stages, movement and attack animations are not sluggish and feel natural. FPS throughout the level is stable enough even during chaotic battle.  Some minus points though, there are no deep customizations like AA or refresh rate and some commonly supported resolutions are not supported. But overall, I'd say the job well done.
And lastly, controller support is great - and I expect it so much because this is a platformer. I wouldn't even give the game a damn great review if it had poor support, but this Foul Play is just apt at adapting controller support. Dinput and Xinput are both supported, moreover each buttons can be customized in game. No complaints from me on this aspect really.
Funny thing is, metacritic user score gives this 69/100. Don't listen - it deserves more. A recommended game from me.

First of all, I will like to say that I love Capcom games, from Megaman to Resident Evil (including Street Fighter, obviously), but there are certain things with Street Fighter V that I cannot let pass anymore.
Street Fighter V's gameplay mechanics are great. I think this is the most balanced Street Fighter to date and is accesible to everybody. The problem is that this is an online-only game and the network has having problems since day one. There are a few modes that can be played solo, like story mode, but you will finish them too quickly that you won't have too much taste out of them.
Trust me, when a game's network has have too many maintenances over one year spam clearly something is wrong, and you can quickly find out when you try online matches. First, you cannot choose your opponent out of a list like SF IV, the game automatically choose him for you, keeping in mind only connection stability measure by bars. When I played SF IV, a 3 bars connection was at least decent, on SF V the bars don't mean anything because you will suffer from lag or roll back even with a "4 bars" connection. Clearly that isn't a 4 bars connection and something is terrible wrong with the netcode that hasn't been revised by Capcom in all this time. And I'm just talking about Casual Matches, don't ever try Rank because is a rage quitting fest.
Overall, the game mechanics are really good but are overshadowed by a poor netcode that doesn't let you play the game at its finest, and since this is an online-only game I cannot recommended in this state. Maybe this will changed in the future, but we will also have more options in the fighting game genre, like Tekken 7, Injustice 2 and Marvel vs Capcom Infinite, so I don't see how we will return to Street Fighter V.

I can't give this game a totally 100% positive review so take the thumbs up with a grain of salt.
While it's fun to play there is too much emphasis on the honor system and too many players know it.
I can't say that there aren't any honest players out there but in all seriousness the number of people who actually play fairly are few and far between especially people with larger friends lists.
One of the biggest rules the game employs is NO OUTSIDE CHAT. This includes, Facebook chat, skype, etc and is to keep the game fair. Now, if you're in a game and six of the fifteen players are Skyping that's six people who can gang up and take the remaining eight down without having to worry about being killed by the Veteran or being shot by the Vigilante. Random chance or not this is a HUGE advantage over the other players and ruins the whole experience.
With that being said the game, when layed properly, is fun and can become addicting to a scary level. It allows for critical thinking and can sometimes give you an adrenaline rush when your character's life is on the line and sweating out the fear of being accused regardless of being accused correctly or not.
For what they're asking it's worth it but in the end you risk being consumed by the hivemind of cheaters who will ruin the game for you at some point or another.

This game is not terraria. comparing it terraria is pretty much meaningless, the only thing they really have in common is that they are  both 2D. Starbound focuses on space technology, quests, and role playing while terraria focuses on exploration and adventure.
Starbound has very good building mechanics and atmosphere. The sound track is absolutely lovely and good enough to listen on its own. However Starbound lacks content compared to the vast size of the universe. This used to be a much bigger problem, but they have slowly been scaling back the randomness of the universe and increasing content. Its not really like Starbound lacks content, but that as a player you have to visit more worlds to find it. The vast majority of time playing this game could be spent just searching for a specific species. going from planet to planet, hoping there is a village or outpost there. One benifite though is that everyone is in the same universe, and some users have begun indexing the planets they visit which can assist other players hoping to find specific things.
A final tip though, start making a base as soon as you start. You might be able to fit all your stuff in your ship, but it will not be as fun and will be very cramped.
This game is most definitely a work in progress. However i am now confident that it will continue evolving and is worth a playthrough. Just don't be looking for a replacement for terraria.

My favorite part of Dominique Pamplemousse is probably what polarizes it most: that "trying hard to look like you're not trying hard" sort of style. The crude choppy claymation, the characters singing with the quality of a middle school musical, severely shoehorned rhymes, it's something that you'll find charming or downright annoying.
Next is the setting, the style is clearly made too look like 1940's black and white crime dramas, and includes most of the tropes. BUT you get these references that clearly place this in present day (twitter, auto-tune, etc.), and the dissonance that this creates is as unique as it is hilarious.
All of the plot exposition is in song, which as I've said before you'll love or hate. Each character has their own melody that reflects their personality. The plot itself, however, isn't very remarkable and you'll see the twist coming a mile away.
The gameplay is definitely the weakest element of the game, very simple point and click mechanics and puzzles that aren't very difficult to solve, it's just a means to an end to carry the exposition.
Oh, and the main character is genderqueer, which I wasn't expecting. The game doesn't really make this a main part of the story or anything, it's just a passing fact, which I found pretty cool. And the way they deflect other characters' prodding question as to their sex/gender is both masterful and hilarious.

Dominique Pamplemousse is a very easy game with a short play time and few puzzles. That statement doesn't sound too appealing, so why would I recommend it?
It is unique. Visually the game is pleasing and pictured from simple cardboard and plasticine type models. The main interest in the game is the singing of the characters. They sing in a kind of poetic way and with voices that are clearly meant to confuse certain issues. The main character him/herself is rather an enigma. One voice sounds just like the character 'Rudi' from Steve Wright's Radio 1 afternoon show of the late eighties / early nineties ('Let me innn, Let me innn')
The story itself is straightforward, though with a couple of neat twists and turns. It's probably almost impossible to fail in this game as it mostly told through exhausting all the dialogue options. There are a couple of easy puzzles in there too though.
I honestly don't think I could have stood the game had it been much longer, as the voices are of limited appeal after a while, but for the hour and a half to two hours it takes to play it, this was thankfully not an issue.
There is an interesting choice to be made at the end, which I guess gives it some replay value.
For the low price, it's a good couple of hours worth of entertainment.

This game is a real love-letter to most things sci-fi/point n' click adventure games! If you're a total nerd for such things, like I am, you'll enjoy the many, many references to all sorts of classics in these genres.
PROS:
- very funny dialogue
- amusing characters
- interesting storyline, quite unique really
- great protagonist
- top-notch voice acting
- nice animation style
- pretty cool soundtrack
- mostly fair puzzles that don't leave you groping for a walkthrough if you just acquit yourself!
- at least 20 hours of gameplay, even for the experienced adventurer (I hope!)
CONS:
- a little repetitive in terms of the environments/jokes, but this is necessary because of the story structure
- the jokes are often a bit puerile and not as witty/accessible as I'd like to see
- I don't really care about swearing, but sometimes it's a bit over the top
- dialogue puzzles can be a bit too long, but I prefer inventory puzzles so I'm biassed
WARNINGS:
- adult themes throughout
- slightly nasty animation sometimes (gore, vomit)
- a lot of expletives
As you can see, personally I love this game, I was scraping the barrel a bit for the CONS, that section was more my attempt to try to imagine things from others' perspectives. This game is fully recommended here.

At its best, Blackwake is one of the funniest games I've ever played.  I personally prefer those moments where you have a crew with a good sense of humor than to just win the round. With such a crew, it doesn't even matter if your ship is sinking and everything is going down the drain, You'll laugh loudly in the process and have the time of your life. These moments have been fairly common to me while playing, but it all comes down to using the mic yourself and at least let out a "yaaar" once in a while.
You don't have to be social in Blackwake, and it's possible to play the game without the use of a microphone. but the game is made with communication in mind so it's a must if you want to get the full experience. Other players are mostly happy as long as you're able to tell your crew that you need supplies downstairs, follow captains orders and basic stuff like that.
To be somewhat effective in this game, you really need a captain that knows what they're doing and a crew that are willing to do the orders they bark out. Playing as a crew member you'll be spending your time scouting for eneny ships, firing and reloading cannons and repairing the ship, sails and killing erupting fire with buckets of water..The tasks are simple but when those cannonballs start flying through your ship and you run around working those holes, you'll be thankful for the simplicity, because it can get pretty intense, at least with a headset. There's also the possibility of locking down enemy ships with grappling hooks to finish it off and the other way around. Ths is where your weapons get useful
Playing as the captain of a ship is different and in some sense more challenging than crew member. You'll need some ability to manage multiple people and tell them what to do and when to do it. And you MUST have a microphone and the will to use it if/when playing as captain on populated servers. Nobody likes a silent captain. Good captains keep the crew informed about their actions in time for the crew to be prepared and ready..
You'll spend most of your time in one position steering the ship in position to fire the broadside cannons on the enemy as well as evading incoming threats by staying out of their range and the angle of their devastating broadside cannons. This is the easy part. The real challenge isn't that or the enemy ships, it's your crew and how you manage it. The difference between firing off a full broadside at the right moment and individual cannons firing off cannonballs at their own convenience is the difference between winning a round or losing it.  Take control and demand respect. Your crew should only fire the cannons when you say so.
It's a type of game I jump in and out of for an hour or two rather than a game I play for full evenings and nights, but I fully recommend this game for its simple yet amazing gameplay and hilarious approach.

And the game never provides hints that you should do any of this - all you know is that you have to distract a shop clerk.
Earlier in the game, you have to break a globe. To do that, you have to use the right object on the right precise spot on the globe. But that's not quite enough, as doing that perfectly will still result in the game indicating you've done the wrong thing. Before it will work - before you get even a hint that you've done the right thing, figured the puzzle out - you have to successfully find the one "Figure" in a huge mass of "Figures." The "Figure" looks no different than the "Figures" and you have no way of knowing that you have to find the "Figure," but you will not be allowed to proceed in the game, even to do the exact thing you should be doing, until you happen to accidentally run your mouse over that one "Figure" amidst the larger zone of "Figures".
That's how the game works - although all adventure games should include some fun trial and error potential, this game takes it to ludicrous levels. Randal's Monday is everything that's ever been wrong with puzzles in adventure games.
Granted, the plot gets interesting as you get further into it, and the Clerks connection is very cool, but the adventure gameplay is terrible, the jokes fall flat, and the main character is too much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to possibly sympathize with. All of the geek-culture references the advertising highlights are certainly present - not particularly funny nor worked into the plot at all - they're just kind of there, like a random picture of Donkey Kong on a calendar. Oh, look, it's Donkey Kong. Do you care? No, because you haven't yet figured out that you have to use the glue on the phone after you use the razor on the glue.
Lots of potential, but it's just not very fun to play.
