I backed Trackless on Fig and later  tested the early beta and RC.
Trackless is a good atmospheric game with simularities to Shadow Gate and Kings Quest. It takes two of the best aspects of both games and merges them with an interesting, and often gorgeous art style, and beautifully haunting OST.
Trackless uses text parsing in the form of (mostly) verbs to solve various puzzles. Where it differs from Kings Quest and Shadow Gate is in the use of typing in specific single verbs. The more complex the verb the higher the score. There is no score cap as in Kings Quest and the game is in a 3rd person 3D format with some 2D art mixed in.
Scoring higher points gets you credits which are used to purchase various items in the game world. These items lead can lead to aiding in puzzle solving and completing acheivments. Some are also just for fun. I would have liked to see more items to spend some of the credits on but there is a fair amount.
The puzzles, for the most part, are easy and enjoyable. The challenge comes from finding more obscure verbs, but you can get away with the use of simple ones. For puzzle depth you can get out of it what you want to put into it. It has a sliding scale difficulty based solely on the player and how much effort they want to put into finding better verbs. I think this is a unique, and interesting, approach to difficulty scaleing. My only critscism to the puzzles is I found some verbs that were not accepted :P But I can't expect every related verb to be in the games libraries!
The art and atmosphere are exellent but it is mixture of being really great to more simplistic. It is executed well however and really works with the atmosphere of the game. All the NPC and lot of the objects you interact with are rendered in a 2D format. I applaud the method used to execute this nicely and it makes for a unique art aesthetic.
There are some minor bugs but nothing that breaks the game much :D. They actually make it quirky and fun and I would not go so far as to really think of them as bugs. They add a fun dimension to the game exploration. There are regular save points at specific locations should you encounter one. All the game breaking bugs have been fixed and Aubrey is very "on the ball" about addressing any issues.
The game itself is linear but has multiple endings and some branching story archs. The game is on a track but is executed in such a way that it feels semi open. There are some very cool easter eggs and some of them are difficult to find. I played through the game multiple times to fully appreciate everything it has to offer.
The music is outstanding and composed and implimented in such a way as to make the atmosphere really stand out. I can think of several moments where the haunting track mixed with visuals were memorable. Like some scene in a film that you just could never forget and has stuck with you for years. The ambient sound effects are subtle and sometimes have to be strained to hear. But the music track fades out for these moments and you can hear the wind blowing on the plains and in the mountains, hear the waves lapping against the shore, or the water dripping in a cave.
The VO are not the greatest. Mostly due to the quality of the recording equipment and the area recorded in. But the acting is ok. One of the actors is by a professional and that acting is good. I dont feel the VO detracts from the game and is optional.
The story is excellent but I wont talk about it because of spoilers. But I commented to Aubrey that this game reminded me a lot of Robert Silverburg's Kindoms of the Wall. The stories themselves are very dissimilar but they share a certain thematic event and an alieness to them.
Trackless is a hard game to rate...as is any indie game. I dont put much stock in number ratings. I think the commentaries are much more important.  But I can say I would give this game an 8/10. With the break down being
Story 10
Atmosphere 10
Music and ambient sound 10
Art 8 or 9
Voice acting 7 or 8
Puzzle quality 10
Overall fun 10

Current Playtime: 68 hours.
The most recent entry to the Fallout franchise as of 2017, and at the same time one of the worst according to a lot of people. To me - a first time player of the series - the game made a very mediocre impression at best. While I really wanted to enjoy the game to get my fun out of the money, I really can't say it was that fun overall.
The setting is usual for the Fallout Franchise; Taking place in post-apocalyptic America, this time in Boston/Massachusetts. While the setting is great and still fresh, the game makes it really hard to enjoy the world and it's narrative, the latter not being very complex to begin with. It feels dumbed down, and as a lot of veterans to the series will tell you, the roleplaying elements of Fallout 4 are almost gone or vague to the point of taking away the player's control to predict what your character will say when you choose a dialogue option.
Another stone in the pathway is the poor optimization on PC. When first running the game, I had problems keeping the game at 20 FPS. Used some optimization fixes, and even then it never got me above 60 FPS. And that's sad considering that my PC can run Overwatch on Medium settings, but not Fallout 4 on lowest settings!
Speaking of the game's technical problems, the performance isn't the only thing that might bother people. Animations look extremely stiff as well, and that wouldn't even be that much of a problem if the questlines and dialogues were as varied and complex as in New Vegas, but they aren't. As mentioned above, the new dialogue system alongside vague dialogue options pretty much kill off the roleplaying aspect.
Another thing that kind of kills the roleplaying aspect is the fact that your choices do not matter, if you get choices at all, and that you cannot decide what kind of character you want to be. Even if you don't want to, your character will have goals and motivations that the story will progress towards, although you may not care about it at all, therefore taking away your ability to roleplay the way you want like you could in previous games.
And last but not least; The combat gameplay. The guns are extremely generic. Out of my head, I can only remember seeing less than 15 gun types in the entirety of the game so far, excluding special reward guns that can only be found once. So even the gunplay can't make up for it, especially because most guns feel like you are stinging your enemy at best.
The only real upside that was memorable about the game for me was the Soundtrack played by your Pip Boy. However, when I looked up some of my favourite songs, I realized that some have been included in Radio Mods for Fallout 3 and New Vegas years before Fallout 4s release, so it is possible that Bethesda didn't even look up those songs themselves.

+ Art style is decent enough
+ References to just about every cult phenomenon you can think of (although the constant references get pretty grating after a while)

Overall, it might be worth picking up in a sale if you love point and clicks and have exhausted your Steam backlog, particularly if you fancy a more adult themed (yet still light hearted) p&c game - there aren't that many out there. Otherwise, there are better games for you to spend your money and time on.

TL;DR: great characters and humor, with occasionally flawed puzzle design
Randall Hicks is the perfect character to star in a modern point-and-click adventure.  This self-serving young everyman is part Marty McFly and part Philip J. Fry, and the game's writers would give a knowing nod if they heard those references.  All the sci fi pop culture humor works for two reasons.  First,  it's not 'inside jokes' only hardcore nerds will get, and second, the game doesn't make the references, by themselves, into punchlines.
So the writing, characters, and dialogue are great.  The gameplay, however, suffers from some unintuitive puzzles.  For example...
*SPOILER*
You acquire a dried out marker, and you need to get it working again.  So my first thought is, get it wet.  There are multiple water sources, and they're 'real' interactive objects used in other puzzles.  But nope, they don't work for the marker.  So my second thought is, it needs more of a solvent, like alcohol.  There's a bar you can enter, and you can get the bartender to give you drinks!  Does that work?  Nope!  But is alcohol at least the right liquid?  Yep!
I'm stumped - I can't form any other logical connections.  What's the solution?  Go to your friend's apartment (but only the second time you go there).  Go into his kitchen, and look for a mug.  Not a beer mug, but a coffee mug.  And not that mug, that's just noninteractive scenery.  Click on the other, identical-looking mug.  That one's interactive, and it has lefterover booze in it you can use to reconstitute the marker.
I don't know what the designers were thinking on that one.  There's no 'hook' to use the player's reasoning skills.  Thankfully, there's a built-in hint system, and it's apparently enough for people since nobody's written a full walkthrough.
There's nothing that makes me more sick than seeing game corporations use modding for their marketing campaign.

This is the first game I'm writing a review for... because in my opinion it's the first game that feels important enough for me to write a review about. I'll try and keep it spoiler-free but if you haven't played the game yet then stop reading right now, cause it's hard to get past spoilers reading the reviews to this game. This is a game you can't inform yourself about, you have to experience it.
I was lucky. I went in completely blind seeing this as a 'psychological horror game' in my recomendations list... and I'm hella glad about that. That was by far the most intense experience I have ever had in a game. Simply because it caught me off guard. Usually these cheap horror games provide little to no story, tons of jumpscares, 1 hour playtime and mediocre level design, which I can look past as long as I'm entertained and as long as they are cheap enough.
This game is the complete oposite of that. It has a great and important storyline, a playtime of roughly 6 hours, decent voice acting, memorable map design and takes horror to another level than just simple jumpscares, because the story itself terrifies you.
And as someone else mentioned before: (That would be where the spoilers beginn)
Having praised the story now, let's talk about the game a bit:
You walk around a dreamlike world with different levels. You're Enola and your task is to find your girlfriend. You solve puzzles to get further in the game, and to get the next story pieces. The gameplay is just about fine, I didn't experience any bigger bugs or anything worth mentioning, I'm used to Indiegames. I'm used to old engines and graphics, so I don't even bother complaining about it, I rather look at the game and ask myself: given the engine and the graphics, does the game look and play good?
And it does, the level design is always memorable, props weren't reused too often and the gameplay was decent... nothing really to complain here, maybe that some levels were a bit to big and took ages to explore.
The puzzles you are given vary in type, some easy, some hard, and I don't remember any of them not working (maybe some restarts but as I said... used to that)
Looking around the levels you find documents and lamps which tell you the story. The voice acting and writing was really good, I liked it a lot.
With a length of 6 hours the game was well worth its money. Being a story driven walking/puzzle simulator though it felt streched at some points, but given the story I was motivated enough to go on.
So to sum it up:
- a 'straight-to-the-guts'-brutal and important story
- decent level design
- voice acting
- puzzles
- 6 hours game time... on the one hand a lot for the money, on the other hand too long for a game you should finish in one sitting
- some minor bugs
- the endings... can't keep up with the story itself
I really recommend playing this game, and also if you get tired... forcing yourself to finish it. It has such an important story that needs to be experienced by more people, it's really eye-opening and makes you think about a lot of things after you've finished it. It's 1,50 on sale (I wish I would have paid more, no joke) so just grab it and give it a try, but be prepared for a disturbing and in many ways different horror game. If you can look past the graphics and some minor bugs and if you are an Indie-Horror-Fanboy like me, you shouldn't even think about skipping this game.
I wish all of luck and success for the developer's future projects, I hope they can keep up with this little masterpiece!

Foul Play... where do I start?
Well for one, this game was a risk to release. Not that it's unfinished, but it would probably be disregarded as "another  mindless brawler". But it is not that. This game is amazing. It isn't perfect, but it is awesome when you play it right.
Yes there is a right and wrong way to play this. Before I get to that though here are the pros and cons.
PROS
Fantastic and humorous storyline.
Believable characters who also have awesome dialogue.
Original concept of the audience being your score, also you can't die on bosses that would be otherwise frustrating.
Fair but challenging enemies.
Co-Op actually has benifits other than playing with your friend.
Awesome combos that are unique
Parrying is the best thing in brawlers since magic in Castle Crashers.
Those 4th wall breaks do.
Extremelly fluent combat that never cancels your moves unless you get hit.
The art style is utterly beautiful and fits perfectly with the game.
CONS
Sometimes the joke of being in a play is too forced.
Getting high combos can be hard on large enemies when it doesn't tell you you can't parry them.
The learning curve suddenly jolts up, although it smooths out later on.
The crowd cares very little for a climax. Why can't you get bonus points for being in a tough spot then pulling through.
By itself rating 8.5/10
But there is a way to play the game that just makes your time with the game the best. Be immersed. It is hard since it constantly reminds you that it is a game. But once you feel like the character, the game truly feels like a hunt against daemons. Get a friend to play this. You two voice the characters like you really mean it. Once you feel like you are in the game, it feels like you are preforming for a live audience about YOUR adventures. This game will leave you wanting more.
With friend and immersion 10/10

Rated negative because of Creation Club. Bethesda, if you want to reward modders for their hard work, you're better off hiring them as freelancers and sell their creations as an outright DLC. Microtransaction-style implementation has earned the hate of so many people, it would be foolish to launch another attempt without expecting outrage from the community. You have been warned.
That said, here's my honest take on Fallout 4.
My god. Where to begin...
Main story, compared to the likes of New Vegas, is nothing to write home about, with the exception of Far Harbor. Limited dialogue choices make for a stricter characterization of the protagonist.
But the rest. Weapon and armor customization, settlement creation. A big, highly-detailed world to roam in. Fast, fluid, intuitive gunplay. Surprises in almost every new location to be found. Enemies that continue to challenge the player no matter how high their level is, keeping them alert almost all the time.
And then there are the mods.
They used to call these kind of games a sandbox. Fallout 4 is no sandbox - it's a huge desert.
Real recommendation: get it on a sale. It's a good game otherwise, just marred by questionable marketing tactics.

TL;DR: Fun co-op, great presentation, but shallow gameplay and a short campaign not worth multiple playthroughs.
The presentation of the game is without a doubt its best feature: the backgrounds are shifted by stage hands, extras in costume pretend to be werewolves, and every object earned or lore page unlocked has flavorful text included.  The set pieces are wonderful, and you'll find yourself chuckling at the background gags or soaking in the atmospheric cutouts of spooky castles and ancient pyramids.
It's a pretty standard beat-em-up with a token leveling system in place that grants you more moves, though you might not find the advanced skills as useful as your basic starting countestrikes.  This game's mastery is based around countering your enemy's moves when they telegraph them, and its very satisfying to contunually float when you are able to chain multiple air grabs off of different enemies.
Unfortunately strategies for the levels and bosses are pretty basic, and when you've seen the same lines of text many times in order to get a level's achievements, the story's charm starts wearing thin.  Co-op mode is definitely the way to go, as single player becomes repetitive quickly.  The game is great for a playthrough with a buddy, but is probably too shallow to make getting all of the achievements much fun.

~* Spoiler Free Review *~

Gameplay

The gameplay itself is fairly simple--assuming you use the guide. The puzzles were just challenging enough to be fun (for me, as a casual gamer), but I can't imagine playing without the guide and not getting frustrated, as many of the puzzles are not intuitive. Of course, if you're a hardcore gamer, you're probably going to have an easier time figuring things out, but I have a low frustration point and found the guide immeasurably useful. Beyond that, mechanics are simple--basically walking simulator/point-and-click. The atmosphere was on point, and there was just enough interesting backdrop to make a little exploration fun. There are a lot of glitches, but I will not cover them here as they are generally well-covered in other reviews as well as the community guide. Having said that, none of them were game-breaking for me, merely mildly annoying is all.

Story

And here is where this game absolutely excels. The story is dark and honest, and I found myself getting pulled deeper and deeper into the devastating and yet oddly hopeful world the devs created. I agree with many other reviews that sexual abuse survivors should tread extremely carefully. As one myself, I thoroughly enjoyed the story but, as evidenced by my hours played, had to step away often to take a breather and at one point, my anxiety medication. That said, if you feel you can play this game and be safe, please do. However, I think the story is even more important to those who have not experienced what survivors have. It offers a deep glimpse into how evil can sometimes beget evil, and may help others to understand how hard it is to fight the darkness inside you, particularly when the darkness is not of your own making. Do you escape the monster and carry on with your life, or do you let the hate inside you grow and consume you until there's nothing left? It may be easier to make this choice within in the safety of a video game than in real life, but as far as Enola goes? Not that much easier. Thanks for reading and play with care!

To be clear on this point, I did receive this game for free, however, it was from one of those sites where you enter in to game giveaways. In other words, I didn't get After The End: The Harvest from the developer.
After The End: The Harvest is a sprawling open-world game with graphics on par with SNES and the Sega CD consoles. It is heavily story-oriented, though, for those who care more about running around & doing what you want the way you want, then you'll be pleasantly surprised with how the game doesn't try to grab you by the arm, yanking you from one story-objective to the next. Do you want to play as a good, altruistic character? You can. Do you want to let loose with your inner Darth Vader? You can. Would you rather walk that grey line between the two while giving the middle finger to Jedi- & Sith-types both? You can.
There are a plethora of quests (almost all optional), pet hunting (a la Pokemon), many forms of weapons, spells, & gear. This includes things like space craft, grappling hooks, swords, laser guns, ship upgrades & gear for your pets. Yes, like Pokemon, you can equip a pet to follow & fight with you on your travels through the galaxy. Also, like the rpgs of the past, there isn't an encumbrance or slot limit for what you're carrying. Both your character & your pets level up while completing quests, slaying monsters,... and by killing the occasional space cop or innocent if you're of the mind.
Also, did I mention that this game has crafting? No? Well, then let me elaborate on this mechanic a bit: This isn't a game where you harvest plants & minerals. Instead, you loot. (There's a lot to loot.) All crafting takes place by combining two items together. For instance, if you need a lockpick, then you craft (if I remember correctly) wood & a steel rod (I've a bad memory, sorry if this is incorrect) & now that pesky door isn't a problem anymore. You have this spell, yet it isn't quite what you want. You can combine it with another spell/component & now you have a hybrid spell.
There are a large number of planets & moons that you can visit via your legally- or illegally-acquired space vessel (which, btw, aren't carbon copies of each other). There are space battles, pet battles with certain NPCs & so much more that I've yet to even stumble across.
I've played this game through most of beta & have seen where the game started, watched it continue to evolve, & where it has ended up. I have to be honest here & say that, in many ways, this game has qualities reminicent of the Bethesda Fallout games & The Elder Scrolls games. Obviously, After The End: The Harvest isn't a 3D game, yet it has some similar game & gameplay elements rooted in its playstyle, options, & spirit.
This game is very reasonably priced considering what you get & the replayability it offers. Also, the developer has written new systems for the RPGMaker game engine since it couldn't do certain things that the dev wanted for his game (e.g., space battles for one). The developer, going by the handle TheSworn, is extremely active on the forums, answering general questions, giving tips, responding to bug reports & quickly pushing out fixes. Oftentimes, these come in the form of small hotfixes (typically an hour or two after the bug was reported) or they are bundled with a larger, scheduled patch if it is very near release.
In short, I greatly recommend this game for those who appreciate a good story, tens of hours of gameplay (more if you do side quests or your own thing, such as catching all the pets, etc.), & if you like story quests that don't have only one outcome, but many based on how you have played the game so far & how you've previously interacted with the quest-giver or specific NPCs along the way.
I know that, at the time of this review, Steam lists my play time at 29.2 hours, however, oftentimes I'm playing After The End: The Harvest (among other titles) offline due to living in the sticks (literally, I'm in the middle of the woods) & the nearby town that I get my internet through is small & doesn't invest much in the phone/DSL lines, thus, my connection & connectivity are rather poor.

Review in Progress - written for early access version 0.9u3 - 29May2017
--- The game's description and screenshots are very accurate for what you're getting here: an expansive open-universe RPG with the look and feel of an old action-adventure SNES game. 17 hours in at this point and still very much driven to continue item scavenging, creature collecting, achievement hunting and just generally exploring for exploring's sake.
--- Among the BIGGEST selling points for After the End so far has been developer interaction. I thought it best to offer up a few questions and bugs into the forums and was immediately greeted with answers and bug fixes. There's not much more I could ask for in an Early Access game.
--- The game does still require some polish, though nothing that's made the game unplayable.
- New players are encouraged to read the game's manual (here on the store page or in the discussion forums) about the controls. There was a semi-frustrating amount of time setting my controller up and even still I require the help of JoyToKey to get things exactly how I want them. It's fine for me now, but most will likely require a little more effort than what ought to be a simple button-remapping options menu.
- My only other major complaint are the filters used during the night in the day/night cycle. The game provides you with a flashlight and lantern, but you're still going to have 90% of your vision interfered with (not by 'dark' per se, but more by a haze) during a large enough portion of gameplay (regardless of whether you're inside a structure or not).
- There are other smaller issues I can attribute to being in early access (some repeating merchants, a vague crafting system, weapon and combat balance) but again, nothing so off-putting as to prevent me from enjoying the experience... and surely nothing that the developers won't be interested in fixing.
--- The game itself really works for me. Once you're given control of your ship and a home base, you're tasked to hunt down the 4 titans, find helpful NPCs to bring back and complete a couple other optional sidequests for some early cash. However, these are merely suggestions on how to start; the universe is now yours to explore at this point.
- I've honestly had the most fun hopping from planet to planet at random. If you can't visit one due to an unfavorable climate (such as excessive heat or radiation), you explore elsewhere until you find the proper hull modifications that will let you move safely.
- Plenty of weapons to play around with: Melee, ranged with ammo, upgradable magic spells, an active pet, a kickass grappling hook that deals some respectable damage or simply hopping in your ship and tagging enemies on the open world from a distance.
- And it's all packaged into the standard RPG systems: Find and equip better gear, level up for better stats and complete quests for rewards and story advancement.
--- And for as much as I've played so far, I still feel like there's a lot to look forward to in terms of existing content and what's to come as the game develops towards a 1.0 version.
- Even from someone who's been burned by early access titles in the past, I'm more than willing to give a thumbs up to a title that feels like an enjoyable throwback with a developer who seems dedicated to actively making a better game.

I don't know if Chucklefish had some sort of staff change, if the lead developer of the game "Tiy" got amnesia'd somehow mid-development and had to pull a whole new concept out of his♥♥♥♥♥after forgetting how to make what they had keep going, or the five people on the Chucklefish page that kept commenting "when is the game coming out???" pressured the developers into releasing the game haphazardly, but the condition the game released felt like an enormous downgrade. Rather than finish up what they already had in order to get the game to a "finished" state, Chucklefish's idea was to instead, and suddenly, cut the project down in size by removing anything unfinished and haphazardly implement an out-of-the-blue "story" structure just to bridge the gap of missing parts.
Numerous things such as cosmetics, armor, weapons, biomes, planets, mobs, bosses, furniture, blocks, and even more were outright removed from the game for no reason other than the haphazard release date that Chucklefish forced themselves didn't leave time to complete them. Hell, some things that WERE actually complete were outright removed too for seemingly no reason. For example, originally, every race was able to craft a melee weapon of each type for each tier - an axe, spear, hammer, broadsword, shortsword, knife, and possibly others I'm forgetting. Not only this, but each race had a completely unique name and appearance for each weapon of each tier from the other, even if they were statistically identical. At release date, these were all removed for absolutely no mentioned reason; not only could only two weapons of a type be crafted per tier, but every race now shared the same generic melee weapon, bar Novakids. Also, a suprisingly unique mechanic amongst other survival-based sandboxes, a 'heat' mechanic, would be removed along with all survival mechanics during an alpha update but nowhere to be seen with the reimplementation of the survival difficulty at release.
Numerous promises were left unfufilled. Each playable race having their own unique opening, story and ending were gone in favor of the universally hated Terrene Protectorate. Each race having their own unique ability - Novakids casting a natural glow in the dark, Florans regenerating themselves in the sunlight - would be nowhere to be seen aside from the already added mechanic that Novakids could only craft guns and all other races could only craft melee weapons. Novakids, the seventh and fan-made race that was officially accepted and said to be as flush with the game as the other races when the game was finalized, would have no representation in the underwhelming "campaign," no villages or tenants to meet or recruit, and would even still be using placeholder inspect quotes. While the second and third issues would later be added post-release, the first has yet to be remedied. Additionally, it was once stated that beating the game without ever fighting would be possible; you'd be able to humbly live farming animal and plant products and selling them. In the final game, you can farm animal and plant products...using tedious processes that were made even MORE complicated from the alpha, and to either be sold for minimal pocket change compared to exploring and looting, or to be used to make weapons to fight with. Additionally, the customization system would go on to be jarringly dull; some cosmetic items would recieve a visual downgrade, the dyeing system would be added and extremely limited, and as stated above, cosmetic items would be removed for no concievable reason, limiting character personalization. But don't worry! They'd be replaced by new cosmetic items...that are either hideous backer-created cosmetics that look terrible, don't match with anything and are never worn by anone ever, or just the old sprites for removed armors with their stats stripped and rebranded as cosmetics.
Numerous perfectly functional mechanics would be reworked for no reason. In addition to the removal of what was made of the unique racial weapons and the heat mechanic, the tech system would be the biggest and easiest-to-note victim of this odd choice. What was once a diverse system that let the player customize themselves how they see fit and give them an advanced sense of control and fast movement that rivaled Minecraft's simplicity, or even surpassed Terraria's and its similar usage of movement-enhancing accesories like running boots or wings, would later become a clunky and watered-down niche that feels and looks like an afterthought in terms of functionality. What was once a lovely variety of seven-ish techs per slot, each with their own uses, would be boiled down into four, with one being a starter version of the tech, and the other three being complete upgrades and thus rendering the first completely irrelevant once the others are obtained. The four slots you once had to mix and match with near-complete freedom would later be decreased to essentially three, with one slot being locked into only having the progressional 'nano-protection' techs that protect the player from increasingly dangerous planetary atmospheres, and later exactly three when the envirnomental protection techs were turned into mandantory equippable items. The racial system of mechs initially planned, with each race having a Mech that could be built or deconstructed around them that matched their race, would be removed at launched and revived later as an unusual new system with mechs that resembled less of serious combat mechs and more of what looked like child-sized gundams that have a limited and non-rechargeable usage on planets, can't navigate doors, can't scale sharp terrain, can't interact with usable objects, and can't even be brought on the game's missions without modding.
Also, let's talk about that campaign. What was, as preached previously, originally going to be seven unique campaigns with unique cinematics, levels and fights that all intertwined at certain points and with Starbound's core exploration and sandbox elements would instead be a single, lazily-written story with cheesy, unimpresive characters, a laughable opening and ending that both end up meaning almost nothing that literally forces you to go out and aimlessly ♥♥♥♥ around until you miraculously manage to find all the♥♥♥♥♥♥the random hag in front of the giant laggy vortex in the Outpost wants you to find before sending you to one of the most thematically one-note levels ever made to fight through unbalanced enemies and environmental hazards that no matter your armor, can kill you in like three hits, only to go fight a boss that probably has less health and damage resistance than whatever the weakest normal enemy in the stage does, and only to have a miniscule chance to get an important rare weapon or trophy. There are only seven mandantory levels not counting the tutorial. Seven. Short. Levels. Worst of all, there's not even a way to truly reset the game without uninstalling it and reinstalling it; if you make a new character and go back to the outpost after beating the game, while the questline itself gets reset and the playeris free to do them over again, all the NPCs remain at the central area, able to buy things from and interact with, and the gate that teleports you to the final level and boss remains unsealed, allowing the annoyed player to simply go "♥♥♥♥ it" and sequence break right to the end of the game if they want.
This game could've been so much better.

Dark Gates is a grid-based party dungeon-crawler, with lite RPG elements.  It is essentially a virtual boardgame representation based on the 'classics' of many years ago.  The objective is to explore the dungeon reach the Dark Gates and destroy the "Unnamed" beast that threatens to destroy the lands.
Exploration take place on a procedurally created dungeon across multiple levels and resembles a grid containing rooms.  Encounters occur with creatures that can inhabit a tile. Encounter options consist of either: combat, negotiating or bribing.  Combat takes place using WEGO-UGO, otherwise the party can pass unhindered.  Characters attack using melee, ranged or magic spells.
Permadeath ensures characters die and leave the party.  Yet the game allows you to replace dead members of if you find it on your adventure, use the Resurrection spell to revive them.  As you progress you can find clues as to the location of the Dark Gates where your goal lies.
+ Randomly generated dungeon.  Albeit very similar as not much to distinguish one from another.
+ Get to choose your party from 20 or so archetypes.  You may recognize some very familiar faces! :)
+ Simple mechanics.  Quick gameplay.
+ Party gains gold and characters experience which can be used to upgrade their skills.
+ Easy to get into.
+ Straightforward to gain achievements.  Most can be gained quickly.
- No character generation.
- No loot to pick-up and inventory to equip characters from.
- Bare-bone interface/instructions, resulting in a steep learning curve at the very beginning.
- Either too short.  Or too long! Mostly because there is no point of reference telling you which staircase is the nearest to the Dark Gates.  Major oversight!
- Party position not saved.  Rather progress and state of the dungeon is.  You have to essentially re-trace previous steps and then continue.
- No mouse controls, 100% keyboard driven.
* Nice clean-cut artwork.
* A range of encounter options: Fight, Negotiate, Bribe; that are dependent on a range of character skills.
* Decent range of magic spells which are fixed but, can be added to through exploring the dungeon.
* Basic, if pretty animated combat & spell effects.
* Very limited party organization and configuration.
* Artwork, music & sounds combine well to generate a decent ambience.
* Its fairly replayable but, very repetitive!
I dont think this game will appeal to anyone but purists of old dungeon crawl boardgames, or this genre of video games.  Maybe if the game also allowed character generation and had a loot and inventory system it would be more of a game that I could recommend.
Overall its just too basic, too simplistic to grab the attention of modern-day gamers.  Unless youre like me and enjoy trying out and/or experiencing different games.  I liked it but you can be sure it will not be for most players.  It takes a brave developer to release a game like this, so Dark Gates should be admired for what it is!  Playing it was fun but only consider getting it if you feel the need to kill a few hours with a short, basic boardgame adaptation that is basically okay!

Personal Rating: 4.5/10
So normally with a negative review, I would just say it's a bad game and that I personally don't recommend it, but I'll make an effort to justify myself. Also, I would like to state that this should not discourage the developer from making games like this.
Pros:
+The game touches on the genre of dungeon crawling, which even though I find extremely boring and repetitive, has a following of retro gamers
+It is quite cheap (I got it for free)
Cons:
-The controls are entirely based on keyboard, which I assume is to give it an older feel. Even though other reviews say it's simple, the controls just to start a new game use a lot of keys that aren't obvious and you'll need guidance (6, 7, M, Space, etc.). Using enter would have been more obvious.
-There is no explanation! You start the game and are immediately prompted to select a team (The characters all look like they were created by a LotR fanatic btw). There is no intro, tutorial, or even small explanation about the stats you are looking at. They will  have some ability called "Dark Gates" that is never explained, but ends up being the ability to open doors in the dungeon without getting hurt (that aspect is the game's only unique feature). The effect of the stats is not explained at all, and there are also spells available for some characters. Thankfully, those are a bit more explained, but again, not having played the game before, the gravity of each one is quite mysterious. Also, the thing I assume is the "cost" of each spell is simply a number before its name, which if you don't pay attention, you'll mistake as just a numbering system.
-Since the game starts abruptly, there is no storyline given. There is no plot or quest. It just becomes pointless.
-The players to select are all preset instead of random. I found two humans that had all the same stats, except one had a slight advantage in agility. I'm sure if someone studied the game, they could determine the best picks for a "dream team". Also would make replay experience repetitive.
-I think this is a bug, but when I tried to load a save, I was basically prompted to the selection screen, but with the selections preset. That means I could select a completely new team, which seems like "cheating". Also, I was placed in the very start, even though the map still had my explored areas. Navigating tile by tile is already annoying, don't make me retrace my steps...
-Combat is a bit weird. I have to be careful with what I select. The characters frequently auto-play (due to there only being one attack option), but I was expecting to have to press Enter, and so I have made someone else do something right after. It is also hard to tell sometimes which character option is selected.
-The whole negotiation and bribing system doesn't make sense. The bribing system is in place to justify the need of looted gold from battles. The negotiation I assume was a feature to "spice up the game". I guess I'll just chat with the spider so it'll let me go? The one time it worked, a group of ghosts got scared. Is diplomacy about fear?
-Repetetive! The whole thing is simply walking down narrow aisles (full of dead-end, one-tile rooms which need to be opened with special skill cause they are DARK GATES!) and fighting hostile mobs (all your typical fantasy mob like spider, troll, ghost, dark knight, etc.) that progressively get harder by having higher health and attack power (not smarter AI though).
All in all, I would not spend any money on this. This game seems like one that should be available to play online for free. It doesn't have advanced graphics, or large memory space needed, or special features, so I don't see why it needs to be a stand-alone. It is not hard to program and the graphics match the quality of resources available to developers for free online. Even free, I don't think I'll ever play this game again.

The fourth entry in the series, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Lockdown is a tactical shooter that was released for PS2, Xbox, Gamecube in 2005. There was even a mobile phone version of the game released the same year. The game was slightly redesigned and then released for PC in 2006; the changes included the removal of sections that contained sniper gameplay and story-related cutscenes, along with the inclusion of redesigned levels and... better helmets.
Lockdown takes place in 2009 and pits the Rainbow force up against Global Liberation Front, a worldwide terrorist organization that have stolen a man-made nanotech virus that is code-named Legion. The virus itself is an aerosol that induces fatal hemorrhaging in those who are unlucky enough to come into contact with it. Through 16 missions, it's up to the Rainbow team to eliminate the Global Liberation Front and stop the spread of Legion before it claims too many casualties. The story, for a tactical shooter, is pretty solid and it's told through a series of debriefing videos at the start of each mission.
That being said, the plot of the game is pretty well the only thing going for it, everything else is completely horrid. The enemy AI is among the worst that I've ever seen in any title, often they will stand there and stare at you while you massacre them; if they do manage to finally pull the trigger, their chances of making contact with you are extremely slim... even at point-blank range. Not only that, but the three squad members that you command are as useful and spry as a bag of bricks; their AI is almost just as bad, they often get stuck on each other, walk in front of you as you're firing, ignore your "follow" commands, and more. Their aim is also terrible, but slightly better than the enemy. If you do not tell them to breach and clear, they're happy to stand there and let you do 100% of the dirty work.
For those that are unaware, older Rainbow Six games did not have regenerating health, but instead three blocks of health that must last you for the entire mission. Even though the enemies have a slim ratio to smack you with a bullet, it almost always seems like when they finally do land a hit, you're down for the count; this is more of an issue if you have two out of three health blocks left. The damage that you receive is very inconsistent. This can be tedious and frustrating, since instead of having checkpoints, Lockdown relies on a manual save system. If you haven't saved your game before dying, you must start from the very beginning of the level.
The badness doesn't just stop at shoddy AI with characters who will sometimes dance and flail around like they're on speed, but the level design is absolutely awful. The only thing that the cramped spaces do, is cause you and your team to fall all over each other and make it that much harder to get through doorways. There's also something that constantly blocks your field of vision, such as giant trees, that makes it impossible to see some enemies before it's too late; with their wonderful AI, they're happy to wait until you're right up on them before they do anything at all.
Another down note... the optimization of Lockdown is screwed up at best. My game consistently fluctuated from anywhere between 40-200 FPS at any given time, all the while still seeming to stutter as I walked. If VSync is enabled, it looks like you're hobbling with a broken ankle. The game also crashed on me if I experienced repeated deaths; I guess it finally gave up on me.
At the end of the day, the only thing good about Lockdown is its theme song, the rest is utter garbage. In fact, this game really has it all covered when it comes to being awful; inconsistent damage received, crappy enemy and squad AI, bad level design, shoddy optimization, crashing, enemies that are too easy to kill, and for some reason the menu of the game is the only part that won't render in 1080p... go figure. Only if you're a hardened Tom Clancy and/or Rainbow Six fan should you pick this title up. It shouldn't even be bought as a joke to see how many laughs you can get out of it, it'll just turn to frustration by your tenth one-shot.

Rainbow Six Lockdown is the 4th entry in Rainbow Six franchise. It actually was made for consoles first, in 2005 by Red Storm. It would then be ported to PC in 2006, apparently reworked somewhat. But not enough, thus you still control only one squad and there is no planning stage. But hey, look at those helmets on rainbow six characters! Apparently, that was number one complaint from fans about console version. Quite a priority.
It also was released on Xbox, Gamecube and PS2. Yea, they are different enough from PC, at least levels aren't all that same.
Also, I think that this is v1.0 version, while there exist a v1.1 patch. But it only seems to fix multiplayer things.
Multiplayer community here is quite dead. Actually, online multiplayer servers are dead. Ubisoft shut them down. Some say that they could login with UPlay account, didn't work for me last time I tried. But oh well, still can use some programs, you know them.
And well, what can I say. The game got literally "consolized", as much as I hate this term. No planning. Only one squad. You can play only as main hero. Everybody has huge health now, unless headshot. Infinite pistol ammo, even though it makes sense gameplay-wise. Game became nothing more but a generic lame action realistical shooter that we had more than enough in 2000s. To be honest, Rainbow Six ports on consoles already had similar thing going for them, but it's the first time developers decided to bring this to PC where it's not really needed.
Which wouldn't be so bad had AI had not been so terrible. I am mostly talking about teammates AI. If you take a look at their AI separate from gameplay, then it's quite an improvement, as they learned to take cover and peek around corners, instead of just following you in straight line. But once you actually play it, then oh boy. They have messed up priority, ignoring terrorist with shotgun, they are often incompetent with their shooting and they can be way too happy to rush forward, often getting headshotted by you.
Hostages also are quite horrific to deal with. They seem to have same AI as teammates, happy to rush into next room and take cover. Heck, they are annoying like no other tactical game ever had, as policeman hostages would whine "police, here!" and "somebody help me!" while following you.
And you don't have as much tactics anymore. After all, you control only one squad, not even individual members. And with their horrible AI, you are pretty much a lone wolf with few lives walking behind you. The only times that they matter is that they can take orders on how to enter through the door. Shotgun, hammer, breach, grenades. They still screw up grenades, which also aren't as good as used to be either, as flashbang works like grenade that stuns, with small radius. And even then, teammates may die embarresingly during cleaning of room, easily.
Since there is little left of tactical part, they could at least make action really good. But nope. Developers decided that PC audience are some crazy hardcore people who hate any story or cutscenes fluff with all their heart and removed it pretty much in this version of a game. We don't even get intel to pick up anymore in these linear levels, so exploration feels empty, as tehre are no pickups at all. Which harms level design that is linear with some pathways.
Not to mention that you will easily blast through the game as it now allows quickscamming of save and loading. And motion detecter with regenerative battery, which I abused heavily.
Also, yea, it also includes modes like Terrorist Hunt, Terrorist Hunt in reverse map, Lone Wolf. Barely noticed difference. And multiplayer, which is dead, so no commers.
Overall, a game on PC that lacks on both tactical and action fun. Just a generic realisticalish lame shooter.

I want to start of with saying that the game isn't bad, it's not good either.  If it were a bad game I could come into the reviews and talk about how the movement is clunky, or how a psychological horror should contain some horror, or how the story quickly became convolunted.  If it were a good game I could praise the psychological aspect, that tackled questions of justified homicide, or the story-telling, which actually was fairly good despite the lacking plot.  If the game were either of these, it would make writing this review so much easier.  Sadly, the game falls into the mediocre section.
In Enola, you play as Enola as she discovers the truth about her lover's past life.  It's about living through the painful memories of said loved one, from her first love, to her abusive job, to her most painful of memories.  And it ends with forgiveness or revenge.  Multiple endings and I managed to end on the 'Happy' ending.
The problem of Enola is not with the actual plot, I actually enjoyed it when I understood it, the problem lays with the pacing.  One moment I'm in a mansion, the next I'm in a church, than I found myself in a factory filled with 'bad people', murderers, rapists, people just doing their jobs, etc.  The lamps and letters, which are the primary plot devices, barely helped with the explanations on where I was or why I was there.  Half the time I didn't know if it was Enola, her lover, or Tony the Tiger speaking to tell me about the awesome new toys that they had devised for my displeasure (I apologize, the developer pointed out my mistake, there are names displayed when activating the lamps).  The overarching story may have made some form of sense, but the settings barely did.
Here's the problem, that's the only thing I can really talk about when it comes to the game.  The jumpscares are standard, the gameplay is Amnesia-like, the voice-acting is subpar, all of these are minor complaints, or praises, that are usually tossed into an opinion at the last minute to get the word count up.  There is nothing to point out about this game, no fantastic characters, no horrifically bad models, nothing.
Here comes the part I hate most, can I recommend the game?
As it stands, the game is a perfect example of Average.  Can I recommend average?  With so many games in the psychological horror genre your game needs a little something to stand out in the crowd and Enola does not offer anything different.
Unfortunatly, unless it's on sale and you've money to throw away, I do not recommend Enola for casual or hardcore gamers.
Thank you for your time.

In response to the developer.
First: I apologize.  You are right, the lamps have names displayed.
Second:  I think the best comparison of your game is a cross of Dear Esther and Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  There was so much focus on making Dear Amnesia that you forgot what made the games special in the first place.  In Amnesia there's pacing and slow progression.  Our initial confusion is explained in timely order where the story is coherently told as we progress further and further into it's madness.
Imagine a fine restaurant where you order a ribeye steak.  Does it arrive with mac'n'cheese, chocolate pudding, and an Icehouse beer?  No, it comes with potatoes, spring salad, and fine Cabernet Sauvignon.  Is the former dish good?  Sure, but the latter pairs them.  It complements them, it adds a sense of logical progression where each of the dishes inspires and fulfils the others.  Amnesia is this fine dish, all the elements, the setting, the gameplay, the scares, they all work in tangent with each other.  They make sense.  Amnesia is not a overcooked sirloin with american cheese heaped onto it.
I can understand the appeal of making a 'game' like Dear Esther, which I feel is what you wanted to do before you realized that throwing stones into holes has better gameplay than DE.  But DE is an experience, it's purely a story and that's okay.  Why?  Because it knows that it is a story.  There are no subpar puzzles in DE, no sudden changes in scenery, and no wild jumpscares where one has to mash their keyboard to escape.  Honestly, DE feels so nice because it feels like they made the world then made individual stories to explain the part of the world you are in while staying true to the overarching story; old man explores his home for the last time.  You've got the simple overarching story down ("Enola discovers her lover's dark past" is nicely simple), but the world is messy and the individual stories become lost in confusion.
Am I confusing you?  If so, I once again apologize.  Sometimes the problem with one game is best explained with a comparision to a similar formula.  I appreciate your acceptance of a bad review and resolute to become better off it.  I hope that you are able to find reviewers who are able to give better feedback on positive changes that can be made rather than a casual reviewer who had to look up the proper wine pairing for a rib eye steak.

I want to keep this review brief but rich. I won't be discussing the issues of Creation Crap and paid mods, as it's a topic for thousands of people to discuss with. I want to talk strictly about the gameplay experience.
If you're buying this game for a rich, colorful and tear-dropping story - move your hands from your wallet. The main story is as you'd expect from recent Bethesda titles, it doesn't really branch off into many parts of the game world, relatively linear and quite short on playtime if you follow it from quest to quest. You'll meet a few interesting characters who are usually the richest in personality and backstory, but that's about it...
What captivated me, especially recently, since I got back into the game just a few days ago, is the gameplay. And trust me when I say this: it's a really solid post-apocalyptic survival RPG. "Survival" meaning gameplay revolving around hard earned food and water, facing enemies that are several levels higher than your character, smart use of strategy and inventory management.
However, all that comes only when you switch game difficulty to "Survival" (don't worry, it came built into the game since launch, unlike whatever Bethesda are marketing for Skyrim on Creation Crap).
Difference between "Very Hard" and "Survival" might look small on paper, but once you spend your first half hour out in the Wasteland you'll understand that you've just been kicked out of your comfort zone and left there to experience a nuclear blast 5km from ground zero (no pun intended).
Although Survival Mode comes with the vanilla game you might want to look up some Survival oriented mods on Nexus Mods. I would specifically suggest something for allowing quicksaves and console use, since Survival Mode only allows you to save during sleeping and disables console completely.
I advise you to use those mods since knowing Bethesda games are prone to crashing and texture glitching, I don't think anyone would be too happy to replay 2h worth of game time just because some radroach's AI scripting went haywire and crashed the game.
However, if a proper post-apocalyptic survival isn't your cup of tea or if you enjoyed Fallout 3, game still has normal shooter RPG gameplay on standard difficulties. I just wanted to review the game as it is marketed, as a post-apocalyptic survival role-playing game.
Like I said before, game supports modding, the modding scene is just as big as Skyrim's and allows you to customize your gameplay with your wildest fantasies.

If you, or a loved one, have ever experienced trauma regarding sexual assault or abuse, this game might not be for you. It is purposefully cruel in that it exploits the inherent darkness of love, trauma, redemption and revenge. Ultimately though, the narrative is pure and delivers a positive message on loving relationships dealing with trauma. This review may contain spoilers.
Enola is a story-driven game with an intricate plot that needs to be pieced together in a non-linear fashion by navigating a dark, tense atmosphere reflecting psychological despair. You play as Enola, the female protagonist, who has to survive a macabre world conjured by the tortured memories of her lover, Angelica. This world has fragments reminiscent of Silent Hill, but in a different way. This game pushes the emotional boundaries of the player to make them feel desolated and isolated in an already surreal and tormented world. The gameplay is mainly driven through first-person exploration and puzzle solving. I must reiterate that this game is not easy, especially for players who have experienced trauma. You will learn about disgusting acts of violence committed to your lover as you try to navigate a nightmarish landscape.
Most of the obstacles you face in the game are hellish mechanical contraptions designed by the most disturbed minds. In addition, there are a few enemies, dubbed ‘Shadow Man’ or ‘Monsters’ that will attempt to sexually assault you, and you must fight back and escape. Enola is also a thematically driven game. Your morality, your thoughts on justice, redemption, revenge and forgiveness will be put to the test. At one point, you will be tasked with deciding whether to ‘spare’ or ‘kill’ people who have committed a series of crimes of varying degrees. These choices are incredibly crucial, and will determine the sort of ending you obtain. Moreover, at least in my personal experience, they made me reflect on my opinions regarding punishment and to what extent I will become a ‘monster’, or kill, in order to save the life of my partner. Enola is also beautifully designed through the Unreal Engine. Mansions reminiscent of Victorian-era architecture, underworld cavern levels that transition into industrial hellscapes and red skies brewing an apocalyptic storm are but few examples of a unique and interesting creative design.

If you like adventure games, you must give Bastion a try.
The art, aesthetics, music, lore, and especially the great narration all combine to provide you with a refreshing adventure experience. The levels are very detailed, and the routes you can take are assembled in front of you as you walk (you can easily fall off the map, which will result in some health loss). There are many destructable objects in the game - this is indicated by the object flashing red whenever you hit it (most objects can be destroyed).
As you play, a narrator comments on certain things you do. For example, you may come across a mechanical bull and, if you decide to attack it, the narrator will say something like: "the kid (you) gave him exactly what he deserved." The music also changes appropriately when you are in the heat of battle.
The controls are very easy to use, however, the feedback prompts can get annoying (for example, when you are at less-than-half health, the keyboard key "F" will appear next to your character, along with "heal." These button reminders can be helpful, as the game will prompt you to block if you are taking constant damage, however, it can become repetitive if you arleady have mastered the controls.
There are many weapons to unlock, and you can equip two at a time; you can also use your shield by pressing/holding shift. Blocking right before the moment an enemy's attack hits you will result in an autoattack. You reflect enemy projectiles if you block with the correct timing. There are a variety of special "secret moves" available, and you can equip one - you have to have the specific weapon the skill is bound to equipped. Later, you will also be able to select things like drink passives (provide bonuses like extra health) or "god" artifacts that make enemies stronger, but also provide you with a bonus to experience. Everything is upgraded with experience that comes in the form of little blue collectibles. You can select between uo yo 6 different upgrades for each weapon ( 3 active at a time).
The game consists of you collecting cores/shards in each level in order to bring the "Bastion" base to life - each core you collect usually opens a new building slot in the Bastion, allowing you to select which building type you would like to build first (ex: armory for equipping weapons and skills, or distillery for equipping passive drinks). There are a variety of buildings, each unlocked for building as you progress through the story.
There are also weapon challenge levels, where you have to perform a task like destroying a number of items with the hammer within a time frame. Each challenge level has 3 difficulty tiers, and beating the time for that tier yields a prize (1st place is always a secret move).
The learning curve is very good, however, the game can get difficult if you use a lot of god trinkets (to increase enemey characteristics) - I equipped a total of 4 and would die from most enemies within 4-5 hits.
The game is very charming and I strongly recommend it if you like adventure games with very nice aesthetics and narration.

Lengthy video review:
Full text/photos here:
MMORPGs aren’t a booming genre like they once were. The glory days of raiding have passed, and though you can still find it if you look, I believe most people have noticed the time and money-sink that they usually turn into. Sometimes I do miss those days, I spent 7 years in World of Warcraft, so it’s hard not to look back fondly… There were some great PvP moments that make me wish I had been youtubing back then, but overall the stress of not getting that drop you “need” detracts a lot from the pure joy of the game. This is what makes It’s A Wipe so ingenious… You still get to enjoy the feeling of an MMO-raid, but you aren’t going to rip your hair out if something for your class doesn’t drop this week. Herding around your team of 10 to try and defeat a raid boss is harder than it sounds, because even though you’re supposed to be in control, this simulates a real life raid by having people go AFK to check their emails… Sometimes missing a heal when it’s most critical. Obviously the humor is there, the concept is interesting… But there are some fundamental flaws, let’s get into that while we look at It’s A Wipe.
There are nine dungeons in this game, which all offer their own challenges, and will require different strategies to beat. If you’re used to managing a raid, setting up primary tanks and target order shouldn’t be a problem. The real strategy comes once the fight starts, since you’ll need to realize when to change gears before it’s too late. Did the mob get an early crit? Spam heals before he drops the tank! Is AoE damage overpowering your casters? Maybe it’s time to retreat and bring an extra druid. The recruiting system has potential, but could use some work. Currently the only skill I’ve seen is Battle Rez, and the only perks Alchemy and Herbalism (both serving the same function). It could get quite interesting to have a few more in the mix, or even just a couple guys with no skills having upgraded gear available. As it stands though, sorta bare-bones. There are a variety of items in the shop, but you’ll honestly only be buying the potions unless you don’t feel bad about embezzling guild money into a sweet mount or companion pet, which isn’t visible.
Besides fighting the bosses, and people derping away in combat, you will be forced to worry about the morale of your guild. You know that rogue that you dragged through three dungeons? Well, he’s upset about the one drop he didn’t get, so he’s decided to leave the guild. I know, I know… It was you that geared him up. I’m sure you’ll have no problem gearing up another one right? Riiiight? Well, yes I do. Even the players who say they don’t care about loot under the personality tab secretly care deep down. Some days you will need to while away some hours chatting with your guild members, listening to their problems, and boosting their morale… This will upset guild members who “demand attention” under the personality tab, though. The entire game presents an intricate balance that I find quite intriguing, and quite difficult… Even on the “normal” setting. But then, when was a raid (or guild management) ever supposed to be easy?
On the downside, there is very little actual gameplay to speak of. It’s a great game for when I don’t want to really “play” a video game… But don’t feel like vegging out on Netflix either. You set up the roles for the guild, and unless something goes terribly you’ll usually just be clicking “Stick With The Plan”. The humor isn’t engaging enough to hold me during EVERY round of combat, so sometimes people will change roles or switch rows without my noticing… Easily leading to a wipe if not corrected. The art style, while nice-looking, is not animated in any way, nor are any upgrades reflected on the character model aside from increasing their stats. It’s an interesting game that lacks a few key fundamentals during execution. The raids are well-designed though, and switching up classes between playthroughs offers some nice replayability. It can certainly scratch that itch I didn’t remember I had, but there is lots of room for improvement, and while it won’t be everyone’s cup of tea, the price is low enough that I’d say it’s worth giving it a chance.
Summary: A MMO guild-management strategy game with plenty of potential.
Final Score: 6/10 for raid designs and replayability. 8/10 with more perks/abilites.

It's A Wipe is worth the money for the nostalgia factor, but most of the game feels relatively spartan in features or gameplay. Generally, the game consists of managing a sitcom-version of a guild raiding party in an indirect fashion with breaks in between; additional characters or other amusing features that one think to find in a game about managing a guild are absent.
Further, the game is quickly over -- there seems to be only 7-8 raids -- and some of the mechanics really need some work, particularly infighting over loot. This can make the game frustrating and the game itself seems to have relatively little replayability; which is odd given that the overall concept of the game, if developed, could provide for a fascinating guild management game.

With that said, it's five dollars and I had trouble not liking it. For that price you get what you might expect. I would tepidly recommend the game and hope the developer fleshes out the features of it.

This game might not be for the newer generation of gamers. If you are used to Super Mario Bros, The Elder Scroll games, or D&D type games like Baldur's Gate, then you probably won't appreciate this game. Dark Gates is an old school (as in late 1970s, early 1980s) style fantasy board game. If you would like to see where this game got some inspiration from search for the SPI games "Deathmaze" and "Citadel of Blood". When comparing Dark Gates to those SPI classics, you can't help becoming excited. I LOVED those old solo games where all the pieces were chits, and 2 six-sided dice. There wasn't much of a back story, and most of the game play was random. Dark Gates captures the style, fun and atmosphere of those SPI classics. If you are an old school gamer (NOT necessarily an old school video gamer), then you will appreciate this game. If you want fancy graphics, lots of diversity in the dungeon levels, and lots of equipment, quests, and hundreds of monsters, you probably are better off looking elsewhere.
I would recommend this game highly to those who enjoy solo or small party fantasy board games, even if you may have never experienced the SPI classics mentioned above. This game definitely has the feel of a classic/vintage board game.
[PROs]
Similar in Style and Play to classic SPI board games from the 70s/80s.
Numerous Heroes to experiment with in order to get a party that best suits your game playing strategy.
Large levels with many monsters, locked doors, and various objects to interact with that may result in a bonus, or punishment to the player, or party.
Basic ability to upgrade your hero's skills, mastery, vitality, resistance and more.
A nice, yet not long and drawn out back story that quickly explains the history and existance of the labyrinth and the unnamed boss who you ultimately must defeat.
Each time you play the dungeon/labyrinth is randomly designed, and stocked.
[CONs]
Movement can feel slow and might annoy some players, but others who enjoy those old board games might appreciate this. I got used to it.
While there are many heroes to choose from, you cannot create your own customized hero from scratch.
Basic upgrading of one's heroes. Not much depth when compared to leveling and upgrading heroes in D&D, or other fantasy style games.
Spell casting costs health, NOT mana thus if you are not careful and you cast a spell that costs more health than the caster has, the casting will cause the caster to die.
Dungeon levels are the same textures, and graphics. Not much differences in the looks of level 1 2, or 3.
[In Closing]
Dark Gates is a fun, old school (potentially painful to newer generations of gamers) fantasy style board game with light RPG/tactical features. For many years I wished for a computerized version of Deathmaze or Citadel of Blood and was extremely happy when I first stumbled upon this game in one of it's earliest releases. I've stuck with the game ever since and have beaten it a few times and STILL always enjoy coming back to it!
Get the comic book if it is available here on Steam as it also gives a little background/story about the game and a group of heroes who were entering the labyrinth to seal the Dark Gates!

The game features a very generous sized 2D open world universe which contains galaxies full of planets and moons that can be
entered and explored at will. There is also sections of deep space which sit between the galaxies filled with
more areas. Space itself contains no loading screens and entering a planet is pretty seamless. Gameplay consists of on foot Zelda
like combat were weapons have different attack ranges. You can have also duel wield some really
crazy weapon combos. There is traditional weapons like swords and modern weapons like guns and flamethrowers. Magic too. Spaceship combat is in real time and ships can be equipped with all kinds of gear and accesories. The spaceship
can be called at anytime while exploring a planet so no need to worry about it getting lost.On foot monsters also run away when your flying past on your ship which is a really cool touch.  Make sure you have fuel
because flying without it, could leave you crash landing into an alien ocean.
You can also have a monster pet which helps
you fight! Planets can be fully explored on foot and also have their own villages, quests and dungeons. Most quests are also
pretty open ended so you can tackle them in various ways. Npc's around the game can also be killed which can then trigger local guards to attack and hunt you down.
The games systems seem simple initially but are suprisingly deep for a cheap game.
Combine and craft items, equip runes to alter stats, battle pets, manage your karma. It's like a little universe in your hands for $5!
Story has been changed since early access, but the 1.0 version story really went into
a direction i wasn't expecting. Getting your ship in the tutorial sections took a little longer then in the earlier version but I think it was partly my fault as I couldn't help but explore rather
then follow the story. Lots of backstory stuff in general to explore too. The introduction of the game makes you think the story will be
your traditional you are the ones stuff but it is so much more then that. This is a great game which deserves more
praise for a first time effort from a dev. I really hope you get to enjoy this awesome game!

Dark Gates simulates old-school board games like "DeathMaze." It's a minimalist idea, to be sure, but one that it does very well. The player selects 6 characters to form a party (many are multi-class and can use both melee and ranged weapons, as well as offensive and defensive magic). Once they breach the front entrance of the labyrinth (there's a back story that explains its existence, but it's typical fare), movement tiles are revealed in a similar fashion to "Dungeon Quest" in order to simulate the Fog of War. There are doors that may or may not be trapped, events to find, chests to open, and, of course, encounters. Each game is randomly generated.
Party members can be replaced or swapped at will, and they can be upgraded as their exp increases. The usual stat increases are here, but there are also Masteries that can be raised (such as the bonus they get to their melee weapon) and Skills (such as a bonus to successfully navigating Traps).
This may not be the popular opinion, but I actually like this game. I've been playing the DRM-free version for the last six months (as I write this review, Dark Gates has been on Steam less than a week), and I appreciate that it feels like an old-school board game. I don't even have a problem with hitting Enter (a common complaint is that the mouse is not used, although it should be noted that the game does claim full gamepad support), because rolling dice would take just as long, if not longer. It's not supposed to be Skyrim; it's a board game. The description even states that it "tries to capture classic tabletop RPG experience," and it  easily achieves this goal. Does it have amazing hi-rez ultra smooth graphics with Oculus support? No, but why would it? The graphics are perfectly serviceable for what it is.
(EDIT: The developer has recently addressed the complaint of hitting Enter too often, by automating this process somewhat. )
Dark gates is a simple game with simple rules. It might be too slow-moving for some, and I'll admit that the sound gets old very quickly. But, in my opinion, the very things that irritate some players are what make the game work for me. Gameplay isn't overly convoluted, which makes it easy to pick up and play in 5 minute increments  or for an hour. The Fog of War keeps things interesting, as does the opportunity to try to settle encounters either through force or diplomatically (by Negotiating or Bribing). Different monsters have different abilities to keep things tense (for example, spiders cast webs over random party members, making them unable to fight). That said, I do believe that $10 US is too much for what this game is. I'd recommend it, but at a price half that, as it really feels more like an iOS game than something designed for PC.
Dark Gates is a lite, board game-inspired time waster. There is nothing particularly deep or strategic about it; this isn't an RTS by any means. Those players who are looking for something simple to pass the time will enjoy it. All others should steer clear. For me, it's a fun and interesting diversion when I don't want to think too hard or button mash.
Recommended, but make sure you know what you're getting before pulling the trigger.
[One quick aside: There is misinformation around that states the game doesn't tell you what the controls are, which kind of baffles me. Every time the screen changes, the keys that are usable on that screen are displayed as icons. You can see this in the game's screen shots if this is a concern.]
