Long story short, the owners of the original Planetary Annihiliation are angry with the developers, and rightfully so. The original cost was somewhere around $60-$80, which was expensive. Then, the developers go around and apparently outright abandon that game's development in favor of this game. And, I do admit that is a sly and conniving move, but we are not here to rate the morality of the developers, per say, we are here to rate the product that they provide. And, I must say, I can tell you that it is a quality product, and just what I wanted from the game when I originally watched the game's Kickstarter trailer in 2012. And, no, this should not have been a DLC, this should have been the original game.
Admittedly, like I said, this is what the original game should have been. Those who say that Titans are overpowered are downright incorrect. They can be a nice trump card to turn the tides, but that is about it. For instance, 10 basic bombers can make quick work of an undefended Siesmic Titan. So, Titans are not the end-all-be-all. You must coordinate your forces to support one another, in a way that all of there advantages can be leveraged.
All of the forces (land, sea, air, and orbital) from the basic and advanced factories are divided into, more or less, these roles: building, light, heavy, repair, AA, and scout. Obviously, with their respective unit names. Buildings consist of resource and storage (metal and energy), factories (land, sea, air, and orbital), defensive [turrets (laser, AA, and artillary), anti-nuclear silos, orbital defense cannons, orbital rail guns, torpedo defense, and walls], offensive (nuclear silo, missile silo, and inter/intraplanetary unit launcher).
Interplanetary travel is surprisingly fluid and intuitive. Simply select an orbital unit or projectile that is capable of interplanetary travel, and right-click your destination. Simple as that.
Titans come in varying flavors. Some use melee attacks, some projectiles, some lightening, one can be a planet destroyer on its own, and one can make interplanetary invasion far easier (teleporters). Just let me be clear, they are not overpowered. They tank your economy once construction begins; if you don't have tens of advanced builders building them, it will take forever; left unprotect, they will be made quick work of; but when used in conjuction with a proper supporting force, you can make your enemies cower.
This is where the game starts to look a bit like Universe Sandbox. You can weaponize a planet, moon, or asteroid. Strap enough celestial rockets (Halleys) onto any of the three, and you can use them as weapons of war. +1 in my books. If that wasn't enough, construct 5 arming buildings on a metal planet, and use it as your weapon to counter incoming celestial nuisances, or don't bother with invading your enemy, just wipe them off the face of the universe in one fell swoop. Death Star anyone?
Some of the games features are pretty cool, too. For instance, if a player randomly disconnects, it pauses the game. You can pause the game for everyone, if you have to go to the bathroom or do some other thing. Twitch and community videos are easily available on the main menu. And, everyone's replays are automatically uploaded to a community pool of replays in-game, which is great for references and just simple videoplayback. Just a  side note, the HUD is fairly minimal. It is focused around being tall/long and narrow along the edges of the screen, with a few dropdown/popout menus. However, the unit icons can get pretty obstructive as the game progresses.
I also find the artstyle to be very tasteful. It is fairly minimalistic with smooth pastels, when zoomed out, but when you zoom in, the plants, water, terrain, effects, and units have nice textures with just the right amount of detail. It is a nice contrast to the more realistic visuals of Supreme Commander, and I welcome that.
My only real gripe with this game is the freakin' orbital battleship. Massproduce and dominate with those. Launch hundreds of solar panels and build loads of orbital factories, and you will dominate time and time again. Not like you heard it from me or anything. Really annoying. It doesn't allow for any diversity in tactics and long term strategy. I admit, they consume a lot of energy, but at least make the orbital defense cannon a tad bit more powerful. I don't really want to have to put one every other meter, so my skies are battleship-free.

If you're looking for a serious tactical shooter, this isn't quite what you're looking for.  While lacking the more linear style levels of the console counterpart, the PC version of Lockdown has larger levels, more open levels (still not as large and open-ended as Rainbow Six 3's, or its predecessors).  The gunplay is very strange, it feels like a mix between Counter Strike and Rainbow Six 3, where your character is swift and nimble, but fire-fights are still extremely deadly and tactics and strategy are still required to overcome enemies.  I'd say that the sound design exceeds Rainbow Six 3's, along with the level design, although the gameplay is much more fast paced.
No longer are you carefully planning your movements and decisions before striking your targets, as this is more about cover-based shooting.  Commanding your squad takes a back seat to the action and its relegated more to a standard FPS with the Rainbow Six skin on it, but lacks the elements that truly made it Rainbow Six.  If you're not a purist, you'll be able to find some joy in it, as it's not broken, plays very smoothly, and is made very competently, the only problem is the design behind most of it where it's trying to be a tactical shooter, but lacks the dedication to really commit to the genre.

I can't in good conscience consider this a good game I can recommend, but it was interesting watching it fail at what it's trying to do, and at least it's an original concept.
The only way I can describe it is as a stop motion musical in a point & click framework. It mostly fails at all these three things, mainly by looking, sounding and playing as the work of an amateur. The art style is distinct, but the stop motion isn't all that good. Still, it's charming. The music and highschool-musical-theater singing are also kinda charming, at least once you realize that the singing is off key and rather bad "on purpose", but you still can't call them good. The point & click elements are barely there, with no real choices and no real puzzles, just serving to move you forward in the story.
I think what really tipped this over to no for me was the story. It's very much on the nose. It's got some points to make, and instead of building them organically into its storytelling, it just repeats them over and over. We are never really allowed to empathize with the characters: Instead of watching them deal with the world and its problems we are being told what their problems are and are expected to feel something from that. Good storytelling doesn't really work that way. So if one of the goals of the game was to make us think about gender and the economy, it very much falls flat. Instead of sounding humorous and lighthearted as it seems to attempt to, it feels awkward and preachy.
So an interesting little amateur experiment, the first commercial game of a single developer working on their own, trying out a relatively novel idea. I didn't regret the cup of coffee I paid for it with the discount, because the aesthetic is charming and  because it didn't overstay its welcome, but that doesn't mean it's a good game.

--Sorry, had to get that out, just played through it in one sitting and the rhythm, and sometimes lack thereof, is catchy in ways.  Hideously catchy.
I love claymation, and even though this is super low-end budget style, I liked the characters and backgrounds.  Animation is not very varied but it gets a... thing of sort... across.
After the first scene or so, the overt cheesiness of the constant amateur singing of the majority of the dialogue wore away.  It really is nice how the music score rolls right along and the dialogues always queue up to hit the beat right when they ought to.  It's a neat effect requiring only momentary pause, and feels really natural in a sort of... absurd impromptu musical.  I liked the score quite a bit and, partnered with the timing of the singing, it honestly felt like the most polished part of the game.
The plot is admittedly pretty silly and nothing worth writing home about, but it might give you a weird kind of chuckle.
The gameplay was very simple, a brief point and click adventure.  I've played a handful of point and clicks, and this one, while it required no massive leaps in logic (which is good), it was far too easy (which is bad).  Regarding variation, there's far more interrogation of the characters (which makes sense given the musical platform) than there are backgrounds to be searched and interacted with.  Finally, there isn't a lick of puzzle element in this game, which I find to be kind of irregular for the genre, but to each its own, I guess.
The kicker, it was super short, a shade more than an hour.  (Additional "playtime" was spent waiting for card drops.)
To sum it up, weirdly catchy tunes, too easy, odd visuals, and too short.
Get it on sale if you're feeling frisky, I guess.

Very nice game in general, with an original historical background. You play a  SS Standartenfuhrer, who chooses to get involved in a plot to assassinate Hitler, using his authority in the Gestapo. What called my attention is that the character you play -intentionally or not- is not the typical "good guy". He's far from noble, actually. His main reason for being disenchanted with Hitler was that he saw
in the concentration camps (apparently he was cool with it when it was only the Jews). Mild mild spoiler (not really, but just in case:
. This is unusual, and was very interesting for me during the gameplay.
THE GOOD:
+ Nice visuals, with beautiful artwork in the cut scenes.
+ Excellent attention to detail, especially with historical elements.
+ The music isn't overwhelming or annoying; sound effects are cool.
+ Different dialog options. It doesn't change the main outcome, but you may learn more or less, according to what you choose.
+ The plot was believable, historically accurate within the context of this fictional little story, and made sense.
THE NOT SO GOOD:
* Two of the "mini-games" inserted in the game are exclusively about luck, rather than skills, and losing them may block your game, forcing you to use a previously saved game.
* The first mini-game was quite poorly explained.
* The game has you picking up stuff you don't need at the moment. This is a common trait of most point-and-click games, but it kind of spoils the immersion.
* Voice acting was... not that good. Some characters were ok, others less so.
* Even though the main plot was somewhat solved, many point were left open in the hopes of part 2. But let's hope!
THE HORRIBLE:
- The pronunciation of German words was preposterous, especially by certain characters. Every time someone said "Wehrmacht", I felt like someone was scratching a blackboard. Note that I'm not German, and I'm cool with actors pronouncing "Gestapo" instead of "Geshtapo", but some of it was too bad even for me.
- The woman who did the voice of "Victoria". That was the worst part of this game, and the worst I ever heard. I heard kids in elementary school reading from history books better than this lady did her lines. PLUS: she pronounced the word "Fuhrer" as "fur-r", and that wasn't the worst part of her "acting".
(Another reviewer deemed her probably the worst voice actress in the history of gaming, and I agree)
Not mind-blowingly good, but I recommend it. I had a very good time playing it, and I'm looking forward to playing the next one!

From the outset Stroke of Fate: Operation Valkyrie attracted my attention. Being an adventure ánd a history buff, makes this sort of game always trigger my interest. The additional novelty of the fact that - in a WWII nazi setting - you were supposed to do some policework merely added to the curiosity.
But I'm affraid it's al been rather of a letdown. Oh the backgrounds and artwork are nice, very nice indeed. And the idea to portray or tell a lot of Nazi history via the game's objects is pretty cool. However the way these things are worked out in the game, it just doesn't come up with the goods. The clumsy clunky movement of the main character doesn't help. But above all the uninspired English voiceacting is abominable. It could have added much to the atmosphere and mystery of the game. Now most lines (especially the ones of the 'supporting' roles - and there are a lót of them) seems they are delivered with as much enthusiasm and gusto, let alone craftsmanship, as a talking concrete slab. Even though in the original Russian version some of this might be better, here it is lost in translation (as I fear a lot of the script is too).
Also the storyline can't seem to decide upon a thriller, historical fiction or a narrative of events that really happened with which you interact.
This all leaves the game basically flawed, though the puzzles are descent and sometimes a bit difficult to grasp. And you do want to know 'what happens next' so you do play out the game. But aren't gripped.
Could have been a lot better. And an overhaul with different voiceactors might actually do it a lot of good...

Rainbow Six Lockdown is set up to be a squad based tactical shooter, where you and your team breach doors, rescue hostages, and take down the bad guys. You have up to four team members at a time, and you issue fairly straightforward commands to them. They are fairly mindless and sometimes stand stupidly while being fired on. It's not so bad, though - the enemy does the exact same thing. Both of you are dealing with not-so-bright comrades so it all evens out.
Really, the thing to remember in single player is that it is all a training mode for multi-player. You always get far better challenges playing against live humans than against computer-driven drones. So consider this your training grounds to get used to the commands. On one hand the game is a bit challenging - you can't survive infinite hits with a gun before you go down. It is much more realistic than many games in that sense. On the other hand, once you get even a basic grasp of how the tactics work, you should be able to rip through many of the missions without any need for cover or caution. The enemy is fairly clueless and you can usually kill them long before they start to take action.
Lockdown is worth a look and gives a solid decent amount play time, however people new to the series would be better to start on another Rainbow six game as this is certainly not a highlight of the series.

Randal's Monday is not the most playable of point-and-click adventures.  Attempting to capitalize on nerd culture by overloading the game with every possible pop culture geek reference isn't enough to make up for poor game design, bad acting and terrible sound quality.
.
The basic plot is interesting enough: jerkwad main character (named after the two main characters in Clerks, and voiced by one of the actors of those characters) steals his best friend's engagement ring during a night of drunken debauchery, then pawns it the next day to pay his rent.  That's when things take a turn for the terrible - he loses his job, his best friend commits suicide, and the prophetic bum in the alley keeps telling him how cursed he is.  Well, with a name like Randal Hicks, what'd you expect?
Like any other point and click, most of this game is just a matter of matching the right inventory object to the scenario.  Unfortunately, some of these connections are tenuous at best, and more often completely inconceivable.  Relying on the hint system becomes practically a necessity to avoid insanity - and even THEN, the hint system misses some important steps, leading to frustration over missing one tiny item in a place you were sure you'd searched thoroughly before.
From the very beginning of the game, it's obvious that the actors weren't even in the same room when recording the script:  dialogue sounds stilted and volume and tone is often mismatched.  Frequently, the responses don't even seem to follow what the original character was even saying, leading to a lot of confusion while trying to follow the story.  While it makes sense for the characters to talk and act incoherently in the first scene (the "let's get drunk at the bar" wedding shower), there's no real excuse for it after that.  Sadly, their acting never lives up to the potential of the game, and certainly doesn't match up to the semi-star-caliber cast (Jeff Anderson ("Randal Hicks" who played Randal Graves in Clerks), Jason Mewes (Jay in both this game and Clerks), two voice actors from Thomas the Tank Engine, etc,)
Sound quality also suffered - often changing volume in mid scene, making it hard to hear the characters, or making it suddenly loud.  Unacceptable in a game of this simplistic a design.  Fire that sound guy immediately!
The soundtrack is actually really good, and if you're just in it for the geek references, well, this is so full as to render the rest of the game irrelevant.
I'm normally a lot more forgiving about video games, but when there's this much wrong with it, it becomes a complete disappointment.  I got it on sale for $5, but still wish I had waited.   Save your money, or buy some TellTale games instead.

As both a nerd and a huge fan of Daedalic's point-and-click adventures, I bought Randal's Monday thinking this was just the game for me.
Boy, was I ever wrong.
First of all, it should noted that Daedalic is just the publisher of this game.  The game was actually developed by a different studio, and it shows.  There were spelling errors, a glitchy interface, and the ending narration kept repeating itself over itself, so at one point I had three narrators talking to me at once.  Yikes.
The humor in this game is crude in nature, by which I mean puking♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥/gore/excessive swearing.  For some people, this is right up their alley.  Personally?  I was not amused.  Don't get me wrong: the occasional non-crude thing was funny.  I really enjoyed the four characters who show up near the end of the game to help you (I won't mention who they are, to avoid spoilers).  But for a comedy game, way too many jokes fell flat.
And to make matters worse, the main character is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  My guess is that, after the success of Rufus in the Deponia trilogy, Daedalic wanted to make another Rufus-y character, but wanted to up the ante.  However, by increasing the main characters snark and self-centeredness, they lost a lot of the charm that made Rufus likeable.  And no one wants to get stuck playing as a main character they hate.
I will give this game a hand, however, for its abundance of nerdy references.  Randal's Monday is over flowing with references to famous movies, video games, TV shows, etc: Star Wars, Back to the Future, Clerks, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Portal, Fallout, Bioshock, Resident Evil, A Clockwork Orange, Pulp Fiction, Game of Thrones, the Sopranos, just to name a few.  Seriously, it would take forever to list all of the media referenced in this game.
If you hardcore love nerdy references, and aren't bothered by the excessive vomitting, gore, and generally dumb-assery, then give this game a shot.  Maybe buy it on sale.  Otherwise, don't bother.  There are plenty of other point-and-click adventures that are more worthy of your time.

I was a huge fan of Burnout 3. I still am - very few games still carry the same sense of speed and absolutly pure fun it was. Paradice has the awful job of being in the same series as 3, which is already setting itself up for failure.
Pretending that Paradice is actually a racing game not part of the Burnout franchise, it's actually not bad. It's got a decently-sized free-roaming sandbox to drive around, but to tell you this is what drove me away from my inital purchase of the game years ago.
The single player falls flat. You start a race by driving up to an intersection, and after being given a route to one of the 8 finishing points, you and a lot of other cheating, rubberbanding AI race to the finish. Although the races rely on steet smarts on finding the quickest way to the finish, the game is kinda kneecapping iself by only giving 8 possible finish points. There's a lot of crazy tracks you could do just in and around the dam alone, but because all of the tracks are sprints only, really cool stuff like that can't happen.
And becuase they have it in a sandbox, the speed had to be turned down for it to be possible to actually navigate around. If the game happened at a pace that matched Burnout 3, then collisions would be everywhere and it would be impossible to dive at full speed. I miss geing cartoonishly fast in racing games. :(
The online, if you can find anyone to play with, is crazy fun however and makes the sandbox absolutly shine. It's like being invited to a socal gathering where the host somtimes puts on fun games and challenges for everyone to do. One moment you're trying to beat a strager's best split time down the highway and next thing you know you're the target in a giant game of Get Rekt Manhunt.

This is one of those games you play when you're curious to try something new yet different at the same time.  It has a lot to offer, with its respectively large world, creative use of RPG Maker VX Ace scripts, and various options for combat.  The controls are tricky to get used to, but provide a lot of fun once you get the hang of it.  The game also does a great job at while encouraging you to explore as much as you can, never throwing you off track.
The game does have a couple glaring issues though.  This is mostly due to its alpha nature, but the game is quite buggy at the moment.  It even crashes occasionally, which is very frustrating if you're not the type who saves often.
I have noticed though that the dev is very quick to fix bugs, usually correcting them no more than a day or 2 after reporting.  Even if the game does come off as a little haphazardly thrown together, there is an effort to iron out any problems people find.
If you would like any further opinions or even a blind playthough, I have actually done a Let's Play of it on my Youtube channel.  You can find it here!

This could have been a neat "tongue-in-cheek" approach to a management game. It is, however, not. The game is so poorly put together that it hurts to play. The whole experience begs to be excused by the fact that it's a "joke game", But the joke stops being funny after the first fight, then there is only frustration left. If I got paid 10$ every hour for playing this, I would say no in a heartbeat. If it was free, I would feel robbed. Paying for it? I will regret it forever. Give it a miss, folks.
The whole premise of leading a guild is also flawed. This game only focuses on the annoying parts of leading a guild. There is no feeling of achievement after completing a raid, just a list of items to distribute, none of which have any appearance or or quality indication on them. At the end of a raid, all you get is some numbers that you give to a member of the raid, and all the others get mad, which removes the want for more gear. There is no reason to wish for progression because the reward is just more grief.
Besides getting the feel of the position of raid leader completely wrong, the game is also relentlessly boring. There is no automization whatsoever, like there would be in a good raid group. If a raid is easy, the raid leader does nothing. here, no matter how easy the boss/trash you're at is, you still have to command every single goddamn turn, which means you just sit there for 10 minutes clicking the same 2 buttons after you know you've allready won. Even turning up the combat speed to "ludicrous" it is still slow as balls, every turn taking way longer than it should. It all adds up to being incredibly boring.
If the game nailed the essence of leading a raid, the responsibility, the challenge, the strategic overview needed, and the amazing feeling of accomplishment after finally downing a boss, this would have been a really interesting experience. As it stands though, it's all just annoying.
TL;DR: It's boring and lame and it sucks. do not buy

I just want to start by saying RPG Maker or not this game is very unique and I've never played anything like it.
I still haven't finished the game, and dont even know how close iam to finishing but I dont really care. I could just run and fly around this galaxy for ever!! If you are a fan of retro rpg's like Final Fantasy, and adventure games like Zelda, then GET THIS GAME! I cant wait to see what the future holds for this game and the single developer. I played and enjoyed it  when it was still V0.07, but the recent updates have really made it into something else. Kind of like a retro Skyrim in space.
A few experiences from my adventure so far.
Started a new game, killed the tutor Mr Moreton with no hesitation with a walking stick.
Parents didn't believe that their child was so blodthirtsy.
Participated in some sort of apocalypse which had me slinging shotgun rounds at hybrids while trying to find my car. Really made it feel like I was in the middle of a Walking Dead apocalypse.
Introduction section was really fun!
I did not expect the game to open up afterwards as much as it did. After the intro section I found myself  waking up on the planet Seria. Planets are very decently sized and seem to have a lot of things to do. There is a quest log which gives you quests but I decided to go explore instead of following it. Ran into grey aliens that wanted to capture residents from my home village for food. An undeground pit full of snake monsters, galactic soldiers who wanted to arrest me, and even a poor woman looking for her Mr Kitty.  After exploring and looting everything on my path I continued on with my main quest, which was to investigate a crash site.
I finally tracked down the crashed ship and received a spaceship and spacesuit. I really like that the spacesuit let you breathe in space and also gives you a boost jump which you can use to climb mountains. I like the fuel mechanics in the game but I wish that your ship wouldnt crash and get a gameover if rou run out of fuel. You can find and buy fuel all over the place and save at anytime so its not really much of a problem.
Flying into space is really cool and as simple as just flying out the borders of the planet. I ended up taking the ship and exploring space. The map in space doesn't make it look like its particularly big, but over 8 hours in and I'm still finding new places and enemies.  Another cool thing is that you can actually drift off of an asteroid and end up landing on a planet. I only remember a few locations but it can be used as a really effective fast travel method once your start learning your way around space. As far as I know so far I have never run into any sort of boundaries which i Love!
You can just keep flying and flying without ever stopping. No invisible walls here!
Since receiving the ship and exploring space, I have doomed villagers on the moon by turning off atmosphere generators and then looting their dead bodies, crafted lockpicks and broke into locked buildings, bought a house on planet Hopa, taken on bounties and explored ruined space stations. I still feel like I've only broken the surface. The ambience on the game is really good as well and sounds pretty amazing with headphones.
I dont know what some of the reviews meant about controls but I have no problem with them. I play by using the mouse and keyboard and if you really want the developer says you can use a controller and some software but I haven't tried it yet.
The one negative I have is that there is a lot to get your head around in terms of features and options and I think it would be nice to have a few more tutorials but otherwise this game is just a gem. Please keep up the amazing work!!!

I saw this game on sale, and thought "What the heck, I'll go for it." I had an hour before I had to leave for work, so I thought I'd give it a go. I'm normally a guy who shows up early just because better safe than sorry.
So I would say this game is pretty spot on. Think of a group of raiders, in any game you could play. World of Warcraft, Ever Quest, Final Fantasy Online - just to name a few. Then, take that group, and think of them as real people (we all know that you picture some guy playing a chick character just to stare at pixel booty all day) - Not to say they aren't, but the perception of most people is to look at who they are, and assume everyone else is a robot or just some random nobody.
This game is full of comedy - Everything from "Killalot talks about his political views" to a person "Afking in the middle of combat to check his email" - And will remind you of what really happens. I love when I tell a tank to take over agro, and the tank (who is better geared and more able to do so) cannot pull agro off the first tank. I love when a mage just happens for wander into creature range and gets attacked wildly. I love when the healers forget to heal because they think a tank is good, and start to dps, letting the poor tank die because the fight required a focused heal at specific times. Just like in real MMOs.
This game is easily one of the more addictive games, and as my first day playing, it has already caused me to come close to being late to work AND caused me to rush home just to try to see how far I can make it after the fact.

Fun game for the price.  Battles require thought after the early dungeons are out of the way, and keeping everyone happy about loot is a bit of a challenge.  Your raid's strength grows noticeably over time, and some of the character actions can be amusingly nostalgic if you've ever raided in an MMO (like someone going link dead, or a mage deciding to tank).  MMO experience can help you get a handle on strategy quickly, but I don't think it's a requirement to enjoy the game.
The character quirks don't impact the gameplay too much, so luck isn't a huge factor.  Fights boil down to managing the raid strategy (like DPS, healing, and tanking priorities) and figuring out boss patterns.  I'm impressed by how well the game simulates the raid management experience ("WHY DID YOU DRINK THAT POTION INSTEAD OF HEALING THE TANK?!?") without getting bogged down in micromanagement.  Fights can drag on at times, but hey, they're raids.  They do that.
It would be great if characters had more personality, or if raid groups could be bigger, or if character abilities were more varied.  For the price, though, those aren't complaints - just wishes for a DLC/sequel someday.

I'm a game developer, and the person that made this game is a good friend of mine, just to be clear. That being said, it's easy for me to be complimentary to the game, because it's good.
Which is a relief, because lying to a friend of yours about how good their game is difficult. But I played this through in a single session, which is not something I do often as a game developer with two small children.
TRACKLESS is a brilliantly modern take on classic adventure gaming, one that I can recommend pretty unequivocally. You move around with WASD+Mouse, but to interact with objects, you get a text parser interface. The twist is that you only ever put in one word at a time, only verbs, and the game grades you on your input.
This solves a lot of the design issues and frustration that come with text parser interfaces in the past. Learning what syntax or phrases the game will recognize, whether or not to include articles like "the" and so on--all the kind of stuff that typically has you fighting the interface of the game rather than enjoying it with games like Zork and many older text adventures.
What I can't emphasize enough is that TRACKLESS is a really relaxing, atmospheric game that is perfectly balanced for minimizing the frustration that tends to come with adventure games. We've all been there, even playing our favorite classic adventure games: you can't solve a puzzle and the game just stops cold. You can't progress. Not only does the single-word parser system of TRACKLESS eliminate a lot of the potential confusion, there are multiple verbs that can be used to solve a given puzzle. Which totally avoids the common frustration of the genre.
Say for example you know you have to interact with a book. The most basic word you can think of relating to it, like "open," the game will hint is an "OK" word (i.e. it will pass the puzzle), but it won't get you the most points. So what I found is that once I understood that I had a word that would allow me to progress (the source of frustration is not being able to move forward in a puzzle game), I was no longer in a hurry, and I liked the challenge of really thinking about the more accurate, higher scoring word to use. The pressure was totally off.
Which is the main thing about this game. It's all about vibe, atmosphere. There's not any conflict or angsty interpersonal conflict. You're basically yourself, taking a trip on a train to a tourist site. That's it. "That's it?" you might ask, incredulous, but I think it's an elusive sort of alchemy for a game to capture the particular emotional arc of taking a really good trip. After finishing the game I had questions I kept turning over in my head but I felt very satisfied. Peaceful, even.
Anyone who has traveled to a foreign country, and dawdled in a public square, looked at statues and wondered should enjoy this game. Due in no small part to Makeup and Vanity Set's really wonderful soundtrack. (Full disclosure: we worked with him on our game, too, so I'm not going to pretend like I'm not biased to really enjoy his music).
The graphics too are quite unusual, TRACKLESS looks like nothing else out there. Like wandering through a little paper world. It's 3d, but also kind of 2d. hard to describe. But I thought it was very evocative, home spun charm. Like someone made a little diorama that you bend over to look into, but suddenly you're inside that world.
RECOMMENDED FOR: Anyone who prizes atmosphere, great music, ambience, setting, sense of place, light puzzling or relaxing games. Anyone that enjoys indie games with a strong vision of a single person.
NOT RECOMMENDED FOR: If you have no patience for mechanically light games or games not driven by combat.

You are The Wanderer, which seems an odd title, as you clearly weren't a wanderer before the start of the game, unless you just wandered around town.  Maybe all the other people in town are wanderers too? Anyway, you're a character sprite you choose from a list of character sprites with no backstory because the plot's not really written yet.  A Beautiful Woman chased by The Bad Guys crashes near your house, so you naturally do the heroic thing, and steal her ship for yourself so you can go joyriding and see the universe, meet strange and fascinating new people, then murder them and loot their corpses for their stuff! Ostensibly, you are doing this to find The Beautiful Woman's soul because she's apparently now your Love.  (So what if you're a girl, you apparently swing that way!) You have to rescue her soul because The Bad Guys... umm... think it would taste great with jam? Or maybe just put it in a lava lamp or something? Anyway, you have to go to The Centre to find it and beat the game.  This amounts to fighting several giant Bad Guys, and one slightly bigger giant Bad Guy who shows he means business because he's a different color than the others and deals marginally more damage.
Along the way, you'll meet several alien races, most of which are hostile because The Harvest swept up all the good races, and took them to a Higher Plane of Existence.  Basically, it's the Rapture, but with dinosaurs and little gray men instead of the Antichrist.
The new version brought with it a "sci fi" pack of portraits, so the little gray men no longer use standard RPGMaker elf portraits, and now means the weapon dealers have a face that looks like a discarded cicada shell, and the catgirls look like goth girls with witch hats.  The dev assures us that none of the art is final, but it's somewhat amusing in its current state, anyway.
The game really only has about 3 required missions, and the rest are basically you just visiting random places, being asked to pick a side in some battle between two opposing races, and murdering whichever side strikes your fancy or didn't give a bid.  In some senses, it's a bit like Skyrim in that regard, although also like Skyrim, it tends to wind up with me walking into some alien base, killing everything, then accidentally hitting a self-destruct button, and then being told "Congratulations, I just completed a quest I didn't actually accept!"  Gee, I hope I didn't miss any important lead-up to that.  I wonder who I just killed?
Enemies range from wolves and lizardpeople and skeletons you kill by the dozen with a couple strong attacks to giants that take shooting for a full minute while dodging their fireballs and chugging potions like crazy while trying not to think about whether the junk made by those red imp guys are really without any side effects when you take 40 times the reccomended dosage.  The fireballs are slow enough to make them easy to dodge if you stand further than 4 tiles away, but many weapon attacks tend to force you to stay still for a second or so, and so it's best to dodge, then shoot. A lack of ability to aim your character without stepping a tile towards your enemy is also an annoyance, as there's a rather small finite number of tiles on the screen to start with, and the player character is such a cool customer, (s)he never bothers to go at more than a walking pace.  So what if you're being followed by a flaming boulder rolled by a living volcano, you didn't pick the character who wears leather pants and shades at night to break your cool!
Weapons range from projectiles with various blast patterns to melee weapons you sell to buy more ammo for the projectile weapons.  The low number of frames of animation mean an enemy is already hitting you by the time the axe appears, so melee combat is essentially impossible to dodge and comes down to spamming the attack button to kill it before it kills you.  Save your potions, abuse your ranged weapons.
Currently, a few imbalanced weapons make the game fairly easy, as stun weapons can paralyze even a titan that by all rights should squish you like a bug.  Magic and projectiles in general need reworking, as they tend to be either easily evaded or, in the case of some spells, are impossible to evade and hit 20 times in a row with enough damage to kill you if you aren't spamming the potion button like crazy.
It takes some clear references from Secret of Mana and Legend of Zelda. Some of the monsters are clearly in the art style of Secret of Mana. You have a "grappleshot" to cling to posts, bombs to open caves blocked by rocks, etc. You can even find outright expies where "Dink" is asked to fight "Cannondork" to save "Princess Xena"...
While it undoubtably has helped speed development, as there are a lot of scripts available for RPG Maker "off the shelf" at this point, the biggest limitation of this game seems to be its engine.  It would play better without the RPG Maker engine, whether it's because the RPG Maker engine is so badly optimized that even these graphics lag the game, or because it forces the game to stick to a grid-based system, when free-form movement would better suit the game.
Early access games should generally be rated on how they are, rather than what you hope they might someday be.  What it IS is still clearly under development at a pre-alpha level.  (There are some towns that just don't have doors because the shop interiors haven't been made yet...) That said, for the dirt-cheap price they're asking for it at this early state, it's more than enough entertainment to justify itself.  I give this game 8 stunlocked final bosses I kill with a weapon I got in the first village out of 10.

Abysmal.
You can see my old review here:
but it is for an older version of the game. I link it mainly because for its humour and so you can see my interactions with the developer.
So here's my review of this version on steam right now:
The game does not inspire confidence from the start when you change resolution and see that the title screen doesn't get scaled and so at 1920p for example it sits uncomfortablly at the top middle of the screen. The options by the way are basically just the resolution, music and sound on and off and a selectable theme. (There are no other themes, just "default").
The game does not work with steam overlay so you can't take screenshots easily.
You pick 6 of the pre-made adventurers on the start screen. You will notice at this point that the graphics are hand-drawn and pretty amateur-looking. In my original review I call the adventurers "Melty Face People" which became a bit disturbing when I learned they were based on photos of people who were cursed by a witch in a previous life and so had decided to back this game.
You will notice you are moving round the dungeon very slowly. Every step you take with your party of MFP (Melty Face People: do pay attention, 007) you see the ground ahead of you fade up with a little animation, and the movement keys do not auto-repeat.
Some squares are empty, some have monsters on. You can fight them or attempt to negotiate with them like some kind of bad♥♥♥♥♥new man, quiche-empathizing-with ("we could be dealing with a new form of life, number 1!") Captain Piccard. Negotiation never seems to work so it's on to the combat. Oh god, the combat...
At this point we get to the problem of controls:
1 The game  doesn't tell you what the keys are.
2 You can't change the keys. In my 7DRL entry last year, written in a week, you can change the keys. This game has been in development for years and you can't. This is absolutely inexcusable. Don't try to defend this, it's just awful.
3 You can't use the mouse.
4 You will have to press Enter *** 18 times every single combat round *** .
That is not an exaggeration. That is a fact. Six adventurers, and for each one you see an icon on the adventurer; you press enter; an options menu comes up (at least at the start it only seems to offer 'attack'); you press enter to select this attack; an icon appears on a monster; you press enter to confirm. That's 3x Enter for each of Six Adventurers, EVERY COMBAT ROUND. (And that's accepting the defaults, not counting the arrow keys you have to use to select option other than attack or target other than the default). Is this game secretly sponsored by keyboard manufacturers?
Also the animations in the combat are tediously slow and unskippable so you can't even just hammer the Enter key wakka-wakka-wakka because you have to wait.
Then there are squares with doors. If you attempt to move onto them you will get a display listing your adventurers and be told to select one to bash the door in. You will get really really familiar with this display.
Once you're in the room there can be a dungeon feature to interact with (that character to do the action selecty screen again) which can give good or bad results.
If you're really unlucky there will be a monster in the room and you will have to fight it. Oh god, no, please no.... Enter Enter Enter Enter...
There isn't much text in the game but it's available in multiple languages. (See I said something positive about the game!) Oh, what little text there is has mistakes in it in English. (Aaaand we're back to nasty).
The game is a horrible, ugly, slow-paced, boring, crash-prone, keyboard destroying, option-light, soul-destroying game of Melty Face People vs. the cardboard monsters. I urge you not to buy it.

OK, so I don't usually write reviews but really felt I had something to say about this one because of the mixed response it's been getting from the community.
Personally, I can understand the mixed reviews, but honestly, from my own perspective, this is a really, really good game. Yes, for sure it's incomplete, and I'm looking forward to the full story-mode version coming in summer (which I think will help promote longevity for this game), and yes, I want arcade mode with incrementally increasing difficulty, which I imagine they'll add at some point (but for now I don't think they've made any promises on this? Correct me if I'm wrong).
So, here's the deal. Really, what this game needs is a Dummies Guide to How to Enjoy SFV, starting with making good use of training mode, of course, but also going on YouTube for basic, intermediate, and advanced guides. Learn about footsies, combos, crush counters, and man does this game open up as something you can perfect not just for weeks, or even months, but potentially years. Watch tourmaments on YouTube for inspiration. There's so much you can engage with outside the game that can help you enjoy it more when you load it up.
And I'm serious. I can see this game as possibly dominating the genre for 2, maybe more, years to come.
That being said, again, I understand the mixed reviews, and I think it comes down to what kind of player you are. If your like me, and you can get obsessively hooked into training, perfecting, and really learning the details, I have no hesitation in recommending this game to you. I'm only a few hours in and I know this game is going to be with me at least through summer 2016, almost certainlyu longer, because story-mode will be a great new thing to get into in June. However, if you're the kind of player that likes a story, or plot, or a sense of immediate advancement when you game, then I wouldn't recommend this game to you, yet, and advise you to wait until the summer update.
As for the finer details, the game works fine (I had a problem with needing to unplug my WACOM tablet, but that's all), the frames are silky smooth, the servers are working fine for me, and I'm OK with waiting times for games as I'm happy training while I wait, which is usually around 2 or 3 minutes. I haven't bothered playing the mini-story modes yet.
My personal score at this early stage in my play is 7 out of 10. I imagine this might increase to an 8 or 9 when the summer update drops. Oh, and buy it on Amazon. It's only £22 there, and you get the steam key. For that price, it's well worth it.

There's two ways the game can go for you. This will either be a charming, lovable, funny little game. Or an annoying, boring, droned out mess. For me personally, it's certainly the first option. The game is VERY linear. It isn't really hard. It isn't all that long either. Knowing all the right options you could probably beat the game in like, 30 minutes. Many people are complaining about the awful singing. These people have missed the gag in that. The singing is supposed to be bad, that's the comedy of it. I feel as if the story is pretty original for what it is. I've always had an interest in stop motion animation this game has....LIMITED stop motion. Typically the same re-hashed animations in different scenes. If there was a nit pick problem from me this would probably be it. You really start to notice the reuse of animations and it gets a little bland in that respect. But the charm of the backdrops, characters, designs, and soundtrack make up for it. The soundtrack fits the atmosphere the game is going for very well. It's weird, wonky, and oddly amusing to listen to. However, staying in one area for too long. You'll notice the looping nature of the tracks, which CAN get a bit grating. The games fun comes from the humor in the characters jokes, as well as the laughs from the absolutely awful singing. First off, if you were a victim of♥♥♥♥♥♥ sexual abuse, child abuse, and/or any of above, it is best not to play this game. Steer clear from it. This will probably trigger your past moments. I know there are people in this world who are victims of such things, and playing this made it feel so real. I'm not kidding.
Right. Now onto the review.
Enola is a psychological story about your girlfriend named Angelica. You play as Enola, and yes you're a girl, and I'm talking about the girl on girl lesbian love, not best friend love. About Angelica...let's just say she did not have a pleasant past.
Graphics:
I love the detail of the objects and stages in the game. The only problem, however, are the human figures you come across. They were kinda weird and didn't sync right. I find that the areas get more disturbing in Nightmare Mode than Normal Mode. It's not gorey based or anything, but has some blood in it and pictures that will easily burn into your brain. Other than that, the areas of the game give it more of a vintage style with a hint of steampunk.
Voice Acting:
The voice acting is pretty good. Whoever did Angelica's voice did a great job, especially when it comes to expressing her sorrow and anger. Astrid's voice sounds a bit weird...like an evil teenage high school student-type voice. Enola's voice acting was okay, except at the beginning of the ending, it sounded like she just recited her lines. However, her crying and screaming were good. Finally, "The Monster's" voice acting was spot-on perfect. The guy really put himself in the game there, acted like a monster for sure. Out of all the voice actors, I'd pick him to be the best.
Gameplay:
The game has a small, yet simple inventory system. It counts the lamps you come across during the game, as they reveal a little extra at the end of the good ending. As for the difficulty curve, it's more of a "spike up" at certain times, as a few times you'll feel so stumped that you may have to search or check for guides for help.
In the game, you come across choices of murdering certain people, which will affect the ending. The game as a save feature, where you interact with Music Boxes to save. There is a battle system. Randomly, you come across shadowy figures and you must click the mouse and mash the W,A,S,D keys to defend yourself.
With the recent update, it has two modes: Normal and Nightmare. Nightmare mode is like a small expansion pack with increase difficulty and to collect crystals, which will reveal Angelica's and Enola's moments together. Collecting crystals will affect the ending as well.
The problem I have with this game is the constant bugs. So far, there is only one gamebreaking bug and one bug that is fixable using the console. Otherwise, most bugs are either aesthetic and/or annoyances that can kill you. Luckily, the game gives you plenty of moments to save. The developer is also active in assisting players to this day (and even assisted me with my guides for the game :D ), which I must give props for. The console is also enabled to help combat the bugs as well or to speed through the game.
Story:
The story focuses on Enola and Angelica. As I said, Angelica did not have a pleasant past so start to feel here. You play as Enola, her girlfriend. One day, she just disappears, and suddenly you're in a strange world. As you play through the story, you understand Angelica's traumatic past, her parents, and how she met Enola. You come across letters that communicate with you and lamps that reveal Angelica's parent's past and some facts about Enola. I could reveal more, but I think the first paragraph at the beginning of the review will give you an idea of what it is like.
Overall:
Regardless of the many bugs and some strange stuff with the graphics, Enola is an indie horror game that shines. What makes the game awesome is the immersive story and great voice acting that makes you feel for the characters in the story. Most horror enthusiasts think that it takes blood, gore, and disfigured people to make you scared. However, Enola apparently knows which strings to pull to make you feel disturbed, sad, and even scared without the above.
Pros:
-Great horror story.
-Unique characters.
-Pretty good graphics.
-Great voice acting.
Cons:
-Buggy at certain points of the game, but you can still play through without coming across them.
-Some weirdness in graphics related to human models.
-Increase of difficulty at certain points of the game.

RotMG has had something of a checkered past. From it's storied inception at the hands of indie dev Wildstorm Studios to it's dubious sale to Kabaam, and now this latest chapter as the game is once again sold to Deca Games. Let's be clear. The time with Kabaam were some dark days. But it speaks to the resiliency and devotion of the fanbase/community that so many players soldiered on through the bad times and stayed with this game for so long.
Kabaam's handling of bugs and duping was poor. Really poor. One of the biggest issues when I last player the game about two years ago was that the "Amulet of Resurrection"... the only item in the game that could save your character if it was "killed" was normally a very expensive and difficult to acquire item. But so many people were duping them that the in game economy was flooded with them and no one was dying. Turn and churn is a really big part of this game so when no one dies the game stagnates. Kabaam handled this complex issue with a sledgehammer turning all the amulets into "Amulets of Zombification." I personally felt violated. They went into my vault inventory and took items I had earned and replaced them with something far inferior without asking me or discussing it with me. I was already furious.
Then they completely botched their communication with the community. Telling us that this new amulet had a 5% chance of turning your character into a Zombie and thus... failing to save it. When your character is dead in RotMG it's dead. Nothing is saved.  So when you lose a maxed character with great gear it's a big deal to a lot of players. And it turned out that the Amulet that was supposed to only have a 5% chance of letting us die was in fact about 95%. Everyone started dying and turning into zombies. I lost a maxed 8/8 Huntress that turned into a Zombie and I was furious. I walked away from the game and hardly looked back despite having three other maxed characters. Time passed.
Kabaam eventually created a pet system to replace the Amulet. No your pets can't save you if you die. But by grinding and grinding you can create a pet so powerful that bosses and dungeons that were super dangerous are far less so. But other than the introduction of a lot of new dungeons and content that seems to be the end of Kabaam's major changes. And bugs and duping have persisted this entire time.
For example there's a bug that if you try and drag an item into your inventory and someone else snags the item (often with the reviled "auto pickup" programs that many players now must use to compete with multi-boxers and hackers) before you get it all the way into your inventory it creates a "ghost" of that item. This ghost will not disappear. And it can block and make useless as many as four inventory slots. And with only 8 slots on the base character that can really hamper your ability to pick up items. What's worse the "ghost" cannot be dispelled without reloading the program entirely. Merely going to the Nexus, your vault or changing realms works. The item "ghost" even persists in the loading screen. And while I understand this was done to fix a duping bug a better solution SURELY should have been found in the two years that have passed since I first encountered it.
But despite these issues RotMG is one of the most consistently fun and addicting games I've ever played. And with the sale to Deca games there's hope that their profession of being fans and devotees of the game themselves will lead to long needed fixes and improvements. For example, there's no way to play fullscreen. The game was originally designed to play on a small computer monitor inside a web browser and that initial design has never been improved upon. Despite the game being years old and being passed to it's 3rd developer and losing a lot of its playerbase there is still no way to play it full screen. In Steam you can stretch the window to make it bigger than the tiny default window... but beware, because if you don't keep the aspect ratio correct... and there is no way to constrain it, you can throw off the way the game is presented to you. The best case scenario is some menus will only present half their information and some ads may block your inventory. The worst case is thinking there is a monster in a certain spot when it is actually a bit closer to you and to the left. It can get you killed if you aren't careful.
Another issue is the HP and Mana Pots. Not the stat pots but the blue and red potions that you use to replenish lost HP or magic power while in a fight. Initially Kabaam, in a rather blatant money grab, made it so when you ran out of these pots and hit the hot key to use one the system would automatically take five "Gold" (the in game currency that is purchased for real world money) and sell you the pot instead of telling you that you were out. After much furor from the community Kabaam implemented an off switch for this in the controls. However I have found that if you do shut off auto purchasing these pots and then hit the hot key when you are out of them and in a fight a large UI box pops up, covering much of your fighting area, and asking you if you want to buy the pot for 5 gold as you are out. It's horrifying. It almost got my 8/8 Knight killed twice in a five minute period. Really freaked me out and it's a really poor implementation.
Additionally I'd say there are issues altogether with the way these pots are sold. Mana and HP Pots are super easy to get. A high level character is so powerful that the low level mobs that drop them get mowed down like bowling pins by maxed out characters. Yet it can be time consuming and annoying to be farming baby mobs just so you have a bit of healing and magic replacement for the dungeons and big fights you actually want to be doing as a maxed character. And purchasing these pots at 5 Gold is a ridiculous and usurious price to charge for something so easily obtained and unimportant to the game. It's like charging a person for putting air in their tires. Sure there are coin operated air compressors but I have yet to run into a service station that doesn't simply turn it on for free. Because while we all realize you need air in your tires it isn't something of great value or scarcity. The same goes for these pots. They are neither valuable nor scarce but you need them. And high level players wasting time scouring the land for them is sort of silly. My hope is that this new owner, Deca Games; in addition to making many other improvements and bug fixes, sees the wisdom in reducing the price for these items and encouraging their use at the same time. For example you can carry up to six of each of these pots for a total of twelve. Can you imagine how much more gold Deca would sell and how more often these micro purchases would be made if they simply offered to top your inventory off for one gold? Imagine... you're going out to the realm and you want to head to the god lands or someone is opening a dungeon in the Nexus. You hit a button and for one gold you get your HP and Mana pots inventory filled up. I'd do this at least once almost every time I played. Probably for multiple characters.
Right now gold is roughly 100 to 1 in real world to in game value. So one dollar US is equal to 100 Gold. So at the current rate buying HP and Mana pots to fill your inventory of six each would cost a staggering sixty cents. More than half a dollar for something so unimportant. Thus I and most players have NEVER purchased them. But if it was 1 gold to fill er up. You bet your♥♥♥♥♥I'd use it.
Deca Games is doing a lot of giveaways and has proclaimed this and the following four weeks the "Month of the Mad God." There's a lot of celebrating and they've done an excellent job of energizing and motivating the community on social media. Lets hope that energy carries over to improvements and new content for the game. But even if it doesn't. RotMG is crazy fun.

As someone who wanted to revist the R6 franchise after years of an absence, I cannot believe I'm going to say this:
This game is the most guilty pleasure I have ever found in a modern-military/tactical-shooter, and it's because it's so bad at being both a competent game and a MMS/TSS.
The story is nonexistent with Tom Clancy's typical phobias of Cold War 2 and of Marxism terrorists going to take over the world with what's given in the PC version. There are no cutscenes in-between missions like the Xbox version, and for some reason this game is structured entirely different from the Xbox version.
I don't think this story-method is inherently flawed. A game that puts you into missions with concise briefings can be an interesting way to tell a story in this genre. With actual characters and time to talk things over with your teammates for quiet time, I think you can pull twists off and engage the player than any dumb modern-military shooter.
As I played the game I felt like a cadet given the scrapest of intel and told to get the job done with lives resting in my hands (which would live for tomorrow whether they died ro not in the mission). These intel could be better utilized to figure out choke-points or learn more about the R6 Heads by what they don't tell you in black-marks or hide in the briefings vs. the debriefings.
Honestly, I'd love for a MMS to do this narrative justice. Or maybe an anti-war game would be better given the quality of game stories that genre has made.
What works in this game is actually surprising.
For starters, the level-design feels quite nice and colorful. There are a variety of settings that each keep the corridor shooters just slightly more interesting to keep playing.
You have desserty middle eastern places, universities, caves, bunkers, urban areas, hospitals, morgues, catacombs, junglely areas and more. A lot of these areas are typical for MMS, and yet the level design and color palatte feel refreshing.
The aesthetic and detail of the game also reminds me of FEAR with the lighting effects and the reference humor on the walls. Ubisoft games, fake ads, fake product placement and more that made me question why were they here in the first place. The game's environments and gun-models look great still for today, but the humans all look like abominations of early 3D gaming.
Everything else about this game... is godawful.
The AI, whether your squad(s) or the enemies are hilarious to watch in their failure. Your AI will clear rooms walking backwards into gunfire; the enemies will spray their guns toward you moving them left-to-right like Rambo, and yet missing you all the time; your AI will flashbang themselves when breaching a room; the enemies will run around you at times to find the right spot to die at; your AI will stay "in cover" while the enemies are filling him/her with holes behind him/her or shooting him/her at an angle.
As much as I save-scummed my way through this
game, I chuckled all the way through with how serious the situations were contrasted with the game's AI. It is almost self-aware.
The gunplay is all right, I suppose, but the guns are all cosmetic and audio differences, and the default loadouts are decent enough to get your through the game. I varied up my guns because you can only stick with the loadout you are given at the start, so be sure to have plenty of ammo for the situationis.
Glitches galore, and random moments plague this game worse than any Ubisoft game released in 2014. And it's still not patched.
I got my money's worth out of this game with just the single-player shennanigans. Almost. On Mission 15, however, the game infuriated me to stop.
You see, there's an area where an enemy is directly at the ladder where you need to drop down . If you don't have a grenade to kill him, it's game-over; there is no way to lure him up, shoot him from above, or send your squad-mates to kill him. And this is the third section of the level, so you'll have to restart the entire mission. Oh joy..
Putting that game-breaking design-desicion aside, I wanna recommend this game ONLY if you buy this game as a part of the R6 pack on a steep Steam sale and you want a jarring experience for a mechanically sufficient tactical shooter with the dumbest AI I have ever played with in all FPSs.

I was really hyped to play another Daedalic adventure and nothing from the visuals gave any signs that it wasn't one. The style of the drawings is identical to the style of Edna and Harvey so naturally I thought that this was a game developed by Daedalic.
Launching the game the first time I was surprised that it didn't pop up the standard Visionnaire tool that every other Daedalic adventure game had. Actually the engine used in Randal's Monday is somewhat better performance wise than the Visionnaire engine. So I thought Daedalic had finally developed a new engine, no big deal.
However, slowly a suspicion started creeping up that Randal's Monday might have been made by some B team. The dialogue is uncharacteristically long and frankly quite boring. The inventory system is hell due to the fact that you can only use an item once before having to select it again. And the biggest telltale sign of all: the puzzle design and sequencing was seriously lacking.
Let's talk about how the inventory system works for a bit. You have a standard inventory icon in the lower left side of the screen that opens up into a comic book. In this comic book you can fit around 20 objects per page and oh boy are you going to carry more than 20 pieces of stuff constantly. To combine things from different pages in your inventory you first have to select thing 1, flip the page, and select thing 2. Simple enough, right? Now try doing it 20 times. I swear it took more than an hour of my life of just doing this to complete the game. I would understand if this system was developed to discourage rubbing things against eachother mindlessly, but many of the game's puzzles are based around combining random objects.
Then there are the puzzles. Half of the time the objective is quite clear and you know what you generally need to do to proceed. However, the thing you need to do is derailed by massive and logic free detours so that most of the time you're really not sure what you are doing. I found myself asking myself "Why am I doing this?" on numerous occasions. And there's weren't just picking up small objects either. The reason for entire hour long puzzles is sometimes revealed only at the end when you receive something useful without previously knowing of its existence.
Then there's the story. Not worth it. Trust me.
I really do feel bad about criticizing this game so heavily and I hope Nexus Game Studios goes on to develop more adventure games. There's some serious talent there if they get a decent writer and work out some of the problems Randal's Monday had.

OK, so I don't usually write reviews but really felt I had something to say about this one because of the mixed response it's been getting from the community.
Personally, I can understand the mixed reviews, but honestly, from my own perspective, this is a really, really good game. Yes, for sure it's incomplete, and I'm looking forward to the full story-mode version coming in summer (which I think will help promote longevity for this game), and yes, I want arcade mode with incrementally increasing difficulty, which I imagine they'll add at some point (but for now I don't think they've made any promises on this? Correct me if I'm wrong).
So, here's the deal. Really, what this game needs is a Dummies Guide to How to Enjoy SFV, starting with making good use of training mode, of course, but also going on YouTube for basic, intermediate, and advanced guides. Learn about footsies, combos, crush counters, and man does this game open up as something you can perfect not just for weeks, or even months, but potentially years. Watch tourmaments on YouTube for inspiration. There's so much you can engage with outside the game that can help you enjoy it more when you load it up.
And I'm serious. I can see this game as possibly dominating the genre for 2, maybe more, years to come.
That being said, again, I understand the mixed reviews, and I think it comes down to what kind of player you are. If your like me, and you can get obsessively hooked into training, perfecting, and really learning the details, I have no hesitation in recommending this game to you. I'm only a few hours in and I know this game is going to be with me at least through summer 2016, almost certainlyu longer, because story-mode will be a great new thing to get into in June. However, if you're the kind of player that likes a story, or plot, or a sense of immediate advancement when you game, then I wouldn't recommend this game to you, yet, and advise you to wait until the summer update.
As for the finer details, the game works fine (I had a problem with needing to unplug my WACOM tablet, but that's all), the frames are silky smooth, the servers are working fine for me, and I'm OK with waiting times for games as I'm happy training while I wait, which is usually around 2 or 3 minutes. I haven't bothered playing the mini-story modes yet.
My personal score at this early stage in my play is 7 out of 10. I imagine this might increase to an 8 or 9 when the summer update drops. Oh, and buy it on Amazon. It's only £22 there, and you get the steam key. For that price, it's well worth it.

Bastion is one of the last Xbox Live Arcade games I missed in my Steam library. While this is not the best, nor my favorite indie game, it is still a wonderful game that everyone should try out.
The story is told by The Stranger who is telling the whole story through very well-written narration with a cool voice. That is in fact one of the major good things of this game.
The graphics, while not the most beautiful of indie games, have a nice style and the idea of raising pieces of land makes for some quite nice visuals.
As previously mentioned, the narration is wonderful and the music is really good too.
The gameplay is quite simple but really fun and at times challenging. The whole game is played in a top-down isometric perspective and the main focus is one finding a certain object (for example, a core) while fighting your way through waves of enemies. It all works well and I haven't ecountered a single glitch. You'll get to use several different weapons, both melee and long-range.
Aside from the main story, there's quite a lot to do on the side. Every weapon has trial/challenge area and later in the game you'll get to visit optional areas (a kind of a battle arena). After beating the game, you also unlock New Game Plus and Score Attack Mode so you might wanna complete the game a few times. With all that in mind: the game has quite a big longetivity and replay value.
SCORE: 8.5/10

Bastion is a fantastic game that needs to be experienced. It provides:
-An arsenal of weapons that are given to you throughout the game at a very good pace. Being curious to what the weapons could be and their functions gave me a lot of motivation to keep going.
-Fantastic narration, voice acting was done perfectly. Narration gives descriptions of the main protagonists, "The Kid", actions throughout the world and explains the story throughout the play through.
-Very well stylised art style. Everything about how the game looks is very unique and detailed. The detail in the environments and wildlife of Bastion immerses the player in the world and lore of the Bastion.
-Story is very well done and complimented by both the narration and the lore of the world. It contains a very good amount of mystery that keeps the player compelled to explore and further unravel the "Calamity."
-You can have two weapons on you that you can switch between in combat allowing the player to choose his or her play style. To test your proficiency with the weapon there are proving grounds and they are arenas that will test your ability to use that weapon with the goal being a 3-Tier prize. Proving grounds, like all the areas in Bastion, contain its own lore and once you have achieved first prize in the proving grounds you gain an attachment towards that weapon and area because of the hardships endured by the player to get first prize.
-The difficulty in the game can be modified through shrines which allow you to choose certain gods that have different things that increase difficulty in exchange for a fragment increase. This was a very good way to put more depth into combat as you would have to become more cautious and think about the situation and how to handle it depending on your chosen shrines.
-The soundtrack is very well done and has to heard along with gameplay to be experienced fully. It is able to give another layer of immersion and intensity in combat situations.
-There is a combat mechanic called counter-blocking that allows the player to return the damage of an enemy's attack back to them with a well-timed block. This mechanic was very satisfying and felt very good when done in the chaos of combat.
As with all games Bastion does have its flaws:
-Combat gets repetitive with some weapons containing only one primary function "shoot" while others contain a "shoot" and "charge" modifier. Whilst the combat scenarios were technically different combat had lost its satisfaction near the end.
-Without the use of shrines the game became to easy especially if you upgraded your weapons and combat wasn't as satisfying. The difficulty curve is very evident and done logically but the combat was still too easy without the use of shrines.
Fantastic - 9.5/10

An enjoyable game thus far. I truly felt like an explorer on a new frontier, overcoming adversity through self-sufficiency, battling against insurmountable odds (on higher threat levels, naturally) to colonise this brave new world(s). The title menu music really does set the mood--a lone ship traversing the blackest depths of the void, taking me to the very heart of vast, immortal suns.
I know that some dislike it for the delay in release, but I'd rather Chucklefish take longer to polish it than release an obvious beta (like certain "AAA" companies have done in the past).
Perhaps we've been conditioned to see indie game developers as money grubbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s--there certainly have been cases where developers pushed releases further and further back, until it became apparent that they were nothing but thieves. But I don't believe we should lose faith in the developers simply because of a missed deadline. Chucklefish may have some issues, but they are undeniably showing effort in pushing out a release. Few complained about Watch_Dogs being pushed back (until it was released), because they thought that a better product would come out of it. What's a couple years more to wait? It's not like Chucklefish is merely saying that they're updating the game--they actually are pushing out updates for us to play with.
Everyone's entitled to their own opinion, of course, and I can understand where much of the impatience and anger is coming from. I, for one, will continue to put my faith in Starbound. (I do hope hunger can be added back in, however.)

Dominique Pamplemousse is a fun but short detective story claymation musical. The game has a really interesting premise, but it tends to get buried under the creator’s “messages”.
Dominique Pamplemousse is a crowd-funded adventure game made by an independent developer, Deirdra Kiai. On paper. In reality it is a claymation musical with little gaming involved.
The presentation looks amateurish and cheap, but it seems like an artistic choice; I have to admit, it adds a warm, welcoming atmosphere. The same cannot be wholeheartedly said about the singing (all done by the creator itself), as it is often off-key. Which, oddly enough, fits the plot: the player takes the role of the titular character, a private detective, who is hired to find a pop star, but eventually gets entangled in the shady voice-manipulation plots of a record company.
For the most part, the story works. Except when it is stopped to repeatedly convey Deirdra’s message about gender identity and financial issues. These out-of-place topics don’t ruin the game, but they certainly made this cheap, short, but sweet title a little less excellent.
