How much can you really complain about a Free To Play game?
As it turns out, quite a bit. Which isn't really a surprise to anyone that's ever played a game like Warframe.
Or Trove.
I'll start with the pluses, since I should at least try to be fair. Trove devs correctly understood that the most entertaining thing about Minecraft is starting a new world fresh and then running wild all over it, and made this a core part of the Trove experience. You select the difficulty of the world you want to enter, jump in, and enter a randomly generated instance map full of dungeons to pillage and bosses to kill. When you want to do it again, you just return to the hub and repeat the process with a new instance map. And unlike Minecraft, which can sometimes feel quite empty and desolate, you share instances with other players, and dungeons and other structures are common, which makes the worlds feel more robust and alive.
You also are not gimped as far as movement is concerned. Very quickly, you will earn the ability to jump three, five, twelve, twenty times in a row, giving you a lot of height and control in the air. There are also wings that can be used to glide very long distances, as well as flying mounts.
The Trove devs also understand that most people who like building simulators enjoy decorating. Trove has a vast list of decorative objects to build with, and most of them need to be unlocked by exploring and raiding dungeons, which is a great incentive to seek out specific biomes and pillage them for the biome-specific crafting recipies.
If only they could have stuck with their basic idea, this game would have been one of the best Free To Plays out there.
But they did not.
For starters, the servers are awful. And I mean bad. Really, really bad. No matter how good your rig is, no matter what company provides your internet service, regardless of whether you have a supercomputer or a toaster, or where you happen to live on Planet Earth, Trove will lag. And crash. And lag some more. You will get kicked from the game. Your game will crash, repeatedly. There is nothing you can do about it. It doesn't matter how solid your connection is, or how good of a machine you have. You could be using fiber optics in Europe, or running a toaster in Australia. You will experience regular, common blowouts, and that's all there is to it.
Secondly, the game has gone hard, HARD pay-to-win. The main advertising point of the game, besides being a better and free version of Minecraft, was the classes, of which there are many. And surprisingly, most of them are pretty good. What a pity you will never unlock any of them. In the original iteration of the game, back in ye olden times, classes could be obtained one of two ways: you could buy them for a large amount of in-game currency, or you could unlock them with a Class Token. Class Tokens are items that are occasionally given away during events and streams, and can be purchased for the premium cash currency at the in-game store.
You can probably see this coming from a mile away, but guess what? After about a year of running the game this way, they nixed the ability to buy the classes with in-game currency. Classes can now only be obtained through direct purchase with money, or indirect purchase through a Class Token, itself an item that must be bought with real money.
This change is a slap in the face to the player base. Not all classes are created equal. Some are absolutely more powerful than others, and you NEED better classes to seriously attempt the highest levels of play. What's more, there is already a system of leveling, called Mastery, that gives you rewards at certain tiers of player level. It would have been child's play to simply grant players Class Tokens at regular Mastery intervals during their progression, or to even award the player a Class Token every time they max out the Class Level of a Class they have already unlocked. At least then you could earn the ability to get more classes by progressing and playing the game. People who were impatient or more casual could pay for their tokens, while the more dedicated players earned them.
But no. Trion decided to double-down on their greed, and the game suffers greatly for it. This one single change took a fun but unstable game, and turned it into a Skinner's Box of sadness and regret.
The third problem pales in comparison to the second, but it still needs to be said: your cornerstone, which is to say, the area you have to build on that is persistant and can be summoned to your location out in the field during instances, is not nearly large enough. The reason everyone makes their base a giant tower exactly as wide as the size of the cornerstone itself, is because it's the only real way to get anything done. Even though the variety of decorations avaliable is fantastic, the fact that you are gimped so hard when it comes to showing them off and putting together a persistant base makes the whole endeavor seem kind of pointless. After all, if it doesn't look good in a needle tower of stone or glass, then it isn't going to see much use. The idea of mobile bases in a free-range Minecraft MMO was a fantastic idea, but in the end, it falls flat, because you get a 20 x 20 space to do it in. No castle, mansion, or giant treehouse for you.
At the end of the day, I can't recommend Trove. This game is not what it used to be, and the only reason the User Reviews are "Mostly Good" is because we all (rightfully) adored it when it first came out.
But Trion has destroyed what used to be good in this game, and it is now nothing more than elaborate trap designed to guilt you into paying for dozens of cash shop items through false emotional investment.
There is a great, worthwhile game to be found in the endless-instance mobile-base freeform-MMO Minecraft formula. But Trove ain't that game.
Just go play Terraria.

TLDR; This game is really fun. If you like RTS games with a good balance of micro vs macro (with more emphasis on the macro) then you should buy this game. Outside of the 1000 pound gorilla of RTS, its one of the more active RTS communities around, so you can pretty easily find MP games. Its got somewhat steep system requirements (8GB ram) but I could still play it on my intel gfx laptop acceptably with low settings, and its pretty cheap/easy to get 8GB these days.
If you look at the past reviews, there are many people who aren't reviewing the game itself, but more based on how they feel the company could have handled kickstarter, etc better. I have no insight into any of that. I am a newcomer to the game, which was just recently updated for the first time in 7 months. My review will be based on the game state AS IT IS TODAY, which is really what you should be concerned about anyway if you're considering getting the game!
PS: While Uber may have made some PR missteps, they are a TRUE indie company that dev'ed and self-published this game beholden to no publishers or external investors. I applaud this approach, as it seems many "indie" game companies these days are not really independent at all...
On the surface PA:Titans doesn't do a ton of things that other RTS haven't done before, but considering how well-explored this genre is thats not really surprising. This is a game from some of the creators of Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander, and it shows clearly. You can (and should) build up tons of units and multiple bases (even across multiple planets!). There are rushing strategies, counters for those strategies, and some tiered advancement plus special units called titans which can be a major payoff, or be your doom. I feel like the game is pretty well balanced overall.
One of the things PA Titans does really well is the introduction of planets as... actual planets. They are fully connected, spherical platforms upon which you set forth to conquer your enemies. Each planet really doesn't feel that different than playing on a 'normal' flattened RTS map, save one thing: There are no corner or side bases. While maps have land and other features to create choke points, you must always be aware that the enemy could literally come from any side, or even ABOVE, as satellites and weapons can be launched in orbit. (Might as well mention it here, you can build a huge engine on the side of the planet and literally launch it into another planet!)
Something the planet and lack of traditional corner bases does is really emphasize the 'strategy' in the RTS acryonym. While the classics like WC, SC, etc are almost more about actions-per-minute than actual gameplay, PA Titans (by nature of being a bit more macro focused combined with the planet system) seems to reward solid scouting, flexibility, and counterplay. Sure, you can commit yourself to a super-Dox rush (think zerglings), and it might just work, but if your opponent scouts you out and builds some quick counters, that huge deathball of yours could be wiped and your opponent could change the momentum dramatically.
The latest update added a built-in mod manager that is probably one of the best I've ever used. Its simple and straightforward to install and use the mods. There are some great community mods, including a whole new faction for some added variety! I recommend at least starting with these mods:
- Ubermap (for traditional RTS overview map)
- Legion Expansion
- PA Chat for Titan & Classic (in-game community chat room)
- Infinite Build (switches factories to continuous build by default)
There are tons more, including map packs, so start with the above and tailor it to your liking.
There are a few strange omissions from the game, such as the lack of a fullscreen resolution changer. You either run in 'borderless window' or windowed mode. If you want a different overall fullscreen resolution you'll need to change your desktop res then relaunch the game. Other than that, I haven't run into any obvious bugs or issues. Multiplayer worked very well, including a traditional LAN-play and self-hosted server option, which you just don't see often enough anymore. Kudos to the devs for adding that feature.
Performance could be better on low-end systems, given the relatively simple graphics. On a typical gaming PC (if you're not running 8+GB these days, what are you thinking?) you'll have no issues, and you don't really miss out on anything if you need to turn down a few graphics settings. Considering the sheer volume of units and projectiles, not to mention planets, that this game is pumping out, I think the performance is quite good.

Enola is probably one of the most bizzare horror games i've ever experienced. You play as Enola, a woman who is searching  through what seems to be her girlfriend, Angelica's subconcious. Along the way you learn of some very disturbing and terrible events in Angelica's life that caused her to get locked away in her own thoughts.
When the game tells you that some parts of the game are disturbing and cruel, they aren't talking about small blood splatters. There is torture, nudity, and plenty of examples of the darker side of human sexuality which add more depth to the game than triggering content.
The puzzles in this game are rather clever, changing up the style and raising the stakes with each completion. If you like to think outside the box, this game will fit with your style of thinking. Some puzzles are as simple as "put this on that thing" or "press these three buttons", and other take a bit more though using subtle clues in notes and in the world itself.
I did only play the basic game and didn't attempt nightmare mode, so your experience could possibly change completely if you attempt to conquer that beast. It was a twisted ride that i'm glad I got off, but could see myself coming back to in the future.

There you are, happily enjoying your weekend when all of a sudden, Monday comes along and ruins everything.
For most of us, it marks the death of free time and the beginning of five days of drudgery.
It’s little wonder that Monday is the most hated day of the week.
There are only fifty two of them a year, It feels like more doesn’t it?
And for Randal, the anti-hero of Daedalic Entertainments point and click adventure “Randals Monday” every day is Monday!
If you’ve seen the movie Groundhog Day (and if not, go and watch it now, I’ll wait...)
You’ll remember that funny man Bill Murray is trapped in time, living the same day over and over again until he “gets it right”.
Well that is the premise for Randals Monday.
After a Sunday evening of heavy drinking with his friends, Randal wakes on Monday morning to what will turn out to be a very bad day.
He doesn’t know it yet, but he’s about to have a row with his landlord, lose his job and discover that his best friend has committed suicide.
So, you’re expecting a dark, gritty drama. A point and click adventure through the melancholy and futility of existence right?
Not so my friend, this game is a comedy!
If you’re familiar with Lucas Arts adventure games of old, Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle etc. then you’ll know what to expect with regards to game play.
You’ll point and click your way around Randals world, combining increasingly bizarre objects at random in a desperate attempt to try and find a solution to which ever obstacle is blocking your progress in the story.
Point and click adventure games live and die on the quality of two things, the writing and the puzzles. The quality of the writing to be found here is a little uneven. There are lines that will genuinely make you chuckle, but not every “funny” hits home.
I guess it’s down to personal taste.
The puzzles themselves range from the logical (Convince a down trodden sales man to make a call as a distraction) to the insane! (Attract a rat, kill it and marinate its corpse in water then use the stench to obtain some soap!)
Fear not though, there is a comprehensive hints system built into the game to help you navigate your way through the craziness.
The story itself is an interesting (and mostly funny) tale, revolving around a cursed ring, an alcoholic friends suicide, his girlfriends’ reaction and a pawnshop (amongst other places).
Events that you set in motion during the day will impact events when you relive that day again.
So even though you’re experiencing the same day, over and over, each iteration of it plays out differently depending on your previous actions.
A good example of this is when you alter the date of an event on a poster to todays date, After you sleep and wake on that same Monday morning, that event will now be taking place.
This is so well implemented in the story telling that you really don’t notice the bizarreness of it all whilst playing.
I should probably also mention the quality of the voice acting, which is very good throughout and complements the fittingly cartoony graphics perfectly.
If you like your pop culture references, then you’ll find plenty to love in Randals Monday.
I’m not going to spoil them for you here; the fun is spotting them in the game and patting yourself on the back for your cultural cleverness.
I will say that I particularly enjoyed the prison elements of the game, where the story pays homage to one of my favourite films of all time <cough>  <Shawshank Redemption>  <cough>
So we’ve got a contemporary, comedy, vaguely supernatural, sci-fi, parody tale here so, whatever your genre of choice, you should find something to enjoy in Randals Monday, but it’s not all genre busting, cultural reverence, There is a down side.
The main character, Randall, is just so damn unlikable.
I imagine he was intended to be a comedic anti-hero, someone who we wouldn’t mind bad things happening to but who also has elements of roughish warmth that help endear him to the player and make him relatable.
Unfortunately, this doesn’t work for me; he just comes across as a selfish and conceited jerk.
If you like point and click adventure games, dark comedy and more pop culture references than should be humanly possible to squash into a game, then you’re going to enjoy Randals Monday.
It does tell an intriguing and entertaining tale which even Randal himself can’t spoil.

The Good: Some interesting quests; a few good laughs with lots of geeky references; generally smart voice acting; great artistic quality; Jay is awesomely profane.
The Bad: Too much banal conversation; repetitive tasks with arduous backtracking and time-consuming transitions between locations; many poorly-clued quests and misleading feedback; unpleasant characters; Randal is dull and annoying.

Bastion is a fantastic game that needs to be experienced. It provides:
-An arsenal of weapons that are given to you throughout the game at a very good pace. Being curious to what the weapons could be and their functions gave me a lot of motivation to keep going.
-Fantastic narration, voice acting was done perfectly. Narration gives descriptions of the main protagonists, "The Kid", actions throughout the world and explains the story throughout the play through.
-Very well stylised art style. Everything about how the game looks is very unique and detailed. The detail in the environments and wildlife of Bastion immerses the player in the world and lore of the Bastion.
-Story is very well done and complimented by both the narration and the lore of the world. It contains a very good amount of mystery that keeps the player compelled to explore and further unravel the "Calamity."
-You can have two weapons on you that you can switch between in combat allowing the player to choose his or her play style. To test your proficiency with the weapon there are proving grounds and they are arenas that will test your ability to use that weapon with the goal being a 3-Tier prize. Proving grounds, like all the areas in Bastion, contain its own lore and once you have achieved first prize in the proving grounds you gain an attachment towards that weapon and area because of the hardships endured by the player to get first prize.
-The difficulty in the game can be modified through shrines which allow you to choose certain gods that have different things that increase difficulty in exchange for a fragment increase. This was a very good way to put more depth into combat as you would have to become more cautious and think about the situation and how to handle it depending on your chosen shrines.
-The soundtrack is very well done and has to heard along with gameplay to be experienced fully. It is able to give another layer of immersion and intensity in combat situations.
-There is a combat mechanic called counter-blocking that allows the player to return the damage of an enemy's attack back to them with a well-timed block. This mechanic was very satisfying and felt very good when done in the chaos of combat.
As with all games Bastion does have its flaws:
-Combat gets repetitive with some weapons containing only one primary function "shoot" while others contain a "shoot" and "charge" modifier. Whilst the combat scenarios were technically different combat had lost its satisfaction near the end.
-Without the use of shrines the game became to easy especially if you upgraded your weapons and combat wasn't as satisfying. The difficulty curve is very evident and done logically but the combat was still too easy without the use of shrines.
Fantastic - 9.5/10

Enola is touted as being, and I quote, a psychological adventure game that delves into the inherent darkness of love, death and revenge. Other reviewers claim the game to be both challenging, dark and emotional. Those reviews and this one prove one thing, everything is subjective and opinions are like♥♥♥♥♥holes, in that we all have one. For those of you who trust my opinion and find it lining up with your own I will bring my recommendation for this game to the very front of this review to save you the kind of time I lost whilst desperately trying to enjoy the experience that is Enola. Do not buy this game, even when it inevitably comes on a sale, do not buy this terrible game. If my recommendation is not enough, or you just wish to read more about my experience and the incredibly small amount of good in Enola, then please read on.
Enola is a game of two halves. One half is a walking game as you explore the mind of the protagonist and the woman she seeks to help. The other half is filled with puzzles reminiscent of my 90s point and click days. The problem is that neither half has gameplay, something I personally enjoy in my video games. Now some will say that this is not your average video game, it is the joyous thing called an ‘experience’ and to a point they would be correct but sadly the developers decided to add gameplay to this ‘experience’ and what they added is nothing short of dull, tedious and instantly forgettable. If Enola was truly an ‘experience’ and did away with the puzzle sections and the, so called, jump-scares then the game would be getting a different review from this writer but it did not and so this is what you get.
Let’s deal with the first half and the majority of what you will be doing whilst playing Enola, walking. You meander around the world of your in-game lovers mind made real, Angelica. It is a dark and sombre place, filled with what would be if seen in your own real life, macabre and tortuous set pieces, fragments of a disturbed and abused mind. It is not a pretty place to be in more ways than one. As I wandered around this world I could easily see how this could have been a scary, tense place filled with shadows and voices haunting you at every corner and around ever pillar. Sadly this never happens because it seems the devs simply do not have the skills required to create the world they wanted to and this is a shame. It is not just the level of graphics in the game, though the Unreal 3 engine is capable of so much more, because whilst graphics do not make a game they do help when it comes to atmosphere. Neither is it the audio, indeed there are various sections where the audio kicks in perfectly and actually throws a couple of chills the players way and the voice acting is extremely good and a cut above everything else. No, the problem lies in direction and game design. The parts are there but they mostly come off as amateur and underfunded and in a game whose sole purpose is to place you in dark and tense moments of horror they fail miserably and make those odd five minutes of genuine fear a weak and uninspired mess. In my humble opinion, Enola needs to lose much of it’s walking and exploration and gain more set pieces with a concentrated focus on tight and tense moments.
Sadly the second half of the game is no better, the puzzle section. Be warned, there are some spoilers ahead should you choose to purchase this game despite my warnings.
Puzzles are like Marmite in that some love them and some loathe them. I admit that I am in the latter camp unless they form an actual part of the game and are not, as they often are, just thrown in to spread the game out regardless of game style or relation to the main story. Unfortunately the puzzles in Enola are merely there in an attempt to add some kind of game to the meandering of the first half. At least one puzzle did actually fit with the narrative, one based around Hours, Weeks and Days but again the lack of direction shows and the answer is given to you directly at the side of said puzzle. It became less a puzzle and more a “oh, I read this for the answer without doing anything”. In short it became instantly redundant. Other puzzles include moving various dials, pressing various buttons and generally doing nothing that has not been done before in a million previous and equally painful games. One particular ‘mind bender’ that bothered me the most was a room filled with numbers and a small clue chalked on the floor where you get to pick two numbered buttons from several available. As it turned out you had to choose the prime numbers despite nothing ever being mentioned that Angelica was a Math nerd or that she had any interest in Math whatsoever. It was just random. It was as if the developers pulled the puzzle out of thin air, which I am fairly sure they did. It did not fit, barely any of the puzzles fit with the narrative and those few that do are so easy they may as well not exist at all.
I played the game on the new Nightmare mode which supposedly gives you more revelations about a traumatic past, new areas to explore and three new endings. This at least shows that the developer is seemingly continuing to expand and improve the game though I cannot say exactly how much content this adds because I only ever played this new mode and I cannot tell you if the ending was good, bad or which one I ended up with because I never finished the game. Over four hours in and I simply gave up. I tried, I really did, but after four hours of wandering, doing pointless puzzles and going over the same area three to four times in a vain effort to find the next chapter of my experience I found that I simply no longer cared what happened to the protagonist, her lover or any other party in the game. Yes, I did at some small point experience remorse for what these girls had been put through and I get that Angelica was sent on a rampage of torture and death after experiencing her pain and others but it was not enough to keep me caring past the faults of the game. I, like her, just wanted it to end but unlike poor Angelica I could simply turn it off, un-install it and with luck never venture back into her Universe.
So, we end up back to my own personal recommendation for this game. Should you buy it? Whilst I do understand that this may be a first game for the Devs and it is probably a learning experience that with luck they will take in and gain from I simply cannot suggest to anyone to purchase Enola. It drips with ideas and it does have around twenty minutes of actual tense moments in the four plus hours I played but this game is not worth actual money. In my opinion the game should be free and used heavily as a learning tool and then maybe a few more games down the line they can come up with something worth both your time and your hard earned cash. As it stands, if you want jump-scares, if you want tension, if you want a story that drags you to its conclusion, buy something else. Sorry.

Honestly, I don't know where to start with this game. I'd heard from friends that it was a pretty good game, and I've owned the soundtrack for quite some time before I even looked at the game.
The game's got an isometric (topdown) view, which is fine with me; just harkens back to things like Diablo and Baldur's Gate. I found the platforming to be kind of tricky in places, but that's coming from someone who's not the greatest at platforming games. The art/graphics were pretty nice, even for being cartoon-like in fashion.
I had good fun with the environment, which is largely destructable and can also be used to provide you some temporary cover from enemy projectiles, and oftentimes give you some spendable resources when they're broken. I also really enjoyed the wide variety of weapons and their upgrades, which you can choose to better fit your playstyle. The different buildings you add to the Bastion have a lot of interesting things to offer, from drinks that grant you different bonuses which can also be switched out, to parts that can be used to upgrade your weapons and more special abilities that can be used in conjunction with certain weapons, and even a building that can be used to tailor the difficulty of your game in different ways you can choose.
I kind of wished the game had a mini-map for the levels, but I suppose it does encourage exploration of each level... and believe me, you want to explore because you can usually find loot and goodies tucked away in the corners and deadends.
I'll outright say that I wasn't very good at the different Proving Grounds (only managed to completely master one of them), but I think they present a good challenge for people who -are- good at that kind of thing, and the better you do at them, the more prizes you get for upgrades and skills. The good news is, if you're like me and not very good at that kind of thing, you don't need to master the different Proving Grounds to finish the game.
With all that said, I still found the soundtrack to be awesome, the game had a stirring story, and the action and style of the game was thoroughly enjoyable. Great game, give it a shot.

I've followed this game since the very first announcement of its development. Terraria had just announced it was halting updates, and Starbound popped up in the distance. Everyones hopes were so high and everyone was tossing money at chucklefish as soon as they could.
With 150+ hours into the game, all spread across multiple versions of the game ranging from the very first publically playable version to the current game, and even into modded and nightly versions. As 2016 rolls around and the games end goal comes into view, its entirely clear that this game on the whole was a dissapointment, and I dont have a problem saying this with confidence anymore. I've given it and the dev team more than enough time to prove me wrong, and while the game has certainly improved as time went on, it pales in comparison to anything it competes with.
I cant with a clear consious recommend this game. I'd highly suggest against it, actually. Very few aspects of this game function and feel better than anything other titles that inspired the game do. Games such as Terraria, Castlevania, Metroid, you name it all do their respective inspired functions better.
Seriously, Instead of giving chucklefish money, you're better off putting your play time into Terraria. You'll have way more fun, I absolutely guarentee it.
Edit: You want me to comment on the gameplay? Fine, heres some comments about what I find unpleasant about the gameplay: The combat is very uninteresting and predictable compared to its competitors IE Hammers do the most damage and are the most reliable melee weapons, guns are generally weaker and will take you longer to kill anything, dificulty ramp up is very real with dungeons which I'm more ok with than just rolling through content like was previously possible, but its just frustrating for every single individual npc encounter in dungeons to be life threatening. Movement in the game is very flat and uninteresting, you're generally able to jump over any obsicals and the movement tech you get is usually not needed and really dosent help as much as movement improvements in other games. The cold/heat system I believe is coming back, which is a plus, but the hunger system coming back only brings back a relatively annoying factor. Late game scaling is extremely frustrating, and raiding end game dungeons without mods to improve healing items is damn near impossible if you arent willing to spend 20 minutes in a bed after every single fight you take damage in, because for some reason health regen does not scale up with how much health you have based on your high tier armor, making every single healing source take many many more and much longer to heal you. I dont have time to sit and grind out every problem I have with this games actual mechanics, but with 150 hours I've more than experienced early into late game of every version since it was first available. They made it slower by making it not the best strategy to just grind out metals in deserts which is good, but then made it a painfully slow grind with the pickaxe change. I appreciate the tool being gived more usefulness, but it feels like they could have just changed the way pickaxes worked instead of make them generally useless.

Each and every game made is a different answer to the question "Why play this?" A good answer is an unexpected one and relies not on what is said but how is said. So when Sleeping Dogs tells me that I get to do consequence-free Triad enforcing, then buy and buy stuff with the fruit of my labors or succeed in Karaoke it is abundantly clear that sometimes not thinking can be just as fun as thinking.
The player stars as Wei, an undercover police officer infiltrating the Sun On Yee criminal organization using all the well-established fictional ways of doing so. Sleeping Dogs' level of realism can only be described as "this makes no damn sense whatsoever." In an early mission Wei and his goofball friend take a shipment from their rivals with force. After Wei beats down two waves of thugs the survivors flee in a car and the friends give pursuit, ramming enemy reinforcements off the road along the way. Finally they claim their prize of.... worthless knock-offs of luxury watches. Why on Earth would anyone use so much muscle to guard something with no value? And why are there no repercussions afterwards, let alone any mention of the event? The answer to A is because the plot demanded comedy and the answer to B is that the game must go on. B also applies to the Hong Kong police who make the Skyrim guards look like unrelenting angels of justice. Should the police pursue Wei he just rams them off the road and the police department immediately forgives and forgets.
Sadly the writing does not work on it's own either, even if separated from the game mechanics. Wei has enough skill to make Jason Bourne look like a mall cop and people are always telling Wei how awesome he is. The reason the Triads suspect him is that he is too good to be true, as they say to each other behind Wei's back! The women Wei dates are there to literally say "Oh, Wei, you are so resourceful!" and little else. Wei carves a bloody swathe through Hong Kong and when his handler quite reasonably tells him that he is too dangerous Wei uses the "mavericks get results" defence that of course works and Wei gets to continue. In another instance a short questline is ended with Wei being told he just got more done than the entire Drug Division accomplished in the last six months. Even more insufferable are the scenes where Wei is torn between the police and the underworld. In all the scenes Wei gets to be right and ultimately I was relieved when some thug punched his face in a non-scripted event.
But while the story is best ignored there still are reasons to play. Wei is unsymphatetic due to his inhuman perfection but the city of Hong Kong is symphatetic for the opposite reasons. The vendors are nothing short of hilarious, with a man selling cheap tea reminding that the gods are watching, a clothes booth owner immediately reassuring a new customer that all his merchandise is completely genuine and legal and a junk food seller telling that no man is a man without a pork bun in his hand. It takes no small effort to get a grown man excited about shopping and this is the games biggest triumph. Running around buying everything from awareness bands to canarie cages and luxury sports cars described as being "For the man who has everything and wants everyone to know it" never got old even on my replay. The same smorgasbord philosophy extends to the activities that let you succeed in Karaoke, be the street racer king or beat down a fight club's worth of contenders for money to live out any lingering consumerist fantasy.
By now the fundaments of criminal sandboxes are so familiar and well-established that they require no descriptive detail apart from saying that they are there and they work as do the meat-and-potatoes sights and sounds. I was happy, however, with placing the emphasis on melee instead of gunplay as well as the close combat system itself. It requires a bit of a learning process as well as stacking bonuses for full effect. You should also know that it is extremely violent, particularly the environmental finishers where you toss thugs into furnaces or impale them on meat hooks, so it is best to consider this before purchase. Wei accumulates XP in three different trees and expands his array of moves and attacks at a steady pace. All in all the game is dangling a juicy carrot worth pursuing quite succesfully. There are many minigames and collectibles along the way, mostly harmless. The DLCs can be split into two categories. All the smaller ones, every single one, are the Square Enix assembly line junk we all know and should be skipped. Some of them even force considerable bonuses on a new game that makes it best to disable them manually with some jury rigging -- or not buy them at all in the first place. There are three larger ones, Nightmare in North Point, Zodiac Tournament and Year of the Snake. I have yet to play but would recommend Googling first and waiting for a sale. The base game is self-sufficient and expanding it can wait.
Sleeping Dogs is ultimately best described in song. The kitschy sleaze-pop of the soundtrack original Yellow Fever sounds like a cheap knock-off that somehow winds up being value for dollar even though it should not. As I played the guilty part of guilty pleasure wore off and I can recommend Sleeping Dogs for anyone in the mood for the digital equivelant of the Chinese all-you-can-eat buffet available anywhere.

Blackwake is an online, server-based pirate game. You're on a ship, running around, loading canons, fixing holes, firing at other ships, and maybe even boarding their ship for some FPS. As a game developed by only two people, it has problems that many early access titles have, but the devs are constantly on online forums checking in on what people have to say, and fixing and adding more to the game every other week.
Pros:
- Fantastic sound, music and voice lines: The voice lines have been done so well that you'd be forgiven for spamming them in-game. The music is very atmospheric and the sound effects feel realistic. The strongest aspect of this game for me.
- Very immersive.
- Sense of scale is great, you can feel yourself slowly lose the fight if your team isn't performing as well as you, and even if your entire crew is performing wonderfully, one ship can find it very difficult to turn the tides.
- Nothing is as hype as jumping off of the sails onto an enemy ship.
- Great FPS elements.
Cons:
- Not so many bugs, but bugs can definitely be present in at least 1/25 games. Swivel's aren't as accurate as you would want them to be, and it's inconsistent leading me to think of bugs.
- Server format is best for quick, get-in and have fun play, but it's hard to have any sense of accomplishment post-game except for level, which would have been acquired anyway.
- Interface and loading speeds could be faster, but given that it's early access and has a small dev. team, I wouldn't call it the end of the world.
- With bad captain, the game can get boring as you get canonballs drilled into your ship.
Neutral:
- This game definitely gets exponentially more entertaining the more of your friends are playing it.
Overall, I definitely really recommend Blackwake to anyone who's interested in a naval combat game and even to those who aren't. It's a great introduction into server-based games like Chivalry, the community is very friendly (Usually) and the servers are modded really well. The developers are active and working hard on the game. Even in it's current state with no additions, I wouldn't have hesitated to buy it and recommend it to others.

After playing the game a good bit on multiplayer I decided to come back and rewrite my review. My original opinion still stands: It is a game with a really  cool premise that I supported 100% before it was released. I absolutely love the original Total Annihhillation and when this game was announced I nearly crapped my pants.  Total Annihillation with PLANETS? meteor bombardment! Endless,  emotionless mechanisms of war fighting on desolate planets. This will truly be the greatest thing since sliced bread, or so I thought.
Unfortuanately the execution is severely flawed. The only way you can get any enjoyment out of the game is to have lighning reflexes that function quicker than your brain.  This is a problem that stands in most RTS games but its nosignificantly worse in Planetary Annihillation.  Your opponent can literally go straight for orbital and stop you from doing anything. But what makes it so untolerable is that there is literally nothing you can do to stop it except build orbitals faster that he/she/it (im sure its mostly robots that play this game) can. Or ground based orbital defense, but good luck. By the time you get those up your enemy will already have 100 guys coming for you and probably will be cockroaching to another planet.
Another good point is the planets. I thought reviewers were just being whiny when they were complaining about the scale of the game. I mean FFS its called PLANETARY Annihillation. But I found that it was a valid point. can you imagine how horrible it is to manage multiple bases on different planets while trying to micromanage attack groups on others? It's a nightmare, and to make it worse any of your bases can be attaked from any angle, including space. Because of that I wouldn't recommend playing it with more than maybe 2-3 planets.
Total Annihillation and Supreme commander were both much better games and are cheaper to get anyway. I would recommend Total Annihillation if you can deal with the bad pathfinding. It was the first 3d RTS  so untis are kinda confused on where to go. Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is a decent game to, but never really resonated with me due to the fact that there isn't a hold position command. But either one of those would be am infinitely better choice than getting Planetary Annihillation.

I greatly enjoyed the first Sanctum.  It was different, and with that free build aspect that allows players to come back again an again, constantly trying to create the 'Perfect' defense grid.  Seeing this on 'Free-To-Play' I decided to try it out.
Sadly, Sanctum 2 leaves me... disappointed.
The graphics are improved greatly, and the back-story is first-class.  The extra bits within the missions also add to the sense that you are 'in' the world.  There are some great ideas tucked into this game.
But... this is supposed to be a 'Tower Defense' game first.  And the tower building options are oh so limited.  You get a set number of blocks to build the maze per wave, which would be fine, if you could mount a weapon on all of them.  But Coffee Stains have imposed a limit on the number of tower weapons you can have.  I suspect it is a limit per player, so great if you're playing as a group of three or four.  But for single player?  It's just too limiting.  It be okay if you had a perk that allowedyou to build extra towers, but I haven't see one yet.
While it makes sense, story wise, for the creatures to attack you, in practice it just gets fustrating with the respawning after death.  And two of the three bosses are just annoying, as they can rip yuor maze apart easily... and after other followed b warm of lesser critters.  Combined with the limted nuber of towers you get, and only two weapons per player, a Boss can totally ruin everything.
Maybe I'm jaded because it's clear - to me - that this game has been heavily slanted for multiplayer sessions.  My advice?  unless you're going to be playing with a group of friends, or don't mind random people dropping into your game, then stick with the original Sanctum.

I'm not sure if "adventure game" is the right label for it, but I enjoyed Dominique Pamplemousse for what it was. From the continuous off-key singing to the charming stop motion clay animation, the game endeared itself to me and sweetened the deal with a protagonist with a sense of humor and a lack of respected pronouns. While I was disappointed by its shortness and clunky story delivery, I was never bored with this unique little point-and-click, and I'll probably pick up the soundtrack because I enjoyed the catchiness of the music.
My only genuine complaint was the game's illusion of choices when you in fact have absolutely none -- something that wouldn't have been frustrating at all if it had been longer or could be failed (such as by arousing suspicions by asking the wrong questions, something that is actually present in the game but is stopped by Dominique announcing they won't make such a mistake.) The addition of easter eggs, more story, or additional game art would have done this game a great deal of good.
All in all, not quite worth its asking price of $4.99 save for the fact that its creator absolutely should go on to make better, more extensive games in the future, because the talent and ingenuity is clearly present. Snag it on sale, or damn the economy and support a genuinely unique indie title that's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off bunches of dudebro gamers.

First up, yes, this game does have some fairly "heavy" and/or "dark" themes that it explores.  Get over it, boys and girls!  Are we seriously at a stage in human development where art forms purporting to work in the "horror" genre need to wear kid gloves?  For ♥♥♥♥'s sake.  GROW UP.  On to the next non-controversy, then...

Yes, this is basically just a "walking simulator", with a couple of tricky puzzles, a bit of timing-based "trap" avoidance, a couple of enemies to outrun or hide from, and a tiny bit of "combat" governed by quick-time button mashing.  So why I am about to give it a pretty decent review?  'Cause within these confines, and given its obvious low-budget/"indie" credentials, IT'S REALLY GOOD.
It's moody, atmospheric, interesting, and even has a couple of decent "jump scares" for added measure.  Is it going to frighten the bejesus out of you more than, say, Outlast?  No.  Not on an immediate, "superficial" level, certainly.  Is it going to completely change/"shatter" your world?  Probably not, unless you're one of the big babies I alluded to in the first paragraph of this review.  It's a game, it's a short game, but it's a GOOD game.  Not earth-shattering...but good.  Solid.  Well worth playing.  Possibly not worth the full asking price of $14.99, so you may want to wait for a sale.
But if you want a genuinely intriguing - if largely derivative - "indie" horror game with a bit of a story, you can do a heck of a lot worse than this.  Plus, as an added bonus, it has LESBIANS, if that's the kind of thing that floats your boat (though it's not quite as good as Gone Home, just for the record, and the end "boss battle" is just straight-up ♥♥♥♥ing LUDICROUS).

Verdict: 8/10.

Buy? Maybe.
-=TL;DR=-
Foul Play is a very simple side-scrolling beat 'em up that plays much like Castle Crashers, in the vein of a stage play as acted by the players. Gameplay is focused on performing well by maintaining combos, avoiding hits and completing level based challenges, instead of survival and managing lives/continues/respawns. It's a clever take on the genre that makes for a somewhat interesting experience, but in spite of the description's "rewards performance over pummeling" the gameplay does get fairly repetitive and it's easy to loose interest after a few levels.
-=Presentation=-
Foul Play is easily comparable to Castle Crashers due to it's art style and simplistic combat - it looks and almost plays quite like a Flash game even though the game doesn't seem to be in Flash. Animation is fluid like Castle Crashers, but certainly won't win any awards. The old British comedy will probably put off some players, not because it's bad, but it's a style of comedy that won't make alot of people laugh. I never felt that any of the jokes were bad or purile, nor did it put me off at all, but I didn't laugh. The game is cartoonish, attacks have that "PISH! POW" as expected and enemies eyes turn into "X's" when they "die" (in which humorously, the enemy actors will be pulled off screen or sneak off screen". Backgrounds gradually fall in the back, as if the props were being managed by an amateur. The director is often seen in the background even on the scene itself, as if he not aware how fast the play is moving. They're all nice touches. The soundtrack fits the theme very well and I do like the menu music, though it's nothing spectacular, it's just good and fits the game well. The game plays at 60FPS, though, doesn't reach my 2560x1080 resolution
-=Gameplay=-
The way to win is the complete the level without dropping the "Mood-o"meter" low, which is the visual metric of how well you are performing. You maintain and grow this meter by performing big combos, maintaining those combos, reversing attacks, avoid being hit and activating a "special" that doubles your combo count output. The gameplay is very forgiving: Combos allow a good 2-3 seconds after you last hit for you to continue hitting enemies (making managing the screenspace key), reversable attacks have a near infinite window for you to counter them and if you can't block it, you can easily dodge a good bit out of the way. Staying alive is extra easy and I'm honestly not sure you can die unless you simply don't perform well enough for the meter - you can usually spam a few attacks here and there to keep yourself in the game. There is still a challenge of keeping your combo going, as you can lose it from being hit or not keeping enemies near you to attack, and the game offer various combo, attack and time challenges. This style of gameplay makes the game potentially more valuable for the completionist.
Combat does get a little boring fairly soon. While Foul Play gives the player new moves at a very reasonable pace, it's generally most effective to mash the attack button and/or spam reversals, as enemies constantly attack. There are moments where it's definitely handy to dodge whether to avoid damage or make it to an enemy fast enough to keep a combo going. Some moves are fun, like the Stunning Piledriver or multi-hit air attack, but the gameplay is very repetitive as you constantly slap enemies with your cane and throw them around with the same two slam attacks. There's a second uppercut style attack, but there is really no reason to use it as air combos aren't awarded more than normal combos and doing so can knock enemies out of your range, causing you to lose a combo.
The game offers Local and Online co-op, though, finding a game seems impossible - I've only seen 0 games in the server browser and that was even when I played the game shortly after it came out. You will likely have to find somebody in the community hub or elsewhere to play with.
-=Conclusion=-
Foul Play offers a unique and lightly fun experience, allowing players to challenge themselves by completing goals, versus beating up and staying alive. The combat becomes dull fairly quickly and after a while, I became disinterested in finishing the game, even though I was halfway finish and trying judiciously to get this off my backlog. For most players, the $15 price point may be a bit too high for the repetitive gameplay, lack of online players, and potentially non-entertaining comedy. The price seems fair for somebody who would really enjoy this game and expect to beat all the challenges, as that is the arguably the best part of this game - seeing if you can complete them on a game that is very easy, though providing some challenges that might feel just slightly out of reach. This surely isn't a must-buy and you would be missing out on the performance based gameplay, though it's nothing revolutionary. However, the game is certainly not bad and there are many worse games you could buy, but you may feel the lack of value shortly after playing.

Okay, I'm likely to get some hate for this post, but since I feel like being in the minority, Ima do it anyway.
Let's get one thing straight; Realm of the Mad God (ROTMG) is a good, fun game. Yes, you read that correctly. It has it's flaws, but overall, I'd say it's a good, fun game. Why is this review negative? We'll get to that in a minute. In the meantime; THE POSITIVES!
If you've never played, ROTMG is a 2D top-down shooter type game, that plays somewhat rougelike, with the exception of vaults that you can keep, although it has minimal storage unless you buy more with real $$$. It has lots of dungeons to explore, metric TONS of enemies to slash through, and many different classes to play, each with their own playstyle and abilities.
The main 'goal' of the game is to kill "The Mad God; Oryx." However, with practice and teamwork, this is easily achieved. What most players consider to be a worthy challange is "Maxing" all eight (8) stats on their character (Becoming an 8/8, or "Fully Maxed" player) Using stat upgrade potions, dropped from various enemies and bosses.
It IS fun, it has quite a bit of content, especially for a newcommer, and in fact, with how often you die*, you could say it has great replay value too, needing to put in more hours, create more characters, try different playstyles, die more after you find a playstyle that doesn't work too well*, "8/8" the characters the survive long enough for you to do so, ect.
However, those asterisks that you may've seen: Death. Death is more common than air in ROTMG. You go into almost any realm, I can GURANTEE that someone has died in it. This may not seem that big a deal, about two (2) people die IRL every second, (True Fact) so why is a big deal here? The problem comes when you realize that you can sometimes spend LITERAL YEARS on some of these characters, (Which, I have done, Though not documented due to playing via website and not Steam) and even spend real $$$ too. Then, it's not okay.
Also, you may notice, I keep bringing up the subject of..... the dreaded.... MICROTRANSACTIONS! D;
Yes, they're here, and they are PLENTIFUL. It's called "gold", and it's used for EVERYTHING. Want to change your character's name? Gold. Wanna buy some equips without trading? Gold. Wanna upgrade your pet without wasting away in the eternal pit of hell named "EUNorth2"? GOLD.  Wanna have more than one character at a time, or more vault space for those characters?
Frankly, I find it worse than playing a mobile game with how much this "Free" game tries to rob you blind whilst playing it.
Another tick aganst this game is the characters; Something which SHOULD be a positive addition to this game. The problem? They're unbalanced as all heck. Some characters like, "Priest," "Necromancer," and "Mystic" are almost un-playable, with how much they struggle to obtain even the most common of loot. They are easily out-damaged, hard to/impossible get any equips that make them worth playing, and just generally ignoreable.
On the other side of the spectrum: "Wizard" and "Warrior." Where to even begin with this duo...? Let's start with the main reason for playing these two classes: The stats. Both have the highest ATK (Attack) Stat possible in the game without equips, and Wizard in particular, can achieve the highest total ATK, and highest DPS (Damage Per Second) in the game. Warrior, also pumps out an impressive amount of DPS, and can also be configured to have the highest total DEF (Defense) Stat in the game, short of being invincible. This makes them extremely Overpowered, and makes playing any other class not recommended at best, and downright pointless at worst.
There's one more point I'd like to make before ending this review; Pros. Here's the thing: Pros are inevitable. If you have a game, people will get good at it. Those good people will continue to be good, and will be better than other players. Problem is, in a pay-to-win game that's otherwise
, Having so many "Pros" that can easily out-damage you on bosses, Get to & Kill events faster than you,  and generally be more effecient than you at the game, can be VERY frustrating.
This, is the biggest point to me, because of a fact; No matter how much you play this game, or even how much money you decide to spend, SOMEONE WILL BE BETTER THAN YOU. This kills the ENTIRE point of a video game to me; Something to pour your extra hours into, untill you become the best you can be, and feel the sense of accomplishment, and feel like you did something worthwhile.
In sum, This game is fun, but only if you can settle for having some features of the game locked away behind solid-gold prison bars, and accepting the fact that you will never be the best player.

Being a psychological horror fan, I can never get enough of complex stories that need to be pieced together, spliced with dark tense atmospheric environments reflecting the nature of psychological despair. They're the kind of games I'm always on the hunt for, and the games from my youth that I miss the most.
I bought Enola on a whim because it was described as a psychological horror, and I have to say, Enola delivers; the story is intricate and full of moral grey areas which slowly unfold as you explore the environment, the puzzles are well designed and remind me of old school point-and-clicks or classic survival horror games, and the atmosphere is just tense enough to keep you on edge all the way through, even the pacing is executed beautifully.
Enola may not be an action packed game with all the bells and whistles of mainstream titles, but it has a slight retro charm (in all the best ways) which brings me back to playing my favorite horror titles as a kid. For an indie game, and clocking in at over six hours of gameplay, it is well worth the price point. If you're a fan of retro horror point-and-clicks or psychological horror titles, you will love this. If Silent Hill 2 and Gone Home had an indie child, it would be this game.

Once again, close friends and strangers of the internet, I'm back to review a game. I rarely feel the need to instantly write a review for a game; I generally like to replay the game so that I can see it from multiple angles (with the exception of FarCry 3-Blood Dragon. I've suffered enough. However, this game is still making my hands tremble from excitement some 12 seconds after I finished it. Without any further build-up, I give you...
Developed by Supergiant Games, Bastion sets place is a post apocalyptic world (Man, this steam sale I really went all out in Post-apocalyptic games) I don't really want to give too much away about the story (That's a lie, I really do want to, but for you, loyal or disloyal reader, I won't), the whole experience really is a journey more that a game. The excellent storytelling by voice actor Logan Cunningham was exceptional. This guy has the sexiest voice since Morgan Freeman. Seriously, his voice is like velvet. I loved the story all the way through. I did feel like it was balancing on the edge of getting repetitive like some kind of tight rope walker of dullness, but it never crossed that line, creating a rich game with plenty of replay value (Blood Dragon, Take note)
Okay, now to something I can never seem to appreciate outside of the video gaming world.
This game was beautiful. It removed all need for me to go outside or even leave my chair. The way the world generated itself around you did a great many things including
1. Add to the uniqueness of the game
2. Create a need for completionist to search every single edge with the hope it might create a secondary path
and, subsequently
3. Make REPLAY VALUE (*Cough Cough Blood Dragon)
The art design of the characters, enemies, scenery and weapons was truly something to be admired. Hats off to Jen Zee, the god in human form who made this exist.
The music of this game was a delicacy. I know I say this a lot with my reviews but I'm seriously considering putting the soundtrack on my phone. It always perfectly supported the art style, the story at that point and Logan Cunningham's sexy voice (Call me!)
The combat was smooth and also commendable. Players had the choice of 13 different weapons (Excluding the battering ram) and were required to choose a melee and a range as well as a special move. The special moves were never over powered but they certainly did aid combat and contrasted against what was never dull combat. The combat in itself was great. There was a countering system which, though difficult to perform, were occasionally the only way to do serious damage to an enemy (This often depended on the weapons you chose.) The weapons you chose definitely affected the game. Weapons varied in range, speed and some required reloading and cooldowns. I choose to use the hammer and the duel pistols, however I'm sure everyone who's played this game will have less then positive opinions on my loadout. It really does depend on the individual play styles. The weapons could be upgraded, which was both significant and necessary to the game.
Along with the main story line, there were also trials that you could do on the side for each specific weapon. Receiving a high score would earn you either third, second, or first prize depending on how quickly you completed the trial, how well you completed the trial or how many shots it took you to complete the trial. The rewards ranged from an upgrade for a specific weapon, the games currency or even a special move if you took first place. I was discouraged to say the least when I couldn't unlock the special move for my duel pistols and could have easily spent another half an hour if my fingers weren't about to start bleeding. This was a great way to add extra content and add to the depth of the game (This is the last reference I'm making to Blood Dragon)
One great addition to the game was basically a wave based combat system in which you fought off waves of enemies whilst receiving back-story for one specific character. This was a great way to add depth and extra content to your game. I hope whoever came up with this idea was given a raise. (The back-story for the characters was well written and well voiced by the very sexily voiced Logan Cunningham.
Finally, Something I never really explored in the game was the ability to use the shrine. This basically granted bonus XP or currency, but made huge effects onto the game (enemies respawing after you killed them, more enemies, more health and powerful enemies ect. Some shrines even did the reverse, making the game easier.
Alright, if I haven't convinced you yet, go visit a doctor. This game deserves your money. Go get it now.

Bastion is one of my favourite games ever. First of all, everything about it is stunning. The voice acting, music, artwork, and design are all top notch; I immediately downloaded the soundtrack in the middle of my first playthrough. It's a pretty short game - it usually takes me about 8-10 hours to finish if I mess around in it, but I replay it over and over. There are different modes to unlock after you finish the first story mode that allow for different ways to enjoy it, although as far as I can tell only one new thing appears, besides some amusing (if subtle) commentary changes.
-The play style is basically point-shoot and it's sort of like a 3D platformer, but I haven't played any games like it before, so it gets a +1 for being original.
-The story isn't the most original but it is compelling and fun to listen to (it's narrated by one of the characters), and I always get a bit choked up at the end.
-There are a ton of weapon possibilities, since there are maybe 15 different weapons to choose from and you can have two at a time, plus a 'special' skill of which there are a lot more (25 maybe? Not sure).
-It's also not particularly difficult, but there are up to 10 'idols' available that can make it basically impossible (yay, 'chivos!).
-The story is mainly linear, with some 'detour' areas until the very last little bit, where you have to make two decisions. Neither of them are "good vs evil!", which I like a lot because both times the decisions are hard to make and during my first playthrough I knew I'd be playing it over again so that I could choose the other. Each time it's heartwrenching, despite the fact that I've tried all four combinations. Even though the story stays the same (besides the outcome), I enjoy the replays, as I've already mentioned.
Overall, probably 8/10 from me, but only because it's so short and there aren't enough tracks.

All the world's a stage...  In this frantic 2-d button-mashing-tastic brawler game with Mr. Pringle and his rogue-like sidekick with a black bandana you go around kick baddies' butts castle crasher style! It can indeed become very repetitive were it not for the clever yet amusing character dialogues/monologues plus ability to deck out your character with special charms unlocked only via challenges presented in most scenes per act.  The challenges themselves can be quite difficult to achieve ranging anywhere from as simple as perform a flawless scene to reaching as high as x200 hit combo in a scenario.  Charms equippe grant special abilities such as giving you extra combo stacks after a successful parry of enemy attack or increase duration until combo wears off under which you must start accumulating them all over again.  Grinding out high combo stack can boost audience mood drastically and also bring you high score multipliers--activating showstopper effect can accelerate this effect and help you reach high stacks faster but cannot be activated too frequently.  Efficiency requires timing the activation at favourable windows of opportunity to facilitate earning high combos and score.
Very good game overall if you fancy castle crasher style gameplay, albeit solo most of the time--online multiplayer is dead.  Despite the lack of a live online community, you can always grab your trusty fellow sidekick to deliver the performance of a century in local co-op action.

Randal's Monday, a game developed by Nexus Game Studios, puts you into the shoes of the man Randal, himself. You will be challenged to find a way to break out of a strange cycle you find yourself in after snatching something off your friend. Little do you know, the ramification of that action, and what turns out to be a Groundhog Day effect, as you will be forced to live the same Monday over and over and over again, but there is something odd that seems to be going on, the day is the same but things seem to be changing from Monday to Monday. Will you be able to make everything right, or will everything fall into chaos?
Graphically this game reminds me of the Deponia series. It has the same depth of field as well as the cartoony look to the characters. Speaking of characters, you are going to meet all minds of characters, and just like everything else in the game, each time you see them, well each Monday, that is, there might be slight changes to them. You will get to explore a comic book store, a bar, a nerd convention, a therapist's office, your apartment, your friend's apartment, a pawn shop, and more. Each area has some very unique individuals that you will get to deal with, and of course they all look like they feel out of a nerd convention. Oh and did I mention the posters, and items that have been placed throughout the game that scream nerd-cred. I'm talking lightsabers, Watchmen posters, energy blades, Hal 2000, and of course soooo much more.
The sounds of the game basically continue with the nerdy theme. The voice acting is also something that really makes this game. It doesn't hurt to have the voice behind Randal in the movie Clerks, voicing the main character by the same name, but the dialogue and the rest of the choices for voices definitely make this game highly enjoyable.
The controls for this game are pretty straight forward. We are talking about a point click adventure game where the majority of the game will be spent pointing the mouse and clicking. Now of course you will have to be on the lookout for opportunities to combine items from your inventory together, or with objects in the world.
So I think I personally built this game up a little too much in my head. I knew it was going to be oozing nerdy, and it did just that, but there is something about this game that started to grate on my nerves, and that was the constant need to go back and forth for little items. Of course these items would then be used to advance the game, but there were plenty of times where only a person who constantly did patrols of each location opened with the current iteration of the game, and trying all items on everything would be able to not miss a thing. Saving grace of this game is the hint section. Now of course, apparently, uncovering a hint kills a kitten, but sometimes it just has to happen, otherwise you will get so lost that the frustration will be too much to take.
I just feel like this game just misses the mark, not by much, but enough that this might not be the game that everyone expected. That being said it is a fun game, with lots of humor in it, and definitely deserves a look. This is a point and click adventure game, and yes I know that back in the day this  you never know what items you might need was just the norm, but I guess with the evolution of gaming, and the genre in general it just feels off. Now of course I'm not expecting everything to be handed to me, but some of the stuff is still a far stretch to connect the dots. So for this I've got to give the game an 7.8 out of 10.

I want to go ahead and say that I'll be doing a review when I actually beat the game as well. Enola is one of those games that isn't going to be remembered for it's graphics, or framerate, or anything really game related. Enola is a psychological horror game (to me at least so far) that's all about exploring the darkness of the mind of your girlfriend, Angelica, and discovering what the mind does to you after a series of terrible events. Without giving t much aware, Angelica went through some pretty godawful things in her past, and it's haunted her to this day, so far that she descends into madness, and you, Enola, have to take a step into that madness to save the woman you love.  Now, off the bat, this game doesn't look as good most, and the sound isn't great, but for what the game is going for in terms of: creating a world that makes no sense and isn't for the weak of willed, or stomachs. The game throws you into creepy mannequin ladies, an eerie island, and cryptic clues scattered everywhere as to what's going on. From what I've played through so far, it's an interesting game with a lot of interesting ideas, even if it could look better. The controls are a bit stiff, but my experience so far has been a great build-up to whatever resolution lies as the end of this mystery. If you want a dark but interesting thriller kind of game, I reccommend this so far. I don't know if this will be my final opinion though,  so I can't completely confirm it yet, but so far it's be enjoyable enough to reccommend to others!

I don't usually play VN's, but this one caught my eye. I wasn't expecting much when I bought it, but what I got out of it was a good 30 hours of surprisingly complex character development, adorableness, and quite a few "squee soo cute" moments. It's a bit pricy, but considering how much I got out of it, I'd say it's totally worth it.
There were a few s❤x  scenes, but nothing that didn't feel deserved and natural in the flow of the character's relationships. They definitely weren't the focus of the game, more of just a culmination of hours of watching the character's develop their relationships. If you're looking for something s❤xy, then you'll be disappointed, but if you come into this looking for an adorable and surprisingly complex (despite the tropes) VN about various girls falling in love you'll be pleasantly surprised.
As you'd expect, I do have a few complaints. The first would be that only some scenes are voice acted. The voice acting that is there is excellent, but it does make the remainder of the VN feel a bit bare in comparison. In addition, the soundtrack could have used more variety. There's only a few songs you'll be hearing repeatedly throughout the whole experience, usually one per "mood". What is there is good, (escpecially A A Ai, Youka's song), but it can get tiring after a while.
One final thing to note: the Steam overlay causes issues with the game. If you want to experience it properly you'll want to launch it directly from the game folder. I noticed that text tended to lag and certain videos (like the end game credits) failed to load properly if launched from Steam. This will throw off your hour count unfortunately, but it's really all you can do.
Overall I'd give this a 8/10. Highly recommended!

The base game, Planetary Annihilation was a bit out of balance - the developers admitted to that, which is good, and their compensation was TITANS; free for the original Kickstarters, and significantly discounted for owners of the orginal PA.
TITANS is absolutely mammoth in content, pun intended - like its predecessor, it features combat ranging from ground skirmishes to space engagements, to Death Star target practice and to asteroids being turned into weapons of mass destruction. And of course, the Titan units for which this game is named; giant, towering behemoths capable of wiping out armies in seconds. Fret not; they can still be killed, though it takes a pretty damned long time to down them (depending on how you play).
This game is very, very resource demanding - it outright refused to run on my laptop, and even with an NVIDIA GT 720, it's pretty resource hogging. Large, large amounts of units will slow the passage of time, which is incredibly frustrating, as with large amounts of planets. Try to keep systems at or under three planets for best all-around performance.
TITANS has quickly earned its place as my favorite RTS game on Steam, due to the variety of tactics and unit combinations you can employ. I strongly recommend it, though users on lower-tier systems and on laptops would do well to avoid this game, as much as it aches to say.

Blackwake is an intensely team-oriented game that alternates between the mechanical loading and repairing of your ship, the carefully-timed firing of cannons (using the scoreboard as your scope), and the fierce musket and sword interactions that occur upon boarded ships. As a captain, you must assign these tasks and command a crew of real people to keep your ship in working order while destroying the enemy ships, all whilst steering around friendlies and into firing positions.
This game can feel like working a job, but it can also feel like winning the Superbowl. The variety of players you will meet and work with as a team makes or breaks your ability to win. Only by working together as a well-oiled machine, by doing what needs done for the ship over what you want to do, can you reign victorious in this game.
PROS:
- amazing community of players
- intensely satisfying when played well
- simple roles to follow / easy to learn
NEUTRAL:
- you should get a mic to play this game
- lots of repetetive actions as a crew member
- still an Alpha game, getting better
CONS:
- if your crew / captain sucks, so will the game
- some racism ocasionally observed
- not many game variants
TLDR:
Blackwake is fun. Buy if you want to play an intense team-based game!

Mystery Castle is a casual puzzle game, many intresting and unique ways of solving the various puzzles exist.  Just remember... don't push the wooden boxes into the Lava.. because you know.. lava burns stuff..  With the obvious stuff out of the way lets get right into the review..
You play as a Wizard, doing what Wizards typically do.. exploring strange towers, on this Adventure a Dwarf introduces himself..  (BTW Dwarfs Rule)  He explains that the Wizard needs to help him collect the Dwarven booty (no not that kind of booty, but Diamonds).  After explaining how they will split the loot (with the Wizard doing all the work) you are left to your own devices.   What follows is a fun game which at times will test your mind, at other times will test your patients, and sometimes you'll be left wondering what the heck you're doing..  The best thing to remember is this game will be a fun ride for Puzzle fans of all ages..
The game features numerous levels, comprised of various different levels.  You're tasked with collecting 5 items which will open a door to progress in the tower.  Various elements stand in your way.. Lava, endless gaps, monsters, etc etc etc.  The game puts the Casual in casual gaming.  Outside of needing to complete X amount of stages to unlock a new hub nothing else seems locked.  You can complete stages in any order you wish, getting frustrated with a stage you just can't seem to figure out... pfft... ignore it and move onto the next one.
I can't begin to describe how awesome the ability to skip around at your leisure was, nothing drains the desire to play a game faster than running into a stage that you just can't seem to get past.  Another awesomely casual feature is the lack of a time limit..  No need to run around like a chicken with no head trying to finish the stage in 14 seconds but finishing it 14.5 seconds and missing out on that flawless run.  You can stop, use your mind, think and then act upon your thoughts.
Fun, Casual Gameplay
No frustrating time limit
Ability to skip around stages and play at your own pace
Dwarves
More levels than you can shake a stick at
Boss fights
Too many to count
No reason to replay the game once you finish the stages

The price is more than worth the content you receive and the game offers a great value for your dollar.  Even without having much replay value, the unique content you do get more than makes up for it.  So what are you waiting for... buy this game now,, don't wait, don't pass go, buy it immediately..
